families.name: KRAB zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs)
families.def: The large, rapidly evolving KRAB-ZNF family; long idiosyncratic motifs, frequently derived from transposable elements. Most ZNF### genes without a separate entry.
families.short: KRAB zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs) are the largest family of DNA-binding proteins in the human genome: roughly 350 to 380 genes, most named only ZNF followed by a number. Each combines a KRAB repression domain, which recruits the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1 and the histone methyltransferase SETDB1, with a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers that reads a long, protein-specific stretch of DNA. Most of those stretches lie inside transposable elements, and the family has expanded and diversified alongside successive waves of element invasion. This atlas entry is therefore a bucket, not a motif: its 587 matrices come from 304 different proteins, run from 4 to 38 bp, and mostly do not resemble one another. A hit identifies one protein's site, not a family motif.
families.long:
## The factors

Human KZFPs number about 350 in the original survey and 378 in the most complete census, the largest group of transcription factors encoded by tetrapods (Imbeault et al. 2017; de Tribolet-Hardy et al. 2023) [PMID:28273063,37730438]. The architecture is uniform: an N-terminal KRAB domain, a variable linker, and a tandem array of 4 to more than 30 C2H2 fingers. The KRAB domain binds the corepressor KAP1/TRIM28 (Friedman et al. 1996) [PMID:8769649], which in turn scaffolds the H3K9-specific methyltransferase SETDB1, HP1 proteins and DNA methyltransferases, producing H3K9me3 heterochromatin over the bound site (Schultz et al. 2002) [PMID:11959841]. The genes sit in clusters, heavily on chromosome 19, built by repeated gene and segment duplication; the family traces back more than 400 million years, to a common ancestor of coelacanths and tetrapods (Imbeault et al. 2017) [PMID:28273063]. Selection has acted specifically on the finger residues that touch DNA, so recent paralogues diverge in specificity while their scaffolds stay similar (Emerson and Thomas 2009) [PMID:19119423]. Not all are simple repressors: across 101 KZFP interactomes, those conserved up to placental mammals essentially recruit KAP1, while a subset of more ancient ones interact instead with genome-architecture and RNA-processing factors (Helleboid et al. 2019) [PMID:31403225]. Expression is not restricted to stem cells. This entry carries 304 distinct gene symbols, 191 of which have two or more matrices.

## The motif

There is no family consensus and one should not be invented. Every protein's finger array differs, and each finger specifies roughly three base pairs through a few residues in its recognition helix, so a 10-finger protein can specify 30 bp. That is what the data show: median consensus length 17 bp, 360 of 587 matrices at least 15 bp, 214 at least 20 bp, median information content 16.3 bits, and 149 matrices above 20 bits. The longest is a 31 bp, 50.7-bit model for ZNF550. Family cohesion is 0.37, against values above 0.8 for entries that really are one motif, and the listed representative (CIS-BP M07723, GCTCCCTGC) is just the matrix nearest the centre of a diffuse cloud. Typical examples: ZNF558 ATTTGATGAAAGACATAAATCTACAAATC (29 bp), ZNF611 TCTGGGATGTGAGGAGCGCCTCTGC (42 bits), ZNF75D TGTAATGAATGTGGGAAAGCCTTCA. Recent paralogue pairs are not separable: ZNF417 and ZNF587 share TGGCGCCCAACATGGG, and the same holds for ZNF75A/ZNF75D, ZNF354A/ZNF354B and the ZNF33A/ZNF33B archetypes. A minority of matrices have the opposite problem, being short or low-complexity and therefore non-specific: 24 are under 8 bp, and models for ZNF212 (a TC repeat), ZNF613 (poly-T) and ZNF746 (poly-C) carry high nominal information but no factor-specific content.

## Where it acts

Overwhelmingly inside transposable elements: endogenous retroviral LTRs, L1, SVA and Alu. Most KRAB-containing C2H2 proteins bind specific endogenous retroelements, from currently active families to ancient ones, and also show widespread binding at regulatory regions (Najafabadi et al. 2015) [PMID:25690854]. Critically, most element targets have lost all transposition potential, so KZFPs are using conserved element fragments as regulatory platforms long after any arms race ended, creating a largely species-restricted layer of epigenetic regulation (Imbeault et al. 2017) [PMID:28273063]. The chromatin context is usually H3K9me3-marked and closed: many KZFPs bind within closed chromatin, each recognizing a distinct set of repeats (Razavi et al. 2026) [PMID:42557260], so these sites are routinely absent from accessibility-based catalogues. A separate niche is the 3' end of the zinc-finger genes themselves, where ZNF274 recruits KAP1 and SETDB1 (Frietze et al. 2010) [PMID:21170338]. Occurrence counts track the copy number of the target element subfamily, from hundreds to tens of thousands of loci.

## Biology and disease

Depleting TRIM28 in human or mouse embryonic stem cells derepresses a broad range of transposable elements, which is the baseline phenotype for the family (Imbeault et al. 2017) [PMID:28273063]. Individual proteins show how element control becomes gene control. ZNF558 evolved as an L1 suppressor but now regulates a single target, the mitophagy gene SPATA18, in human but not chimpanzee forebrain progenitors, with its own expression set by a variable tandem repeat that differs between the two species (Johansson et al. 2022) [PMID:34624206]. More broadly, KZFPs act as context-specific switches that gate element-derived regulatory modules, and mutations in KZFP genes are an emerging cause of human developmental disorders (Davis et al. 2026) [PMID:41720928]; Bruno et al. 2019 review the arms race and its consequences for mammalian traits [PMID:31518518]. Imprinting (ZFP57), pancreatic development (ZNF808) and the SVA/L1 restriction factors ZNF91 and ZNF93 have separate entries.

## Reading a hit

Start from the gene symbol on the matrix, not the family. Then check the evidence: of the 285 HOCOMOCO models here, 224 are ChIP-only (evidence code P) and 160 are graded C, with only 49 at grade A, and in vitro codes (S, M) are rare. A ChIP-derived KZFP motif is in practice the consensus of the element the protein sits on, so a match may mean only "this is that element". Long, high-information motifs will not arise by chance in a small interval, but they will match every copy of the parent element, so genome-wide enrichment is usually a statement about repeat content. Seventeen matrices here have their closest neighbour in a different family: three resemble ETS motifs, two each MAZ, CTCF, ZNF24 and TBX, and one each STAT, YY1, HNF4, E2F, ZNF384 and ZFP57. That is the expected failure mode of ChIP-derived models, and a reason to check short KZFP hits against the better-characterized families. Finally, most KZFPs are expressed at low levels in restricted contexts, so a sequence match without expression evidence in your cell type is weak.
families.caveats: This entry is a family of proteins, not a motif: cohesion 0.37, with 587 matrices from 304 genes whose sites are largely unrelated. Never report it as a consensus. Most models are ChIP-derived (224 of 285 HOCOMOCO entries, 160 graded C), and for KZFPs that usually means the matrix is the consensus of a transposable element, so a hit may amount to repeat annotation rather than evidence of binding. Recent paralogue pairs such as ZNF417/ZNF587 share a motif outright. Seventeen matrices most closely resemble motifs of other families, including ETS, CTCF and MAZ. Check the gene symbol, the evidence code, the repeat track, and whether the protein is expressed in your cells.

timeline.finding: A conserved 75-residue N-terminal region, named the Krüppel-associated box, was found in about a third of the hundreds of human Krüppel-like zinc-finger genes, defining the family as a subfamily rather than a scatter of individual genes.
timeline.methods: sequence comparison, zoo blots, northern blots
timeline.open: Nothing was known about what any of these proteins bound, or how the KRAB domain repressed.

timeline.finding: KAP-1/TRIM28 was cloned as the corepressor that binds the KRAB domain and is required for its repression, giving the whole family a single shared effector.
timeline.methods: two-hybrid cloning, repression assays
timeline.open: How KAP-1 silenced chromatin, and which genomic sites KRAB proteins occupied, were both unknown.

timeline.finding: KAP-1 was shown to bind SETDB1, an H3K9-specific methyltransferase, and KAP-1, SETDB1, H3K9me3 and HP1 were found together at a silenced promoter, supplying the chromatin mechanism behind KRAB repression.
timeline.methods: biochemistry, in vitro methyltransferase assays, immunofluorescence, ChIP

timeline.finding: ZNF91 and ZNF93 were shown to have evolved to repress SVA and L1 elements shortly after those elements began to spread, and the L1PA3 subfamily was shown to have escaped ZNF93 by deleting its binding site, establishing the arms-race model for the family's expansion.
timeline.methods: comparative genomics, ancestral-sequence reconstruction, reporter and repression assays
timeline.open: Whether the arms race described two primate genes or the whole family was untested, as targets were known for only a handful of KZFPs.

timeline.finding: A recognition code derived from thousands of C2H2 finger domains, combined with ChIP, gave motifs for large numbers of zinc-finger proteins and showed that most KRAB-containing members bind specific endogenous retroelements while also binding regulatory regions.
timeline.methods: bacterial one-hybrid, protein-binding microarray, ChIP-seq, inferred recognition code
timeline.open: Motifs inferred from a code or from ChIP peaks could not separate the protein's own specificity from the sequence of the element it sits on.

timeline.finding: ChIP-exo across a large fraction of human KZFPs put the root of the family at a common ancestor of coelacanths and tetrapods and showed that most bound transposable elements have lost all transposition potential, revising the arms race from an ongoing conflict into a largely finished one whose products are reused as regulatory platforms.
timeline.methods: ChIP-exo in human cells, phylogenetics
timeline.open: It remained unclear how many bound element copies are actually repressed in any given cell type.

timeline.finding: Interactomes for 101 KZFPs showed that members conserved up to placental mammals essentially recruit KAP1, while a subset of more ancient ones instead bind genome-architecture and RNA-processing factors, so the family is not uniformly a set of heterochromatin repressors.
timeline.methods: affinity purification-mass spectrometry

timeline.finding: Systematic profiling of poorly characterized human transcription factors found that many KZFPs bind within closed chromatin at protein-specific sets of repeats, sites that accessibility-based catalogues miss, and KZFP mutations were argued to be an emerging cause of human developmental disorders.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq of tagged factors in living cells; review of human genetics
timeline.open: For most individual KZFPs there is still no loss-of-function phenotype, so the functional consequence of this binding is unmeasured.

open: It is unsettled what fraction of KZFP-bound transposable-element copies are actually repressed in a given cell type rather than simply occupied: TRIM28 depletion derepresses elements broadly, yet most individual KZFP knockouts published so far change little.

Whether a ChIP-derived KZFP motif records the protein's own finger preferences or merely the consensus of the element it sits on is usually impossible to decide from the model alone, and in vitro evidence exists for only a minority of the matrices in this entry.

How much of the family is functionally redundant is unknown: recent paralogue pairs such as ZNF417/ZNF587 share a motif outright, and no systematic test has shown whether their proteins are interchangeable at those sites.
Whether the ancient, non-KAP1-interacting KZFPs act as repressors at all is unresolved, since their interactomes point to genome architecture and RNA processing rather than to heterochromatin.

families.name: Q50 homeodomain (DLX/MSX/LHX-type, TAATTA)
families.def: Palindromic TAATTA read by homeodomains with glutamine at position 50, grouped by that specificity rather than by gene family: DLX1-6, MSX1-3, LHX1-9, ALX1/3/4, PRRX1/2, SHOX/SHOX2, EMX1/2, VAX1/2, EN1/2, GBX1/2, BARHL1/2, BARX1/2, UNCX, ARX, ESX1, HLX, HMX1-3, MEOX1/2, MNX1, NOTO, HESX1, ISL1/2, ISX, LBX1/2, LMX1A/1B, DBX1/2, EVX1/2, GSX1/2, TLX1-3, and the Q50 paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP, SEBOX, PDX1.
aka: Q50 paired-like factors (RAX, VSX, PHOX2, PROP1)
families.short: About half of the roughly 200 human homeodomain proteins carry glutamine at position 50 of the domain and read the palindromic hexamer TAATTA. This family gathers 275 published motifs for 89 gene symbols: DLX1-6, MSX1-3, the LIM-homeodomain proteins LHX1-9 and ISL1/2, ALX1/3/4, ARX, PRRX1/2, EMX, EN, GBX, BARHL, LMX, SHOX, VAX and TLX, plus the paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP and SEBOX and, from another family again, PDX1. Grouping follows the specificity a protein actually has rather than its gene family. Many of these proteins also bind cooperatively as dimers on TAATNNNATTA palindromes, which is where most real discrimination lies; a single TAATTA match carries almost no information.
families.long:
## The factors

The homeodomain is a 60-residue module: three alpha-helices around a hydrophobic core, with helix 3 in the major groove and a flexible N-terminal arm in the adjacent minor groove. The human genome carries about 235 functional homeobox genes [PMID:17963489], and roughly half of the encoded homeodomains have glutamine at position 50, the last residue of the recognition helix - the residue this family is named for.

Eighty-nine gene symbols and 275 motifs are grouped here. The core set is expected: DLX1-6; MSX1-3; the LIM-homeodomain proteins LHX1-6, LHX8/9 and ISL1/2, which contact DNA through the homeodomain but assemble via LIM domains and LDB1; the aristaless-related ALX1/3/4, ARX and PRRX1/2; and EMX, EN, GBX, BARHL, BARX, DBX, GSX, EVX, HMX, LBX, LMX, MEOX, SHOX, TLX, VAX, UNCX, MNX1, HLX, ESX1, HESX1, ISX and NOTO.

The family also holds proteins whose gene families would suggest otherwise: the paired-like factors VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP and SEBOX, plus PDX1. In standard classifications these sit beside OTX, CRX, PITX and GSC [PMID:17963489,26464018], but they carry glutamine at position 50, not lysine, and their measured motifs are TAATTA-type; the atlas groups by the specificity a protein actually has, so they belong here rather than in HD_K50.

## The motif

Position 50 is a specificity switch: substituting it in Drosophila Paired transfers the preference of Fushi tarazu or Bicoid onto that protein [PMID:2572327], and the reciprocal change in Bicoid converts it into an Antennapedia-class binder [PMID:2500253]. Site selection with six different residues at position 50 each gave a distinct specificity, all sharing the TAAT core and differing only in the bases immediately 3' of it [PMID:8692913].

Structurally, the invariant Asn51 hydrogen-bonds the second adenine of 5'-TAAT-3' while Arg3 and Arg5 of the N-terminal arm read the minor groove there [PMID:1977522]; the position-50 side chain points at the next two. Glutamine accommodates T:A, giving TAATTA and TAATTG; lysine instead contacts C:G, giving TAATCC [PMID:8692913]. Information is confined to those six base pairs, so most models here are 6-8 columns wide.

Longer models are dimeric [PMID:23332764]. Paired-like homeodomains bind palindromes with two TAAT half-sites three base pairs apart (the P3 site, TAATNNNATTA) cooperatively, with up to 300-fold enhancement; residue 50 sets the spacing and the central bases [PMID:7901121], and the rules for which homeodomains can do this have recently been derived [PMID:42675056]. Thirty-five of the 112 HOCOMOCO models here are 11 bp or longer: ALX4, PHOX2B, PROP1 and MIXL1 TAATTAGATTA, ARX TAATCTAATTAG, LMX1B TTAATTAATT, DRGX and PHOX2A TAATTTAATTA.

Paralogues are not separable. Cohesion is 0.84 across 275 models, the medoid is GBX1 (JASPAR MA0889.2), and the data consensus reads CTAATTA - the same site with one flanking base. Real outliers exist: BARHL1/2 prefer TAAACG, HMX1-3 and ISL1/2 give NKX-like TAAGTG models, MEOX1/2 TAATGA, VSX1/2 a distinctive TAATTAGC, and methyl-HT-SELEX models for LHX1/6/8/9, LBX2 and PRRX2 a CpG-containing TAACGA variant [PMID:28473536]. Surveys quantify the point: 168 mouse homeodomains resolve into at least 65 binding activities [PMID:18585359] and 84 Drosophila homeodomains into 11 specificity groups [PMID:18585360] - real variation, but finer than a PWM resolves.

## Where it acts

TAATTA sites sit in AT-rich distal enhancers rather than CpG-island promoters, and occupancy is strongly cell-type restricted. The motif is extremely common: at human base composition this self-complementary 6-mer is expected some two million times in 3.1 Gb, so even restricting to the ~4.5 million mapped DNase I footprints [PMID:32728250] leaves far more matches than any factor occupies. Members share enhancers and compete on the same sites: DLX and MSX are the classic antagonistic pair in craniofacial and limb enhancers, while VSX1/2 and RAX act in retinal progenitors, PHOX2A/2B in autonomic neurons and NOBOX in oocytes. Characterized enhancers usually contain double TAAT cores or several cores within a few hundred base pairs; one archetype here is named EMX/PAX.

## Biology and disease

Human mutations are typically heterozygous and dosage-sensitive, and produce sharply localized defects. An MSX2 homeodomain substitution causes autosomal dominant craniosynostosis and MSX2 haploinsufficiency enlarged parietal foramina; MSX1 causes selective tooth agenesis, DLX3 tricho-dento-osseous syndrome, recessive ALX3 frontorhiny, SHOX deletion the short stature of Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis and Turner syndrome, LMX1B nail-patella syndrome, LHX3 combined pituitary hormone deficiency, HESX1 septo-optic dysplasia and ARX X-linked lissencephaly. The paired-like members add PHOX2B in congenital central hypoventilation syndrome and neuroblastoma predisposition, VSX2 in microphthalmia, RAX in anophthalmia and NOBOX in premature ovarian failure. Many pathogenic substitutions lie inside the homeodomain and alter DNA binding or cooperativity directly [PMID:42675056].

## Reading a hit

A TAATTA match says a Q50-class homeodomain could bind, and little else. No published matrix separates DLX5 from LHX2 or EN1 from MSX1; report the hit as a Q50 homeodomain site, not a gene. The site is too common to be informative on its own, so a bare hit means little without expression data, accessibility and ideally a second TAAT core three to five base pairs away. Evidence that these proteins bind TAATTA is strong: 107 of 112 HOCOMOCO models have in vitro HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX support and only five are ChIP-only. That is not the same as saying their ChIP peaks sit on TAATTA; peak sets routinely carry other factors' motifs [PMID:25070602]. Two members are flagged as resembling other families, but not for that reason: an HT-SELEX-only VENTX model (VENTX.H14CORE.1.S.C, grade C) reads AATTTGCATA, close to the POU octamer, which co-bound partners in ChIP cannot explain, and a low-information CIS-BP VSX2 model (TATATT) matches WT1. Six CIS-BP entries (DBX1, DBX2, LHX3, HLX, OTP, SEBOX) are transferred from mouse orthologues, SEBOX at only 79% domain identity; archetype names such as DLX/LHX are majority labels, not claims of separability.
families.caveats: Trust the family, not the member. A TAATTA match identifies a Q50-class homeodomain site; the 89 gene symbols here are not distinguishable by matrix, and the expected genome-wide frequency of the hexamer (order 10^6) means an isolated hit is close to uninformative. Require expression, accessibility and preferably a dimeric TAATNNNATTA arrangement. In vitro support for the motif is strong (107 of 112 HOCOMOCO models have SELEX evidence), but ChIP-derived peaks often carry other proteins' motifs. Separately, one grade-C HT-SELEX VENTX model reads an octamer-like AATTTGCATA; it is not a ChIP artifact, and whether VENTX genuinely prefers that sequence is untested. Membership follows measured specificity, not gene family: VSX1/2, RAX/RAX2, PHOX2A/2B, NOBOX, MIXL1, VENTX, PROP1, DRGX, BSX, OTP, SEBOX and PDX1 are paired-like or CDX/PDX genes that carry Q50 and read TAATTA.

timeline.finding: Two groups show that homeodomain residue 50 (residue 9 of the recognition helix) switches DNA specificity. One substitution lets Bicoid (K50) recognize Ultrabithorax and Fushi tarazu sites, and changing residue 50 of Paired confers Fushi tarazu or Bicoid specificity. This is the origin of the Q50/K50 distinction.
timeline.methods: Yeast transcription-activation assay; in vitro DNA binding of mutant homeodomains
timeline.open: Which bases residue 50 reads, and how, was unknown.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the engrailed homeodomain, a Q50 protein, on DNA: the N-terminal arm lies in the minor groove with Arg3 and Arg5 near the 5' end of TAAT, and the recognition helix lies in the major groove with Ile47 and Asn51 contacting its 3' end.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How the residue-50 side chain discriminates the bases 3' of TAAT was not resolved.

timeline.finding: Paired-class homeodomains bind cooperatively as dimers to palindromic TAAT sites, with up to 300-fold enhancement. Residue 50 sets the preferred half-site spacing, the central bases and the strength of cooperativity.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection, EMSA
timeline.open: Which other residues allow or prevent cooperative dimerization.

timeline.finding: In vitro selection with six different residues at position 50 gives six distinct specificities, all on a TAAT core and differing in the bases immediately 3' of it. This is the position-50 rule in its general form.
timeline.methods: In vitro genetic binding-site selection

timeline.finding: The full human catalogue (235 functional homeobox genes in 11 classes) places VSX, RAX, PHOX2, PROP1 and other Q50 paired-like genes in the same PRD class as the K50 OTX, PITX and GSC genes. Gene family and residue 50 therefore give different groupings.
timeline.methods: Genome survey, phylogenetic classification
timeline.open: Which grouping better predicts binding was left to the binding surveys that followed.

timeline.finding: Genome-scale surveys, protein-binding microarrays for 168 mouse homeodomains (at least 65 distinct activities) and bacterial one-hybrid selection for all 84 Drosophila homeodomains (11 specificity groups), yield a catalogue of specificity-determining residues in which position 50 is one of several. They also show variation within the TAATTA group that is finer than a single PWM captures.
timeline.methods: Protein-binding microarrays, bacterial one-hybrid selection

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX of human TFs (830 profiles, 239 distinct specificities) shows that homodimer spacing and orientation matter widely. Data of this kind underlie the TAATTA monomer and P3-dimer (TAATNNNATTA) models of the Q50 paired-like proteins in this family, settling that they read Q50 sites despite their gene family.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX, ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Analysis of the 36 human paired-like homeodomains derives 11 rules for cooperative binding to the P3 site. It identifies residues that keep Antennapedia-class homeodomains from binding cooperatively, and 11 of 12 tested disease variants change cooperativity but not affinity.
timeline.methods: Structural, biochemical and bioinformatic analysis; quantitative DNA-binding assays
timeline.open: Whether P3 cooperativity selects genomic targets in vivo for the Q50 paired-like factors.

open: Gene classification and measured specificity disagree for the Q50 paired-like factors. Nomenclature places VSX, RAX, PHOX2, PROP1 and their relatives in the PRD class with the K50 OTX, PITX and GSC genes, while their in vitro models are TAATTA-type almost without exception. It is not established whether their shared capacity for P3 dimer binding, rather than the monomer site, is what sets them apart in vivo from other Q50 proteins.

How about 89 proteins with indistinguishable monomer models reach distinct targets is unresolved. Dimer spacing, LIM-domain partners such as LDB1, and specificity differences finer than a PWM (at least 65 activities among mouse homeodomains) have each been proposed, but none has been shown to account for paralogue-specific occupancy genome-wide.

Whether the CpG-containing TAACGA variant in methyl-HT-SELEX models for LHX1, LHX6, LHX8 and LHX9 is bound at methylated genomic sites is untested. Unmethylated HT-SELEX models for the same four proteins read TAATTA, and methyl-SELEX shows only that many homeodomain proteins prefer methylated CpG in vitro.

families.name: Unnamed zinc-finger archetypes
families.def: Archetype motifs whose only label is the generic token ZNF, so nothing is claimed beyond the structural class. This is not one motif: it is a set of long, distinct zinc-finger matrices, many of them matching transposable-element sequence.
families.short: Not a motif but a label gap. The Vierstra footprint atlas groups redundant matrices from several databases into archetypes, each named after the factor groups whose motifs clustered into it. For 256 of the 693 archetypes in this atlas that name collapses to a generic token, ZNF, ZFP, ZBTB, ZSCAN or ZKSCAN, so the only claim being made is that some C2H2 zinc finger binds here. These 256 matrices are long, high-information and almost entirely unrelated to one another: not one has a close match to another member of this entry. A hit means you matched a specific, reproducible zinc-finger matrix whose protein was never named, and the useful next step is to find that matrix's nearest named neighbour.
families.long:
## The factors

None is named, and that is the point of the entry. Human C2H2 zinc fingers number around 700, the largest structural class of transcription factors in the genome, and roughly half carry a KRAB, SCAN, BTB or SET domain in addition to their finger array (Schmitges et al. 2016; Lambert et al. 2018) [PMID:27852650,29425488]. Specificities for most of them were determined in bulk screens rather than by individual study (Najafabadi et al. 2015; Schmitges et al. 2016) [PMID:25690854,27852650], and several hundred putative human transcription factors had no motif of any kind until very recently (Jolma et al. 2026) [PMID:42557334]. An archetype is a cluster of similar matrices drawn from several source collections, built to remove redundancy before annotating DNase I footprints genome-wide; the reference footprint atlas delineated about 4.5 million footprints across 243 human cell and tissue types and used archetypes as the motif vocabulary for them (Vierstra et al. 2020) [PMID:32728250]. An archetype identifier encodes accession, factor-group label and structural class, as in AC0403:ZNF:C2H2_ZF. Here the label field is generic for all 256 members: ZNF for 226, ZBTB for 12, ZFP for 9, ZSCAN for 5, ZKSCAN for 2, and mixed generic tokens for 2. The class field is C2H2_ZF for 248 of them. The only assertion any of these names carries is the protein fold.

## The motif

There is no consensus: 256 matrices here are 256 different things. Median consensus length is 14 bp, with 116 members at 15 bp or longer and 40 at 20 bp or longer; median information content is 15.3 bits, with 50 members above 20 bits and a maximum of 45.9 bits over 28 bp. Cohesion is 0.33, the lowest kind of value in this atlas, and the diagnostic number is starker still: of the 218 members that have any within-entry neighbour, not one scores above 0.9 similarity and 184 score below 0.7. The listed representative AC0620 (CCTCAGCCTCC) is a centroid, not a consensus. What an individual matrix is, however, is often recoverable from the data even though the label withholds it. AC0403 (TTGCGCCACTGCACTCCAGCCTGGGCAA, 45.9 bits) is essentially the CIS-BP matrix for ZNF496; AC0286 (AGTGGCTTTTTCTACCTCACAATACAAC, 43.3 bits) is essentially the CIS-BP matrix for ZNF737; AC0408 is the CIS-BP matrix attributed to ZNF445 and AC0339 is the ZSCAN29 site, an inverted pair of GTCTAC hexamers. More generally, 206 of the 250 archetypes that have a cross-family neighbour match it at 0.9 or better, so an unnamed archetype is usually a named protein's motif with the name dropped. Base composition is 55% GC overall, and the long, high-information members have the profile expected of transposable-element sequence read by KRAB zinc fingers (Imbeault et al. 2017) [PMID:28273063].

## Where it acts

Archetypes were built to annotate accessible, footprinted DNA, so an archetype in this set was seen in DNase I cleavage data in at least some of the 243 profiled cell and tissue types (Vierstra et al. 2020) [PMID:32728250]. That is real evidence that a protein occupies some of its matches, without saying which protein. Beyond that, distribution follows the matrix. The GC- and CT-rich members, of which the representative CCTCAGCCTCC is one, will accumulate at promoters and CpG islands and will be difficult to separate from the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1 and E2F pools. The long AT-containing members will accumulate in repeat-rich intronic and intergenic DNA. Many zinc fingers of this kind bind within closed chromatin at protein-specific sets of repeats and are therefore systematically under-represented in accessibility-based catalogues (Razavi et al. 2026) [PMID:42557260].

## Biology and disease

This entry cannot support a biological claim, and treating it as though it could is the main way to misuse it. The processes the underlying proteins control are described in the entries that do have names: transposable-element silencing and its domestication for the KRAB zinc fingers, imprinting for ZFP57, promoter regulation for the SCAN and BTB groups. What can be said is that the gap is closing. Systematic in vitro and in vivo screens have produced motifs for just over half of 332 previously uncharacterized human transcription factors, adding roughly 130 distinct motifs to the known vocabulary, most of them associated with a single protein (Jolma et al. 2026) [PMID:42557334]. Some archetypes here will become assignable to one of those proteins, but the archetype label will not change until the clustering is rebuilt.

## Reading a hit

Do not report "a ZNF motif". Report the archetype accession, its length and its information content, then do three things. First, look for the nearest named matrix in JASPAR, HOCOMOCO or CIS-BP: for 82% of the members here that neighbour scores 0.9 or better, and it usually supplies the protein name the archetype lacks. Second, check the repeat annotation, because a matrix longer than about 20 bp is frequently a fragment of a transposable element, in which case matches are element copies rather than independent regulatory sites. Third, look at base composition: a GC- or CT-rich archetype cannot be separated from the general GC-box pool and should not be attributed to a specific protein. Two members are explicitly flagged as belonging elsewhere, AC0408 to the ZFP57 entry and AC0339 to the ZNF24/ZSCAN29 motif. And keep the semantics straight: the archetype name is a statement about which matrices clustered together, never a claim that a protein called ZNF binds this sequence.
families.caveats: This is a label gap, not a motif family: 256 archetypes whose names carry no information beyond "C2H2 zinc finger". Cohesion is 0.33 and no member resembles another above 0.9 similarity, so there is no consensus and the representative matrix is only a centroid. A hit tells you which archetype you matched and nothing about which protein. Resolve it by finding the nearest named matrix, which scores 0.9 or better for 206 of the 250 members that have a cross-family neighbour. Check the repeat track, since many of the long members are transposable-element sequence and their matches are element copies. GC- and CT-rich members cannot be separated from the general GC-box pool.

timeline.finding: A review of C2H2 recognition established the working rule that each finger contacts about three base pairs through a few helix residues, while concluding that no general recognition code allows a motif to be read off an array's sequence; interactions between neighbouring fingers and linkers complicate prediction.
timeline.methods: review of structures and phage-display selections
timeline.open: Specificity for an uncharacterized zinc-finger protein could not be predicted, only measured.

timeline.finding: A survey of more than 1,000 transcription factors across 131 eukaryotes showed that closely related DNA-binding domains almost always share sequence preferences, licensing motif inference for about a third of known eukaryotic factors and creating the inferred, cross-species labels that fill databases such as CIS-BP.
timeline.methods: protein-binding microarrays, motif inference by DNA-binding-domain identity
timeline.open: Inference was weakest exactly where zinc-finger arrays differ most, among recent paralogues.

timeline.finding: A recognition code inferred from thousands of natural C2H2 domains, combined with protein-binding microarrays and ChIP, produced motifs for large numbers of previously unmeasured zinc fingers and showed that this class recognizes more motifs than all other human transcription factors combined.
timeline.methods: bacterial one-hybrid, protein-binding microarray, ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Direct profiling of 131 human C2H2 proteins gave motif models for 78 that had none, and found that their protein-protein interactions are nearly as diverse as their motifs, so a zinc finger's effector function cannot be guessed from its accessory domain either.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, affinity purification-mass spectrometry, expression profiling after knockdown

timeline.finding: The reference footprint atlas clustered redundant matrices from several collections into archetypes and named each after the factor groups it contained; clusters with no named majority took a generic token, which is the origin of the ZNF, ZFP and ZBTB labels in this entry.
timeline.methods: DNase I footprinting in 243 cell and tissue types, motif clustering
timeline.open: An archetype's name reported which matrices clustered, not which protein binds, and the clustering was never revisited as new motifs appeared.

timeline.finding: The Codebook effort determined specificities for 332 putative and poorly characterized human transcription factors in more than 4,000 experiments, producing motifs for 177 of them and adding roughly 130 distinct motifs, most tied to a single protein; in vitro motifs proved strongly enriched in cellular binding sites.
timeline.methods: multiple in vitro and in vivo assays, cross-validated
timeline.open: Half of the targeted factors still yielded no motif, and the archetype labels here were not rebuilt against the new models.

timeline.finding: Binding locations for 166 poorly characterized human transcription factors showed that about half associate with promoters and enhancers at shared conserved motif matches, while the other half bind largely unique sets of repeat sequences in closed chromatin, a compartment that footprint-derived archetypes systematically under-sample.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq of tagged factors in living cells

open: It is unresolved whether an unnamed archetype that matches a named matrix at 0.9 or better is that protein's motif or a motif shared by several zinc fingers, because similarity alone cannot distinguish the two and the archetype clustering has not been rebuilt since the recent motif surveys.

How well any of these in vitro or footprint-derived models predict occupancy in living cells remains contested: the Codebook data report that in vitro motifs are strongly enriched in cellular binding sites, while in-cell profiling of poorly characterized factors finds half of them binding closed-chromatin repeats that accessibility-based atlases never sampled.

Whether the long, high-information members of this entry are transposable-element sequence read by KRAB zinc fingers or genuine composite regulatory words has not been tested member by member; the base composition is consistent with the first reading but no repeat annotation has been published for the archetype set.

families.name: Other C2H2 zinc fingers
families.def: C2H2 factors and archetypes that are not KZFPs and have no dedicated entry.
families.short: The remainder of the C2H2 zinc-finger class: factors that are neither KRAB zinc-finger proteins nor members of a family with its own entry. Ninety-six named genes appear here, from well-studied cases such as ZNF335, ZNF341, ZFAT and ZFTA to dozens of ZNF numbers with almost no literature. What they share is the fold, and little else: the 168 matrices in this entry are mutually unrelated, with a cohesion of 0.38 and a median length of 12 bp. The evidence behind them is nonetheless much better than for the KRAB group, with 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models at the top grade and many supported in vitro. A hit here identifies one named protein at best, never a family motif.
families.long:
## The factors

About 700 human proteins carry C2H2 zinc fingers, the largest structural class of transcription factors in the genome, and roughly half also carry a KRAB, SCAN, BTB or SET domain (Vaquerizas et al. 2009; Schmitges et al. 2016; Lambert et al. 2018) [PMID:19274049,27852650,29425488]. This entry holds most of the remainder that lack a dedicated family: 96 named genes plus two generic archetype labels, heterogeneous in every respect other than the fold. A few are well characterized. ZNF335/NIF-1 is a component of a vertebrate-specific trithorax H3K4-methylation complex. ZNF341 is a nuclear transcription factor that binds the STAT3 promoter. ZFTA, formerly C11orf95, is best known as a fusion partner in ependymoma. Others carry different modules: ZXDA, ZXDB and ZXDC; ZFP64 and ZFP91; ZNF423, a relative of the EBF-binding zinc fingers; MZF1, which has a SCAN domain but is filed here; and the NET-family proteins ZNF503 and ZNF703, with only one or two fingers. Most of the rest, from ZNF16 through ZNF865, received their motifs from bulk C2H2 screens rather than individual study (Najafabadi et al. 2015; Schmitges et al. 2016) [PMID:25690854,27852650]. Zinc fingers with distinctive, well-mapped sites — CTCF, EGR, WT1, KLF/SP, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF143, ZNF263, ZNF281, ZNF384, ZNF410 and ZNF768 — have their own entries and are not included here.

## The motif

There is no family consensus; cohesion is 0.38 and the representative (CIS-BP M08388, CCCGGCCTCC) is only a centroid. Median consensus length is 12 bp and median information content 13.9 bits, with 59 matrices at 15 bp or more, 33 at 20 bp or more, and 26 above 20 bits. In practice they fall into three groups. First, long element-like matrices: ZNF146 (OZF) CTTTTTTATGGCTGCATAGTATTCC at 41 bits, with ZNF260 giving nearly the same sequence, so those two are not distinguishable; also ZNF280A TCTCTCCAGTGTGAATTCTCTGAT and ZNF121 CCTGGGCAACATAGCAAGACCCC. Second, simple-repeat matrices, which look informative but are not specific: ZNF646 and ZNF865 are both (TG)n at 31 and 27 bits, and ZNF48 is a GA repeat. Third, and hardest, short GC-rich matrices: ZNF740 GTGGGGGGGG, ZNF395 and SLC2A4RG both GCCGGCCGG, ZNF575 GCTGCGGCAGCAG, RLF CCGCCGCTTTT, ZXDA GCAGGGGC and ZXDB CAGGGG. These are near-indistinguishable from one another and from the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF281, EGR and GLI motifs, each of which has its own entry. Twenty-one matrices have their nearest neighbour outside the family: four are essentially a KLF/SP GC-box (three ZNF574 models and the archetype AC0466), two the SIX homeodomain motif (both ZNF32 models), two the BCL11 motif (both ZNF296 models), and single cases point to ZNF281, VEZF1, GLI, YY1, EBF, ZIC, PRDM, NFKB, ETS, ETV2/ETV6, posterior HOX and ZNF384. The clearest single case is basonuclin 2: the JASPAR BNC2 matrix is TGAGTCA, the canonical AP-1 site, at 0.99 similarity to the AP-1 entry.

## Where it acts

Mostly promoters and promoter-proximal regions. The GC-rich majority lands in CpG islands, joining a crowded pool of interchangeable GC-box models; the small number of long, element-like matrices lands in repeat-rich sequence. Systematic profiling of 166 poorly characterized human transcription factors found that nearly half associate with known promoters and enhancers, often co-localizing at conserved motif matches, while the other half bind largely non-overlapping sites in repeat-rich closed chromatin (Razavi et al. 2026) [PMID:42557260]. Members of this entry are split across both behaviours and mostly unassigned.

## Biology and disease

Three members have clear, mapped human phenotypes. Biallelic ZNF335 mutations cause severe microcephaly with small somatic size and neonatal death; Znf335-null mice are embryonic lethal, the protein is required for neural progenitor self-renewal and neuronal differentiation, and it directly regulates REST/NRSF (Yang et al. 2012) [PMID:23178126]. Loss-of-function mutations in ZNF341 cause a recessive form of hyper-IgE syndrome: ZNF341 binds the STAT3 promoter, and its loss lowers basal STAT3 mRNA and protein, abolishes STAT3 autoinduction, and removes T helper 17 cells while leaving an excess of T helper 2 cells (Béziat et al. 2018) [PMID:29907691]. ZFTA is the 5' partner of the recurrent ZFTA(C11orf95)-RELA fusion that drives oncogenic NF-kB signalling in supratentorial ependymoma; the driver is the fusion, not the wild-type factor (Parker et al. 2014) [PMID:24553141]. For most members here no loss-of-function phenotype has been published, which reflects absence of study rather than absence of function; these are the proteins recent systematic efforts were designed to characterize (Jolma et al. 2026) [PMID:42557334].

## Reading a hit

Identify the protein, then ask whether the matrix can carry the identification. Three checks settle most cases. Is it GC-rich and shorter than about 12 bp? Then it is one of many interchangeable GC-box models and should not be attributed to a specific protein without orthogonal evidence. Is it a simple repeat, as for ZNF646, ZNF865 or ZNF48? Then it is not a motif in any useful sense. Does it have a high-similarity neighbour in a different family? Twenty-one matrices do, and for those the label should be treated as unresolved. Evidence here is comparatively good: 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models are grade A and many carry in vitro codes (S or M) alongside ChIP [PMID:37971293], so a grade-A model with both kinds of support, such as ZFAT's GCAGATTCGTCA or ZFTA's GTGGCCCC, deserves more weight than a grade-C ChIP-only model such as ZNF711's. Two CIS-BP models, for ZNF652 and ZNF691, are transferred from mouse orthologues at 0.97 to 0.99 DNA-binding-domain identity, a safe transfer [PMID:25215497]. Finally, because many of these proteins co-localize at the same conserved sites, a match in an occupied promoter does not tell you which zinc finger made the contact.
families.caveats: This entry is the leftover of a structural class, not a motif: 96 named proteins, 168 matrices, cohesion 0.38, no consensus. Read a hit as naming one protein at best. Short GC-rich members are interchangeable with each other and with the SP/KLF, MAZ, VEZF1, ZNF281, EGR and GLI motifs, and simple-repeat members such as ZNF646, ZNF865 and ZNF48 carry no factor-specific information. Twenty-one matrices most closely resemble a motif from another family; the clearest is the JASPAR BNC2 model, which is the AP-1 site. Evidence is better than in the KRAB group, with 39 of 93 HOCOMOCO models at grade A, so check the evidence code before trusting any label.

timeline.finding: A manually curated census of 1,391 human transcription factors established C2H2 zinc fingers as the largest class and documented how few of them had been studied individually, which is the condition this entry still records.
timeline.methods: curation of sequence and expression data
timeline.open: Binding specificities were unknown for the great majority of the class.

timeline.finding: ZNF335 was identified as a cause of severe microcephaly with small somatic size and neonatal death, shown to be required for neural progenitor self-renewal, and placed in a vertebrate-specific H3K4-methylation complex that directly regulates REST/NRSF, the first clear disease mechanism for a member of this leftover group.
timeline.methods: human genetics, null and conditional mouse knockouts, RNA interference, postmortem human tissue

timeline.finding: Measuring preferences for more than 1,000 factors across 131 eukaryotes showed that closely related DNA-binding domains almost always share motifs, which is the basis for the cross-species inferred models that fill out CIS-BP, including the mouse-derived entries in this family.
timeline.methods: protein-binding microarrays, inference by DNA-binding-domain identity
timeline.open: How far identity can be pushed before a transferred motif becomes wrong was set by convention, not by measurement.

timeline.finding: A recognition code derived from thousands of natural C2H2 domains, with protein-binding microarray and ChIP data, supplied motifs for a large share of the proteins in this entry and showed that the class recognizes more distinct motifs than all other human transcription factors combined.
timeline.methods: bacterial one-hybrid, protein-binding microarray, ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Direct functional analysis of 131 C2H2 proteins produced motif models for 78 that had none and found that their co-activator and co-repressor partners are nearly as diverse as their motifs, so members of this group share neither a site nor an effector mechanism.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, affinity purification-mass spectrometry, knockdown expression profiling

timeline.finding: Loss-of-function mutations in the previously uncharacterized ZNF341 were shown to cause a recessive hyper-IgE syndrome, with ZNF341 binding the STAT3 promoter and its loss abolishing STAT3 autoinduction, demonstrating that an unstudied zinc finger can carry a specific, non-redundant regulatory role.
timeline.methods: human genetics, patient cells, reporter and binding assays

timeline.finding: Systematic characterization gave motifs for 177 of 332 poorly characterized human factors, while in-cell profiling of 166 of them found about half at promoters and enhancers, frequently co-localizing with each other at the same conserved motif matches, and the rest at unique repeat-rich sites in closed chromatin.
timeline.methods: multiple in vitro and in vivo binding assays; ChIP-seq in living cells
timeline.open: Co-localization at shared motif matches leaves open which factor makes the DNA contact at any given occupied site.

open: Whether the short GC-rich models in this entry, such as those for ZNF740, ZNF395, SLC2A4RG, ZXDA and ZXDB, represent genuinely distinct specificities or one degenerate GC-box read by many proteins is unresolved: each has its own in vitro model, yet they cannot be separated from one another or from the SP/KLF and MAZ motifs by sequence.

The simple-repeat models for ZNF646 and ZNF865, both (TG)n, carry grade-A evidence including in vitro assays, so it is unclear whether these proteins truly recognize dinucleotide microsatellites or whether repeat-rich bound regions dominate both the in vitro selection and the ChIP peaks.

The JASPAR BNC2 matrix is the canonical AP-1 heptamer at 0.99 similarity, and nothing published settles whether basonuclin 2 occupies AP-1 sites through its own fingers, through co-binding with a bZIP partner, or whether the model is simply mislabelled.

Because about half of the poorly characterized factors surveyed in cells converge on the same conserved motif matches, it is not known for most members here whether an occupied site reflects direct recognition by the named protein or co-binding with another factor at the same element.

families.name: RXR and its heterodimers
families.def: DR1-DR5 direct repeats of AGGTCA. RXRA/B/G, RARA/B/G, THRA/THRB, VDR, PPARA/D/G, NR1H2/3 (LXR), NR1H4 (FXR), NR1I2/I3 (PXR/CAR).
families.short: This family covers retinoid X receptors (RXRA/B/G) and the receptors that heterodimerize with them: retinoic acid receptors (RARA/B/G), thyroid hormone receptors (THRA/THRB), the vitamin D receptor (VDR), the PPARs, the liver X receptors (NR1H2/NR1H3), FXR (NR1H4) and the xenobiotic sensors PXR and CAR (NR1I2/NR1I3). Every member reads the same hexameric half-site, AGGTCA (more precisely RGKTCA), so the half-site sequence tells you nothing about which receptor bound. What does carry information is how two half-sites are arranged: direct repeats separated by 1 to 5 bp (DR1 through DR5), inverted repeats and everted repeats. Spacing and orientation, not half-site identity, are the readable signal here.
families.long:
## The factors

RXRA, RXRB and RXRG are the shared partner of much of the nuclear receptor superfamily (Mangelsdorf and Evans 1995; Evans and Mangelsdorf 2014) [PMID:8521508,24679540]. The partners collected here are RARA/RARB/RARG (retinoic acid), THRA/THRB (T3), VDR (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3), PPARA/PPARD/PPARG (fatty acids, fibrates), NR1H3/NR1H2 (LXRalpha/beta, oxysterols), NR1H4 (FXR, bile acids) and NR1I2/NR1I3 (PXR, CAR, xenobiotics). All share a C4 double-zinc-finger DNA-binding domain (DBD) with a C-terminal extension (CTE). Heterodimers are permissive (PPAR:RXR, LXR:RXR, FXR:RXR, where an RXR ligand alone activates) or non-permissive (RAR:RXR, THR:RXR, VDR:RXR); RXR also homodimerizes [PMID:8521508]. Expression ranges from near-ubiquitous (RXRA, RARA) to narrow (PPARG in adipocytes; PXR and CAR in liver and intestine). It is the largest family here: 106 models, 19 gene symbols.

## The motif

The half-site is AGGTCA, written RGKTCA when the degeneracy is spelled out (Moutier et al. 2012) [PMID:22661711]. It is the same hexamer the estrogen receptor reads; two hexamers make an element, and the variables are orientation and gap:

- Direct repeat (DRn): both half-sites on the same strand, AGGTCA-(n)-AGGTCA. Heterodimers read n = 1 to 5 (Rastinejad et al. 1995) [PMID:7746322].
- Inverted repeat (IRn): head to head, AGGTCA-(n)-TGACCT. IR0 is the classic palindromic thyroid element; IR1 is the FXR element.
- Everted repeat (ERn): tail to tail, TGACCT-(n)-AGGTCA. ER6 is a documented PXR and thyroid element.

The gap is read by the CTE: in the RXR-THR DBD heterodimer on a DR4 the thyroid receptor's CTE lies in the minor groove across the spacer, measuring its length directly (Rastinejad et al. 1995) [PMID:7746322]; five residues in the second zinc finger set the tolerated spacing (Umesono and Evans 1989) [PMID:2500251]. The intact PPARgamma-RXRalpha complex shows the same asymmetry in full-length receptors (Chandra et al. 2008) [PMID:19043829].

The usual assignments are the 3-4-5 rule: DR3 for VDR, DR4 for THR, DR5 for RAR, established by showing that adding or removing one spacer base converts a thyroid element into a retinoic acid or vitamin D element and abolishes the original response (Umesono et al. 1991) [PMID:1648450]. DR1 is used by PPAR:RXR and RXR homodimers; the PPAR element also needs a 5' extension (the malic enzyme PPRE is AACTAGGTCAAAGGTCA) and has fixed polarity, PPAR on the 5' half-site and RXR on the 3' (IJpenberg et al. 1997) [PMID:9242684] - visible in the HOCOMOCO PPARA/PPARG models, acTaGGtcAAAGGTCA. LXR:RXR uses DR4; the FXR (NR1H4) models here are inverted repeats with a single-base spacer, AGGtCAnTGACCt. The PXR, CAR and VDR models drift from AGGTCA towards a GTTCA-type half-site (JASPAR NR1I2 tGAACTcnaTGAACT, VDR GAGTTCA). In vivo the rule is looser than it sounds: RAR-RXR occupies DR0, DR2, DR5, DR8 and IR0 elements in mouse cells and binds these non-canonical spacings about as well as DR2 and DR5 (Moutier et al. 2012) [PMID:22661711].

What is distinguishable is the spacing class, and only sometimes the receptor. The JASPAR DR1 matrices for RXRA, RXRB, RXRG, PPARD and THRB are 0.997-0.998 similar - effectively one model. By contrast the THRB everted-repeat and PXR/CAR/VDR GTTCA models sit far from anything outside the family (best outside match 0.62-0.70), so those two shapes genuinely separate.

## Where it acts

Mostly distal enhancers, with some promoter-proximal elements such as the VDR sites at CYP24A1. Occupancy is ligand-modulated re-use of pre-existing sites, and is small relative to motif counts: 2,776 VDR-occupied positions after calcitriol in lymphoblastoid cells, with 229 genes changing expression (Ramagopalan et al. 2010) [PMID:20736230]. Sharing between heterodimers is extensive - in mouse liver PPARalpha occupies 71-88% of LXR-RXR binding regions, and sequential ChIP indicated they use degenerate shared elements mutually exclusively (Boergesen et al. 2012) [PMID:22158963]. Co-occurring motifs are typically CEBP in adipocytes (Nielsen et al. 2008) [PMID:18981474] and liver, SPI1 in macrophages.

## Biology and disease

Retinoid signalling through RAREs patterns the anteroposterior axis, limbs and face; the PML-RARA fusion in acute promyelocytic leukemia blocks it and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid. THRB mutations cause resistance to thyroid hormone, VDR mutations hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, and PPARG mutations familial partial lipodystrophy type 3; VDR binding regions are enriched near autoimmune and cancer association loci (Ramagopalan et al. 2010) [PMID:20736230]. PPARgamma and PPARalpha are the targets of thiazolidinediones and fibrates, LXRs drive reverse cholesterol transport, FXR agonists treat cholestatic liver disease, and PXR and CAR induce CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, a major source of drug-drug interactions.

## Reading a hit

Report the architecture, not the label. A bare AGGTCA occurs roughly a million times per haploid genome and means nothing on its own. Measure the gap between the two hexamers and state DR1-DR5, IRn or ERn; that narrows the candidates more than any motif name here does. Then accept the limit: a DR1 is compatible with RXR homodimers, PPAR:RXR, HNF4, COUP-TF/NR2F and TR2/TR4 [PMID:8521508], and no PWM separates them. Watch the counting convention - the same 13 bp element is DR1 if the half-site is called as AGGTCA and 'GGTCA with a 2 bp gap' if it is called as GGTCA. JASPAR's explicit dimer entries (RXRA::VDR MA0074.1, Pparg::Rxra MA0065.3) name both partners but still cannot say which heterodimer bound a site. Prefer in vitro evidence codes (S, M, SM) for claims about direct binding: ChIP-only models here often carry flanking or partner signal, for instance RXRA.H14CORE.3.P.B (gGGkganvvagAGGTCAaGG). One Vierstra archetype here, AC0094:NR1H/WT, is the AT-rich model TATTATAT with no half-site at all - a clustering artefact, and a reminder that archetype names describe a majority of members, not a verified specificity (Vierstra et al. 2020) [PMID:32728250].
families.caveats: Treat a hit here as evidence for the superfamily half-site plus a spacing class, never for a receptor. Many DR1 matrices for RXRA/B/G, PPARD and THRB in this collection are 0.997 similar - effectively interchangeable - and the same DR1 is used by HNF4, COUP-TF and TR2/TR4 outside this family. Only the THR everted repeats and the PXR/CAR/VDR GTTCA-type half-sites separate cleanly. A lone AGGTCA occurs about a million times per haploid genome and is not evidence of anything. ChIP-derived models frequently include partner or flanking signal, and one Vierstra archetype placed here (AC0094:NR1H/WT, TATTATAT) contains no half-site at all.

timeline.finding: RXR binds cooperatively with RAR and directly enhances DNA binding by the vitamin D3 and thyroid hormone receptors, identifying it as the shared heterodimer partner of several hormone pathways.

timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, hydrogen-deuterium exchange
timeline.open: Whether the compact domain arrangement seen in the crystal holds for other heterodimers or in solution.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide, RAR occupies many DR0, DR8 and IR0 elements in addition to DR1, DR2 and DR5, and recombinant RAR-RXR binds the non-canonical spacings about as well as DR2 and DR5, loosening the spacing code derived from reporter assays.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq, in vitro binding, reporter assays

timeline.finding: In mouse liver PPARalpha occupies 71-88% of LXR-RXR binding regions, and sequential ChIP indicates the two heterodimers use the shared degenerate elements in a mutually exclusive way.

open: The arrangement of full-length heterodimers on DNA is disputed: the PPARgamma-RXRalpha crystal structure shows a compact complex in which the PPARgamma ligand-binding domain touches the DNA-binding domains, whereas solution scattering and FRET of three heterodimers show an extended, asymmetric shape with the ligand-binding domains toward the 5' end of the element.

How strictly half-site spacing selects the partner in cells is unresolved: the 3-4-5 rule came from reporter assays, but genome-wide RAR binding includes DR0, DR8 and IR0 elements, and LXR and PPARalpha share most of their liver sites, so occupancy may depend more on which receptors and ligands are present than on spacing.

The physiological RXR ligand is not settled: 9-cis-retinoic acid binds and activates RXR in vitro but is barely detectable in most tissues, and other candidates, including 9-cis-13,14-dihydroretinoic acid and polyunsaturated fatty acids, have been proposed; this bears on how permissive heterodimers are activated in vivo.

families.name: Forkhead (FOX)
families.def: RYAAAYA core. FOXA1-3, FOXB1/2, FOXC1/2, FOXD1-4, FOXE1, FOXF1/2, FOXG1, FOXH1, FOXI1, FOXJ1-3, FOXK1/2, FOXL1/2, FOXM1, FOXN1-4, FOXO1/3/4/6, FOXP1-4, FOXQ1, FOXR1/2, FOXS1.
families.short: Forkhead box (FOX) proteins are a family of about 50 human transcription factors that bind DNA as monomers through a ~100-residue winged-helix domain, named for the two loops, or wings, that flank its three-helix core. Nearly all of them read the same seven-base element, RYAAAYA, usually written GTAAACA or, on the opposite strand, TGTTTAC. The family includes the FOXA pioneer factors that engage nucleosomal DNA and open liver, prostate and breast enhancers; the insulin- and stress-controlled FOXO proteins; FOXC, FOXE, FOXG and FOXL factors needed for eye, thyroid, forebrain and ovary development; and the proliferation factor FOXM1. Because the DNA-contacting residues are almost invariant across the family, a forkhead match tells you that a FOX protein could bind there, but rarely which one.
families.long:
## The factors

The human genome carries about 50 forkhead box genes in 19 subfamilies, FOXA through FOXS [PMID:20650821]. Each
encodes one copy of the forkhead (winged-helix) domain: roughly 100 residues in which three
alpha-helices pack against a short three-stranded beta-sheet. Helix H3 lies in the major groove
and supplies the base-specific contacts, while two extended loops - wing 1, between strands
beta2 and beta3, and wing 2 at the C-terminus - fold over the phosphate backbone and reach into
the flanking minor groove. The first co-crystal structure, of HNF-3gamma (FOXA3) on DNA, showed
that this fold is essentially that of linker histone H5 and that it bends DNA by about 13
degrees [PMID:8332212]. Binding is monomeric in the usual case, but FOXO1 (and, in the same assays, FOXO3,
FOXM1 and FOXI1) also homodimerizes on a palindromic element using wing 1 [PMID:33577686]. Expression ranges
from near-ubiquitous (FOXK1/2, FOXO1/3, FOXJ3) to sharply restricted: FOXA1-3 in endoderm-
derived epithelia, FOXE1 in thyroid, FOXG1 in telencephalon, FOXL2 in granulosa cells and
eyelid, FOXI1 in inner ear and renal intercalated cells, FOXM1 in cycling cells.

## The motif

The literature consensus is RYAAAYA (R = A/G, Y = C/T), seven base pairs, most often realized as
GTAAACA [PMID:7957066,23836653]; the medoid model of the 106 collected here is exactly GTAAACA, matching the databases.
Specificity comes almost entirely from H3 contacts to the central AAA run and the following
pyrimidine, several of them water-mediated, which is why that core tolerates so little variation
and the flanks so much [PMID:8332212,7957066]. The FOXO field calls the same element the DAF-16 binding element, core
TTGTTTAC, and distinguishes it from the weaker insulin-response sequence in the IGFBP1 promoter [PMID:10880363].
Longer models in the data are one of three things: an extended monomeric site with AT-rich
flanks (HOCOMOCO FOXA1, TTGTTTACTTAA); a perfect palindrome, GTAAATATTTAC, which is two RYAAAYA
half-sites head-to-head with no spacer and corresponds to the wing-1 homodimer site (HOCOMOCO
FOXD3, FOXD2, FOXB1, FOXC1; CIS-BP FOXC2); or a composite with a partner, as in the JASPAR
models FOXO1::ELK1, FOXO1::ELK3, FOXO1::ELF1 and FOXO1::FLI1, where most of the information
content is the ETS GGAA core, not the forkhead site. Two members are real exceptions. FOXM1
models carry almost no information (2.1 bits in CIS-BP) because FOXM1 reaches chromatin mainly
through cofactors and non-canonical sequences [PMID:26100407]. FOXH1 (FAST-1/FAST-2) models read AATCCACA,
equivalently TGTGGATT - the activin/Smad response element - and not RYAAAYA at all [PMID:8878477]. Otherwise
FOXA, FOXB, FOXC, FOXD, FOXI, FOXK, FOXL, FOXO, FOXQ, FOXR and FOXS are not separable by
sequence [PMID:23836653].

## Where it acts

Forkhead sites are AT-rich and enhancer-biased: depleted from CpG-island promoters, enriched in
distal tissue-specific elements, and frequently on nucleosomal rather than naked DNA. FOXA1 and
FOXA2 bind a nucleosomal site that overlaps the linker-histone position [PMID:9427758], displace H1, and hold
liver enhancers in an accessible but nucleosome-occupied state [PMID:27058788]. ChIP-seq typically recovers tens
of thousands of FOXA1 sites per cell type, most of them distal, and which ones are used depends
on the partner present: androgen receptor in prostate, estrogen receptor alpha and GATA3 in
luminal breast, HNF4A and CEBP in liver. FOXA1 is required for almost all ER-chromatin contacts
and for tamoxifen-dependent ER activity [PMID:21151129]. FOXO sites sit at insulin- and oxidative-stress-
responsive promoters and enhancers (IGFBP1, G6PC, SOD2) and are switched off by AKT-driven
nuclear export, not by loss of the site. RYAAAYA is short - with two degenerate positions it is
expected on the order of three million times in a 3.1 Gb double-stranded genome - so occupancy
is set by chromatin and partners, not by the element.

## Biology and disease

Forkhead loss-of-function is usually severe. FOXC1 mutations cause Axenfeld-Rieger malformations
and early-onset glaucoma [PMID:9620769]; FOXL2 mutations cause blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus
syndrome, and the recurrent FOXL2 C134W substitution is present in most adult granulosa cell
tumors [PMID:19516027]; FOXE1 variants affect thyroid development; FOXG1 mutations produce a Rett-like
encephalopathy. FOXA1 is the clearest cancer story. It is altered in roughly a third of prostate
cancers, and the most common class of activating mutation clusters inside the wing-2 loop of the
forkhead domain, increasing chromatin mobility and driving a luminal androgen-receptor program;
other classes truncate the C-terminus or rearrange the locus [PMID:31243372]. FOXA1 is also amplified or mutated
in breast, bladder and salivary tumors and sets the response to endocrine therapy. FOXM1 is
overexpressed in most carcinomas and drives cell-cycle gene expression [PMID:26100407].

## Reading a hit

A GTAAACA/TGTTTAC match identifies a forkhead site, not a forkhead protein. All of FOXA, FOXO,
FOXK, FOXC and FOXD read this element with the same residues, the models in all four databases
collapse onto one cluster (cohesion 0.78, no member with out-of-family nearest neighbors), and
the archetype names make the point explicitly: AC0042 is "FOXA/FOXB", AC0039 is "FOXD/FOXK",
AC0093 is "FOXC/HOXA". Deciding which FOX protein is involved requires expression data, ChIP, or
a partner site. The element is common enough to occur millions of times by chance, so a single
match in a region of unknown function is weak evidence. Prefer the in vitro models when you need
"this protein binds this sequence": 24 of the 30 HOCOMOCO entries here carry HT-SELEX or methyl-
HT-SELEX evidence (S or M in the fourth field), and only six are ChIP-only. Treat the FOXO1::ETS
and FOXJ2::ELF1 composite models as ETS motifs with a forkhead flank, and treat FOXM1 and FOXH1
models as not representing RYAAAYA.
families.caveats: High confidence that a match is a forkhead site; very low confidence about which of the ~50 FOX proteins binds it. Sequence cannot separate FOXA from FOXO, FOXC, FOXD, FOXI, FOXK, FOXL or FOXQ, and the Vierstra archetype names (FOXA/FOXB, FOXD/FOXK, FOXC/FOXK) reflect that rather than resolving it. The element is short and AT-rich, so it occurs millions of times by chance; treat matches as candidates that need chromatin or expression evidence. Two labels in this family do not represent RYAAAYA: FOXM1 models are near-uninformative, and FOXH1 models are the activin/Smad response element. Four CIS-BP entries are mouse-derived (FOXJ1, FOXM1, and the inferred FOXS1 and FOXB2 models at 79% and 93% DBD identity).

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection with four human forkhead proteins gives a shared core, RTAAAYA, with the paralogues differing in the flanking positions; domain swaps map those flank differences to two subregions of the forkhead domain.

open: Whether FOXM1's forkhead domain contributes sequence specificity in cells is unsettled: its ChIP peaks lack the forkhead motif and sit at cell-cycle promoters bound through the MuvB complex, which argues for recruitment by protein partners, yet a DNA-binding-deficient FOXM1 is not recruited, which argues that direct contact with some non-canonical sequence is still required.

Which palindromic arrangement forkhead dimers use is not settled: the crystallized FOXO1 dimer site is GTAAACATGTTTAC, two complete half-sites abutting head to head, whereas many HT-SELEX FOXA, FOXB, FOXC and FOXD models read GTAAATATTTAC, in which the half-sites overlap by two bases, and FOXC2 bound the FOXO1 site only as a monomer.

families.name: KLF / SP (GC-box)
families.def: GC-box GGGGCGGGG and CACCC-box. KLF1-17, SP1-9.
families.short: The SP and KLF proteins are about 26 human transcription factors that each use three C2H2 zinc fingers to read a nine- to ten-base GC-rich element. Two classical forms of that element exist: the GC-box GGGGCGGGG, found in the SV40 21-bp repeats and in most CpG-island promoters, and the CACCC-box CCACACCC of erythroid promoters such as beta-globin. In vitro selection puts the family consensus at CCACGCCC, which is the same site read from the other strand. Because all 26 proteins share the same finger code, sequence alone cannot say which one is bound; a GC-box hit identifies the family and, given how common GC-rich sequence is in promoters, often identifies very little else.
families.long:
## The factors

The mammalian SP/KLF family comprises roughly 26 genes - SP1 to SP9 and KLF1 to KLF17/18 - unified under a single nomenclature by Suske et al. (2005) [PMID:15820306]. Each protein carries three Cys2-His2 zinc fingers at its C terminus; the SP subgroup additionally has the Sp-box and a buttonhead box, while the KLF subgroup is more variable outside the fingers. SP1 was the first mammalian sequence-specific activator purified, isolated as the factor that activates the SV40 early promoter through its 21-bp repeats (Dynan and Tjian 1983) [PMID:6313230], and its DNA-binding activity was mapped to the C-terminal zinc-finger region (Kadonaga et al. 1987) [PMID:3319186]. The KLF branch was opened by the cloning of erythroid Kruppel-like factor, KLF1/EKLF, as a CACCC-element-binding protein (Miller and Bieker 1993) [PMID:7682653]. Older aliases persist: KLF1 = EKLF, KLF2 = LKLF, KLF4 = GKLF, KLF9 = BTEB1, SP7 = Osterix. Expression splits the family into broadly expressed members (SP1, SP2, SP3, KLF6, KLF7, KLF9-KLF11, KLF13, KLF16) and restricted ones (KLF1 in erythroid cells, KLF2 in lymphocytes and endothelium, KLF4 and KLF5 in gut and skin, SP4 in neurons, SP7 in osteoblasts, SP8 and SP9 in limb bud and forebrain, KLF17 in oocytes). They bind DNA as monomers.

## The motif

Three fingers read nine to ten bases, three per finger, following the Zif268 code. Two canonical forms are described in the literature. The GC-box, GGGGCGGGG, is the Sp1 site. The CACCC-box, CCACACCC, is the erythroid form found in the beta-globin promoter [PMID:7682653]. The 100 matrices collected here converge on a third way of writing the same thing: the medoid (SP3, JASPAR MA0746.3) is GCCACGCCCAC, and in vitro selection models across the family read CCACGCCC or, on the opposite strand, GGGCGTGG. Which of these a given paralogue prefers is a graded matter, not a switch. Matrices for SP1-SP4 and most KLFs keep a CpG in the central triplet (GGGGCGGGG, GGGCGTGG), whereas KLF1, KLF3, KLF4 and KLF5 tolerate A or T there and yield the CACCC-type models seen in this atlas (KLF4: TGGGTGTGGC; KLF9: GCCACACCCAC). Structurally, the Klf4 three-finger domain has been solved bound to fully methylated DNA at 1.85 A, where an arginine and a glutamate contact the 5-methyl group and binding to methylated DNA is only slightly tighter than to unmodified DNA (Liu et al. 2014) [PMID:24520114]; methyl-SELEX across 542 human factors confirmed that many C2H2 proteins, KLFs included, are methylation-tolerant rather than methylation-blocked (Yin et al. 2017) [PMID:28473536]. Several HOCOMOCO models here span 18-23 positions and contain two copies of the core, reflecting how often these sites occur in tandem. With 100 matrices from 27 gene labels and a cohesion of 0.84, the honest summary is that this family has one motif: no matrix distinguishes SP1 from SP3, or KLF10 from KLF11.

## Where it acts

GC-boxes are the characteristic element of CpG-island promoters and are the reason many housekeeping promoters have no TATA box. They cluster with NRF1, NFY and ETS sites in the same promoters, while CACCC-type sites dominate erythroid regulatory elements such as the beta-globin promoter and locus control region. The family's real problem is neighbors, not partners. The gastrin EGF-response element GGGGCGGGGTGGGGGG binds Sp1 and, independently, ZBP-89/ZNF148 (Merchant et al. 1996) [PMID:8943318]. When the CT/GC-rich element of the IL-3 promoter was used as a bait, the clones recovered were EGR1, EGR2 and DB1/VEZF1 (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994) [PMID:8035792]. In other words, a single GC-rich element can be a legitimate binding site for members of four or five different families in this atlas.

## Biology and disease

Sp1-null mouse embryos are retarded and die around day 11, yet Sp1-/- cells grow and differentiate, so the requirement is developmental rather than cell-autonomous (Marin et al. 1997) [PMID:9160753]. KLF1 is required for beta-globin transcription and activates the beta-globin promoter through its CACCC box but not the gamma-globin promoter; swapping the two CACCC boxes showed that this selectivity is set by the overall structure of the beta promoter, not by the CACCC sequence itself (Asano and Stamatoyannopoulos 1998) [PMID:9418858]; dominant human KLF1 mutations cause severe anemia, including congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type IV (Kulczynska-Figurny et al. 2020) [PMID:33339573]. KLF4 is one of the four factors in the original reprogramming cocktail for induced pluripotent stem cells [PMID:16904174]. SP7/Osterix is required for osteoblast differentiation, and its mode of action is unusual (below).

## Reading a hit

A hit identifies the GC-box family and nothing narrower. Beyond that, ask three questions. Is the site informative at all? GGGGCGGGG and CCACGCCC are very common in GC-rich sequence, so a match inside a CpG-island promoter carries little information by itself. Which matrix matched? Of the 100 profiles here, 45 come from HOCOMOCO and many rest on ChIP-seq evidence at grade B or C; the grade-A models (KLF3-KLF5, KLF10, KLF12-KLF14) carry in vitro support and are the ones worth trusting for "this protein binds this sequence". Two HOCOMOCO models are not GC-box motifs at all: SP7.H14CORE.0.P.B and SP9.H14CORE.0.P.B are AT-rich (TAATTACAGGTT). For SP7 this is understood - amino-acid differences in the Sp7 zinc-finger domain reduce its affinity for the GC-box, and Sp7 reaches osteoblast enhancers inside Dlx-containing complexes bound to AT-rich motifs (Hojo et al. 2016) [PMID:27134141] - which makes the SP7 ChIP motif a textbook case of a factor "having" its recruiter's motif. One CIS-BP matrix labelled SP5 (M03682_2.00) is not from a human protein at all: it is transferred from a Drosophila melanogaster protein at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity. Finally, MAZ/PATZ1, ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1, EGR and WT1 all read GC- or GA-rich sequence, and where a match scores well against both a GC-box and a GGGAGGG model, sequence cannot decide between them.
families.caveats: A match tells you the GC-box family, not the member: 100 matrices from 27 gene labels share essentially one motif. GC-rich nine-mers are also very common, so a hit in a CpG-island promoter may be no more than a statement about base composition. Most matrices are ChIP-derived at grade B or C; prefer the grade-A in vitro models. Two HOCOMOCO models labelled SP7 and SP9 are AT-rich and are not this motif - for SP7, indirect recruitment by Dlx factors explains it - and one CIS-BP matrix labelled SP5 is inherited from a Drosophila protein. Overlap with MAZ, ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1, EGR and WT1 is frequently unresolvable from sequence alone.
