timeline.finding: Sp1 is purified from HeLa cells as a promoter-specific activator that footprints and activates the SV40 early promoter through its tandem 21-bp repeats, defining the GC-box as a sequence-specific activator site.
timeline.methods: Biochemical fractionation, DNase I footprinting, in vitro transcription of deletion mutants
timeline.open: The site was defined on one viral promoter, and the protein's DNA-binding domain was unknown.

timeline.finding: Cloning of Sp1 maps its sequence-specific, zinc-dependent DNA binding to three C-terminal zinc fingers.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, truncation mapping of bacterially expressed fragments

timeline.finding: EKLF (KLF1) is cloned as an erythroid-restricted protein with three Kruppel-type fingers that binds CCACACCCT, an essential element of the beta-globin promoter, opening the KLF branch and the CACCC-box form of the motif.
timeline.methods: Subtractive cDNA cloning, binding-site prediction from finger sequence, gel shift, co-transfection
timeline.open: Whether GC-box and CACCC-box factors are separable specificities or variations on one was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Sp1-null mouse embryos die around day 11, yet many putative Sp1 target genes are expressed normally and CpG islands remain methylation-free, contradicting the expectation that Sp1 is broadly required for GC-box promoters and island protection.
timeline.methods: Gene targeting in mice and ES cells
timeline.open: Whether other SP paralogues compensate at GC-boxes was not tested.

timeline.finding: Swapping CACCC boxes between the beta- and gamma-globin promoters shows that EKLF's selective activation of beta-globin is set by the overall promoter structure, not by the sequence of the CACCC box: the gamma promoter stays inactive even with the beta CACCC box in place.
timeline.methods: Promoter swap and repositioning constructs in transient transfection
timeline.open: Which features of promoter architecture confer the selectivity was not identified.

timeline.finding: A unified nomenclature groups the mammalian three-finger GC-box and CACCC-box binders into one SP/KLF family, SP1-SP9 and KLF1-KLF17.
timeline.methods: Sequence classification and nomenclature

timeline.finding: The 1.85 A structure of the Klf4 three-finger domain on fully methylated DNA shows an arginine and a glutamate contacting the 5-methyl group, with affinity only slightly higher than for unmodified DNA; methylation-sensitive SELEX across 542 human factors in 2017 then showed that many factors are not blocked by CpG methylation, and some prefer it.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays; methylation-sensitive SELEX

timeline.finding: Sp7/Osterix ChIP-seq and binding studies show that amino-acid differences in the Sp7 fingers reduce its GC-box affinity and that Sp7 reaches osteoblast enhancers in Dlx-containing complexes on AT-rich motifs, which explains why the SP7 ChIP motif is not a GC-box.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, transgenic enhancer assays, binding and interaction mapping
timeline.open: Whether other SP members with AT-rich ChIP motifs, such as SP9, are recruited the same way was not examined.

open: How individual SP/KLF paralogues reach different targets when their matrices cannot be told apart is not settled: the globin promoter-swap experiments point to promoter architecture rather than site sequence, and how much the graded preference for a central CpG versus a CACCC triplet contributes in vivo has not been measured across the family.

Whether GC-box binding by SP factors helps keep CpG islands unmethylated is unresolved: islands stayed methylation-free in Sp1-null embryos, which argues against a requirement, but redundancy among SP1, SP3 and other paralogues could mask one.

The SP9 ChIP model in HOCOMOCO is the same AT-rich sequence as the SP7 model, which suggests, but does not establish, that SP9 is also recruited indirectly through homeodomain partners rather than binding GC-boxes at those sites.

families.name: SOX (HMG box)
families.def: AACAAT / (A/T)(A/T)CAA(A/T)G. SOX1-21, SOX30, SRY; plus SOX-OCT composite sites.
families.short: SOX proteins are the 20 human transcription factors built around a single SRY-type HMG box, a 78-residue L-shaped domain that binds DNA entirely in the minor groove, wedges a hydrophobic residue between base pairs and bends the double helix by 70-80 degrees. They read a six- to seven-base core usually written AACAAT, or CATTGTT/ATTGTT on the opposite strand. A SOX protein bound alone does little; transcriptional output comes from a partner factor on an adjacent site, most famously OCT4 in the SOX-OCT composite element of pluripotency enhancers, and from dimeric palindromic sites used by SOX8, SOX9 and SOX10. The family covers sex determination (SRY, SOX9), cartilage (SOX9, SOX5, SOX6), neural stem cells (SOX2), neural crest and melanocytes (SOX10) and endothelium (SOX17, SOX18).
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have 20 SOX genes: SRY (group A), SOX1/2/3 (B1), SOX14/21 (B2), SOX4/11/12 (C), SOX5/6/13
(D), SOX8/9/10 (E), SOX7/17/18 (F), SOX15 (G) and SOX30 (H). Each carries one HMG box of about
78 residues folded into a twisted L: three alpha-helices whose concave face lies against DNA.
Unlike almost all other transcription factors, recognition happens entirely in the minor groove.
Side chains intercalate between base pairs - isoleucine 13 in SRY - widening the groove,
unwinding the helix and bending it by 70-80 degrees [PMID:7774012]. That distortion is the point: SOX proteins
are as much architectural as regulatory, and one bound alone generally neither activates nor
represses. Output depends on a partner factor at an adjacent site, which is why the same SOX
protein behaves differently in different tissues [PMID:24086078]. Two subgroups add dimerization hardware. SOXD
proteins (SOX5, SOX6, SOX13) carry a coiled-coil that makes them obligate dimers or
heterodimers; SOXE proteins (SOX8, SOX9, SOX10) carry a short DIM domain immediately N-terminal
to the HMG box that supports cooperative homo- and heterodimers [PMID:26013289]. SOX2 and SOX11 can also bind
DNA on the nucleosome surface and are bona fide pioneer factors [PMID:32350470].

## The motif

The core is six to seven bases, conventionally written AACAAT and equivalently ATTGTT or CATTGTT
on the other strand; the medoid of the 87 models here is CATTGTT, the reverse complement of
AACAATG. The SRY consensus determined by site selection is (A/T)(A/T)CAA(A/T)G [PMID:8190643]. Information is
concentrated on the CAA/TTG centre, which is where the intercalating residue inserts and where
groove width is most constrained [PMID:7774012]; the outer positions are AT-preferring largely because AT-rich
DNA is easier to bend. Site selection on Sox4, Tcf1 and yeast Ste11 showed the functional
element is really 10-12 base pairs, with residues C-terminal to the HMG box reading the 3'
flank [PMID:10867006]. Many models here are dimeric: CIS-BP SOX8 AACAATGTGCAGTGTT (28.8 bits), CIS-BP SRY,
SOX15, SOX7 and SOX2 AACAAT(A/G)(n)CATTGTT, HOCOMOCO SOX9 ATSAATTGCAGTSAT. All are head-to-head
inverted repeats of the core with a two- to four-base spacer, consistent with the finding that
SOXE dimers tolerate a range of spacings rather than a fixed one [PMID:26013289]. Within the family sequence
does not separate members: SOX1, SOX2 and SOX3 are interchangeable on DNA, as are SOX8, SOX9 and
SOX10 apart from their preference for dimeric sites, and the Vierstra archetypes are labelled
"SOX" or "SOX/SRY", not a protein. One overlap reaches outside the family: HOCOMOCO SOX4, SOX11,
SOX13 and one SOX2 model read CCTTTGTT, whose reverse complement AACAAAGG also satisfies the
TCF/LEF Wnt response element CTTTGWW. SOX and TCF/LEF share the HMG fold and their consensus
sequences differ at essentially one position, so CTTTG-type hits are genuinely ambiguous between
the two families.

## Where it acts

SOX sites are enhancer-biased and usually appear as one half of a composite element. The best
characterized is the SOX-OCT element, where a SOX core abuts the octamer ATGCAAAT: SOX2 and OCT4
occupy it at the FGF4, UTF1, NANOG and POU5F1 enhancers [PMID:7590241], and the crystal structure of the
POU/HMG/DNA complex showed that the two proteins assemble in different conformational
arrangements depending on which enhancer's spacing they are given [PMID:12923055]. Other named partnerships
include SOX2 with PAX6 at the lens DC5 element, SOX9 with SOX5/SOX6 at the COL2A1, COL9A2 and
COL11A2 enhancers, SOX10 with MITF at melanocyte enhancers, and SOXF factors with ERG and FLI1
in endothelium. Because AACAAT is only six bases it is expected roughly 1.5 million times in a
3.1 Gb double-stranded genome, far more often than it is occupied; nucleosome position matters,
since SOX2 and SOX11 bind at superhelical location 2, distort the DNA there and help detach the
terminal nucleosomal DNA [PMID:32350470].

## Biology and disease

SRY is the testis-determining gene [PMID:1695712], and HMG-box point mutations that abolish DNA binding or
bending cause 46,XY sex reversal [PMID:7774012]. SOX9 mutations cause campomelic dysplasia with XY sex
reversal [PMID:7990924]; Sox9 is required for cartilage formation, and a mutation in the dimerization domain
alone gives skeletal disease without sex reversal, showing that the dimeric and monomeric
activities are separable [PMID:12837698]. SOX10 mutations cause Waardenburg syndrome type 4 (Waardenburg-
Hirschsprung disease) and peripheral demyelinating neuropathy [PMID:9462749], and SOX10 is the lineage-
dependency factor of melanoma. SOX2 mutations cause bilateral anophthalmia, SOX2 is one of the
four Yamanaka reprogramming factors, and its locus is amplified in squamous carcinomas of lung
and esophagus. SOX17 and SOX18 are required for endothelial and lymphatic development, and SOX11
is a diagnostic marker in mantle cell lymphoma.

## Reading a hit

A CATTGTT/AACAAT match identifies a SOX-family site, not a SOX protein: all 20 members read it
with the same fold and the same contacts, and the archetype labels ("SOX", "SOX/SRY") say so.
Expression data is the practical discriminator. Even the family assignment is soft at the
boundary with TCF/LEF, because CTTTG-type variants fit both. The core is short enough to occur
by chance more than a million times, so an isolated match means little; look for a partner site
- an octamer, a second SOX core in inverted orientation, a MITF E-box - before treating it as
functional. Of the 36 HOCOMOCO models here, 27 carry HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX evidence and
nine are ChIP-only; the ChIP-only ones (SOX5, SOX6, SOX11, SOX13, SOX30, some SOX2 and SOX17
models) are the likeliest to have absorbed a partner's preference. Two CIS-BP entries (SOX1,
SOX11) are mouse-derived at 100% DNA-binding-domain identity, which does not affect specificity;
no member of the family has out-of-family nearest neighbors.
families.caveats: A hit tells you a SOX-family HMG box could bind; it does not tell you which of the 20 proteins. SOX1/2/3, SOX8/9/10 and SOX4/11/12 are mutually indistinguishable from sequence, and the Vierstra archetypes are named "SOX" or "SOX/SRY" for that reason. The core is six bases and occurs over a million times by chance, so isolated matches are weak evidence; SOX proteins also need a partner factor to do anything, so a lone SOX site rarely predicts regulation. CTTTG-type variants overlap the TCF/LEF Wnt response element and cannot be confidently assigned to either family. Nine of the 36 HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only and may reflect a partner's specificity.

timeline.finding: SRY is identified in the sex-determining region of the human Y chromosome and found to carry a DNA-binding motif shared with the nuclear HMG proteins HMG1 and HMG2, defining the family the other SOX genes were later named for.
timeline.methods: Positional cloning, sequence comparison
timeline.open: Whether SRY bound DNA sequence-specifically, and what sequence, was not known.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection defines the SRY consensus as (A/T)(A/T)CAA(A/T)G, a six- to seven-base AT-rich core.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection
timeline.open: Left open whether the other SOX proteins read the same core, and how such a short site could be selective.

timeline.finding: SOX9 mutations are shown to cause campomelic dysplasia with autosomal sex reversal, establishing that SOX proteins outside SRY control both skeletal development and testis determination.
timeline.methods: Translocation breakpoint cloning, mutation analysis

timeline.finding: The NMR structure of the SRY HMG box on its site shows an L-shaped domain binding entirely in the minor groove, with a side chain intercalated between base pairs, the helix unwound and bent by 70-80 degrees, and explains sex-reversal point mutations at the atomic level.
timeline.methods: Multidimensional NMR

timeline.finding: Sox2 is identified as the factor that acts with Oct-3 on the FGF-4 enhancer, and only the Sox2-Oct-3 pair activates transcription: the first demonstration that a SOX protein works through an adjacent partner site.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, EMSA, reporter assays

timeline.finding: Site selection on Sox4, Tcf1, MatMc and Ste11 shows that sequence-specific HMG-box factors read 10-12 base pairs, not the 6-8 assumed, with residues C-terminal to the box contacting the 3' bases.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection, footprinting with deletion mutants

timeline.finding: Two results separate SOX functions that one motif cannot: the crystal structure of a POU/HMG/DNA complex shows Oct4 and Sox2 adopting different arrangements on different enhancers, and a SOX9 mutation outside the HMG box abolishes cooperative dimer binding at chondrocyte enhancers while leaving monomeric binding and sex determination intact.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; human genetics with EMSA and reporter assays

timeline.finding: Cryo-EM structures of SOX2 and SOX11 DNA-binding domains on nucleosomes show them binding and distorting DNA at superhelical location 2 and detaching terminal nucleosomal DNA, giving a structural basis for SOX pioneer activity.
timeline.methods: Cryo-electron microscopy
timeline.open: Did not establish which genomic SOX sites are engaged in this nucleosomal mode in cells.

open: Whether CTTTG-type sites are genuine SOX preferences is unresolved: HOCOMOCO SOX4, SOX11 and SOX13 models read CCTTTGTT, which also satisfies the TCF/LEF Wnt response element, and three of those four models are ChIP-only, so the sequence may belong to a co-occupying TCF/LEF protein rather than to the SOX protein named on the label.

How spacing constrains SOXE dimer sites is unsettled: the palindromic models in these databases carry a two- to four-base spacer, but SOXE proteins were shown to bind cooperatively over a range of spacings, so it is unclear whether the recurring spacer reflects a real optimum or the selection scheme that produced the models.

What makes paralogues with identical motifs occupy different sites in vivo is still open: expression, partner factors and nucleosome engagement are all invoked, and no sequence feature has been shown to separate SOX1 from SOX2 or SOX8 from SOX9 and SOX10.

families.name: NeuroD / Atonal / ASCL
families.def: Class II neural E-box CAGATG / CAGCTG. NEUROD1/2/4/6, NEUROG1-3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1-3, PTF1A, FERD3L, BHLHA9/15, BHLHE22/23, MSGN1, FIGLA, NHLH1/2.
families.short: Class II basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) proteins of the Atonal, achaete-scute, Olig and NSCL groups — NEUROD1/2, NEUROG1-3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1-3, PTF1A, BHLHA15, FIGLA, MSGN1, NHLH1/2 and relatives — bind DNA only as heterodimers with the broadly expressed class I E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12. The dimer reads a six-base E-box, CANNTG; this group prefers CAGATG (CATCTG on the opposite strand), with CATATG and CAGCTG as the two common variants. These factors are commitment switches for progenitors in the nervous system, inner ear, retina, pancreas, intestine and presomitic mesoderm, and several of them — ASCL1, NEUROD1, NEUROG2, ATOH1 — are the active ingredients of direct reprogramming protocols that convert fibroblasts into neurons.
families.long:
## The factors

This family collects the tissue-restricted ("class II") bHLH proteins whose DNA-binding domains are closest to *Drosophila* atonal and achaete-scute. In the atlas it spans NEUROD1/2 (and NEUROD4/6), NEUROG1/2/3, ATOH1/7/8, ASCL1/2, OLIG1/2/3, PTF1A, FERD3L, FIGLA, BHLHA9, BHLHA15 (MIST1), BHLHE22/23, MSGN1 and NHLH1/2 — around twenty human genes. The binding unit is a ~60-residue basic helix-loop-helix domain: a basic segment that lies in the major groove, followed by two helices separated by a loop that pack into a parallel four-helix bundle with the partner subunit. Almost none of these proteins binds DNA usefully on its own. The functional species is a heterodimer with a class I E-protein — TCF3 (E12/E47), TCF4 (ITF2) or TCF12 (HEB) — which are expressed in nearly every cell type. The crystal structure of the E47-NEUROD1 bHLH dimer on the insulin-gene E-box shows why heterodimers dominate: the E47-NEUROD1 interface is as extensive as the E47 homodimer interface, while NEUROD1 homodimers are unstable [PMID:18069799]. Expression of the class II partners is narrow and largely non-overlapping: NEUROG1/2 in neural progenitors, NEUROD1 in newly born neurons and pancreatic islets, ATOH1 in cerebellar granule, inner-ear hair-cell and intestinal secretory progenitors, ASCL1 in ventral telencephalon and autonomic and neuroendocrine lineages, OLIG2 in motor-neuron and oligodendrocyte precursors, PTF1A in pancreas and cerebellum, BHLHA15 in exocrine secretory cells, FIGLA in oocytes, MSGN1 in presomitic mesoderm. "Neural" describes most of the family, not all of it.

## The motif

The site is a six-base E-box, CANNTG, an imperfect palindrome in which each monomer reads one CAN half-site. A glutamate in the basic region hydrogen-bonds the cytosine and adenine of its half-site and an adjacent arginine contacts the guanine on the complementary strand; these contacts are what make CA...TG invariant. The central two positions are the variable ones, and in the E47-NEUROD1 structure no side chain contacts them directly — specificity there comes from backbone contacts, DNA deformability and flanking sequence [PMID:18069799]. That is the single most important fact for interpreting hits: CAGATG, CAGCTG and CATCTG (the reverse complement of CAGATG) differ at positions the protein barely touches.

The data reflect this. The representative model is `gaCAGATGG`, and the 82 motifs split into three overlapping groups: CAGATG (mostly ChIP-derived, for NEUROD1/2, NEUROG2, ATOH1, PTF1A), CATATG (almost all HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX models, covering NEUROG1/2/3, OLIG1/2/3, ATOH1/7, BHLHE22/23, NEUROD1/2, BHLHA15) and CAGCTG (ASCL1/2, NHLH1/2, PTF1A, FERD3L, ATOH8, BHLHA9), with a CACCTG minority for FIGLA and some ASCL1 and PTF1A models. Genome-wide comparison of NEUROD2 and MYOD binding found CAGCTG shared between them and CAGATG as the NEUROD2-preferred site, so CAGCTG is the least diagnostic of the three [PMID:22445365]. The flanks add a little: FERD3L models read GTAACAGCTGTTGC, NHLH models CGCAGCTGCG, and PTF1A ChIP gives an E-box followed after about five bases by a TTC, the TC-box of the trimeric PTF1 complex with RBPJ or RBPJL. Overall cohesion is 0.81 and no member is flagged as belonging elsewhere, but the CATATG and CAGCTG subgroups are separated by more than the usual paralogue-level noise.

## Where it acts

These are enhancer factors. Sites are distal, AT-rich rather than CpG-island-associated, and binding is largely confined to E-boxes that are already in accessible chromatin, so the same motif is used by different family members in different cell types with little overlap. Typical genome-wide occupancy is thousands to tens of thousands of sites per factor, a small fraction of the available E-boxes. Frequent neighbours are SOX (SOX2, SOX10), POU (POU3F2/BRN2), LHX and RFX motifs in neural enhancers, and in the pancreas FOXA, PDX1 and RBPJ/RBPJL. The named composite element in this family is the PTF1 site: an E-box and a TC-box about one helical turn apart, bound by PTF1A together with RBPJ (PTF1-J) or RBPJL (PTF1-L).

## Biology and disease

These factors are commitment switches. *Atoh1* loss removes cerebellar granule neurons, inner-ear hair cells and the intestinal secretory lineage [PMID:10364557]; *Neurog3* loss removes all four pancreatic endocrine cell types [PMID:10677506]; *Olig1* and *Olig2* couple motor-neuron and oligodendrocyte specification, and *Olig2* loss removes both [PMID:11955447]; *Neurog1* is required for the proximal cranial sensory ganglia, whose precursors are never determined in its absence [PMID:9539122], and *Neurog1* and *Neurog2* are required for the two successive waves of dorsal root ganglion neurogenesis, Neurog2 mainly for the early trkB- and trkC-positive neurons and Neurog1 for most trkA-positive ones [PMID:10398684]; the proneural framework these knockouts established is set out in a review [PMID:12094208]. ASCL1 also drives progenitor proliferation, not only differentiation, which is why proneural activity and cell-cycle exit are not synonymous [PMID:21536733]. In humans, biallelic *PTF1A* mutations cause pancreatic and cerebellar agenesis [PMID:15543146]. ASCL1 and NEUROD1 define transcriptional subtypes of small-cell lung cancer and OLIG2 marks oligodendroglial tumours. The same commitment function underlies direct reprogramming: ASCL1 with POU3F2 and MYT1L converts fibroblasts to functional neurons [PMID:20107439], and NEUROD1, NEUROG2 and ATOH1 are used in comparable protocols.

## Reading a hit

A CAGATG, CATATG or CAGCTG match tells you a class II bHLH-E-protein heterodimer could bind, and nothing about which one. All ~20 members are indistinguishable from sequence; the Vierstra archetype `AC0084:OLIG/NEUROG:bHLH` says so in its name. Chance matters: a fixed six-mer is expected roughly 750,000 times per strand of a 3.1-Gb genome, so a bare E-box hit is close to uninformative without conservation, accessibility or expression evidence. Which motif version you scan with changes the answer — the in vitro (HT-SELEX) models say CATATG while the ChIP models say CAGATG or CAGCTG [PMID:23332764]. Members with only ChIP evidence (HOCOMOCO fourth-field `P`, e.g. `NDF1.H14CORE.0.P.B`) support "this factor occupies these regions", not "this factor binds this sequence"; the S and M models do the latter. One outlier deserves naming: the Vierstra archetype `AC0461:ASCL:bHLH` has the consensus ACACGACGC, which is not an E-box and matches nothing else in the family.
families.caveats: A hit identifies the family, not the factor: all twenty-odd members read the same six-base E-box and cannot be told apart from sequence, which is why one Vierstra archetype here is named OLIG/NEUROG rather than after a protein. The three variants CAGATG, CATATG and CAGCTG differ at positions the protein does not directly contact, so a scan tuned to one will miss or misrank the others, and CAGCTG in particular is shared with E-protein homodimers, MYOD, TWIST and TCF21. Six-mers are far too common to be evidence on their own. ChIP-only models (HOCOMOCO evidence letter P) show occupancy, not binding specificity.

timeline.finding: NeuroD is identified as a neuronal differentiation factor: ectopic expression converts Xenopus ectoderm into neurons, showing that one tissue-restricted bHLH protein can impose neuronal identity.
timeline.methods: expression cloning, Xenopus embryo overexpression
timeline.open: Which E-box variant NeuroD reads, and with which partner, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Neurogenin is placed upstream of NeuroD as a determination gene, giving the vertebrate family the same two-tier organization as the Drosophila proneural genes.
timeline.methods: expression analysis and overexpression in mouse and Xenopus
timeline.open: Whether family members differ in target sequence or only in timing and expression domain.

timeline.finding: Knockouts show single members are required for whole lineages: Atoh1 for inner-ear hair cells (1999), Neurog3 for all four pancreatic endocrine cell types (2000), Olig1/Olig2 together for motor neurons and oligodendrocytes (2002).
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting
timeline.open: The non-redundant phenotypes could not be explained by DNA-binding differences, since the proteins read the same E-box.

timeline.finding: Biallelic truncating PTF1A mutations are shown to cause pancreatic and cerebellar agenesis in humans, carrying the family's lineage-commitment role into monogenic disease.
timeline.methods: linkage analysis and positional cloning in two families

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the E47-NEUROD1 bHLH heterodimer on the insulin-gene E-box CATCTG shows a heterodimer interface as extensive as the E47 homodimer interface and no side-chain contact with the two central base pairs.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: With nothing contacting the central bases, what sets the CAGATG/CATATG/CAGCTG preference measured in solution was left unexplained.

timeline.finding: ASCL1 with POU3F2 and MYT1L converts fibroblasts directly into functional neurons, showing these factors act as commitment switches outside their normal lineage.
timeline.methods: combinatorial factor screening, electrophysiology
timeline.open: Why only a small subset of genomic E-boxes is engaged during conversion.

timeline.finding: Side-by-side genome-wide mapping of NEUROD2 and MYOD finds a shared CAGCTG site plus factor-specific sites (CAGATG for NEUROD2, CAGGTG for MYOD); transcription tracks only the factor-specific sites, and occupancy is confined to E-boxes already in accessible chromatin.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and expression profiling in two differentiation systems
timeline.open: The relative weight of sequence and chromatin in choosing targets remained contested.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX models for NEUROG1-3, OLIG1-3, ATOH1/7 and NEUROD1/2 read CATATG rather than the ChIP-derived CAGATG, so the in vitro preference of these proteins differs from the site recovered from chromatin.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Whether the CATATG/CAGATG difference reflects partner proteins, chromatin or selection conditions was not resolved.

open: In vitro and ChIP-derived models of the same proteins disagree about the two central bases: HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX models for NEUROG1-3, OLIG1-3 and ATOH1/7 read CATATG, while ChIP models for NEUROD1/2, NEUROG2, ATOH1 and PTF1A read CAGATG or CAGCTG, and it is unsettled whether partner proteins, chromatin context or the selection protocol accounts for the shift.

What selects member-specific targets in vivo is unresolved, because the one solved class I/class II structure shows no side-chain contact with the variable central bases; flanking sequence, DNA shape, cooperating factors and pre-existing accessibility have all been proposed, and the NEUROD2/MYOD comparison argues that sequence chooses the program while chromatin decides which sites are available.

Whether proneural activity is separable from proliferative activity is open: ASCL1 drives both cell-cycle exit and progenitor expansion, and which targets or conditions tip that balance has not been settled.

The Vierstra archetype AC0461:ASCL:bHLH has the consensus ACACGACGC, which is not an E-box and matches nothing else in the family; whether it captures a real secondary binding mode of ASCL factors or is a footprint-clustering artifact is unknown.

families.name: POU (octamer)
families.def: Octamer ATGCAAAT and MORE/PORE dimer sites. POU1F1, POU2F1-3, POU3F1-4, POU4F1-3, POU5F1/OCT4, POU5F1B, POU6F1/2.
families.short: The octamer ATGCAAAT is the site read by the 16 human POU-domain factors, including OCT1/POU2F1, OCT2/POU2F2, PIT1/POU1F1, the BRN2/BRN1 group (POU3F1-4), the BRN3 group (POU4F1-3) and OCT4/POU5F1. What makes the family unusual is the binding unit: a POU-specific domain and a homeodomain joined by a flexible linker, so the two halves of the site can be re-arranged. The same proteins therefore also form dimers on the PORE and MORE elements and sit next to SOX partners in the SOX-OCT composite elements that control pluripotency genes. Hits matter because octamer elements drive immunoglobulin and snRNA promoters and because OCT4 occupancy of SOX-OCT sites is a defining feature of pluripotent cells. The motif is short and AT-rich, so it is common.
families.long:
## The factors

Sixteen human POU genes fall into six classes: POU1F1 (PIT1), POU2F1-3 (OCT1, OCT2, OCT11/SKN-1a), POU3F1-4 (OCT6, BRN2, BRN1, BRN4), POU4F1-3 (BRN3A/B/C), POU5F1 (OCT4) together with the retrogene-derived POU5F1B locus, and POU6F1/2. All of them use one composite DNA-binding unit, described from sequence in 1988 and named after PIT1, OCT1, OCT2 and *C. elegans* UNC-86 [PMID:3215510,2905684]: an N-terminal POU-specific domain (POU-S), a four-helix bundle whose helix-turn-helix resembles the bacteriophage lambda and 434 repressors, tethered by a flexible 15-27 residue linker to a C-terminal POU-homeodomain (POU-HD), a conventional 60-residue three-helix homeodomain [PMID:8156594,7622033]. Expression is class-restricted. POU2F1 is essentially ubiquitous; POU2F2 is lymphoid [PMID:2905684]; POU5F1 is confined to pluripotent and germ cells; POU3F and POU4F members mark defined neural, retinal and inner-ear lineages; POU1F1 is restricted to the anterior pituitary.

## The motif

The core is the 8-bp octamer ATGCAAAT, first noted as a conserved element upstream of immunoglobulin genes [PMID:6425835]. The 1994 crystal structure of the OCT1 POU domain on an octamer site showed why the site is bipartite: POU-S grips the 5' ATGCA half and POU-HD the 3' AAAT half, the two domains bind opposite faces of the duplex, and the linker is disordered and contacts no bases [PMID:8156594]. The 3' half is a TAAT-type homeodomain site read in the reverse orientation; POU-S contributes most of the base-specific contacts, which is why the ATGC block is the least tolerant part of the site. Because the linker tethers rather than spaces, the half-sites can be rearranged: two POU domains dimerize on the PORE (ATTTGAAATGCAAAT) or on the MORE (ATGCATATGCAT) using two non-overlapping surface patches, and only the PORE arrangement recruits the coactivator OBF-1/POU2AF1 [PMID:11136971,11583619]. Pooled across JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetypes, this family's consensus is tTATGCaAATt - the octamer plus its usual flanking T - but cohesion is only 0.68, because many HT-SELEX models for POU3F, POU4F and POU6F members report homeodomain-half arrangements (TGCATAAT, ATTAATTATGCA, TAATTA, TCATTA) instead of the full octamer [PMID:23332764]. Those are configuration variants of one binding unit, not separate specificities [PMID:7622033].

## Where it acts

Octamer sites are classically promoter-proximal, in immunoglobulin heavy- and light-chain promoters, the histone H2B promoter and snRNA promoters [PMID:6425835,7622033]. The best-characterized POU enhancer elements are composite: an OCT4 octamer immediately adjacent to a SOX HMG site. OCT4 and SOX2 dimerize in different relative orientations on the FGF4 and UTF1 enhancers, and it is the arrangement of the two boxes in the DNA, not a switch in the proteins, that sets the geometry [PMID:12923055]. The Vierstra archetype set recovers POU5F/NANOG and POU2F/POU3F clusters, reflecting how routinely these sites are found with partner motifs. Because the octamer is only 8 bp and AT-rich, an exact match is expected on the order of 10^5 times in 3.1 Gb, so the great majority of matches are unoccupied in any one cell type; occupancy tracks which POU class is expressed. Methyl-SELEX places several POU factors among those whose affinity is changed by CpG methylation in flanking positions, although the octamer core itself has no CpG [PMID:28473536].

## Biology and disease

POU5F1/OCT4 maintains the pluripotent state and is one of the four factors that reprogram human fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells [PMID:18035408]. POU2F2 with OBF-1 drives immunoglobulin promoter activity in B cells, and the PORE-versus-MORE distinction is the structural explanation for that coactivator dependence [PMID:11136971,11583619]. POU3F2 and POU3F3 pattern the neocortex; POU4F1-3 specify sensory neurons, retinal ganglion cells and inner-ear hair cells; POU1F1 controls the growth hormone and prolactin genes. Mendelian loss of POU1F1 causes combined pituitary hormone deficiency [PMID:1509262], and mutations in POU3F4 and POU4F3 cause X-linked and autosomal dominant deafness respectively [PMID:7839145,9506947]. In cancer, POU2F3 defines a tuft-cell-like subtype of small-cell lung carcinoma [PMID:29945888], and POU5F1 is re-expressed in germ cell tumors.

## Reading a hit

A good octamer match tells you that a POU factor could bind; it does not tell you which one. The in vitro models for POU2F1, POU2F2, POU2F3, POU3F1-4 and POU5F1 are all the same 8-9 bp [PMID:23332764], so treat a hit as "POU family" unless expression data narrow it. Do not read a bare TAATTA or TCATTA match as POU: that is the homeodomain half alone and is shared with most of the homeodomain superfamily, which is exactly why two low-information CIS-BP and Vierstra entries in this family have nearest neighbours in the HOX and Q50 groups. Conversely, a full PORE, MORE or SOX-OCT composite is much stronger evidence, because the spacing constraint is specific. HOCOMOCO ids are informative here: PO2F1.H14CORE.0.PS.A and PO5F1.H14CORE.2.SM.B carry in vitro (S/M) support, whereas the P-only models such as PO3F2.H14CORE.0.P.B come from ChIP alone and may reflect co-binding.
families.caveats: A hit identifies the POU family, not a paralogue: the octamer models for OCT1, OCT2, OCT4 and the BRN proteins are interchangeable at 8-9 bp. The family is only moderately cohesive (0.68) because HT-SELEX returns several linker configurations, and the lowest-information members reduce to TAAT cores indistinguishable from the rest of the homeodomain superfamily; three entries here have nearest neighbours in other homeodomain families. ChIP-derived (P-grade) POU models can capture partner motifs, particularly SOX sites in pluripotent cells. Exact octamers occur roughly 10^5 times genome-wide, so a match alone is weak evidence without expression or footprint support.

timeline.finding: The octamer is found about 70 bp upstream of the transcription start of every immunoglobulin gene examined, as ATTTGCAT in light-chain genes and its exact inverse ATGCAAAT in heavy-chain genes, conserved while the surrounding sequence has diverged.
timeline.methods: Comparative sequence analysis of immunoglobulin promoters
timeline.open: That the element was a binding site for a tissue-specific factor was a proposal, not yet tested.

timeline.finding: Cloning of OCT1 and comparison with OCT2, PIT1 and UNC-86 define the POU domain: a POU-specific box plus a homeobox subdomain, about 160 residues, that carries all the octamer-binding activity; ubiquitous OCT1 and lymphoid OCT2 read the octamer indistinguishably.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, deletion mapping, sequence comparison
timeline.open: How two subdomains in one polypeptide divide an 8-bp site between them was unknown.

timeline.finding: The OCT1 POU domain-octamer structure shows POU-S on the 5' ATGC half, docked like the lambda and 434 repressors, and POU-HD on the 3' AAAT half, docked like other homeodomains, with an invisible linker and no protein-protein contact between the two.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography (3.0 A)
timeline.open: With no contact between the domains, the source of their cooperativity was unexplained.

timeline.finding: Unlinked POU-S and POU-HD polypeptides still bind the octamer cooperatively (coupling energy about 1.6 kcal/mol), and the linker behaves as a tether with an effective concentration of about 3.6 mM rather than as a fixed spacer.
timeline.methods: Quantitative DNA-binding assays with isolated subdomains

timeline.finding: POU dimers assemble in two configurations, on the PORE (ATTTGAAATGCAAAT) and the MORE (ATGCATATGCAT); only the PORE dimer recruits OBF-1, because the MORE dimer interface uses the same OCT1 residues that contact OBF-1. Crystal structures in 2001 showed the two non-overlapping interface patches.
timeline.methods: Binding and transactivation assays, mutagenesis; X-ray crystallography (2001)

timeline.finding: A structure of the OCT1 POU domain and SOX2 HMG domain on the FGF4 enhancer element, plus modeling and mutational tests, shows that OCT4 and SOX2 assemble in different relative arrangements on the FGF4 and UTF1 enhancers, and that the enhancer DNA, not the proteins, sets the arrangement.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, model building, mutational validation

timeline.finding: Systematic HT-SELEX of human POU proteins gives the octamer for POU2F, POU3F and POU5F1B proteins but homeodomain-led arrangements such as TGCATAATTAAT and CTCATTA for POU4F and POU6F proteins, so the in vitro preference of the family is a set of linker configurations rather than one octamer.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Whether these alternative arrangements are what POU4F and POU6F proteins occupy in vivo was not tested.

timeline.finding: Methyl-HT-SELEX across 542 human factors finds that many homeodomain proteins bind CpG-methylated sites differently from unmethylated ones; POU models from this kind of assay include CpG-containing MORE-like variants (for example POU2F2, GAATATGCGCAT) that the canonical octamer, which has no CpG, cannot capture.
timeline.methods: Methyl-HT-SELEX, crystallography

open: Which DNA configuration POU3F proteins use in vivo is unsettled in the data: their JASPAR HT-SELEX models read the monomeric octamer (TATGCAAAT), whereas the HOCOMOCO models that incorporate ChIP-seq for POU3F1 and POU3F2 (PO3F1.H14CORE.1.PS.A, PO3F2.H14CORE.0.P.B) read the palindrome CATGAATATTCAT, a two-site arrangement the octamer does not describe.

How often POU5F1 binds the octamer on its own rather than as part of a SOX-OCT composite is unresolved: the in vitro POU5F1 models are the bare octamer, the ChIP-derived ones carry the adjacent SOX half-site, and genome-wide data have been read both as cooperative assembly and as largely independent binding of the two factors.

Whether POU4F and POU6F proteins occupy the full octamer or the homeodomain-led arrangements their HT-SELEX models give (TGCATAATTAAT, CTCATTA) is not resolved; the latter are close to generic homeodomain sites, so the answer decides whether these proteins can be told apart from other homeodomain factors by sequence at all.

families.name: ETS class I (ETS1/ERG/FLI1)
families.def: GGA(A/T) core, ACCGGAAGT. ETS1/2, ERG, FLI1, FEV, ETV1/4/5, ETV6/7, ERF, ETV3, ELK1/3/4, GABPA, SPDEF.
families.short: ETS proteins are a family of 28 human transcription factors that each bind DNA through a single ~85-residue winged helix-turn-helix domain and read a nine-base site whose informative part is the four-base core GGA(A/T). The class I members - ETS1 and ETS2, ERG, FLI1, FEV, the PEA3 proteins ETV1/4/5, the ternary complex factors ELK1/3/4, the repressors ERF and ETV3, and GABPA - select essentially the same sequence, ACCGGAAGT, so a match names the class rather than a protein. These sites sit just upstream of a large fraction of human promoters and, in enhancers, next to RUNX, GATA, PAX and SRF sites. Class I also contains every ETS gene recurrently rearranged in cancer: ERG in prostate cancer, FLI1 and ERG in Ewing sarcoma, ETV1 and ETV4 in both.
families.long:
## The factors

The human genome contains 28 ETS genes. All encode one copy of the ETS domain: about 85 residues
folded as a winged helix-turn-helix, three alpha-helices packed on a four-stranded antiparallel
beta-sheet, that binds DNA as a monomer [PMID:8602247,21548782]. Profiling the DNA-binding preference of every human and
mouse ETS protein split the family into four classes, and class I is by far the largest: the ETS
subfamily (ETS1, ETS2), the ERG subfamily (ERG, FLI1, FEV), the PEA3 proteins (ETV1, ETV4,
ETV5), the ternary complex factors (ELK1, ELK3, ELK4), the repressors ERF and ETV3, and GABPA [PMID:20517297].
GABPA is the structural exception: it functions only in complex with the ankyrin-repeat subunit
GABPB, which it recruits using the ETS domain plus a carboxy-terminal extension [PMID:9461436]. Several class I
proteins carry autoinhibitory segments flanking the ETS domain that are relieved by partner
binding [PMID:10075931,21548782]. Expression ranges from near-ubiquitous (GABPA, ELK1, ERF, ETV3) through
lymphoid-enriched (ETS1), endothelial and hematopoietic (ERG, FLI1), to narrowly restricted
(FEV). SPDEF is grouped here in this atlas, but biochemically it is the sole class IV factor and
prefers a GGAT core [PMID:20517297,21548782].

## The motif

The site is nine base pairs, ACCGGAAGT, and nearly all of its information is in the GGA(A/T)
core [PMID:21548782]. Two invariant arginines in recognition helix H3 hydrogen-bond the two core guanines; a
conserved tyrosine (Tyr395 in ETS1) supports the interface; a lysine in the wing contacts DNA 5'
of the core and a lysine in the H2-H3 turn contacts the opposite strand 3' of it [PMID:8602247,21548782]. The core is
read base by base, the flanks indirectly, through sequence-dependent backbone geometry [PMID:21548782]. The
flanks separate subfamilies, and separate them weakly: class I prefers A three bases 5' of the core and disfavors C there, the ELF/EHF group
prefers C at that position (CCCGGAAGT), SPI1/SPIB/SPIC use a purine-rich 5' flank (AGAGGAAGTG),
and SPDEF alone prefers GGAT [PMID:20517297]. Quantitatively, different ETS proteins vary only about ten-fold in
affinity for the same consensus, whereas one protein's affinity across variant sites spans five-
to eighty-fold [PMID:21548782]; sequence therefore grades site quality much better than it identifies a
paralogue, and no class I member is separable from another by motif alone. The CCGG contains a
CpG, and methylating it blocks binding [PMID:20019798,21548782]. Tandem arrangements are a distinct case: GGAA
microsatellites of four or more consecutive repeats are the response elements of the EWS-FLI1
fusion [PMID:18626011,21548782], and some models grouped here (JASPAR MA0149.1, archetype AC0561) are GGAA repeats rather
than single sites.

## Where it acts

ETS occupancy follows two logics. At promoters it is largely redundant: a strong CCGGAAGT sits
20-40 bp upstream of the transcription start site in CpG-island housekeeping promoters - roughly
a quarter of human promoters carry an ETS site near the start site [PMID:17652178,21548782] - and different ETS proteins
bind interchangeably, with most GABPA-occupied promoters in Jurkat cells also occupied by ETS1 [PMID:17652178,20019798].
These sites lie in hypomethylated CpG islands, so the CpG in the core stays unmethylated [PMID:21548782]. At
distal, DNase-sensitive enhancers, occupancy is factor-specific, the sequence departs from
consensus [PMID:17652178,20019798], and specificity comes from composite elements: ETS1 with RUNX1 at AGGA(A/T)GTGG, which
binds more than 30-fold cooperatively and marks over a thousand ETS1-specific regions in T cells [PMID:10075931,20019798,21548782];
ETS with GATA in hemogenic endothelium, where FLI1, GATA2 and SCL cross-regulate through
neighboring sites [PMID:17962413]; ETS1 with PAX5 at the mb-1 promoter, where Gln22 of the PAX5 paired domain
hydrogen-bonds Tyr395 of ETS1 [PMID:11779502,21548782]; the ternary complex factors with SRF at serum response elements [PMID:11715049,21548782];
and ERG with the androgen receptor in prostate cancer, where the two share about 44% of sites [PMID:21548782].
The ETS-IRF composite element (EICE) belongs to the SPI1 subfamily and is described there.

## Biology and disease

Class I factors run housekeeping transcription, growth-factor responses and lineage programs.
Gabpa-null mouse embryos die before implantation [PMID:15199140], consistent with GABPA's occupancy of
housekeeping promoters. Ets1 loss impairs T-cell and natural killer cell development. ERG and
FLI1 are required for endothelial and hematopoietic specification. The clinical weight of the
class is oncogenic rearrangement: TMPRSS2-ERG and related fusions place ERG, ETV1, ETV4 or ETV5
under androgen control in roughly half of prostate cancers [PMID:16254181,21548782], and EWSR1-FLI1 or EWSR1-ERG defines
Ewing sarcoma, where the fusion's prion-like EWSR1 domain converts GGAA microsatellites into de
novo enhancers [PMID:18626011,28844694].

## Reading a hit

Treat a single match as weak evidence. The four-base GGAA core is expected about 12 million times
per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome and the full nine-mer ACCGGAAGT on the order of 10,000 times per
strand by base-composition arithmetic; CCGG-containing words are rarer than that because the
genome is CpG-depleted, but the site is still common enough that isolated hits mean little
without context: conservation, accessibility, a nearby partner site, or a promoter position close
to the start site. A hit identifies an ETS site, not an ETS protein: ETS1, ERG, FLI1, ELK1
and GABPA are not distinguishable from sequence. ChIP-derived models carry partner signal:
HOCOMOCO's ChIP-based ETS1 model (ETS1.H14CORE.1.P.B) has consensus ACAGGAAGTGG, whose trailing
GTGG is the RUNX1 half-site of the ETS1-RUNX1 composite [PMID:20019798], and several other ChIP-derived ETS
models converge on CAGGAAG rather than the in vitro CCGGAAGT [PMID:20019798,21548782]. Half of the JASPAR entries grouped
here (16 of 32) are CAP-SELEX heterodimer models such as ERF::SREBF2 or ETV5::FIGLA, where much
of the matrix is the partner's site, not an ETS site. Finally, consensus strings are stored on
either strand: GABPA's JASPAR model reads CACTTCCTGT, the reverse complement of ACAGGAAGTG.
families.caveats:
A hit tells you the family, not the member: all class I ETS proteins select the
same nine-mer in vitro and differ only in weak flanking preferences, so a "FLI1 site" and an
"ERG site" are the same sequence. The core is short and frequent, so a match outside an
accessible, conserved or composite context is expected by chance. Sixteen of the 32 JASPAR models
here are CAP-SELEX heterodimers whose matrices are partly a bHLH, FOX, HOX or SREBF site; four
models here are GGAA repeats rather than single sites and will hit any GGAA microsatellite; and the
ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO models (evidence letter P) include RUNX-extended and CAGGAAG variants that
reflect partners and indirect binding rather than intrinsic ETS specificity. SPDEF is placed in
this family here but reads GGAT and is biochemically its own class.

timeline.finding: The ETS domain is named as a new DNA-binding motif shared by the ETS proteins and shown to recognize a purine-rich core centred on GGA.
timeline.methods: Sequence comparison across ETS proteins, DNA-binding assays
timeline.open: How one short domain read so small a core, and whether family members differed in what they bound, was unknown.

timeline.finding: The first ETS domain-DNA crystal structure (PU.1) shows a winged helix-turn-helix contacting ten base pairs through a loop-helix-loop: two arginines of the recognition helix read the GGA core, a wing lysine binds 5' of it and a turn lysine 3' of it on the opposite strand.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: No base contacts outside the core were seen, so the flanking preferences that separate subfamilies were left to indirect readout.

timeline.finding: Outlier-expression analysis finds ERG and ETV1 overexpressed in prostate cancer through fusion to the 5' end of the androgen-regulated TMPRSS2 gene; 23 of 29 tumors examined by FISH carry an ERG or ETV1 rearrangement.
timeline.methods: Cancer outlier profile analysis, FISH, RT-PCR, androgen stimulation of cell lines
timeline.open: Which genomic sites the overexpressed ETS proteins act through, and whether they differ from those of the endogenous ETS factors, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Promoter-array ChIP for three ETS proteins in a T-cell line finds that redundant occupancy is the rule: consensus sites near the start sites of housekeeping genes are shared, while factor-specific sites diverge from consensus, lie farther away, and include an ETS1-RUNX1 cooperative site.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip on promoter microarrays, motif analysis
timeline.open: Promoter arrays could not see enhancers, where specific occupancy turned out to concentrate.

timeline.finding: EWS-FLI1 regulates targets such as NR0B1 through GGAA microsatellites; the NR0B1 repeat binds the fusion in vitro and in vivo, is necessary and sufficient for regulation, and activity depends on the number of consecutive GGAA motifs.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip, in vitro binding, reporter assays, genome-wide sequence analysis
timeline.open: Whether repeat binding was a property of the FLI1 ETS domain or required the EWS portion of the fusion was not settled.

timeline.finding: ETS1 ChIP-seq in Jurkat T cells separates redundant occupancy with GABPA at housekeeping promoters from ETS1-specific occupancy at T-cell enhancers, which carry either a CpG-free CAGGAAGT variant or an ETS-RUNX composite; more than a thousand specific regions show AGGA(A/T)GTGG.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, DNase I sensitivity, in vitro binding
timeline.open: FLI1 and ERG also co-occupy sites with RUNX1 in stem cells, so how specific the composite is for ETS1 was left open.

timeline.finding: DNA-binding profiles of all human and mouse ETS proteins, from two in vitro methods, fall into four classes; every cancer-linked ETS factor (ERG, ETV1, ETV4, FLI1) is in class I, and ChIP-seq for one member of each class confirms that the small in vitro differences affect site choice in cells.
timeline.methods: High-throughput microwell binding assay, protein-binding microarrays, ChIP-seq
timeline.open: Members within class I remained indistinguishable, so paralogue specificity had to come from elsewhere.

timeline.finding: Wild-type FLI1 occupies canonical ETS sites but not GGAA repeats, whereas EWS-FLI1 binds repeats, recruits BAF complexes and opens de novo enhancers, and needs the tyrosines that drive phase transitions of the EWSR1 prion-like domain to bind them. This revises the earlier view that the EWS portion contributes only transcriptional activation.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in mesenchymal stem cells and Ewing sarcoma cells, mutagenesis, proteomics, in vitro phase-transition assays

open: How class I paralogues reach different genomic sites despite indistinguishable in vitro preferences is only partly explained: ETS-RUNX composites account for some ETS1-specific enhancers, but RUNX1 also co-occupies sites with FLI1 and ERG, and the contributions of partner choice, autoinhibition and relative expression level to the remaining specific sites have not been separated.

Why ChIP-derived models converge on CAGGAAG while in vitro models give ACCGGAAGT is unresolved: one reading is an intrinsic ETS1 preference for the variant that confers specificity, the other is that the A simply removes a CpG whose methylation would block binding at enhancers outside protected CpG islands.

Whether binding to GGAA microsatellites is an intrinsic property of the ETS domain or a neomorphic property of the EWSR1 fusion is contested: in vitro and reporter work found binding that scales with repeat number and reported that several wild-type ETS proteins bind repeats, while in cells wild-type FLI1 does not occupy repeats and EWS-FLI1 needs its prion-like-domain tyrosines to do so.

The databases cluster SPDEF models with class I, whereas in vitro profiling makes SPDEF the sole class IV factor with a GGAT core; whether SPDEF also uses GGAA sites in cells, or the clustering reflects only the shared CCGGA flank, is not established.

families.name: AP-1 (FOS/JUN)
families.def: TRE/AP-1 site TGA(C/G)TCA. FOS, FOSB, FOSL1/2, JUN, JUNB, JUND, BATF, BATF2/3, JDP2, ATF3, and FOS::JUN heterodimers.
families.short: AP-1 is the collective name for dimers of the JUN proteins (JUN, JUNB, JUND) with the FOS proteins (FOS, FOSB, FOSL1, FOSL2), together with the related basic region-leucine zipper partners ATF3, JDP2 and BATF/BATF2/BATF3. They bind the seven-base TPA response element TGA(C/G)TCA, two TGAC half-sites read one per subunit, and also the one-base-longer cyclic-AMP response element TGACGTCA. FOS and JUN were among the first proto-oncogenes described, and AP-1 activity rises within minutes of growth-factor, cytokine, ultraviolet or oxidative stimulation. The site is one of the most frequently occupied sequences in accessible chromatin, concentrated in distal enhancers, where AP-1 binding helps keep regions open for other factors. Because every member reads the same seven bases, a match names the family rather than the protein.
families.long:
## The factors

AP-1 is a dimer pool rather than a single protein. The JUN subfamily (JUN, JUNB, JUND) and the FOS subfamily (FOS, FOSB, FOSL1/FRA-1, FOSL2/FRA-2) are basic region-leucine zipper (bZIP) factors: a roughly 60-residue module in which a basic region lies along the DNA major groove and an adjacent leucine-rich heptad repeat forms a parallel two-stranded coiled coil with the partner subunit. Fos proteins barely homodimerize and need a Jun partner; Jun homodimerizes weakly and prefers Fos, a bias the c-Fos-c-Jun crystal structure traced to an asymmetric network of interhelical electrostatic contacts in the zipper [PMID:7816143]. Three further groups join the same pool and read the same site: ATF3, JDP2, and the immune bZIPs BATF, BATF2 and BATF3. JUN, JUND, FOSL1, FOSL2 and ATF3 are broadly expressed; FOS and FOSB are immediate-early genes whose transcription rises within minutes of stimulation; BATF and BATF3 are largely confined to lymphoid and dendritic lineages. Measuring DNA specificity for 102 bZIP dimers showed that about 72% of heterodimer motifs are simply the partners' half-sites joined [PMID:28186491], which is why this pool behaves as one motif.

## The motif

The classical site is the 7 bp TPA response element (TRE), TGA(C/G)TCA, written TGASTCA [PMID:3034433]. It is two TGAC half-sites in opposed orientations sharing a central base, one read by each subunit. TGACTCA and TGAGTCA are exact reverse complements, so these are not two variants but one site seen from either strand. The 8 bp cyclic-AMP response element (CRE), TGACGTCA, is the same half-site pair with one extra base between them, and Jun-, ATF3-, JDP2- and BATF-containing dimers bind it as well [PMID:1827203,28186491]. Information sits almost entirely on TGA and TCA; the central base and the flanks are weakly constrained, although an A or T immediately outside each half-site is common, giving the ATGACTCAT of many models. In the crystal structure the coiled coil is flexibly joined to the basic regions and the heterodimer does not occupy the asymmetric TGAGTCA in a unique orientation, which is the structural reason no base distinguishes the Fos half from the Jun half [PMID:7816143]. The 77 models gathered here bear this out: the JASPAR dimer matrices FOS::JUN, FOSL2::JUNB, FOSL2::JUND and BATF::JUN each have a same-family neighbour at 0.99 similarity or better. The consensus derived from these models is ATGACTCA, but the highest-information members - BATF3, BATF2, FOS, JUNB, JDP2 and ATF3 - are the 8 bp ATGACGTCAT. That split follows evidence type rather than biology: in vitro selection recovers the CRE as the higher-affinity site for these dimers, whereas ChIP-derived models recover the 7 bp TRE, which is what cells actually occupy. BATF models carry a second element, a TTTC placed two or three bases from the TRE: the AP-1-IRF composite element (AICE) through which BATF dimers recruit IRF4 or IRF8 [PMID:22983707].

## Where it acts

AP-1 sites are enriched at distal enhancers rather than in CpG-island promoters [PMID:31034924], and AP-1-like footprints are among the most frequently recovered classes in genome-wide DNase I footprint maps. The site is genuinely common: a 7-mer of this composition is expected roughly 4 x 10^5 times in 3.1 Gb of human sequence, so most matches are not functional. AP-1 occupancy is better described as collaborative than instructive: AP-1 binding raises local accessibility and licenses glucocorticoid receptor binding at shared elements [PMID:21726817], and AP-1 motifs are among the sequences that lineage-determining factors use to prime enhancers in macrophages and B cells [PMID:20513432]. Named composites include the AICE with IRF4 and IRF8, the NFAT-AP-1 composite of the IL2 and CSF2 enhancers, and glucocorticoid receptor tethering sites.

## Biology and disease

AP-1 converts short-lived signals - growth factors, cytokines, ultraviolet light, oxidative stress - into transcription, and its targets span proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, wound repair and bone remodeling. Mice lacking c-fos are osteopetrotic because osteoclasts fail to form, and have hematopoietic defects [PMID:1465144,7939685]; c-jun-null embryos die in mid-gestation with hepatic failure [PMID:8371760]. Batf3-null mice lack CD8-alpha-positive (cDC1) dendritic cells and prime cytotoxic T cells poorly [PMID:19008445]. In cancer AP-1 acts in both directions depending on tissue and member: JUN is amplified in dedifferentiated liposarcoma, FOS and FOSB are recurrently rearranged in epithelioid hemangioma, and FOSL1 is elevated in many epithelial tumors, while JUNB and JUND can be growth-suppressive.

## Reading a hit

A TGASTCA match identifies the family, not the member: nothing in the sequence separates FOS from FOSB or FOSL1/2, or JUN from JUNB or JUND, and the ATF3, JDP2 and BATF models are equally close. At seven informative bases a single occurrence in a promoter is not evidence of regulation; ask instead whether it falls in accessible chromatin in your cell type. The site is also hard to separate from its siblings. If your match is TGACGTCA, the CREB/ATF family is at least as likely, and ATF6/CREB3 if the 3-prime flank is GTGG. If GC extensions flank the core, as in TGCTGACTCAGCA, read MAF; if only the 3-prime side is GC, as in TGACTCAGC, read NFE2/BACH. ChIP-derived AP-1 models are also prone to indirect recovery: a JUN-like motif is one of a handful repeatedly enriched in ChIP-seq datasets for unrelated factors, accounting for up to 45% of peaks in some sets [PMID:25070602]. One CIS-BP entry labelled ATF3 in this family (M07822) is a CACGTG E-box whose nearest neighbours are USF motifs; treat it as out of place here.
families.caveats: An AP-1 match is one of the safest family calls in this atlas and one of the least informative member calls. All 13 proteins share the motif, so a hit licenses "an AP-1-family dimer could bind here" and nothing more; it does not say which subunits, whether the site is occupied, or whether occupancy activates or represses. The 7 bp core occurs a few hundred thousand times in the genome, so require accessibility, conservation or allelic evidence before calling a site functional. Half of the models here come from ChIP-seq, and AP-1 motifs are a well-documented contaminant of ChIP-seq peaks for unrelated factors, so an AP-1 motif under someone else's peak is not evidence that the two proteins interact.

timeline.finding: AP-1 purified from HeLa cells footprints a conserved TGACTCA in the TPA-inducible enhancers of metallothionein IIA, SV40 and collagenase, and multimerized copies of the site confer TPA inducibility.
timeline.methods: DNA-affinity purification, DNase I footprinting, in vitro transcription, reporter transfection
timeline.open: AP-1 was a 47 kDa activity, not yet a named gene product or a dimer family.

timeline.finding: Fos/Jun and ATF/CREB proteins form selective cross-family heterodimers whose DNA specificities differ from either parent, blurring the earlier one-family-one-site split between TRE and CRE.
timeline.methods: In vitro dimerization and DNA-binding assays
timeline.open: Which dimers prefer the TRE and which the CRE was not mapped systematically.

timeline.finding: Gene targeting shows the members are not redundant in vivo: c-fos-null mice are osteopetrotic with altered hematopoiesis, traced in 1994 to a block in osteoclast differentiation, and c-jun-null embryos die in mid to late gestation with impaired hepatogenesis.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockouts, bone-marrow transplantation
timeline.open: Why members that share one DNA motif have distinct knockout phenotypes was not explained by DNA specificity.

timeline.finding: The c-Fos-c-Jun bZIP heterodimer crystal structure on TGAGTCA shows each basic helix reading one half-site, a coiled coil flexibly joined to the basic regions, and no unique orientation of the heterodimer on the asymmetric site.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Genome-wide maps recast AP-1 as an enhancer factor that works collaboratively: AP-1 maintains accessibility needed for glucocorticoid receptor recruitment, and AP-1 motifs co-occur with lineage-determining factors at macrophage enhancers.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, DNase-seq
timeline.open: Whether AP-1 opens closed chromatin on its own or only maintains sites opened by others was not settled.

timeline.finding: BATF-containing AP-1 dimers bind cooperatively with IRF4 or IRF8 at AP-1-IRF composite elements (AICEs), explaining the TTTC extension seen in BATF models.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in TH17 cells, cooperative DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: A JUN-like motif is one of a few motifs repeatedly enriched in ChIP-seq peaks for unrelated factors, making up to 45% of some datasets, so an AP-1 motif under another factor's peak is not evidence of interaction.
timeline.methods: Meta-analysis of hundreds of ChIP-seq datasets
timeline.open: The proposed cohesin-associated loading-station mechanism was not tested.

timeline.finding: DNA specificity of 102 bZIP dimers: 72% of heterodimer motifs are the partners' half-sites joined, 12% are variably spaced half-sites and 16% are emergent sites not predictable from either partner.
timeline.methods: SELEX-seq-based cognate site identification, EMSA-FRET, comparison to ChIP-seq
timeline.open: How often the emergent heterodimer sites are used in cells was shown only for ATF3.

open: Why in vitro selection and ChIP-seq disagree for this family is not explained: HT-SELEX models for JUN, FOS, ATF3, JDP2 and BATF3 rank the 8 bp CRE TGACGTCA highest, while ChIP-seq models for the same proteins recover the 7 bp TRE TGASTCA, and the genomic rarity of the CpG-containing CRE, its methylation, and the cellular partner pool have not been separated as explanations.

Whether AP-1 acts as a pioneer that opens nucleosomal DNA itself, or as a collaborator that maintains accessibility at sites selected with lineage-determining factors, is not settled by the genome-wide studies cited here.

Why AP-1 motifs turn up under ChIP-seq peaks for unrelated factors is not established: genuine co-binding at shared open enhancers and a non-specific recovery mechanism (the proposed cohesin-associated loading station) predict different things, and neither has been confirmed.

Which FOS, JUN, ATF or BATF dimer occupies a given site in a given cell cannot yet be predicted, because partner choice can change specificity in vitro (the 16% of emergent heterodimer sites) and the in vivo dimer pool is rarely measured.

families.name: Anterior HOX (HOX1-8)
families.def: TAAT core with PBX/MEIS cooperativity; paralogue groups 1-8: HOXA1-A7, HOXB1-B8, HOXC4-C8, HOXD1-D8.
families.short: The 39 human HOX genes sit in four clusters and specify position along the head-to-tail axis. This family covers paralogue groups 1 to 8 - the anterior and central HOX proteins - with 75 motifs for 27 gene symbols. Their homeodomains read the generic TAAT core, written TAATTA for groups 1-3 and shifting to TAATGA or TAATGG for groups 4-8. On their own these proteins are essentially interchangeable in vitro: no matrix separates HOXA5 from HOXB5 or HOXC6. Real sequence discrimination appears only in complex with the TALE cofactors PBX and MEIS, which build a bipartite site, ATGATTNATNN, whose HOX half-site shifts stepwise along the cluster.
families.long:
## The factors

HOXA1-A7, HOXB1-B8, HOXC4-C8 and HOXD1-D8 make up this family, together with unassigned HOXA/HOXB/HOXC/HOXD archetypes: 27 symbols, 75 motifs. Each protein is a single homeodomain with short flanking regions, expressed in a spatially restricted, colinear pattern - genes at the 3' end of a cluster are expressed earliest and most anteriorly - and controlled in part by retinoic acid. Immediately N-terminal to the homeodomain most of them carry a hexapeptide motif (IYPWMK and variants) that docks into a pocket of the TALE-class cofactor PBX1-4 (extradenticle in Drosophila); MEIS1-3 and PKNOX1/2 form the second TALE arm. Anterior HOX proteins bind cooperatively with PBX in a hexapeptide-dependent manner, shown for HOXB4, HOXB6 and HOXB7 but not for HOXA10, and grafting the HOXB7 hexapeptide onto HOXA10 confers cooperativity [PMID:7729685].

## The motif

The invariant feature is the four-base core 5'-TAAT-3'. When the DNA preferences of four Drosophila HOM proteins were compared directly, Ultrabithorax, Antennapedia and Deformed all preferred TAAT while Abdominal-B preferred TTAT, and Ubx and Antp were indistinguishable outside the core; the residues responsible lie in the homeodomain N-terminal arm, not at position 50 (all HOX proteins have glutamine there) [PMID:7914870].

Within this family the bases 3' of the core drift with cluster position. JASPAR and HOCOMOCO in vitro models give CTAATTAC for groups 1-3 (HOXA1, HOXA2, HOXB1, HOXB2, HOXD1, HOXD3), TTAATGA for groups 4-5 (HOXA4, HOXB4, HOXC4, HOXD4, HOXA5) and TAATGG/TAATTG for groups 6-8 (HOXA6, HOXA7, HOXB8, HOXD8). The family medoid is HOXA6 (HOCOMOCO HXA6.H14CORE.0.SM.B) and its trimmed consensus is TAATGA, which is why the data consensus for the family reads TAATGA rather than the TAATTA usually quoted for anterior HOX; both are the same 6-bp window with a different 3' base, and cohesion across the family is 0.87.

The cofactor site is where specificity actually lives. Binding-site selection with PBX-HOX heterodimers returned the bipartite sequence 5'-ATGATTNATNN-3', with PBX contacting ATGAT and HOX the more variable TNATNN half; across HOXB1 to HOXB9 and HOXA10 the HOX half-site core shifts stepwise from TTAT to TGAT in an order that matches gene position in the cluster [PMID:8657149]. Crystal structures explain both halves: the HoxB1-Pbx1-DNA complex at 2.35 A shows the hexapeptide bound in a pocket created by the three-residue TALE insertion [PMID:10052460], and the HoxA9-Pbx1 structure shows that N-terminal arm residues determine sequence preference indirectly, without contacting bases [PMID:12923056]. SELEX-seq on all eight Drosophila Hox proteins with Exd showed the same principle quantitatively: latent specificity differences emerge only in the complex, group into three classes that follow colinearity, and correspond to differences in minor-groove shape [PMID:22153072], the same readout mechanism worked out structurally for Sex combs reduced [PMID:17981120].

## Where it acts

Anterior HOX sites are in embryonic distal enhancers, not CpG-island promoters, and in vivo occupancy tracks accessible, PBX/MEIS-marked regions. Counting matters: TAATTA is expected on the order of two million times in 3.1 Gb, while the ATGATTNAT composite is expected a few hundred thousand times - still common, but two orders of magnitude more specific. Two ChIP-derived models in this family make the point directly: HOXB4 and HOXB7 ChIP-seq models read TGATTGATG, the PBX-HOX composite, while HT-SELEX models for the same two proteins read TTAATGA. Archetype analysis of DNase footprints likewise puts a HOXB/PBX composite (TTGATTAAT) in this family.

## Biology and disease

Anterior HOX genes set segmental identity in the hindbrain, branchial arches and axial skeleton. Hoxa2 loss in mouse produces a homeotic transformation of the second branchial arch toward first-arch identity [PMID:7903601]. In humans, homozygous HOXA1 loss of function causes brainstem malformation with inner-ear, cardiovascular and cognitive involvement [PMID:16155570], and a HOXB1 founder mutation causes hereditary congenital facial palsy, reproducing the Hoxb1 null mouse phenotype [PMID:22770981]. Anterior HOX genes are also downstream of retinoic acid signaling in the hindbrain, and PBX1 itself is oncogenic as the E2A-PBX1 fusion in acute lymphoblastic leukemia [PMID:7729685].

## Reading a hit

A bare TAAT or TAATTA hit is close to meaningless. It does not identify a HOX protein, does not distinguish anterior HOX from the large Q50 homeodomain family that reads the same core, and occurs so often that genome-wide scans return millions of matches. The only sequence configuration with real discriminating power is the PBX composite ATGATTNATNN, and even that identifies a class, not a paralogue [PMID:22153072,27066866]. Evidence quality is good for the in vitro claim - 21 of 23 HOCOMOCO models here have HT-SELEX support - but ChIP-derived HOX motifs should be assumed to be cofactor composites or, worse, unrelated: in a direct comparison the most enriched motif in HOXA2 ChIP-seq peaks was not bound by HOXA2 in vitro at all [PMID:34940502]. Three flagged members are informative rather than wrong: a HOXB2::ELK1 model is a measured heterodimer site dominated by its ETS half, two footprint archetypes labelled HOXC/HOXD and HOXC/HOXA are posterior-type (TTTTATTG), and an archetype labelled HOXB/BARHL is plain TAATTA.
families.caveats: Treat a match as "anterior/central HOX-type TAAT site" at best. The 27 gene symbols here are not separable by matrix, and the core is shared with the ~200-member Q50 homeodomain class, so a TAATTA hit does not even establish that a HOX protein is involved. Expect millions of genome-wide matches; require the PBX composite ATGATTNATNN, expression data and accessibility before treating a site as HOX-bound. ChIP-derived models for these factors are suspect: the two ChIP-only HOCOMOCO models in this family are PBX-HOX composites rather than HOX sites, and published comparisons show the top motif in HOXA2 peaks is not one HOXA2 binds in vitro. Three CIS-BP entries come from mouse orthologues.

timeline.finding: Site selection with PBX-HOX heterodimers defines the bipartite site ATGATTNATNN, PBX on ATGAT and HOX on TNATNN; the HOX half-site core shifts stepwise from TTAT to TGAT across HOXB1-B9 and HOXA10 in cluster order, through the HOX N-terminal arm. This is the first sequence readout that tracks colinearity.

HOX proteins look interchangeable as monomers but not in complex.
timeline.methods: SELEX-seq, DNA-shape prediction
timeline.open: Whether vertebrate HOX-PBX-MEIS complexes separate paralogues within a group, not only classes.

timeline.finding: The most enriched motif in HOXA2 ChIP-seq peaks is one HOXA2 does not bind in vitro, so a motif learned from HOX ChIP data need not be a HOX site.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq motif enrichment, in vitro binding assays

open: Whether members of one anterior paralogue group (for example HOXA4, HOXB4, HOXC4 and HOXD4) differ in DNA preference at all is unresolved: the cofactor studies separate classes along the cluster, not members of one group, and the in vitro models in this family cannot be told apart.

How much of in vivo target choice is DNA readout is unsettled. PBX-HOX complexes show colinear sequence preferences in vitro, yet the top motif in HOXA2 ChIP-seq peaks is not bound by HOXA2, which suggests that accessibility and partner proteins select many occupied sites.

Whether the 3' drift in human monomer models (TAATTA for groups 1-3, TAATGA or TAATGG for groups 4-8) matters in vivo has not been tested directly. The alternative is that it is overridden by the PBX composite, where the HOX half-site follows its own TTAT-to-TGAT progression.

How much the hexapeptide matters in vivo is debated: structures and in vitro binding make it the main PBX contact, while the genetic work reviewed by Merabet and Mann describes HOX-TALE interactions that persist without it in some contexts.

families.name: Posterior HOX (HOX9-13, AbdB-like)
families.def: TTTTATKR / TTAT core preferred by paralogue groups 9-13: HOXA9-A13, HOXB9, HOXB13, HOXC9-C13, HOXD9-D13.
families.short: HOX paralogue groups 9 to 13 - the Abdominal-B-like or posterior HOX proteins - read a different core from the rest of the homeodomain superfamily. Where most homeodomains require TAAT, these prefer TTAT, and their in vitro sites extend to TTTTACGAC (equivalently GTCGTAAAA on the opposite strand). This family collects 63 motifs for the 16 posterior HOX genes: HOXA9-A13, HOXB9, HOXB13, HOXC9-C13 and HOXD9-D13. The longer, AT-rich site makes these motifs considerably rarer and more informative than a bare TAAT hit, but the 16 paralogues remain indistinguishable from each other. Groups 9-10 partner with PBX, groups 11-13 with MEIS instead.
families.long:
## The factors

Sixteen genes, 63 motifs: HOXA9, HOXA10, HOXA11, HOXA13, HOXB9, HOXB13, HOXC9-C13 and HOXD9-D13. These are the 5' genes of each HOX cluster, expressed latest and most posteriorly under colinearity, and they pattern the posterior trunk, the limb autopod and the urogenital tract; HOXA9 and HOXA10 are also central to hematopoietic progenitor regulation.

Cofactor usage splits the group. Paralogues 9 and 10 still form cooperative complexes with the TALE protein PBX1, although HOXA10 lacks a canonical hexapeptide and uses a tryptophan-containing motif instead [PMID:8657149,9079637]. Paralogues 11, 12 and 13 do not bind PBX1a [PMID:9079637] and instead heterodimerize with MEIS1, which was identified as a common retroviral integration site in myeloid leukemias where Hoxa9 is co-activated; the heterodimer occupies a composite target with a MEIS1 half-site (TGACAG) adjacent to an Abd-B-like HOX site (TTTTACGAC) [PMID:9343407], and HOXA9 additionally forms trimeric complexes with PBX2 and MEIS1 in myeloid cells [PMID:10082572].

## The motif

The defining difference is the core. In a direct comparison of four Drosophila HOM proteins, Abdominal-B bound a site with an unusual TTAT core while Ultrabithorax, Antennapedia and Deformed all preferred TAAT; the responsible residues lie in the homeodomain N-terminal arm, and the same arm differences are conserved in the vertebrate Abd-B-like proteins [PMID:7914870]. Concretely, posterior HOX homeodomains begin GRKKRVPYTK or TRKKRCPYTK where anterior ones begin GKRARTAYTR or RKRGRQTYTR. Position 50 is glutamine throughout, so this split is not a position-50 effect; the HoxA9-Pbx1 crystal structure showed directly that these arm residues set specificity without contacting bases, through DNA conformation, and that the posterior hexapeptide adopts a different conformation from the anterior one [PMID:12923056].

In vitro models across the family converge tightly. HOCOMOCO HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models for HOXD9, HOXA10, HOXA11, HOXC9-C12 and HOXD10-D12 read TTTTACGAC, with the group-13 genes (HOXA13, HOXB13, HOXC13, HOXD13) shifting the last base to give TTTACGAG. CIS-BP and JASPAR models for several of the same genes report the variant TTTTATTGC/TTTTATTGG, and the family medoid is HOXC9 (HOCOMOCO HXC9.H14CORE.1.S.C) at TTTATGAC. A degenerate rendering of the same core is often written TTTTATKR, including in this atlas's own family definition; it describes the 5'-TTTAT-3' core with the 3' bases left ambiguous and is not a separate site. Cohesion is 0.89, among the highest of the homeodomain families here, and no member is flagged as belonging elsewhere.

Paralogues are not separable. Nothing in these matrices distinguishes HOXA9 from HOXD9, and the only within-family distinction with support is group 13 versus groups 9-12. ChIP-derived models look different from the in vitro ones because they capture the cofactor composite: HOXA9, HOXC9 and HOXC10 ChIP models read TGATTTATGG, that is, the PBX half-site ATGAT followed by a posterior TTAT half-site, consistent with the finding that within the PBX composite the HOX half-site core shifts stepwise from TTAT to TGAT along the cluster [PMID:8657149].

## Where it acts

Posterior HOX sites are in distal developmental enhancers, prominently in the limb autopod regulatory landscape 5' of HOXD and in hematopoietic progenitor enhancers. Unlike TAATTA, the site is genuinely rare: at human base composition the 9-mer TTTTACGAC is expected only a few tens of thousands of times in 3.1 Gb, so a strong full-length match is worth taking seriously. Co-occurring motifs are the informative context - MEIS (TGACAG) for groups 11-13 and PBX (ATGAT) for groups 9-10 [PMID:9079637,9343407] - and in leukemia HOXA9 sites overlap extensively with MEIS1 occupancy [PMID:22072553].

## Biology and disease

Human posterior HOX mutations produce distinctive limb and urogenital phenotypes. HOXD13 polyalanine expansion causes synpolydactyly [PMID:8614804]; HOXA13 mutation causes hand-foot-genital syndrome [PMID:9020844]; HOXA11 mutation causes amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with radioulnar synostosis [PMID:11101832]. HOXB13 carries the recurrent germline G84E variant that raises prostate cancer risk [PMID:22236224]. In leukemia, the NUP98-HOXA9 fusion arising from t(7;11)(p15;p15) drives myeloid transformation, and deregulation of the HOXA9/MEIS1 axis is the shared downstream program of MLL-rearranged and NPM1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia, making it an active therapeutic target [PMID:27258906].

## Reading a hit

A full TTTTACGAC or TTTTATTG match is one of the more informative homeodomain hits available, because the site is long and rare. What it does not do is name a protein: all 16 posterior HOX genes share it, and a hit should be reported as a posterior/Abd-B-like HOX site. Two further practical points. First, matches truncated to TTTAT are no more specific than a generic AT-rich homeodomain hit and should not be counted. Second, five of the 30 HOCOMOCO models in this family are ChIP-only and four more combine ChIP with SELEX; the ChIP-derived versions are PBX-HOX composites (TGATTTATGG) rather than HOX monomer sites, so scanning with them tests for the composite element, not for the HOX protein. One JASPAR entry here, HOXD12::ELK1, is a measured heterodimer motif whose information is dominated by the ETS half-site and will match ETS-driven promoters.
families.caveats: Better than most homeodomain families, but still a class-level call. All 16 posterior HOX paralogues share one motif, so report a hit as "Abd-B-like/posterior HOX", never as HOXA9 or HOXD13. The strength of the call depends on match length: the full 9-mer TTTTACGAC is expected only tens of thousands of times genome-wide and is meaningful, whereas a TTTAT-only match is an ordinary AT-rich homeodomain hit. Five of 30 HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only and read the PBX-HOX composite TGATTTATGG rather than the monomer site; scanning with these tests for the composite element. The HOXD12::ELK1 entry is a heterodimer motif dominated by its ETS half.

timeline.finding: Abdominal-B, the Drosophila founder of the posterior group, prefers a TTAT core where Ultrabithorax, Antennapedia and Deformed prefer TAAT. N-terminal arm residues are responsible, and the differing arm residues are conserved in the vertebrate Abd-B-like HOX proteins.
