timeline.finding: Binding-site selection with a purified c-Myc bHLH-LZ fragment identifies CACGTG as the first sequence-specific MYC site.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection (SAAB imprinting)
timeline.open: MYC alone bound DNA poorly; the partner that makes binding efficient was not yet known.

timeline.finding: MAX is identified as the bHLH-LZ partner of MYC, MYCN and MYCL; the MYC-MAX heterodimer binds the E-box under conditions where neither protein binds alone.
timeline.methods: cDNA expression-library screen, protein interaction assays, EMSA

timeline.finding: MAD (MXD1) heterodimerizes with MAX on the same site and antagonizes MYC, turning MAX into the hub of an activator-repressor network.
timeline.methods: Expression-library screen, EMSA, transactivation assays
timeline.open: How a shared site could give opposite outcomes depending on the MAX partner.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the MAX bHLH-LZ homodimer on CACGTG defines the parallel four-helix-bundle fold and the basic-region contacts to each half-site.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography (2.9 Å)

timeline.finding: Structures of MYC-MAX and MAD-MAX on CACGTG show the same DNA contacts as MAX-MAX; partner choice is set by the leucine zipper, so activator and repressor dimers read one site.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography (1.9-2.0 Å)

timeline.finding: In cells, MYC occupies a high-affinity class of CpG-island promoter E-boxes regardless of its level and spreads to low-affinity and non-E-box sites when overexpressed; genome-wide mapping in B cells then places most of >4,000 bound loci at CpG-island promoters.
timeline.methods: Quantitative ChIP; ChIP-PET
timeline.open: Whether occupancy at open promoters reflects E-box recognition or non-specific DNA binding.

timeline.finding: Amplifier model: at high levels MYC accumulates at essentially all active promoters and raises the output of the existing expression program rather than switching on a new gene set.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, RNA-seq with per-cell normalization
timeline.open: Direct and indirect effects of MYC on RNA output were not separated.

timeline.finding: The amplifier and E-box-driven views are both revised: promoter invasion and RNA amplification prove separable, with MYC directly activating and repressing discrete gene sets, and MYC-MAX genomic occupancy tracks Pol II more closely than E-boxes despite strong in vitro 8-mer preferences.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and expression profiling in lymphomagenesis; universal PBM; ChIP-seq meta-analysis
timeline.open: How much of MYC's effect at a given promoter depends on contacting an E-box.

open: Whether elevated MYC uniformly amplifies all active genes or activates and represses discrete gene sets is unresolved: studies in lymphocytes, ES cells and tumour cells support amplification, while lymphoma and fibroblast studies that separate direct from indirect effects support selective regulation.

How far the E-box directs MYC occupancy is disputed: MYC-MAX shows strong CACGTG and flanking 8-mer preferences in vitro, but genome-wide occupancy follows promoter-proximal Pol II and CpG-island accessibility more closely than E-box presence.

Two database models disagree with the canonical CACGTG: the JASPAR MXI1 model (MA1108.3) reads CACATG and a methyl-HT-SELEX HOCOMOCO MYCN model reads aCGCGCgc; whether these are genuine secondary specificities or assay artifacts has not been established.

families.name: NFAT
families.def: GGAAA core; NFATC1-4 (Rel-homology) and NFAT5/TonEBP.
aka: nuclear factor of activated T cells
families.short: NFAT sites are read by five proteins with a Rel-homology DNA-binding domain: the calcineurin-regulated NFATC1, NFATC2, NFATC3 and NFATC4, plus the structurally distinct, calcium-independent NFAT5 (TonEBP). Unlike NF-kB, the calcineurin-dependent NFATs bind as monomers to a short GGAAA core, usually written TGGAAA and only about six informative bases long. Because that is too little information to specify a site on its own, NFATs typically work in composite elements, most famously the NFAT-AP1 element of the interleukin-2 promoter, where NFAT and a Fos-Jun dimer touch each other on adjacent DNA. NFAT activity is controlled by dephosphorylation and nuclear import, which is why cyclosporin A and tacrolimus, which inhibit calcineurin, are immunosuppressive.
families.long:
## The factors

Five human proteins carry an NFAT DNA-binding domain. NFATC1 (NFAT2), NFATC2 (NFAT1), NFATC3 (NFAT4) and NFATC4 (NFAT3) share a Rel-homology region related to that of NF-kB, preceded by a long regulatory domain packed with serine-rich motifs and SP boxes. In a resting cell that domain is heavily phosphorylated and the protein is cytoplasmic; a sustained rise in cytosolic calcium activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates it and exposes a nuclear localisation signal [PMID:8397339,12975316]. Nuclear export kinases such as GSK3, CK1 and DYRK reverse this, so NFAT shuttles continuously and its nuclear concentration tracks calcium in near-real time [PMID:12975316]. NFATC1 and NFATC2 dominate in lymphocytes, NFATC3 in thymocytes, NFATC4 in heart, skeletal muscle and brain [PMID:9143705]. NFAT5 (TonEBP) is the outlier: it keeps the Rel-homology fold but lacks the calcineurin-docking regulatory domain, is activated by hypertonicity rather than calcium [PMID:10051678], and binds DNA as an obligate homodimer that completely encircles the double helix [PMID:11780147]. That structural work also made the family's relationship to NF-kB explicit, since DNA-bound NFAT5 adopts an NF-kB-like arrangement [PMID:11780147].

## The motif

The core is GGAAA, normally written with its 5' T as TGGAAA, and the databases converge on a very short model: the representative in vitro-supported HOCOMOCO entry is ATGGAAAAT, of whose nine positions about six carry real information. The Rel-homology domain contacts the GGAA bases through basic residues in the equivalent of NF-kB's L1 loop [PMID:9510247], but a monomer covers only one half-site's worth of DNA, so total specificity is low - TGGAAA occurs roughly every 2 kb in random sequence. Two features add length in practice. First, many NFAT models in these databases are two half-sites in opposed orientation (for example TTTCCATGGAAA, or TTTCCNNTAACGGAAAA), reflecting genuine NFAT dimers on pseudo-palindromic, kB-like sites; the HIV-1 LTR tandem kB element is the structural example [PMID:12949493,18462673]. Second, the classic arrangement is the NFAT-AP1 composite element of the interleukin-2 distal antigen-receptor response element, where NFAT and Fos-Jun bind adjacent sites and form a continuous protein-DNA interface across 15 bp [PMID:9510247]. That partnership leaves a visible mark on the motif collections: the ChIP-derived NFATC1 and NFATC2 models here read TGGAAAAANTGAGTCA - the NFAT core spliced to a canonical AP-1 site, which is a property of the element, not of the protein. NFAT5 differs slightly, preferring a TonE-like TGGAAANNYNY, but not enough to separate it from NFATC1-4 by score. Within NFATC1-4 there is no usable discrimination at all: family cohesion is 0.87 and several members' models are effectively identical.

## Where it acts

NFAT sites are enhancer elements far more often than promoter elements, and they are not CpG-island features. Occupancy is strongly cell-type restricted because it depends both on calcium signalling and on chromatin a lineage factor has already opened; in T cells the relevant regions are co-occupied by AP-1, and frequently by RUNX1, ETS1, GATA3 or TBX21 depending on the subset. Composite elements with recognised names include the interleukin-2 ARRE-2 (NFAT-AP1) [PMID:7565783,9510247] and the tandem kB/NFAT element of the HIV-1 long terminal repeat, which NFAT and NF-kB can each occupy [PMID:12949493]. Cooperation with AP-1 is not optional for much of the programme: NFAT mutants that cannot recruit Fos and Jun activate a different, largely non-overlapping set of genes [PMID:10970869].

## Biology and disease

The calcineurin-NFAT axis is the main transcriptional output of antigen-receptor signalling, driving interleukin-2, interleukin-4, interferon-gamma, CD40LG and FASLG in T cells [PMID:9143705,15928679], and contributing to the anergy programme when NFAT acts without AP-1 [PMID:15928679]. Beyond immunity, NFATC1 is required for osteoclast differentiation downstream of RANK and for heart valve development, and NFATC3 and NFATC4 contribute to cardiac hypertrophy [PMID:12975316]. The pathway is a first-line drug target: cyclosporin A and tacrolimus block calcineurin and are standard immunosuppressants in transplantation, and their renal and neurological toxicity reflects how broadly the pathway is used [PMID:12975316]. NFAT5-null mice show that the lymphoid microenvironment is osmotically stressful, with impaired lymphocyte function and renal medullary defects [PMID:15247420], and NFAT5 drives osmolyte-transporter genes under hypertonic conditions [PMID:10051678].

## Reading a hit

A bare TGGAAA match is weak evidence. With six informative positions the site occurs hundreds of thousands of times in the human genome, so one match carries essentially no information unless supported by clustering, conservation, or an adjacent partner site. Look for composites: a TGGAAA within about 15 bp of a TGASTCA is far more convincing than either alone, and tandem or inverted GGAAA repeats indicate the dimeric mode. A hit cannot distinguish NFATC1 from NFATC2, NFATC3 or NFATC4, and only marginally separates NFAT5, so report it as NFAT-family. Check the evidence code before trusting a model: HOCOMOCO entries with S or M in the fourth field come from HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX and are statements about the protein, whereas the ChIP-only NFATC1 and NFATC2 models here are demonstrably contaminated by the composite element's AP-1 site - scan with those and you are scoring AP-1 as much as NFAT. Note also that the Vierstra archetype AC0682 is labelled NFATC/ZNF because unrelated zinc-finger motifs clustered with it, not because those factors share a specificity.
families.caveats: This is a short, low-information motif and that dominates everything else. Six informative bases make chance matches overwhelmingly more common than real sites, so an isolated TGGAAA should not be reported as an NFAT site; require a composite (usually AP-1 within about 15 bp), a tandem or inverted pair, or independent occupancy data. No model separates NFATC1-4, and NFAT5 only weakly, so a hit is family-level. Several ChIP-derived NFATC1 and NFATC2 models in these databases include the AP-1 TGAGTCA alongside the NFAT core: that is the partner's motif riding along, and it inflates apparent specificity. Finally, occupancy requires calcium signalling, so matches in an unstimulated cell are mostly inactive.

timeline.finding: NFAT-1 is identified as a complex, formed only with nuclear extracts of activated T cells, that binds a functional sequence of the interleukin-2 enhancer and appears minutes before IL-2 transcription; a similar activity binds the HIV-1 LTR.
timeline.methods: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays; reporter transfection
timeline.open: The proteins in the complex, including whether AP-1 was part of it, were unknown.

timeline.finding: NFATp is shown to be a substrate of the calcium-activated phosphatase calcineurin and to bind DNA together with Fos and Jun, linking calcium signalling to the NFAT-AP-1 composite site.
timeline.methods: Protein purification, dephosphorylation and DNA-binding assays
timeline.open: The DNA-binding domain and its relationship to other families had not been defined.

timeline.finding: The structure of the NFAT, Fos and Jun DNA-binding domains on the IL-2 distal ARRE shows an extended NFAT-AP-1 interface and a continuous groove recognizing 15 bp, explaining why the composite element binds cooperatively.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How NFAT binds sites that have no adjacent AP-1 site, and whether it can dimerize, were not addressed.

timeline.finding: TonEBP (NFAT5) is cloned as a Rel-like protein that binds the tonicity-responsive enhancer and activates transcription in response to hypertonicity, extending the family beyond calcium signalling.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, DNA-binding and reporter assays

timeline.finding: NFAT1 mutants that bind DNA normally but cannot recruit Fos-Jun still induce TNF and IL-13 but not IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, GM-CSF, MIP1a or Fas ligand, separating AP-1-dependent and AP-1-independent NFAT programmes in one cell type.
timeline.methods: Mutant-protein expression in T cells; mRNA and promoter assays

timeline.finding: DNA-bound TonEBP/NFAT5 is an obligate dimer that adopts an NF-kB-like structure and completely encircles its DNA target, giving a direct structural link between the NFAT and NF-kB families.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; DNA-binding kinetics

timeline.finding: NFAT1 binds the HIV-1 LTR kB site cooperatively as a dimer whose asymmetric interface differs from the symmetric Rel dimer, showing that the calcium-regulated NFATs, previously viewed as monomeric binders, can also occupy kB-like sites as dimers.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How often NFAT dimers form on genomic sites, as opposed to viral and model elements.

open: Whether NFAT prefers a methylated CpG immediately 5' of its core is unresolved: the literature and ChIP-derived models read TGGAAA, but several HOCOMOCO models built from methyl-HT-SELEX for NFATC1-4 and NFAT5 read ACGGAAA, consistent with a 5-methylcytosine standing in for the thymine, and whether methylated CGGAAA sites are bound in cells has not been shown in the work cited here.

Which binding mode NFAT uses at a given genomic site - a monomer on a lone GGAAA, a cooperative complex with Fos-Jun, or a dimer on a kB-like site - cannot be predicted from sequence: all three are structurally established, but their genome-wide shares are unknown.

families.name: Divergent forkhead sites (FOXP dimeric / FHL)
families.def: Forkhead factors whose preferred site is not the canonical RYAAAYA: FOXP1-4 dimeric TGTTTAC repeats, and the alternate FHL/GACGC site used by FOXN1/N4 and bispecifically by FOXN2/N3, FOXJ2/J3.
families.short: This entry collects the forkhead factors whose preferred site is not the ordinary RYAAAYA element. Two things are going on. FOXN1 and FOXN4 read a completely unrelated five-base sequence, GACGC, called the forkhead-like or FHL motif, using the same recognition helix in a shifted register; FOXN2, FOXN3, FOXJ2 and FOXJ3 are bispecific and bind both FHL and canonical sites. Separately, the FOXP proteins (FOXP1-4) are the only forkheads that can form a domain-swapped dimer, and their highest-information models are a head-to-head pair of forkhead half-sites rather than a single one. The factors matter clinically: FOXN1 loss causes human athymic immunodeficiency, FOXP2 a speech disorder, and FOXP3 the autoimmune syndrome IPEX.
families.long:
## The factors

Seven of the human forkhead proteins sit here. FOXN1 is restricted to thymic epithelium and skin
keratinocytes; FOXN4 to retinal and spinal neural progenitors; FOXN2, FOXN3, FOXJ2 and FOXJ3 are
broadly expressed. FOXP1, FOXP2 and FOXP4 are expressed in brain, lung, heart and lymphocytes,
and FOXP3 almost only in regulatory T cells. All carry the same ~100-residue winged-helix domain
as the rest of the family - three alpha-helices on a small beta-sheet, with wing 1 and wing 2
gripping the backbone - so nothing about the fold predicts their unusual specificity. What
distinguishes the FOXP subfamily structurally is a single substitution: a proline conserved in
other FOX proteins is an alanine in FOXP1-4, which allows the domain to swap helices with a
second copy of itself [PMID:16407075]. In the FOXP2 and FOXP3 crystal structures the swapped dimer is real, and
in the FOXP3 ternary complex with NFAT1 on the interleukin-2 promoter it bridges two separate
DNA duplexes rather than two half-sites on one [PMID:16407075,21458306]. IPEX-causing FOXP3 mutations map either to the
DNA-binding surface or to this dimer interface [PMID:16407075], and interface mutants bind DNA normally but
cannot suppress T cell activation [PMID:21458306].

## The motif

There is no single consensus for this family, which is why one is not given. The FHL site is
GACGC, five bases with no resemblance to RYAAAYA [PMID:9108066,23836653]. The FOXN1 co-crystal structure at 1.6 A shows
why the same protein can read either: the recognition helix sits in the major groove in both
cases, but the FKH and FHL sequences are contacted in two distinct modes with partially
different registers, using a mixture of direct and water-mediated hydrogen bonds, and a single
alternative side-chain rotamer in the recognition helix is a major determinant of which mode is
used [PMID:31914405]. The FoxN3 structures make the same point from the other side: FoxN3 adopts essentially one
conformation on both sites and uses the same amino acids to touch different bases, while the DNA
shape differs between the two complexes [PMID:30826165]. Bispecificity of this kind has arisen repeatedly and
independently in forkhead evolution and is generally not explained by changes in the known
specificity-determining residues [PMID:23836653]. The FOXP side of the family looks different again. Most FOXP
models here are ordinary canonical sites (JASPAR FOXP1, FOXP2, FOXP3, FOXP4 all GTAAACA;
HOCOMOCO FOXP1 TGTTTACT), but the highest-information models, CIS-BP FOXP3 (25.6 bits) and
Vierstra AC0285 (24.8 bits), are ATTTGTCATACAAAT: two RYAAAYA half-sites in their ACAAAT flavor,
facing each other, with a three-base spacer. Whether that arrangement is bound by the domain-
swapped dimer or by two independent monomers is not settled by the available structures, which
show the swapped dimer holding two different DNA molecules [PMID:16407075,21458306].

## Where it acts

Because GACGC is only five bases, it is expected several million times in the genome and carries
almost no positional information on its own; FOXN1 needs its C-terminal region for high-affinity
binding, and its affinity drops on DNA containing 5-methylcytosine [PMID:31914405], so methylation state and
flanking sequence matter more here than for canonical forkhead sites. FOXN1 acts at thymic
epithelial enhancers controlling the genes that make the thymus permissive for T cell
development, and at hair keratin genes in skin. FOXP1 and FOXP2 occupy large numbers of distal
sites in brain and lymphoid cells, often with co-repressors of the NuRD and CtBP families rather
than with a named composite element; FOXP3 works in a multiprotein complex on T cell enhancers
together with NFAT, RUNX1 and ETS factors, which is how the IL2 promoter site was solved [PMID:21458306]. JASPAR
contains a CAP-SELEX composite, FOXJ2::ELF1, in which most of the information is the ETS GGAA
core [PMID:26550823].

## Biology and disease

FOXN1 null mice and rats are the classical nude strains: no thymus, no hair. Human FOXN1
mutations produce the same picture - congenital alopecia, nail dystrophy and severe T cell
deficiency - and the human nude phenotype was the first clinical description of this [PMID:10206641]. FOXP2 was
identified through a family with a severe developmental speech and language disorder segregating
with a forkhead-domain mutation [PMID:11586359]. FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX (immune dysregulation,
polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked) [PMID:11137993], and FOXP3 is the lineage-defining factor of
regulatory T cells. FOXP1 haploinsufficiency causes intellectual disability with autistic
features, and FOXP1 is recurrently translocated and overexpressed in diffuse large B-cell
lymphoma and MALT lymphoma. FOXN3 and FOXJ3 have weaker phenotypes; FOXN4 is required for
retinal amacrine and horizontal cell production.

## Reading a hit

A GACGC match alone means very little: five bases, no degeneracy assumed, and no way to tell
FOXN1 from FOXN4 or from a bispecific FOXN2/FOXN3 or FOXJ2/FOXJ3. Use it only in combination
with expression evidence or with a longer model that includes the flanks. A canonical RYAAAYA
match cannot be assigned to this family at all, since FOXP1-4, FOXJ2, FOXJ3, FOXN2 and FOXN3 all
also read the ordinary site and are indistinguishable there from the 40-odd other forkheads. The
dimeric ATTTGTCATACAAAT model is specific enough to be worth something, but it appears in only
two of the 29 models here and is labelled FOXP3 in one database and simply "FOXP" in the other.
HOCOMOCO contains no FOXN model at all; the two CIS-BP FOXN entries (FOXN1, 3.3 bits; FOXN4, 5.2
bits) are inferred from mouse proteins at 99% and 95% DNA-binding-domain identity. Treat
FOXJ2::ELF1 as an ETS motif: its nearest neighbors across all four databases are ETV-family
motifs, not forkhead ones.
families.caveats: Moderate confidence in the family as a concept, low confidence in member assignment. The FHL site GACGC is too short to be informative alone and is not distinguishable between FOXN1, FOXN4 and the bispecific FOXN2/FOXN3, FOXJ2/FOXJ3 proteins. Most FOXP and FOXJ models in these databases are ordinary RYAAAYA sites, so a hit on them says "forkhead", not "divergent forkhead". Only two models capture the FOXP head-to-head arrangement. The FOXN1 and FOXN4 CIS-BP models are inferred from mouse orthologs, and HOCOMOCO has no FOXN entry. The JASPAR FOXJ2::ELF1 composite is dominated by its ETS half and its nearest neighbors are ETS motifs.

timeline.finding: The DNA-binding domain of the nude gene product (Whn, now FOXN1) selects an 11-base consensus built around an invariant ACGC, unrelated to the forkhead sites then known; the zebrafish and amphioxus orthologues read the same sequence.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, reporter assays
timeline.open: Why a forkhead domain should read a sequence unrelated to the canonical site was unexplained.

timeline.finding: Forkhead-domain mutations in FOXP2 and FOXP3 are found to cause, respectively, a severe speech and language disorder and the IPEX autoimmune syndrome, making the FOXP subfamily clinically central.
timeline.methods: Human genetics: linkage, breakpoint mapping, mutation screening

timeline.finding: The FOXP2 forkhead domain on DNA forms a domain-swapped dimer, made possible by an alanine in place of a proline conserved in other FOX proteins; disease mutations in FOXP2 and FOXP3 map to the DNA-binding surface or to the swap interface.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Whether the swapped dimer forms in cells, and what DNA arrangement it binds, were open.

timeline.finding: In the FOXP3-NFAT1 complex on an IL2 promoter oligonucleotide, the FOXP3 swapped dimer bridges two DNA molecules; IPEX and structure-guided interface mutants keep DNA binding but lose dimerization and regulatory T cell suppressive function.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, mutagenesis, in vitro and in vivo suppression assays
timeline.open: Did not show whether the dimer can also occupy two half-sites on one duplex, as the head-to-head selection models imply.

timeline.finding: Profiling forkhead domains across the family's phylogeny shows that the FHL-type alternative specificity arose repeatedly, that some forkheads are bispecific for FKH and FHL sites, and that most specificity changes are not at the known DNA-contacting residues.
timeline.methods: Protein-binding microarrays, phylogenetic inference
timeline.open: Proposed, but did not show, that conformational rearrangement of the DNA-binding domain explains bispecificity.

timeline.finding: Co-crystal structures of the FoxN3 DNA-binding domain on an FKH site and on an FHL site show the protein in a similar conformation, using the same residues to contact different bases, while the DNA shape differs between the two complexes.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: The 1.6 A FOXN1-FHL structure indicates that FKH and FHL sites are bound in two distinct modes with partially different contact registers, with one alternative side-chain rotamer in the recognition helix as a key determinant; FOXN1 also needs its C-terminal region for high-affinity binding and binds methylated DNA poorly.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays
timeline.open: Its emphasis on register and side-chain rearrangement sits uneasily with the FoxN3 account, in which protein conformation is unchanged and DNA shape carries the difference.

open: Whether the head-to-head FOXP model ATTTGTCATACAAAT is bound by the domain-swapped dimer or by two monomers is unresolved: the FOXP2 and FOXP3 structures show the swapped dimer bridging two separate DNA molecules, whereas the selection-derived model places two half-sites on one duplex three bases apart.

How bispecific forkheads read two unrelated sites is not settled: the FoxN3 structures attribute it mainly to differences in DNA shape with an unchanged protein conformation, while the FOXN1 structure points to a shifted contact register and an alternative side-chain rotamer in the recognition helix.

Whether the bispecific factors FOXN2, FOXN3, FOXJ2 and FOXJ3 use the FHL site in cells is not established: their FHL preference rests on in vitro microarray and structural data, the only ChIP-supported model among them in the four databases (HOCOMOCO FOXJ2, grade A) is an ordinary RYAAAYA site, and HOCOMOCO has no FOXN model at all.

families.name: GLI
families.def: GACCACCCA. GLI1-3, GLI4, GLIS1-3, ZIC-adjacent sites.
families.short: GLI factors are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that read the nine-base site GACCACCCA and form the transcriptional output of the Hedgehog pathway. Humans have three canonical members: GLI1, an activator that is itself a Hedgehog target gene, and GLI2 and GLI3, which are made as full-length activators but are partially degraded into N-terminal repressors when Hedgehog signaling is off. The related GLIS1, GLIS2 and GLIS3 proteins read a close variant, GACCCCCCAC. Binding is monomeric and the informative bases are concentrated at the 3' end of the site, which fingers four and five contact directly. GLI sites control limb and neural-tube patterning, and pathway mutations cause polydactyly syndromes, basal cell carcinoma and SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma.
families.long:
## The factors

Three canonical human GLI proteins, GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3, are the vertebrate counterparts of
Drosophila Cubitus interruptus. Each carries five tandem C2H2 zinc fingers and binds DNA as a
monomer. GLI2 and GLI3 are bifunctional: an N-terminal repressor domain and a C-terminal
activation domain flank the finger array, and limited proteolysis removes the activation domain to
leave a repressor [PMID:10693759,39576500]. GLI1 lacks the N-terminal repressor region and is a dedicated activator; because
GLI1 transcription is itself induced by Hedgehog signaling, GLI1 mRNA is widely used as a pathway
readout. GLI2 and GLI3 are broadly expressed during development, whereas GLI1 accumulates only
where the pathway is active.

The GLIS subfamily, GLIS1, GLIS2 and GLIS3, is the nearest relative: Kruppel-like proteins with
five fingers whose DNA-binding domains are close enough to GLI that their motifs cluster together [PMID:14500813],
but whose expression is largely non-overlapping (GLIS3 in thyroid, pancreatic islets and kidney,
GLIS2 in kidney, GLIS1 in a restricted set of tissues and in oocytes). A fourth entry, GLI4
(ZNF767P), is annotated as a family member but the matrices assigned to it in these databases do
not resemble a GLI site; treat it separately.

## The motif

The consensus GACCACCCA was defined by selecting genomic fragments bound by recombinant GLI: the
protein protected 23-24 bases at each site, and all recovered sites contained the same nine-base
core [PMID:2105456]. The crystal structure of the five GLI fingers on a high-affinity site explains the shape of
the information content. Finger one makes no DNA contact; fingers two through five wrap into the
major groove without the strictly periodic geometry of Zif268; and fingers four and five make
extensive base contacts across a conserved nine-base-pair stretch whose conformation is
intermediate between B- and A-form DNA [PMID:8378770]. The consequence is that the 3' half of the site
(reverse-strand TGGGTGGTC) carries most of the specificity while the 5' flank is tolerant.

Systematic affinity measurements of every single substitution show a wide dynamic range [PMID:16413481], and
reporter assays with natural promoters show that many low-affinity variants still drive strong
activation at moderate GLI concentrations [PMID:20070907]. So "non-consensus" GLI sites are functional, and a
strict consensus search under-counts real elements. The GLIS paralogues prefer GACCCCCCAC, with the
central ACC replaced by CCC [PMID:23332764]; the databases keep GLI and GLIS as separate matrices, but their
cross-similarity is high enough that only strong matches can be assigned to one subfamily. The data
consensus here, GACCACCCACgdcG, is the same core with a weakly informative 3' extension.

## Where it acts

GLI binding is mostly at distal enhancers rather than core promoters, and GLI sites are not a
CpG-island feature. ChIP of GLI activators in Hedgehog-responsive mouse neural tissue recovers on
the order of a thousand high-confidence regions, enriched at known pathway components (Ptch1, Gli1,
Hhip) and at patterning genes (Foxa2, Nkx2-2), with the motif recovered de novo [PMID:17442700]. Because the
informative core is nine bases with degenerate flanks, exact matches occur tens of thousands of
times in the human genome and the great majority are never occupied. Occupancy tracks pathway
activity and chromatin: the same sequence is silent in tissue where GLI2 and GLI3 are not
stabilized. Frequent neighbors in Hedgehog-responsive enhancers include SOX2, FOXA2 and NKX
factors, and ZIC proteins, which bind an overlapping sequence and can physically associate with GLI
zinc fingers.

## Biology and disease

Hedgehog ligand binding to PTCH1 relieves inhibition of SMO, which blocks the phosphorylation of
GLI2 and GLI3 by PKA, GSK3 and CK1 and thereby blocks their processing [PMID:39576500]. In the unstimulated state
GLI3 is converted into a truncated repressor, GLI3R; in the developing limb this produces a graded
anterior-to-posterior distribution of repressor that patterns the digits [PMID:10693759]. SUFU sequesters GLI
proteins and opposes the pathway.

Gli2-null mice lack a floor plate and show reduced Shh responses [PMID:9636069]; Gli1-null mice are viable and
only reveal defects in combination with a Gli2 mutation [PMID:10725236], consistent with GLI2 being the principal
activator and GLI1 an amplifier. Truncating GLI3 mutations cause Greig cephalopolysyndactyly
syndrome, while frameshifts in the middle third of the gene, which leave a repressor-like product,
cause Pallister-Hall syndrome [PMID:20301619,15739154]. GLI1 was originally cloned as an amplified, highly expressed gene in
a human glioma [PMID:3563490], and Hedgehog-driven tumors (basal cell carcinoma, SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma)
signal through GLI even when the initiating lesion is in PTCH1 or SMO [PMID:39576500]. On the GLIS side, biallelic
GLIS3 loss causes neonatal diabetes with congenital hypothyroidism [PMID:16715098], GLIS2 (NPHP7) loss causes
nephronophthisis [PMID:17618285], and GLIS1 improves the efficiency of somatic-cell reprogramming [PMID:21654807].

## Reading a hit

A GACCACCCA match identifies the GLI/GLIS class and nothing finer. GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 have
effectively the same matrix, so no sequence argument distinguishes them; assignment to a member
comes from expression or ChIP data. More importantly, a hit does not tell you the sign of the
output, because GLI3R binds the same site as GLI2 full-length activator. With nine informative
bases the site is common enough to occur by chance in any few-kilobase window, so an isolated match
is weak evidence; conservation, open chromatin in a Hedgehog-responsive tissue, and proximity to
other pathway targets all help. Conversely, the functional importance of low-affinity variants
means absence of a consensus match does not exclude GLI regulation. In HOCOMOCO, the GLI2 and GLI3
models carry in vitro support (HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX, grade A), whereas the GLI1 model is
ChIP-only at grade C; the GLI4 entries are ChIP-only and do not look like a GLI site at all.
families.caveats: A hit tells you "GLI/GLIS", never which paralogue and never whether the factor present is an activator or the GLI3 repressor. The nine-base core occurs frequently by chance, so isolated matches carry little weight without conservation or Hedgehog-responsive chromatin. GLI and GLIS matrices differ at only one or two central positions, so weak matches cannot be assigned to a subfamily. Low-affinity, non-consensus sites are demonstrably functional, so consensus searching both over-calls inert sites and misses real ones. The GLI4/ZNF767P matrices in these databases are ChIP-derived and unlike the GLI site; the Vierstra archetype carrying that motif is named GLI but groups poorly with the rest of the family.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection from total human DNA with a recombinant GLI protein recovers three sites, each footprinted over 23-24 bases and each containing GACCACCCA.
timeline.methods: Genomic binding-site selection with PCR recovery, DNase I footprinting
timeline.open: The consensus rested on three natural sites; which positions were essential was not tested.

timeline.finding: Crystal structure of the five GLI fingers on a high-affinity site: finger 1 makes no DNA contact and fingers 4 and 5 make most base contacts across a nine-base-pair stretch, explaining why the 3' half of the site carries most of the specificity.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: A single site was solved; how variant sites are tolerated was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Hedgehog-regulated, PKA-dependent processing of GLI3 produces a repressor distributed as an anterior-posterior gradient in the limb, so the same site can receive activator or repressor input.
timeline.methods: Biochemical analysis of GLI3 processing in chick and mouse limb; human syndrome and chick talpid2 mutants
timeline.open: How an enhancer distinguishes activator from repressor bound to the same sequence.

timeline.finding: High-throughput affinity measurements for GLI1-3 across single-substitution variants of the site give a quantitative specificity model, used to predict Hedgehog-responsive enhancers genome-wide.
timeline.methods: High-throughput in vitro binding-affinity assay, computational enhancer prediction, transgenic mouse reporters
timeline.open: Many natural GLI target sites scored as low affinity, raising the question of whether they were functional.

timeline.finding: ChIP of an epitope-tagged GLI activator in differentiating mouse neural progenitors identifies direct targets, including enhancers of Nkx2-2 and Nkx2-1, confirmed in transgenic embryos.

timeline.open: Coverage was limited to candidate loci rather than the whole genome.

timeline.finding: Reporters carrying every single substitution of the site show that many low-affinity variants activate strongly at moderate GLI concentration, revising the view that only consensus GACCACCCA sites are functional.

timeline.open: Reporter assays in cultured cells do not show how affinity is used to read the Hedgehog gradient in tissue.

timeline.finding: A large HT-SELEX survey of human transcription factors gives the GLIS paralogues a GACCCCCCAC site, which differs from the GLI1-3 site GACCACCCA at the central ACC.

open: Why many functional Hedgehog-responsive enhancers use low-affinity GLI sites is unresolved: one view is that weak sites restrict the response to cells with high activator levels and so sharpen the readout of the Hedgehog gradient, the other that weak sites are simply sufficient at moderate GLI concentration and are not selected against.

Whether GLI activators and the GLI3 repressor occupy the same genomic sites in vivo, or whether some sites are read preferentially by one form, is not settled; the three proteins share one matrix in vitro, so any difference would have to come from chromatin, partners or site arrangement.

Whether GLI4 binds a GLI-type site at all is unknown: the only matrices assigned to it are ChIP-derived and share a TGGCATTCAAGGCC consensus unrelated to GACCACCCA, and a Vierstra archetype labeled GLI carries the same sequence.

families.name: PRDM
families.def: PR/SET-domain zinc fingers. PRDM1/BLIMP1 (AAAG(T/C)GAAAG), PRDM4-6, PRDM9 (recombination hotspots), PRDM10/13/14/15/16.
families.short: PRDM proteins are zinc-finger transcription factors defined by an N-terminal PR domain, a variant of the SET methyltransferase fold, followed by a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers that does the DNA binding. The family is heterogeneous and does not share one motif: each member's finger array reads its own sequence, and those sequences are unrelated to one another. The best-characterized members are PRDM1/BLIMP1, which binds an interferon-regulatory-factor-like AAAGTGAAAG site and drives plasma-cell differentiation; PRDM9, whose rapidly evolving finger array selects meiotic recombination hotspots and underlies a mouse hybrid-sterility phenotype; PRDM14, in naive pluripotency; and PRDM16, in brown adipocyte and craniofacial development. A hit labelled PRDM should be interpreted per member, never as a family-level call.
families.long:
## The factors

The PRDM proteins take their name from the PR domain, a diverged SET domain of about 130 residues,
followed by a variable number of C2H2 zinc fingers [PMID:22669819]. Humans have roughly 19 PRDM genes. This family
groups the ones for which a motif has actually been measured: PRDM1, PRDM4, PRDM5, PRDM6, PRDM9,
PRDM10, PRDM13, PRDM14, PRDM15 and PRDM16. MECOM (historically PRDM3) is kept as a separate family
here because its two zinc-finger clusters behave differently from a single array.

Only some PR domains are catalytically active. PRDM9 is a genuine histone H3 lysine-4
trimethyltransferase, first described in mouse as Meisetz, and that activity is required for meiotic
prophase [PMID:16292313]. For most other members the PR domain has no demonstrated methyltransferase activity and acts
as a protein-interaction surface; PRDM1/BLIMP1, for instance, works by recruiting histone deacetylase
and methyltransferase cofactors rather than by modifying histones itself [PMID:22669819]. Expression is mostly
restricted. PRDM1 appears in plasma cells, effector T cells, keratinocytes, primordial germ cells and
placenta; PRDM9 essentially only in meiotic germ cells; PRDM14 in embryonic stem cells and germ cells;
PRDM16 in brown and beige adipocytes, craniofacial mesenchyme and hematopoietic stem cells. Few PRDMs
are broadly expressed, so the plausible member behind a hit is usually decided by cell type rather than
by sequence.

## The motif

There is no family consensus, and the data in this atlas show that plainly: member motifs range from the
GTTTCAAG core of PRDM4, through the IRF-like AAAGTGAAAG of PRDM1, to GGTCTCTAAC for PRDM14 and G-rich
models for PRDM9 and PRDM16. Cohesion across the family is low, about 0.5, and the medoid motif
(ACTTTCACT, the PRDM1 site on the reverse strand) is simply the most central member, not a shared
element.

PRDM1/BLIMP1 is the clearest case. Its zinc fingers read an approximately 10-bp site built on a GAAAG
core; the optimal selected sequence is close to AAAGTGAAAG, which overlaps a subset of
interferon-stimulated response elements, so BLIMP1 and IRF1/IRF2 compete for the same DNA with
comparable affinities [PMID:15494505]. In vivo, several motif variants are needed to capture BLIMP1 occupancy, and
binding is sensitive to CpG methylation [PMID:20421211]. The reverse-complement rendering ACTTTCACTTT is the same site
and is what several database entries display.

PRDM9 is different in kind. Its DNA-binding module is a minisatellite-encoded tandem array of roughly a
dozen C2H2 fingers, one of the fastest-evolving coding sequences in mammals, polymorphic within humans
and between mouse strains [PMID:20044539]. Human hotspots are enriched for a degenerate 13-mer, CCNCCNTNNCCNC, which
the common human A allele recognizes [PMID:19165926,20044539]; crystal structures of the human PRDM9 finger array on DNA explain
the base contacts, and the C allele reads a different sequence [PMID:26833727]. Because the array differs between
alleles, no single PRDM9 matrix is correct for all individuals, and the JASPAR and CIS-BP PRDM9 models
are approximations of one allele's preference at best.

## Where it acts

PRDM1 sites sit in promoters of genes it represses, including IRF-dependent immune programs, in both
CpG-poor and CpG-island promoters, with the methylation-sensitive variants biased to the latter [PMID:20421211]. PRDM9
sites are the defining feature of meiotic double-strand-break hotspots: tens of thousands of them,
typically 1-2 kb wide, mostly outside promoters, and in mouse directed away from functional elements
such as transcription start sites. PRDM14 and PRDM15 sites are concentrated at enhancers and promoters
of pluripotency and signaling genes in stem cells. PRDM16 sites are found at brown-fat enhancers, where
PRDM16 acts less as an autonomous sequence reader than as a partner of adipogenic factors [PMID:18719582], which matters
for interpreting its ChIP-derived motif.

## Biology and disease

PRDM1 knockout blocks plasma-cell formation and specification of primordial germ cells; in humans PRDM1
is inactivated by mutation and deletion in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, where it behaves as a tumor
suppressor [PMID:16492805]. PRDM9-null mice are sterile with arrested meiosis [PMID:16292313]; PRDM9 allele identity changes hotspot
usage in human families [PMID:20044539]; and one PRDM9 allele is the mouse hybrid-sterility gene, with sterility
reversible by swapping the finger array [PMID:26840484]. PRDM14 loss destabilizes naive pluripotency and PRDM15 loss
does the same through WNT and MAPK-ERK targets. PRDM16 loss impairs brown-fat identity [PMID:18719582], and PRDM16 mutations found in nonsyndromic
left ventricular noncompaction and dilated cardiomyopathy were proposed to cause the cardiomyopathy of
1p36 deletion syndrome [PMID:23768516], an attribution others consider unlikely [PMID:24387995]; PRDM5 loss-of-function causes brittle cornea syndrome [PMID:21664999]; PRDM6
variants cause nonsyndromic patent ductus arteriosus [PMID:27181681]. PRDM10 and PRDM16 also appear as fusion partners
in soft-tissue tumors and leukemia.

## Reading a hit

Treat a PRDM hit as a hit on one named member. Sequence cannot tell you which PRDM bound, because the
members do not share a motif and the family label spans unrelated sites. Check which member the
underlying matrix is labelled with, then whether that member is expressed in your cell type. For PRDM1
the site is short and IRF-like, so an IRF or ISRE explanation is at least as likely as BLIMP1 unless
BLIMP1 is present [PMID:15494505,20421211]. For PRDM9 a match is meaningless outside meiotic germ cells, and allele-dependent
even there. Several PRDM entries rest on ChIP-only evidence, where the motif may belong to a partner;
the EBF-like HOCOMOCO PRDM16 model (PRD16.H14CORE.0.P.B) is one. The HOCOMOCO PRDM13 model, which
matches a SNAI-type CAGGTG E-box, is not: PRD13.H14CORE.0.PSGI.A adds HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq
to ChIP-seq at grade A, so indirect binding does not explain it. Both are flagged as inconsistent with
their labels by their nearest neighbours across databases.
families.caveats: This family has no shared motif, so a family-level hit means little; only the member-specific matrix matters. Cohesion across members is about 0.5, and two entries contradict their labels: the HOCOMOCO PRDM16 model (TCCCCTGGGA) resembles an EBF site and rests on ChIP-seq alone, where a partner motif is the simpler explanation, while the PRDM13 model (GCAGGTGG) is a SNAI-type E-box despite grade-A in vitro support, so it is either a genuine E-box-like preference or a mislabel. PRDM1 evidence is strong and includes in vitro selection, but the site overlaps IRF elements, so IRF1, IRF2 or an ISRE is a competing interpretation. PRDM9 matrices describe one allele of a polymorphic finger array and are interpretable only in meiotic germ cells. Short G-rich PRDM models match frequently by chance.

timeline.finding: PRDI-BF1, a five-zinc-finger protein, is identified as a repressor that binds the PRDI element of the human interferon-beta promoter and is proposed to act by displacing its activators.
timeline.methods: Sequence-specific binding to PRDI; cotransfection reporter assays
timeline.open: The binding site was known only as PRDI; its relation to IRF sites and to B-cell differentiation was not yet recognized.

timeline.finding: Mouse Blimp-1, the orthologue of PRDI-BF1, is cloned as a zinc-finger factor induced in, and able to drive, the maturation of B cells into immunoglobulin-secreting cells.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; transfection of B-lymphoma lines
timeline.open: Its DNA-binding specificity had not been defined.

timeline.finding: The optimal BLIMP1 site is determined and found to match the subset of IRF sites containing GAAAG; BLIMP1, IRF1 and IRF2 bind such sites with similar affinities and compete at the IFNB promoter.
timeline.methods: In vitro site selection; EMSA competition and dissociation constants; ChIP; cotransfection
timeline.open: How many genomic BLIMP1 sites are shared with IRFs was unknown.

timeline.finding: Meisetz (PRDM9) is shown to be a histone H3 lysine-4 trimethyltransferase expressed only in germ cells entering meiotic prophase; knockout mice of both sexes are sterile.
timeline.methods: Histone methyltransferase assays; gene knockout in mouse
timeline.open: What targets PRDM9 to particular sites in the genome was not addressed.

timeline.finding: A degenerate 13-mer, CCNCCNTNNCCNC, is found to recruit crossovers to at least 40% of human recombination hotspots.
timeline.methods: Population-genetic hotspot maps (HapMap Phase 2); motif enrichment
timeline.open: The protein that reads the 13-mer was unknown.

timeline.finding: PRDM9 is identified as the major determinant of hotspot location: the human consensus allele is predicted, and shown in vitro, to bind the 13-mer, and PRDM9 finger-array alleles track hotspot usage in mice and humans.
timeline.methods: Mouse strain genetics; zinc-finger recognition prediction; in vitro binding; human association
timeline.open: Because the finger array is highly polymorphic, a single matrix could describe only one allele.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide BLIMP1 promoter occupancy shows that several motif variants are needed to capture its specificity, that binding is methylation-sensitive, and that only a subset of occupied sites overlap IRF motifs.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip; motif discovery and enrichment; knock-down

timeline.finding: A crystal structure of PRDM9 allele A fingers 8-12 on hotspot DNA explains its base contacts and allele-specific affinities, and humanizing the mouse PRDM9 finger array repositions hotspots and restores fertility in sterile hybrids.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; in vitro binding of allelic variants; humanized-allele mouse genetics
timeline.open: Why symmetric binding of both homologues is needed for fertility remains mechanistically unexplained.

open: Whether PRDM16 loss causes the cardiomyopathy of 1p36 deletion syndrome is disputed: Arndt et al. (2013) mapped a minimal deletion to PRDM16 and found PRDM16 mutations in noncompaction and dilated cardiomyopathy, while de Leeuw and Houge (2014) argued that PRDM16 loss is unlikely to explain the cardiomyopathy in the deletion syndrome.

The HOCOMOCO PRDM13 model (GCAGGTGG) looks like a SNAI-type E-box, yet it carries in vitro support (HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq, grade A), so it is unresolved whether PRDM13 genuinely reads an E-box-like site or the model is mislabelled; the EBF-like PRDM16 model, by contrast, rests on ChIP-seq alone, where a partner motif is the simpler explanation.

How PRDM9 binding leads to fertile meiosis is not settled: hotspot position follows the allele's binding specificity, but in hybrid mice fertility tracks whether PRDM9 binds both homologues symmetrically, and the downstream step that requires symmetry is unknown.

Which BLIMP1 sites are direct high-affinity targets and which are competitive IRF-overlapping sites is only partly resolved: in vitro selection gives one AAAGTGAAAG-like site, while promoter occupancy needs several motif variants that differ in CpG content and methylation sensitivity.

families.name: ATF6 / CREB3 (ER stress)
families.def: ERSE / UPR elements, TGACGTGG-like. ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L1-L4, XBP1.
families.short: This group collects the endoplasmic-reticulum-tethered basic region-leucine zipper factors ATF6 and ATF6B together with the CREB3 (OASIS/Luman) family - CREB3, CREB3L1, CREB3L2, CREB3L3 and CREB3L4 - and XBP1. All are made as inactive precursors and released by regulated proteolysis or, for XBP1, by IRE1-mediated mRNA splicing, so their activity reports stress in the secretory pathway rather than a signaling kinase. They bind an asymmetric, CRE-like element, TGACGTGG, equivalently CCACGTCA on the opposite strand, whose CCACG half is the ATF6-contacted part of the ER stress response element ERSE (CCAAT-N9-CCACG). Their targets are ER chaperones, ERAD components and secretory-pathway genes. The members are not separable by sequence, and several of their matrices are indistinguishable from an ordinary CRE or a CACGTG E-box.
families.long:
## The factors

Two related sets of bZIP proteins share this element, and both are membrane-tethered. ATF6 (ATF6A) and ATF6B (CREB-RP) are type-II transmembrane proteins of the ER; accumulation of unfolded protein in the ER lumen releases them for transport to the Golgi, where site-1 and site-2 proteases cleave off a soluble nuclear fragment, the 50 kDa p50ATF6 [PMID:10564271,11163209]. The CREB3 family - CREB3 (Luman/LZIP), CREB3L1 (OASIS), CREB3L2 (BBF2H7), CREB3L3 (CREB-H) and CREB3L4 (AIbZIP) - is processed the same way, but the members are tissue-restricted: CREB3L1 in osteoblasts and other secretory cells, CREB3L2 in chondrocytes, CREB3L3 in liver and intestine, CREB3L4 in prostate, while CREB3, ATF6 and ATF6B are broad [PMID:31334233]. XBP1 groups here by motif but is produced differently: IRE1 excises 26 nucleotides from its mRNA, shifting the reading frame to yield the active bZIP XBP1s [PMID:11779464]. Because the bZIP domains are closely related, all of these proteins dimerize with one another to varying degrees, and ATF6-XBP1s heterodimers are documented.

## The motif

The element is best written as the 8 bp TGACGTGG, or CCACGTCA reading the other strand [PMID:10856300]. It is asymmetric: one half is the CRE half-site TGACG, the other is CCACG (CGTGG on the top strand), so a single subunit reads a CRE-like half and the other reads a G-rich half. The functional promoter element in which ATF6 acts is composite. The ER stress response element ERSE has the consensus CCAAT-N9-CCACG [PMID:9837962], and p50ATF6 binds CCACG only when the general factor NF-Y occupies the CCAAT box nine bases away [PMID:11112790]; a second element, ERSE-II, has the shorter arrangement ATTGG-N-CCACG and is also ATF6-dependent [PMID:11112790]. The mammalian UPRE, used in reporter work, is the TGACGTG(G/A) core alone [PMID:11779464]. The 26 models collected here give a consensus of GGTGACGTGGC, with the highest-information examples (JASPAR ATF6 MA1466.2, CIS-BP ATF6 and ATF6B) reading TGATGACGTGGCA. Members are not distinguishable: the ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L3, CREB3L4 and XBP1 models sit above 0.95 similarity to one another, and the Vierstra archetype AC0633 is named CREB3L/XBP precisely because their motifs clustered. Two kinds of drift within the family matter in practice. Some entries collapse to a plain CRE - the HOCOMOCO ATF6A HT-SELEX model is TGATGACGTCAT and JASPAR CREB3L4 MA1475.2 is GTGACGTCA - and are then indistinguishable from CREB/ATF. Others collapse to a CACGTG E-box - JASPAR Creb3l2 MA0608.1 is GCCACGTGT and the CIS-BP CREB3L1 model is TGCCACGTGTAC - and are then indistinguishable from USF, MITF or TFE3 motifs. Both drifts follow from the shared ACGT core.

## Where it acts

This family works mainly at promoters, and its canonical targets are the ER chaperone and quality-control genes: HSPA5 (GRP78/BiP), HSP90B1 (GRP94), CALR [PMID:9837962], and ERAD components including HERPUD1, SEL1L and EDEM1. These promoters are CpG-island-associated and the elements are promoter-proximal rather than distributed across enhancers, which distinguishes this family's genomic distribution from AP-1. XBP1s occupancy is nonetheless condition- and cell-type-specific, with distinct target networks in different tissues [PMID:17612490], so the shared motif does not imply a shared target set. The obligate partner for ERSE function is NF-Y at the CCAAT box; ATF6 and XBP1s also co-occupy UPR promoters with ATF4, whose amino-acid response elements lie at overlapping loci. CREB3-family factors additionally act at secretory-pathway and lipid-metabolism promoters outside the classical chaperone set [PMID:31334233].

## Biology and disease

These factors implement the transcriptional arm of the unfolded protein response and, more broadly, adjust secretory capacity to demand. XBP1 is required for plasma cell differentiation, the extreme case of secretory expansion [PMID:11460154], and Xbp1-null mice also fail in hepatocyte development. CREB3L1/OASIS is required for bone formation in mice [PMID:19767743], and biallelic CREB3L1 loss causes a recessive form of osteogenesis imperfecta in humans [PMID:31207160]. CREB3L2 is the 3-prime partner of the recurrent FUS-CREB3L2 fusion that defines low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma [PMID:21406083], in which the CREB3L2 bZIP supplies DNA binding to a chimeric activator. Biallelic ATF6 variants, including multi-exon deletions, cause achromatopsia with foveal hypoplasia [PMID:32271167], a phenotype that localizes an ER-stress transducer to cone photoreceptor development. Prolonged signaling through this arm, with ATF4 and CHOP, drives apoptosis rather than adaptation [PMID:23624402].

## Reading a hit

A TGACGTGG match is a reasonable family call and no kind of member call: ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3, CREB3L1 to CREB3L4 and XBP1 are interchangeable at this resolution, and only expression data can narrow it. Before trusting the call, check which half-sites you actually matched. If the 3-prime half is GTCA rather than GTGG, you have a plain CRE and CREB/ATF is at least as likely; if the match is CACGTG with no TGAC half, you have an E-box and the USF/MITF/TFE families are better explanations. A functional ATF6 site normally comes with context: look for a CCAAT box about nine bases away (ERSE) or an ATTGG one base away (ERSE-II), and for promoter proximity. All ten HOCOMOCO models here carry in vitro evidence in their code (S or M), which supports direct binding, but three members - CREB3L1, CREB3L2 and CREB3L4 - also contribute truncated models such as ACGTGG and ACGTGGC that will match far too often to interpret on their own.
families.caveats: The family is internally cohesive, but its motif is the least distinctive in the bZIP set because it is built on an ACGT core shared with the CRE and with CACGTG E-boxes. Several matrices in this collection have drifted to one or the other: two read as plain CREs and two as E-boxes, so an unqualified hit may not even be in the right family. A match also does not tell you which of the eight proteins is bound, nor that any of them is expressed, nor whether the ER stress pathway is active. Because ATF6 needs NF-Y at a CCAAT box to work at ERSE, an isolated CCACG with no CCAAT nearby is weak evidence of a functional UPR element.

timeline.methods: Lymphoid chimeras from Xbp1-deficient cells

open: Whether the CRE-like and E-box-like matrices recorded for some members are selection artifacts or genuine alternative specificities is unresolved: the HOCOMOCO ATF6A HT-SELEX model and JASPAR CREB3L4 MA1475.2 read as the plain CRE TGACGTCA, while JASPAR Creb3l2 MA0608.1 and the CIS-BP CREB3L1 model read as CACGTG E-boxes, so the same proteins are represented by matrices pointing to two different neighboring families.

Which of XBP1's cell-type-specific targets are bound directly through the UPRE, and which through other motifs or partners, is open; genome-wide XBP1 occupancy found different motifs at functionally distinct target sets.

Why loss of ATF6, which is broadly expressed and shares its motif with ATF6B and XBP1s, causes a disease confined to cone photoreceptors is not explained; ATF6B transcripts are also present in cones, so simple redundancy does not account for it.

families.name: TWIST / HAND
families.def: E-box CATCTG/CAGATG bound by TWIST1/2, HAND1/2, TCF21, MESP1/2, SCX.
families.short: TWIST1/2, HAND1/2, TCF21, SCX and MESP1/2 are class II basic helix-loop-helix factors of mesoderm and neural crest. They bind the E-box CANNTG as heterodimers with the ubiquitous E-proteins TCF3/TCF4/TCF12, with each other, or as homodimers, and this group prefers CAGATG (CATCTG on the opposite strand). Because the two central E-box bases are barely contacted by the protein, the distinction from the muscle E-box CAGCTG and the neural CATATG is weak. TWIST has one genuinely diagnostic feature: a double E-box with the two boxes five bases apart, which aligns two TWIST-E47 dimers on one face of the helix so they can tetramerise. The family runs craniofacial, cardiac, tendon and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes.
families.long:
## The factors

TWIST1, TWIST2 (DERMO-1), HAND1 (eHAND/Thing1), HAND2 (dHAND/Thing2), TCF21 (capsulin/epicardin/POD1), SCX (scleraxis) and MESP1/MESP2 make up this family. All are class II bHLH proteins of mesodermal and neural-crest lineages, and all bind DNA as dimers: heterodimers with the ubiquitous class I E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, homodimers, and heterodimers with each other. The TWIST1-HAND2 pairing matters functionally, because different dimer species have different activities and the balance between them is set post-translationally. Phosphorylation of conserved helix I residues, regulated by protein kinase A and protein phosphatase 2A, shifts TWIST1 and HAND2 dimer choice, and mutations that alter that balance produce limb and craniofacial phenotypes overlapping the TWIST1 loss-of-function syndrome [PMID:15735646]. TWIST1 additionally carries a C-terminal WR ("Twist-box") domain that dimerises, allowing two TWIST1-E47 dimers to assemble into a tetramer [PMID:25762439]. Expression is lineage-restricted but broad within those lineages: TWIST1/2 in cranial and limb mesenchyme, dermis and many mesenchymal tumours; HAND1 in extraembryonic mesoderm, left ventricle and trophoblast; HAND2 in right ventricle, branchial arches and sympathoadrenal cells; TCF21 in epicardium, kidney, lung mesenchyme and vascular smooth muscle; SCX in tendon; MESP1/2 in nascent mesoderm.

## The motif

The core is again a six-base E-box, CANNTG, with each monomer reading one CAN half-site. This family's preference is written CAGATG, or equivalently CATCTG read on the other strand, and that is what the data give: the representative model is `CCAGATGT` (CIS-BP TWIST1 and JASPAR TWIST1 MA1123.3 agree exactly), with HOCOMOCO TWIST1 ChIP models reading ACATCTG. The distinction from the muscle E-box CAGCTG and the neural CAGATG/CATATG is weak by construction — the two central bases are the ones that vary, and in the one solved class I/class II structure on an asymmetric E-box (E47-NEUROD1 on CATCTG) no side chain contacts the central base pairs directly [PMID:18069799]. Expect substantial cross-matching.

The one feature in this family with real discriminating power is architectural rather than compositional. High-resolution mapping of TWIST occupancy in human and *Drosophila* genomes found that TWIST, and not other bHLH proteins tested, prefers a double E-box with the two boxes separated by five nucleotides; the spacing aligns two TWIST-E47 dimers on the same face of the helix so that the WR domains can contact each other and form a stable tetramer [PMID:25762439]. The data carry that signature: `TWST2.H14CORE.0.P.B` reads CAGCTGGNNNCCAGATGT, two E-boxes five bases apart, in a single model.

Cohesion here is the lowest of the E-box families at 0.76, and label agreement is poor for most members. TCF21 has one high-grade model reading AACAGCTGG (a myogenic-type site) and another reading CATATGGT (a NeuroD/Atonal-type site). MESP1/MESP2 models read CATATG or CACCTG. The HAND models are the weakest: `HAND1.H14CORE.0.P.B` and `HAND2.H14CORE.0.P.B` are nearly identical to one another (TCTGGNTTNTGTCA) but resemble nothing else, and JASPAR's Hand1 MA2123.1 (CCAGACCT) and Hand1::Tcf3 MA0092.2 (GTCTGGCA) are not recognisable E-boxes at all, while the one HT-SELEX HAND2 model reads GCACCTGC. Three mutually inconsistent HAND2 models exist across the four databases.

## Where it acts

These are enhancer factors in mesenchymal, cardiac and neural-crest chromatin, not CpG-island promoter factors. TWIST1 sites occur in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) programmes alongside SNAI, ZEB, TEAD and AP-1 motifs; the double E-box is the TWIST-specific arrangement. HAND2 sites sit in the core regulatory circuitry of the adrenergic/noradrenergic state of neuroblastoma, co-occurring with PHOX2B, GATA3, ASCL1 and TBX2 motifs in large super-enhancer clusters, and the same circuit can switch to a mesenchymal state with an entirely different motif complement [PMID:28740262,28650485]. TCF21 acts in smooth-muscle and fibroblast enhancers; the coronary artery disease association at 6q23.2 maps to an enhancer regulating *TCF21* expression rather than to coding variation [PMID:23874238].

## Biology and disease

TWIST1 haploinsufficiency causes Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, with coronal craniosynostosis, facial asymmetry and limb anomalies; both founding reports identified loss-of-function and missense changes clustered in the bHLH domain [PMID:8988166,8988167]. TWIST1 is also required for EMT-associated metastasis in mammary tumour models [PMID:15210113]. *Hand1*-null mouse embryos die with extraembryonic and cardiac defects [PMID:9500550]; *Hand2* (dHAND) loss disrupts right ventricle and branchial-arch development and sympathetic neuron differentiation [PMID:9171826]. *Mesp1* is expressed in heart precursors and required for a single heart tube [PMID:10393122]. HAND2 is a dependency of adrenergic neuroblastoma [PMID:28740262]. TCF21 variation contributes to coronary artery disease risk through smooth-muscle phenotype.

## Reading a hit

A CAGATG or CATCTG match says a class II bHLH-E-protein dimer of this general kind could bind. It does not tell you which factor, and the separation from the NEUROD/ATOH family (CAGATG/CATATG) and the MYOD family (CAGCTG) is one or two bases at positions the protein barely touches. If you want evidence that a site is genuinely TWIST-type rather than generically bHLH, look for the double E-box with a five-base spacer; a single E-box will not settle it [PMID:25762439]. Treat HAND1 and HAND2 models with particular caution: all of the HAND ChIP-derived models in this family are HOCOMOCO grade B with `P` (ChIP-only) evidence, they do not look like E-boxes, and they match nothing else in the collection, which is the expected signature of an indirect or low-quality model rather than of a HAND recognition sequence. One CIS-BP TWIST2 model is inherited from the mouse protein at 100% DBD identity, which is harmless. Because the family's own members disagree about their preferred site, do not use a hit to assign a specific paralogue.
families.caveats: This is the least cohesive of the E-box families in the atlas (cohesion 0.76), and its members disagree with each other. TCF21 has one high-grade model reading a myogenic AACAGCTGG and another reading a NeuroD-type CATATGGT; HAND2 has three mutually inconsistent models across the four databases. The HAND1 and HAND2 models from ChIP are nearly identical to one another, are not recognisable E-boxes, and resemble nothing else in the collection — treat them as unreliable rather than as HAND recognition sequences. A single CAGATG or CATCTG hit identifies the general class II bHLH site, not the factor. Only the five-base-spaced double E-box discriminates TWIST specifically.

timeline.finding: Two groups report that heterozygous TWIST1 loss-of-function and bHLH-domain missense mutations cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, placing the family in human craniofacial and limb development.
timeline.methods: positional cloning and mutation screening in families
timeline.open: Whether the missense changes act by abolishing DNA binding or by some other mechanism was not determined.

timeline.finding: Mouse knockouts show the HAND factors are required for cardiac and neural-crest development: dHAND/Hand2 loss disrupts the right ventricle, branchial arches and sympathetic neurons (1997), and Hand1 loss causes extraembryonic and cardiac failure (1998).
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting
timeline.open: No DNA recognition sequence had been established for either HAND protein.

timeline.finding: Twist1 is shown to be required for metastasis in a mouse mammary tumour model, tying the family to epithelial-mesenchymal transition in cancer.
timeline.methods: RNAi knockdown in a mouse tumour model

timeline.finding: Twist1 and Hand2 are found to antagonise each other in a dosage-dependent way, with dimerization partner choice set by phosphorylation of conserved helix I residues; several Saethre-Chotzen mutations alter that phosphorylation, so the syndrome is reframed as misregulated dimerization rather than simple loss of DNA binding.
timeline.methods: mouse genetics, phosphorylation and dimerization assays
timeline.open: Whether different dimer species also differ in preferred DNA sequence, rather than only in activity.

timeline.finding: The E47-NEUROD1 bHLH structure on the asymmetric E-box CATCTG shows that no side chain contacts the central base pairs, which explains why CAGATG, CATCTG and CAGCTG assignments cannot be separated by sequence across the class II bHLH families.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: The 6q23.2 coronary artery disease association is mapped to an enhancer that modulates TCF21 expression rather than to coding variation, making this family's regulatory sites the disease-relevant element.
timeline.methods: fine mapping, reporter and allele-specific assays in vascular cells

timeline.finding: High-resolution occupancy mapping in human and Drosophila finds that TWIST, unlike other bHLH proteins tested, recognises a double E-box with a preferred five-nucleotide spacer that aligns two TWIST-E47 dimers on one face of the DNA for WR-domain-mediated tetramer formation, so target specificity comes from architecture rather than from a distinct core sequence.
timeline.methods: ChIP-exo-type occupancy mapping, molecular modelling, binding kinetics
timeline.open: Most database models for this family are still single E-boxes, so how much of TWIST occupancy genome-wide requires the spacing is unsettled.

timeline.finding: Two independent super-enhancer studies place HAND2 in the core regulatory circuitry of the adrenergic state of neuroblastoma, alongside PHOX2B, GATA3 and ASCL1, with an alternative mesenchymal state built on a different factor set.
timeline.methods: H3K27ac super-enhancer mapping and ChIP-seq in tumours and cell lines
timeline.open: Whether HAND2 occupancy in that circuit reflects direct DNA recognition or recruitment by its partners.

open: Whether the HAND proteins have a definable recognition sequence is unresolved: the HAND1 and HAND2 ChIP models in HOCOMOCO are nearly identical to each other, are not recognisable E-boxes and match nothing else in the collection, and the one HT-SELEX HAND2 model reads GCACCTGC instead, so three mutually inconsistent HAND2 models coexist across the four databases.

How general the TWIST double E-box is remains open: the five-base-spaced arrangement was found to be conserved between human and Drosophila and is required for TWIST-induced EMT, yet nearly every database model for this family is a single E-box, and what fraction of genuine TWIST1 sites carries the spacing has not been established genome-wide.

It is not known whether the phospho-regulated choice between TWIST1 homodimers, TWIST1-E-protein heterodimers and TWIST1-HAND2 heterodimers changes the preferred DNA sequence or only the transcriptional output, so the single matrix stored per factor may be averaging over dimers with different specificities.

TCF21's placement in this family is contradicted by its own models, one high-grade model reading the myogenic site AACAGCTGG and another the NeuroD-type CATATGGT, and it is unsettled whether TCF21 genuinely reads a TWIST-type site or has been grouped here by domain similarity alone.

families.name: HES / HEY (N-box)
families.def: Class C bHLH-Orange repressors reading CACGYG (and the N box CACNAG); the CACGTG form is shared with the MYC/USF/MITF/CLOCK E-box families. HES1-7, HEY1/2, HEYL, HELT.
families.short: HES1-7, HEY1/2, HEYL and HELT are the vertebrate hairy/Enhancer-of-split relatives: bHLH repressors with an Orange domain that sets partner choice and a C-terminal WRPW or YRPW peptide that recruits TLE/Groucho corepressors. Most are direct Notch targets, so their activity reports Notch signalling. They read a genuinely different site from the class II bHLH activators — a proline in the basic region shifts preference away from CANNTG. Two sites are described: the functionally defined N box CACNAG, and the higher-affinity CACGYG (CACGTG or CACGCG) that the database matrices actually capture. HES1 autorepression through N boxes generates a two-hour expression oscillation; HES7 drives the somite segmentation clock.
families.long:
## The factors

HES1-HES7, HEY1, HEY2, HEYL and HELT are the vertebrate relatives of *Drosophila* hairy and Enhancer of split, and they are structurally distinct from the class I and class II bHLH proteins that read E-boxes. Three features define them. First, a proline in the basic region, which is why this group is sometimes called the proline-bHLH class and why its sequence preference differs from CANNTG [PMID:12548545]. Second, an Orange domain, a two-helix module immediately C-terminal to the bHLH that restricts which partners a given member will dimerise with. Third, a C-terminal tetrapeptide — WRPW in HES proteins, YRPW in HEY proteins — that recruits TLE/Groucho corepressors [PMID:17586813]. They are repressors, not activators. Most are direct transcriptional targets of Notch signalling through RBPJ/CSL, so their expression reports Notch activity [PMID:17329370]: HES1 broadly, HES5 in neural progenitors, HES7 in presomitic mesoderm, HEY1/HEY2/HEYL in cardiovascular and endothelial tissue. HES2, HES3, HES4 and HES6 are divergent; HES6 does not behave like a canonical repressor [PMID:17329370]. Crucially, these proteins repress by two routes. They bind DNA and recruit corepressors, and they also sequester class II activators: HES1 reduces E47-driven transcription and blocks MyoD- and MASH1-driven differentiation, which requires no HES site at all [PMID:8524259].

## The motif

Two different sites are attributed to this family, and the distinction matters. The site defined functionally is the N box, CACNAG, the Enhancer-of-split recognition sequence through which HES1 represses transcription [PMID:1340473]. *Drosophila* hairy was then shown to prefer a non-canonical site, CACGCG, and mutating a single CACGCG in the *achaete* promoter abolishes hairy-mediated repression in cells and produces ectopic sensory organs in flies [PMID:7958930,7958929]. Different papers call this site a class C site or a class B E-box; the nomenclature is not consistent, so it is safer to write the sequence than the class name.

What the databases contain is neither of these. Twenty-four of the 26 motifs assigned here read CACGTG or CACGYG, usually with GG/CC flanks: GGCACGTGCC. The representative model is JASPAR HEY1 MA0823.1 (CACGTGCC), and almost all the HOCOMOCO models carry in vitro evidence (`S` or `SM`), so this is a real binding preference measured in vitro, not an artefact. Genome-wide, HEY1, HEY2 and HEYL bound preferentially to CACGYG, but a large fraction of efficiently bound promoters contained no E-box at all, implying additional, loosely defined binding modes [PMID:22615585]. The honest summary is that the high-affinity in vitro site is CACGYG, the classical repression site is the lower-affinity N box CACNAG, and the database matrices capture only the former. The atlas's data consensus CACGTGCC therefore disagrees with the ontology definition's N box for a documented reason rather than by error.

CACGTG is a problem sequence. It is the canonical palindromic E-box of MYC/MAX, USF1/2, TFE3/TFEB/MITF, SREBF1/2, BHLHE40/41, ARNT and the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer. The Vierstra archetype `AC0068:HEY/CLOCK:bHLH` states this in its name. Two further Vierstra archetypes here, `AC0263:HES` and `AC0264:HES`, have low-information consensuses (CACACTT, CNCACGT) that resemble nothing else in the family and should not be used as HES models. Two CIS-BP entries, for HES4 and HEYL, are inferred from mouse proteins at 91% DNA-binding-domain identity.

## Where it acts

Unlike the E-box families, HES/HEY sites are promoter-proximal. Chromatin immunoprecipitation of HEY factors in HEK293 cells, cardiomyocytes and mouse hearts found binding clustered in proximal promoter regions, disproportionately at genes encoding transcriptional regulators and developmental control proteins [PMID:22615585]. CACGTG contains a CpG, so these sites are enriched in CpG islands and their occupancy is sensitive to DNA methylation. HES1 binds N boxes in its own promoter, and that negative feedback loop, combined with short protein and mRNA half-lives, generates a roughly two-hour oscillation in HES1 expression [PMID:12399594]. Neighbouring RBPJ/CSL sites are common, because these genes and their targets are Notch-responsive.

## Biology and disease

HES and HEY proteins are the main transcriptional output of Notch signalling. Hes1 and Hes5 maintain neural progenitors and delay neuronal differentiation; removing them causes premature neurogenesis and progenitor depletion [PMID:10205173]. Hes7 drives the segmentation clock in presomitic mesoderm, and its loss disorganises somite formation [PMID:11641270]; in humans, *HES7* mutations cause spondylocostal dysostosis with vertebral and rib malformations [PMID:23897666]. HEY1, HEY2 and HEYL are strikingly redundant, which is why single knockouts are often mild and combined losses phenocopy each other in the heart [PMID:22615585]. HES1 acts downstream of activated NOTCH1 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

## Reading a hit

A CACGTG hit is one of the least specific results a scan can return: on sequence alone it is compatible with at least eight other families, several of which (MYC/MAX, USF, MITF, CLOCK-BMAL1) are far more abundantly expressed in most cell types than HES or HEY. Treat a CACGTG match as a "class B E-box" hit and resolve it with expression and co-factor evidence, not with motif scores. If you are specifically after Notch-effector repression, the functionally validated site is the N box CACNAG, which the database matrices will not find for you; scan for it separately and expect weak scores. The individual HES and HEY paralogues cannot be distinguished. Finally, remember that these proteins can repress without binding DNA, by titrating E-proteins and class II activators, so the absence of a site is not evidence that HES or HEY is not acting on a gene.
families.caveats: The site the databases model, CACGTG, is the canonical palindromic E-box shared with MYC/MAX, USF1/2, TFE3/TFEB/MITF, SREBF, BHLHE40/41, ARNT and CLOCK-BMAL1 — one Vierstra archetype here is named HEY/CLOCK for exactly that reason — so a hit is weak evidence for HES or HEY specifically. The classically defined repression site, the N box CACNAG, is lower affinity and is not represented by these matrices, so a scan will miss it. Two low-information Vierstra HES archetypes resemble nothing else in the family. HES4 and HEYL models are inferred from mouse proteins. HES and HEY also repress without binding DNA, by sequestering E-proteins, so absent sites do not exclude their involvement.
