timeline.finding: Mammalian HES1 and HES3 are cloned as relatives of Drosophila hairy and Enhancer of split; HES1 represses through the N box CACNAG and separately reduces E-box-driven activation by E47 without binding that site, defining the two repression modes at the outset.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, gel shift and reporter assays
timeline.open: The relative importance of DNA-bound repression and activator sequestration in vivo.

timeline.finding: Drosophila hairy is shown to be a sequence-specific repressor that prefers the non-canonical site CACGCG rather than the N box, and mutating a single CACGCG in the achaete promoter abolishes repression in cells and produces ectopic sensory organs in flies — direct genetic evidence tying one site to one phenotype.
timeline.methods: binding-site selection, cell reporter assays, transgenic flies
timeline.open: Whether vertebrate HES proteins share the CACGCG preference or use the N box.

timeline.finding: Domain swaps place repression specificity outside the bHLH: the bHLH and Orange domains antagonise specific activators such as Scute, while the C-terminal WRPW tetrapeptide represses through corepressor recruitment, so two separable mechanisms operate.
timeline.methods: chimeric proteins assayed in Drosophila sex determination

timeline.finding: Hes1 and Hes5 are established as the Notch effectors that hold neural progenitors undifferentiated, with premature neurogenesis and progenitor depletion on their loss.
timeline.methods: mouse knockouts and progenitor assays

timeline.finding: Dynamic rather than static repression emerges: Hes7 is shown to be required for ordered somite segmentation (2001), and Hes1 is shown to oscillate with a roughly two-hour period driven by negative autoregulation through N boxes in its own promoter plus short mRNA and protein half-lives (2002).
timeline.methods: mouse mutants, serum-synchronised cultures, mathematical modelling
timeline.open: Whether oscillation depends on the precise affinity of the autoregulatory N boxes.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide mapping of HEY1, HEY2 and HEYL finds binding clustered in proximal promoters of transcriptional regulators, a clear preference for class B E-boxes CACGYG rather than the N box, extensive redundancy among the three proteins, and many efficiently bound promoters with no E-box at all.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip/ChIP-seq and microarray profiling in cells, cardiomyocytes and mouse heart
timeline.open: What the factors recognise at the E-box-free promoters was left undefined.

timeline.finding: HES7 mutation is shown to cause spondylocostal dysostosis in a large human family, carrying the segmentation-clock mechanism into human skeletal disease.
timeline.methods: linkage and sequencing in an extended family

open: Which site this family actually uses is unsettled: repression was defined functionally through the N box CACNAG and, in Drosophila, through CACGCG, whereas the in vitro matrices in these databases read CACGTG/CACGYG, and it is unresolved whether the N box is a genuine lower-affinity site used in vivo or an early assignment that the newer binding data supersede.

A large fraction of promoters efficiently bound by HEY proteins contain no E-box, and whether that reflects tethering by other DNA-binding factors, a degenerate site that position weight matrices do not capture, or indirect ChIP signal has not been determined.

How much HES/HEY repression requires DNA binding at all is unquantified: these proteins also repress by sequestering E-proteins and class II activators, a mode that needs no site, and the in vivo balance between the two mechanisms is unknown.

No paralogue-level sequence difference has been demonstrated within the family, and the two low-information Vierstra archetypes grouped here, AC0263:HES (CACACTT) and AC0264:HES (CNCACGT), resemble neither the CACGYG models nor each other, so whether they capture any real HES binding mode is doubtful.

families.name: STAT
families.def: GAS TTCnnnGAA and ISRE-like. STAT1-4, STAT5A/B, STAT6.
families.short: The seven human STAT proteins - STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT6 - sit latent in the cytoplasm until a receptor-associated JAK kinase phosphorylates a single C-terminal tyrosine. Two phosphorylated monomers then pair through reciprocal SH2-phosphotyrosine contacts and clamp around DNA at a gamma-interferon activation site (GAS): the short inverted repeat TTCNNNGAA. Spacing is almost the only sequence feature that distinguishes them, with STAT6 preferring a four-base spacer and the rest a three-base spacer, so a GAS match names the family and not the member. STATs convert essentially every cytokine, interferon and several growth factor signals into transcription, and germline or somatic STAT mutations cause immunodeficiency, allergy, growth failure and leukemia.
families.long:
## The factors

Seven genes: STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT6. All share one architecture - an
N-terminal domain, a coiled-coil, a DNA-binding domain built on an immunoglobulin fold like those of
NF-kappaB and p53 [PMID:9630226], a linker, an SH2 domain, and a C-terminal transactivation domain carrying the
conserved tyrosine. The protein is latent in the cytoplasm; a receptor-associated JAK phosphorylates
that tyrosine, and two monomers pair by reciprocal contacts between the SH2 domain of one and the
phosphotyrosine tail of the other, producing a C-shaped clamp that encircles the DNA [PMID:9630226,9671298]. The
phosphotyrosine site of the SH2 domain is structurally coupled to the DNA-binding domain, so
dimerization and DNA binding are not independent [PMID:9630226]. Which STAT is active is set by the cytokine, not by
the DNA: STAT1 homodimers by interferon gamma, STAT1-STAT2 plus IRF9 (ISGF3) by type I interferons,
STAT3 by the IL-6 family, STAT4 by IL-12, STAT5A and STAT5B by the IL-2 family, growth hormone,
prolactin and erythropoietin, and STAT6 by IL-4 and IL-13 [PMID:28323260]. STAT5A and STAT5B have no measured
difference in DNA-binding specificity [PMID:11053426].

## The motif

The GAS element is TTCNNNGAA: two TTC/GAA half-sites facing each other across a three-base spacer,
often written TT(N)5AA [PMID:7708771]. Spacer width is the only substantial selectivity available. STAT6 prefers
four spacer bases, TTCNNNNGAA, but still binds three-base sites reasonably well; STAT1 and STAT5
prefer three, and STAT5A tolerates four weakly; none of them binds a lone half-site [PMID:11053426]. In reporter
assays, a five-base TT-to-AA spacing is generally permissive, four favors STAT3-containing complexes
and six favors IL-4-activated complexes [PMID:7708771]. Within the three-base class, STAT1, STAT3, STAT4 and STAT5
are not separable by sequence, and the consensus that the models here agree on, TTCCTGGAA, is
compatible with all of them. Two further arrangements matter in practice. First, tetramers: contacts
between N-terminal domains let two dimers bind tandem, individually weak GAS sites cooperatively [PMID:8896455], so
genuine STAT5 targets are often clusters of poor matches rather than one good one, and scanning for a
single strong site will miss them. Second, ISGF3: when STAT1 and STAT2 act with IRF9 they read an
ISRE rather than a GAS, with the STAT pair on the 5' GGAA and IRF9 on the second GAAA repeat [PMID:29317535]. That is
why several STAT-labelled models here look like ISREs - HOCOMOCO STAT1.H14CORE.1.P.B
(TCAGTTTCRTTTTCC), HOCOMOCO STAT2.H14CORE.0.P.B (GGAAANHGAAACTGA) and JASPAR STAT1::STAT2.

## Where it acts

STAT occupancy is signal-dependent and transient: sites become occupied within minutes of cytokine
exposure and are vacated as the STAT is dephosphorylated and exported [PMID:28323260]. Targets are both
cytokine-inducible promoters and, more often, enhancers, where STATs cooperate with the
lineage-defining factors of the responding cell. The practical consequence is that a GAS match in an
unstimulated cell type usually corresponds to nothing: the motif is present in the genome whether or
not the pathway is on. Type I interferon signaling shifts the element as well as the factor, from GAS
to ISRE, so the same STAT1 protein leaves different footprints depending on which interferon acted.

## Biology and disease

Human genetics has produced an unusually clear catalogue. Gain-of-function STAT1 mutations impair
IL-17 immunity and cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis [PMID:21727188]. Dominant-negative mutations in the STAT3
DNA-binding domain cause hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome - a disease of DNA binding specifically, since the
mutant protein dimerizes but cannot read its site [PMID:17676033]. Somatic STAT3 mutations, mostly in the SH2 domain,
occur in large granular lymphocytic leukemia [PMID:22591296], and activating STAT5B mutations recur in T-cell
leukemias. Loss-of-function STAT5B mutations cause growth hormone insensitivity with severe short
stature and immune dysfunction [PMID:13679528]. Germline gain-of-function STAT6 mutations cause severe early-onset
allergic disease [PMID:36758835]. Together these establish that STAT dosage and DNA-binding competence, not just
pathway activation, are rate-limiting in vivo.

## Reading a hit

Be conservative. TTCNNNGAA specifies only six bases, so it is expected on the order of several
hundred thousand times per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome; STAT matches are among the least specific in
this atlas, and this family is the least internally cohesive of the ETS/IRF/STAT group. The evidence
behind the models is also weaker than elsewhere: every HOCOMOCO model assigned here is ChIP-derived
(evidence letter P, grade B) with no in vitro HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model, all nine JASPAR
models are ChIP-seq, six of them from mouse rather than human experiments (Stat2, Stat4, Stat5a,
Stat5b, Stat6, Stat5a::Stat5b), and two CIS-BP entries are transferred from mouse proteins on
DNA-binding-domain similarity - one of which is the motif this atlas selects as the family
representative. "This protein binds this sequence" therefore rests largely on in vivo co-occupancy
plus older in vitro studies. Expect confusion with IRF: the ISRE-shaped STAT models cross-match IRF
motifs, and in this atlas most nearest neighbours of STAT1.H14CORE.1.P.B, STAT2.H14CORE.0.P.B and
JASPAR STAT1::STAT2 are labelled IRF, while the JASPAR mouse Stat2 model's best match anywhere lies
outside the STAT family. The discriminator is orientation: a GAS is an inverted repeat (TTC facing
GAA), an ISRE is a direct repeat of GAAA. Finally, no STAT paralogue can be named from sequence -
STAT5A versus STAT5B is impossible - so use the cytokine, the time point and the cell type.
families.caveats:
A GAS match names the family, never the member: STAT1, STAT3, STAT4 and STAT5 read
the same three-spacer inverted repeat, STAT5A and STAT5B have no measured specificity difference, and
only STAT6's preference for a four-base spacer gives partial leverage. The element is short enough to
occur hundreds of thousands of times by chance, and occupancy is signal-dependent, so a hit in an
unstimulated cell type usually means nothing. Evidence is weaker here than for most families: all
HOCOMOCO models assigned to STAT are ChIP-only, all JASPAR models are ChIP-seq and two-thirds of
them are mouse, and two CIS-BP entries - including the family representative - are inferred from
mouse proteins. Expect overlap with IRF, since ISGF3 (STAT1-STAT2-IRF9) reads the ISRE, not a GAS.

timeline.finding: Natural STAT elements vary but share the form TT(N)5AA; synthetic sites show that the 5-bp TT-to-AA spacing binds STAT complexes generally, 4 bp selects complexes containing Stat3 and 6 bp selects the IL-4-activated complex, with matching effects on transcription.
timeline.methods: EMSA with synthetic and natural sites, reporter transfection
timeline.open: How the dimer read the half-sites, and whether spacing was the only source of selectivity, was unknown.

timeline.finding: Purified phosphorylated Stat1 binds strong and weak sites with similar equilibrium affinity but leaves weak sites far faster; two dimers bind tandem sites (not head-to-head sites) more stably than one site, and this cooperativity needs the N-terminal domain.
timeline.methods: In vitro DNA binding with purified phosphoprotein, mass spectrometry, domain truncation
timeline.open: How often natural targets depend on tandem weak sites was not measured.

timeline.finding: Crystal structures of a phosphorylated STAT1 dimer and a STAT3beta dimer on DNA show an immunoglobulin-fold DNA-binding domain and a C-shaped clamp around the DNA held by reciprocal SH2-phosphotyrosine contacts structurally coupled to the DNA-binding domain.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Side-by-side selection and affinity measurements for STAT1, STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT6 confirm near-identical specificity: STAT6 prefers four-base spacers but binds three-base sites fairly well, STAT1 and STAT5 prefer three, STAT5A weakly tolerates four, none binds a lone half-site, and STAT5A and STAT5B do not differ.
timeline.methods: In vitro selection from random oligonucleotides, quantitative affinity measurements, comparison with natural sites
timeline.open: STAT3 and STAT4 were not part of the comparison.

timeline.finding: A STAT5B mutation is found in a patient with growth hormone insensitivity, linking STAT5B to growth hormone signaling in humans.
timeline.methods: Patient genetics, functional studies

timeline.finding: De novo heterozygous mutations in the STAT3 DNA-binding domain cause hyper-IgE syndrome; the mutants are non-functional alone and dominant-negative with wild-type STAT3, and patient cells show greatly reduced STAT3 DNA binding.
timeline.methods: Patient sequencing, DNA-binding and reporter assays

timeline.finding: Heterozygous STAT1 mutations in the coiled-coil domain cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis by gain of function: they impair nuclear dephosphorylation and impair IL-17 immunity. Previously described disease-causing STAT1 alleles were all loss-of-function.
timeline.methods: Whole-exome sequencing, functional assays in patient cells

timeline.finding: Structures of the IRF9 association domain and its complex with the STAT2 coiled-coil domain explain the selective STAT2-IRF9 pairing in ISGF3; a model of ISGF3 on an ISRE puts the STAT pair on the 5' GGAA repeat and IRF9 on the second GAAA repeat.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, EMSA, structural modeling, reporter assays
timeline.open: The full ISGF3 complex on DNA has not been solved.

open: No high-throughput in vitro model exists for any STAT in these databases: every HOCOMOCO model is ChIP-only and every JASPAR model ChIP-seq, so whether the spacer-base preferences in the TTCCNGGAA consensus are intrinsic, or reflect partners and chromatin, has not been checked against the older selection and affinity data on a common footing.

How ISGF3 contacts the ISRE is inferred from a docked model rather than a structure, so whether the ISRE-shaped STAT1 and STAT2 ChIP motifs record STAT base contacts or only IRF9 binding within the complex is unresolved.

Whether STAT3 has a spacer preference of its own is unsettled: reporter and binding work found that a 4-bp TT-to-AA spacing selects STAT3-containing complexes, while the systematic comparison that found the STATs near-identical did not include STAT3, and the ChIP-derived STAT3 models here read the ordinary three-base-spacer TTCNNNGAA.

families.name: C/EBP
families.def: TT(G/A)CGCAA palindrome. CEBPA/B/D/E/G, and DDIT3 (CHOP) heterodimer sites.
families.short: The C/EBP family - CEBPA, CEBPB (NF-IL6), CEBPD, CEBPE, CEBPG, with DDIT3 (CHOP) as a heterodimer partner - binds the palindromic element TT(G/A)CGCAA, most often written as the 10-mer ATTGCGCAAT. These are basic region-leucine zipper proteins; the leucine zipper itself was first described in C/EBP, and the family's distinctive DNA contacts centre on an arginine that is conserved in C/EBPs but not in other bZIPs. Family members control hepatic and adipose metabolism, the acute-phase response, and granulocyte maturation, and CEBPA and CEBPE are mutated in human myeloid disease. The paralogues are indistinguishable from sequence. The boundary with the CREB/ATF family is genuinely blurred: CHOP-containing dimers and ATF4 read a hybrid half-C/EBP, half-CRE site, and CpG methylation converts a CRE into a C/EBP-alpha site.
families.long:
## The factors

Five C/EBP proteins bind DNA as this family: CEBPA, CEBPB (also NF-IL6 or LAP/LIP), CEBPD, CEBPE and CEBPG. All are basic region-leucine zipper (bZIP) factors, and the leucine zipper was in fact first proposed from the C/EBP sequence [PMID:3289117], with the scissors-grip model of DNA recognition advanced for the same family a year later [PMID:2683088]. CEBPA, CEBPB, CEBPD and CEBPE have N-terminal activation domains; CEBPG has essentially none and works mainly through heterodimers. Expression differs sharply even though the motif does not: CEBPB and CEBPG are broad, CEBPA is concentrated in liver, adipose tissue, lung and granulocytes, CEBPD is stress- and cytokine-inducible, and CEBPE is restricted to the granulocyte and eosinophil lineages. Alternative translation initiation produces short LIP isoforms of CEBPA and CEBPB that dimerize and occupy sites without activating, so the same motif can be read as an activator or a competitive repressor depending on isoform ratio. DDIT3 (CHOP/GADD153) is included here because it is an obligate C/EBP partner, but its basic region is substituted at positions that matter for C/EBP-site contact, so CHOP-C/EBP heterodimers bind a different, hybrid sequence rather than the C/EBP palindrome [PMID:8657121]. C/EBPs also pair outside the family, notably with ATF4 and with NF-kappa-B subunits.

## The motif

The consensus is the palindrome TT(G/A)CGCAA, usually presented with flanks as ATTGCGCAAT [PMID:8632009]. It is an inverted repeat of the half-site TTGC, one half per subunit. The C/EBP-alpha crystal structure resolved the contacts across ATTGCGCAAT and identified Arg289 as the keystone residue: it hydrogen-bonds to an adenine in the half-site, to the DNA backbone, and to Asn292, the asparagine invariant across bZIPs [PMID:12578822]. A second residue explains the family boundary. Val296, which is alanine in most other bZIPs, discriminates against purines and restrains the invariant Arg300; mutating it to alanine strongly increased C/EBP-alpha binding to CRE sites while leaving C/EBP-site affinity intact [PMID:12578822]. In other words a single side chain, not a different reading frame, separates the C/EBP site from the cyclic-AMP response element. Common variants replace the central CG: ATTGCACAAT and ATTGCGTAAT are both well represented among the 25 models here, as are half-degenerate forms in which only one TTGC half is intact. Methylation adds a twist in the same direction: CpG methylation of the CRE TGACGTCA, and of the half-sites CGTCA and CGCAA, increases C/EBP-alpha binding, and methylated promoters bound by C/EBP-alpha lose that binding when demethylated [PMID:21059933]. The paralogues are not distinguishable - JASPAR CEBPB MA0466.4 and CEBPE MA0837.3 are 0.997 similar, and every CEBPA, CEBPD and CEBPG model here falls within 0.95 of the family medoid. What does look different is the CHOP-partnered and ATF4-adjacent set: JASPAR Ddit3::Cebpa, HOCOMOCO DDIT3 and JASPAR CEBPG MA1636.2 all read ATGATGCAAT-like sequences, which is the C/EBP-ATF composite element (CARE), half CRE and half C/EBP [PMID:10085237].

## Where it acts

C/EBP sites occur at both promoters and enhancers, with less CpG-island bias than the CRE. In macrophages and adipocytes they are among the motifs that lineage-determining factors use when priming enhancers, and C/EBP-beta co-occupies acute-phase promoters with NF-kappa-B while C/EBP-alpha and C/EBP-beta act with PPARG at adipocyte enhancers and with RUNX1 and SPI1 at myeloid enhancers. The named composite element is the CARE, TTGCATCA or TGATGCAAT, at integrated-stress-response genes including DDIT3 itself, TRIB3, ASNS and ATF3; there C/EBP-family proteins and ATF4 occupy the same element [PMID:10085237]. On frequency: the exact palindrome TTGCGCAA is expected of order 10^4 times in 3.1 Gb before allowing for the genome's CpG depletion, while its non-CpG relatives TTGCACAA and TTGTGCAA are several-fold more common, so scans at usual thresholds return large numbers of C/EBP-like matches.

## Biology and disease

Cebpa-null mice die soon after birth from hypoglycemia, with no hepatic glycogen and disrupted adipose tissue [PMID:7652557]. Cebpb-null mice survive but their macrophages fail at bacterial killing and tumor cytotoxicity [PMID:7530603]. Cebpe-null mice have impaired granulopoiesis, myelodysplasia and early lethality [PMID:9371821], and in humans loss-of-function CEBPE mutation causes neutrophil-specific granule deficiency, a disorder of defective secondary granules and recurrent bacterial infection [PMID:10359588]. Dominant-negative CEBPA mutations that truncate the N-terminus define a recurrent subtype of acute myeloid leukemia [PMID:11242107], and germline CEBPA variants cause familial AML [PMID:15575056]. C/EBP-beta and C/EBP-delta are the transcriptional arm of the IL-6 acute-phase response. DDIT3/CHOP, acting with ATF4, raises protein synthesis during sustained ER stress to the point of cell death [PMID:23624402], which makes the CARE element a control point for stress-induced apoptosis.

## Reading a hit

A full ATTGCGCAAT palindrome is among the more distinctive bZIP matches: TTGC half-sites are not shared with AP-1, CREB/ATF, MAF or NFE2/BACH, so the family call is comparatively safe. The member call is not available at all. CEBPA, CEBPB, CEBPD, CEBPE and CEBPG give one motif, and which of them is bound is a question about expression, not sequence. A lone TTGC half-site is not interpretable. The real ambiguity is with the C/EBP-ATF composite: if your match reads ATGATGCAAT or TTGCATCA, it is a CARE, and ATF4 in the CREB/ATF family accounts for it as well as any C/EBP does; the DDIT3 and CEBPG matrices here are the same element. Methylation cuts both ways: a methylated CRE can be a genuine C/EBP-alpha site, and a CGCAA-containing hit may require methylation to be occupied. None of the 25 models is flagged as belonging elsewhere, and the in vitro (HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX) models agree with the ChIP-derived ones, which is the reassuring case for a ChIP-heavy family.
families.caveats: C/EBP is one of the more trustworthy family calls in this atlas: the motif is cohesive across all four databases, its in vitro and ChIP-derived models agree, and the TTGC half-site is not shared with the other bZIP families. Do not read a member into it - the five paralogues are identical at this resolution, and the biological consequence differs between them and between full-length and LIP isoforms of the same protein. Two caveats are specific. Matches of the form ATGATGCAAT are C/EBP-ATF composites and are equally well explained by ATF4. And because methylated CpG creates C/EBP-alpha sites at half-CRE and half-C/EBP sequences, a scan run without methylation data will both miss real sites and over-call unmethylated ones.

timeline.finding: A periodic array of leucines every seventh residue in C/EBP, also present in Fos, Jun, Myc and GCN4, is proposed to form an interdigitating dimerization helix, the leucine zipper.
timeline.methods: Sequence analysis and helical modeling
timeline.open: The zipper was a hypothesis, and how the adjacent region contacts DNA was not addressed.

timeline.finding: The scissors-grip model places the basic regions of a zipper-linked dimer in the major groove of a dyad-symmetric site, explaining why bZIP sites are abutted half-sites.
timeline.methods: Sequence comparison of 11 basic regions, chemical probing of protein-DNA complexes
timeline.open: No atomic structure of a bZIP-DNA complex yet existed.

timeline.finding: Knockouts separate member functions despite a shared motif: Cebpa-null mice die of neonatal hypoglycemia, Cebpb-null macrophages fail to kill bacteria, and Cebpe-null mice (1997) fail to make functional neutrophils.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting

timeline.finding: Random site selection shows the C/EBP family members share one consensus, RTTGCGYAAY, so the paralogues are not separable by sequence preference.
timeline.methods: PCR-mediated random site selection

timeline.finding: CHOP-C/EBP heterodimers cannot bind classic C/EBP sites but select a distinct core, PuPuPuTGCAAT(A/C)CCC, giving CHOP a dual role as inhibitor and direct activator.
timeline.methods: PCR-based selection, DNase I footprinting, methylation interference
timeline.open: How much CHOP's own DNA binding contributes in cells, as against sequestering C/EBP partners, was unresolved.

timeline.finding: At the Gadd153/CHOP promoter, C/EBP-beta, ATF4 and ATF3 bind in sequence to one C/EBP-ATF composite site during stress, defining the half-CRE, half-C/EBP element shared with the CREB/ATF family.
timeline.methods: EMSA and supershift, reporter assays

timeline.finding: The C/EBP-alpha bZIP crystal structure on ATTGCGCAAT shows Arg289 as the keystone contact and Val296 as a residue that excludes CRE binding; V296A gains CRE affinity without losing C/EBP sites.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, mutagenesis

timeline.finding: Reversing the usual rule that CpG methylation blocks binding, methylation of the CRE and of CGTCA and CGCAA half-sites creates C/EBP-alpha sites, and demethylation removes C/EBP-alpha from methylated tissue-specific promoters.
timeline.methods: DNA-binding assays, transfection, ChIP in primary keratinocytes, 5-azacytidine and DNMT1 depletion
timeline.open: The genome-wide fraction of C/EBP sites that depend on methylation, and whether other paralogues share the preference, were not measured.

open: How much of C/EBP-alpha's genomic binding depends on methylated CpG is unclear: methylation of CGTCA and CGCAA half-sites creates binding at some tissue-specific promoters, but whether this is a minor class of sites or a general feature, and whether the other C/EBP paralogues share it, has not been established.

Whether the CEBPG matrices describe CEBPG or its partners is unresolved in the databases: the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO model and JASPAR MA1636.2 read as the C/EBP-ATF composite ATTGCATCAT, while the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models read as the C/EBP palindrome, consistent with a protein that works mainly as a heterodimer.

How CHOP acts at DNA is not settled: CHOP-C/EBP heterodimers are excluded from classic C/EBP sites and select a distinct core in vitro, while genome-wide ChIP-seq places CHOP together with ATF4 at shared directly induced genes, and the relative weight of inhibition by sequestration and direct activation in cells is unknown.

families.name: ETS epithelial (ELF/EHF)
families.def: AACCGGAAGT with distinct 5' preference. ELF1-5, EHF, ELF2.
families.short: ELF1, ELF2, ELF3, ELF4, ELF5 and EHF are the ELF branch of the ETS family. They bind the same GGA(A/T) core as every other ETS protein through the same winged helix-turn-helix domain, but prefer a C where class I ETS factors prefer an A three bases 5' of the core, giving the ten-base site ACCCGGAAGT. ELF3, ELF5 and EHF are the epithelium-specific "ESE" members, expressed in gut, salivary gland, breast, airway, cornea, prostate and bladder epithelium; ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 are broader, with strong hematopoietic expression. These factors set and maintain epithelial differentiation - mammary alveolar cell fate, intestinal goblet cells - and in airway epithelium EHF represses CFTR; they are recurrently mutated or silenced in carcinomas of the bladder, biliary tract, cervix and breast.
families.long:
## The factors

Six human genes make up this group: ELF1, ELF2 (NERF), ELF3 (ESE-1/ESX), ELF4 (MEF), ELF5 (ESE-2)
and EHF (ESE-3). Each has a single ETS domain of about 85 residues - three alpha-helices on a
four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet, a winged helix-turn-helix - that binds DNA as a monomer,
with no obligate dimerization partner of the kind GABPA requires [PMID:8602247,21548782]. Binding profiles of all human
and mouse ETS proteins place the ELF proteins in class II (subclass IIa), separate from the large
class I group and from ETV6/ETV7 [PMID:20517297]. Expression splits the group in two. ELF3, ELF5 and EHF, together
with SPDEF, form the epithelium-specific ETS ("ESE") subfamily: ELF3 is highest in
gastrointestinal tract, salivary gland, bladder, liver and prostate; ELF5 is restricted to
salivary gland, breast and bladder with some lung, kidney and skin; EHF covers salivary gland,
esophagus, prostate, colon, skin, bladder and breast [PMID:30200227]. ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 are more widely
expressed, with prominent hematopoietic and lymphoid expression.

## The motif

The literature writes the class II site as CCCGGAAGT, differing from the class I consensus
ACCGGAAGT at a single position: the base three steps 5' of the GGA core, where class I strongly
disfavors C and the ELF group accepts or prefers it [PMID:20517297,21548782]. With the extra 5' adenine that most
in vitro models here include, the site reads ACCCGGAAGT, which is what the motifs assigned to this
family agree on. The recognition chemistry is identical to the rest of the family: two invariant
arginines in helix H3 hydrogen-bond the two guanines of GGA, a wing lysine contacts DNA 5' of the
core and a turn lysine contacts the opposite strand 3' of it [PMID:8602247], so the core is read directly and the
flanks through backbone geometry [PMID:21548782]. That makes the discriminating information one or two low-content
positions, and the six ELF/EHF proteins are not distinguishable from each other by sequence: the
JASPAR models for EHF (MA0598.4) and ELF3 (MA0640.3) have the identical consensus CACTTCCTG.
One variant is worth recognizing. CCGGAAGT contains a CpG, and methylating that CpG blocks ETS
binding [PMID:21548782,28473536]; the methylation-aware HOCOMOCO models for ELF2, ELF3 and ELF4 in this family instead read
CAGGAAGT, a form with no CpG. Whether that is cause or coincidence, both forms are in wide use and
a scan should allow CAGGAAG as well as CCGGAAG.

## Where it acts

Two contexts dominate. ELF1, ELF2 and ELF4 contribute to the redundant ETS occupancy of
CpG-island promoters, where a strong consensus 20-40 bp upstream of the transcription start site is
bound interchangeably by many ETS proteins [PMID:20517297,21548782]; a hit there is a poor basis for naming a factor. The
ESE members act mostly at epithelial enhancers and tissue-specific promoters, where their sites
are frequently non-consensus and sit among other epithelial regulators. Documented examples
include EHF in bronchial epithelium, where it is induced by inflammatory mediators and represses CFTR
from an airway-selective element 35 kb upstream of the CFTR promoter [PMID:29572268,30200227]; EHF across enhancers that define corneal epithelial identity [PMID:24142692];
and ELF5 at genes of the mammary alveolar program, including repression of SNAI2 [PMID:18316476,23086238]. Because the
motif is short and its family-discriminating positions weak, cell type - which ELF genes are
actually expressed - is usually more informative about which protein is bound than the sequence is.

## Biology and disease

The ESE factors maintain epithelial differentiation. Elf5-null mouse embryos die by about E7.5
from a trophoblast defect [PMID:15650748,30200227], and loss of a single Elf5 allele blocks mammary alveolar development in
pregnancy [PMID:15650748,18316476]; ELF5 also holds cells in an epithelial state by repressing SNAI2, and its loss promotes
epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metastasis in breast cancer models [PMID:23086238]. About 30% of Elf3-null
embryos die around E11.5 and survivors have abnormal small intestinal epithelium with reduced
goblet cells [PMID:30200227]. The consequences in human cancer are mostly loss of function: ELF3 is recurrently
mutated in roughly 6% of bladder cancers, mucinous ovarian cancers, cholangiocarcinomas and
gallbladder cancers, about 10% of ampullary carcinomas and about 13% of cervical adenocarcinomas,
with a large share of inactivating alleles [PMID:30200227]; EHF is downregulated with promoter methylation in
prostate cancer [PMID:30200227]. Ehf-null mice are born at Mendelian ratios but develop skin papillomas, corneal ulcers and heightened
colitis susceptibility, and gut-specific deletion impairs goblet cell differentiation [PMID:34180969].

## Reading a hit

A match identifies an ELF/EHF-type ETS site, and it does so only weakly. The sequence separating
this family from class I ETS is a single flanking base, so a hit that scores well for ELF3 will
almost always also score well for ETS1, ERG or ELK1, and the reverse; if you need to know which
protein is bound, use expression and ChIP data, not the motif. The GGAA core is expected millions
of times per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome, so context - accessibility, conservation, an epithelial
enhancer, neighboring sites - has to carry the inference. Evidence quality is uneven within the
family: ELF1, ELF2, ELF3, ELF4 and ELF5 all have in vitro (HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX) HOCOMOCO
models, but EHF's only HOCOMOCO model here is ChIP-derived, so "EHF binds this sequence" rests on
weaker evidence than for its relatives. Two of the three Vierstra archetypes grouped here
(AC0452:ELF, AC0645:ELF) [PMID:32728250] have GGAT-containing consensus sequences and match motifs outside this
family better than motifs inside it; treat them as loosely attached. Consensus strings also appear
on either strand - CACTTCCTG and CAGGAAGTG are the same site.
families.caveats:
The one base that distinguishes this family from class I ETS is a low-information
flanking position, so in practice a hit means "an ETS site" and not "an ELF site", let alone a
specific ELF protein; the JASPAR EHF and ELF3 models are literally the same consensus. Which of
the six proteins is bound has to come from expression or ChIP, not from sequence. Within the
family, EHF's only HOCOMOCO model here is ChIP-derived rather than in vitro, so its label carries
less weight than ELF1-ELF5, which have HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX support. Two of the three
Vierstra ELF archetypes in this family have GGAT-type consensus sequences and their nearest
neighbours lie outside the family. Allow both CCGGAAG and the CpG-free CAGGAAG form when scanning.

timeline.finding: Elf5-null embryos die before E7.5, and loss of one Elf5 allele arrests mammary alveolar development in pregnancy through an epithelial-autonomous defect; a second knockout line confirmed the embryonic lethality and traced it to loss of extraembryonic ectoderm.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockout, mammary transplantation
timeline.open: Which Elf5 target genes, and which DNA sites, carry the mammary phenotype was unknown.

timeline.finding: Elf5 specifies the secretory alveolar lineage: knockout prevents formation of secretory epithelium, inducible overexpression drives alveolar differentiation and milk secretion in virgin mice, and CD61+ luminal progenitors accumulate without it.
timeline.methods: Knockout, inducible transgenic overexpression, flow cytometry of mammary progenitors

timeline.finding: Profiling all human and mouse ETS proteins puts the ELF proteins in class II, which tolerates the C three bases 5' of the core that class I rejects, a difference traced to a single leucine where class I carries phenylalanine or tyrosine; ETV6 and ETV7 are split off as class IIb, and ELF1 ChIP-seq peaks are strongly promoter-enriched.
timeline.methods: High-throughput microwell binding assay, protein-binding microarrays, site-directed mutagenesis, ChIP-seq
timeline.open: No sequence feature separated one class IIa ELF protein from another.

timeline.finding: Elf5 suppresses the epithelial-mesenchymal transition in mammary development and breast cancer metastasis by directly repressing Snail2.
timeline.methods: Conditional knockout, EMT and metastasis models, MMTV-neu tumour model, clinical breast cancer samples

timeline.finding: EHF promotes corneal epithelial fate through both activating and repressing target genes, with likely interplay with KLF4 and KLF5.
timeline.methods: Transcriptome time course, loss of function, ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Methylation-sensitive SELEX across 542 human transcription factors finds ETS-family proteins generally inhibited by CpG methylation, which bears directly on the CpG inside CCGGAAGT.
timeline.methods: Methyl-HT-SELEX
timeline.open: How methylation shapes which ELF sites are used in cells was not measured.

timeline.finding: In bronchial epithelium EHF targets inflammation and wound-repair genes, and an siRNA screen of about 1500 factors identifies it, with KLF5, as one of the strongest repressors of CFTR, acting at an airway-selective element 35 kb upstream of the CFTR promoter.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, RNA-seq after depletion, siRNA screen, ChIP in primary bronchial epithelial cells
timeline.open: How the cystic fibrosis modifier variant near EHF changes EHF activity was not established.

timeline.finding: Ehf-null mice are born at Mendelian ratios but develop facial skin papillomas, preputial or vulval abscesses and corneal ulcers and are more susceptible to colitis; gut-specific deletion impairs goblet cell differentiation and enhances Apc-initiated adenomas. This overturns the 2018 review statement that no Ehf deletion phenotype had been reported.
timeline.methods: Germline and intestine-specific knockout mice

open: Why the methylation-aware HOCOMOCO models for ELF2, ELF3 and ELF4 read CAGGAAGT while the unmethylated in vitro models read CCGGAAGT is not established: the A may simply avoid a CpG whose methylation blocks ETS binding, or it may be a genuine second preference that persists in cells.

Two footprint archetypes grouped here read GGAT, whereas the ESE literature describes ELF3, ELF5 and EHF as GGAA binders and class II proteins as more sensitive than class I to the A-to-T change that creates GGAT; whether these archetypes record real ELF binding at GGAT sites or SPDEF-like footprints is unresolved.

Whether ELF3 acts as a tumour suppressor or a tumour promoter depends on context and is unsettled: inactivating, often heterozygous, mutations in bladder, ovarian and biliary cancers argue for loss of function, while amplification in colorectal and gastric cancer and raised expression in prostate cancer and mutant cervical adenocarcinomas point the other way.

families.name: HSF
families.def: Heat-shock element, inverted nGAAn repeats. HSF1/2/4/5, HSFY1/2.
families.short: Heat shock factors bind the heat shock element (HSE), an array of the 5-base unit nGAAn in alternating orientation: nTTCn-nGAAn-nTTCn and longer runs. The DNA-binding domain is a winged helix, and HSF proteins trimerize through a coiled coil so that three subunits each read one 5-base unit, with further trimers loading cooperatively onto longer arrays. Humans have HSF1, HSF2, HSF4, HSF5 and the Y-linked HSFY1/HSFY2. HSF1 is the stress-inducible member, held inactive as a monomer until proteotoxic stress triggers trimerization. HSEs drive heat shock protein genes, and HSF1 activity also supports malignant transformation; HSF4 mutations cause congenital cataract.
families.long:
## The factors

Human HSF1 is the stress-responsive member, kept as an inactive monomer by intramolecular
coiled-coil interactions and by chaperone binding, and converted on proteotoxic stress into a
DNA-binding trimer that is further tuned by phosphorylation, acetylation and SUMOylation [PMID:20628411]. HSF2 is
developmentally and differentiation-regulated, binds many of the same elements, and forms
heterotrimers with HSF1 [PMID:17213196]. HSF4 is expressed mainly in lens and other epithelia and, unlike HSF1, is
constitutively trimeric and can act as a repressor at HSF1 targets [PMID:20628411]. HSF5 is poorly characterized
and largely testis-restricted. HSFY1 and HSFY2 lie in multicopy on the Y chromosome within the
AZFb interval and are expressed in testis [PMID:22158087]. All members share an N-terminal winged-helix DNA-binding
domain followed by hydrophobic repeats (HR-A/B) that mediate trimerization; the domain is among the
most conserved DNA-binding domains in eukaryotes.

## The motif

The recognition unit is 5 bases, nGAAn, and a functional heat shock element is an inverted array of
at least three of them [PMID:3146692,2590940]. The classical rendering is nTTCnnGAAnnTTCn; the two permutations,
head-to-head and tail-to-tail repeats of the 5-bp unit, bind with similar affinity and with
striking two-fold symmetry, which was the original evidence that the unit and not a longer
palindrome is the recognition module [PMID:2590940]. HSF binds arrays cooperatively, so four, five or six units
give progressively higher affinity and are common in strongly inducible promoters [PMID:1899357]. The crystal
structure of an HSF DNA-binding domain showed a three-helix bundle capped by a four-stranded
antiparallel beta sheet, a winged-helix variant of the helix-turn-helix motif [PMID:8284672], and the human HSF1
structure in complex with DNA showed how the trimer positions three such domains around the helix [PMID:26727489].
Each domain reads GAA in the major groove, so most of the information sits on the GAA/TTC triplets,
but the flanks are not free: the two positions just 5' of each GAA affect whether an element works
[PMID:3146692], and the in vitro models here fix them as the TA of TTCTAGAA, with a weaker CG preference
in GAAcgTTC. That is why database models for HSF1, HSF2 and
HSF4 look like TTCTAGAA-cg-TTC or aGAA-cg-TTCTAGAA: they are the same three-unit array written with
different phase and strand. The HSFY and HSF5 models are different in a real way, favoring TTCGAA
and CGTTCGAA arrangements, so the family separates loosely into an HSF1/2/4 group and an
HSFY/HSF5 group; overall cohesion (0.66) is the lowest in this batch. Within the HSF1/2/4 group no
member is distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

HSEs are promoter-proximal at the classic targets: HSPA1A/HSPA1B, HSP90AA1, DNAJB1, HSPB1 and the
other chaperone and co-chaperone genes carry clustered HSEs within a few hundred bases of the
start site, usually with a paused RNA polymerase already engaged so that induction is a release
step rather than a recruitment step [PMID:35687139]. HSF1 is also found at thousands of distal enhancers, and the
enhancer repertoire differs between stress types: heat shock and oxidative stress drive HSF1 and
HSF2 to partly distinct gene and enhancer sets [PMID:35687139]. GAGA-type factors and, in mammals, SP1 and NF-Y
occupy the same promoters; NF-Y binds the CCAAT boxes of several heat shock promoters. In cancer
cells, HSF1 occupies a large set of non-chaperone genes that is distinct from the classical heat
shock program [PMID:22863008], and in tumor stroma it drives a separate program in cancer-associated fibroblasts.
HSF1 also localizes to sex chromatin during meiotic repression.

## Biology and disease

Hsf1-null mice are viable but lack thermotolerance, show tissue-specific failure of stress-inducible
chaperone expression [PMID:12112007], and develop demyelination and protein aggregate accumulation in the CNS;
Hsf1 is also required for oocyte meiosis. HSF1 activity extends lifespan in C. elegans together
with chaperones, linking the pathway to proteostasis in aging [PMID:20628411]. In cancer, HSF1 supports malignant
transformation through a transcriptional program distinct from the heat shock response [PMID:22863008], high
nuclear HSF1 predicts poor outcome in breast cancer, and loss of Hsf1 suppresses lymphoma in
p53-deficient mice. HSF4 mutations in the DNA-binding domain cause autosomal dominant lamellar and
Marner cataract [PMID:12089525], and a homozygous splice mutation causes recessive congenital cataract; Hsf4-null
mice develop cataract with reduced gamma-S-crystallin. HSF2 contributes to inducible hsp expression
through heterotrimerization with HSF1 rather than acting alone [PMID:17213196]. HSFY copy loss accompanies AZFb
deletions in azoospermia, though targeted studies argue HSFY genes are not themselves required for
spermatocyte maturation [PMID:22158087], so the association may be positional.

## Reading a hit

A three-unit HSE is reasonably informative, and models here reach 17-21 bits, so a good match is
worth following up. Two specific traps make this family riskier than that number suggests. First,
nGAAn arrays overlap other purine-rich motifs. A GGAA core is the ETS recognition sequence and
GGAAA is the NFAT core, so loose HSF models score on ETS and NFAT sites and vice versa; one
Vierstra archetype in this family is explicitly labelled HSF/NFATC for that reason. A single
nGAAn unit is worthless as evidence. Second, and more concretely, several ChIP-derived HSF1 models
in these collections are not HSEs at all but resemble the tRNA internal B-box promoter element
(GTTCGAANNC) [PMID:2109308]: consensus strings such as GGGTTCGAATCCC appear in CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and Vierstra
entries labelled HSF1 or HSF, and these are the entries whose label agreement with the rest of the
family is lowest. Treat a GGGTTCGAATCC-like match as a possible tRNA gene rather than an HSE. The
evidence codes help: HSF1, HSF2 and HSF4 grade-A or grade-B models built on SELEX plus methyl-SELEX
(PSM, SM) give the canonical three-unit HSE, while the B-box-like models are ChIP-only (P). Finally,
a genuine HSE hit does not mean the gene is stress-inducible, because HSF2 and HSF4 occupy the same
elements constitutively and HSF4 can repress there.
families.caveats: The 5-base unit nGAAn is useless alone; require at least three alternating units. nGAAn arrays cross-score with ETS (GGAA) and NFAT (GGAAA) sites, and one archetype here is labelled HSF/NFATC for that reason. Several ChIP-only models labelled HSF1 or HSF match the tRNA B-box (GGGTTCGAATCC) rather than an HSE and have the lowest label agreement in the family; a hit of that shape may be a tRNA gene. The family also splits into an HSF1/2/4 group and a distinct HSFY/HSF5 group, and cohesion is the lowest in this batch. A hit does not imply stress-inducibility, since HSF2 and HSF4 bind the same elements constitutively.

timeline.methods: Promoter deletion mutants, synthetic element transfer, transfection, S1 mapping
timeline.open: What bound the element, and whether the palindrome or a smaller unit was the recognition module.

timeline.finding: Heat shock elements are modular, built from GAA blocks in alternating orientation at 2-nucleotide intervals, giving a 5-nucleotide periodicity; functional elements need three or more blocks, and the two nucleotides upstream of each GAA affect competence.
timeline.methods: Synthetic element mutagenesis, reporter assays

timeline.finding: The minimal site for stable binding by Drosophila HSF is an inverted repeat of the 5-bp unit nGAAn; head-to-head and tail-to-tail arrangements bind equally, footprints grow with each added unit, and cross-linking indicates HSF binds as a trimer.
timeline.methods: EMSA, DNase I footprinting, protein cross-linking

timeline.finding: HSF binding is cooperative both within a trimer and between trimers: occupying one of two adjacent trimer sites raises binding to the second by more than 2000-fold, explaining why strong heat shock promoters carry multiple elements.
timeline.methods: Quantitative DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: The 1.8 A structure of the HSF DNA-binding domain is a three-helix bundle capped by a four-stranded antiparallel beta sheet, a variant of the helix-turn-helix fold.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: The domain was solved without DNA, so base contacts were inferred.

timeline.finding: In highly malignant human cancer cells HSF1 drives a transcriptional program distinct from the heat shock response, including many non-chaperone genes, and the program is active in primary breast, colon and lung tumors and associated with metastasis and death.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, expression profiling, analysis of patient tumors

timeline.finding: Cocrystal structures of the human HSF1 DNA-binding domain with heat shock element DNA, compared with the paralogue Skn7, show that single amino acid changes in the domain can switch DNA-binding specificity, and support a model of the trimer embracing the element.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, comparative mutagenesis, structural modeling
timeline.open: Whether natural paralogues such as HSFY use such substitutions to read different sites.

timeline.finding: HSF1 and HSF2 bind distinct genes and enhancers in oxidative stress and heat shock, release paused RNA polymerase II at promoters, and HSF1 occupies many chaperone genes under oxidative stress without activating them.
timeline.methods: PRO-seq, ChIP-seq

open: The GGGTTCGAATCC-like models labelled HSF1 or HSF are ChIP-only and match the tRNA B-box, and whether they reflect genuine HSF1 occupancy at tRNA genes or contamination of HSF1 peak sets by heavily occupied tRNA loci has not been established.

Whether HSFY and HSF5 have their own specificity is not resolved: the in vitro HSFY1 models favor TTCGAA-type arrays unlike HSF1/2/4, and the two low-grade HSF5 models disagree with each other (ACGTTCYA versus AACATTCCA, the latter resembling a TEAD site); single-residue changes can switch HSF specificity, but in vivo targets of HSFY and HSF5 are unknown.

families.name: ZIC
families.def: GLI-like CCTGCTGNG. ZIC1-5.
families.short: ZIC1 to ZIC5 are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger proteins whose DNA-binding domains are the closest relatives of GLI outside the GLIS subfamily, and which read a GLI-like site. In vitro selection gives an optimal ZIC site almost identical to the GLI consensus but bound with lower affinity; modern high-throughput measurements extend it to GACCCCCCGCTGTG, whose reverse complement, CACAGCAGGGGGT, is how several databases write the same motif. ZIC proteins also bind GLI zinc fingers directly and can raise or lower GLI-dependent transcription. They act mainly in dorsal neural tube, neural crest, somites and cerebellum, and human mutations cause holoprosencephaly (ZIC2), X-linked heterotaxy (ZIC3) and Dandy-Walker malformation (ZIC1 with ZIC4).
families.long:
## The factors

The ZIC family has five human members, ZIC1 to ZIC5, each with a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers
that is more similar to the GLI fingers than to any other vertebrate zinc-finger class. ZIC1 and
ZIC4 are a divergently transcribed pair on chromosome 3q24; ZIC2 and ZIC5 are a similar pair on
13q32; ZIC3 sits alone on Xq26 [PMID:23443491]. They bind as monomers. In addition to binding DNA, ZIC proteins
associate physically with GLI zinc fingers and, depending on cell type, either enhance or suppress
GLI-dependent transactivation [PMID:11238441,11053430], so part of their activity is exerted as a GLI cofactor rather than
through their own site. Expression is largely neural and paraxial: dorsal neural tube and roof
plate, neural crest, somites, and, postnatally, cerebellar granule cells. ZIC2 is also expressed in
early epiblast and embryonic stem cells.

## The motif

The first systematic definition of the ZIC site used gel-shift-based target selection with ZIC1,
ZIC2 and ZIC3 and recovered a sequence almost identical to the GLI binding sequence, but bound with
lower affinity than GLI [PMID:11053430]; consistently, reporter activation by ZIC proteins depended less on the
presence of a GLI site than GLI1 activation did, and ZIC proteins activated many promoters lacking
one [PMID:11053430]. Circular-dichroism comparisons of ZIC, GLI and GLIS finger domains on DNA support a shared
recognition mode [PMID:18298960].

High-throughput SELEX extends the site to a 13-14 base element usually written GACCCCCCGCTGTG [PMID:23332764]. Its
5' half, GACCCCCC, is the GLIS-like version of the GLI core, and the 3' extension GCTGTG is what
distinguishes ZIC from GLI and GLIS in practice. Several databases write the same element on the
other strand, as CACAGCAGGGGGT or the shorter CNCAGCAGG, and the ontology form CCTGCTGNG is the
reverse complement of that short core; none of these is a different motif. The data consensus here,
CNCAGCAGGGGGCC, is the reverse-strand form of the full site. One real subtlety is visible in the
collection: the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX versions of the ZIC motif differ at a central CpG
(CAGCGGGGGG versus CAGCAGGGGG), so cytosine methylation shifts the measured preference at that
position [PMID:28473536], and different database entries for the same protein can look inconsistent for that reason.
No experiment distinguishes ZIC1 from ZIC2, ZIC3, ZIC4 or ZIC5 by sequence; the JASPAR
Zic1::Zic2 entry is modeled as a dimer but its consensus is the same short core.

## Where it acts

ZIC sites are enhancer elements. In mouse embryonic stem cells ZIC2 occupies thousands of
enhancers, both active and poised, and works with the Mbd3/NuRD chromatin-remodeling complex to regulate
genes linked to differentiation [PMID:25699711]; later work describes ZIC2 acting first as a priming factor on closed chromatin during
neural induction and then as an activator at established enhancers [PMID:42033229]. In the cerebellum and dorsal
neural tube ZIC occupancy overlaps with GLI-responsive elements, which is expected given the shared
core, and ZIC and GLI compete or cooperate at the same sequences. Because the informative part of
the site is roughly nine to thirteen bases with a GC-rich core, matches are common in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, and the motif overlaps in scoring space with GLI, GLIS and, at the CAGCAGG core,
with simple CAG-repeat and E-box-adjacent sequence.

## Biology and disease

Gli/Zic factors together pattern the vertebrate neural plate by defining domains of differentiation,
with ZIC activity dorsal to the SHH-dependent ventral domains [PMID:9634234]. Heterozygous ZIC2 loss-of-function
causes holoprosencephaly type 5, characteristically with a middle-interhemispheric variant and
distinctive facial features [PMID:29442327]; ZIC3 mutations cause X-linked heterotaxy with complex congenital heart
defects and laterality reversal [PMID:29442328]; heterozygous deletion of the linked ZIC1 and ZIC4 pair causes
Dandy-Walker malformation [PMID:15338008], and mouse work shows that combined Zic1 and Zic4 loss disturbs several
developmental programs in the cerebellar anlage rather than one [PMID:21307096]. ZIC5 was identified in Xenopus as a
neural-crest regulator [PMID:23443491]. Beyond development, ZIC family members are recurrently deregulated in
tumors, most consistently by promoter hypermethylation and silencing; ZIC1, for example, is
downregulated by promoter hypermethylation in gastric cancer [PMID:19135984].

## Reading a hit

Treat a ZIC match as "ZIC family", never as a specific paralogue: all five members share one motif.
Then treat it cautiously as "ZIC rather than GLI". The two families were defined on essentially the
same 5' core, and separating them depends on the 3' GCTGTG extension, which carries relatively
little information; a short or weak match can belong to either, and a ZIC hit inside a
Hedgehog-responsive enhancer is as likely to be a GLI site. Note also that a real ZIC effect need
not require a ZIC site at all, since ZIC proteins act as GLI cofactors and in reporter assays
activate promoters lacking the site. The GC-rich core makes the motif frequent in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, so isolated matches are weak evidence. In the data behind this family, one Vierstra
archetype labelled ZIC (AC0536) has the consensus GACCACCC and matches the GLI family better than
its own; that is the expected failure mode for this pair, not a claim that the label is wrong.
families.caveats: The five ZIC paralogues are indistinguishable by sequence, so a hit names the family only. The larger problem is the GLI boundary: ZIC and GLI were defined on nearly the same core, ZIC binds the GLI consensus in vitro (with lower affinity), and the two are separated only by a weakly informative 3' extension, so weak matches cannot be assigned to one family. One Vierstra archetype labelled ZIC in these data in fact scores closest to GLI. In vitro entries for the same ZIC protein can also disagree at a central CpG because the methyl-SELEX and standard SELEX preferences differ there. Finally, ZIC can act on GLI-dependent transcription without occupying its own site.

timeline.finding: zic is cloned from mouse cerebellum as a zinc-finger gene expressed in granule-cell precursors, naming the family and placing its zinc fingers closest to the GLI fingers.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, in situ hybridization
timeline.open: No binding site had been measured; the GLI similarity was a sequence inference.

timeline.finding: Zic2 and Gli proteins are shown to pattern the frog neural plate into alternating domains, Zic2 inducing neural crest and inhibiting neurogenesis while Gli does the opposite, establishing the two as a functionally paired system.
timeline.methods: Xenopus expression and overexpression assays
timeline.open: Whether the antagonism was exerted through shared DNA sites or through protein interaction.

timeline.finding: Gel-shift target selection gives ZIC1, ZIC2 and ZIC3 a site almost identical to the GLI site but bound with lower affinity, and ZIC and GLI proteins are shown to associate physically through their zinc-finger domains and to modulate each other's activity.
timeline.methods: EMSA-based site selection with mutational analysis, reporter assays, co-immunoprecipitation
timeline.open: Because ZIC proteins also activated promoters lacking the site, how much of their activity is site-dependent was unclear.

timeline.finding: Heterozygous deletion of the linked ZIC1-ZIC4 pair is identified as a cause of Dandy-Walker malformation, giving the family its first human cerebellar phenotype.
timeline.methods: Human deletion mapping in patients, mouse expression analysis

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX extends the ZIC site to a 13-14 base element, GACCCCCCGCTGTG, whose 3' GCTGTG extension is what separates it from the GLI and GLIS versions of the shared GC-rich core.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Whether the low-information 3' extension is used to partition sites in vivo.

timeline.finding: ZIC2 is mapped genome-wide in mouse embryonic stem cells and found at thousands of enhancers, where it is required for normal differentiation, moving the family from a patterning gene to a measured enhancer-binding factor.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, proteomics of associated complexes, differentiation assays

timeline.finding: Methyl-HT-SELEX shows that the measured ZIC preference shifts at the central CpG, so the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models of the same protein differ (CAGCGGGGGG versus CAGCAGGGGG).
timeline.methods: Methylation-sensitive SELEX across 542 human factors
timeline.open: Whether methylation-dependent ZIC binding occurs at methylated regulatory DNA in cells.

timeline.finding: During neural induction from mouse embryonic stem cells, ZIC2 binds de novo to closed distal enhancers and raises their accessibility at pluripotency exit, then activates a subset of those primed enhancers, so one factor occupies the same sites in two mechanistically different roles; ZIC3 compensates for its loss in the pluripotent state.
timeline.methods: Genome editing in mESC-derived neural progenitors, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, transcriptomics
timeline.open: What converts a primed ZIC2-bound enhancer into an active one is not identified.

open: How much of ZIC activity runs through the ZIC site itself is unsettled: ZIC proteins activate reporters lacking the site and bind GLI zinc fingers directly, yet genome-wide maps show them occupying thousands of enhancers in a sequence-dependent way.

Whether the 3' GCTGTG extension is actually used in cells to partition sites between ZIC and GLI/GLIS is unknown; it is the only feature separating the two families in vitro, and it carries little information.

Whether the methylation-dependent shift at the central CpG, seen when HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models of the same ZIC protein are compared, has any counterpart at methylated enhancers in vivo has not been tested.

Nothing in the measured specificities separates ZIC1 from ZIC2, ZIC3, ZIC4 or ZIC5, yet their loss-of-function phenotypes differ sharply (holoprosencephaly, heterotaxy, Dandy-Walker malformation); whether that reflects expression domains alone or unmeasured differences in site preference or partner use is open.

families.name: ZNF24 / ZSCAN-type promoter ZFs
families.def: SCAN-domain zinc fingers with defined promoter motifs. ZNF24, ZSCAN4, ZKSCAN1/3, ZSCAN21/22/29.
families.short: A small group of SCAN-domain C2H2 zinc fingers with defined, experimentally supported binding sites at promoters and microsatellites: ZNF24 (also known as ZNF191 and ZSCAN3), ZSCAN4, ZSCAN21, ZSCAN22, ZSCAN29, ZKSCAN1 and ZKSCAN3. They are grouped by domain architecture and a promoter-proximal style of binding, not by a shared motif: the seven proteins read at least five unrelated sequences. ZNF24 binds a TCAT tetranucleotide repeat, ZSCAN4 a CA-repeat core, ZSCAN29 an inverted pair of GTCTAC hexamers, ZKSCAN3 GGCTAGCCC and ZKSCAN1 CCTACTATG. Reported functions are equally varied, from repressing VEGFA transcription to repressing autophagy genes and protecting telomeres in early embryos.
families.long:
## The factors

Seven proteins, all C2H2 zinc fingers with an N-terminal SCAN domain, an approximately 80-residue leucine-rich module that mediates self-association and selective association with other SCAN proteins (Williams et al. 1999) [PMID:10567577]. The NMR structure of the MZF1 SCAN domain is a domain-swapped dimer of five-helix monomers, with helix 3 forming the core of the interface and a dissociation constant near 600 nM (Peterson et al. 2006) [PMID:16950398], so these factors are expected to act at least partly as dimers. ZKSCAN1 (7q22.1, formerly ZNF139/ZNF36) and ZKSCAN3 (6p22.1, formerly ZNF306) additionally carry a KRAB domain and can recruit TRIM28. ZNF24 (18q12.2) has been published under several names, including ZNF191, mouse Zfp191 and the alias ZSCAN3, and is 94% identical to its mouse orthologue (Li et al. 2006) [PMID:17064688]. SCAN genes generally sit in tandem clusters and carry between 3 and 14 fingers (Edelstein and Collins 2005) [PMID:16139965]. The wider SCAN group is split across this atlas: other ZSCAN and ZKSCAN genes have a separate entry, and MZF1 itself is filed under other C2H2 zinc fingers.

## The motif

Not one motif. Cohesion is 0.44, and the 24 matrices form roughly seven tight per-protein clusters. Every matrix has a near-identical partner in the family (median best within-family similarity 0.96), but that partner is almost always the same protein measured again in another database. ZNF24 reads a TCAT tetranucleotide repeat: JASPAR MA1124.1 and CIS-BP M08093 both give CATTCATTCATTC and the HOCOMOCO model is TGAATGAATGAATG, the reverse complement. That agrees with the literature, in which ZNF191/ZNF24 binds the polymorphic intronic TCAT repeat HUMTH01 of the tyrosine hydroxylase gene, and allele length changes both the amount and the pattern of binding (Albanese et al. 2001) [PMID:11532988]. ZSCAN29 reads GTCTACAC; its methyl-SELEX model is ATAAACGTCTACAC and the related unnamed archetype AC0339 reads GCGTAGACGTCTACAC, that is GTAGAC followed by GTCTAC, an inverted repeat of the same hexamer. That is the arrangement a SCAN-mediated dimer contacting two half-sites would produce, but no structure or mutagenesis has tested it. ZSCAN4 reads GCACACVCTGAAA, whose core is a CA repeat, consistent with mouse Zscan4 recognizing a subset of (CA)n microsatellites (Srinivasan et al. 2020) [PMID:32219172]. ZKSCAN3 reads GGCTAGCCC, ZKSCAN1 CCTACTATG (its JASPAR entry gives the reverse complement), ZSCAN22 the CT-rich CCTCCTCCCTCAGAC, and ZSCAN21 a weak nine-bit CTCAGCACT. Two pairs are inseparable: ZSCAN1, in the other SCAN entry, matches the ZSCAN4 motif at 0.95, and a grade-A HOCOMOCO model for the KRAB zinc finger ZNF500 is GCGTCTACACTANCC, the ZSCAN29 site.

## Where it acts

TCAT and CA repeats are ubiquitous microsatellites, so ZNF24- and ZSCAN4-type matches are common and mostly lie outside regulatory elements. ZNF24 has one precisely mapped functional site, an 11 bp element in the proximal VEGFA promoter (Jia et al. 2013) [PMID:23212515]. ZKSCAN3 occupies the promoters of more than 60 autophagy and lysosome genes, with MAP1LC3B and WIPI2 confirmed as direct targets, and responds to starvation in the opposite direction to TFEB (Chauhan et al. 2013) [PMID:23434374]. Mouse Zscan4 is restricted to two-cell embryos and a small, transient subpopulation of embryonic stem cells, where it localizes to telomeres and to nuclease-resistant, histone-dense microsatellite regions (Zalzman et al. 2010; Srinivasan et al. 2020) [PMID:20336070,32219172].

## Biology and disease

Zfp191-null mouse embryos are severely growth-retarded and die around embryonic day 7.5, and no homozygous embryonic stem cell lines can be derived; tyrosine hydroxylase expression is unaffected, so the phenotype is a proliferation defect rather than a TH defect (Li et al. 2006) [PMID:17064688]. ZNF24 represses VEGFA: overexpression produces VEGF-like vascular defects in zebrafish that VEGF rescues, reduces tumour angiogenesis in a breast cancer xenograft, and ZNF24 and VEGF levels are inversely correlated in human breast tumours (Jia et al. 2013) [PMID:23212515]. Silencing ZKSCAN3 induces autophagy and lysosome biogenesis (Chauhan et al. 2013) [PMID:23434374]. Zscan4 knockdown shortens telomeres, raises sister chromatid exchange and karyotype abnormalities, and drives embryonic stem cells to crisis by passage eight (Zalzman et al. 2010) [PMID:20336070]; its loss also increases DNA damage in two-cell embryos in a transcription-dependent manner (Srinivasan et al. 2020) [PMID:32219172].

## Reading a hit

Which protein the hit belongs to matters much more than the family label. Repeat-based matches, ZNF24's (TCAT)n and ZSCAN4's (CA)n core, will number in the tens of thousands genome-wide and are not evidence of occupancy; for ZNF24, repeat length is part of the signal, so genotype the repeat rather than scoring a fixed-width matrix. ZSCAN4 and ZSCAN1 share a motif, and so do ZSCAN29 and ZNF500, making those labels interchangeable from sequence alone. The evidence is mixed: five of the seven HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only (evidence code P), while ZSCAN4 and ZSCAN29 have in vitro support (codes SM and M). The ZSCAN21 model carries about nine bits and should not be scanned by itself. The ZSCAN22 matrix is CT-rich and hard to separate from the many other CT- and GC-rich zinc-finger matrices in this atlas.
families.caveats: This entry holds seven proteins with at least five unrelated motifs; cohesion is 0.44 and there is no family consensus, so read a hit as a hit to the named protein. Two of the motifs, ZNF24's TCAT repeat and ZSCAN4's CA-repeat core, are microsatellites that match tens of thousands of loci by chance. ZSCAN4 cannot be distinguished from ZSCAN1, nor ZSCAN29 from the KRAB zinc finger ZNF500. Five of seven HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only, so for those the enriched sequence may belong to a partner rather than the tagged protein. The ZSCAN21 model is too weak to scan on its own.

timeline.finding: The SCAN box was shown to be an oligomerization domain that mediates self-association and selective association with other SCAN-bearing zinc fingers, which is the only property all seven proteins in this entry share.
timeline.methods: yeast two-hybrid, co-immunoprecipitation, in vitro association assays

timeline.finding: ZNF191, later renamed ZNF24, was cloned as a protein binding the TCAT motif of the polymorphic intronic microsatellite HUMTH01 in the tyrosine hydroxylase gene, and common allele lengths were shown to silence reporter expression quantitatively and to change both the amount and the pattern of ZNF191 binding.
timeline.methods: protein purification and cloning, electrophoretic mobility shift assays, reporter assays
timeline.open: Because the TCAT core is ubiquitous in the genome, it was unclear whether this binding mattered anywhere other than at HUMTH01.

timeline.finding: The NMR structure of the MZF1 SCAN domain, a domain-swapped dimer of five-helix monomers with a dissociation constant near 600 nM, provided the physical model for dimerization in this group and the expectation that some of its sites should be dyadic.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, fluorescence polarization

timeline.finding: Zfp191-null mouse embryos were found to be severely growth-retarded and to die around embryonic day 7.5, with no homozygous ES cell lines derivable, while tyrosine hydroxylase expression was unaffected, so the factor's essential role is in cell proliferation rather than in the TH regulation that first identified it.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, blastocyst outgrowth, RNA interference

timeline.finding: Zscan4 was shown to be expressed transiently in about 5% of mouse ES cells at any time, to localize to telomeres, and to be required for telomere maintenance and karyotype stability, with knockdown driving cells to crisis by passage eight.
timeline.methods: live reporter imaging, knockdown, telomere and karyotype analysis
timeline.open: No DNA sequence was assigned to Zscan4, so whether its telomeric localization was sequence-directed was unknown.

timeline.finding: Two members were given mapped target sets in the same year: ZNF24 was shown to repress VEGFA through an 11 bp element in the proximal promoter, with vascular consequences in zebrafish and xenografts, and ZKSCAN3 was shown to repress more than 60 autophagy and lysosome genes, acting opposite to TFEB under starvation.
timeline.methods: reporter and gel-shift mapping, zebrafish and xenograft models; ChIP-seq, knockdown, autophagy assays

timeline.finding: Direct profiling of 131 human C2H2 proteins, giving models for 78 that had none, supplied most of the remaining matrices in this entry and showed that these proteins' co-factor repertoires are as varied as their motifs, undercutting any expectation of a shared SCAN-family mechanism.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, affinity purification-mass spectrometry, knockdown expression profiling

timeline.finding: Zscan4 was shown to recognize a subset of (CA)n microsatellites characterized by low nuclease sensitivity and high histone occupancy, to bind nucleosomes and protect them from disassembly under torsional strain, and to prevent DNA damage in two-cell embryos in a transcription-dependent way, replacing the telomere-centered account with a sequence- and nucleosome-based one.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and in vitro binding, nucleosome assays, embryo depletion experiments

open: Whether ZNF24 binding at TCAT repeats is functional beyond HUMTH01 is unresolved: allele length changes binding and reporter output at the tyrosine hydroxylase locus, yet tyrosine hydroxylase expression is normal in Zfp191-null embryos and the repeat occurs at tens of thousands of other loci.
ZSCAN29 and the KRAB zinc finger ZNF500 carry essentially the same grade-A motif, and nothing published says whether the two proteins genuinely share a site or one of the models is mislabelled.

The inverted GTAGAC-GTCTAC arrangement at the ZSCAN29 site is what a SCAN-mediated dimer contacting two half-sites would produce, but no structure or mutagenesis has tested half-site organization for any member of this entry.

For Zscan4 it is unclear how much of the binding is driven by the (CA)n sequence itself and how much by the nucleosome-dense, nuclease-resistant chromatin in which those microsatellites sit, since the protein binds nucleosomal DNA directly.

families.name: Grainyhead (GRHL)
families.def: AACCGGTT. GRHL1-3, TFCP2, TFCP2L1, UBP1.
families.short: The Grainyhead/CP2 family binds the palindrome AACCGGTT through an immunoglobulin-like DNA-binding domain that shares a fold with p53 but differs from it in important details. Six human members split into two branches: the epithelial GRHL1, GRHL2 and GRHL3, and the more broadly expressed TFCP2 (LSF/CP2), TFCP2L1 and UBP1 (LBP-1a). They bind as dimers, and many real elements are doubled, giving 16-26 bp tandem sites. GRHL factors control epidermal barrier formation, neural tube and palate closure, and epithelial identity, and they sit at the epithelial end of EMT regulation. Human mutations cause Van der Woude syndrome and nonsyndromic cleft palate.
families.long:
## The factors

Six human genes belong to this family. The grainyhead-like branch, GRHL1, GRHL2 and GRHL3, is
epithelial: GRHL1 and GRHL3 in epidermis and periderm, GRHL2 in most simple and stratified
epithelia including airway, gut and bladder. The CP2 branch, TFCP2 (also LSF or CP2), TFCP2L1
(CRTR-1) and UBP1 (LBP-1a), is more broadly expressed and includes the factor originally
characterized on the alpha-globin promoter [PMID:8157699]. All six share a roughly 250-residue region that carries
both DNA binding and dimerization, inherited from Drosophila Grainyhead (also called NTF-1 and
Elf-1), and the Drosophila and human domains are interchangeable enough that the family was
recognized by that conservation [PMID:8196641,12175488]. Crystal structures of the GRHL1 and GRHL2 DNA-binding domains
showed a closely similar immunoglobulin-like core sharing the overall fold of the p53 DNA-binding
domain while differing in the DNA-contacting elements [PMID:29309642]. GRHL1 binds its recognition element as a
dimer, and target-site selection is parsimonious: two conserved arginine residues make most of
the base-specific contacts [PMID:29309642].

## The motif

The consensus is the 8-bp palindrome AACCGGTT, often written with flanking A/T as AAACCGGTTT.
Because selection rests on a small number of arginine contacts, the central CCGG is the most
constrained part and the flanking AA/TT contribute the rest. The palindrome means the two halves
are equivalent, and dimer binding is the normal mode. A conspicuous feature of this family's
models is doubling: HOCOMOCO entries for TFCP2, TFCP2L1, UBP1 and GRHL3 span 15-26 columns and
contain two AACCGGTT-like units, sometimes in the arrangement AACCGGTT-N(2)-AACCGGTT. That is a
genuine property of Grh/CP2 elements rather than a modelling artifact [PMID:9668115], and it is why the highest
information content in this family (about 20 bits) comes from CP2-branch models rather than from
the single-site GRHL models. Degenerate variants are common and legitimate: AACAGGTT, AACTGGTT and
AACCAGTT all appear as database consensuses, reflecting tolerance at the central positions. No
member is reliably distinguishable from another by sequence. The GRHL and CP2 branches are similar
enough that Vierstra collapses them into archetypes named GRHL/TFCP, and this family's cohesion
(0.78) is limited mainly by the mixture of single-site and doubled models, not by disagreement
about the core.

## Where it acts

Grh/CP2 sites occur at both promoters and enhancers, with a strong bias toward epithelial
differentiation loci: the epidermal differentiation complex, tight junction and desmosome genes,
transglutaminases, and the genes of the cornified envelope. GRHL3 binding is highly dynamic: when
progenitor keratinocytes differentiate it binds mainly at super-enhancers, whereas when they migrate it
binds mainly at promoters, together with REST [PMID:28445475].
GRHL2 also occupies enhancers in pluripotent cells during exit from naive pluripotency and in
airway basal cells during mucociliary regeneration. Common neighbors are KLF4 and TP63 in
keratinocytes, IRF6 in periderm (IRF6 binds an enhancer near GRHL3 and is needed for Grhl3 expression in periderm [PMID:22931925],
although Irf6;Grhl3 double-heterozygous mice show no epistasis [PMID:24360809]),
and AP-1 at differentiation enhancers. GRHL factors recruit Trithorax-group complexes to switch on
differentiation genes [PMID:22829784], and in cancer they sit in a mutually repressive loop with ZEB1 and the
miR-200 family that keeps cells epithelial [PMID:26887977]. The palindrome is 8 bp, so chance matches are frequent;
doubled sites are much rarer and much more indicative.

## Biology and disease

Grhl3-null mice fail to form a skin permeability barrier [PMID:15831758] and develop spina bifida that is
resistant to both inositol and folate supplementation, identifying Grhl3 as the gene behind the
long-studied curly tail mouse [PMID:14608380]. Grhl3 is also required for eyelid closure and urothelial
differentiation. In humans, dominant GRHL3 mutations cause Van der Woude syndrome, the commonest
syndromic form of cleft lip and palate, in families without IRF6 mutations [PMID:24360809]; separate GRHL3 coding
variants, including a common susceptibility allele and rare truncating variants, cause and predispose
to nonsyndromic cleft palate [PMID:27018472]. GRHL2 variants are associated with age-related hearing impairment [PMID:17921507],
and GRHL2 has both oncogenic and tumor-suppressive effects depending on context, promoting the
epithelial phenotype in breast, ovarian and prostate cancer while restraining metastatic
dissemination. TFCP2 appears in cancer as a fusion partner: EWSR1-TFCP2 and FUS-TFCP2 fusions define
an aggressive intraosseous spindle and epithelioid rhabdomyosarcoma with frequent ALK
overexpression, often in the jaw and skull [PMID:33382123].

## Reading a hit

An AACCGGTT match identifies the Grh/CP2 family and no individual member. That matters because the
two branches have different biology: a hit could correspond to epithelial GRHL2 or to broadly
expressed TFCP2, and only expression or ChIP data can tell you which. At 8 bp with a palindromic
core, single matches occur often by chance, so treat a lone AACCGGTT the way you would treat any
8-mer: as a hypothesis. A doubled site, two AACCGGTT-like units within about 20 bp, is a much
stronger signal and is the form in which many validated elements occur. Also note that models in
this family differ in width by a factor of three, from 8 to 26 columns, so scores from different
databases are not comparable and a "weaker" hit may simply reflect a narrower model. The evidence
base is mixed but reasonable: several HOCOMOCO models for GRHL1, GRHL3, TFCP2, TFCP2L1 and UBP1
rest on in vitro selection (evidence codes SM, SB, S), which supports direct binding, whereas the
GRHL2 models here are ChIP-only (P) and their degenerate variants (AACAGGTT, CCGGTTTGGCCAG) should
be read as descriptions of GRHL2 peaks rather than of GRHL2's intrinsic specificity.
families.caveats: A hit names the family, not the member, and the family spans two branches with different expression: epithelial GRHL1-3 versus broadly expressed TFCP2, TFCP2L1 and UBP1. The 8-bp palindrome occurs frequently by chance, so single matches are weak; doubled AACCGGTT units within about 20 bp are much more convincing. Model widths in this family range from 8 to 26 columns, so scores across databases are not comparable. Degenerate variants such as AACAGGTT come mostly from ChIP-only GRHL2 models and describe peak composition rather than intrinsic specificity; the in vitro-supported models converge on AACCGGTT.
