timeline.open: What normal TEL does, and which DNA sites it binds, was unknown.

timeline.finding: Tel-null embryos die at E10.5-11.5 with a yolk sac angiogenic defect and intra-embryonic apoptosis while yolk sac hematopoiesis is spared; chimeras built from Tel-null ES cells (1998) show TEL is needed to establish hematopoiesis of all lineages in the bone marrow, though not in yolk sac or fetal liver.
timeline.methods: Gene targeting, ES-cell chimeras

timeline.finding: The structure of the native TEL SAM (PNT) domain interface confirms the head-to-tail helical polymer first seen in a mutant, and shows flat interacting surfaces without obvious pockets.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How polymerization contributes to DNA binding and repression at genomic sites was not addressed.

timeline.finding: ER71 (ETV2) acts downstream of BMP, Notch and Wnt in specifying FLK1+ mesoderm: enforced expression induces FLK1+ mesoderm and blood and endothelium from ES cells, and Er71-deficient embryos die early with severe blood and vessel defects resembling Flk1-null mice.
timeline.methods: ES-cell differentiation, gain and loss of function, knockout mice

timeline.finding: Systematic in vitro profiling splits ETV6 and ETV7 off from the ELF proteins as class IIb, marked by a strong preference for A at the fourth core position that tracks a tyrosine-to-histidine substitution in the ETS domain.
timeline.methods: High-throughput microwell binding assay, protein-binding microarrays, site-directed mutagenesis
timeline.open: ChIP-seq was done for one member of the other classes but not for ETV6 or ETV7, so whether the class IIb preference matters in cells was untested.

timeline.finding: Consecutive-affinity SELEX of transcription factor pairs recovers 618 heterodimeric motifs, most of them composite sites markedly different from either partner's motif; this is the assay behind the ETS-HOX, ETS-bHLH and ETS-FOX heterodimer models that make up four of the seven JASPAR entries here.
timeline.methods: CAP-SELEX, crystallography
timeline.open: How many of these DNA-dependent pairs form in cells was not measured.

timeline.finding: Germline ETV6 missense variants segregating with dominant thrombocytopenia and diverse hematologic cancers in three kindreds abolish DNA binding, mislocalize the protein and reduce repression in a dominant-negative manner.
timeline.methods: Family sequencing, functional assays

timeline.finding: The two ETV6 PNT self-association interfaces are mapped in detail: monomeric variants keep a stable helical-bundle fold on association, and alanine scanning identifies hydrophobic and salt-bridge hot spots.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics, surface plasmon resonance

open: Whether this is a motif family at all is doubtful: its models cluster with ETS class I in every database, the published classification puts ETV6 and ETV7 in their own class IIb, and ETV2's in vitro models are indistinguishable from class I, so the grouping reflects a clustering outcome rather than a shared sequence preference.

Whether ETV6 and ETV7 polymers select clustered ETS sites in the genome is unresolved: PNT-domain self-association supports cooperative binding to neighboring sites in vitro, and three models here are doubled sites, but genome-wide evidence that the repressors prefer site clusters is not reported in the sources cited here.

families.name: NF-kB / Rel
families.def: kB site GGGRNNYYCC. NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB, REL.
families.short: The kB site is the element read by the five mammalian Rel/NF-kB proteins: NFKB1 (p105/p50), NFKB2 (p100/p52), RELA (p65), RELB and REL (c-Rel). They bind DNA only as dimers, through a shared Rel-homology region, so the site is pseudo-palindromic and is usually written GGGRNNYYCC, each subunit reading one guanine-rich half. What makes these factors unusual is that they are pre-made and held in the cytoplasm by IkB proteins, then released within minutes by inflammatory cytokines, microbial sensing, antigen receptors or DNA damage. The same kB site can therefore be empty in a resting cell and heavily occupied after stimulation. kB sites lie in promoters and enhancers of cytokine, chemokine, adhesion-molecule and pro-survival genes, and are the usual first evidence that a regulatory region is inflammation-responsive.
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have five Rel/NF-kB proteins. RELA (p65), RELB and REL (c-Rel) are synthesised in mature form and carry C-terminal transactivation domains. NFKB1 and NFKB2 are made as the longer precursors p105 and p100 and are processed to p50 and p52, which lack transactivation domains; p50 and p52 homodimers are therefore usually repressive unless they recruit a coactivator such as BCL3. All five share an N-terminal Rel-homology region of roughly 300 residues built from two immunoglobulin-like beta-barrel domains, with a nuclear localisation signal at its C-terminal end. The same region performs both jobs: the N-terminal barrel makes most base-specific contacts and the C-terminal barrel forms the dimer interface [PMID:7530332,7830764]. Five subunits allow fifteen dimers in principle; the abundant ones are p50:RELA (the "classical" NF-kB of canonical IKK signalling), p50:REL, and p52:RELB, which is the output of the non-canonical, NIK-dependent pathway [PMID:18267068]. RELA and NFKB1 are broadly expressed; REL and RELB are enriched in lymphoid cells and dendritic cells. Activity is controlled after translation rather than by transcription: IkBa, IkBb and IkBe, and the unprocessed p105 and p100 tails, mask the nuclear localisation signals, and signal-induced IKK phosphorylation triggers their degradation [PMID:18267068]. The IkBa/NF-kB crystal structure showed how one IkB simultaneously blocks the NLS and distorts the DNA-binding surface [PMID:9865694].

## The motif

The kB site is 9-11 bp and is conventionally written GGGRNNYYCC; a recent structural review writes it GGGRNNNYCC, and the difference is real: the number of central, low-information positions depends on which dimer is bound [PMID:31501881]. Crystal structures of the p50 homodimer, the p52 homodimer, and the p50:p65 heterodimer on the interferon-beta kB site show that each subunit reads one half-site, with conserved arginine, histidine and glutamate residues from loop L1 hydrogen-bonding the 5' GGG triplet [PMID:7530332,7830764,9384586,11970948]. p50 and p52 prefer a 5-bp guanine-rich half-site, giving longer and more nearly symmetric sites such as GGGGATTCCCC; RELA, RELB and c-Rel prefer a 4-bp half-site (GGAA), giving shorter sites such as GGGAATTTCC [PMID:31501881]. All the information sits in the GGG and in the CC of the opposite half; the middle two or three positions are close to free. A protein-binding-microarray and surface-plasmon-resonance survey of eight dimers found three specificity classes rather than five, and showed that dimers readily occupy "non-traditional" sites that contain only one good half-site - so NF-kB binding in vitro is more permissive than the palindromic consensus implies [PMID:22101729]. The four databases assembled here agree closely (cohesion 0.83) and their NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB and REL models differ mainly in half-site length, not in the recognised bases. Two entries, JASPAR RELB (MA1117.2) and CIS-BP M08161, are half-site-only models (ATTCCCC); most of their nearest neighbours in motif space fall outside this family, and they should not be used for scanning.

## Where it acts

kB sites occur in both promoters and enhancers, and are not associated with CpG islands. In a stimulated macrophage or lymphocyte, NF-kB occupies thousands of sites, a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of consensus matches in the genome; occupancy is largely confined to chromatin already made accessible by lineage-determining factors, so the cell type, not the motif, decides which kB sites are usable [PMID:20066094]. The best-characterised composite element is the interferon-beta enhancer (the PRDII kB site together with IRF3/IRF7 and ATF2/JUN sites), whose assembled enhanceosome has been modelled atomically [PMID:17574024]. More generally, kB sites co-occur with AP-1 (TGASTCA), IRF/ISRE, STAT (GAS) and C/EBP sites at inflammatory enhancers, and in myeloid cells with SPI1/PU.1.

## Biology and disease

NF-kB was found as an activity binding the immunoglobulin kappa light-chain enhancer [PMID:3091258] and was soon recognised as the general transcriptional output of innate and adaptive immune signalling: cytokine and chemokine induction, antigen-receptor responses, lymphoid organogenesis and germinal-centre B-cell programmes through RELB/p52, osteoclast differentiation downstream of RANK, and survival genes including BIRC3 and BCL2L1 [PMID:18267068]. Mouse knockouts separate the subunits: loss of Rela is embryonic lethal, with massive hepatocyte apoptosis [PMID:7603567] that is prevented by also deleting TNF [PMID:10077625]; Relb-null mice develop multiorgan inflammation and have fewer thymic dendritic cells [PMID:7834753]; and Nfkb1 (p50)-null mice develop normally but have multifocal B-cell and immune-response defects [PMID:7834752]. In humans, heterozygous loss-of-function NFKB1 variants are among the more frequent monogenic causes of common variable immunodeficiency [PMID:34473196], and NFKB2 variants cause hypogammaglobulinaemia with adrenal insufficiency [PMID:24140114]. Constitutive NF-kB activity is a defining feature of activated-B-cell diffuse large B-cell lymphoma [PMID:11748286], Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma, where NIK and TRAF3 lesions activate the non-canonical pathway [PMID:17692805].

## Reading a hit

A kB match says a Rel dimer could bind, not that one does. Because NF-kB is regulated by nuclear entry, a kB site in an unstimulated cell is usually unoccupied; a match is therefore a statement about potential, and it should be checked against accessibility or ChIP data from the relevant stimulus and cell type. The element is also common: with four strongly constrained positions and a degenerate centre, 10-bp matches occur many thousands of times per genome, so match count alone carries little weight. The subunits are not separable from sequence. At most, a long, symmetric site with a 5-bp GGGGA half-site slightly favours p50- or p52-containing dimers, and a short GGAA half-site favours RelA, RelB or c-Rel; no model distinguishes RELA from REL. Evidence codes help: the HOCOMOCO NFKB1 and NFKB2 core models carry in vitro SELEX or methyl-SELEX support (PS, PSM), whereas the RELA, RELB and REL models are ChIP-only, grade B, and describe where those proteins were found rather than what they bind directly. Since NF-kB works within enhanceosomes, ChIP-derived NF-kB models can be pulled toward IRF, AP-1 or STAT sequences contributed by partners.
families.caveats: Treat a kB hit as family-level and conditional. It identifies Rel/NF-kB, never which of the five subunits: the databases' NFKB1, NFKB2, RELA, RELB and REL models differ mainly in half-site length. Because NF-kB activity is controlled by nuclear entry rather than by expression, most matches in any given cell state are unoccupied, and a match is not evidence of an active site without accessibility or stimulus-matched ChIP data. The RELA, RELB and REL models in HOCOMOCO are ChIP-derived only (grade B), so partner motifs from enhanceosome co-binders can bleed into them. Avoid the half-site models (JASPAR MA1117.2, CIS-BP M08161) for genome scans; they match promiscuously.

timeline.finding: NF-kB is identified as a nuclear activity in B-cell extracts that binds a short sequence in the immunoglobulin kappa light-chain enhancer, the element later called the kB site.
timeline.methods: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays with nuclear extracts
timeline.open: Which proteins made up the activity, and whether it existed in a latent form outside B cells, were unknown.

timeline.finding: Two independent crystal structures of the p50 homodimer on kB DNA show the Rel-homology region as two immunoglobulin-like domains: loops of the N-terminal domain contact the bases across the 10-bp site and the C-terminal domains form the dimer interface.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Both structures were homodimers on palindromic sites; how RELA-containing heterodimers read asymmetric sites was not shown.

timeline.finding: The IkBa/p50:p65 structure shows how NF-kB is held latent: IkBa tethers the sequences next to both nuclear localization signals and shifts the p65 N-terminal domain into a position incompatible with DNA binding, so a kB site stays empty until IkB is degraded.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: An atomic model of the interferon-beta enhanceosome places NF-kB, IRF3/IRF7 and ATF2-JUN on one continuous composite element; the scarcity of local protein-protein contacts implies that cooperative occupancy comes from DNA conformation and coactivators rather than direct factor-factor binding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of enhancer subcomplexes combined into a composite model
timeline.open: Whether such tightly packed, sequence-invariant composites are typical of kB enhancers or peculiar to virus-inducible promoters.

timeline.finding: Microarray and surface-plasmon-resonance measurements on eight NF-kB dimers define three specificity classes and many non-traditional kB sites bound through a single consensus half-site, revising the view that the palindromic GGGRNNYYCC describes what NF-kB binds.
timeline.methods: Protein-binding microarrays, surface plasmon resonance
timeline.open: How often the non-traditional sites and the dimer-specific classes are used in cells.

timeline.finding: Of 90 NFKB1 variants from patients with CVID or related conditions, 59 were loss-of-function or hypomorphic in a kB reporter assay, against 2 of 260 variants from the general population, establishing NFKB1 haploinsufficiency as a cause of autosomal-dominant CVID.
timeline.methods: Reporter assays in NFKB1-deficient cells; variant enrichment analysis

open: Whether the kB sequence selects which Rel dimer binds in cells is unsettled: structures and microarray surveys show dimer-specific half-site preferences and specificity classes in vitro, but in cells occupancy is dominated by pre-existing accessible chromatin and by which dimers a given stimulus releases from IkB.

How much NF-kB regulation runs through non-traditional sites carrying only one consensus half-site is unknown: such sites are bound with measurable affinity in vitro, but the palindromic models used for scanning score them poorly, so genome scans would miss them if they are functional.

families.name: RUNX
families.def: TGTGGT core (ACCACA). RUNX1/2/3 with CBFB.
families.short: RUNX sites are read by RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 through the Runt domain, a 128-residue immunoglobulin-like fold in the same structural class as NF-kB and p53. The core is a six-base element, TGYGGT, written ACCRCA on the other strand, and it is the retroviral enhancer "core" site originally described for core-binding factor. None of the three proteins binds efficiently alone: all require the non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB, which clamps the Runt domain into its DNA-bound conformation and raises affinity substantially. RUNX1 is the hematopoietic member and one of the most frequent targets of chromosomal translocation in leukemia; RUNX2 controls osteoblast differentiation and RUNX3 gut and immune programmes. The three paralogues are indistinguishable by sequence preference.
families.long:
## The factors

RUNX1 (AML1, CBFA2), RUNX2 (CBFA1) and RUNX3 (CBFA3) each carry one Runt domain near their N terminus. The domain is about 128 residues and adopts an s-type immunoglobulin fold, placing RUNX in the same structural superfamily as NF-kB, NFAT, STAT and p53 rather than with any classical helix-turn-helix family [PMID:10404214]. It binds DNA as a monomer, but not effectively on its own: the shared subunit CBFB (CBFbeta, PEBP2beta) makes no DNA contact yet is required in practice. Two crystal structures of the Runt domain-CBFB-DNA ternary complex showed how - CBFB stabilises the DNA-bound conformation of the domain's C-terminal "tail" and "wing", which together clamp the phosphate backbone across both grooves, and the extended tail contributes most of the NF-kB-like base-specific major-groove contacts [PMID:11257229,11276260]. Expression is largely complementary: RUNX1 in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and lymphocytes, RUNX2 in osteoblasts, chondrocytes and some epithelia, RUNX3 in gut epithelium, sensory neurons and T and NK cells. All three interact with CBFB and with the same corepressor and coactivator machinery, so which one is present is usually a matter of cell type rather than of DNA sequence.

## The motif

The core is six bases. Binding-site selection with core-binding factor gave the consensus PyGPyGGTPy [PMID:8445737], most compactly written TGYGGT, and its reverse complement ACCRCA is equally common in the literature. The Y at position three is the one genuinely ambiguous base, and it explains a discrepancy visible in these databases: ChIP-derived models for all three paralogues read TGTGGTT (ACCACA), whereas HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX models for RUNX2 and RUNX3, the JASPAR RUNX2 model, and the Vierstra archetypes read TGCGGTT (ACCGCA) [PMID:23332764]. Both are correct readings of TGYGGT; in vitro selection favours the C variant, genomic occupancy the T variant. Structurally, the guanines of the GG step are read by arginine and lysine side chains from the Runt domain tail in the major groove, while the flanking T and the distorted, bent B-form geometry of the site account for the rest of the specificity [PMID:11257229,11276260]. Six informative positions is little, and the databases compensate in two ways. Some models extend one or two positions into the flank; others are tandem repeats of the core (AACCGCAAAAACCGCA, GTGGTTTTTGTGGTTT). RUNX enhancers do tend to carry paired sites, but the tandem models are not read off enhancers: the HOCOMOCO ones come from HT-SELEX (RUNX3.H14CORE.1.S.B) and methyl-HT-SELEX (RUNX2.H14CORE.2.M.C) on random ligands, which recovered two cores at a fixed spacing [PMID:23332764]. Every structure of the complex shows a monomeric Runt domain [PMID:11257229,11276260], so whether a pair of cores is bound cooperatively is unresolved rather than excluded. No model distinguishes RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 - family cohesion is 0.86 and the three ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO consensuses are character-for-character identical. Note also that one CIS-BP RUNX1 entry was measured on the mouse protein, whose Runt domain is identical to the human one at 100% identity.

## Where it acts

RUNX motifs are enhancer features more than promoter features, and are not enriched in CpG islands. In hematopoietic cells RUNX1 occupies tens of thousands of sites, and its motif is one of the commonest in the accessible chromatin of blood lineages; RUNX2 shows the same pattern in osteoblasts. The characteristic arrangement is a composite with ETS. Cooperative binding of ETS1 and core-binding factor to adjacent sites was described at the T-cell receptor enhancers [PMID:8264651], and genome-wide work later showed that the ETS-RUNX composite is what distinguishes ETS1's T-cell-specific enhancer occupancy from its redundant, consensus-driven occupancy at housekeeping promoters [PMID:20019798]. RUNX sites also co-occur with GATA (the GATA-RUNX pairing at hematopoietic enhancers), with SPI1/PU.1 in myeloid cells, with TCF/LEF and with AP-1.

## Biology and disease

Runx1-null mice fail definitive hematopoiesis and die in mid-gestation with central nervous system hemorrhage [PMID:8565077]; the Cbfb knockout reproduces this, which was the genetic demonstration that the partner subunit is required in vivo [PMID:8929538]. Runx2-null mice have no bone formation at all because osteoblasts arrest before maturation [PMID:9182763], and heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in human RUNX2 cause cleidocranial dysplasia [PMID:9182765]. RUNX3 silencing by promoter hypermethylation and loss of expression was linked causally to gastric carcinoma [PMID:11955451]. RUNX1 is among the most frequently rearranged genes in human leukemia: t(8;21) creates RUNX1-RUNX1T1 in acute myeloid leukemia, t(12;21) creates ETV6-RUNX1 in the commonest subtype of childhood B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and inv(16) fuses CBFB to MYH11; germline RUNX1 mutations cause familial platelet disorder with predisposition to myeloid malignancy [PMID:28179279]. Most of these lesions keep an intact Runt domain and convert RUNX1 into a repressor at its normal sites [PMID:28179279].

## Reading a hit

TGYGGT is short. Expect roughly one match every few hundred base pairs per strand, so an isolated hit is close to meaningless; weight matches by clustering, by conservation, and above all by the presence of a partner site. An adjacent ETS core (GGAA/GGAT) within a few base pairs, or a nearby GATA site, turns a weak RUNX match into a plausible composite element. The hit cannot name the paralogue, and it cannot distinguish RUNX from CBFB-containing complexes generally, since CBFB has no motif of its own - a "CBFB site" in any database is a RUNX site. Decide which variant to scan with deliberately: an in vitro TGCGGT model will score differently from a ChIP-derived TGTGGT model on the same sequence, and neither is wrong. The HOCOMOCO RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 primary models are ChIP-only (grade B); because RUNX travels in composites with ETS and GATA, ChIP-derived RUNX models can absorb flanking partner information, and conversely ETS models derived from T-cell ChIP can absorb the RUNX core.
families.caveats: A six-base core means chance matches dominate: treat a lone TGYGGT as no evidence and look for a composite, most often an ETS core within a few base pairs or a nearby GATA site. The three paralogues cannot be told apart - the ChIP-derived RUNX1, RUNX2 and RUNX3 models here are identical, so a hit is RUNX-family and the responsible protein follows from cell type. CBFB has no motif of its own, so any database entry labelled for it is a RUNX motif. Be deliberate about the variant: in vitro models read TGCGGT, ChIP models TGTGGT, and they score real sequence differently. All three primary HOCOMOCO models are ChIP-only.

timeline.finding: Selected-and-amplified binding-site footprinting with core-binding factor defines the consensus PyGPyGGTPy, and ethylation interference shows phosphate contacts spanning 9 bp around the core.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection (SAAB); ethylation interference
timeline.open: How the DNA-binding alpha subunit and the partner beta subunit divide the work of recognition was not known.

timeline.finding: ETS1 and core-binding factor bind cooperatively to adjacent sites in the T-cell receptor beta enhancer, and site selection shows that the relative spacing and orientation of the two sites are loosely constrained.
timeline.methods: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays; mutagenesis; binding-site selection

timeline.finding: Runx1-null and Cbfb-null mice share one phenotype - no definitive hematopoiesis and mid-gestation hemorrhage - showing that the non-DNA-binding CBFB subunit is required for RUNX1 function in vivo.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting (two independent knockouts)

timeline.finding: Runx2 (Cbfa1) is required for bone formation in the mouse, and heterozygous RUNX2 mutations cause human cleidocranial dysplasia.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting; human linkage and mutation analysis

timeline.finding: The DNA-bound Runt domain is an S-type immunoglobulin fold, structurally related to the DNA-binding domains of NF-kB, NFAT, p53 and the STATs rather than to helix-turn-helix factors, and NMR of the ternary complex maps the surface that binds CBFB.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy

timeline.finding: Two crystal structures of the Runt domain-CBFB-DNA complex show a monomeric Runt domain clamping the DNA and CBFB acting allosterically, stabilising the DNA-binding loops without itself contacting DNA.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Whether CBFB changes sequence preference or only affinity.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide ETS1 occupancy in T cells separates redundant promoter binding with other ETS proteins from ETS1-specific enhancer binding, and one route to that specificity is an ETS-RUNX composite that supports cooperative binding.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq; DNase I hypersensitivity

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX yields a RUNX2 model built on ACCGCA (TGCGGT) with paired cores, whereas ChIP-derived RUNX models favour TGTGGT, so in vitro and in vivo collections now disagree at the one ambiguous position of TGYGGT.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Whether the C variant is intrinsically preferred and rare in vivo because of CpG depletion and methylation, or favoured by the assay.

open: Why in vitro selection favours TGCGGT while ChIP-derived models favour TGTGGT is not settled: the C variant may be the higher-affinity site that is scarce in the genome because CpG is depleted and usually methylated, or the preference may be shifted by selection conditions, including the absence of CBFB from most selection experiments.

Whether paired RUNX cores are bound cooperatively is unresolved: every structure shows a monomeric Runt domain, yet HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX recover two cores at fixed spacings from random ligands, which would be unexpected for fully independent binding.

families.name: CENP-B / pogo / Tigger
families.def: CENP-B box TTCGTTGGAA and related pogo-family transposase-derived domains. CENPB, TIGD1-7, POGK, JRK, CENPBD1.
families.short: The third and largest of the atlas's domesticated-transposase families. CENP-B, the Tigger-derived TIGD1 to TIGD7 proteins, POGK, JRK and CENPBD1 all carry DNA-binding domains descended from pogo, a Drosophila DNA transposon whose Tigger relatives left more than a hundred thousand fossil copies in the human genome. CENP-B itself recognizes the 17-base-pair CENP-B box, which recurs in alpha-satellite DNA - so a CENP-B box match is almost always centromeric or pericentromeric, not a regulatory site. Sixteen motifs cover twelve symbols, most of them sharing a bipartite pattern of a TTCG/CGAA block and a CCCG/CGGG block read by two helix-turn-helix domains. Cohesion is low at 0.48 and one model is flagged suspect.
families.long:
## The factors

In 1996 a survey of human interspersed repeats identified two roughly 2.5 kb elements with coding capacity, Tigger1 and Tigger2, that closely resemble pogo, a DNA transposon of Drosophila, and that probably mobilised at least fourteen families and more than a hundred thousand degenerate short copies carrying 14 to 25 base-pair terminal inverted repeats [PMID:8643651]. The deduced pogo and Tigger transposases turned out to be very similar to CENP-B, the major mammalian centromere protein - the observation that first suggested CENP-B has a transposase origin [PMID:8643651]. This family collects the human descendants of that lineage: CENPB itself, the Tigger transposable element derived proteins TIGD1 through TIGD7, POGK, JRK (jerky) and CENPBD1. TIGD7 was in fact isolated as a Jerky/JRK-like gene [PMID:15487591], and the wider pogo group also contains POGZ, which is not filed here.

Their host functions have diverged completely. CENP-B is a centromeric chromatin protein. Jerky, in Drosophila, facilitates cell-specific Wnt/Wingless signalling by modulating beta-catenin-TCF activity [PMID:21399610], and in mouse it is associated with translationally inactive neuronal mRNA. Several TIGD genes have no characterised function at all. What they retain in common is the recognition module, which is exactly what makes this family readable as a motif family and unreadable as a functional one.

## The motif

CENP-B binds a 17 base-pair sequence in centromeric alpha-satellite (alphoid) DNA, purified from HeLa nuclear extract as the protein that recognizes it, with an affinity of about 6 x 10^8 M^-1, and the major protein-DNA complex contains two DNA molecules [PMID:1730770]. The 129-residue DNA-binding region forms two helix-turn-helix domains that occupy adjacent major grooves; the DNA is kinked at both recognition-helix contacts, the larger kink reaching 43 degrees through an arginine-rich helix that bridges the phosphate backbone, giving an overall bend of 59 degrees [PMID:11726497]. The box recurs in alpha-satellite at regular intervals, roughly every other repeat unit [PMID:11726497,17115329].

The atlas models for CENPB, tCCCGCaTnntACGAA in HOCOMOCO and CCCGcdTnnwaCGAA in CIS-BP and Vierstra, are written on the strand opposite the way the box is conventionally quoted: the CCCG block at their 5' end corresponds to the CGGG block at the 3' end of the box, and their 3' CGAA corresponds to the box's 5' TTCG. Read in either orientation the bipartite architecture is visible, two conserved blocks separated by a tolerant spacer, exactly matching the two-helix-turn-helix structure. The same signature runs through the family: JRK gives CCTCgrTTAACCGGAA, TIGD7 ttCnnTAATTCGGAC, TIGD4 ACCCCGTTAaTAcGAaC, TIGD3 TATGCAGgTAAcCGda, TIGD5 cccbtTATAACGC and POGK TCGACcTtAgGTCGACa. These are long, information-rich models of 12 to 26 bits with grade A HOCOMOCO evidence [PMID:42557334], but they are not the same site as each other, which is why family cohesion is only 0.48. The tail is weak: TIGD1 gives TATTGCG, CENPBD1 TACGta at 4.1 bits, TIGD6 aaCGAA at 3.4 bits, and the Vierstra archetype AC0265 collapses to CG and is flagged suspect with SAND as its alternative family. Two CIS-BP models, for TIGD2 and TIGD6, are transferred from Monodelphis domestica, and a third for POGK is a PBM construct at only 73 percent domain identity.

## Where it acts

For CENP-B the answer is unusually definite: its sites are in alpha-satellite arrays at centromeres and pericentromeric regions, distributed through higher-order repeat units [PMID:17115329], and they are functional there. Both the CENP-B box and alphoid sequence context are required for de novo centromere chromatin assembly on synthetic repeats in the human artificial chromosome assay, including recruitment of CENP-A, CENP-C and CENP-E [PMID:12460987]; combining CENP-B box positive and negative synthetic repeats improves artificial chromosome formation further [PMID:35563684]. Alpha-satellite arrays differ in their CENP-B box content [PMID:17115329], and the box has arisen independently more than once - it is present in some New World monkey satellite lineages with separate origins [PMID:31813924]. The other members are nuclear proteins of unremarkable distribution whose genomic occupancy is poorly mapped.

## Biology and disease

The centromeric role of the box is not matched by a requirement for the protein: Cenpb null mice are viable with no apparent abnormalities [PMID:9740654], so CENP-B is best understood as facilitating centromere assembly rather than being essential to it. This is the standard picture for domesticated transposases, whose retention reflects opportunistic recruitment rather than indispensability. Jerky loss in mouse produces an epilepsy phenotype [PMID:7550318], and the fly orthologue modulates Wnt signalling through beta-catenin-TCF [PMID:21399610]. The Tigger and POGK members remain largely uncharacterised; POGZ, a pogo relative outside this family, is a well-established neurodevelopmental disorder gene, which is a reason to expect more phenotypes here.

## Reading a hit

Check repeat annotation first. A CENP-B box match will nearly always fall inside alpha satellite, and in that context it is a structural feature of the centromere, not a candidate enhancer; counting matches is effectively counting satellite repeat units, and satellite arrays are poorly resolved in most reference assemblies, so occurrence counts are unreliable. For the rest of the family, the long grade A models for JRK, POGK, TIGD3, TIGD4, TIGD5 and TIGD7 are individually specific and mutually distinct, so a hit can be assigned to a member rather than only to the family - but almost nothing is known about what those sites do, and there is no occupancy evidence to corroborate them. Discard the CENPBD1, TIGD6 and TIGD1 models, the cross-species transfers, and the suspect CG archetype.
families.caveats: This is a low-cohesion family (0.48) whose members do not share one site: only CENPB, and the models labelled CENPB, correspond to the CENP-B box, and those are written reverse-complement to the usual rendering of the box. A CENP-B box hit is almost always inside alpha satellite and should be read as centromeric structure, not regulation; match counts there track satellite copy number and assembly quality rather than biology. Four models are effectively uninformative (CENPBD1 4.1 bits, TIGD6 3.4 bits, the suspect CG archetype AC0265, and TIGD1's seven-base TATTGCG). Two CIS-BP models are transferred from Monodelphis domestica and one POGK model from a PBM construct at 73 percent domain identity. No member except CENPB has published occupancy data to corroborate its motif.

timeline.finding: CENP-B was purified from HeLa nuclear extract as the protein that binds the 17 bp CENP-B box of alpha-satellite DNA, with direct binding shown by mobility shift, Southwestern blotting and DNase I protection, a binding constant of about 6 x 10^8 M^-1, and a major complex containing two DNA molecules.
timeline.methods: Oligonucleotide affinity purification, EMSA, Southwestern blotting, DNase I footprinting
timeline.open: Whether CENP-B is needed for centromere function.

timeline.finding: An insertional mutation in mice inactivated jerky, a novel gene related to CENP-B, and caused whole-body jerks, generalized clonic seizures and epileptic brain activity.
timeline.methods: Transgenic insertional mutagenesis, EEG, gene cloning
timeline.open: Whether the jerky protein binds DNA, and at which sites.

timeline.finding: Tigger1 and Tigger2, 2.5 kb human DNA transposon fossils resembling Drosophila pogo, were identified along with more than 100,000 degenerate short copies; their deduced transposases were very similar to CENP-B, implying that CENP-B is a domesticated transposase.
timeline.methods: Computational analysis of human interspersed repeats

timeline.finding: Cenpb null mice were viable and fertile with normal mitosis and meiosis, contradicting the proposal that CENP-B performs a vital role in organizing centromeric chromatin.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting
timeline.open: What the conserved CENP-B box does if the protein that binds it is dispensable.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the 129-residue CENP-B DNA-binding region on the CENP-B box showed two helix-turn-helix domains in adjacent major grooves, a kink-straight-kink DNA path with a 43 degree kink made by phosphate bridging from an arginine-rich helix, and an overall bend of 59 degrees.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Synthetic repeats with mutated CENP-B boxes failed to form mammalian artificial chromosomes or assemble CENP-A, CENP-C and CENP-E, showing that the box and alphoid sequence are both required for de novo centromere assembly in human cells despite the viability of Cenpb null mice.
timeline.methods: Synthetic alphoid arrays, artificial chromosome formation assay, ChIP
timeline.open: Why a box required for de novo assembly is dispensable in the whole animal.

timeline.finding: Phylogenetic analysis of centromere satellite repeats in three New World monkeys placed the CENP-B box at a different location in each species, supporting multiple independent origins of the box rather than inheritance from a common ancestor.
timeline.methods: Phylogenetic analysis of satellite repeat units

timeline.finding: A multi-assay survey of poorly characterized human transcription factors found that CENP-B- and Brinker-domain proteins give long, information-rich motifs, and that JRK binding in both ChIP-seq and GHT-SELEX is enriched on the Tigger15a elements it derives from, with predicted sites in their terminal repeats; this supplied occupancy data for a family member other than CENP-B.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX, SMiLE-seq, protein-binding microarrays, ChIP-seq
timeline.open: Whether the TIGD and POGK sites likewise mark their ancestral transposon fossils.

open: Why the CENP-B box is required for de novo centromere assembly on synthetic alphoid DNA while Cenpb null mice are viable and fertile is unresolved; current work places CENP-B in the balance between CENP-A chromatin and heterochromatin rather than as an essential centromere component, but whether it matters only for establishment is not settled.

Whether the long motifs of JRK, POGK and the TIGD proteins describe host regulatory sites or remnants of ancestral transposon recognition is open: JRK binding is enriched on the Tigger15a elements it descends from, with predicted sites in their terminal repeats, but what that binding does for the host has not been shown.

It is not known whether JRK's DNA specificity bears on its reported cellular roles, since the fly orthologue acts as a beta-catenin-TCF coactivator and mouse Jerky has been described in association with neuronal mRNA, neither of which has been tied to the motif.

families.name: PRD-like / primate-specific (CRX-like)
families.def: Divergent paired-like homeodomains of germline and early embryo: DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1, ARGFX, RHOXF1/2, DUX-like TPRX paralogs.
families.short: PRD-like homeobox genes are a small set of rapidly evolving, single-homeodomain factors, ARGFX, DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1 and RHOXF1/2 among them, that are expressed almost exclusively in the oocyte, the cleavage-stage embryo and the germ line. Several arose by retrotransposition of a CRX-like ancestor within mammals, and several have been lost or pseudogenised in other lineages, so there are no mouse orthologues for much of the group. Most of them select a short K50-type homeodomain site, TAATCC, in vitro; ARGFX instead prefers a TAATTA palindrome. They are candidate drivers of human zygotic genome activation, acting at promoters derived from endogenous retroviral repeats. The evidence base is thin and largely in vitro, and the motifs are short.
families.long:
## The factors

The PRD-like class, as defined in the standard classification of human homeobox genes, contains ARGFX,
DPRX, LEUTX, TPRX1 and its relatives, RHOXF1 and RHOXF2, and several others [PMID:17963489]. Their names record features of
the domain itself: ARGFX is "arginine-fifty homeobox" and LEUTX is "leucine-twenty homeobox", after the
residue at those positions of the homeodomain [PMID:17005330,17963489]. Each protein is small, carries one homeodomain, and has no
other recognisable DNA-binding or dimerisation module. Evolutionarily this is the most volatile corner of
the homeobox repertoire: the genes arose in eutherian mammals, several by retrotransposition from a
CRX-like ancestor, and they have been repeatedly pseudogenised or deleted, so there is no one-to-one mouse
counterpart for ARGFX, DPRX or LEUTX [PMID:17005330,27296695]. Expression is correspondingly narrow. LEUTX, TPRX1, DPRX and ARGFX
are detected in the oocyte and in 4- to 8-cell human embryos and essentially nowhere else [PMID:26360614,27296695]; RHOXF1 and
RHOXF2 are expressed in human oocytes and male germ cells [PMID:23482336]. Because the genes are off in every accessible
adult tissue, almost nothing is known about them from conventional cell-line work.

## The motif

Most members select TAATCC, written GGATTA on the other strand: a canonical homeodomain TAAT core followed
by two positions specified by residue 50 of the recognition helix, which is the position that separates
K50-type factors (TAATCC) from Q50-type factors (TAATTG or TAATTA) [PMID:2572327]. DPRX and RHOXF1 models extend this to
GATAATCC, and TPRX1 to AWCGGATTA. ARGFX is the exception and reads CTAATTAG, a TAAT/ATTA palindrome of the
Q50 type, consistent with its unusual residue 50 [PMID:28473536]. Information content is low throughout. The strongest
model in the family carries about 15 bits, most carry 8 to 13, and several are 6-mers or shorter; one
CIS-BP TPRX1 entry has 2 bits and reduces to "At", which is why the representative consensus computed from
the data is uninformative and should not be used. There is no single family consensus: the honest
description is two shapes, a K50 TAATCC site shared by most members and an ARGFX-specific TAATTA
palindrome. Crucially, the TAATCC form is not distinguishable from the site of the much better known K50
factors CRX, OTX1/2, PITX1-3 and GSC; nearest-neighbour similarity to motifs outside this family reaches
0.99 for several members [PMID:23332764,18585359].

## Where it acts

What is known comes from early-embryo transcriptomics rather than from chromatin maps. PRD-like binding
sequences are enriched at transcription start regions active at the 4-cell stage in human embryos, and a
substantial fraction of the promoters concerned are derived from repeat families, including MLT2A1/HERVL
long terminal repeats and Alu elements [PMID:26360614]. Overexpression of nine of these genes in human cells activated
overlapping sets of embryo-specific targets [PMID:27412763], and LEUTX and the TPRX proteins converge on the 8-cell-stage
program [PMID:27578796,36074823]. Outside those windows the sites are not occupied by these factors, because the proteins are
absent; any match in somatic chromatin is far more likely to be read by a K50 factor such as CRX in
photoreceptors, OTX2 in brain and retina, or PITX proteins more broadly. No composite element involving a
PRD-like factor has been named and characterised.

## Biology and disease

The central proposal is that these factors help drive human zygotic genome activation, the handover from
maternal transcripts to embryonic transcription that in humans occurs around the 4- to 8-cell stage.
LEUTX is expressed in a sharp pulse at that point and its manipulation changes 8-cell-stage gene
expression [PMID:27578796]; depletion of the TPRX proteins impairs zygotic genome activation and subsequent development [PMID:36074823],
which is currently the strongest functional evidence in the group. The RHOXF cluster is regulated by DNA
methylation and histone H1, is imprinted in mouse, and its methylation state and expression have been
associated with human male infertility [PMID:23943794], but no PRD-like gene is an established Mendelian disease gene. The
absence of mouse orthologues for most members means there are no informative knockouts, and human
embryo work is limited in scale, so almost every functional statement in this family rests on a small
number of studies.

## Reading a hit

Treat a TAATCC match as a K50 homeodomain site and stop there. It does not identify a PRD-like factor; the
same sequence is read by CRX, OTX and PITX proteins, which are expressed in far more tissues and have far
more supporting data. Almost all motif evidence for this family is in vitro: HOCOMOCO models for ARGFX,
DPRX, RHOXF1 and RHOXF2 are built on HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX only, with quality grade B, and the
JASPAR models are HT-SELEX [PMID:37971293,28473536]. Only TPRX1 and LEUTX have HOCOMOCO models with any in vivo component. One
JASPAR entry labelled RHOXF1 in this family is in fact the mouse Rhox11 protein-binding-microarray motif,
consensus CGCTGTAAA [PMID:18585359], which resembles nothing else here; the mouse Rhox cluster is a lineage-specific
expansion rather than a set of RHOXF1/2 orthologues, and that model should not be transferred to human
sequence. Unless your material is oocyte, cleavage-stage embryo or germ line, the prior on PRD-like
occupancy is very low.
families.caveats: Low-confidence family. The shared motif is a 6-base K50 homeodomain site, TAATCC, that occurs by chance roughly every few kilobases and is indistinguishable from the CRX, OTX and PITX site, so a hit almost never identifies a PRD-like factor. Several models in the family carry under 3 bits and cannot be scanned meaningfully. The evidence is overwhelmingly in vitro selection on recombinant protein; only TPRX1 and LEUTX have any in vivo support. One JASPAR entry labelled RHOXF1 is a mouse Rhox11 microarray motif with an unrelated consensus. Because the genes are expressed only in the oocyte, early embryo and germ line, matches in somatic data should be attributed elsewhere.

timeline.finding: Swapping the single residue at position 50 of the homeodomain recognition helix is shown to be necessary and sufficient to convert the DNA preference of one homeodomain into another, establishing the K50/Q50 rule that later separates TAATCC readers from TAATTA readers.
timeline.methods: site-directed mutagenesis and in vitro DNA binding in Drosophila Paired
timeline.open: Said nothing about which mammalian proteins carry K50 domains, and the PRD-like genes had not yet been found.

timeline.finding: Genome annotation names ARGFX, DPRX, TPRX1 and DUXA as rapidly evolving homeobox genes whose processed pseudogenes imply germline expression, proposes that they are divergent derivatives of CRX, and places them in the PRD-like class of the human homeobox catalogue.
timeline.methods: comparative genome annotation and phylogenetics
timeline.open: Expression was inferred from retrotransposed pseudogenes rather than measured, and no protein had been shown to bind DNA.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX on recombinant human proteins yields the first directly measured PRD-like specificities, including the K50-type TAATCC site assigned to RHOXF1.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: The same site is selected by CRX, OTX and PITX proteins, so in vitro selection could not say which factor uses it in cells.

timeline.finding: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 348 human oocytes, zygotes and blastomeres shows that ARGFX, DPRX, LEUTX, DUXA and DUXB are transcribed across the 4- to 8-cell transition, and that promoter motifs enriched at these stage-specific transcription start regions often overlap Alu and other repeats.
timeline.methods: single-cell RNA-seq of human preimplantation embryos with transcript far 5'-end quantification and de novo motif discovery
timeline.open: Motif enrichment is correlative; no PRD-like protein had been shown to occupy those promoters in an embryo.

timeline.finding: A phylogenetic reconstruction derives the group, renamed ETCHbox genes, from tandem duplication of Crx on the forerunner of human chromosome 19 in the stem lineage of placental mammals, with repeated gene loss, and argues from ectopic-expression transcriptomes that they tune an 8-cell-to-morula program rather than drive genome activation generally.
timeline.methods: phylogenomics plus RNA-seq after ectopic expression in cultured human cells
timeline.open: Revises the earlier retrotransposition account toward tandem duplication without settling the origin of every member.

timeline.finding: Overexpression studies in human embryonic stem cells separate the group into activators and repressors, with LEUTX activating a large share of the genes upregulated at embryo genome activation and DPRX acting as a counterbalancing repressor at the 8-cell stage.
timeline.methods: cloning of embryo transcript variants plus overexpression and RNA-seq in human embryonic stem cells
timeline.open: Forced expression in a stem-cell line is not evidence that the endogenous protein does the same in an embryo.

timeline.finding: Methylation-sensitive HT-SELEX adds models for ARGFX and DPRX and shows that many extended homeodomain proteins prefer methylated CpG-containing sites, a preference traced to hydrophobic contact with the 5-methyl group.
timeline.methods: methyl-HT-SELEX with supporting structural analysis
timeline.open: ARGFX selects a Q50-type palindrome unlike the rest of the group, and why it diverged is unexplained.

timeline.finding: Knockdown of TPRX1, TPRX2 and TPRXL in human embryos causes defective zygotic genome activation and impaired preimplantation development, the first loss-of-function evidence that a PRD-like factor is required in human embryos.
timeline.methods: ribosome profiling and RNA-seq of human oocytes and embryos plus knockdown in embryos
timeline.open: Whether the TPRX proteins act through the TAATCC sites they select in vitro was not established by occupancy data in embryos.

open: The origin of the group is unsettled: the original annotation derived ARGFX, DPRX and TPRX1 by retrotransposition from a CRX-like ancestor, whereas the later phylogenomic reconstruction derives them by tandem duplication of Crx on a dynamic region of the chromosome-19 forerunner.

It is disputed whether these factors drive human zygotic genome activation broadly or only tune a narrow 8-cell-to-morula program: the embryo transcriptome and LEUTX overexpression work treats them as genome-activation regulators, while the comparative study argues their targets are a restricted set of stage-specific genes rather than the activation wave itself.

No PRD-like protein has been shown to occupy a TAATCC site in a human embryo; every specificity model comes from in vitro selection or from forced expression in stem cells, so the in vivo site of each factor remains unknown.

The RHOXF1 motif label is unresolved: one JASPAR model under that name is a mouse Rhox11 microarray motif with an unrelated consensus, and whether the mouse Rhox cluster, a lineage-specific expansion, has any specificity relationship to human RHOXF1 and RHOXF2 has not been tested.

families.name: PAR bZIP (HLF/NFIL3/DBP)
families.def: Proline- and acidic-rich bZIPs binding TTATG(T/C)AA. HLF, NFIL3/E4BP4, DBP, TEF.
families.short: The PAR bZIP group contains three proline- and acidic-amino-acid-rich basic region-leucine zipper activators - DBP (albumin D-site binding protein), HLF (hepatic leukemia factor) and TEF - together with NFIL3 (E4BP4), which lacks the PAR domain, represses rather than activates, and yet reads the same site. That site is the palindrome TTACGTAA, written in much of the literature as TTATG(T/C)AA. It differs from the cyclic-AMP response element at only the outermost bases of each half-site, TTAC in place of TGAC. DBP, HLF and TEF accumulate with circadian rhythms in liver and suprachiasmatic nucleus, and NFIL3 oscillates in antiphase, so the same element can be activated or repressed depending on time of day. This is the most internally consistent bZIP family in the collection, and its four members are indistinguishable by sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

PAR stands for proline- and acidic-amino-acid-rich, the character of the region N-terminal to the basic region in DBP, HLF and TEF (also called VBP). All three are bZIP activators. NFIL3, better known as E4BP4, is grouped with them because its DNA-binding specificity is the same, but it is structurally distinct: it has no PAR domain and it carries a repression rather than an activation function [PMID:11316793,12386933], so the two halves of this family do opposite things at identical sites. Expression is informative. DBP, HLF and TEF accumulate with high-amplitude circadian rhythms in tissues where clock gene expression cycles strongly, notably liver and the suprachiasmatic nucleus, while remaining near-constant in most other brain regions [PMID:15175240]. NFIL3 cycles in antiphase to DBP, which makes the pair a repressor-activator switch running on one element [PMID:11316793]. NFIL3 is broadly expressed and prominent in immune cells; HLF is largely restricted, and in human hematopoiesis its expression marks the stem cell state [PMID:1386162,34499717]. Dimerization matters for interpretation: the bZIP class heterodimerizes extensively, and systematic interaction surveys show these networks are highly partner-specific and have been rewired repeatedly over evolution [PMID:23661758], so which sites a PAR protein occupies depends on the partner it has.

## The motif

The palindrome is TTACGTAA: two TTAC half-sites in opposed orientation, one per subunit, usually with A, T or G immediately outside, giving GTTACGTAAT and ATTACGTAAC in the highest-information models here [PMID:8065331]. Much of the older literature writes the site as TTATG(T/C)AA; that form is the same element with one half-site degenerate, and both appear in this collection - HOCOMOCO and JASPAR HLF and NFIL3 models read TTATGTAAC and TTATGCAAC, while the DBP and TEF models read TTACGTAA. The distinction from the cyclic-AMP response element is two bases and no more: TTAC against TGAC at the outer edge of each half-site, with the ACGT core shared. That difference is real but slim, and truncated matrices lose it. This family is unusually coherent. Across 15 models from four databases its internal cohesion is 0.94, the highest of the bZIP families here, and every JASPAR and CIS-BP model in the family sits above 0.97 similarity to another member. Four of the six HOCOMOCO models carry in vitro evidence (HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX), so the claim that these proteins bind this sequence directly rests on more than ChIP. No member is distinguishable, and the family data flags no member as belonging elsewhere and contains no cross-species inferred model. The one model that drifts is CIS-BP M04016 for HLF, GTGACGTAA, which is half a PAR site and half a CRE; the same is true of CIS-BP M04034 for NFIL3, ATGACGTAAT.

## Where it acts

The founding site is the D-site of the rat albumin promoter, from which DBP takes its name [PMID:2331750], and the family's best-characterized targets are hepatic metabolic genes, including cytochrome P450 enzymes and pyridoxal kinase [PMID:8617210,15175240]. DBP, HLF and TEF have similar circadian and tissue-specific expression but measurably different promoter preferences [PMID:8617210], so a shared matrix does not imply a shared target list. Because occupancy is rhythmic and NFIL3 occupies the same elements at the opposite phase [PMID:11316793], a site can be an activator target in one part of the day and a repressor target twelve hours later; a static motif scan cannot express this. In immune cells NFIL3 acts at lineage-specification loci rather than at metabolic promoters [PMID:24663216,25310240]. On frequency: the AT-rich 8-mer is expected of order 10^5 times in 3.1 Gb of human sequence, so an isolated match carries little weight.

## Biology and disease

Single knockouts of Dbp, Hlf or Tef in mice are mild, which is the expected signature of factors that share an element. Mice lacking all three are viable but highly susceptible to spontaneous and audiogenic generalized seizures that are frequently lethal; the mechanism was traced to reduced expression of pyridoxal kinase and hence lower brain pyridoxal phosphate, serotonin and dopamine [PMID:15175240]. NFIL3 has non-redundant immune roles: it is required for commitment to the natural killer cell lineage, where it directly regulates Eomes and Id2 [PMID:24663216], and for the development of a common innate lymphoid cell precursor [PMID:25310240]. HLF is the 3-prime partner of the t(17;19) TCF3-HLF fusion in a rare and aggressive pro-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia, in which the HLF bZIP supplies dimerization and DNA binding to a chimeric activator [PMID:1386162]. In normal human hematopoiesis, HLF expression defines the stem cell compartment [PMID:34499717].

## Reading a hit

A TTACGTAA match is a clean family call by the standards of this class, because the family is cohesive, its models agree across databases, and several rest on in vitro binding data. It is not a member call at all, and here that matters more than usual: DBP, HLF and TEF activate while NFIL3 represses, so the same match is consistent with opposite outcomes, and which applies depends on cell type and on time of day. Check the outer bases before accepting the family. TTAC is PAR bZIP; TGAC is AP-1, CREB/ATF or ATF6/CREB3, and the shared ACGT core means a matrix scan will happily return CREs under a PAR model and vice versa. Two CIS-BP models filed here, for HLF and NFIL3, are themselves half-PAR and half-CRE hybrids. The 8-mer is AT-rich and common, so require accessibility or phase-resolved occupancy data before calling a site functional. Finally, treat a hit in a non-liver, non-immune, non-clock tissue with caution: expression, not sequence, is what limits this family's activity.
families.caveats: Of the eight bZIP families in this atlas, this is the one whose motif models agree best with each other and with in vitro binding data, and no member is flagged as belonging elsewhere. The limits are elsewhere. The site differs from a cyclic-AMP response element by only the outermost base of each half-site, so truncated or low-information matrices will not separate them, and two CIS-BP models here are already half-CRE hybrids. The 8-mer is AT-rich and occurs of order 100,000 times genome-wide. Most importantly, a hit does not indicate direction: DBP, HLF and TEF activate, NFIL3 represses, they occupy the same element in antiphase across the day, and sequence cannot distinguish them.

timeline.finding: DBP is cloned as the activator binding the D-site of the rat albumin promoter; it is liver-enriched at the protein level although its mRNA is widespread.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, expression analysis
timeline.open: The report described DBP as lacking a leucine zipper; its grouping with TEF and HLF as PAR bZIP proteins came later.

timeline.finding: The t(17;19) translocation of pro-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia fuses the E2A activation domain to the bZIP of a new factor, HLF, closely related to DBP and TEF.
timeline.methods: Translocation breakpoint cloning, cDNA characterization

timeline.finding: In vitro binding-site selection gives HLF and E2A-HLF the consensus GTTACGTAAT; HLF also binds related PAR and C/EBP sites, and the chimera is less tolerant of deviations from the consensus.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, EMSA, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether the TTAC half-site or the older TTATG(T/C)AA form better describes in vivo sites was not addressed.

timeline.finding: TEF and DBP accumulate with strong circadian rhythms in liver and bind the same sequences in vitro, yet prefer different promoters; a TEF-DBP fusion carrying the DBP DNA-binding and dimerization domain behaves like DBP, so the preference does not track measured affinity.
timeline.methods: Protein quantification across the day, in vitro binding, co-transfection with domain-swap fusions
timeline.open: How the bZIP region confers promoter preference without changing in vitro affinity was not explained.

timeline.finding: E4BP4/NFIL3 cycles in antiphase to DBP, HLF and TEF, cannot heterodimerize with them, and represses through the same sites they activate, making the family a clock-driven repressor-activator switch.
timeline.methods: mRNA and protein rhythms in SCN and liver, EMSA, reporter assays

timeline.finding: Mice lacking DBP, HLF and TEF develop frequently lethal epilepsy, traced to reduced pyridoxal kinase and lower brain pyridoxal phosphate, serotonin and dopamine.
timeline.methods: Triple knockout mice, transcriptome profiling, metabolite measurement

timeline.finding: NFIL3 is required at the common lymphoid progenitor for NK-cell commitment, directly regulating Eomes and Id2, and for a committed precursor of all innate lymphoid cell lineages, acting through TOX.
timeline.methods: Knockout progenitor differentiation and rescue, clonal assays, binding to regulatory regions

timeline.finding: HLF is one of the most selectively expressed genes in human hematopoietic stem cells, and an HLF reporter marks all stem-cell activity on serial transplantation.
timeline.methods: Bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, genomic reporter knock-in, transplantation

open: Whether the PAR site is better written TTACGTAA or TTATG(T/C)AA is unsettled, and the split follows evidence type: HT-SELEX models for DBP, TEF, HLF and NFIL3 give the symmetric TTACGTAA, while the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO models and JASPAR matrices for HLF and NFIL3 give TTATGTAAC or TTATGCAAC, and whether this reflects depletion of the CpG-containing palindrome in the genome, heterodimer partners in cells, or both, has not been resolved.

Why DBP and TEF, which bind the same sequences in vitro, prefer different promoters is unexplained: in fusion experiments the preference follows the DBP DNA-binding and dimerization domain, yet in vitro affinity does not differ, which points to promoter context or partner interactions that have not been identified.

families.name: SAND domain (AIRE/SP100/GMEB)
families.def: GMEB1/2 (GRE-modulating), SP100, SP140, AIRE, DEAF1-like SAND factors.
families.short: The SAND domain is a small DNA-binding fold named after the four proteins in which it was first recognized: Sp100, AIRE, NucP41/75 and DEAF1. Sequence-specific binding depends on a conserved KDWK motif on the domain's surface, and only some SAND proteins have it. The best-defined members are GMEB1 and GMEB2, which bind as a heterodimer, also known as parvovirus initiation factor, to two CpG-containing tetranucleotide half-sites with flexible spacing: ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases. Binding is abolished by methylation of the CpG in either half-site. AIRE and the speckled proteins SP100 and SP140 lack the KDWK motif and are recruited through chromatin rather than sequence, so motif models attributed to them should be treated as descriptions of where they were found.
families.long:
## The factors

SAND is a fold, not a functional group. The domain was named from Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75 and
DEAF1, and its NMR structure showed a novel alpha-beta fold whose DNA-binding activity maps to a
conserved surface motif, KDWK, which gives the family its alternative name [PMID:11427895,10523663]. Human SAND proteins
fall into distinct groups. GMEB1 and GMEB2 (p96 and p79) were identified twice over: as the
heterodimer that binds the glucocorticoid modulatory element upstream of the tyrosine
aminotransferase gene [PMID:7665613], and as parvovirus initiation factor, the host factor required for
minute virus of mice origin nicking [PMID:10523663]. They carry the KDWK motif, bind DNA cooperatively, and are
ubiquitously expressed [PMID:7665613,10523663,11743720]. DEAF1 (NUDR) is a related KDWK protein that binds TTCG-containing repeats [PMID:9773984];
notably, it has no motif in any of the four databases used here despite being named in this
family's definition. The speckled proteins SP100, SP110, SP140 and SP140L are nuclear-body
components that combine a SAND domain with PHD fingers and bromodomains and act as chromatin
readers in immune cells [PMID:32386862]. AIRE, the autoimmune regulator, is the most important special case: its
SAND domain lacks the KDWK residues required for sequence-specific DNA contact and instead mediates
homodimerization, while its two PHD fingers read histone H3, PHD1 binding H3 tails that are
unmethylated at lysine 4 [PMID:18292755]. AIRE is essentially restricted to medullary thymic epithelial cells [PMID:12376594].

## The motif

For GMEB1/GMEB2 the site is well defined and unusual. Degenerate oligonucleotide selection showed
that the heterodimer, and each homodimer, binds two tetranucleotide half-sites conforming to
ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases [PMID:11743720]; the spacing is genuinely flexible, so the
element is a pair of short half-sites at variable distance rather than a fixed-width motif [PMID:10523663,11743720]. The
invariant feature is the CpG in each half-site, and 5-methylation of those cytosines abolishes
binding completely [PMID:11743720], which makes GMEB an unusual example of a factor whose occupancy is directly
methylation-sensitive at its core. Because CpG is suppressed in vertebrate genomes, such sites
should be rare, yet over half of a sample of 100 human promoters contained at least one, often
within 100 bases of the start site [PMID:11743720]. The models in these databases capture only part of this
grammar. Most GMEB matrices collapse the pair into a single half-site region: the representative
model here is TACGTAA, and JASPAR's GMEB1 and GMEB2 matrices are tACGTa and TACGTAA. One CIS-BP
model, M05735_2.00, does show the doubled form (TACGTACGGTACGTA), which is the two half-sites
resolved. The consequence for scanning is severe: a six- or seven-base ACGT-centered model sits in
the middle of the sequence space used by bZIP factors, since TACGTA, TGACGT and CACGTG all contain
ACGT [PMID:10523663], and the data reflect this directly. Two GMEB1 models have a higher similarity to their
best out-of-family neighbour than to any in-family motif, and the family's cohesion is only 0.70
across 15 motifs. The remaining models are not ACGT elements at all: the ChIP-derived GMEB models
are GCGTCAGCGCG-like, the HOCOMOCO SP100 model is AACGGTTA and the SP140 model is GTCGTCACTA, each
with zero label agreement, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype (AC0160) is a CCAAT-containing element
rather than anything resembling a SAND site.

## Where it acts

GMEB sites are promoter-proximal and, by construction, CpG-containing, so they concentrate in
CpG-island promoters where their methylation sensitivity could make them responsive to DNA
methylation state. The glucocorticoid modulatory element itself modulates the sensitivity of a
glucocorticoid-responsive promoter rather than driving it [PMID:7665613], so GMEB acts as a modifier of another
factor's output. AIRE acts in a completely different regime: in medullary thymic epithelial cells
it associates with super-enhancers [PMID:28135252] and with thousands of promoters of tissue-restricted antigen
genes, and its principal mechanism is releasing stalled RNA polymerase II rather than recruiting it
to a specific sequence [PMID:22203960]. SP140 occupies and maintains repressed loci in macrophages, including
lineage-inappropriate developmental genes [PMID:32386862].

## Biology and disease

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in AIRE cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal
dystrophy (APECED, also APS-1), a monogenic autoimmune disease [PMID:9398839]; Aire-deficient mice lose promiscuous
expression of thousands of tissue-restricted antigens in the thymus and develop multi-organ
autoimmunity, which established the central-tolerance model of negative selection [PMID:12376594]. Missense
mutations in the SAND domain of DEAF1 cause intellectual disability with severe speech impairment
and behavioral problems [PMID:24726472]. Variants at SP140 and SP110 are associated with Crohn disease, multiple
sclerosis and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and SP110 mutations cause hepatic venoocclusive disease
with immunodeficiency [PMID:32386862]. GMEB proteins have no established monogenic disease link, but they are
required for parvovirus DNA replication [PMID:10523663].

## Reading a hit

The central caution is that this key mixes proteins that read sequence with proteins that do not. A
match to a GMEB model is a real, if weak, claim: look for the second CpG half-site within nine bases
and check the methylation state, because an unmethylated CpG is part of the site rather than
incidental. A match to an AIRE, SP100 or SP140 model is much harder to interpret. The three are not alike. AIRE's SAND domain lacks the KDWK residues, and its only motif here is a Vierstra archetype that reads as a CCAAT-type element. SP100's SAND domain does carry KDWK, since the SAND structure itself was solved from Sp100b [PMID:11427895], and the SP100 and SP140 models are grade A in HOCOMOCO with in vitro selection support (HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq, plus PBM for SP140) as well as ChIP. Those two are measurements of direct binding, even though their nearest neighbours lie in other families. The general risk for the ACGT-centered GMEB models is
confusion with bZIP sites, which share the same four-base core and are far more abundant [PMID:10523663,7665613]; a TACGTA
match in a promoter is more likely to be a CRE-like or MAF-like element than a GMEB site.
families.caveats: Split this family in two before trusting anything. GMEB1 and GMEB2 have the KDWK motif and a real, if unusual, site: two CpG-containing half-sites with a 1-9 base spacer, abolished by CpG methylation. But the matrices compress this to a six- or seven-base ACGT core that overlaps bZIP space, and two GMEB1 models here match an out-of-family motif better than any relative. AIRE is the real exception: its SAND domain lacks the KDWK residues and its only model is a Vierstra archetype that reads as a CCAAT-type element. The SP100 and SP140 models are grade A with in vitro selection support, so they do record sequences those proteins bind, but their nearest neighbours lie in other families. Treat the AIRE model as a record of where AIRE was found rather than of a sequence it reads. DEAF1 has no motif here at all.

timeline.finding: The factor binding the glucocorticoid modulatory element (GME) far upstream of the tyrosine aminotransferase gene is a novel, ubiquitous complex of two proteins, GMEB1 and GMEB2, distinct from the CREB/ATF proteins that also bind the element.
timeline.methods: Partial protein purification, gel shift, size-exclusion chromatography
timeline.open: The proteins' sequences, family and recognition rules were unknown.

timeline.finding: Parvovirus initiation factor is cloned as the p96/p79 heterodimer (GMEB1/GMEB2), placed in the KDWK family, and shown to bind two PuCGPy half-sites that can be spaced 1 to 15 nucleotides apart.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, recombinant protein, DNA-binding and promoter assays
timeline.open: The exact consensus and spacing optimum.

timeline.finding: NMR structure of the Sp100b SAND domain defines a new alpha/beta DNA-binding fold, with the conserved KDWK motif on a positively charged helical surface that mutagenesis and chemical-shift mapping identify as the DNA-binding surface; the NUDR (DEAF1) SAND domain alone suffices for DNA binding.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, mutagenesis, chemical-shift perturbation

timeline.finding: Selection and dissociation-rate analysis define the GMEB consensus as ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY with an optimal spacer of six; CpG methylation of the half-sites abolishes binding, yet over half of 100 human promoters carry a site.
timeline.methods: Degenerate-oligonucleotide selection, dissociation kinetics, gel shift
timeline.open: Whether methylation regulates GMEB occupancy in cells.

timeline.finding: AIRE is reported to be a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein whose dimers and tetramers bind ATTGGTTA and TTATTA motifs.
timeline.methods: Gel shift and competition assays with recombinant protein
timeline.open: The motifs were not tied to AIRE target genes in thymic epithelium.

timeline.finding: Aire-deficient mice lose ectopic expression of peripheral tissue-restricted antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells and develop autoimmunity that depends on Aire in thymic stroma, establishing AIRE's role in central tolerance.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, expression profiling, thymic transplantation

timeline.finding: In medullary thymic epithelial cells AIRE binds essentially all Pol II-rich start sites and activates its targets by releasing stalled RNA polymerase II, not by recognizing specific promoter sequences. This is at odds with the earlier report of sequence-specific AIRE binding.
timeline.methods: Transcript mapping with mRNA-spanning probes, ChIP-seq for AIRE and Pol II

open: Whether CpG methylation regulates GMEB binding in cells is open: methylating the half-site CpGs abolishes binding in vitro, but the proposal that this controls occupancy in vivo rests on that biochemistry.

Whether AIRE has any intrinsic sequence preference is disputed: an early in vitro study reported AIRE oligomers binding ATTGGTTA and TTATTA motifs, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype AC0160 carries ATTGGTTA on its reverse strand, whereas genome-wide work finds AIRE at essentially all Pol II-rich start sites, acting by releasing stalled polymerase rather than by sequence recognition.

Whether SP100 and SP140 bind DNA directly through their SAND domains is unsettled: their HOCOMOCO models are grade A and supported by in vitro assays (HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq, plus PBM for SP140) as well as ChIP, yet the motifs (AACGGTTA, GTCGTCACTA) share little with the GMEB half-site beyond a CpG, and their nearest neighbours lie in other families.

The permitted GMEB half-site spacing differs between studies: the cloning work reported spacings of 1 to 15 nucleotides, whereas selection combined with dissociation-rate analysis gave 1 to 9 with an optimum of six.

families.name: EGR
families.def: GCGTGGGCG. EGR1-4, WT1.
families.short: EGR1 to EGR4 are immediate-early transcription factors whose three C2H2 zinc fingers read a nine-base GC-rich site, GCGTGGGCG, also written GCGGGGGCG. The first of these proteins, EGR1, is better known to structural biologists as Zif268: its complex with DNA was the crystal structure that established how zinc fingers recognize DNA, three bases per finger, and it remains the reference for the C2H2 recognition code. EGR proteins are induced within minutes by growth factors, serum and neuronal activity, so their sites sit in the promoters of rapidly inducible genes. All four paralogues share the same matrix, and the WT1 tumor suppressor binds essentially the same sequence, so a hit names a site rather than a protein.
families.long:
## The factors

EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 are four paralogous immediate-early transcription factors, each with three Cys2-His2 zinc fingers and a set of aliases reflecting their independent discovery: EGR1 is also Zif268, NGFI-A, Krox-24 and zif/268; EGR2 is Krox-20; EGR4 is NGFI-C (Christy and Nathans 1989; Patwardhan et al. 1991) [PMID:2510170,1906159]. Their mRNAs are induced within minutes of exposure to growth factors, serum, mitogens or neuronal activity, which is what "immediate-early" means here: the protein is largely absent from unstimulated cells. EGR1 is broadly inducible; EGR2 is prominent in Schwann cells and the developing hindbrain; EGR3 in neurons and muscle spindles; EGR4 is largely restricted to brain. All four bind DNA as monomers. One further protein must be kept in mind: the Wilms tumor suppressor WT1 has a closely related four-finger domain and recognizes essentially the same site (Rauscher et al. 1990) [PMID:2244209]. WT1 is a separate family in this atlas, but it is not separable from EGR by sequence alone.

## The motif

The site is nine base pairs, usually written GCGTGGGCG or GCGGGGGCG; the reverse-complement form, CGCCCACGC, is how several matrices in this atlas are stored (the medoid, CIS-BP M04461_2.00, is CCGCCCACGCA, which is TGCGTGGGCGG read from the other strand). Recognition is the textbook case. The 2.1 A crystal structure of the three Zif268 fingers bound to a consensus site showed the fingers lying in the major groove and wrapping part way around B-DNA, each finger contacting a three-base subsite through residues at positions -1, 3 and 6 of its recognition helix (Pavletich and Pabo 1991) [PMID:2028256]; the structure was later refined to 1.6 A (Elrod-Erickson et al. 1996) [PMID:8939742] and became the basis of the general C2H2 code (Wolfe et al. 2000; Zhang et al. 2024) [PMID:10940247,38754172]. Random-site selection showed that EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 all bind and activate from GCGGGGGCG and from a family of closely related variants, with only modest differences among them (Swirnoff and Milbrandt 1995) [PMID:7891721]. The atlas data agree emphatically: 15 matrices, four gene symbols, cohesion 0.90, and the JASPAR profiles for EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 are all the same 11-mer, ACGCCCACGCA. Nothing distinguishes the paralogues. The useful comparison is outward, to the other GC-rich families. EGR's signature is the CACGC / GCGTG triplet immediately adjacent to a GGGCG block; the KLF/SP GC-box, GGGGCGGGG, lacks it, and the KLF/SP in vitro consensus CCACGCCC shares the pentamer CCACG with the reverse complement of the EGR site but places it differently. Where a nine-mer matches both models at comparable scores, sequence cannot decide, and that situation is common.

## Where it acts

EGR sites are promoter-proximal and GC-rich, concentrated near CpG islands and in the promoters of rapidly inducible genes. Because EGR protein appears only after stimulation, occupancy is condition-dependent in a way that the sequence does not reveal: the same site can be empty in a resting cell and bound minutes after serum addition. The classic co-occurrence problem is with the GC-box factors. When the CT/GC-rich element of the human IL-3 promoter (positions -76 to -47) was used as bait in an expression screen, the clones recovered were EGR1, EGR2 and the unrelated zinc-finger protein DB1/VEZF1; in gel-shift assays DB1 bound the element constitutively while EGR1 bound only after T-cell activation (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994) [PMID:8035792]. That single experiment is a compact demonstration of both the overlap and its resolution: the same element, different factors, distinguished by condition rather than by sequence. EGR sites also overlap WT1 sites directly, and the two proteins compete at shared sequences [PMID:2244209,7862142].

## Biology and disease

Egr1-null mice are viable but females are infertile because of a specific failure to produce luteinizing hormone beta, identifying EGR1 as the factor required for LH-beta expression (Lee et al. 1996) [PMID:8703054]. Egr2/Krox-20 null mice fail to myelinate peripheral nerves, establishing EGR2 as a control point for Schwann cell myelination (Topilko et al. 1994) [PMID:7935840], and human EGR2 mutations cause hereditary myelinopathies in the Charcot-Marie-Tooth and congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy spectrum (Warner et al. 1998) [PMID:9537424]. EGR1 has been implicated in growth-factor responses, apoptosis and tumor suppression in various tissues, though the direction of effect is context-dependent and the literature is not settled. EGR3 and EGR4 have narrower documented roles, largely neuronal.

## Reading a hit

A match identifies the EGR site, not an EGR protein - and possibly not even an EGR protein, since WT1 binds the same sequence. The evidence that EGR factors really bind this sequence is unusually good: the HOCOMOCO models for EGR1, EGR2 and EGR3 carry combined ChIP and HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX evidence at grade A, so the label is in vitro supported, not ChIP-inferred. Two entries in the family are weaker and should not be used alone: EGR4.H14CORE.0.S.B is an eight-position model whose nearest neighbors across the databases lie outside this family, and the Vierstra archetype AC0262:EGR carries only 5.6 bits, too little to call anything. One archetype is explicitly named AC0519:EGR/WT, which is the clustering telling you that the EGR and WT1 motifs merged. Practically: a nine-base GC-rich site is common in promoters, so treat an isolated hit as weak evidence; and because EGR proteins are stimulus-induced, a real site may be unoccupied in whatever cell state you sampled.
families.caveats: EGR1 to EGR4 share one matrix, so a hit names the family at best. Worse, WT1 binds essentially the same nine-base site, and one Vierstra archetype in this family is explicitly labelled EGR/WT - a strong EGR match is also a candidate WT1 site. Overlap with the KLF/SP GC-box is frequent and often unresolvable from sequence. The in vitro evidence behind the EGR label is good (grade-A HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX models for EGR1-EGR3), but the EGR4 HT-SELEX model and the low-information AC0262 archetype should not be used on their own. Because EGR proteins are stimulus-induced, occupancy depends on cell state, not sequence.
