timeline.finding: Zif268 (EGR1) expressed in bacteria binds sites upstream of its own gene and in other promoters; footprinting and methylation interference give the high-affinity consensus GCGTGGGGCG.
timeline.methods: DNase I footprinting, methylation interference, synthetic oligonucleotide binding
timeline.open: How three zinc fingers specify a GC-rich site was unknown.

timeline.finding: Site selection with the zinc-finger region of the Wilms tumor protein WT1 recovers sequences similar to the EGR-1 consensus, so the EGR site is not unique to EGR proteins.
timeline.methods: Selection from degenerate oligonucleotides, gel shift
timeline.open: Whether WT1 and EGR1 prefer different variants of the site was not tested.

timeline.finding: The 2.1 A crystal structure of the three Zif268 fingers on a consensus site shows the fingers following the major groove, each making its primary contacts in a three-base subsite, mostly on the G-rich strand; refinement to 1.6 A in 1996 sharpened the contact map.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Whether the contacts seen in the crystal account for the full binding energy and site length was not measured.

timeline.finding: Krox-20 (Egr2)-null mice fail to myelinate peripheral nerves; in 1998 EGR2 mutations were found in human hereditary myelinopathies, making EGR2 the best-supported disease gene in the family.
timeline.methods: Gene targeting in mice; mutation screening in patients

timeline.finding: Random-site selection shows EGR1, EGR2, EGR3 and EGR4 select nearly the same consensus, but revises the site: binding tolerates more divergence than assumed, contacts not apparent in the crystal structure contribute substantially to binding energy, and an optimal site is at least 10 bp rather than 9. EGR4 (NGFI-C) binds with more than threefold lower affinity than the others.
timeline.methods: PCR-mediated random site selection, gel shift, dissociation kinetics
timeline.open: Whether the EGR4 affinity difference changes its targets in vivo was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Egr1-null female mice are infertile because of LH-beta deficiency, and a canonical EGR site in the LH-beta promoter is needed for synergistic activation with SF-1, giving the clearest single physiological target of an EGR site.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, promoter mutagenesis and co-transfection

timeline.finding: An updated review of C2H2 structures restates the recognition code: positions -1, -4 and -7, counted back from the first zinc-coordinating histidine (the classical helix positions 6, 3 and -1), read the 5', central and 3' bases of each triplet, positions -5 and -8 also contribute, and residue identity maps onto base identity (Arg, Lys or His for G; Asn or Gln for A; Glu for T or 5-methylcytosine; Asp for C).
timeline.methods: Review of crystal structures

open: How long the EGR site is depends on which evidence is used: the Zif268 structure and most matrices treat it as a 9-bp site, whereas random-site selection found that an optimal site is at least 10 bp and that contacts not seen in the crystal contribute substantially to binding energy.

Whether the four EGR paralogues differ at the sequence level in any way that matters in cells is unresolved: their selected consensus sites are nearly identical, yet EGR4 binds with more than threefold lower affinity, and the one EGR4 in vitro model here is shorter than the others and clusters with matrices outside the family.
Which of EGR1 and WT1 occupies a shared site when both are expressed, and whether their effects on the target gene oppose each other, has not been settled beyond individual promoters.

EGR1's role in cancer is disputed: it has been described as a tumor suppressor in some tissues and as growth-promoting in others, and the literature has not settled what determines the direction of effect.

families.name: MITF / TFE (CLEAR)
families.def: CLEAR/M-box GTCACGTGAC. MITF, TFE3, TFEB, TFEC.
families.short: MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC are bHLH-LZ factors that dimerize only with each other, because a three-residue insertion kinks their leucine zipper. They read a canonical E-box core with a preference for T and A flanks, giving the palindromic 10-mer GTCACGTGAC, known as the CLEAR box in lysosomal and autophagy promoters; at the weaker CATGTG form of the core the 5' T is not merely preferred but required, and that version is the melanocyte M-box (TCATGTGA) of the pigmentation genes. MITF is the lineage factor of melanocytes and is mutated in Waardenburg syndrome type 2A and predisposes to melanoma; TFEB and TFE3 run the lysosome-autophagy program downstream of mTORC1 and are recurrently rearranged in renal cell carcinoma. The four paralogues cannot be told apart from sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC form the MiT/TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) factors. MITF was identified from the mouse microphthalmia locus, where mutations cause loss of melanocytes, deafness and small eyes [PMID:8343963]; the three TFE genes were then recognized as a discrete family that dimerizes internally - each member homodimerizes and heterodimerizes with the others, but not with MYC, MAX or USF [PMID:7958932]. The structural basis is a three-residue insertion that kinks the leucine zipper, which excludes the other bHLH-ZIP proteins from the dimer interface and explains why MiT/TFE factors, despite reading the same DNA core, form a closed dimerization set [PMID:23207919]. Expression is what separates them: MITF is restricted (melanocytes, mast cells, osteoclasts, retinal pigment epithelium) and has multiple isoforms driven from alternative promoters, TFE3 and TFEB are broadly expressed and act as the general lysosomal-autophagy arm, and TFEC is largely myeloid. All four are regulated post-translationally rather than only transcriptionally; TFEB in particular is phosphorylated by mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface and held in the cytoplasm until nutrient stress releases it [PMID:22692423]. The atlas assigns 14 motifs here (4 JASPAR, 6 HOCOMOCO, 4 CIS-BP) across all four symbols, cohesion 0.94, with TFE3.H14CORE.0.PSM.A as the representative.

## The motif

The core is the canonical E-box CACGTG, read as two CAC half-sites by the histidine-glutamate-arginine triad in each basic region, exactly as in MAX [PMID:23207919]. What distinguishes MiT/TFE is the flanking base, but the requirement is specific to one form of the core. At a CATGTG E-box a 5' T is essential: MITF bound TCATGTGA and not the same E-box lacking the T, correctly predicting that the CATGTG box of the P gene would not be bound, and the E-boxes of the tyrosinase, TRP-1, TRP-2 and QNR-71 promoters carry the T without exception [PMID:9819381]. That T-flanked CATGTG is the classical melanocyte M-box [PMID:1321344,7958932]. At a CACGTG E-box the same work saw no specific requirement for the flanking sequence [PMID:9819381], even though every MiT/TFE model in these databases is built with a T and the reciprocal A around the core, giving the palindromic 10-mer GTCACGTGAC. In the lysosomal literature that 10-mer is called the CLEAR element (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression And Regulation), GTCACGTGAC, found in the promoters of most lysosomal hydrolase, subunit and trafficking genes [PMID:19556463]. So the M-box and the CLEAR box are one arrangement described in two fields, a T/A-flanked E-box, differing only in the central base pair of the core. Two consequences follow. First, MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC are not separable from one another by sequence: pairwise similarity among their models in this atlas is 0.97-0.995. Second, the motif is essentially identical to the USF motif, and very close to BHLHE41 and CLOCK-BMAL1 models, so the T/A flanks buy discrimination against MYC-MAX but not against those. The family data also contains lower-information, ChIP-derived variants (a grade-C TFEB model reading gTCACATG) that lose the 3' half entirely.

## Where it acts

MiT/TFE sites are promoter-proximal and CpG-island-associated. The CLEAR network was defined as a few hundred coordinately regulated lysosomal and autophagy genes carrying the element within the first few hundred base pairs of the transcription start site [PMID:19556463,21752829], and TFEB ChIP-seq recovers that set plus autophagosome-formation genes [PMID:21752829,21617040]. MITF occupancy is layered on top of a melanocyte-specific accessibility landscape: the same GTCACGTGAC sequence is used at pigmentation genes (TYR, DCT, TYRP1, PMEL), at lysosome-related genes in melanosome biogenesis, and at proliferation genes, and MITF co-occupies melanocyte enhancers with SOX10 and the AP-1 machinery. TFEB and TFE3 occupancy is switched by subcellular localization rather than by motif availability - the sites are present and often accessible even when the factor is cytoplasmic [PMID:19556463,22692423].

## Biology and disease

MITF is the lineage-determining factor of the melanocyte: loss-of-function alleles cause the mouse microphthalmia phenotypes and, in humans, Waardenburg syndrome type 2A (deafness with pigmentary anomalies) [PMID:8343963,7874167] and Tietz syndrome. The recurrent MITF E318K substitution, which impairs SUMOylation, raises melanoma risk and also associates with renal cell carcinoma [PMID:22080950,22012259]. TFEB and TFE3 drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy downstream of mTORC1 and starvation [PMID:21617040,22692423], and are involved in lysosomal storage disease biology as therapeutic targets. Translocations involving these genes are diagnostic in cancer: promoter substitution at t(6;11)(p21;q13) drives TFEB overexpression in a distinct renal cell carcinoma subtype, and TFE3 fusions define another renal carcinoma group [PMID:12837690] and alveolar soft part sarcoma.

## Reading a hit

A GTCACGTGAC or TCATGTGA hit identifies a T/A-flanked E-box. That is a real narrowing - it argues against MYC-MAX - but it does not name the factor: USF1/USF2, BHLHE41, CLOCK-BMAL1 and all four MiT/TFE proteins share it. Within the family, a hit cannot distinguish MITF from TFE3, TFEB or TFEC; the usual discriminator is expression, so a hit in melanocyte data suggests MITF and a hit in a starvation experiment suggests TFEB, and neither inference comes from the sequence. ChIP-derived MiT/TFE models are additionally biased toward active CpG-island promoters. Prefer the HOCOMOCO models with in vitro (S or M) support.
families.caveats: The T/A flanks make this motif distinguishable from MYC-MAX but not from USF1/USF2, BHLHE41 or CLOCK-BMAL1, which prefer the same extended palindrome; a GTCACGTGAC hit therefore names a group, not a protein. Within the family MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC share one motif at 0.97-0.995 similarity, so assignment relies entirely on which factor is expressed and, for TFEB/TFE3, on whether it is nuclear at the time. Several models here are ChIP-only and low grade (a grade-C TFEB model reduces to gTCACATG), so they encode promoter context as much as intrinsic specificity. Prefer HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX-supported models when the question is direct binding.

timeline.finding: Mutagenesis of the TRP-1 promoter identifies the M box, an 11-bp element conserved between the melanocyte-specific TRP-1 and tyrosinase promoters, as a positive regulatory element.
timeline.methods: Promoter mutagenesis, transfection, DNA-protein binding assays
timeline.open: The M-box-binding factor was not identified.

timeline.finding: The mouse microphthalmia locus, whose alleles affect pigmentation, eye size, bone resorption, mast cells and hearing, is shown to encode a bHLH-ZIP protein.
timeline.methods: Insertional mutagenesis, positional cloning, expression analysis

timeline.finding: MITF binds DNA as a homodimer or as a heterodimer with TFEB, TFE3 or TFEC, defining the MiT family, and activates pigmentation genes through the M box.
timeline.methods: EMSA, dimerization assays, reporter assays
timeline.open: Why MiT proteins do not partner other bHLH-ZIP factors.

timeline.finding: A T immediately 5' of a CATGTG E-box is essential for MITF binding in vitro and in vivo, while no flank requirement was seen for CACGTG; pigmentation-gene E-boxes carry the T without exception.
timeline.methods: EMSA, reporter assays, cross-species promoter comparison
timeline.open: Later database models show a T/A flank around CACGTG as well, which this work did not detect.

timeline.finding: Most lysosomal genes share a promoter-proximal GTCACGTGAC element (CLEAR) and are coordinately regulated by TFEB, which translocates to the nucleus under lysosomal storage stress.
timeline.methods: Promoter motif analysis, expression meta-analysis, TFEB overexpression

timeline.finding: A germline MITF E318K substitution that impairs SUMOylation is associated with melanoma and with renal cell carcinoma.
timeline.methods: Whole-genome sequencing, linkage, case-control association, functional assays

timeline.finding: TFEB localization is set by phosphorylation, by ERK2 in response to nutrients and by lysosomal mTORC1 at Ser211 with 14-3-3 retention, so CLEAR occupancy is switched by nuclear entry rather than by site availability.
timeline.methods: Phosphosite mapping and mutagenesis, kinase inhibition, localization imaging

timeline.finding: MITF crystal structures show a three-residue shift in the leucine zipper that kinks one helix and restricts heterodimerization, and an Ile212 nonpolar contact that explains M-box binding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, mutagenesis, mouse and human mutant analysis

open: Whether the T and A flanks that every MiT/TFE model carries around CACGTG are a real binding preference or a property of the sequences the models were built from is untested: gel-shift and in vivo assays found the 5' T essential at CATGTG but no flanking requirement at CACGTG.

Whether the M-box is more MiT/TFE-selective than the CLEAR box is not settled: the MITF structure attributes M-box binding to an Ile212 contact that related factors lack and reports that several of them bind the M-box weakly, but the JASPAR USF1 model also reads a T-flanked CATGTG (GTCATGTGAC).
Whether MITF isoforms differ in DNA recognition is unclear: an alternatively spliced exon outside the bHLH-ZIP modulated DNA binding in vitro, but none of the database models resolves isoforms.

families.name: YY1 / YY2
families.def: AAnATGGCggc. YY1, YY2, ZFP42/REX1.
families.short: YY1 is a ubiquitously expressed zinc-finger protein that binds a short CCAT-centered site, usually written CGCCATNTT or, on the other strand, AANATGGCGGC. It sits at or just inside the transcription start site of a large fraction of CpG-island promoters, works as an activator at some and a repressor at others, and is found on both the enhancer and the promoter side of enhancer-promoter contacts. Two retrogenes derived from YY1, YY2 and ZFP42/REX1, share the same zinc-finger domain; YY2 binds the same consensus more weakly, and REX1 prefers divergent sites that still contain the CCAT core. Because the motif is short and concentrated in CpG islands, a YY1 match is one of the most common hits in promoter sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

YY1 (Yin Yang 1) has four C2H2 zinc fingers at its C terminus and belongs to the GLI-Kruppel class;
its Drosophila counterpart is Pleiohomeotic (Pho). It was described independently in the same period
as a repressor whose activity is relieved by adenovirus E1A [PMID:1655281] and as an initiator-binding protein that
directs and activates transcription in vitro [PMID:1720509], and it also appears in the older literature as NF-E1,
delta factor and UCRBP. It binds DNA as a monomer and is expressed in essentially all cell types.

The family in these databases has three human members. YY2 and ZFP42 (REX1) are both retrogenes
generated from YY1 in placental mammals [PMID:17478514], and their zinc-finger domains remain highly similar to
YY1's. Motif measurements show that YY2 binds the same consensus as YY1 but with much lower
affinity, while REX1 binds sequences divergent from YY1's that nevertheless share the CCAT core [PMID:17478514].
ZFP42/REX1 is best known as a pluripotency marker in embryonic stem cells. All three are assigned
here to a single family because their matrices are not separable.

## The motif

The literature core is CCAT. The short consensus most often quoted is CGCCATNTT, and the
reverse-strand form AANATGGCGGC is what several databases show, including the form used in the
ontology entry for this family. Selection experiments give a longer high-affinity version,
GCCGCCATTTTG, and the endogenous sites at Peg3 (GGCGCCATNTT) and Xist (CCGCCATNTT) are longer than
the classic motif [PMID:18950698]. Substituting three residues in the first zinc finger, to mimic Drosophila Pho,
collapses specificity to a bare GCCAT, showing that the four fingers contribute jointly rather than
modularly and that the flanking information depends on finger one [PMID:18950698]. The data consensus here,
CCGCCATYTT, is the same site.

The cocrystal structure of the YY1 zinc fingers on the adeno-associated virus P5 initiator explains
an unusual property. Upstream of the start sites the protein contacts both strands, whereas
downstream the contacts are essentially restricted to the template strand, leaving the non-template
strand free [PMID:8942976]. That asymmetry is what allows YY1 to sit over an initiator, support TBP-independent
initiation with a fixed direction, and bind a preformed transcription bubble or a DNA/RNA hybrid [PMID:8942976].
Functionally the site is orientation-sensitive in context: in the c-fos promoter YY1 bends DNA and
its effect depends on which way the site points [PMID:8276234]. Sequence alone does not distinguish YY1 from YY2,
and only partially separates ZFP42.

## Where it acts

YY1 is a promoter factor first. Its motif is strongly enriched at CpG-island promoters, where it
co-occurs with a characteristic set of partners at active promoters, including HCFC1, ZNF143,
THAP11 and GABP [PMID:23539139], and it binds within a few tens of base pairs of the transcription start site far
more often than at a distance. It is also present at active enhancers, and the observation that it
occupies both sides of many enhancer-promoter pairs led to the proposal that YY1 acts as a general
structural contributor to enhancer-promoter loops [PMID:29224777], in loose analogy to CTCF at structural loops.
YY1 is additionally reported as a CTCF cofactor at the X-inactivation choice [PMID:17218270], and as the mammalian
Pho counterpart that helps recruit Polycomb complexes, an activity that requires both DNA binding
and interaction with YAF2 [PMID:24285299]. Because the informative site is short and CpG islands are the preferred
context, matches are extremely dense in promoter sequence: a YY1 hit near a TSS is close to the
default expectation rather than a discovery.

## Biology and disease

YY1 is dosage-sensitive in humans: de novo heterozygous variants and deletions cause Gabriele-de
Vries syndrome, an intellectual-disability syndrome with movement abnormalities in which patient
cells show transcriptional and chromatin dysfunction [PMID:28575647], consistent with partial loss of a general
promoter factor rather than a tissue-restricted one. Mouse YY1 mutants show homeotic transformations
of the axial skeleton and interact genetically with the Polycomb gene Ring1 [PMID:16624538], placing YY1 in the
PcG-dependent regulation of Hox genes. At the molecular level YY1 has been assigned both activating
and repressing roles at different promoters, often through the cofactor it recruits (HDACs and
Polycomb components on one side, coactivators and the basal machinery on the other), which is why
the same motif cannot be read as a sign. YY1 is frequently reported as overexpressed in tumors,
though the causal claims there are much less settled than the developmental genetics.

## Reading a hit

A YY1 match is common enough that on its own it is close to uninformative, particularly inside a
CpG island. Treat it as a family-level call: YY1, YY2 and ZFP42 are not separable by sequence, and
YY2 in particular binds the same consensus. A hit tells you nothing about direction of effect,
because YY1 activates at some promoters and represses at others. Position matters more than score:
a site within tens of base pairs of a TSS, in the orientation seen at initiators, is a more credible
YY1 element than a stronger match in intergenic DNA. Finally, YY1 has been used as a positive
control in so many ChIP experiments that the motif is over-represented in derived models generally;
if a ChIP-derived matrix for some unrelated factor looks like AANATGGCGGC, indirect or
co-occupancy-driven enrichment at active promoters is the first explanation to consider, not a new
specificity.
families.caveats: The site is short, CpG-island-associated and present at a large share of active promoters, so a hit is expected rather than informative and should be weighted by position relative to the TSS. YY1, YY2 and ZFP42/REX1 all descend from the same zinc-finger domain and cannot be told apart from sequence; YY2 binds the identical consensus with lower affinity. A match says nothing about activation versus repression, since YY1 does both depending on the cofactor recruited. And because YY1 sits at essentially all active promoters, an AANATGGCGGC-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data is more likely promoter co-occupancy than that factor's own specificity.

timeline.finding: Two groups describe the same protein from opposite directions: as a repressor of the adeno-associated virus P5 promoter whose repression is converted to activation by adenovirus E1A, and as an initiator-binding protein that sets the start site and activates transcription in vitro.
timeline.methods: Promoter deletion and reporter assays, protein purification, in vitro transcription
timeline.open: Why one protein gave activation in one assay and repression in the other.

timeline.finding: At the c-fos promoter YY1 bends the DNA, and whether it represses depends on the orientation of its site, showing the element is read in context rather than as a free-standing word.
timeline.methods: Circular permutation bending assays, reporter constructs

timeline.finding: The cocrystal structure of the four YY1 zinc fingers on the AAV P5 initiator shows contacts to both strands upstream of the start site but essentially template-strand-only contacts downstream, explaining how YY1 can sit over an initiator and leave the non-template strand accessible.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: The structure covered one site; the contribution of each finger to flanking specificity was not tested.

timeline.finding: Phylogenetic analysis identifies YY2 and ZFP42/REX1 as retroposed copies of YY1 that arose in placental mammals; YY2 keeps the YY1 consensus at much lower affinity while REX1 has diverged, retaining only the CCAT core.
timeline.methods: Comparative genomics across 62 YY1-related sequences, binding-site selection

timeline.finding: The functional YY1 site is longer than the classic CGCCATNTT: the Peg3 and Xist elements and an independent selection give GCCGCCATTTTG with higher affinity, and swapping three residues of finger 1 for the Drosophila Pho version collapses specificity to GCCAT, so the four fingers act jointly rather than modularly.
timeline.methods: Gel-shift assays on endogenous sites, binding-site selection, zinc-finger mutagenesis

timeline.finding: Genome-wide occupancy places YY1 in a fixed company of factors at active CpG-island promoters, coinciding with HCFC1, ZNF143, THAP11 and GABP, which sets the baseline expectation that a YY1 site near a TSS is unremarkable.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq across human cell lines

timeline.finding: De novo heterozygous YY1 variants and deletions are shown to cause Gabriele-de Vries syndrome, establishing that this broadly expressed promoter factor is dosage-sensitive in human development.
timeline.methods: Exome sequencing in a patient cohort, patient-cell transcriptomics and chromatin profiling

timeline.finding: YY1 is proposed to be a general structural regulator of enhancer-promoter loops, by analogy to CTCF at larger loops: it binds both enhancers and promoter-proximal elements, and deleting its sites or depleting the protein disrupts looping and expression.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, chromosome-conformation assays, site deletion and degron-based protein depletion in mouse embryonic stem cells
timeline.open: Whether loss of looping is a direct structural effect or a consequence of losing transcription at the same promoters was not separated.

open: Whether YY1 is a general structural component of enhancer-promoter loops is unsettled: the proposal rests on co-occupancy at loop anchors plus site deletion and protein depletion in a small number of cell lines, and an alternative reading is that YY1 marks active CpG-island promoters, so the contacts it is credited with follow from transcription rather than cause it.

Nothing in the sequence predicts whether YY1 will activate or repress a given promoter; the recruited cofactor (Polycomb and HDACs versus coactivators and the basal machinery) is the usual explanation, but no context feature has been shown to determine the choice.

Whether ZFP42/REX1 belongs with YY1 as a motif family member is debatable: selection experiments say its sites have diverged from YY1's apart from the CCAT core, yet its HOCOMOCO model (GGCAGCCATTTT) is close enough to the YY1 model to be pooled here.
What YY2 does that YY1 does not is unresolved, since it binds the same consensus with much lower affinity and no distinct target class has been established for it.

families.name: E-proteins (TCF3/4/12)
families.def: Class I bHLH E-box CAGCTG/CACCTG heterodimer partners. TCF3/E2A, TCF4/ITF2, TCF12/HEB, TCF15, TCFL5.
families.short: TCF3 (E2A/E12/E47), TCF4 (E2-2) and TCF12 (HEB) are the broadly expressed class I bHLH proteins that serve as the general dimerization partners for tissue-restricted bHLH factors - MYOD in muscle, ASCL and NEUROD in neurons, TWIST in mesenchyme, TAL1 in blood - and are sequestered by ID proteins. They bind the class-A E-box, written CACCTG or equivalently CAGGTG, and also CAGCTG. Because most functional sites are heterodimeric, only one half-site is read by the E-protein itself. E2A loss abolishes B-cell development; TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, TCF12 loss causes coronal craniosynostosis, and TCF3 is a recurrent fusion partner in pre-B leukaemia.
families.long:
## The factors

The E-proteins are TCF3 (E2A, whose splice isoforms are E12 and E47), TCF4 (E2-2, ITF2) and TCF12 (HEB, HTF4). They are class I basic helix-loop-helix proteins: broadly expressed, lacking a leucine zipper, and defined by the fact that they are the general dimerization partners for the class II, tissue-restricted bHLH factors. The HLH motif itself was recognized by comparing the immunoglobulin enhancer-binding E12/E47 proteins with Drosophila daughterless, MyoD and MYC [PMID:2493990], and the following paper showed the central property directly: heterodimers between different HLH proteins form readily and bind a common DNA sequence [PMID:2503252]. That is what E-proteins do. TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 heterodimerize with MYOD and MYF5 in muscle, ASCL1, NEUROD and ATOH in neural tissue, TWIST1 and HAND in mesenchyme, TAL1 and LYL1 in blood, PTF1A in pancreas, and OLIG proteins in glia, as well as with each other [PMID:10611221,26555048]. They are also the targets of the ID proteins (ID1-ID4), which have an HLH but no basic region and therefore sequester E-proteins into non-binding dimers [PMID:2156629]. This family also collects TCFL5, a more distant protein, and the ontology lists TCF15; in the current data, motifs exist for TCF3, TCF4, TCF12 and TCFL5. The atlas assigns 13 motifs here (5 JASPAR, 4 HOCOMOCO, 4 CIS-BP), cohesion 0.87, representative TCF4 (MA0830.3).

## The motif

E-proteins read the class-A E-box, most often written CACCTG or, equivalently, CAGGTG - these are the same six base pairs read from opposite strands, which is worth keeping in mind when comparing database consensus strings. The other class-A variant, CAGCTG, is also bound; together the preference is CAG[C/G]TG on one strand. The immunoglobulin enhancer sites that defined the family, muE5 and kappaE2, are of this type [PMID:2493990,2503252]. The E47 crystal structure showed how the site is read: a parallel four-helix bundle with one basic helix per monomer in the major groove, a glutamate contacting the CA of each half-site and an arginine the guanine on the complementary strand - the same chemistry as MAX, with the residue at one position determining class A versus class B preference [PMID:7926781]. Because heterodimers are the functional unit, the real in vivo site is often asymmetric: one half-site is read by the E-protein and the other by the tissue partner, so MyoD-E47 and TAL1-TCF3 sites differ from E-protein homodimer sites mainly in one half. Systematic binding-site selection comparing MyoD and E2A complexes established this early [PMID:2174572], and it is the reason paralogue assignment from sequence fails here. In the atlas data, TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 models are mutually similar at 0.96-0.995, so they are one motif. Two entries are not: the TCFL5 models read tCACGCGC, which is not an E-box, and the JASPAR Tcf12 model MA0521.3 is a bare CAGCTG whose nearest neighbour across all four databases lies outside this family. These two account for the modest cohesion score.

## Where it acts

E-protein sites are found at both promoters and enhancers, but the striking pattern is that their genomic distribution is essentially that of whichever partner is expressed. In B cells, TCF3 occupies the immunoglobulin heavy- and light-chain enhancers and the B-lineage gene set; in muscle, E-protein occupancy coincides with MyoD enhancers; in the T-lineage, TCF12 and TCF3 sit at TAL1 and thymocyte enhancers. Because CAGCTG and CACCTG contain no CpG, they are not depleted in mammalian DNA and occur very frequently - a 6-bp palindrome is expected roughly every 4 kb. The practical consequence is that E-proteins appear in an unusually large number of ChIP datasets, both as the tagged factor and as the apparent motif inside someone else's peaks, because they are physically present at almost every class-II bHLH site in every tissue that expresses one.

## Biology and disease

E2A/TCF3-null mice lack B cells entirely and fail to initiate immunoglobulin gene rearrangement [PMID:8001124,8001125], which established E-proteins as required for lymphoid specification rather than merely modulatory. Human disease follows the paralogues. TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and autonomic dysfunction [PMID:17436254], and a common marker in intron 4 of TCF4 was one of three loci, with the MHC region and NRGN, significantly associated with schizophrenia in a 2009 combined genome-wide scan [PMID:19571808]. TCF12 loss-of-function, acting through its partnership with TWIST1, is a frequent cause of coronal craniosynostosis [PMID:23354436]. TCF3 is a recurrent fusion partner in pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, where the t(1;19) translocation joins the TCF3 activation domain to the PBX1 homeodomain [PMID:1967983]. ID protein overexpression, which titrates E-proteins away from DNA, is a common feature of tumours and of proliferating progenitors [PMID:26555048].

## Reading a hit

A CACCTG or CAGCTG match identifies a class-A E-box. It does not identify an E-protein, and it certainly does not identify which one: TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 share a single motif. Worse, the same core is read by MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, TWIST/HAND, TAL1/LYL1, TFAP4, ZEB1/2 and SNAI-associated E-boxes. Most real E-protein sites are occupied by a heterodimer, so only one half of the match belongs to the E-protein at all. Treat an E-protein motif inside someone else's ChIP peaks as expected co-occupancy rather than evidence of indirect binding artifact - and treat an E-protein ChIP peak as most likely marking the partner's locus. The TCFL5 models here are not E-boxes and should not be scanned as such.
families.caveats: TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 share one motif at 0.96-0.995 similarity, so a hit names the E-proteins at best, never a paralogue. The class-A core is also read by MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, TWIST/HAND, TAL1/LYL1, TFAP4 and ZEB, contains no CpG and is not depleted, so it occurs by chance every few kilobases. Most genuine sites are heterodimeric, meaning half the match belongs to the partner. E-proteins consequently show up in a very large number of ChIP datasets as the apparent motif inside other factors' peaks; that is real co-occupancy, not necessarily mislabelling. The TCFL5 models assigned here read tCACGCGC, which is not an E-box, and one JASPAR Tcf12 model is a bare CAGCTG whose nearest neighbours lie outside this family.

timeline.finding: Cloning of the kappaE2-binding proteins E12 and E47 reveals a shared helix-loop-helix motif, also present in daughterless, MyoD and MYC, required for both dimerization and DNA binding.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning, sequence comparison, mutagenesis, EMSA

timeline.finding: Heterodimers between E12, E47 or daughterless and tissue-specific HLH proteins such as MyoD and achaete-scute bind the kappaE2 site with high affinity, more strongly than most homodimers.
timeline.methods: In vitro translation, EMSA with mixed proteins
timeline.open: Which half of a heterodimer site each partner reads.

timeline.finding: Id, an HLH protein without a basic region, binds MyoD, E12 and E47 and blocks their DNA binding, establishing sequestration of E-proteins as a regulatory mechanism.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, EMSA, transfection

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection shows that MyoD and E2A homo- and heterodimers share the CA..TG core but differ at flanking and internal positions, consistent with half-site recognition.
timeline.methods: Selected and amplified binding-site (SAAB) imprinting

timeline.finding: The E47 bHLH crystal structure on CACCTG shows a parallel four-helix bundle distinct from MAX and nonequivalent contacts to the two half-sites.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Two independent E2A knockouts lack B cells, with the block before immunoglobulin DH-JH rearrangement, establishing E-proteins as required for B-lineage specification.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting (two independent lines), hematopoietic analysis

timeline.finding: De novo TCF4 deletions and basic-region missense mutations cause Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, the first human disorder attributed to a class I bHLH defect.
timeline.methods: Array CGH, sequencing of patients

timeline.finding: Heterozygous TCF12 mutations account for a substantial fraction of coronal craniosynostosis, and Tcf12/Twist1 double-heterozygous mice show that TCF12-TWIST1 heterodimer dosage controls suture development.
timeline.methods: Exome sequencing, transactivation assays, compound-heterozygous mice

open: How well the E-protein models describe sites in cells is uncertain: most functional sites are heterodimer sites in which the E-protein reads only one half, binding-site selection showed that MyoD and E2A complexes differ at flanking and internal positions, and the database models come from single-protein in vitro selections or from ChIP peaks that include partner sites.

Whether TCF12 differs from TCF3 and TCF4 in preferring CAGCTG is unclear: the JASPAR Tcf12 model MA0521.3 and the CIS-BP TCF12 model read CAGCTG, but the HOCOMOCO TCF12 model and JASPAR MA1648.2 read CAGGTG/CACCTG like the other E-proteins.
What TCFL5 binds is unresolved on the data: both of its models read tCACGCGC, a CpG-containing non-E-box site, which does not fit its grouping with the class I E-proteins.

families.name: p53 family
families.def: Two decamers RRRCWWGYYY. TP53, TP63, TP73.
families.short: The p53 response element is bound by three paralogues - TP53, TP63 and TP73 - through a shared, structurally unusual DNA-binding domain that works only as a tetramer. The element is built from two decamers of the form RRRCWWGYYY, usually adjacent but tolerating a spacer, so a full site is 20 bp or more. Each decamer is read by a p53 dimer, and the CATG core at its centre is the part that matters: three of the four hotspot residues mutated in human cancers contact exactly this DNA. Because the element is long and its core is well defined, p53 sites are among the more specific vertebrate motifs, and a good double-decamer match is genuinely informative. What a match cannot tell you is which of the three paralogues is responsible.
families.long:
## The factors

Three human genes encode this DNA-binding domain: TP53, TP63 and TP73. The domain is a beta-sandwich carrying a loop-sheet-helix motif and two large loops held together by a structural zinc ion [PMID:8023157]. The beta-sandwich is an immunoglobulin-like fold of the same structural class as the DNA-binding domains of NF-kB, NFAT, the STATs and the Runt-domain (RUNX) factors [PMID:7830764,10404214]. It works only as a tetramer, assembled through a separate C-terminal oligomerisation domain, and the tetramer is best described as a dimer of dimers: two dimers bind the two decamer half-sites and are further stabilised by protein-protein and base-stacking contacts between them [PMID:16793544]. TP53 is ubiquitously expressed and normally short-lived, kept low by MDM2-mediated degradation until stress stabilises it. TP63 and TP73 are expressed more narrowly - TP63 in basal keratinocytes and other stratified epithelia, TP73 in ciliated epithelia and neurons - and both produce N-terminally truncated dominant-negative isoforms (dNp63, dNp73) that compete for the same element without activating it [PMID:9774969]. All three share a near-identical DNA-contacting surface, which is why they read the same sequence.

## The motif

The consensus was defined by selecting genomic fragments that bind p53: two copies of 5'-PuPuPuC(A/T)(T/A)GPyPyPy-3', now usually written RRRCWWGYYY, separated by 0-13 bp [PMID:1301998]. One decamer alone was insufficient for binding in that assay, and small alterations of the decamer abolished affinity even in multiple copies [PMID:1301998]. The crystal structure of the p53 core domain on DNA explained why: arginine 280 hydrogen-bonds the invariant guanine, lysine 120 and alanine 276 read the adjacent bases, and arginine 248 tracks the minor groove - residues 248, 273 and 282 are among the most frequently mutated in human tumours, so the hotspots are literally the DNA-reading apparatus [PMID:8023157]. Information is concentrated in the central CWWG (in practice mostly CATG) and in the purine and pyrimidine runs that flank it; the outer positions are looser [PMID:18234719,20364130]. Spacing is genuinely contested. The original definition allowed up to 13 bp, but a systematic transactivation study found that even small increases in spacer length sharply reduce activity, while separately reporting substantial transactivation from non-canonical half-sites (a single decamer) and three-quarter sites [PMID:18714371]. Solution and crystal work has since shown that p53 tetramers can form hemispecific complexes in which one dimer sits on a specific half-site and the other on adjacent spacer sequence, with comparable affinity [PMID:28912355] - which reconciles the two observations without settling how much of the genome's real regulation runs through half-sites. Practically, the databases here are split the same way: the high-information models are full double decamers (for example ACATGTCC..GACATGT, 16-20 positions), while several HOCOMOCO secondary models are single decamers or less, and those have markedly lower label agreement. TP53, TP63 and TP73 models are not separable from one another; the family's cohesion is 0.81 mainly because half-site and full-site models are mixed together.

## Where it acts

Most functional p53 elements lie in proximal promoters, within about 1 kb of the start site; distal sites are reported less often, partly because single-gene studies favor promoters, and correlate more weakly with activation [PMID:28288132]. The elements are not CpG-island-associated. The first genome-wide map identified at least 542 high-confidence binding loci [PMID:16413492], far fewer than for most families, and curated censuses converge on a core set of a few hundred directly regulated genes that is largely shared across cell types and stresses [PMID:28288132]. Unlike many factors, p53 does not require a partner site to bind: its element is self-sufficient and often sits in closed chromatin that p53 can open. Co-occurrence is therefore weaker and less stereotyped than for NF-kB or NFAT, though p53 sites are enriched near CCAAT boxes and E2F sites at cell-cycle genes, and p63 sites in keratinocytes co-occur with AP-1, KLF and GRHL motifs.

## Biology and disease

p53 activation by DNA damage, oncogene signalling, ribosomal stress or nucleotide depletion drives cell-cycle arrest (CDKN1A), apoptosis (BBC3, PMAIP1, BAX), senescence, DNA repair and metabolic adjustment [PMID:18431400]. TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, and the common mutations are missense changes in the DNA-binding domain rather than truncations [PMID:8023157] - they produce a full-length protein that cannot read the element and can act dominant-negatively over the tetramer. Germline TP53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome [PMID:1978757]. The paralogues are developmental: Trp63-null mice lack limbs and stratified epithelia entirely [PMID:10227293], and human TP63 mutations cause EEC and related ectodermal dysplasia syndromes [PMID:10535733]; TP73 loss affects ciliogenesis and neuronal survival. TP63 and TP73 are rarely mutated in cancer but their dominant-negative isoforms are frequently overexpressed.

## Reading a hit

A full double-decamer match is one of the more trustworthy motif hits available, because 20 constrained positions are rare by chance. A single decamer is not: it occurs frequently enough to be uninformative on its own, and the half-site models in these collections will match tens of thousands of times per genome. Always check whether the model you scanned with is a full site or a half site. The hit does not identify the paralogue - TP53, TP63 and TP73 read the same element, and in a keratinocyte or a basal breast tumour the more likely occupant is p63. Be aware of provenance: the CIS-BP TP53 motif M03439 is transferred from the mouse protein (91% DNA-binding-domain identity), which is harmless here but is the same mechanism that produces bad motifs elsewhere. ChIP-derived p53 models are relatively clean, since p53 binds its element directly and largely without partners, but the ChIP-only HOCOMOCO models still favour the subset of sites occupied in whichever cell line was assayed. Spacer-containing matches should be treated as plausible but weaker than adjacent decamers.
families.caveats: Trust full sites, distrust half sites. Two adjacent RRRCWWGYYY decamers are specific enough that a match means something; a single decamer is common and several models in these databases are single-decamer or shorter, with correspondingly low label agreement. A hit identifies the p53 family, not the member: TP53, TP63 and TP73 share the element, so in stratified epithelia p63 is often the likelier occupant. Spacer length is unsettled - the original definition allowed 0-13 bp, but transactivation falls off quickly as the spacer grows, so spaced matches deserve less weight than abutting ones. One CIS-BP TP53 entry is inherited from mouse rather than measured on the human protein.

timeline.finding: Mapping p53-binding sites in 18 human genomic clones defines the consensus as two copies of the decamer PuPuPuC(A/T)(T/A)GPyPyPy separated by 0-13 bp; one decamer is insufficient for binding, and hotspot mutants fail to bind.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding and selection of genomic fragments; site mapping
timeline.open: Whether spaced sites and single decamers are functional in cells, as opposed to bound in vitro.

timeline.finding: The structure of the p53 core domain on DNA shows a beta-sandwich scaffold with two zinc-stabilised loops and a loop-sheet-helix motif forming the DNA-binding surface, and places the residues most often mutated in tumours at that surface.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Only one core domain made specific contacts; how four domains assemble on the full double-decamer element was unresolved.

timeline.finding: Crystal structures of core-domain complexes show four p53 molecules self-assembling on two half-sites as a dimer of dimers, stabilised by protein-protein and base-stacking contacts, with the protein-DNA interface varying with sequence in step with measured affinity.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; binding measurements

timeline.finding: The first genome-wide p53 binding map refines the consensus motif and identifies at least 542 high-confidence binding loci, far fewer than the number of consensus matches in the genome.
timeline.methods: ChIP with paired-end ditag sequencing (ChIP-PET)

timeline.finding: Contrary to the 0-13 bp spacer allowance derived from in vitro binding, small increases in spacer length sharply reduce p53 transactivation, while single decamers and three-quarter sites can support substantial transactivation; p63 and p73 behave similarly.
timeline.methods: Reporter assays in yeast and human cells; microsphere binding assay
timeline.open: Why spaced elements are common among validated targets if spacing weakens activity.

timeline.finding: Structures of p53 tetramers on contiguous half-sites show Hoogsteen pairing at the central A-T doublet of each half-site, which strengthens protein-DNA and protein-protein contacts relative to spaced half-sites and gives a structural link between spacer length and affinity.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; computational analysis

timeline.finding: On elements with long spacers p53 forms either a fully specific tetramer or a hemispecific one (one dimer on a half-site, the other on spacer DNA) with comparable affinity, so isolated half-sites can recruit tetramers; half of validated response elements carry 1-18 bp spacers.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; solution binding and DNA-structure assays; cell-based reporter assay

timeline.finding: A census of 3,661 reported direct target genes from 13 high-throughput and many single-gene studies finds limited agreement between studies and concludes that p53 acts directly only as an activator, with gene repression indirect and dependent on p21 - a direct challenge to the long-held view that p53 represses many genes through its own element.
timeline.methods: Meta-analysis of published genome-wide and single-gene data

open: How much p53 regulation runs through spaced elements and half-sites is unsettled: transactivation assays show that spacers weaken activity, yet half of validated response elements contain 1-18 bp spacers and hemispecific tetramers bind them with affinity comparable to full sites.

Whether p53 ever represses transcription directly through its element remains disputed: meta-analysis argues that all p53-dependent repression is indirect and requires p21, whereas earlier single-gene studies reported direct repression from p53 response elements.

families.name: Atypical / composite homeodomain
families.def: Homeodomains in unusual architectures: ZHX1-3, ZFHX2/3, HOMEZ, TSHZ1-3, ADNP, HDX, HMBOX1, PROX1-like, HHEX, POU-less HD archetypes.
aka: ZHX / ZFHX / HOMEZ / TSHZ / HMBOX / HHEX group
families.short: This family collects homeodomains that do not behave like homeodomains. Instead of one small domain in a compact protein, these factors bury one to five divergent homeodomains inside large multidomain proteins, usually alongside many C2H2 zinc fingers: ZHX1-3, ZFHX2 and ZFHX3, HOMEZ, TSHZ1-3, HMBOX1, HDX, HHEX, and the SATB-type CUT-plus-homeodomain proteins. Several were discovered as something else entirely, an AT-rich enhancer-binding protein, a telomere repeat-binding protein, a chromatin scaffold protein. Their motifs are correspondingly heterogeneous: there is no single family consensus, several database models carry almost no information, and where a good motif exists it may be read by the zinc fingers rather than by the homeodomain. Useful as a bucket, not as an identifier.
families.long:
## The factors

What unites these proteins is architecture, not sequence preference. Domain annotation gives the flavour.
ZHX1 and ZHX3 are 873 and 956 residues with five annotated homeobox regions each plus two C2H2 zinc
fingers; ZHX2 has four homeoboxes. ZFHX3, originally named ATBF1, is 3,703 residues carrying four
homeodomains and 23 zinc fingers; ZFHX2 is 2,572 residues with three homeodomains and 12 zinc fingers.
HOMEZ is a 550-residue protein with three homeodomains and a leucine-zipper-like region and no zinc
fingers at all [PMID:12925734]. TSHZ2 and TSHZ3, vertebrate teashirt proteins, have five zinc fingers and a single
homeodomain annotated as atypical. HDX has two homeodomains; HMBOX1 has one, embedded in a POU-like
arrangement. HHEX is the outlier in the other direction, a 270-residue protein with a single homeodomain,
but it homo-oligomerises through a proline-rich region rather than working as a monomer [PMID:18498250]. SATB1 and SATB2
pair a divergent homeodomain with two CUT domains [PMID:26464018]. Several of these proteins were characterised before
anyone called them homeodomain factors: ZFHX3/ATBF1 as the AT-motif binding factor of the human
alpha-fetoprotein enhancer [PMID:1719379], HMBOX1 as HOT1, a direct double-stranded telomere repeat-binding protein [PMID:23685356],
SATB1 as a matrix-attachment-region binding protein with "unusual binding site recognition" [PMID:1505028], and ZHX1 as an
NF-Y-interacting repressor [PMID:10441475].

## The motif

There is no single consensus, and the entry deliberately does not offer one. The three best-supported
models are as follows. HOMEZ, from HT-SELEX, reads TAATCGTTT, about 13 bits: a recognisable TAAT core with
an unusual CGTTT extension, and it is reproduced independently in CIS-BP as TATAATCGTTTT and as a footprint
archetype, so it is probably real [PMID:23332764,25215497]. HMBOX1 gives CTAGTTA, equivalently TAACTAG, supported by both in vitro
selection and ChIP [PMID:23332764]; this is a TAAT-like core with an inverted 3' half. Notably it does not resemble the
TTAGGG telomeric repeat that HOT1/HMBOX1 was reported to bind directly [PMID:23685356], and that discrepancy is not
resolved in the literature. TSHZ2 gives a 15-base CATCAAATGGAATC with high information content and grade A
evidence, and it contains no TAAT core whatever; the most economical reading is that the zinc fingers do
the binding, as they do for *Drosophila* teashirt, and the atypical homeodomain contributes little. The
remaining models are close to empty: ZFHX2 is a bare TAATTA at 5.5 bits, ZFHX3 reduces to AAT at 2.5 bits,
HHEX to AT at 1.9, ZHX1 to AC at 1.3, HDX to a single T. Family cohesion is 0.55, the lowest of the
homeodomain groups, which is the expected signature of a bucket.

## Where it acts

Genuinely varied, and for several members not well mapped. HMBOX1/HOT1 localises to telomeres and
associates with actively processed telomere ends. ZHX proteins act as promoter-proximal repressors in
complexes with NF-Y [PMID:10441475]. ZFHX3/ATBF1 was defined at an AT-rich enhancer element and binds AT-rich sequence
generally [PMID:1719379], which is one reason its motif carries so little information. SATB1 occupies base-unpairing
regions and matrix attachment regions and organises chromatin loops in T cells rather than acting at a
short consensus [PMID:1505028,10716941]. TSHZ3 works at neuronal target genes in cortical projection neurons [PMID:27668656]. The general pattern
is that occupancy for these proteins is determined by protein-protein interaction and by regional DNA
character, AT-richness or repeat content, more than by a short high-information consensus, which is exactly
why motif-based prediction performs poorly for them.

## Biology and disease

Several members have solid human genetics. Somatic mutation and deletion of ZFHX3/ATBF1 occur recurrently
in prostate cancer [PMID:15750593]. Deletion of TSHZ3 causes an autism syndrome with defects in cortical projection
neurons [PMID:27668656]. De novo mutations in ADNP, another large protein with a homeodomain in unusual company, cause a
SWI/SNF-related autism syndrome [PMID:24531329]. HHEX, as PRH/Hex, is required for formation of the vertebrate body axis,
the haematopoietic and vascular systems, liver, thyroid and forebrain, and it can both repress and activate
targets and additionally regulate nuclear export of specific mRNAs [PMID:8096636,18498250]. HMBOX1/HOT1 is a positive regulator of
telomere length: depletion shortens and overexpression lengthens telomeres, and it promotes chromatin
association of telomerase [PMID:23685356]. SATB1 controls thymocyte development [PMID:10716941] through higher-order chromatin
organisation.

## Reading a hit

This is the family where a motif hit licenses the least. Of the 13 models, five carry under 6 bits and
three carry under 3 bits, which means they cannot be scanned meaningfully at all; a "hit" for the CIS-BP
ZHX1 or HDX model is not information. The CIS-BP HHEX model is inherited across species: it was measured on
a *Caenorhabditis elegans* protein at 77% DNA-binding-domain identity and transferred to human HHEX, not
measured on the human protein [PMID:25215497]. The CIS-BP ZFHX2 model is a bare TAATTA whose nearest neighbours across all
four databases are Q50 homeodomain motifs, and the ZHX1 model's nearest neighbours are CpG-binding
MBD/CXXC motifs; both are flagged in the underlying data as probably belonging elsewhere. Only HOMEZ,
HMBOX1 and TSHZ2 rest on direct in vitro selection for the human protein, and for TSHZ2 the motif is
probably the zinc fingers' rather than the homeodomain's. Read a hit here as a statement about sequence
composition, and go to expression and ChIP data before naming a protein.
families.caveats: Treat this family as a bucket label, not an identification. Five of the 13 models carry under 6 bits and three under 3 bits, so they are not scannable; matches to them are noise. The CIS-BP HHEX model is transferred from a C. elegans protein at 77% DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on human HHEX. The CIS-BP ZFHX2 and ZHX1 models sit closer to Q50 homeodomain and MBD/CXXC motifs respectively than to anything in this family. Only HOMEZ, HMBOX1 and TSHZ2 have credible human in vitro motifs, and the TSHZ2 site contains no TAAT core and is likely read by its zinc fingers. For most members, occupancy is driven by partners and by AT-rich or repeat context, not by the consensus.

timeline.finding: ATBF1, later renamed ZFHX3, is cloned as the protein that binds an AT-rich motif in the human alpha-fetoprotein enhancer and turns out to be a 306-kDa protein with four homeodomains and 17 annotated zinc fingers, the first example of homeodomains embedded in a very large multidomain factor.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning and sequence analysis with enhancer binding assays
timeline.open: The protein was defined by binding an AT-rich region rather than a defined consensus, and which of its domains contacts DNA was not determined.

timeline.finding: SATB1 is cloned as a thymus-enriched matrix-attachment-region binding protein that recognizes an AT-rich context indirectly, contacting the minor groove and the sugar-phosphate backbone rather than specific bases, and losing binding when the unwinding potential of the site is removed.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning with missing-nucleoside and chemical interference binding assays
timeline.open: Established that a protein in this group can select sites with no conventional consensus, which no position weight matrix can represent.

timeline.finding: ZHX1 is isolated in a two-hybrid screen for NF-YA partners and found to be an 873-residue protein with five homeodomain motifs and two zinc fingers that is expressed ubiquitously, placing it at promoters through a partner rather than through its own site.
timeline.methods: yeast two-hybrid screening and Northern analysis

timeline.finding: HOMEZ is described as a vertebrate-specific protein combining three atypical homeodomains with leucine-zipper-like motifs and an acidic domain, and is grouped with the ZHX proteins as a distinct architectural subset of the homeobox superfamily.
timeline.methods: comparative genomics and expression analysis across vertebrates
timeline.open: No DNA-binding data; the homeodomains were called atypical on sequence grounds alone.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX on recombinant human proteins gives the first directly measured specificities for members of this group, including the HOMEZ site TAATCGTTT and the HMBOX1 site TAACTAG, both of which deviate from the canonical homeodomain TAAT consensus.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Most members of the group yielded no usable model, and the HMBOX1 site does not resemble a telomeric repeat.

timeline.finding: A quantitative DNA-protein interaction screen identifies HMBOX1, renamed HOT1, as a direct binder of double-stranded TTAGGG telomere repeats that associates with the telomerase complex and acts as a positive regulator of telomere length, a sequence preference different from the one in vitro selection reports for the same protein.
timeline.methods: SILAC-based DNA-protein interaction screen with ChIP, depletion and overexpression
timeline.open: The discrepancy between the telomeric repeat and the selected TAACTAG site has not been reconciled.

timeline.finding: A survey of more than 1,000 transcription factors establishes that closely related DNA-binding domains usually share preferences and uses that rule to infer motifs for about a third of known eukaryotic factors; several models carried in this family, including the human HHEX motif, are inferred from a non-human protein rather than measured.
timeline.methods: protein-binding microarrays across 131 eukaryotes with inference by DNA-binding-domain identity
timeline.open: Whether the identity-based inference rule holds for divergent and atypical homeodomains was not tested separately.

timeline.finding: Heterozygous deletions at 19q12-q13.11 are narrowed to TSHZ3 as the critical gene for an autism syndrome, and Tshz3 mutant mice show altered expression of cortical projection neuron markers, synaptic changes and autism-like behavior, giving one member of this architecturally defined group a defined developmental function.
timeline.methods: human deletion mapping with mouse knockout transcriptomics, electrophysiology and behavior
timeline.open: Does not say whether TSHZ3 acts through its zinc fingers, its atypical homeodomain or through partners.

open: The HMBOX1 specificity is contradictory: an interaction screen reports direct binding to double-stranded TTAGGG telomere repeats, while in vitro selection and the database models give TAACTAG, and no study has established whether the telomeric association is direct binding to a second site class or recruitment by a telomere-bound partner.

It is unresolved whether the high-information TSHZ2 site is read by the zinc fingers or by the atypical homeodomain: the 15-base selected sequence contains no TAAT core, which points to the fingers as in Drosophila teashirt, but there is no structure or domain-deletion binding experiment for the human protein.

For the multi-homeodomain proteins it is unknown whether any of the homeodomains binds DNA in cells at all: ATBF1 was defined by AT-rich binding and ZHX1 was found as an NF-Y partner, both consistent with the homeodomains working as protein-interaction modules, and no domain-by-domain binding data exist.

The inferred human HHEX motif rests on an untested assumption: it was measured on a Caenorhabditis elegans protein sharing 77% DNA-binding-domain identity, and whether identity-based transfer is reliable for divergent homeodomains of this kind has not been evaluated for this group.

families.name: SREBP
families.def: Sterol response element TCACNCCAC plus E-box binding. SREBF1, SREBF2.
families.short: SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 are bHLH-LZ factors made as ER membrane precursors and activated by sterol-regulated proteolysis, so only the cleaved nuclear fragment binds DNA. They are unusual in having dual specificity: a tyrosine replaces the arginine that is otherwise invariant in bHLH basic regions, letting them bind both the palindromic E-box CACGTG and the non-palindromic sterol regulatory element SRE-1, TCACNCCAC. Sites sit in promoters of cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis genes and work with a neighbouring NF-Y CCAAT box or SP1 GC box, which an isolated SRE needs for activity. The pathway controls the LDL receptor, hepatic lipogenesis and the response to statins, and is central to fatty liver disease and insulin resistance.
families.long:
## The factors

SREBF1 and SREBF2 encode SREBP-1 and SREBP-2, basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) factors that are unusual in being synthesized as membrane-anchored precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum. SREBF1 produces two isoforms from alternative first exons, SREBP-1a and SREBP-1c (also called ADD1), which differ in the length of their activation domain [PMID:11994399]. Each precursor has two transmembrane segments and is held in the ER by SCAP; when sterols are low, SCAP escorts it to the Golgi, where sequential cleavage by Site-1 and Site-2 proteases releases the N-terminal bHLH-LZ fragment, which enters the nucleus and dimerizes [PMID:9150132]. Regulation is therefore proteolytic rather than transcriptional at the level of DNA binding, and only the cleaved nuclear form is a transcription factor. SREBP-2 is the principal driver of cholesterol synthesis genes, SREBP-1c of fatty acid synthesis genes, and SREBP-1a is a stronger general activator expressed mainly in proliferating cells and cell lines [PMID:11994399]. Both genes are broadly expressed, with SREBF1 highest in liver and adipose tissue. The atlas assigns 12 motifs to this family (4 JASPAR, 5 HOCOMOCO, 2 CIS-BP, 1 Vierstra archetype) over SREBF1 and SREBF2, with cohesion 0.89 - the lowest in the E-box group - and SREBF1 (MA0595.1) as the representative.

## The motif

SREBP has dual DNA-binding specificity, and this is the single most important fact about the family. It binds the canonical palindromic E-box CACGTG, usually with T/A flanks (ATCACGTGAT), and it also binds a non-palindromic, non-E-box element, the sterol regulatory element SRE-1, written TCACNCCAC [PMID:8402897,7739539]. Mutagenesis of the LDL receptor promoter identified the nucleotides that make SRE-1 an active element [PMID:2298751], and biochemistry then showed the structural cause: in SREBP the arginine that is otherwise invariant in the basic region of every bHLH protein is replaced by a tyrosine, and that single substitution is sufficient to add SRE recognition to E-box recognition [PMID:7739539]. The co-crystal of the SREBP-1a bHLH-LZ bound to an SRE showed a quasi-symmetric dimer with an asymmetric DNA interface: one monomer reads the E-box-like ATCAC half-site with typical bHLH contacts, and the other reads the non-E-box half through entirely different contacts [PMID:9634703]. This is why the atlas cannot give the family one consensus. Roughly half of the assigned models are SRE-type (aTCACCCCAc, or its reverse complement aTGGgGTGAt), including the Vierstra archetype AC0486:SREBF:bHLH; the rest are E-box-type (ATCACGTGAT, ATCACcTGAT, gTCAgGTGAt). The published SRE consensus TCACNCCAC and the data consensus aTCACCCCAc agree, with the databases simply filling the degenerate position with the commonest base, C [PMID:8402897]. The two motif classes are not variants of each other in any alignment sense, and a scan using one will miss the other.

## Where it acts

SREBP sites are promoter-proximal, typically within a few hundred base pairs of the transcription start site of lipid-metabolism genes, and they rarely work alone. An isolated SRE is a weak element; efficient activation requires a co-regulatory factor bound nearby, most often NF-Y at a CCAAT box or SP1 at a GC box [PMID:9271397,9430668]. At the LDLR promoter, synergy with SP1 (or SP3, which can substitute) requires a region of SP1 that includes the buttonhead (Btd) box, whereas the FAS and ACC promoters, which carry two SREBP sites, do not need it [PMID:9271397]; at HMGCS1, SREBP interacts directly with the assembled NF-Y trimer through its bHLH-zipper [PMID:9430668]. Genome-wide mapping of SREBP1 together with NFY and SP1 confirmed that the three co-occupy a large fraction of SREBP-bound promoters [PMID:18654640]. The canonical composite arrangements are the LDLR promoter (SRE-1 plus SP1 sites) and the HMGCS1 promoter (SRE plus NF-Y) [PMID:8314806,9430668]. Because the nuclear form is generated by proteolysis, occupancy is switched by sterol depletion, statin treatment, insulin (for SREBP-1c) or feeding rather than by changes in site availability [PMID:9150132].

## Biology and disease

SREBP-2 activates essentially the whole cholesterol biosynthetic pathway plus the LDL receptor, which is why statin treatment, by lowering hepatic sterols, raises LDLR expression through this pathway [PMID:11994399]. SREBP-1c activates fatty acid and triglyceride synthesis and is induced by insulin and by LXR agonists [PMID:11994399,28849786]. Targeted disruption of Srebf1 in mice causes partial embryonic lethality, and surviving animals show elevated SREBP-2 and increased cholesterol synthesis, an example of cross-compensation within the family [PMID:9329978]. In humans the pathway sits at the centre of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, hypertriglyceridemia and insulin resistance, and SREBP-driven lipogenesis is also co-opted by tumours; reviews describe the physiology as convergent but the pathophysiology as divergent between the two genes [PMID:28849786].

## Reading a hit

Decide first which motif you matched. An ATCACGTGAT hit is a T/A-flanked canonical E-box and is indistinguishable from USF, MITF/TFE, BHLHE41 or CLOCK-BMAL1 sites; it is weak evidence for SREBP on its own. A TCACNCCAC hit is much more specific, because few other human factors read that asymmetric sequence, and it becomes considerably stronger if an NF-Y CCAAT box or an SP1 GC box lies within about 50 bp in a lipid-gene promoter. SREBF1 and SREBF2 cannot be distinguished from each other by sequence, and the SREBP-1a/1c isoforms share one DNA-binding domain entirely. Several HOCOMOCO models here are ChIP-only, and one grade-C model (tCgCGTGA) is a degenerate half-site that should not be used for scanning.
families.caveats: This family has two unrelated motif classes and the databases hold both, so check which one you matched. An ATCACGTGAT E-box hit is shared with USF, MITF/TFE, BHLHE41 and CLOCK-BMAL1 and is weak evidence for SREBP. A TCACNCCAC SRE hit is far more specific, but SREBPs bind it weakly on their own and real elements are usually accompanied by NF-Y or SP1 within about 50 bp. SREBF1 and SREBF2 are indistinguishable by sequence, as are the SREBP-1a and -1c isoforms. Cohesion here is only 0.89 because of the two motif classes, several models are ChIP-only, and one grade-C model is a degenerate half-site not suitable for scanning.

open: How many SREBP target promoters act through the SRE rather than through an E-box is not settled: the classic sterol-regulated promoters (LDLR, HMGCS1) use SRE-type sites, the protein binds E-boxes as well in vitro, and the atlas splits its models roughly evenly between the two classes.

Why SREBP-2 favours cholesterol genes and SREBP-1c lipogenic genes is not explained by DNA sequence: their models are indistinguishable, and proposed explanations rest on activation-domain strength and promoter architecture, such as the number of SREs and the type of co-regulator site.

families.name: CLOCK / BMAL1
families.def: Tandem E-boxes CACGTG of the circadian oscillator. CLOCK, ARNTL/BMAL1, NPAS2.
families.short: CLOCK, BMAL1 (gene symbol ARNTL) and NPAS2 are basic helix-loop-helix PER-ARNT-SIM (bHLH-PAS) transcription factors that form the activating limb of the mammalian circadian clock. BMAL1 pairs with CLOCK or with its paralogue NPAS2 and binds the palindromic E-box CACGTG together with a small set of E-box-like variants. The complex reads seven base pairs rather than six, because a flanking A-T pair next to the core contributes to affinity. Strong circadian promoters usually carry two E-boxes in tandem six to seven base pairs apart, and it is the pair, not a single hexamer, that produces rhythmic transcription. Occupancy oscillates once a day and drives Per, Cry, Rev-erb and thousands of output genes. Because CACGTG is also the core read by MYC/MAX, USF and SREBP, sequence alone cannot assign an E-box to the clock.
families.long:
## The factors

CLOCK, BMAL1 (*ARNTL*, formerly MOP3) and NPAS2 (MOP4) are bHLH-PAS proteins: an N-terminal basic helix-loop-helix domain followed by two PAS domains (PAS-A, PAS-B) and a PAC extension. The bHLH contacts DNA; the PAS domains set dimerization specificity and provide cofactor and small-molecule surfaces. Neither subunit binds DNA productively alone. BMAL1 is the obligate partner, heterodimerizing with CLOCK or with NPAS2 [PMID:9576906]; BMAL2 (*ARNTL2*) is a lower-abundance paralogue. The crystal structure of the mouse CLOCK:BMAL1 bHLH-PAS region shows an asymmetric, interdigitated assembly with three separate interfaces, so the subunits wrap around one another rather than pairing symmetrically (Huang et al. 2012) [PMID:22653727]. CLOCK and BMAL1 are broadly expressed; NPAS2 is enriched in forebrain and some peripheral tissues and can substitute for CLOCK, which is why *Clock*-null mice keep behavioral rhythms (DeBruyne et al. 2006) [PMID:16675400] while *Bmal1*-null mice are arrhythmic in constant darkness (Bunger et al. 2000) [PMID:11163178]. This family holds 12 motifs from JASPAR, HOCOMOCO and CIS-BP labeled ARNTL/BMAL1, CLOCK or NPAS2, with none flagged as probably mislabeled.

## The motif

The core is the palindromic E-box CACGTG. Each basic helix enters the major groove and reads one CAC half-site; because the hexamer is its own reverse complement, the two subunits occupy equivalent halves. A structure of the human CLOCK:BMAL1 bHLH domains on a canonical E-box resolved the hydrogen-bond network and showed BMAL1 Ile80 contacting the base pair immediately 3' of the core, so the recognized unit is 7 bp, CACGTGA, with that flanking A-T pair indispensable; the same study measured single substitutions and defined two high-affinity non-canonical boxes, AACGTGA and CATGTGA (Wang et al. 2013) [PMID:23229515]. This resolves an apparent split in the databases. The methyl-HT-SELEX models CLOCK.H14CORE.0.M.C and NPAS2.H14CORE.1.M.C recover ACACATGT and ACATGTGT, the CATGTG variant, while the grade-A models BMAL1.H14CORE.0.PSM.A and CLOCK.H14CORE.1.PS.A recover CACGTG with a flanking base. The pooled consensus computed from the members is cCACGTGc; it does not contradict the literature 7-mer, because averaging a strand-ambiguous palindrome symmetrizes the flanks. The other commonly cited variant is the E'-box CACGTT. Functionally rhythmic promoters generally carry tandem E-boxes 6-7 bp apart, and the pair rather than either hexamer confers cell-autonomous rhythmicity (Nakahata et al. 2008) [PMID:18177499]; the most information-rich model here, NPAS2.H14CORE.2.S.B, is itself a tandem (CACGTGbnndaCACGTGt, about 21 bits). No member of the family can be told from another by sequence.

## Where it acts

Binding is promoter-biased. ChIP-seq in mouse liver puts most confident sites within a few hundred base pairs of transcription start sites, often in CpG-island promoters, with roughly one to three thousand sites per time point (Rey et al. 2011; Koike et al. 2012) [PMID:21364973,22936566]. Occupancy itself cycles, peaking once per day ahead of the RNA polymerase II and H3K4me3/H3K9ac rhythms it drives (Koike et al. 2012) [PMID:22936566]. Core targets are *Per1*, *Per2*, *Cry1*, *Cry2*, *Nr1d1*/*Nr1d2* and *Dbp*; the wider output program layers E-boxes with D-boxes (DBP/HLF/TEF) and ROREs (ROR/REV-ERB) so that one clock input can generate many output phases (Takahashi 2017) [PMID:27990019]. A specific hexamer is expected about 7 x 10^5 times in a 3-Gb genome under uniform base composition; CpG depletion lowers the real count, but matches still outnumber occupied sites by orders of magnitude.

## Biology and disease

CLOCK:BMAL1 was identified as the activator of *Per1* through E-boxes, with the dominant-negative *Clock* mutation lengthening period (Gekakis et al. 1998) [PMID:9616112]. *Bmal1* loss abolishes free-running rhythms (Bunger et al. 2000) [PMID:11163178] and produces early-onset aging phenotypes including cataracts, sarcopenia and reduced lifespan (Kondratov et al. 2006) [PMID:16847346]. Pancreatic-islet disruption of *Clock* or *Bmal1* causes hypoinsulinemia and diabetes (Marcheva et al. 2010) [PMID:20562852]. In humans the clock is implicated in sleep-phase disorders, metabolic syndrome and shift-work-associated disease, though the strongest Mendelian sleep-timing mutations lie in *PER2* and *CSNK1D* rather than in CLOCK or BMAL1 (Takahashi 2017) [PMID:27990019].

## Reading a hit

A CACGTG match by itself says almost nothing about which bHLH protein bound it: MYC/MAX, MXI1, USF1/2, SREBF1/2, TFE3/MITF, ARNT homodimers and HIF:ARNT all read the same or an overlapping core, and several CLOCK/BMAL models in this family have a closer neighbor in another family than within their own. Features that shift the interpretation toward the clock are a tandem pair 6-7 bp apart, an A or T immediately 3' of the core, a promoter-proximal CpG-island location, and rhythmic accessibility or expression of the nearby gene. The hit cannot separate CLOCK from NPAS2, BMAL1 from BMAL2, or either from an ARNT homodimer. Evidence codes matter: the grade-A BMAL1 and CLOCK models carry in vitro support (HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX), whereas ChIP-only models can reflect tethering to partner factors, and CLOCK/BMAL1 ChIP peaks include many regions with no recognizable E-box.
families.caveats: Treat a hit as "an E-box" first and a clock site only with extra evidence. The core CACGTG is shared with the MYC/MAX, USF, SREBP and MiT bHLH groups and with HIF:ARNT, and in this family several models sit closer to motifs outside the family than inside it. Nothing in the sequence distinguishes CLOCK from NPAS2 or BMAL1 from BMAL2. The non-canonical CATGTG-type models come from methyl-HT-SELEX at grade C and are lower confidence than the grade-A CACGTG models. ChIP-derived versions include indirect binding, so peak-derived motifs are not proof that the tagged subunit touched the DNA. Tandem spacing and rhythmic behavior of the locus are more informative than the match score.

timeline.finding: MOP3, later renamed BMAL1/ARNTL, was identified as the bHLH-PAS subunit that dimerizes with both circadian (CLOCK, NPAS2) and hypoxia (HIF-1alpha) partners, placing the clock E-box inside the wider ARNT-like beta-subunit class.

timeline.methods: Reporter assays with spacing variants in cultured cells
timeline.open: Whether tandem spacing is required at endogenous loci genome-wide or mainly at the core clock promoters tested.
