timeline.finding: Screening with the estrogen receptor DNA-binding domain as a probe isolates two cDNAs (ERR1 and ERR2) encoding receptor-like proteins with no known hormone, founding the estrogen-related receptors as orphan receptors.
timeline.methods: cDNA library screening with an ER DNA-binding-domain probe, sequence comparison
timeline.open: Their DNA target and any activating ligand were unknown.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection with ERRalpha defines its element as a single extended half-site, TNAAGGTCA, and identifies one in the MCAD promoter, linking the receptor to fatty-acid oxidation.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, EMSA, reporter assays
timeline.open: What activates ERRalpha, since it did not activate the MCAD promoter on its own.

timeline.finding: Esrrb-null embryos die at about E10.5 with failed chorion development, too many trophoblast giant cells and too little diploid trophoblast, a defect rescued by wild-type tetraploid extraembryonic tissue.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockout, tetraploid aggregation

timeline.finding: ERRalpha and ERRbeta bind and activate through both the classical ERE and the extended SF-1 response element, sharing targets with ERalpha but not with ERbeta.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding, reporter assays

timeline.finding: The solution structure of the ERR2 (ERRbeta) DNA-binding domain on its site shows that monomeric high-affinity binding needs minor-groove contacts from an AT-hook-like C-terminal extension that packs against the surface other receptors use to dimerize, explaining the required 5' extension.
timeline.methods: NMR solution structure

timeline.finding: Motif discovery in PGC-1alpha-induced genes identifies ERRalpha and GABPA sites as key regulators of oxidative phosphorylation genes, and a synthetic ERRalpha inhibitor blunts PGC-1alpha effects on gene expression and respiration: the two factors are DNA-binding partners through which PGC-1alpha drives this program.
timeline.methods: Expression profiling, computational motif analysis, cellular assays with a synthetic inhibitor

timeline.finding: Genome-wide location analysis in adult heart shows ERRalpha and ERRgamma occupying a common set of promoters for substrate uptake, ATP production and transport, calcium handling and contraction, with NRF-1, CREB and STAT3 sites enriched alongside.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip, expression profiling, motif analysis

timeline.finding: Esrrb is a direct Nanog target that sustains cytokine-independent self-renewal of embryonic stem cells even without Nanog, placing the ERR element in the pluripotency network.
timeline.methods: Inducible Nanog alleles, overexpression and deletion in mouse ES cells, reprogramming assays

open: Whether ERRalpha has an endogenous ligand is disputed: the receptor is constitutively active and regulated mainly through PGC-1 coactivators, while cholesterol has been proposed as an endogenous agonist.

The oligomeric state of ERRs on DNA is unsettled: the DNA-binding-domain structure explains recognition of the extended half-site by a monomer, but ERRalpha and ERRgamma have been described as non-obligatory heterodimers in heart, and the highest-information model in this family (CIS-BP M03412, labelled ESRRG) is a tandem pair of extended half-sites.

Whether ERRs compete with ER at endogenous EREs is not established: ERRalpha and ERRbeta activate consensus EREs in reporter assays, yet every genome-derived ERR model here is an extended half-site rather than an inverted repeat.

families.name: NR4A (NUR77/NURR1)
families.def: NBRE AAAGGTCA monomeric half-site and NurRE. NR4A1/2/3.
families.short: NR4A1 (NUR77), NR4A2 (NURR1) and NR4A3 (NOR-1) are orphan nuclear receptors and immediate-early genes: they are transcribed within minutes of serum stimulation, depolarization or antigen-receptor signaling and their proteins turn over quickly. Unlike most nuclear receptors they bind DNA as monomers, to a single AGGTCA half-site carried on an A/T-rich 5' extension, giving the eight-base NGFI-B response element AAAGGTCA. A separate protein surface, the A box, reads those A-T base pairs in the minor groove. The same receptors can also act as homodimers on the everted NurRE and as heterodimers with RXR. Because a monomeric half-site constrains only eight or nine positions, matches are common by chance, and the AGGTCA core is shared with most of the nuclear receptor superfamily.
families.long:
## The factors

The NR4A subfamily has three paralogues: NR4A1 (NUR77, NGFI-B, TR3), NR4A2 (NURR1) and NR4A3 (NOR-1, MINOR). Each has the standard nuclear receptor layout: an AF-1 region, a DNA-binding domain of two C4 zinc modules, a carboxy-terminal extension containing the A box, and a ligand-binding domain. All three are immediate-early genes induced by serum, growth factors, depolarization, antigen-receptor signaling and stress, with short protein half-lives, so levels are low in resting tissue; NR4A1 was cloned as a nerve growth factor-induced transcript. They are orphans in a strong sense: the NURR1 ligand-binding domain has no accessible ligand pocket, its interior filled with bulky side chains, defining a class of receptors that activate without a ligand (Wang et al. 2003) [PMID:12774125]. The three paralogues are largely redundant: NR4A1-null mice have normal thymocyte apoptosis (Lee et al. 1995) [PMID:7624775]. Ten motifs are collected here across all four sources.

## The motif

The core element is the NGFI-B response element, NBRE, AAAGGTCA, identified by genetic selection in yeast (Wilson et al. 1991) [PMID:1925541]. Its structure explains its length. The two zinc modules read the AGGTCA half-site through the major groove as in other nuclear receptors, while a substructure carboxy-terminal to them, the A box, reaches into the minor groove and reads the three A-T base pairs extending 5' of the half-site; this was the first structure of a nuclear receptor bound to DNA as a monomer (Meinke and Sigler 1999) [PMID:10331876]. Domain swaps had already shown that NR4A1 and SF-1 (NR5A1) bind by the same monomeric mechanism with distinct 5' requirements: an amino group in the minor groove of the SF-1 sequence and an asparagine in the SF-1 A box (Wilson et al. 1993) [PMID:8395013]. The same receptors use two other arrangements: homodimers on the NurRE, an everted pair of NBRE-related octamers with an unusual spacer, which mediates signaling at the POMC promoter (Philips et al. 1997) [PMID:9315652], and heterodimers with RXR on a direct repeat (Perlmann and Jansson 1995) [PMID:7705655]. The collected data agree: the pooled consensus is AAAGGTCA, and five models from three databases give exactly that string. The highest-information model, the Vierstra archetype AC0119:NR4A at 25 bits, is GACCTTTAAAGGTCA: two NBRE octamers head to head with no spacer, not the classic NurRE spacing. Two entries need care. JASPAR NR4A2::RXRA (MA1147.2) is an inverted-repeat dimer model whose nearest neighbors sit outside this family, so it describes a heterodimer, not monomer binding. The archetype AC0114:NR4A/NR2C is flagged in the data as probably belonging with the RXR heterodimers: it is a bare aAGGTCA half-site, exactly what one expects to be ambiguous. Nothing distinguishes the three paralogues by sequence.

## Where it acts

NR4A sites behave like those of other stimulus-induced factors: promoters and signal-responsive enhancers, with occupancy tracking induction of the receptor rather than presence of the motif. They act in T cells, neurons, pituitary corticotropes, macrophages, vascular smooth muscle, liver and adipose tissue, so target programs are cell-type specific. A specific eight-mer is expected about 47,000 times per strand in a 3-Gb genome, so tens of thousands of NBRE matches exist and only a small fraction is ever bound. Composite arrangement matters: NurRE-type pairs and NBRE-RXR direct repeats bind more tightly and are the configurations shown to respond to physiological signals, while a lone NBRE is often weak or non-functional.

## Biology and disease

NR4A2 loss abolishes midbrain dopaminergic neurons in mice and the gene has been examined in Parkinson disease (Zetterstrom et al. 1997) [PMID:9092472]. Although single knockouts are near-normal, the subfamily as a group limits T cell effector function: deleting all three NR4A genes relieves an exhaustion-like program and improves tumor control by CAR T cells (Chen et al. 2019) [PMID:30814732]. In the pituitary, NR4A1 mediates CRH-induced POMC transcription through the NurRE (Philips et al. 1997) [PMID:9315652]. The clearest cancer link is structural: extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma is defined by a translocation fusing EWSR1 to NR4A3, converting the receptor into a constitutive activator (Labelle et al. 1995) [PMID:8634690].

## Reading a hit

A monomeric half-site is much harder to call than a spaced dimer; this is the central practical point. A dimeric element such as a DR3, DR4 or DR5 constrains two 6-bp half-sites plus a fixed spacer, 13-15 positions in all, so a scanner can demand a rare pattern and the arrangement itself is evidence. The NBRE constrains only eight or nine positions, of which six are the AGGTCA half-site shared by most of the nuclear receptor superfamily, so all the family-level information lives in the two or three A-T bases of the 5' extension, and there is no spacer to check. One or two substitutions convert a predicted NBRE into an SF-1 element or into one half of a genuine RXR heterodimer site. Prediction of nuclear receptor elements improves substantially when dimer configuration is modeled, which is unavailable here (Sandelin and Wasserman 2005) [PMID:15563547]. Treat a hit as "a nuclear receptor half-site" first. Provenance is comparatively good here: NR4A1.H14CORE.0.PSM.A is grade A with ChIP, HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX support and NR4A2.H14CORE.0.SM.B has both in vitro assays, so AAAGGTCA is well supported as directly bound. The one NR4A3 model, CIS-BP M00818_2.00, is inferred from the mouse protein at 97% DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured for human NR4A3 (Weirauch et al. 2014) [PMID:25215497].
families.caveats: The sequence identifies a nuclear receptor half-site, not a receptor. AAAGGTCA constrains eight positions, six of which are the AGGTCA half-site used across the superfamily, so tens of thousands of chance matches exist and one or two substitutions turn a predicted NBRE into an SF-1 element or into half of an RXR heterodimer site. Nothing separates NR4A1, NR4A2 and NR4A3. The AAAGGTCA string itself is well supported in vitro (a grade-A HOCOMOCO model with HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX evidence), but the only NR4A3 model is inferred from mouse, one Vierstra archetype in this family is flagged as probably belonging with the RXR heterodimers, and the JASPAR NR4A2::RXRA entry is a dimer model rather than an NR4A monomer motif. Occupancy requires the receptor to have been induced.

timeline.finding: The NGFI-B response element was defined as AAAGGTCA by genetic selection in yeast, showing that the receptor recognizes a single half-site carried on an A/T-rich 5' extension rather than a spaced repeat.
timeline.methods: Genetic selection in yeast with binding assays
timeline.open: Why three extra base pairs 5' of the half-site were needed was not yet explained structurally.

timeline.finding: Domain swaps between NGFI-B and SF-1 established monomer binding as a third paradigm of nuclear receptor-DNA interaction alongside homodimers and RXR heterodimers, and traced the different 5' requirements of the two receptors to residues in the A box.
timeline.methods: Chimeric protein domain swaps with binding and reporter assays
timeline.open: The minor-groove contacts inferred from swaps had no direct structural support.

timeline.finding: NGFI-B and NURR1 were shown to heterodimerize with RXR on a direct repeat and to respond to retinoid signaling, so the same receptors read at least two unrelated DNA arrangements and a monomeric half-site is not the whole story.
timeline.methods: Gel-shift, reporter assays, retinoid response

timeline.finding: Nur77-null mice were found to have unimpaired thymic and peripheral T cell death, overturning the expectation from dominant-negative experiments that the receptor is required for negative selection and pointing instead to redundancy among the three paralogues.
timeline.methods: Mouse germline knockout with immunological phenotyping

timeline.finding: A dimeric arrangement, the NurRE, was shown to mediate CRH-induced POMC transcription in pituitary cells, establishing an everted pair of NBRE-related octamers as the configuration that carries a physiological signal.
timeline.methods: Promoter dissection, gel-shift, reporter assays

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the NGFI-B DNA-binding region on the NBRE showed a single receptor molecule using its zinc modules on the AGGTCA half-site and an A-box substructure reaching into the minor groove of the 5' A-T base pairs, the first structure of a nuclear receptor bound to DNA as a monomer.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: The NURR1 ligand-binding domain was found to have no accessible ligand pocket, its interior filled with bulky side chains, defining a class of receptors that activate without a ligand.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of the ligand-binding domain
timeline.open: Whether the domain can still be targeted pharmacologically.

timeline.finding: Deleting all three NR4A genes in CAR T cells relieved an exhaustion-like transcriptional program and improved tumor control, demonstrating at the level of the whole subfamily the redundancy that single knockouts had obscured.
timeline.methods: Combined knockout in mouse CAR T cells with tumor models and genomics

open: Whether an isolated NBRE is functional in vivo is unsettled: the monomeric element is well measured in vitro, yet the configurations shown to respond to physiological signals are the dimeric NurRE and the NBRE-RXR direct repeat, and a lone octamer is often weak in reporter assays.

Whether the three paralogues have distinct target sets cannot currently be answered: their motifs are identical, single knockouts are near-normal, and the clearest phenotypes appear only when all three are removed together.

Whether the ligand-binding domain can be engaged pharmacologically despite the absence of a conventional pocket remains contested, with the crystal structure showing the interior filled by side chains while small molecules continue to be reported as acting through that domain.

The boundary between this family and the RXR heterodimers is not settled in the data: one Vierstra archetype assigned here is a bare AGGTCA half-site flagged as belonging with the RXR heterodimers, and the JASPAR NR4A2::RXRA entry is a dimer model whose nearest neighbors lie outside the family.

families.name: REV-ERB (NR1D)
families.def: RevDR2 and RORE-like sites. NR1D1, NR1D2.
families.short: REV-ERBalpha (NR1D1) and REV-ERBbeta (NR1D2) are nuclear receptors that lack the helix-12 activation surface and act only as repressors, recruiting the NCoR-HDAC3 complex and binding heme as a ligand. They read the same DNA as the RORs: an AGGTCA half-site with a 5' AT-rich extension (the RORE, or RevRE), and preferentially a direct repeat of two such sites separated by 2 bp, called RevDR2, on which they bind as homodimers. Together with the RORs they form the second feedback loop of the mammalian circadian clock, alternately repressing and activating Bmal1 at the same sites. Loss of both paralogues disrupts circadian behavior and causes hepatic steatosis and metabolic derangement.
families.long:
## The factors

REV-ERB is a two-member nuclear-receptor group: NR1D1 (REV-ERBalpha, historically EAR-1) and NR1D2 (REV-ERBbeta, historically RVR or EAR-1R). The *NR1D1* gene lies on the opposite strand of, and overlapping, the thyroid hormone receptor gene *THRA*, which is how it acquired the name "Rev-ErbA" [PMID:8474464]. Both proteins have the standard receptor architecture — an N-terminal region, a two-module zinc-binding DNA-binding domain (DBD) with a C-terminal extension (CTE), and a ligand-binding domain (LBD) — but with one decisive difference from most of the superfamily: the LBD lacks helix 12 and therefore has no AF-2 surface [PMID:24577401]. REV-ERBs cannot activate transcription. They are dedicated repressors that recruit the NCoR-HDAC3 corepressor complex, and their LBD binds heme as a physiological ligand, so their activity tracks cellular heme and redox state [PMID:7651396,18006707]. Both paralogues are widely expressed, with high levels in liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, brown fat, brain and macrophages, and both are strongly rhythmic, peaking in the early rest phase. NR1D1 protein is short-lived and its abundance oscillates far more than that of most clock proteins.

## The motif

REV-ERBs read the same element as the RORs. A single REV-ERB monomer binds an AGGTCA half-site carrying a 5-6 bp AT-rich 5' extension — the RORE, also called the RevRE in the older REV-ERB literature [PMID:8474464]. Higher-affinity binding requires two such sites arranged as a direct repeat separated by exactly 2 bp, the element named RevDR2, on which REV-ERB binds as a homodimer [PMID:7651396]. The literature writes the core of RevDR2 as AGGTCANNAGGTCA; the motif models collected here retain the AT-rich extensions as well and therefore run 14-18 bp, with a pooled consensus of ANTAGGTCAGTAGGTCA. This is not a disagreement about the element, only about how much flanking sequence a model keeps.

The structural basis is well defined. The crystal structure of the REV-ERBalpha DBD plus CTE bound to RevDR2 shows each zinc module inserting its recognition helix into the major groove of AGGTCA while the CTE runs along the minor groove of the AT-rich extension; the 2-bp spacing is what allows a second protein-DNA interface to form next to the classical one, which is why DR2 and not DR1 or DR4 is the preferred repeat [PMID:9660968]. The same CTE-plus-minor-groove mechanism was described for the monomeric receptor NGFI-B [PMID:10331876].

Neither paralogue is distinguishable from the other, and neither is reliably distinguishable from ROR. The Vierstra archetype AC0123:NR1D/RORC names both groups precisely because their motifs clustered together.

## Where it acts

RevDR2 and RORE sites occur in promoters and enhancers and are not enriched in CpG islands. The canonical target is the *Bmal1* (*ARNTL*) promoter, where two ROREs are occupied by RORs during the day and by REV-ERBs at night; *Cry1*, *Npas2* and *Nfil3* carry the same arrangement [PMID:12150932,16267379,12152080]. In the circadian cis-regulatory grammar, the RORE supplies the late-night phase component and works in combination with E-boxes (CLOCK:BMAL1) and D-boxes [PMID:12152080]. In liver and macrophages, REV-ERBalpha also occupies thousands of tissue-specific enhancers together with lineage factors; in liver these are predominantly HNF6 sites [PMID:26044300].

## Biology and disease

REV-ERB is the repressive arm of the second circadian feedback loop. *Nr1d1*-null mice have a shortened free-running period and altered clock gene amplitude [PMID:12150932]; deleting both paralogues disrupts circadian behavior far more severely and deranges lipid metabolism, with hepatic steatosis and altered bile acid and glucose handling [PMID:22460952]. REV-ERBs also gate inflammatory gene expression in macrophages and set the timing of muscle mitochondrial function [PMID:24577401]. Because the LBD binds heme, synthetic REV-ERB agonists and ROR inverse agonists have been developed as metabolic and immunological tools, and REV-ERB agonists shift wheel-running rhythms and reduce fat mass in mice [PMID:24577401].

## Reading a hit

A RevDR2 or RORE match tells you the site belongs to the ROR/REV-ERB group. It does not tell you which of the four proteins binds it, and the ROR-versus-REV-ERB distinction matters biologically because the two have opposite signs: RORs recruit coactivators, REV-ERBs recruit NCoR-HDAC3 [PMID:24577401]. The two loops compete for identical sequence; the discrimination is temporal and cell-type dependent, not sequence-encoded [PMID:16267379,26044300]. Treat the family boundary between the `ROR` and `REV_ERB` entries in this atlas as a labelling convention, not a specificity claim.

Two further cautions. A single AGGTCA is not a REV-ERB site — that hexamer is shared with ESRRA, NR5A, NR4A and the RXR heterodimer partners [PMID:31175293] — so score the full extended element, and prefer the tandem form when you have it, since RevDR2 is far less likely to occur by chance than a 10-mer monomeric site. Second, ChIP-derived motifs for this family should be read carefully: in mouse liver most REV-ERBalpha ChIP-seq peaks arise from tethering to HNF6 rather than from direct RORE binding [PMID:26044300], so ChIP-only models (HOCOMOCO evidence code `P`, e.g. NR1D1.H14CORE.0.P.B) can carry a partner's specificity. The in vitro models here (evidence `SM`) are the ones that support a direct binding claim.
families.caveats: REV-ERB and ROR sites are the same sequence. A hit here is a ROR/REV-ERB call; nothing in the motif separates NR1D1 from NR1D2, or either from RORA/RORB/RORC, and the Vierstra archetype AC0123:NR1D/RORC says so explicitly. Because the two groups have opposite transcriptional sign, that ambiguity is consequential — resolve it with expression and phase data, not the motif. Require the AT-rich extension; a bare AGGTCA is shared across the superfamily. The tandem RevDR2 form is much more specific than the monomeric site. Finally, ChIP-derived models (HOCOMOCO code P) may reflect tethering: in liver, most REV-ERBalpha peaks are HNF6 sites rather than direct ROREs.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection with purified Rev-ErbAalpha defines its site as a 5-bp A/T-rich sequence adjacent to an AGGTCA half-site, an asymmetric 11-bp element bound by a monomer; the receptor was reported to activate transcription through it.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, EMSA, reporter assays

timeline.finding: A second selection identifies RevDR2, two monomer sites as a 2-bp-spaced direct repeat bound cooperatively by a homodimer 5-10 times more stably; on it Rev-Erb represses, reversing the 1993 conclusion that it is an activator.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection, EMSA, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether natural targets use RevDR2 or single monomer sites was not established.

timeline.finding: The 2.3 A structure of the REV-ERB DNA-binding region as a tandem homodimer on RevDR2 shows a second protein-DNA interface in the minor groove, explaining both the AT-rich extension and the 2-bp spacing.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: REV-ERBalpha is identified as the main regulator of cyclic Bmal1 transcription, and an expression-based promoter survey identifies the REV-ERB/ROR element as the circadian-night cis-element; Nr1d1-null mice keep rhythms but with altered period.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, expression profiling, promoter analysis, reporter assays

timeline.finding: All REV-ERBs (alpha, beta) and RORs (alpha, beta, gamma) act on the Bmal1 ROREs, with opposite sign, and Bmal1 output is the result of their competition at the same elements.
timeline.methods: Reporter assays, expression analysis

timeline.finding: Heme binds reversibly to REV-ERBalpha and regulates its interaction with the NCoR corepressor complex, giving the orphan receptor a ligand and linking it to gluconeogenic gene repression.
timeline.methods: Ligand binding, corepressor interaction assays, hepatocyte gene expression

timeline.finding: Liver ChIP-seq shows NR1D1 and NR1D2 share more than half their binding sites and overlap extensively with BMAL1; double-knockout mice have markedly altered wheel-running behavior and deregulated lipid metabolism.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, double-knockout mice, behavior, transcriptomics

timeline.finding: A DNA-binding-defective REV-ERBalpha separates two modes: clock genes need direct binding at ROREs in competition with RORs, whereas metabolic genes are regulated through tethering to lineage factors such as HNF6, so ChIP-derived motifs mix direct and indirect binding.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, DNA-binding mutant, transcriptomics

open: Whether REV-ERB represses from a single RORE in vivo or needs a pair of sites is not settled: in reporter assays it repressed as a homodimer on RevDR2 but not from a monomer site, yet the in vitro (SM) models in this family are 14-18 bp tandem elements while the ChIP-derived ones (evidence P) are single 9-10 bp sites.

How far REV-ERB activity is tuned by physiological changes in heme is unresolved: heme binds the ligand-binding domain reversibly and promotes NCoR recruitment, but whether cellular heme varies enough to act as a regulatory signal rather than a constitutive cofactor has not been established.

Whether NR1D1 and NR1D2 differ in target choice at all is unclear: their liver cistromes share more than half their sites and their in vitro motifs are indistinguishable, so it is unknown whether the non-shared sites reflect sequence preference or only differences in expression level and timing.

families.name: CTCF
families.def: 19-bp core CCASYAGRKGGCRSYR with upstream module; the insulator/loop-anchor motif. CTCF.
aka: TFClass: more than 3 adjacent zinc finger factors
families.short: CTCF is a single, near-ubiquitously expressed protein whose eleven C2H2 zinc fingers read an asymmetric, roughly 15-20 bp GC-rich sequence, often with a second recognition module a few bases upstream. Tens of thousands of these sites act as insulators and as anchors for cohesin-extruded chromatin loops, so they delimit topologically associating domains and separate enhancers from promoters they should not reach. Because the motif is long, information-rich, and read by a well-characterized finger-to-base code solved in two crystal structures, a CTCF match is one of the few motif hits that predicts real occupancy reasonably often. The site is directional: which strand it lies on determines which way a loop is anchored, and convergent pairs of sites are the ones that form loops.
families.long:
## The factors

CTCF (CCCTC-binding factor) is one protein, not a family. The human gene encodes a 727-residue polypeptide with a central array of eleven Cys2-His2 zinc fingers flanked by N- and C-terminal regions that carry no DNA-binding domain. It is expressed in essentially every cell type examined, and it is extraordinarily conserved: the chicken and human proteins are 93% identical in amino acid sequence (Filippova et al. 1996) [PMID:8649389]. CTCF binds DNA as a monomer; no dimerization interface is required, and its long-range activity comes from partners rather than from self-assembly. The most important of these is cohesin: a short segment in the CTCF N terminus docks onto the SA2-SCC1 (STAG2-RAD21) surface of human cohesin, and a 2.7 A crystal structure of that complex showed the interaction is specifically needed for CTCF-anchored loops and for positioning cohesin at CTCF sites (Li et al. 2020) [PMID:31905366]. CTCF has exactly one paralogue, the testis-restricted CTCFL/BORIS, which carries an almost identical zinc-finger array and is treated as a separate family here.

## The motif

The high-information core is 15 bp. JASPAR's core model (MA0139.2) reduces to RCCASYAGRKGGCRS in IUPAC, which is the sequence most people mean when they write the CTCF consensus; longer ChIP-derived models are also in use (JASPAR MA1929.2 and MA1930.2 span 31 and 33 positions), corresponding to the 33/34-mer that Schmidt et al. (2012) defined from six mammals [PMID:22244452]. The structural basis is unusually well understood. In the Hashimoto et al. (2017) crystal structure, zinc fingers 3-7 each contact three bases of the 15-bp core, with each conserved nucleotide making a base-specific hydrogen bond to a particular side chain; variable positions also make contacts, which is how CTCF tolerates deviation from consensus [PMID:28529057]. Yin et al. (2017) resolved CTCF on protocadherin sites and split the site into four modules: ZF3 reads module 4, ZF4-7 read modules 3 and 2, and ZF9-11 read an upstream module 1, with ZF8 acting as a spacer that absorbs variable distance between modules 1 and 2 [PMID:29076501]. Genome-wide, ZF4-7 anchor CTCF at roughly 80% of targets containing the core motif, while ZF1-2 and ZF8-11 read non-conserved flanks (Nakahashi et al. 2013) [PMID:23707059]. Two consequences matter in practice. The site is asymmetric, so it has an orientation, and a central asymmetric A is part of what makes recognition directional [PMID:29076501]. CTCF is also sensitive to cytosine methylation at position 2 of the core but insensitive at position 12, a difference the structure rationalizes [PMID:28529057]; across 19 human cell types, 41% of variable CTCF occupancy was attributable to differential methylation concentrated at two positions in the recognition sequence (Wang et al. 2012) [PMID:22955980].

## Where it acts

The first genome-wide survey reported 13,804 CTCF sites (Kim et al. 2007) [PMID:17382889]; current ChIP-seq gives tens of thousands per cell type. Sites are GC-rich but are not concentrated in CpG islands the way GC-box promoters are; they are spread across intergenic space, introns and promoter-proximal regions, and lineage-specific expansions have been driven by waves of retrotransposon activity (Schmidt et al. 2012) [PMID:22244452]. Occupied sites are enriched at topologically associating domain boundaries, where they often occur in clusters rather than singly, a redundancy that appears to stabilize boundaries over evolution (Kentepozidou et al. 2020) [PMID:31910870]. The essential partner is cohesin. Loops form preferentially between CTCF sites in convergent orientation (Rao et al. 2014) [PMID:25497547], and deleting or inverting a single site changes the loops formed (de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015) [PMID:26527277,26276636] - the observation that motivated the loop-extrusion model (Sanborn et al. 2015; Fudenberg et al. 2016) [PMID:26499245,27210764] and that single-molecule work later explained as DNA-tension-dependent, orientation-specific blocking of extruding cohesin (Davidson et al. 2023) [PMID:37076620].

## Biology and disease

CTCF was defined functionally as the protein required for enhancer-blocking by vertebrate insulators (Bell et al. 1999) [PMID:10458613] and for methylation-sensitive imprinting control at the H19/Igf2 locus [PMID:10839546,10839547]. Acute degradation of CTCF abolishes CTCF-CTCF loops and TAD insulation while leaving A/B compartments intact, separating those two layers of genome folding (Nora et al. 2017) [PMID:28525758]. In disease, CTCF/cohesin-binding sites are recurrent somatic mutation hotspots in several cancers (Katainen et al. 2015) [PMID:26053496]; in IDH-mutant glioma, hypermethylation disrupts a CTCF boundary and allows an enhancer to activate PDGFRA (Flavahan et al. 2016) [PMID:26700815]; and germline monoallelic CTCF variants cause an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder affecting brain, growth and craniofacial development (Valverde de Morales et al. 2023) [PMID:36454652].

## Reading a hit

This is the one family in the atlas where a position-weight-matrix match genuinely carries predictive weight: sites that match the consensus more closely are occupied more often and more constitutively (Plasschaert et al. 2014) [PMID:24121688]. Even so, only a fraction of genomic matches are bound in any one cell type, and occupancy is conditional on the methylation state of the CpG at core position 2. Report the strand: a CTCF hit without an orientation is half an answer, because loop anchoring depends on it. A hit cannot distinguish CTCF from CTCFL, which share the zinc-finger array. Finally, check which matrix matched. Two Vierstra archetypes labelled for CTCF are not the CTCF motif at all - AC0214:CTCF/ZNF is a poly-T model (tTTTTgTTTTT) and AC0174:CTCF/ZNF is a short C-rich model (tGCCCCCT, 8.4 bits) - and a hit to either says nothing about CTCF. The genuine CTCF models, including the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO core model (CTCF.H14CORE.0.P.B, ChIP evidence, grade B), agree with each other and with two independent crystal structures [PMID:28529057,29076501], so the label itself is not in doubt.
families.caveats: Trust a strong CTCF hit more than almost any other motif in this atlas, but not unconditionally. Only some matches are occupied in a given cell type; occupancy depends on the methylation state of the CpG at core position 2, and a site bound in one lineage may be free in another. The hit cannot tell CTCF from CTCFL/BORIS. Orientation is part of the result, not an afterthought. A single site is weak evidence for a domain boundary, since boundaries are usually clusters of sites. And confirm which matrix matched: two Vierstra archetypes carrying the CTCF label are poly-T or short C-rich models that have nothing to do with the CTCF core.

timeline.finding: A 5' element of the chicken beta-globin domain (the HS4 region) is shown to block the beta-globin LCR enhancer from a reporter directionally, and to protect a transgene from position effects in Drosophila, establishing the vertebrate insulator as an element that can be assayed.
timeline.methods: Stable reporter assays in K562 erythroid cells; transgenic Drosophila position-effect assay
timeline.open: No protein had been identified that bound the element or carried its activity.

timeline.finding: Cloning of human CTCF shows an 11-zinc-finger protein 93% identical between chicken and human that binds diverged c-myc promoter sites with different subsets of fingers (ZF2-7 on the chicken site, ZF3-11 on the human), the first evidence that CTCF is 'multivalent'.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, gel shifts with finger deletions, contact-base mutagenesis, proteolytic protection
timeline.open: Because each known site seemed to use a different set of fingers, no general consensus could be written.

timeline.finding: CTCF is identified as the protein required for enhancer blocking by HS4 and other vertebrate insulators; in 2000 two groups showed that CTCF binding at the H19 imprinting control region is abolished by CpG methylation, so the methylated paternal allele loses the boundary and expresses Igf2.
timeline.methods: Enhancer-blocking reporter assays, binding-site mutagenesis, in vitro methylation-sensitive binding, transgenic mice
timeline.open: How a single DNA-bound protein blocks an enhancer acting from a distance was unexplained.

timeline.finding: The first genome-wide map finds 13,804 CTCF sites in human fibroblasts, mostly far from transcription start sites, fitting a conserved consensus motif, with occupancy largely invariant across cell types.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip, de novo motif discovery
timeline.open: Why a minority of sites vary between cell types, and why most genomic matches are unbound, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Kilobase-resolution Hi-C shows that chromatin loop anchors are usually CTCF-bound and that the two anchoring motifs are overwhelmingly in convergent orientation.
timeline.methods: In situ Hi-C, ChIP-seq, motif-orientation analysis
timeline.open: Whether orientation was causal, and what mechanism could read the orientation of two sites hundreds of kilobases apart, was unknown.

timeline.finding: Deleting or inverting single CTCF sites by CRISPR rewires loops (Sox2, protocadherin and beta-globin loci), showing that orientation is causal; the loop-extrusion model, in which cohesin extrudes DNA until it meets a CTCF site pointing toward it, explains why only convergent pairs form loops.
timeline.methods: CRISPR deletion and inversion with 4C-seq and Hi-C; polymer simulation
timeline.open: Cohesin had not yet been shown to extrude DNA, and how a bound CTCF stops it in one direction only was unknown.

timeline.finding: Two crystal structures of the CTCF finger array on DNA show ZF3-7 each reading three bases of the 15-bp core and explain methylation sensitivity at core position 2 but not 12; on protocadherin sites ZF9-11 read an upstream module, with ZF8 as a spacer.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography with binding assays
timeline.open: The two structures disagree about the C-terminal fingers: one places ZF9-11 in the major groove reading module 1, the other finds ZF8-9 spanning the backbone without base contacts and ZF10-11 not visible.

timeline.finding: A 2.7 A structure shows a segment of the CTCF N terminus docking onto the SA2-SCC1 subunits of cohesin, an interaction required specifically for CTCF-anchored loops. Single-molecule imaging in 2023 then showed CTCF blocks extruding cohesin asymmetrically but in a DNA-tension-dependent way, and can redirect extrusion or shrink loops: a regulator of extrusion, not the simple wall the 2015 model assumed.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, Hi-C of interface mutants; in vitro single-molecule imaging of CTCF and cohesin
timeline.open: How permeable CTCF boundaries are to cohesin in living cells, and what sets DNA tension there, was not measured.

open: What CTCF's C-terminal fingers contribute to recognition is unsettled: the protocadherin-site structures place ZF9-11 in the major groove reading the upstream module, whereas the other crystal structure finds ZF8-9 spanning the backbone without base contacts and ZF10-11 disordered, and genome-wide mutant data assign ZF8-11 to non-conserved flanks.

Why most genomic matches to the CTCF core are unbound in a given cell type is only partly explained: CpG methylation at core position 2 accounts for about 41% of variable occupancy across 19 cell types, and the contribution of chromatin accessibility, flanking sequence and cofactors to the remainder has not been quantified.

Whether CTCF acts in cells as a near-absolute barrier to loop extrusion, as the convergent-orientation rule suggests, or as a leaky, tension-dependent one, as single-molecule assays show, is not resolved, because the rate at which cohesin passes CTCF sites in vivo has not been measured.

How much gene regulation depends on CTCF-anchored loops in general is open: acute CTCF degradation dissolves loops and TAD insulation genome-wide, while the clearest transcriptional consequences come from disrupting individual boundaries such as the PDGFRA boundary in IDH-mutant glioma, and which boundaries matter for expression cannot yet be predicted.

families.name: Estrogen receptors
families.def: ERE: inverted AGGTCA repeat, GGTCAnnnTGACC. ESR1, ESR2.
families.short: The estrogen receptors ERalpha (ESR1) and ERbeta (ESR2) are estradiol-activated nuclear receptors that bind DNA as homodimers on the estrogen response element, a 15 bp inverted repeat of the hexamer AGGTCA with a 3 bp spacer: AGGTCAnnnTGACCT, usually quoted as its 13 bp core GGTCAnnnTGACC. The element differs from the glucocorticoid-type half-site by only two base pairs, and the same 3 bp spacing and dimer geometry are shared with the steroid receptors, so the half-site sequence rather than the architecture is what marks it as estrogenic. ESR1 and ESR2 cannot be told apart by sequence. These sites drive the estrogen program in breast, uterus, bone and liver, and they are the regulatory target of tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors and fulvestrant.
families.long:
## The factors

Two paralogues: ESR1 (ERalpha) and ESR2 (ERbeta), subfamily NR3A. Both have an N-terminal AF-1 region, a C4 double-zinc-finger DNA-binding domain (DBD), a hinge and a ligand-binding domain that binds 17beta-estradiol and, with different consequences, tamoxifen, raloxifene and fulvestrant. They bind as homodimers and can form ERalpha/ERbeta heterodimers. ERalpha is the dominant form in breast epithelium, uterus, liver, adipose, bone and hypothalamus; ERbeta is lower and more restricted, with ovarian granulosa cells, prostate, colon and some immune cells the usual examples, and much of its biology remains contested (Hewitt and Korach 2018) [PMID:29901737,28643774]. Nine motif models fall in this family (JASPAR 2, HOCOMOCO 4, CIS-BP 2, Vierstra 1), all labelled ESR1 or ESR2.

## The motif

The estrogen response element (ERE) is an inverted repeat of AGGTCA with three intervening bases: 5'-AGGTCAnnnTGACCT-3', frequently written as the 13 bp core GGTCAnnnTGACC [PMID:15036253]. It was first defined functionally in the 5' flanking region of the Xenopus vitellogenin A2 gene (Klein-Hitpass et al. 1986) [PMID:3463433] and reviewed in detail by Gruber et al. (2004) [PMID:15036253]. The crystal structure of the ERalpha DBD bound to a consensus palindrome showed a symmetrical dimer reading two 6 bp half-sites separated by three base pairs, and explained how the receptor discriminates its own half-site from the glucocorticoid half-site, which differs by only two base pairs (Schwabe et al. 1993) [PMID:8221895]. Three residues in the first zinc finger decide which of the two half-sites a receptor reads, and swapping them interconverts glucocorticoid and estrogen specificity (Umesono and Evans 1989) [PMID:2500251].

Spacing is the other half of the rule. A 3 bp spacer with the half-sites pointing at each other is an ERE; the same AGGTCA hexamers arranged as direct repeats separated by 1-5 bp are elements for RXR heterodimers instead, and a single extended half-site with a 5' A/T extension is an ERR or NR5A element. The models here are consistent with this: the data consensus is AGGTCAcvnTGnCCt, a 15 bp inverted repeat whose 3' half-site is noticeably more degenerate than the 5' half in ChIP-derived matrices. Common variants are EREs with one or two mismatches, ERE half-sites flanked by SP1 or AP-1 sites, and no ERE at all where ERalpha works by tethering to AP-1 or SP1.

ESR1 and ESR2 are not distinguishable: their models are 0.86-1.00 similar and the Vierstra archetype in this family, AC0122, is labelled ESR/ESRRA because estrogen and estrogen-related receptor motifs cluster together. The confusion runs both ways and is partly biological rather than a labelling error: the CIS-BP ESR1 model M07985 is an extended monomeric half-site (cCAAGGTCA), an ERR-type element, and the family data flags it as belonging with ESRR, while a CIS-BP ESRRA model is a full ERE. ERRalpha and ERRbeta do activate transcription through consensus EREs, whereas ERbeta activity is restricted to the ERE (Vanacker et al. 1999) [PMID:10428965].

## Where it acts

Near-consensus 15 bp EREs are abundant: a genome-wide screen found roughly 70,000 across the human and mouse genomes, enriched near transcription start sites, with only about 1% conserved in the flanking regions of orthologous genes (Bourdeau et al. 2004) [PMID:15001666]. Actual ERalpha occupancy is far smaller and mostly distal: genome-wide mapping in MCF-7 cells placed authentic binding sites predominantly in enhancers rather than promoters (Carroll et al. 2006) [PMID:17013392]. FOXA1 is required for most of that occupancy and reprogramming FOXA1 redistributes ERalpha (Hurtado et al. 2011) [PMID:21151129]; GATA3, TFAP2C and PGR also shape it. ER binding sites differ between tumours and that differential binding tracks clinical outcome (Ross-Innes et al. 2012) [PMID:22217937]. Many peaks contain only a half-site, consistent with indirect or tethered recruitment.

## Biology and disease

EREs carry the estrogen response in mammary and uterine epithelium, bone remodelling, hepatic lipid handling and hypothalamic feedback on gonadotropins. Esr1-null females are infertile, with hypoplastic uteri and hyperemic ovaries that form no corpora lutea, and Esr1-null males have reduced fertility [PMID:8248223]; Esr2-null females are fertile but have fewer and smaller litters because of reduced ovarian efficiency, and older Esr2-null males show prostate and bladder hyperplasia [PMID:9861029]. About three quarters of breast cancers are ER-positive and are treated by blocking the receptor or depleting its ligand. Acquired ESR1 ligand-binding-domain mutations, chiefly Y537S and D538G, are recurrent in endocrine-resistant metastatic breast cancer and make the receptor constitutively active (Robinson et al. 2013) [PMID:24185510]; because they do not change the DBD, the motif itself is unaltered, and the consequence is where and how much the receptor binds rather than what it binds.

## Reading a hit

A full 15 bp ERE is a reasonably specific signal for the estrogen/ERR branch, but it cannot tell ESR1 from ESR2, and it overlaps with ERRalpha and ERRbeta, which bind consensus EREs [PMID:10428965]. Check the spacing and orientation before naming anything: AGGTCA inverted with a 3 bp gap is an ERE, direct repeats are RXR-heterodimer elements, and a lone AGGTCA with a 5' AA is an ERR element. With about 10 informative positions, exact consensus 13-mers occur on the order of 10^3 times per haploid genome and near-matches tens of thousands of times, so most hits are not bound in any given cell. Two of the four HOCOMOCO models here are bare half-sites (AGGTCA, TGACCT) and all four are ChIP-derived (evidence code P), which in this family means they can include tethering signal; there is no in vitro (S/M) model for either receptor in this set. A ChIP peak with no ERE is expected, not anomalous.
families.caveats: A full inverted-repeat ERE is among the more specific nuclear receptor signals, but it marks the estrogen/ERR branch rather than a receptor: ESR1 and ESR2 are indistinguishable by sequence, and ERRalpha and ERRbeta bind consensus EREs too. One CIS-BP model labelled ESR1 in this family is actually an extended ERR-type half-site and is flagged as such. All four HOCOMOCO models here are ChIP-derived, with no in vitro entry for either receptor, so they may carry signal from tethered recruitment via AP-1 or SP1; conversely, many genuine ER peaks contain only a half-site. Near-consensus EREs number in the tens of thousands genome-wide, so pair a hit with accessibility or ChIP evidence.

timeline.finding: A 35 bp segment of the Xenopus vitellogenin A2 5' flank confers estradiol induction on a heterologous promoter in human MCF-7 cells, with the palindrome GGTCACAGTGACC as its essential core: the first functional ERE, and evidence that the element is conserved from frogs to humans.
timeline.methods: Deletion mapping, transient transfection reporter assays
timeline.open: How the receptor tells this palindrome from the closely related glucocorticoid element.

timeline.finding: The 2.4 Å crystal structure of the ER DNA-binding domain shows a symmetrical dimer on two 6 bp half-sites with three intervening base pairs, and explains how it discriminates its half-site from the GR half-site, which differs at two positions.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: ERalpha, ERRalpha and ERRbeta all bind and activate through both the ERE and the SF-1 response element (an extended half-site), whereas ERbeta is restricted to the ERE, so the estrogen and estrogen-related receptors share targets.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether ER and ERR compete for the same sites in cells.

timeline.finding: A genome-wide screen finds about 70,000 near-consensus EREs in the human and mouse genomes, enriched near transcription start sites, with about 1% conserved in orthologous gene flanks; ChIP confirms ERalpha binding at many tested sites.
timeline.methods: Computational screen, in vitro binding, ChIP
timeline.open: Which of these many sites are actually occupied, and why most are not.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide mapping of ERalpha and RNA polymerase II in breast cancer cells places authentic ER binding mostly far from promoters and identifies cooperating factor motifs, revising the promoter-centred picture implied by sequence scans.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip, expression profiling

timeline.finding: Almost all ERalpha-chromatin interactions and estrogen-driven expression changes in breast cancer cells depend on FOXA1, and expressing FOXA1 in other cells alters where ER binds.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, FOXA1 knockdown and ectopic expression
timeline.open: Whether the dependence is a strict hierarchy, with FOXA1 always acting first.

timeline.finding: ER and GR can themselves change where FOXA1 binds, and at a subset of sites the steroid receptor enhances FOXA1 binding rather than the reverse, so the pioneer relationship is dynamic and not strictly one-way.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, DNase-seq, live-cell single-molecule tracking

timeline.finding: A validation of 13 anti-ERbeta antibodies found only one specific for immunohistochemistry; with it, ERbeta protein was detected in testis, ovary and lymphoid cells but not in normal or cancerous breast, contradicting many earlier reports.
timeline.methods: Antibody validation panel, immunohistochemistry, RNA-seq comparison
timeline.open: Which earlier ERbeta expression, binding and target-gene findings survive with validated reagents.

open: Where ERbeta is expressed, and so where ESR2 sites could matter, is disputed: rigorous antibody validation places the protein in testis, ovary and lymphoid cells and not in breast, contradicting a large body of earlier antibody-based work.

Whether FOXA1 acts strictly upstream of ERalpha is debated: depletion studies find that almost all ER binding in breast cancer cells needs FOXA1, while live-cell and genomic studies report that activated steroid receptors can recruit FOXA1 to new sites.

What share of ERalpha's genomic action requires a full ERE is unsettled: many ChIP peaks contain only a half-site or no ERE, which is read either as tethering through AP-1 or SP1 or as direct binding to degenerate elements.

Whether ERalpha binding to extended half-sites (the SF-1/ERR type, TCAAGGTCA) is a significant part of its genomic activity is unclear: ERalpha activates through such sites in reporter assays and one CIS-BP ESR1 model has this form, but genome-wide ER motifs are dominated by the inverted repeat, and the family data assigns that model to the ERR family.

families.name: NF-Y (CBF)
families.def: CCAAT box. NFYA, NFYB, NFYC.
families.short: NF-Y is a heterotrimer of NFYA, NFYB and NFYC that binds the CCAAT box, one of the most frequent elements in eukaryotic promoters. NFYB and NFYC carry histone-fold domains and pair like H2A/H2B, gripping the DNA backbone and bending it; NFYA supplies the only sequence-specific contacts, inserting an alpha helix into the minor groove to read CCAAT. All three subunits are required for binding, so the three gene symbols describe one molecular entity and one motif. NF-Y is ubiquitous, sits at a fixed distance upstream of transcription start sites, and helps open chromatin for cell-type-specific factors. NF-YA is overexpressed and alternatively spliced in several cancers.
families.long:
## The factors

NF-Y, also called CBF and historically CP1, is an obligate heterotrimer. NFYB and NFYC each
contain a histone-fold domain (HFD) and first dimerize with each other; the NFYB/NFYC dimer then
recruits NFYA, and only the complete trimer binds DNA [PMID:9153318]. Yeast HAP2, HAP3 and HAP5 are the
orthologues of NFYA, NFYB and NFYC respectively [PMID:22050321], and the conservation is high enough that subunits
are interchangeable across large evolutionary distances. NFYA exists as two major splice isoforms,
long and short, differing in the glutamine-rich activation region; the short isoform is enriched
in embryonic stem cells. NFYB and NFYC are encoded by single genes with essentially constitutive
expression, so NF-Y activity is regulated largely through NFYA levels and isoform choice [PMID:22050321]. Because
all three subunits are needed, a motif labelled NFYA, NFYB or NFYC in these databases refers to
the same complex and the same site; the three-way split in this family's data (nine models across
three symbols) reflects which subunit was tagged in an experiment, not three specificities.

## The motif

The consensus is the 5-base CCAAT box, generally quoted with flanking preferences as CCAATCA or,
on the reverse strand, TGATTGG [PMID:3476205,22050321]; databases here report both renderings plus CCAATCAG and CATTGGCC.
The crystal structure of NF-Y on a 25-bp CCAAT oligonucleotide explained the division of labor.
The NFYB/NFYC histone-fold dimer binds the sugar-phosphate backbone over about 25 bp, mimicking
the H2A/H2B-DNA interaction in a nucleosome and bending the DNA, but makes no base-specific
contacts [PMID:23332751,12401788]. NFYA contributes the specificity: a short alpha helix inserts deeply into the minor
groove and reads the CCAAT bases directly [PMID:23332751]. This architecture explains two features of the motif.
First, information is concentrated on five bases with modest preferences a few positions to each
side, giving models of 10-14 bits, and the flanking positions matter partly because they set the
DNA's bendability rather than because they are read. Second, NF-Y has nucleosome-like,
non-sequence-specific affinity in addition to its specific contacts, which is why it behaves like
a chromatin protein as well as a transcription factor [PMID:23332751]. Not every CCAAT box is an NF-Y site: the
element was long used as a generic label, and several unrelated families were grouped under
"CCAAT-binding protein", including the C/EBPs and NFI/CTF [PMID:3476205,3398920]. Those are different proteins with
different folds.

## Where it acts

NF-Y is the most positionally constrained factor in this batch. Its CCAAT boxes sit
overwhelmingly in core and proximal promoters, classically between 60 and 100 bp upstream of the
major transcription start site, and frequently in bidirectional promoters [PMID:15647281]. ChIP-on-chip and later
genome-wide work showed that a substantial minority of NF-Y sites nonetheless lie outside core
promoters [PMID:15647281]. NF-Y is bound to a large fraction of cell cycle gene promoters (cyclin A, CDC25C, CDK1)
often together with E2F factors [PMID:12771133], to the Y box of MHC class II promoters where it binds
cooperatively with the RFX complex about 15-20 bp away [PMID:10779326], to the CCAAT boxes of heat shock gene
promoters, and to the globin promoters. It recruits histone acetyltransferases including GCN5/PCAF
and p300, contacts TBP [PMID:12771133,9153318], and imposes H3K4 trimethylation through Ash2L. In embryonic stem cells NF-Y
is required to maintain identity and opens chromatin for lineage-determining factors [PMID:25132174], which makes
it one of the clearest examples of a ubiquitous factor acting as a chromatin accessibility
provider rather than a specificity determinant.

## Biology and disease

NF-Y is essential: loss of NFYA or of the histone-fold subunits is lethal in cells and in mice, and
NF-Y regulates cell cycle progression, cholesterol and lipid metabolism genes, and the
endoplasmic-reticulum stress and heat shock programs. Because the CCAAT box is so widespread, the
downstream consequences are broad rather than tissue-specific. In disease, the clearest links are
quantitative: NF-YA is overexpressed, and its isoform ratio shifted, in breast cancer [PMID:31506469] and in lung
adenocarcinoma, and NF-YA is required for proliferation of epithelial ovarian cancer cells through
EZH2 upregulation [PMID:23360797]. NF-YA splice isoform status has been reported as a prognostic variable in low
grade endometrial cancer. There is no well-established Mendelian disease caused by NFYA, NFYB or
NFYC mutation, which is consistent with the complex being required in every cell.

## Reading a hit

A CCAAT match is 5 bp of information and occurs roughly a million times in the human genome, so a
hit in isolation is not evidence. What makes a CCAAT hit credible is position: an NF-Y site 60-100
bp upstream of an annotated transcription start site, ideally with a preferred flank (CCAATCA or
its reverse complement TGATTGG), is a reasonable prediction, while the same 5-mer in an intron or
a distal enhancer is usually noise. The paralogue problem is unusual here and easy: there are no
paralogues to separate, because NFYA, NFYB and NFYC are three subunits of one complex. Treat all
three labels as synonyms for NF-Y. The main real confusion is with other families historically
called CCAAT-binding. C/EBP factors bind ATTGC-containing palindromes, not CCAAT, and NFI/CTF,
whose old name is literally "CCAAT box transcription factor", binds TTGGC(N5)GCCAA [PMID:3398920]; its GCCAA
half-site contains a CCAAT-like string and will cross-score on loose CCAAT models. If a scan
returns both NF-Y and NFI matches at the same position, they are competing explanations. Finally,
note that every HOCOMOCO model in this family is ChIP-only (evidence code P, grade B) and the
label agreement scores are correspondingly moderate; the structural and biochemical evidence for
NFYA reading CCAAT is strong [PMID:23332751], but these particular matrices are peak-derived.
families.caveats: CCAAT is 5 bp and occurs about a million times in the genome, so only position makes a hit credible: NF-Y sites cluster 60-100 bp upstream of transcription start sites. NFYA, NFYB and NFYC are subunits of one obligate trimer, so the three labels denote one motif, not three specificities, and only NFYA makes base contacts. The recurring confusion is with other families once called CCAAT-binding: NFI/CTF's GCCAA half-site and C/EBP sites will cross-score on loose CCAAT models and are competing explanations, not corroboration. All HOCOMOCO models here are ChIP-derived (grade B), though the structure independently confirms CCAAT reading.

timeline.finding: The structure of the NF-Y trimer on a 25-bp CCAAT oligonucleotide shows the histone-fold dimer binding the backbone like H2A/H2B in a nucleosome, while an NF-YA helix inserts into the minor groove and makes the CCAAT-specific contacts.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, mutagenesis

timeline.finding: In embryonic stem cells and neurons NF-Y binds cell-type-invariant promoters and also cell-type-specific enhancers together with master factors, where it promotes a permissive chromatin conformation; it is required to maintain ES cell identity.

open: How promoter-restricted functional NF-Y binding is remains unsettled: the classical CCAAT box sits 60-100 bp upstream of the start site, but ChIP-on-chip placed 40-50% of NF-Y sites outside core promoters and genome-wide data in ES cells and neurons find NF-Y at cell-type-specific enhancers, so distal CCAAT matches may be real more often than the promoter-position rule assumes.

Whether NF-Y is a constitutive promoter-presetting factor or a regulated one is not settled: its histone-fold subunits are ubiquitous and it occupies promoters broadly, yet on cell-cycle promoters its binding is timed and lost on repression.

Why the flanks matter is unclear: the trimer structure shows base-specific contacts concentrated on CCAAT, yet every model here carries flank preferences (CCAATCA, CCAATCAG), which could reflect DNA shape and bendability or contacts outside the crystallized site.

families.name: BED-type zinc finger
families.def: hAT-transposase-derived BED fingers. ZBED1 (hDREF, TATCGATA), ZBED2/4/5.
families.short: BED fingers are zinc-coordinating DNA-binding modules named for the two proteins in which they were first recognized, Drosophila BEAF and DREF, and they are shared with the hAT superfamily of DNA transposases. Vertebrate ZBED genes arose from at least two independent domestication events of hAT elements, so this is a second family of transposase recognition modules turned into host transcription factors. Nine motifs cover four proteins. Only ZBED1, the human DREF orthologue hDREF, has a strong and reproducible site: all four of its models converge on TATCGCGACAT, a relative of the Drosophila DNA replication-related element TATCGATA. ZBED2, ZBED4 and ZBED5 contribute short, weaker and partly conflicting models.
families.long:
## The factors

The BED finger was described in 2000 as a small zinc-binding DNA-binding domain found in two otherwise unrelated groups of proteins: chromatin boundary-element-binding proteins, of which the Drosophila factors BEAF and DREF gave the domain its name, and hAT-superfamily transposases [PMID:10973053]. Vertebrate ZBED genes are the domesticated descendants of the transposase side of that split. A phylogenetic survey showed they derive from at least two independent domestication events in jawed vertebrate ancestors and form two monophyletic clades: one containing ZBED2, ZBED3, ZBED4, ZBEDX and ZBED6, the other containing ZBED1, with ZBED5 separate again and related to Buster DNA transposons [PMID:23533661]. The family is an unusually clear demonstration that one class of transposon-derived protein module can be recruited repeatedly and independently into quite different host regulatory pathways [PMID:23533661].

Four proteins carry motifs here. ZBED1 is hDREF, the human orthologue of Drosophila DREF, a 694-residue protein that shares only about 22 percent identity with the fly factor [PMID:18155677]; it self-associates through its hATC domain, and that self-association is required both for nuclear accumulation and for DNA binding [PMID:17209048]. ZBED2 is expressed in keratinocytes and aberrantly in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma [PMID:32385160]. ZBED4 is a cone photoreceptor and Muller cell protein of the human retina [PMID:19369242]. ZBED5 is the Buster1-derived member [PMID:23533661]. ZBED6, the best-known domesticated ZBED of all - it is encoded inside an intron of ZC3H11A and represses IGF2 [PMID:20016685] - contributes no motif to this family and is not filed here.

## The motif

ZBED1 dominates the family. Its CIS-BP, JASPAR, HOCOMOCO and Vierstra models all read essentially the same eleven to twelve base pairs, TATCGCGACAT, with pairwise similarities of 0.98 to 1.00 and 17 to 19 bits of information - by some distance the best-supported site in this entry, and the source of the family consensus. Its relationship to the fly element is informative but not exact: Drosophila DREF binds as a homodimer to the palindromic DNA replication-related element TATCGATA [PMID:18155677], while the human in vitro models centre on a TATCG core followed by CGACAT. In human cells, hDRE-like sequences were found within 200 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site in 22 of 79 ribosomal protein genes, and hDREF binds them both in vitro and in chromatin [PMID:17220279].

The remaining models are short and much weaker. ZBED2 gives CGAAACC in JASPAR and CGAAaCt in HOCOMOCO, which agree with each other (similarity 0.92) but carry only about 10 bits. ZBED5 gives the six-base GGwACC. ZBED4 is the problem case: HOCOMOCO reports acCaGAACCAg while JASPAR reports CCCGCcCCGC, and the two are unrelated. Independent in vitro selection with recombinant Zbed4 recovered poly-G tracts and GC-box core signatures [PMID:22693546], which supports the JASPAR model and not the HOCOMOCO one. Overall family cohesion is 0.57, and that number is misleading: it reflects four nearly identical ZBED1 models plus three unrelated short models rather than a graded family.

## Where it acts

ZBED1/hDREF sites sit in promoters of proliferation-associated genes, prominently ribosomal protein genes, where they act as positive elements; hDREF expression and ribosomal protein gene expression both rise from late G1 into S phase, and knocking hDREF down reduces both ribosomal protein transcript levels and proliferation in normal human fibroblasts [PMID:17220279]. ZBED2 acts at promoters co-occupied with IRF1, where it behaves as a sequence-specific repressor of interferon-stimulated genes by antagonising IRF1-mediated activation [PMID:32385160]. ZBED4's sites, on the present evidence, are G-rich and GC-box-like and therefore fall in the same promoter-proximal compartment as the SP/KLF factors.

## Biology and disease

hDREF is required for normal proliferation [PMID:17220279], and its self-association mutants fail to enter the nucleus [PMID:17209048]. ZBED2 is preferentially expressed in the squamous molecular subtype of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and is associated with inferior survival; it represses the pancreatic progenitor programme, enhances motility and promotes invasion, and blunts the growth arrest that follows interferon signalling [PMID:32385160]. ZBED4 is expressed in cones and Muller glia of human retina but only in Muller cells in mouse [PMID:22693546], a species difference worth remembering before transferring mouse data. ZBED6, outside this family, regulates IGF2 and muscle growth and explains a major porcine growth quantitative trait locus - the textbook example of a domesticated transposon becoming a physiologically important repressor [PMID:20016685].

## Reading a hit

Trust the ZBED1 model and treat the rest with caution. TATCGCGACAT is eleven informative base pairs and will be genuinely rare, so a good match in a promoter, particularly a ribosomal protein or other growth gene promoter, is a reasonable ZBED1/hDREF call. The short ZBED2, ZBED4 and ZBED5 models are six to ten base pairs and will match constantly; they need expression and occupancy evidence before they mean anything. For ZBED4, prefer the GC-rich JASPAR model over the HOCOMOCO one, and note that a GC-box-like match cannot be attributed to ZBED4 rather than to any SP/KLF factor. Finally, a BED-finger hit does not distinguish the domesticated factor from an active hAT transposase carrying the same recognition module.
families.caveats: Only ZBED1 has a reproducible, information-rich site; the other three members contribute short models of six to ten base pairs that will match frequently by chance. ZBED4 is internally inconsistent: the HOCOMOCO model (acCaGAACCAg) and the JASPAR model (CCCGCcCCGC) are unrelated, and each has in vitro support: CASTing with recombinant Zbed4 favours the GC-rich JASPAR version, while the HOCOMOCO model is grade A across four assays. Until one is reconciled with the other, treat a ZBED4 hit to either model as unconfirmed. The family cohesion figure of 0.57 is an artefact of four near-duplicate ZBED1 models sitting beside three unrelated ones. ZBED6, the best-studied domesticated ZBED, contributes no motif and cannot be scanned for. Nothing in a BED-finger match separates a domesticated ZBED from an active hAT transposase.

open: The two ZBED4 models disagree and the evidence points both ways: the GC-rich JASPAR model matches the 2012 CASTing selection of poly-G and GC-box sequences, whereas the HOCOMOCO model acCaGAACCAg carries grade A support from four in vitro assay types (HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX, SMiLE-seq and PBM) and shares a GAAnCC-like core with the ZBED2 models from the same clade; which is the protein's direct site has not been settled.

How the human ZBED1 site relates to the fly DRE is unresolved: Drosophila DREF binds the palindrome TATCGATA as a homodimer, while every human ZBED1 model reads TATCGCGACAT, and with only about 22 percent identity between the two proteins it is not known whether this is the same element with diverged flanks or a different recognition mode.

Whether ZBED2 represses interferon-stimulated genes by competing with IRF1 for overlapping sequence or by binding a separate adjacent site is not settled; its short CGAAACC model shares a GAAAC stretch with IRF-type elements, so the two cannot be separated by motif alone.

families.name: HNF1
families.def: GTTAATNATTAAC palindrome. HNF1A, HNF1B.
families.short: HNF1A and HNF1B are the only two members of this family, and they bind an unusually long 13-bp near-palindrome, GTTAATNATTAAC, as an obligate dimer. Each subunit contributes an atypical homeodomain carrying a 21-residue insertion, paired with a POU-specific-like domain that was only recognized once the protein-DNA structure was solved. Because the dimer is rigid, the spacing between the two half-sites is fixed and the resulting motif carries about 15-16 bits of information - among the most specific sites of any homeodomain-related family. The two factors drive liver, pancreatic islet, kidney tubule and intestinal gene expression, and heterozygous loss of either causes a distinct form of monogenic diabetes (MODY3 for HNF1A, MODY5 with renal cysts for HNF1B).
families.long:
## The factors

The family has exactly two human members: HNF1A (historically TCF1, LFB1) and HNF1B (TCF2, vHNF1). Both are modular. An N-terminal dimerization domain of roughly 32 residues forms an intertwined four-helix bundle in the dimer [PMID:11439029]; a central region provides an atypical POU-specific-like fold [PMID:12453420]; and the DNA-contacting homeodomain carries a 21-amino-acid insertion in the loop between helices 2 and 3 that no other homeodomain has [PMID:1985954]. Dimerization is obligate for high-affinity binding, and HNF1A and HNF1B form homodimers as well as heterodimers, so the two proteins compete for and share the same sites [PMID:1985954]. The dimerization domain is stabilized by the cofactor DCoH/PCBD1 [PMID:11439029]. Expression is restricted and partly complementary: HNF1B appears earlier and more broadly in the developing pancreas, liver and kidney, while HNF1A dominates in adult hepatocytes, pancreatic islets, renal proximal tubule, stomach and intestine.

## The motif

The site is the 13-bp near-palindrome GTTAATNATTAAC [PMID:1985954,9047360]. Each GTTAAT half-site is read by one homeodomain, and the central position carries essentially no information, which is why the databases render it as an N. The cocrystal of HNF1A residues 83-279 with a high-affinity promoter showed two identical protein molecules on one site and revealed a second domain structurally similar to POU-specific domains that could not be predicted from the amino acid sequence; atypical elements in both domains create a stable interface, distinguishing HNF1A from the flexible POU-homeodomain proteins whose linker allows half-sites to be rearranged [PMID:12453420]. That rigidity is the whole story of the motif: the half-site spacing cannot vary, so the site is long, palindromic and highly informative. All four collections agree closely - JASPAR MA0046.3 and MA0153.2, the HOCOMOCO A-grade models HNF1A.H14CORE.0.PS.A and HNF1B.H14CORE.0.PS.A, two CIS-BP models and the Vierstra archetype AC0650 all give GTTAATNATTAAC at 13-16 bits [PMID:23332764,32728250], and family cohesion is 0.86. HNF1A and HNF1B are not distinguishable from sequence. One JASPAR entry labelled Hnf1A (MA1991.2) instead reads cCTTTGATcT; its nearest neighbours across all four databases lie in the TCF/LEF family, and CTTTG(A/T)T is the canonical TCF7/LEF1 site, so that model should not be used as an HNF1 motif.

## Where it acts

HNF1 sites sit in the promoters of tissue-specific genes - albumin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, fibrinogen, phenylalanine hydroxylase, pyruvate kinase, and many transporters of the renal proximal tubule [PMID:8598044] - and a systematic survey of vertebrate sequence found them 2.5 to 5 times more frequent in hepatic genes than expected, most markedly in promoter regions, but also common in genes transcribed in cells that lack HNF1, with no sign of counter-selection in the rest of the genome [PMID:9047360]. Genome-scale location analysis in human liver and pancreatic islets placed HNF1A on a large set of promoters shared extensively with HNF4A and ONECUT1/HNF6, with the three factors binding overlapping target sets and each other's genes, so HNF1 hits very often occur in clusters with those motifs rather than alone [PMID:14988562]. Arithmetically the site is rare: with 12 informative positions, an exact 13-mer match is expected only a few hundred times in 3.1 Gb, which is orders of magnitude below a typical 6-8 bp transcription factor site.

## Biology and disease

Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in HNF1A are the most common Mendelian cause of diabetes mellitus (MODY3), and the mutational hotspot in the DNA-binding region was the reason for solving the protein-DNA structure [PMID:8945470,12453420]. Mutations in HNF1B cause MODY5, generally with extrapancreatic features - renal cysts and dysplasia, genital tract malformations and pancreatic hypoplasia - described as renal cysts and diabetes syndrome [PMID:9398836,10484768]. Hnf1a-null mice develop hepatic dysfunction, phenylketonuria from loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase, and a renal Fanconi syndrome, which maps neatly onto the human phenotypes [PMID:8598044]. Biallelic HNF1A inactivation also defines a recognized molecular subtype of hepatocellular adenoma [PMID:12355088].

## Reading a hit

Of all the families in this atlas that derive from a homeodomain, this is the one where a sequence match is most informative. A full GTTAATNATTAAC is long enough that chance matches are rare, and finding one in a hepatocyte, islet, renal tubule or intestinal regulatory region is reasonable evidence of real HNF1 occupancy. Two limitations. First, the hit cannot tell you whether HNF1A, HNF1B or a heterodimer is responsible; use expression, since the two genes are expressed in overlapping but not identical tissues. Second, do not call a single GTTAAT half-site an HNF1 site - on its own it is a generic TAAT-type homeodomain core shared with most of the superfamily. The A-grade HOCOMOCO models carry HT-SELEX (S) support, so the claim that these proteins bind this sequence in vitro is solid [PMID:23332764] and does not rest on ChIP alone.
families.caveats: The two members are indistinguishable from sequence, so a hit means HNF1A, HNF1B or a heterodimer. The full 13-bp palindrome is specific enough that false positives are uncommon, but half-site-only matches (GTTAAT) are generic homeodomain cores and should not be reported as HNF1. One JASPAR model labelled Hnf1A (MA1991.2) is a TCF/LEF-type site (CTTTGAT) and is flagged as such by its nearest neighbours; avoid it. Evidence for the canonical motif is in vitro as well as ChIP-based, so the sequence claim is well supported. Occupancy is still tissue-restricted: outside liver, islet, kidney and gut, a match is unlikely to be bound.
