timeline.open: The rest of the DNA-binding region had no recognizable fold, and how it contributed to the 13-bp site was unknown.

timeline.finding: Heterozygous HNF1A mutations are found to cause MODY3, and Hnf1a-null mice show hepatic dysfunction, a silent phenylalanine hydroxylase gene with phenylketonuria, and renal Fanconi syndrome, fixing the factor's main targets in liver, islet and proximal tubule.
timeline.methods: Human linkage and mutation screening; mouse gene targeting

timeline.finding: A weighted-matrix search of vertebrate sequence finds several hundred candidate sites, 52 of 54 tested bind HNF1, and the sites are 2.5- to 5-fold enriched in hepatic genes and in promoters, but are also common in genes of cells that lack HNF1, with no sign of counter-selection.
timeline.methods: Matrix-based database search with in vitro binding assays
timeline.open: Whether the many sites outside liver genes are ever used was left open.

timeline.finding: An HNF1B mutation is found in MODY (MODY5); in 1999 a pseudo-POU deletion that abolishes DNA binding is shown to cosegregate with diabetes, non-diabetic renal disease and Mullerian aplasia, defining the extrapancreatic syndrome.
timeline.methods: Human mutation screening, pedigree cosegregation, DNA-binding and reporter assays

timeline.finding: The HNF1A dimerization domain is an intertwined four-helix bundle whose N-terminal mini-zipper is complementary to the coactivator DCoH; MODY mutations L12H and G20R destabilize it in different ways.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography (1.7 A), NMR

timeline.finding: The HNF1A 83-279-DNA cocrystal shows two molecules on one site and reveals a POU-specific-like domain that sequence had not predicted; a stable interface between it and the homeodomain, unlike the flexible POU proteins, explains the fixed half-site spacing.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Promoter-wide ChIP in human liver and islets shows HNF1A, HNF4A and HNF6/ONECUT1 occupying extensive overlapping target sets and each other's genes.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip on promoter arrays

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX for human HNF1A and HNF1B returns the same GTTAATNATTAAC palindrome for both, confirming in vitro that the paralogues cannot be separated by sequence.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX

open: Why full-length, high-affinity HNF1 palindromes are common in genes expressed in cells that lack HNF1 is unresolved: a genome-wide matrix survey found them only 2.5- to 5-fold enriched in hepatic genes with no counter-selection elsewhere, and whether those extra-hepatic sites are neutral, used by HNF1B in other epithelia, or used only in development has not been established.

Whether HNF1A homodimers, HNF1B homodimers and HNF1A-HNF1B heterodimers differ in which sites they occupy is not settled; their in vitro models are indistinguishable, so the distinct MODY3 and MODY5 phenotypes are currently attributed to expression pattern rather than to sequence preference.

The databases disagree with the literature over one model: JASPAR MA1991.2, labelled Hnf1A and derived from mouse ChIP-seq, reads the TCF/LEF-type CTTTGAT rather than the HNF1 palindrome, and the literature does not explain whether this reflects co-occupancy with TCF/LEF factors or a mislabelled dataset.

families.name: GFI1 / GFI1B
families.def: AATC core, TAAATCAC(A/T)GC. GFI1, GFI1B.
families.short: GFI1 and GFI1B are six-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger repressors of blood cell development that bind a well-defined AATC-core site, TAAATCAC(A/T)GC. Only fingers 3, 4 and 5 make the sequence-specific contacts; repression comes from the N-terminal SNAG peptide, which docks into LSD1 and pulls in the LSD1/CoREST complex. GFI1 acts in granulocyte, T-cell and hematopoietic stem cell programs, GFI1B in erythroid and megakaryocyte programs, and the two proteins bind indistinguishable sequences, so a motif hit identifies the pair rather than one member. Dominant-negative GFI1 mutations cause severe congenital neutropenia; dominant-negative GFI1B mutations cause gray platelet syndrome. The site is AT-rich, information-dense and unusually specific for a C2H2 motif.
families.long:
## The factors

Two paralogues: GFI1 (growth factor independence 1) and GFI1B, each about 330-420 residues, with six C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers and a 20-residue N-terminal SNAG domain [PMID:8887656]. Gfi-1 was found as the target of provirus integration in rat T-cell lymphoma lines that had been selected for interleukin-2-independent growth, which is how it got its name [PMID:8441411]. The SNAG peptide is the repression module: it inserts into the substrate-binding pocket of the histone demethylase LSD1 (KDM1A) and thereby recruits the LSD1/CoREST/HDAC complex to GFI-bound sites [PMID:17707228], so both proteins work as sequence-specific adaptors for a chromatin-modifying machine rather than as intrinsic repressors. They bind DNA as monomers; the two paralogues share the same DNA-binding surface but differ outside it, and they are largely non-overlapping in expression. GFI1 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells, granulocyte-monocyte progenitors, T cells and inner ear sensory cells; GFI1B in erythroid and megakaryocytic cells. Because they cross-repress each other's genes, their expression domains are largely exclusive despite identical sequence preference.

## The motif

The site was defined by random-oligonucleotide selection with recombinant GFI1 as TAAATCAC(A/T)GCA, with an AATC core whose bases are the most sensitive to mutation; methylation interference and mutant probes confirmed the internal hierarchy, and deletion mapping showed that only zinc fingers 3, 4 and 5 are needed for sequence-specific binding [PMID:8754800] - three adjacent fingers reading roughly nine bases of major groove, which matches the length of the informative region. The family data agrees closely. JASPAR renders GFI1 as AAATCACTGC and Gfi1B as AAATCACAGC; the Vierstra archetype AC0241:GFI/GFI1B reads AAATCACWGC [PMID:32728250]; and the HOCOMOCO grade-A models are written GCTGTGATTT, which is the reverse complement of the same site rather than a different motif. At 12-15 bits this is one of the more informative C2H2 motifs, and the AT-rich AATC core is distinctive enough that false positives are less of a problem than for E-box or GC-box families. Two entries in the data are less useful: a CIS-BP GFI1 model reduced to AATC alone (2.6 bits) and a second Vierstra archetype, AC0394:GFI, reading ATATCAC, which matches the main GFI cluster poorly (0.72). One long HOCOMOCO GFI1B model, AGTGVNNTGCAGTGATTT, looks like two core sites in opposite orientation separated by a variable spacer; whether that reflects a genuine dimeric arrangement or a selection artifact is not settled, and the single-site models are the safer default. GFI1 and GFI1B motifs are 0.96 similar and cannot be separated from sequence.

## Where it acts

GFI sites sit in promoters and enhancers of lineage-restricted blood genes rather than in CpG islands; the motif is AT-rich and therefore under-represented in CpG-island promoters. The best-validated target is ELANE (ELA2, neutrophil elastase), which GFI1 represses in granulocyte progenitors [PMID:12778173]; GFI1 and GFI1B also bind their own and each other's regulatory regions, producing a cross-antagonistic circuit that helps keep the myeloid and erythroid programs apart [PMID:26447191]. Genome-wide, GFI1 co-occupies myeloid enhancers with PU.1/SPI1, RUNX1, and the LSD1/CoREST complex, and GFI1B with GATA1 and TAL1 in erythroid and megakaryocytic cells. Because occupancy depends on LSD1 recruitment, GFI-bound sites are typically nucleosome-depleted regions marked by H3K4 methylation that is then removed [PMID:17707228].

## Biology and disease

Gfi1-null mice have severe neutropenia with an accumulation of atypical immature myeloid cells and heightened inflammatory responses [PMID:11810106]. In humans, heterozygous dominant-negative GFI1 mutations (the recurrent N382S substitution in zinc finger 5) cause severe congenital neutropenia and derepress ELA2, tying the human disease directly to loss of DNA binding [PMID:12778173]. Gfi1b-null mouse embryos die around midgestation with arrested erythroid and megakaryocytic differentiation [PMID:11825872], and in humans a dominant-negative GFI1B truncation causes gray platelet syndrome, with macrothrombocytopenia and platelets deficient in alpha-granules [PMID:24325358]. Both genes appear in leukemia: GFI1 levels modulate the course of myeloid leukemia and a low-expression GFI1 variant is associated with acute myeloid leukemia risk [PMID:26447191], while GFI1B is recurrently affected in myelodysplastic contexts. The clinical genetics of both genes are dominated by dominant-negative alleles rather than simple haploinsufficiency, which is consistent with a protein that occupies sites and recruits a corepressor.

## Reading a hit

This is one of the better-behaved families in the C2H2 world. The AATC-core site is long, AT-rich and information-dense, so a strong match is meaningful and unlikely to be a coincidence in a short query. What a match does not tell you is which paralogue: GFI1 and GFI1B read the same sequence, and the Vierstra archetype name AC0241:GFI/GFI1B is an explicit statement that the two were not separable [PMID:32728250]. Use expression to decide - a granulocyte or T-cell context favors GFI1, an erythroid or megakaryocytic one GFI1B. Evidence types are mostly good: HOCOMOCO GFI1 and GFI1B core models are grade A with PSM evidence (ChIP plus HT-SELEX plus methyl-HT-SELEX), and JASPAR MA0038.3 for GFI1 is HT-SELEX, so the in vitro basis is solid [PMID:28473536]. Two entries warrant care: JASPAR MA0483.2 is a ChIP-seq-derived matrix for mouse Gfi1B, so it carries both a cross-species and an indirect-binding caveat, and the 4 bp CIS-BP GFI1 entry is too degenerate to scan with usefully.
families.caveats: The motif itself is trustworthy - long, AT-rich, 12-15 bits, defined in vitro by site selection and reproduced by HT-SELEX - so a strong match is usually a real GFI-family site. What it cannot do is name the paralogue: GFI1 and GFI1B motifs are 0.96 similar and one Vierstra archetype merges them by name. Resolve the ambiguity with cell type, not sequence. Avoid the 4 bp CIS-BP GFI1 entry (AATC, 2.6 bits), which will match everywhere, and treat the mouse ChIP-derived JASPAR Gfi1B matrix as the weakest member. The extended double-site HOCOMOCO GFI1B model should not be assumed to represent obligate dimeric binding.

timeline.finding: Gfi-1 was cloned as the site of provirus insertion in rat T-cell lymphoma lines selected for interleukin-2-independent growth, identifying a zinc-finger protein whose overexpression contributes to growth-factor independence.
timeline.methods: retroviral insertional mutagenesis, cDNA cloning, Northern blotting
timeline.open: Whether the protein bound DNA directly and at what sequence.

timeline.finding: Random-oligonucleotide selection with recombinant GFI1 defined the site as TAAATCAC(A/T)GCA; methylation interference ranked the AATC core as the critical bases and deletion mapping showed that only fingers 3, 4 and 5 are needed, so three of six fingers carry the specificity.
timeline.methods: site selection, EMSA, DNase I footprinting, methylation interference, finger deletions
timeline.open: How the protein repressed transcription once bound.

timeline.finding: A 20-residue N-terminal region was shown to be an autonomous, position-independent repression domain shared with Snail-family proteins, IA-1 and Gsh-1, and was named the SNAG domain; a single P2A substitution in it abolished repression.
timeline.methods: GAL4 fusion reporters, point mutagenesis, cell-cycle assays

timeline.finding: Germline deletions separated the two paralogues in vivo: Gfi1-null mice are severely neutropenic with excess immature monocytic cells and exaggerated inflammatory responses, while Gfi1b-null embryos arrest in erythroid and megakaryocytic development, despite the two proteins sharing one DNA preference.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, hematopoietic phenotyping
timeline.open: Why two factors with the same binding site have non-overlapping requirements.

timeline.finding: Dominant-negative zinc-finger mutations in human GFI1, including the recurrent N382S change in finger 5, were shown to cause severe congenital neutropenia with derepression of ELA2, linking the human disease to loss of sequence-specific binding rather than to loss of protein.
timeline.methods: patient sequencing, EMSA, chromatin immunoprecipitation, expression analysis

timeline.finding: Purification of Gfi-1b complexes identified CoREST, LSD1 and HDAC1/2 bound through the SNAG domain, and showed that LSD1 depletion derepresses Gfi target genes with increased H3K4 methylation - the repression mechanism implied by the 1996 domain mapping.
timeline.methods: complex purification and mass spectrometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation, knockdown differentiation assays

timeline.finding: A nonsense GFI1B allele was shown to cause autosomal dominant gray platelet syndrome by acting as a dominant negative on wild-type GFI1B, extending the dominant-negative pattern already seen for GFI1 in neutropenia.
timeline.methods: family linkage and sequencing, platelet and megakaryocyte phenotyping, transcriptional assays

timeline.finding: High-throughput in vitro binding including methyl-HT-SELEX, and genome-wide footprint clustering, both reproduced the 1996 selected site; the footprint archetype was named for GFI1 and GFI1B together, formalizing that the two paralogues are not separable from sequence.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX, DNase footprint clustering across cell types

open: The long HOCOMOCO GFI1B model (AGTGVNNTGCAGTGATTT) reads as two core sites in opposite orientation with a variable spacer, and it is unresolved whether GFI proteins genuinely occupy paired sites in that arrangement or whether the model is an artifact of selection, since no structure or in vivo footprint has tested it.

No experiment has separated GFI1 from GFI1B at the sequence level - their models are 0.96 similar and the footprint archetype merges them - so whether their strictly non-overlapping biology rests entirely on expression and partner availability, or partly on unmeasured sequence preferences, is unsettled.

The database entries for this family disagree with each other more than the literature does: CIS-BP renders GFI1 as a 4 bp AATC and GFI1B as AAATCTG, and the Vierstra archetype AC0394:GFI reads ATATCAC and matches the main cluster at only 0.72, and nothing indicates which of these reflects a real secondary preference rather than a poorly estimated model.

families.name: ZNF143 / THAP11 (SBS)
families.def: SPH/SBS element ACTACAATTCCC, bound by ZNF143 and by THAP11 (Ronin) with HCFC1; also ZNF76.
families.short: The SPH element, also called the SBS, is a promoter element read by three proteins that are not close relatives. ZNF143 (originally Staf) and its paralogue ZNF76 are C2H2 zinc-finger activators; THAP11 (Ronin) uses an unrelated THAP zinc-coordinating domain and occupies the same sequence in a complex with the coactivator HCFC1. The site sits close to transcription start sites at thousands of CpG-island promoters, where it drives small nuclear RNA genes transcribed by RNA polymerase II and III and a large set of protein-coding genes, prominently nuclear-encoded mitochondrial and ribosomal ones. The element was once presented as a sequence-specific anchor for chromatin loops; that role has since been retracted, but its promoter activity is well supported.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF143 was cloned as Staf, the selenocysteine tRNA gene transcription-activating factor, a zinc-finger protein that activates an RNA polymerase III promoter [PMID:7641696]; it was soon shown to work on polymerase II promoters as well, including the U6 snRNA gene, whose enhancer-like distal region contains the same element (there called SPH) [PMID:9009278,9776743]. The DNA-binding region is a tandem array of seven C2H2 zinc fingers, with a separate N-terminal activation domain [PMID:7641696]. ZNF76 is the close paralogue and has essentially the same in vitro specificity. THAP11/Ronin is unrelated in fold: its DNA-binding domain is a THAP domain, a zinc-coordinating domain of transposase ancestry that reads adjacent major and minor grooves, and it binds the element as part of a complex with HCFC1 (HCF-1) [PMID:20581084]. ZNF143, THAP11 and HCFC1 occupy overlapping sets of promoters [PMID:23539139,23408857], and the three are individually essential; ZNF143 is deeply conserved in vertebrates, and zebrafish carry two znf143 paralogues.

## The motif

The functional element is bipartite and about 18 base pairs long. The half that carries most of the information is written TCCCAYAATGCA [PMID:9009278]; upstream of it, separated by nothing or a base or two, sits the ACTACAA box, giving the composite form that the ChIP-derived matrices in this family read as ACTACAATTCCCAGCATG (reverse complement CATGCTGGGAATTGTAGT) [PMID:23408857]; the element is more often quoted in the literature in the shortened form ACTACAATTCCC used above. The two halves are contacted by different parts of the finger array, which is why databases built from different assays capture different portions of the site. In this family, the in vitro matrices — the HT-SELEX/methyl-SELEX ZNF76 matrix and JASPAR MA0088.2 (ZNF143) and MA1716.2 (ZNF76) — cover the TCCCACAATGCA half, in the opposite orientation, while the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices and the CIS-BP ZNF143 matrix carry the full bipartite word including ACTACAA. The family-level dataConsensus, CGGGGCATGCTGGGAADTGTAG, is the complete site read on the minus strand, which is why it looks unlike the ACTACAATTCCC form given above. ZNF143, ZNF76 and THAP11 are not distinguishable from sequence: their matrices are each other's nearest neighbours across all four databases.

## Where it acts

This is a promoter motif, not an enhancer motif. Occurrences concentrate within roughly 100-200 base pairs of transcription start sites in CpG islands, often at divergent promoter pairs, and the element is one of the small number of words enriched at bidirectional promoters [PMID:21177654]. It is also a fixture of the type 3 polymerase III promoters (U6, tRNA-Sec, and related small RNA genes), where it works together with the SNAPc complex and the PSE [PMID:9009278]. At protein-coding promoters the element coincides with HCFC1, YY1 and GABP occupancy, making it part of a recurring core-promoter module rather than a stand-alone site [PMID:23539139]. Overlapping ZNF143, THAP11 and Notch1 sites at the same promoters have been described, so occupancy can be competitive [PMID:23408857]. Tens of thousands of matches to the full motif exist in the human genome, but the strongly occupied subset is in the low thousands [PMID:23408857] and is largely invariant between cell types.

## Biology and disease

Depletion of ZNF143 is lethal in cells and in mouse embryos [PMID:39708803,39708805]. Degron experiments place its direct output on nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and ribosomal genes [PMID:39708803,39708805]: loss causes severe mitochondrial dysfunction and blocks proliferation and differentiation [PMID:39708805], and it acts by stimulating transcription initiation at promoters it occupies directly, activating most and repressing some [PMID:39676670]. THAP11/Ronin knockout arrests mouse embryos before implantation and is required for embryonic stem cell self-renewal [PMID:20581084], and mutations in HCFC1 and THAP11 cause an inborn error of cobalamin metabolism with ribosomopathy features [PMID:35013307]. ZNF143 has been reported as overexpressed in several cancers, but the mechanistic claims that received most attention were architectural rather than oncogenic.

The architectural story is the important caution here. ZNF143 was reported to occupy chromatin-interaction anchors and to provide sequence specificity for promoter loops, with and without CTCF [PMID:25645053], and later to mediate CTCF-bound promoter-enhancer loops in haematopoietic stem cells [PMID:33397967]. Two 2025 degron studies overturned this. Acute depletion of ZNF143/ZFP143 in mouse and human cells changed no loops [PMID:39708803,39708805], and one study showed that a widely used ZNF143 antibody cross-reacts with CTCF, which is how the factor came to be placed at loop anchors in the first place [PMID:39708805]. The current view is that ZNF143 is an essential promoter-proximal transcription factor with an unusually long chromatin residence time and no general looping function [PMID:39708803].

## Reading a hit

A confident match tells you that you are almost certainly at a promoter, and it tells you the family, not the protein: ZNF143, ZNF76 and THAP11/HCFC1 all read this word and cannot be separated from sequence. If the hit came from a ChIP peak set, check which antibody was used before concluding anything about loops or CTCF [PMID:39708805], and do not treat co-occurrence with CTCF as evidence of a composite element. Because the site is bipartite, a hit on only the TCCCAYAATGCA half is weaker evidence than a hit spanning both halves, and matrices in this family differ in which half they model; scan with several and compare. The motif is information-rich, so chance matches to the full site are uncommon in a single promoter but not negligible genome-wide.
families.caveats: A match identifies the SPH/SBS element, not a specific protein: ZNF143, ZNF76 and THAP11 with HCFC1 all occupy it, and in vitro data support direct binding for all three. The main hazard is historical rather than motif-based. ChIP-derived ZNF143 peak sets in the literature are contaminated by CTCF cross-reactivity of a common antibody, so any inference from a hit to loop anchoring, CTCF cooperation or three-dimensional architecture is unsafe; the 2025 degron studies found no looping function. Also note that the four databases model different portions of the bipartite site, in opposite orientations, so scores are not comparable across matrices and a partial match may reflect the matrix rather than the sequence.

timeline.finding: Staf is cloned from Xenopus as the factor that binds the 15-bp activator element of the selenocysteine tRNA gene and activates its RNA polymerase III promoter; it has seven C2H2 zinc fingers, a separate acidic activation domain, and a close human relative, ZNF76.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, DNA-binding assays, Xenopus oocyte expression
timeline.open: The binding-site consensus, and whether Staf acted on any gene other than tRNA-Sec, were unknown.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection gives a 19-bp Staf consensus (YYWCCCRNMATSCMYY-RCR), and Staf is shown to drive enhanced transcription of most vertebrate snRNA genes by both RNA polymerase II and III; in 1998 the human factor cloned on the U6 SPH element turns out to be ZNF143.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, footprinting, EMSA, oocyte microinjection, expression cloning
timeline.open: The site was known only from small-RNA genes; how many protein-coding promoters used it was not known.

timeline.finding: Ronin (THAP11), with its coregulator HCF-1, is identified as the binder of a hyperconserved promoter element containing ACTACA that had lacked a known factor; its targets in embryonic stem cells are genes for transcription initiation, splicing and metabolism.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and motif discovery in mouse ES cells
timeline.open: Whether this element and the Staf/ZNF143 site were one element or two neighbours was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide analysis finds ZNF143 sites overrepresented in bidirectional over unidirectional promoters, and ChIP detects ZNF143 at 93% of a tested set of divergent promoters carrying a predicted site.
timeline.methods: Promoter motif analysis, ChIP, dual-reporter assays

timeline.finding: ChIP-seq resolves two ZNF143 motifs at about 3,100 promoter binding events: the canonical 18-bp SBS1 and a 25-bp SBS2 with ACTACAN immediately upstream. ZNF143 binds both with the same affinity; the ACTACA part is the THAP11 site, and the two DNA-binding domains occupy SBS2 mutually exclusively. Separately, HCFC1 is found at about 5,400 active CpG-island promoters, about 90% of them co-occupied by ZNF143/THAP11, YY1 or GABP.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, de novo motif discovery, EMSA with recombinant DNA-binding domains
timeline.open: Whether ZNF143 and THAP11-HCFC1 compete for or share individual sites in cells was left open.

timeline.finding: ZNF143 is proposed as a chromatin-looping factor: integration of ENCODE ChIP-seq with interaction maps places it at loop anchors connecting promoters to distal elements, and binding-altering SNPs alter interactions. A 2021 study extends this to CTCF-bound promoter-enhancer loops in mouse hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, with CTCF and ZNF143 motifs often 37 bp apart in convergent orientation.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and ChIA-PET/HiChIP integration, knockdown and conditional knockout, allele-specific analysis
timeline.open: Neither study depleted ZNF143 acutely, so direct and indirect effects on loops could not be separated, and anchor occupancy rested on antibody ChIP.

timeline.finding: Reversal of the looping model. Two independent degron studies in mouse and human cells find that acute ZNF143/ZFP143 depletion changes no chromatin loops and that ZNF143 acts largely independently of CTCF; one shows that a widely used ZNF143 antibody cross-reacts with CTCF, which is how ZNF143 came to be placed at CTCF loop anchors. ZNF143 is instead an essential promoter-proximal regulator of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial and ribosomal genes, with a chromatin dwell time of over 20 minutes.
timeline.methods: Degron tagging, chromosome conformation capture, single-molecule imaging, re-analysis of antibody specificity in ChIP data
timeline.open: Acute depletion tests loop maintenance; a role in establishing loops at specific loci was not formally excluded.

timeline.finding: Rapid degradation places ZNF143's action at transcription initiation: it binds the promoters of nearly all genes it activates, and represses a subset by occluding initiation sites and promoter elements and by acting as a roadblock to early elongation.
timeline.methods: Degron depletion with nascent-transcription profiling and ChIP-seq

open: Whether the upstream ACTACAA box belongs to the ZNF143 site is doubtful: ZNF143's DNA-binding domain binds the canonical SBS1 and the ACTACA-extended SBS2 with the same affinity and cannot bind the THAP11 site alone, yet the ChIP-derived ZNF143 matrices in this family include ACTACAA, which may record THAP11 occupancy at the same promoters rather than ZNF143 contacts.

How ZNF143 and THAP11-HCFC1 share promoters in cells is unsettled: their DNA-binding domains occupy the composite SBS2 site mutually exclusively in vitro, while genome-wide ChIP places all three proteins at largely the same CpG-island promoters, which could mean alternating occupancy of one site or separate sites within one promoter.

Whether anything of the earlier looping phenotypes survives is open: the 2021 hematopoietic study used multi-day conditional deletion and reported loss of CTCF binding, which acute degron studies did not reproduce, and it has not been shown whether those effects were indirect consequences of transcriptional and mitochondrial failure.

What ZNF76 contributes is unresolved: it shares ZNF143's in vitro specificity and its peaks overlap ZNF143's, but since ZNF143 loss alone is lethal ZNF76 evidently does not substitute, and whether it has targets of its own is not established.

families.name: OVOL (OVO-like)
families.def: CCGTTA core. OVOL1, OVOL2, OVOL3.
families.short: OVOL1 and OVOL2 are C2H2 zinc-finger repressors, the mammalian counterparts of Drosophila OVO/shavenbaby, that bind a short AT-flanked core, CCGTTA (equivalently TAACGG on the other strand). They act mainly as repressors of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, holding epithelial cells in an epithelial state by shutting down ZEB1, ZEB2 and other EMT inducers, and OVOL1 additionally represses its own promoter and MYC. Mouse knockouts show defects in hair follicles, sperm, kidney, mammary ductal morphogenesis and epidermal progenitor arrest. In humans, a promoter point mutation that mis-expresses OVOL2 in corneal endothelium causes posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy type 1. OVOL1 and OVOL2 share one motif and cannot be separated from sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

The OVOL genes are the vertebrate orthologues of Drosophila ovo/shavenbaby (svb), a single locus whose
alternative transcripts supply two genetic functions: svb for the extracellular projections of epidermal
cells and ovo for female germ-cell survival [PMID:9808631,10637336]. Humans have OVOL1 (11q13) and OVOL2 (20p11). A third gene,
OVOL3, is annotated in some species but has no measured motif in these databases and is not represented
here. The proteins carry four C2H2 zinc fingers, of which only about three contribute to specificity [PMID:10637336],
and they bind DNA as monomers. OVOL1 and OVOL2 are epithelial: skin and hair follicle, kidney, mammary
and corneal epithelium, placenta, and germ cells. Both act predominantly as transcriptional repressors;
OVOL1 represses by competing with the activator MYB at overlapping sites and by recruiting histone
deacetylase activity [PMID:17311813], and OVOL2 exists in repressor and non-repressor isoforms whose balance sets its
output [PMID:24735879].

## The motif

The consensus is CCGTTA, usually written with AT-rich flanks, and it appears in these databases in both
orientations: ACCGTTAT (JASPAR OVOL1 and OVOL2) [PMID:28473536] and TAACGGT (HOCOMOCO OVOL2, and the atlas
representative). These are the same element read on opposite strands, so the apparent disagreement
between AT-rich and CG-containing renderings is only a strand convention. The information sits almost
entirely on the six-base core; the flanking A/T positions add affinity but little specificity, which is
why the shortest matrices here carry only about 6 bits.

The site was first defined by random-oligomer selection with the Drosophila OVO zinc-finger array, which
gave a statistically significant 9-bp consensus and showed that the recognition does not follow the usual
zinc-finger contact rules, consistent with the conclusion that some fingers in the array have degenerated
and no longer read bases [PMID:10637336]. Mouse Ovol1 binding sites in genomic DNA converge on the same CCGTTA core [PMID:16636146,17311813], and in OVO ChIP-seq from the Drosophila female germline the top peak motif, TAACGGTAAA, contains
the same core on the other strand, although the authors define the core more permissively as TAACNGT
[PMID:39291827]; the core is conserved from fly to mouse. The permissive hexamer CC/TGTTA is also reported, with high-affinity sites
favouring AT-rich flanks [PMID:17311813].

OVOL1 and OVOL2 are not distinguishable from sequence. Their matrices in all four databases converge
(family cohesion about 0.89, and the best cross-member similarities exceed 0.98), so a hit identifies the
family, not the member. One Vierstra archetype in this family, ACAGTTACA [PMID:32728250], is a variant with a different
third position and does not match the others closely; treat it as a separate, weakly supported model.

## Where it acts

OVOL sites are found in promoters and enhancers of epithelial-identity and EMT genes. Documented direct
targets include ZEB1 and other EMT inducers [PMID:24124593,24735879], MYC (repressed by OVOL1 in embryonic epidermal
progenitors) [PMID:16636146], the OVOL1 promoter itself [PMID:17311813], and in flies the ovarian tumor (otu) promoter, where OVO binds
unusually close to the transcription start site [PMID:11290304]. That proximity to start sites is a recurring feature:
OVO/OVOL sites cluster near TSSs rather than in distal enhancer deserts [PMID:39291827]. In epithelial cells the factors
sit inside a double-negative feedback loop with ZEB1/ZEB2 [PMID:24124593,24735879], so OVOL peaks tend to co-occur with ZEB and
SNAI motifs in the same regulatory regions, and with GRHL and KLF4 motifs that mark epithelial promoters.
The core is only 6 bp, so genomic occurrences are numerous in any sequence composition.

## Biology and disease

Mouse Ovol1 (movo1) knockouts are small, make aberrant hairs, show hypogenitalism with reduced fertility
and develop kidney abnormalities [PMID:9808631]; the epidermal phenotype traces to failure of embryonic epidermal
progenitors to arrest and to de-repression of MYC [PMID:16636146]. Ovol2 deletion blocks mammary ductal morphogenesis,
depletes stem and progenitor pools, and lets epithelial cells undergo EMT in vivo; conversely, forced
expression of the repressor isoform of OVOL2 reverts metastatic breast cancer cells toward an epithelial
state [PMID:24735879]. OVOL1 and OVOL2 can both induce mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition in human cancer cell lines [PMID:24124593].
In human disease, posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy type 1 is caused by point mutations in the
OVOL2 promoter (c.-307T>C and related variants) that switch the gene on ectopically in corneal
endothelium [PMID:26749309,28046031], and OVOL2 maintains the corneal epithelial program by suppressing EMT [PMID:27134177]. Reports in lung,
colorectal and breast cancer describe both tumour-suppressive and context-dependent pro-tumour effects,
and the literature here is not settled.

## Reading a hit

CCGTTA is six informative bases, so chance matches are frequent: expect many hits per megabase and treat
a single match as weak evidence. Sequence cannot distinguish OVOL1 from OVOL2, and in most epithelial
tissues both are expressed, so ChIP-seq in such a cell will not resolve them either. The evidence base
for this family is comparatively good: the HOCOMOCO OVOL1 and OVOL2 models carry in vitro support
(HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX) [PMID:28473536], so "this protein binds this sequence" is well established even though
"this sequence was bound by this protein here" is not. Be alert to the reverse-complement rendering
TAACGGT, which is the same site and is easy to mistake for an unrelated motif. A match in an
EMT-associated promoter alongside ZEB or SNAI sites is more interpretable than an isolated hit, but the
direction of effect still has to come from expression or perturbation data.
families.caveats: The informative core is only 6 bp (CCGTTA / TAACGG), so chance matches are abundant and one hit is weak evidence. OVOL1 and OVOL2 share a single motif - cohesion here is about 0.89 with cross-member similarities above 0.98 - so a match identifies the family, not the member, and ChIP in epithelium cannot separate them either because both are usually expressed. The two strand renderings (ACCGTTAT and TAACGGT) are the same element and are often mistaken for different motifs. Evidence quality is good: the OVOL1 and OVOL2 HOCOMOCO models include in vitro HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX support. The Vierstra ACAGTTACA archetype is a poorly matching variant and should be treated separately.

timeline.finding: A mouse ovo orthologue, movo1 (Ovol1), is cloned; knockout mice are small, make aberrant hairs, have reduced fertility and kidney abnormalities, paralleling the fly epidermal and germline functions.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; gene targeting in mouse
timeline.open: The sequence bound by the vertebrate protein was not known.

timeline.finding: Random-oligomer selection with the Drosophila OVO zinc-finger array gives a 9-bp consensus that matches sites in known target genes but breaks the usual zinc-finger contact rules; only three of the four fingers appear to contribute.
timeline.methods: In vitro random DNA oligomer selection

timeline.finding: OVO is shown to activate ovarian tumor (otu) through a site unusually close to the transcription start, establishing a direct target and a TSS-proximal mode of action.
timeline.methods: Loss- and gain-of-function and promoter-swap transgenes in Drosophila

timeline.finding: Mouse Ovol1 is shown to bind CCGTTA sites to repress c-myc and its own promoter; site selection with recombinant Ovol1 then gives an AT-flanked CYGTTA consensus, and repression combines competition with c-Myb and HDAC recruitment.
timeline.methods: Knockout epidermis analysis; EMSA; ChIP; CAST site selection; reporter assays

timeline.finding: Ovol2 is required for mammary ductal morphogenesis, where it directly represses EMT inducers; its repressor isoform can push metastatic breast cancer cells back to an epithelial state.
timeline.methods: Conditional knockout mice; target binding and expression analysis; forced-expression reprogramming

timeline.finding: Non-coding mutations in the OVOL2 proximal promoter are found to cause the corneal endothelial dystrophies CHED1 and PPCD1, increasing promoter activity in a tissue where OVOL2 is normally not detected.
timeline.methods: Linkage, targeted and whole-genome sequencing in large pedigrees; reporter assays
timeline.open: Which factor acts on the mutated promoter to switch OVOL2 on was not identified.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX with human OVOL1 and OVOL2 yield the ACCGTTA-type models now used in JASPAR and HOCOMOCO, confirming the core in vitro for both paralogues.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX; methylation-sensitive SELEX

timeline.finding: Genome-wide ChIP-seq of OVO in the Drosophila female germline finds binding concentrated near transcription start sites of essential maternal genes, with a TAACNGT motif that is degenerate at a position the vertebrate matrices fix.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq; RNA-seq with hypomorphic and rescue alleles; motif enrichment
timeline.open: Whether the degenerate position reflects a real difference between fly and vertebrate proteins or a ChIP-versus-SELEX difference is untested.

open: How strict the second base of the core is remains unsettled: human in vitro matrices give CCGTTA, mouse Ovol1 site selection allowed C or T there (CYGTTA), and Drosophila OVO ChIP-seq gave TAACNGT, which would also admit the CAGTTA variant seen in the Vierstra ACAGTTACA archetype that this atlas treats as a separate, weakly supported model.

Whether OVOL2 restrains or promotes carcinoma progression is not settled: it induces mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition and reduces metastatic potential in prostate and breast models, while reports in lung, colorectal and breast cancer also describe context-dependent pro-tumour effects.

How the OVOL2 promoter mutations in PPCD1 and CHED1 cause disease is not established: they raise promoter activity and are proposed to create cryptic regulatory sites that switch OVOL2 on ectopically in corneal endothelium, but the factor that binds them has not been identified.

families.name: USF
families.def: E-box with flanking preference GTCACGTGAC. USF1, USF2, USF3.
families.short: USF1 and USF2 are ubiquitously expressed bHLH-LZ proteins, first purified as the adenovirus major late transcription factor (MLTF), that bind DNA as homodimers and heterodimers. They read a canonical E-box core, but with a characteristic extended palindromic preference, GTCACGTGAC: the T and A flanks are what separate a USF site from a MYC-MAX site, which prefers C and G there. Because both proteins are constitutive, USF motifs turn up in a very large number of accessible promoters and CpG islands in every cell type, making USF one of the most frequently recovered motifs in promoter and footprint analyses. Human genetics links USF1 variants to familial combined hyperlipidemia.
families.long:
## The factors

USF1 and USF2 are ubiquitous basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) proteins of about 43 and 44 kDa, originally purified as the factor that stimulates transcription from the adenovirus major late promoter and therefore also called MLTF [PMID:4075392,3403559]. They bind DNA as homodimers [PMID:2249772] and as USF1-USF2 heterodimers; besides the bHLH-LZ they carry a USF-specific region (USR) immediately N-terminal to the basic domain that is required for activation but not for binding. A third gene, USF3 (KIAA2018), encodes a much larger protein with a divergent bHLH and no leucine zipper, and is not a simple USF1/USF2 paralogue. Both USF1 and USF2 are expressed in essentially all tissues, which is one reason USF sites appear in so many promoters. In mice, loss of either gene alone is tolerated and the two cross-regulate asymmetrically, with Usf2 loss reducing total USF DNA-binding activity more than Usf1 loss; combined loss was reported to be embryonic lethal [PMID:9520440]. The atlas assigns 8 motifs to this family (2 JASPAR, 3 HOCOMOCO, 2 CIS-BP, 1 Vierstra archetype) over the symbols USF1, USF2 and USF3, with high cohesion (0.94) and USF1.H14CORE.0.PSM.A as the representative.

## The motif

USF reads the canonical E-box CACGTG, but what defines the family in practice is the extended, strongly palindromic form GTCACGTGAC: a pyrimidine-purine flank on each side that USF prefers and that MYC-MAX does not [PMID:4075392,8052536]. The bHLH-LZ fold places one basic helix in each half of the major groove, where a conserved histidine, glutamate and arginine read the CAC triplet; the crystallographic analysis of the USF b/HLH/Z domain showed the same recognition geometry as Max, with the leucine zipper fixing dimer choice [PMID:8306960]. Because core contacts are shared across the bHLH-ZIP class, almost all of the discriminating information in a USF model sits in the two flanking positions, and in vitro base-preference measurements confirmed that USF and MYC family proteins differ mainly there rather than in the core [PMID:8052536]. Flanking preference of this kind is largely mediated by local DNA shape rather than by new base contacts [PMID:23562153]. Variants matter: the JASPAR USF1 model MA0093.4 is a CATGTG-type site (GTCATGTGAC), so USF tolerates the class-A-like half-site as well. The central CG of the core is a CpG, so occupancy can be modulated by DNA methylation; the HOCOMOCO USF1 and USF2 models carry both HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX support [PMID:37971293]. The HOCOMOCO USF3 model is an outlier: its consensus GgCCACGTGGg has MYC-like C/G flanks and its nearest neighbours across the four databases sit outside this family.

## Where it acts

USF1 and USF2 are promoter factors. They occupy tens of thousands of accessible, mostly promoter-proximal and CpG-island regions in essentially every cell type examined, which makes USF one of the most commonly recovered motifs in promoter analyses and in DNase footprint atlases. Because both proteins are constitutive, USF occupancy is not a cell-type marker; the dependence is on accessibility and on methylation state rather than on a tissue-restricted partner. USF sites are frequently found close to TATA-less initiators, in housekeeping and metabolic gene promoters, and in composite arrangements with other promoter-proximal factors. The Vierstra footprint archetype covering these motifs is labelled AC0066:USF/BHLHE:bHLH - that is, USF motifs cluster with BHLHE40/41 motifs and were not separable in the footprint data [PMID:32728250].

## Biology and disease

USF1/USF2 targets are enriched for lipid and glucose metabolism, stress response and cell-cycle genes, and the pair have been characterized as stress-responsive general regulators rather than as a developmental switch [PMID:16162174]. The clearest human genetic link is metabolic: variants in USF1 are associated with familial combined hyperlipidemia, one of the more common inherited dyslipidemias, in Finnish and subsequently other cohorts [PMID:14991056,15976322]. USF3 is a separate story; a germline compound heterozygous poly-glutamine deletion in USF3 has been reported in predisposition to heritable and sporadic epithelial thyroid carcinoma [PMID:28011713]. Because USF binding is methylation-sensitive, USF sites are also discussed in the context of promoter CpG island hypermethylation.

## Reading a hit

A GTCACGTGAC match is better evidence for USF than a bare CACGTG, but it is not proof. MITF, TFE3, TFEB and TFEC prefer exactly the same extended palindrome, and BHLHE41 and CLOCK-BMAL1 models look very similar; a strong T/A-flanked E-box narrows the candidate set to USF plus MITF/TFE plus BHLHE41 rather than to one factor. USF1 and USF2 are not distinguishable from each other by sequence at all, so a hit identifies USF, not a paralogue. Do not read the USF3 model as a USF site: it is MYC-flanked and clusters away from USF1/USF2. Given the number of genomic E-boxes, treat a single hit as a hypothesis.
families.caveats: The extended GTCACGTGAC form is shared with MITF, TFE3, TFEB, TFEC and BHLHE41, so it narrows a hit to a T/A-flanked E-box group, not to USF. USF1 and USF2 are indistinguishable by sequence. The Vierstra footprint archetype that carries these motifs is labelled USF/BHLHE, which is an explicit statement that USF and BHLHE40/41 motifs did not separate. The HOCOMOCO USF3 model has MYC-like CCACGTGG flanks and its nearest neighbours lie outside this family, so it should not be used as a USF site definition. USF occupancy is also methylation-sensitive because the core contains a CpG, so a sequence match says nothing about binding in a methylated promoter.

timeline.finding: USF is partially purified from HeLa nuclei as a factor that stimulates the adenovirus major late promoter and footprints the palindrome GGCCACGTGACC upstream of the TATA box.
timeline.methods: Reconstituted in vitro transcription, DNase I and MPE-Fe(II) footprinting
timeline.open: The protein's structure and its relationship to other factors were unknown.

timeline.finding: Purified 43- and 44-kDa USF forms bind the major late site with identical affinity, and binding is strongly influenced by neighbouring sequence.
timeline.methods: Protein purification, binding kinetics, in vitro transcription

timeline.finding: cDNA cloning places USF in the MYC-related bHLH-leucine-zipper group and shows that it binds DNA as a dimer.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, in vitro translation, deletion analysis, EMSA

timeline.finding: The USF bHLH co-crystal on CACGTG reproduces the MAX recognition geometry, and the zipper-containing domain forms a bivalent tetramer able to bind two sites.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, hydrodynamic measurements

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection defines the optimum USF site as RYCACGTGRY and shows that the base at ±4 discriminates among E-boxes: a T at -4 inhibits MYC binding but not USF or MAX.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection, oligonucleotide competition
timeline.open: Why a base outside the contacted core changes affinity.

timeline.finding: Usf1 and Usf2 knockout mice are viable with asymmetric cross-regulation of the remaining paralogue, while combined loss is embryonic lethal.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting

timeline.finding: Familial combined hyperlipidemia is linked and associated with USF1 in Finnish families, and the association is replicated in Mexican families in 2005.
timeline.methods: Linkage and family-based association, haplotype analysis
timeline.open: No causal variant or mechanism was identified.

timeline.finding: Flanking sequence beyond the E-box changes bHLH binding through DNA shape, offering a mechanism for flank preferences such as USF's.
timeline.methods: Genomic-context protein-binding microarrays, DNA shape analysis (yeast bHLH factors)
timeline.open: Shown for yeast Cbf1 and Tye7, not directly for USF.

open: Whether USF1 variants cause familial combined hyperlipidemia is not settled: linkage and association were found in Finnish and Mexican families, but no causal variant or mechanism has been established, and one of the associated Mexican SNPs lies in the neighbouring F11R gene, which could not be excluded.

Whether anything in the sequence separates USF sites from MiT/TFE and BHLHE41 sites is unresolved: all prefer GTCACGTGAC, and the Vierstra footprint archetype AC0066 does not split USF from BHLHE40/41.

The databases disagree about the USF1 half-site: the JASPAR USF1 model MA0093.4 reads GTCATGTGAC while the HOCOMOCO and CIS-BP USF1 models read GTCACGTG, and the models do not settle whether USF1 genuinely prefers the CATGTG form at some sites.

Whether USF3 belongs with USF1/USF2 as a DNA-binding factor is unclear: it lacks the leucine zipper, and its well-supported HOCOMOCO model reads a MYC-like GgCCACGTGGg whose nearest neighbours lie outside this family.

families.name: ARID / BRIGHT
families.def: AT-rich interaction domain; ARID3A/B, ARID5A/B.
families.short: ARID stands for AT-rich interaction domain, and this family is restricted to the four human ARID proteins that really do read AT-rich sequence: ARID3A (Bright), ARID3B, ARID5A and ARID5B. Eight motifs converge on a five to eight base-pair AT core - ATTAAT for ARID3B, ATTAAA for ARID3A, AATATT for ARID5A - so the whole family occupies one narrow, information-poor patch of sequence space and is very hard to separate from homeodomain TAAT sites or from AT-rich DNA generally. The many other ARID-domain proteins, including ARID1A and ARID1B in BAF and ARID2 in PBAF, bind DNA without sequence preference and are deliberately excluded from this family.
families.long:
## The factors

The domain was discovered twice in the same year. Bright, a B cell-specific trans-activator, was purified as the protein binding the matrix-associating regions flanking the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer and was recognized as defining a new DNA-binding protein family [PMID:8543152]; the Drosophila protein Dead ringer provided the first structure, and its DNA-binding module was named the AT-rich interaction domain [PMID:10545119]. Bright is now called ARID3A. The human genome encodes fifteen ARID-domain proteins in seven subfamilies [PMID:15640446], but only four are filed here: ARID3A and ARID3B, which together with ARID3C form a subfamily carrying an extended ARID plus a REKLES self-association domain, and ARID5A and ARID5B, the shortest members, which consist of little more than the domain itself.

The exclusion of the rest is deliberate and well founded. Systematic comparison of ARID-family proteins showed that sequence-specific AT-rich binding is a property of the ARID3 and ARID5 subfamilies, while the large ARID-containing subunits of chromatin remodellers - ARID1A and ARID1B in BAF, ARID2 in PBAF, and the yeast Swi1 equivalent - bind DNA with no detectable sequence specificity [PMID:15640446,14982958]. Those proteins are chromatin regulators that happen to contain a structurally similar domain; scanning a genome for a motif attributed to them is not meaningful, and where such a model exists in the atlas, as for ARID1A, it is filed in the CHROMATIN bucket instead. ARID4A/4B and the JARID/KDM5 demethylases are likewise absent.

## The motif

All eight models agree on the same thing and none of them says very much. ARID3B reads ATTAAT in CIS-BP and tATTAAT in JASPAR; ARID3A reads ATTAAA in JASPAR and the five-base AThAA in CIS-BP; ARID5A reads AATATTa and tAATATTg. Information content runs from 9.6 to 11.8 bits for the useful models, and the trimmed consensus is a five- to seven-base AT-only core. Structurally this is expected: the ARID fold contacts the major groove of AT-rich DNA through a helix-turn-helix-like core, with flanking regions contributing affinity [PMID:10545119,35119801], and recent work shows that ARID5A uses intrinsically disordered extensions on either side of the core domain for its DNA and RNA recognition rather than achieving specificity within the domain alone [PMID:38866324].

Two entries should be set aside. The Vierstra archetype AC0374 for ARID5B reads ttdGTATTGT, which is only 0.59 similar to anything else in the family. The CIS-BP model M01661 for ARID5B is the three-base ATa at 3.3 bits and carries no information at all. Four of the five CIS-BP models are transferred from other species - three from Mus musculus, one from Microcebus murinus - but all at 100 percent DNA-binding-domain identity, so the transfers are sound even if the models are short.

Family cohesion is 0.69, which looks respectable, but the discriminating number is the comparison between within-family and out-of-family nearest neighbours: bestOther values run from 0.74 to 0.84, meaning the closest matching model in some other family is nearly as similar as the closest match inside this one. The competitors are obvious - homeodomain families reading TAAT, the HMGA AT-hook models, and any AT-rich model at all.

## Where it acts

Bright/ARID3A was found at nuclear-matrix-attachment regions flanking the immunoglobulin heavy-chain intronic enhancer, and it acts there in a strongly context-dependent way, requiring the right surrounding sequence and partner proteins to activate [PMID:8543152]. ARID5B works at Sox9-regulated genes in chondrocytes, where it recruits the histone demethylase PHF2 [PMID:24276541], and more recently has been shown to coordinate HDAC-mediated repression [PMID:42328790], so both ARID5 proteins are best thought of as sequence-biased recruiters of chromatin enzymes rather than as classical activators. AT-rich cores of this length are extremely abundant, so in practice the location of a real ARID site is set by chromatin context and partner occupancy, not by the motif.

## Biology and disease

ARID5B is the medically prominent member: common germline variants at the ARID5B locus are among the strongest known inherited risk factors for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, identified by genome-wide association and repeatedly replicated [PMID:19684603]. Targeted deletion of the mouse orthologue, originally named Desrt, causes growth retardation and abnormal development of the reproductive organs [PMID:11483573], and Arid5b is required for normal chondrogenesis [PMID:24276541]. ARID5A is an immune regulator that stabilises IL-6 messenger RNA - a reminder that ARID-domain proteins can be RNA-binding as well as DNA-binding [PMID:38866324]. ARID3A/Bright has regulatory roles across human and mouse haematopoiesis, including B cell development and stem cell function [PMID:24678314].

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit in this family as evidence of AT-rich sequence and little more. A five- to seven-base AT core will occur on the order of a million times in the human genome, and it cannot be distinguished from a homeodomain TAAT site, an AT-hook target, or an AT-rich stretch of no consequence. Do not attempt to assign a hit to a particular paralogue: ARID3A, ARID3B and ARID5A models are mutually similar at 0.89 to 0.98. Require expression and, ideally, occupancy data before calling any ARID site, and be aware that an ARID motif call has no bearing on ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2 or the KDM5 proteins, whose ARID domains are not sequence-specific [PMID:15640446].
families.caveats: Every model in this family is a short AT-only core, so a match carries almost no information: expect on the order of a million genome-wide hits and no way to distinguish an ARID site from a homeodomain TAAT site, an AT-hook target or plain AT-rich DNA. Out-of-family nearest neighbours score 0.74 to 0.84, nearly as high as within-family ones. Individual paralogues cannot be separated. Two ARID5B entries are unusable: the CIS-BP model is three bases at 3.3 bits, and the Vierstra archetype disagrees with everything else. Four CIS-BP models are cross-species transfers, though all at 100 percent domain identity. Only ARID3 and ARID5 proteins belong here; other ARID-domain proteins bind DNA non-specifically.

timeline.finding: Bright, a B cell-specific activator of immunoglobulin heavy-chain transcription, was cloned as a protein that binds the minor groove of a restricted AT-rich sequence in matrix-associating regions flanking the heavy-chain enhancer, through a previously undescribed domain shared with SWI1; it activated only when its sites were in their natural context.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, DNA-binding assays, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether the new domain conferred sequence specificity in all the proteins that carry it.

timeline.finding: The NMR structure of the Dead ringer ARID showed a globular fold of eight helices and a short beta-sheet, with DNA studies indicating that a helix-turn-helix reads the major groove while a beta-hairpin and C-terminal helix contact adjacent minor grooves; sequence comparison divided ARIDs into three structural classes.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, sequence analysis

timeline.finding: The ARID-containing SWI/SNF subunits were compared directly: p270 (ARID1A) bound DNA without regard to sequence, excluding an intrinsic role for its ARID in recruiting the remodeller to specific promoter sequences.
timeline.methods: In vitro DNA-binding assays, substitution mutagenesis

timeline.finding: A survey across all fifteen human ARID proteins found that five of seven subfamilies bind DNA without obvious sequence preference, overturning the assumption that the domain is an AT-rich reader by definition; mutagenesis did not support single residues in loop 2 or helix 5 as the specificity determinants.
timeline.methods: In vitro DNA-binding survey, site-directed mutagenesis
timeline.open: What makes the ARID3 and ARID5 subfamilies sequence-specific when the others are not.

timeline.finding: A genome-wide association study found germline ARID5B variants associated with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (rs10821936, odds ratio 1.91), most strongly with the B-hyperdiploid subtype, and replicated the subtype association in an independent cohort.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide association with validation cohort
timeline.open: How noncoding risk variants alter ARID5B function.

timeline.finding: Arid5b was identified as a Sox9 co-regulator that physically associates with Sox9, recruits the H3K9 demethylase Phf2 to Sox9 target promoters and is needed for normal endochondral ossification, framing ARID5 proteins as recruiters of chromatin enzymes rather than classical activators.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, protein-interaction assays, ChIP, knockdown

timeline.finding: NMR-centered biochemistry defined an Arid5a DNA preference and showed that intrinsically disordered regions flanking the core ARID modulate DNA specificity and affinity and are needed for RNA binding; transcriptome-wide iCLIP2 found a weak preference for (A)U-rich pre-mRNA regions.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, high-throughput in vitro RNA binding, iCLIP2
timeline.open: Whether the flank-dependent DNA preference matches the core-only AATATT models in the databases.

timeline.finding: ARID5B was found to assemble a repressor complex with MIER1, C16ORF87, HDAC1 and HDAC2, and CUT&RUN placed it at active promoters and distal regulatory elements, where it represses B-cell proliferation and signalling genes.
timeline.methods: Proteomics, CUT&RUN, transcriptomics
timeline.open: Whether ARID5B occupancy is set by its own AT-rich site or by its complex partners.

open: Whether the core-only models capture ARID5A's DNA preference is untested: the PBM-derived AATATT models treat it as an AT-core reader, whereas the 2024 NMR-based study found that disordered regions flanking the domain modulate specificity and affinity, information that a five- to seven-base model cannot carry.

It is open whether ARID5B occupancy reflects its own AT-rich site or recruitment by its HDAC-containing repressor complex: CUT&RUN places it at active promoters and distal elements, and neither ARID5B model in the atlas is usable to test the question (one is three bases, the other disagrees with the rest of the family).

What determines sequence specificity within the ARID fold is unresolved: mutagenesis did not identify single specificity residues, and so few ARID-DNA complex structures exist that it is not known why the ARID3 and ARID5 subfamilies read AT-rich sequence while five other subfamilies do not.

families.name: DUX / DUXA
families.def: Double homeodomain TAATCTAATCA. DUX4, DUXA, DUXB.
families.short: DUX4 and its relatives DUXA and DUXB carry two homeodomains in tandem within a single polypeptide, an architecture found only in placental mammals and derived from a retrotransposed copy of an ancestral homeobox gene. The two domains bind side by side, head to head, and together read an eleven-base site, TAATCTAATCA, that is far longer and more specific than a single homeodomain site. These genes are normally expressed only for a few cell divisions after fertilisation, where they help switch on the embryonic genome and a set of endogenous retroviral promoters. Misexpression of DUX4 in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, and DUX4 rearrangements define a subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, so this motif marks one of the better understood pathogenic regulatory programs.
families.long:
## The factors

DUX genes exist only in eutherian mammals [PMID:21110847]. Each encodes two complete homeodomains in tandem, joined by a
short linker, in a protein of a few hundred residues. Human DUX4 is encoded inside the D4Z4 macrosatellite
repeat at 4q35, with a nearly identical array at 10q26 and many DUX4L pseudogenes elsewhere [PMID:40855454]; DUXA and DUXB
are single-copy genes. The mouse counterpart is *Dux*. DUX4 has a C-terminal transactivation domain that
binds p300/CBP, so it is a strong activator [PMID:26951377]; DUXA is transcriptionally inert but binds an overlapping set
of sequences and competes with DUX4, and because DUXA is itself a DUX4 target this constitutes a negative
feedback loop that limits the window of DUX4 activity [PMID:37744032]. The ancestral state is a single homeodomain: the
platypus sDUX protein has one, binds DNA as a homodimer, and is already able to activate
zygotic-genome-activation genes and long terminal repeats [PMID:37744032]. Expression of the human genes is confined to
the cleavage-stage embryo, testis and thymus.

## The motif

The site is TAATCTAATCA, about 11 informative positions. The crystal structure of the DUX4 tandem
homeodomains bound to DNA explained its shape. The two domains bind head to head, and the linker between
them makes anchoring minor-groove contacts plus protein-protein contacts that fix their relative
positions, so the spacing between the two half sites is not variable the way it is for two independent
homeodomain monomers. The surprise from that structure is that the two homeodomains, although tandem
duplicates of each other, do not read the same core sequence: an arginine-to-glutamate substitution unique
to primates repositions a key arginine side chain in one recognition helix [PMID:30540931]. That is why the consensus is
not a clean palindrome but an asymmetric TAATC-TAATCA. The same divergence explains why mouse DUX and
human DUX4 have different motifs, and the difference tracks with which retrotransposon promoters each one
can activate [PMID:28459454]. In the assembled data, DUX4 and DUXA models are similar but not identical: DUX4 models read
TAATTTAATCA or TGATTAGGTTA, DUXA models TGATTAAATTA or TGATTTAATCA, with within-family similarities from
0.84 to 1.0 and overall cohesion of 0.89. One low-information entry, a 5.8-bit CIS-BP DUXA model reading
only TGATTG, is flagged in the data as belonging with Q50 homeodomains instead: a six-base TGATTA fragment
is simply a generic paired-like homeodomain half site and carries no double-homeodomain information.

## Where it acts

DUX4 sites are overwhelmingly repeat-resident. DUX4 occupies MERVL/HERVL long terminal repeats,
ERVL-MaLR elements and other retrotransposon promoters, along with conventional promoters of
cleavage-stage genes including ZSCAN4, TRIM43, MBD3L family members, PRAMEF family members, KHDC1L and
LEUTX [PMID:22209328,28459457]. Because the motif sits inside repeat families, the number of genomic matches is large, in the tens
of thousands, and DUX4 ChIP-seq peaks are heavily biased toward repeats [PMID:22209328,26951377]. Where DUX4 binds it recruits
p300/CBP and deposits H3K27 acetylation, so the sites behave as bona fide enhancers and promoters rather
than as passive footprints [PMID:26951377]. In adult somatic tissue these sequences are silent and the motif is not
occupied, because the factors are not expressed.

## Biology and disease

Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is the clearest example of a disease caused by a single
transcription factor being switched on in the wrong tissue. In FSHD1, contraction of the D4Z4 array to
between one and ten units on a permissive 4qA haplotype, which supplies a polyadenylation signal
downstream of the last repeat, allows a stable DUX4 transcript to accumulate in muscle [PMID:20724583]. In FSHD2 the same
end is reached through mutations in chromatin repressors such as SMCHD1 [PMID:23143600]. DUX4 expressed in myoblasts
activates germline and cleavage-stage genes, retroelements and immune mediators, and is cytotoxic [PMID:22209328,37744032].
In normal development, mouse Dux and human DUX4 activate cleavage-stage genes and MERVL/HERVL elements at
zygotic genome activation [PMID:28459457,28459456], and DUX4 also has roles in priming the human embryonic genome beyond
transcriptional activation [PMID:35402882]. Rearrangements that place DUX4 under the IGH enhancer, and related DUX4
fusions, define a distinct subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in adolescents and young
adults; the retained portion is the double homeodomain [PMID:27019113].

## Reading a hit

An 11-base double-homeodomain match is a distinctive shape, but three cautions apply. First, it does not
tell you which DUX protein. DUX4 and DUXA have overlapping specificity and opposite activity, so the same
site can be an activated enhancer or a competitively blocked one. Second, half-site-only matches, TAATCA
or TGATTA, fall straight back into the large generic paired-like homeodomain pool and are not DUX
evidence. Third, one JASPAR entry in this family is the mouse Dux motif, which is genuinely different from
the human one, and the JASPAR DUX4 model and one HOCOMOCO DUX4 model are ChIP-derived from overexpression
systems rather than from in vitro selection on the purified protein [PMID:22209328]. Finally, a match in an ERVL or MaLR
repeat is expected by composition and says little on its own.
families.caveats: The motif shape is good but the label is not resolvable: DUX4, DUXA and DUXB bind overlapping sequences, and DUXA represses what DUX4 activates, so a hit does not predict direction of effect. One JASPAR entry here is mouse Dux, whose motif differs from human DUX4 because of a primate-specific change in one recognition helix; do not transfer it to human sequence. The best DUX4 models are ChIP-derived from forced expression, not from in vitro selection. Because the site lives inside MERVL/HERVL and MaLR repeats, matches are numerous and largely explained by repeat content; outside the cleavage-stage embryo, testis, thymus, FSHD muscle or DUX4-rearranged leukaemia, no DUX protein is present to occupy them.

timeline.finding: Sequencing the partially deleted D4Z4 locus of an FSHD patient identifies an open reading frame with two homeoboxes inside each 3.3-kb repeat unit, the gene later named DUX4.
timeline.methods: cloning and nucleotide sequencing of the contracted repeat array
timeline.open: The repeat was widely regarded as non-coding, and there was no evidence that the predicted gene was transcribed or that its product bound DNA.

timeline.finding: A unifying genetic model shows that repeat contraction causes disease only on a 4qA haplotype carrying a polymorphism that creates a polyadenylation signal distal to the last repeat, stabilizing the DUX4 transcript, which explains why contraction alone is not sufficient.
timeline.methods: haplotype and SNP analysis of patient chromosomes plus transfection assays of transcript stability
timeline.open: It remained unclear what DUX4 does to muscle once the transcript is stabilized.

timeline.finding: DUX4 is shown to activate germline and early stem-cell genes, MaLR retrotransposon long terminal repeats and innate-immune mediators, and these targets are detectable in FSHD muscle but not controls, giving direct support for the misexpression model.
timeline.methods: inducible expression in myoblasts with ChIP-seq and expression profiling of patient muscle
timeline.open: Which of these induced programs is responsible for muscle damage was not resolved.

timeline.finding: FSHD2, which occurs without repeat contraction, is shown to arise from mutations in the chromatin repressor SMCHD1 inherited together with a permissive D4Z4 allele, bringing both forms of the disease under a single mechanism of DUX4 derepression.
timeline.methods: exome sequencing, linkage and D4Z4 methylation analysis in families

timeline.finding: Insertion of D4Z4 repeats containing DUX4 into the IGH locus is found recurrently in Philadelphia-negative B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia of adolescents and young adults, and DUX4-IGH expression in pro-B cells generates leukemia in mice.
timeline.methods: RNA-seq of 73 patient specimens and a mouse transplantation assay

timeline.finding: Three studies establish mouse Dux and human DUX4 as activators of the cleavage-stage program and of MERVL/HERVL elements at zygotic genome activation, and show that the two orthologs have diverged in sequence preference, with motif divergence tracking which retrotransposon promoters each can activate.
timeline.methods: expression profiling, ChIP-seq and knockout or knockdown in embryonic stem cells and embryos
timeline.open: Whether human DUX4 is required for zygotic genome activation in human embryos, rather than merely sufficient in cultured cells, was untested.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the DUX4 tandem homeodomains on DNA shows head-to-head binding with the linker making minor-groove and protein-protein contacts, and reveals that the two duplicated homeodomains read different core sequences because of a primate-specific arginine-to-glutamate change that repositions an arginine in one recognition helix.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography with mutational binding assays
timeline.open: Explains the asymmetric site but not how DUX4 and DUXA, which bind overlapping sequences, are partitioned in cells.

timeline.finding: Comparison of the three human DUX proteins with the single-homeodomain platypus sDUX shows that cytotoxicity is a property of DUX4 and of ancestral sDUX but not of DUXA or DUXB, and that DUXA, itself a DUX4 target, competes for DUX4 sites and antagonizes DUX4 in FSHD patient cells.
timeline.methods: comparative expression, DNA-binding and cytotoxicity assays in human cells
timeline.open: The relative occupancy of DUX4 and DUXA at shared sites in intact tissue has not been measured.

open: What makes DUX4 cytotoxic is unsettled: in human myoblasts the C-terminal p300/CBP-binding region is required for both target activation and cell death, yet the ancestral single-homeodomain platypus sDUX protein is also cytotoxic, so toxicity may not depend on the double-homeodomain architecture or on the primate C-terminus.

Whether human DUX4 is required for embryonic genome activation or only contributes to it is disputed: mouse Dux depletion impairs zygotic genome activation and the 2-cell-like state, whereas DUX4 knockdown in human zygotes altered the activation transcriptome without terminating the embryos, which fits a priming role rather than a switch.

Nothing in the sequence distinguishes a DUX4-occupied site from a DUXA-occupied one, and because the two proteins have opposite transcriptional output, how occupancy is partitioned between them in cells that express both is unknown.

The usability of the mouse Dux motif for human sequence is contested: motif collections list it alongside human DUX4 models, while the comparative work shows that the primate-specific change in one recognition helix gives the two orthologs genuinely different preferences and different retrotransposon targets.

families.name: MAZ / PATZ1
families.def: GGGAGGG G-rich sites. MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF278-like.
aka: TFClass: more than 3 adjacent zinc finger factors
families.short: MAZ, the Myc-associated zinc finger protein, and PATZ1 are broadly expressed C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind short G-rich runs, written GGGAGGG or GGGGAGGGG and read as CCCTCCCC on the opposite strand. MAZ was cloned as the protein binding ME1a1, an element between the c-MYC P1 and P2 promoters. Interest in the motif increased when MAZ turned out to be a second insulator-type element: it colocalizes with CTCF at chromatin boundaries, contacts the cohesin subunit RAD21, and deleting MAZ motifs at the Hox clusters disrupts boundaries much as deleting CTCF motifs does. The single-base difference from the SP1 GC-box, an A where the GC-box has a C, is the only sequence discriminator, and it is thin.
families.long:
## The factors

MAZ is a 477-residue protein with six Cys2-His2 zinc fingers, an N-terminal proline-rich region and several polyalanine tracts. It was cloned by screening with a concatemerized copy of ME1a1, a 16-bp element lying between the c-MYC P1 and P2 transcription start sites that is required for P2 activity, and was implicated in both transcriptional initiation and termination at c-MYC (Bossone et al. 1992) [PMID:1502157]. Older aliases include Pur-1 and ZF87. PATZ1 is grouped here because its motif is not separable from MAZ's. PATZ1 (also MAZR, ZNF278, ZSG) is a POK-family protein: a BTB/POZ domain, an AT-hook and a C-terminal zinc-finger array. The BTB domain forms a homodimer whose crystal structure has been determined, and PATZ1 is ubiquitously expressed with a documented role in T-lymphocyte development, where it targets the CD8 gene, and in interactions with p53 (Piepoli et al. 2020) [PMID:32496219]. Both proteins are broadly expressed, unlike most of the restricted factors elsewhere in this atlas.

## The motif

The site is short: GGGAGGG, often extended to GGGGAGGGG, and CCCTCCCC on the complementary strand [PMID:1502157,11395515]. The data here agree - the medoid (CIS-BP M08290_2.00) is CCCCTCCCC and JASPAR MAZ (MA1522.2) is CCCCTCCC. Why so short for a six-finger protein? Mutational analysis showed that only two consecutive zinc fingers are essential for MAZ to engage its element, just as only two of Sp1's three are essential for the GC-box (Song et al. 2001) [PMID:11395515]; the additional fingers are not all contributing base contacts, so the footprint is 7-9 bp rather than 18. The same study states the two respective sites explicitly: GGGCGG for Sp1, GGGAGGG for MAZ [PMID:11395515]. That single-base difference - A where the GC-box has C - is the practical discriminator between this family and KLF/SP, and it is a thin one. Against the other G-rich families it is thinner still. The HOCOMOCO VEZF1 model VEZF1.H14CORE.0.P.C (GGGGGAGGGGG) has its nearest neighbor across all four databases inside this family, so VEZF1's motif is effectively MAZ's. ZNF281 and ZNF148 models (GGGGGAGGGG) differ only by context, and the ChIP-derived WT1 models fall in the same cluster. Within the family, the labels are not clean either: JASPAR's PATZ1 profile (MA1961.2) is GGGGGCGGGGG, which is a GC-box and will behave like an SP1 matrix, not like a MAZ matrix [PMID:37962376]. None of the four HOCOMOCO models for MAZ or PATZ1 carries in vitro evidence; all are ChIP-only at grade B or C [PMID:37971293], and for two of them the best-matching matrix elsewhere in the databases scores higher than the best match inside the family.

## Where it acts

MAZ and PATZ1 sites are promoter-proximal and concentrated in GC-rich, CpG-island promoters, starting with c-MYC itself. The more interesting location is chromatin boundaries. A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen for genes required for CTCF boundary activity at the HoxA cluster identified MAZ; MAZ colocalizes with CTCF at chromatin borders, interacts with the cohesin subunit RAD21, and deletion of MAZ motifs disrupts gene expression and intra-domain contacts in a way that resembles deletion of CTCF motifs (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2022) [PMID:35145304]. A follow-up study extended this to a small array of zinc-finger proteins that specify distinct Hox boundaries: PATZ1 was required for the thoracolumbar boundary in differentiating motor neurons and in the mouse skeleton, and ZNF263 for cervicothoracic boundaries, each acting with cohesin, with or without CTCF (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2024) [PMID:39173638]. So a G-rich site next to a CTCF site is not necessarily noise [PMID:33558242,35145304].

## Biology and disease

MAZ's documented functions center on c-MYC promoter regulation and on insulation: MAZ knockout disrupts local contacts within topologically associating domains and the expression of genes inside them (Ortabozkoyun et al. 2022) [PMID:35145304]. PATZ1 has a wider documented range, reviewed for its physiological functions and disease involvement (Fedele et al. 2017) [PMID:29186807]: repression of CD8 in lymphocyte development, interaction with p53, and suppression of differentiation with effects on metabolism in human embryonic stem cells (Huang et al. 2024) [PMID:38385086]. The clearest disease link in the family is through PATZ1 gene fusions. EWSR1::PATZ1 defines a rare round-cell sarcoma that was newly categorized in the 2020 World Health Organization classification of soft tissue and bone tumors (Yagi et al. 2024) [PMID:38645952], and MN1::PATZ1 fusions occur in a rare class of CNS neuroepithelial tumors [PMID:34417833]. Note that in a fusion the PATZ1 contribution is usually the zinc-finger array, so the motif is still relevant even when the protein is chimeric.

## Reading a hit

Three cautions. First, the site is short and G-rich, so GGGAGGG occurs constantly by chance, and especially inside CpG islands and G-rich repeats; an isolated match is weak evidence of anything. Second, the family cannot be separated from its neighbors by sequence. A hit here is also a plausible ZNF281, ZNF148, VEZF1 or ChIP-derived WT1 site, and is one base away from an SP1/KLF GC-box. If the question is which protein binds, sequence will not answer it. Third, check which matrix matched: all HOCOMOCO models in this family rest on ChIP-seq alone, and the JASPAR PATZ1 matrix is a GC-box that will pull in SP-family sites. What does make a hit worth following up is context. A G-rich motif immediately adjacent to a CTCF site at a developmental cluster is the configuration in which MAZ and PATZ1 have demonstrable boundary function, and there the motif deletion experiments give the label real support.
families.caveats: A seven-base G-rich site carries little information and occurs frequently by chance, so treat an isolated hit as weak. The family is also not separable from ZNF281/ZNF148, VEZF1 or the ChIP-derived WT1 models - the HOCOMOCO VEZF1 matrix's nearest neighbor across all four databases lies inside this family - and it differs from the SP1 GC-box by a single base. All four HOCOMOCO models here are ChIP-only at grade B or C, and JASPAR's PATZ1 profile is in fact a GC-box. Context helps more than score: a G-rich motif beside a CTCF site at a Hox-type boundary is where MAZ and PATZ1 have demonstrated function.
