timeline.finding: MAZ is cloned as a six-finger protein binding ME1a1 between the c-MYC P1 and P2 start sites; the recombinant protein binds a GA box, GGGAGGG, in the P2 promoter, in the P2 attenuator and at a C2 termination element, defining the motif.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning with a concatemerized site, binding of recombinant fusion protein
timeline.open: Which of the six fingers read the site, and how MAZ sites differ from Sp1 GC-boxes, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Sp1 and MAZ are shown to bind the same GC-rich sites, and DNA binding by each depends mainly on two consecutive fingers (fingers 2-3 of Sp1, fingers 3-4 of MAZ), explaining why a six-finger protein has a 7-9-bp motif; the sites are given as GGGCGG for Sp1 and GGGAGGG for MAZ.
timeline.methods: Finger deletion and mutation, gel shift, reporter assays
timeline.open: What the other four MAZ fingers contribute was not resolved.

timeline.finding: MAZ is found at sites adjacent to CTCF, binds a cohesin subunit, arrests cohesin sliding independently of CTCF and acts as an insulator in reporter assays; CTCF/MAZ double sites retain cohesin better than CTCF-only sites, and MAZ depletion disrupts TAD-internal and boundary contacts.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, protein interaction, enhancer-blocking reporter, Hi-C after depletion
timeline.open: Whether MAZ is needed for any specific developmental boundary in vivo was not tested.

timeline.finding: DNA methylation profiling of 60 mostly pediatric CNS tumors with MN1::PATZ1 or EWSR1::PATZ1 fusions defines a molecularly distinct neuroepithelial tumor class spanning many histological diagnoses.
timeline.methods: DNA methylation profiling, RNA sequencing

timeline.finding: An independent genome-wide CRISPR screen for CTCF boundary function at HoxA identifies MAZ; MAZ motif deletions derepress posterior Hox genes beyond CTCF boundaries and cause homeotic transformations in mice, so the G-rich motif next to a CTCF site has a measurable function.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen, biochemical interaction, motif deletion in ES cells and mice

timeline.finding: Cohesin-bound sites lacking CTCF and MAZ reveal further zinc-finger insulators: PATZ1 is required for the thoracolumbar Hox boundary in motor neurons and mouse skeleton, and ZNF263 for cervicothoracic boundaries, acting with cohesin with or without CTCF.
timeline.methods: Cohesin ChIP-seq, knockout in differentiating motor neurons and mice

timeline.finding: In HOCOMOCO v14 all four MAZ and PATZ1 models are ChIP-only (grade B or C), and the JASPAR 2024 PATZ1 profile is a GC-box rather than a GA box, so the databases do not give an in vitro-supported motif for either protein.
timeline.methods: Database curation of ChIP-seq-derived models

open: How MAZ contributes to CTCF boundaries is not settled: it can stall cohesin on its own, but CTCF is also preferentially retained at sites MAZ occupies, and whether MAZ acts as an oriented barrier like CTCF or mainly stabilizes CTCF binding has not been resolved.

Whether PATZ1 prefers a GA box or a GC-box is unclear: the JASPAR PATZ1 profile is a GC-box (GGGGGCGGGGG), the HOCOMOCO PATZ1 models are GGGAGGG-type, and none of the HOCOMOCO models for either PATZ1 or MAZ has in vitro support that could decide between them.

PATZ1's role in cancer is contested: it has been described both as a tumor suppressor and as an oncogene depending on tumor type, and in the fusion tumors it is not established whether the PATZ1 fingers bind their normal targets.

families.name: HIC1 / HIC2
families.def: TGCC(A/G) HiRE sites. HIC1, HIC2.
families.short: HIC1 (hypermethylated in cancer 1) and HIC2 are BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressors with five Kruppel-like C2H2 fingers. Their optimal site, defined by site selection, is (C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC, with a GGCA core read by fingers 3 and 4; databases usually render the same element on the opposite strand as TGCC(A/G), which is why the family is often listed with a short TGCC consensus. The BTB domain blocks binding to a single site but supports cooperative binding to several, so genuine targets carry multiple sites. HIC1 sits at 17p13.3, is induced by p53, is frequently silenced by promoter hypermethylation in tumors, and represses SIRT1; heterozygous mouse mutants develop tumors.
families.long:
## The factors

Two paralogues: HIC1 and HIC2 (also HRG22). Each has an N-terminal BTB/POZ domain, a central region containing a conserved GLDLSKK motif that binds CtBP, and five Kruppel-like C2H2 zinc fingers at the C terminus [PMID:15231840,23566242]. HIC1 was cloned from 17p13.3, a region frequently deleted or hypermethylated in human tumors and deleted in Miller-Dieker syndrome, and was identified as a p53-inducible gene [PMID:7585125]. The BTB domain has an unusual and important effect on DNA binding: it inhibits binding of the full-length protein to an isolated site while mediating cooperative binding to probes carrying several concatemerized sites, a property shared with other BTB/POZ proteins [PMID:15231840]. Repression works through CtBP and through recruitment of HDAC-containing complexes, and HIC1 also localizes to distinct nuclear bodies, into which it can sequester other proteins [PMID:16724116]. HIC1 is widely expressed in adult tissues and silenced epigenetically in tumors; HIC2 is expressed in the developing cardiovascular system and is much less studied. There is no evidence that the two heterodimerize preferentially over homodimerizing.

## The motif

Selection and amplification of binding sites with recombinant HIC1 gave the optimal sequence 5'-(C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC-3' [PMID:15231840]. In silico and functional follow-up narrowed the essential element to a GGCA core contacted by zinc fingers 3 and 4 [PMID:15231840], so of the five fingers only two carry most of the base-specific contacts - which explains why the informative region is short even though the domain could cover more sequence. The database matrices all describe this same element on the complementary strand, which is why they look different at first glance: JASPAR Hic1 (MA0739.2) reads ATGCCAAC, JASPAR HIC2 (MA0738.2) and CIS-BP M02902 read ATGCCC, the HOCOMOCO HIC1 grade-A model reads ATGCCA, and the Vierstra archetype AC0477:HIC reads ATGCCCAC [PMID:23332764,32728250,37971293]. Reverse-complementing ATGCCCAC gives GTGGGCAT, which contains the GGGCA of the selected consensus. This is a strand convention, not a conflict, but it does mean the widely quoted "TGCC(A/G)" form of the consensus is a four- or five-base fragment of a longer selected site and is far too short to scan with. Information content of the database models is low, 7-11 bits. HIC1 and HIC2 models are 0.98 similar and cannot be separated by sequence. One archetype in the family, AC0435:HIC reading GGCAACC, matches the main HIC cluster poorly (0.74) [PMID:32728250] and should be treated as a divergent model rather than an independent confirmation.

## Where it acts

HIC1 sites occur in promoters of genes it represses, and because the full-length protein needs cooperativity, functional HIC1 elements usually come in clusters [PMID:15231840] - a single TGCC match in a promoter is not a HIC1 element in any meaningful sense. Validated targets include SIRT1, ATOH1, EPHA2 and Wnt-responsive genes [PMID:16269335,23566242]; HIC1 also attenuates Wnt signaling by a non-DNA route, recruiting TCF4 and beta-catenin into nuclear bodies away from their target promoters [PMID:16724116]. The element is GC-rich and CpG-containing, so matches concentrate in CpG-island promoters, the same territory as SP/KLF and other GC-box readers. HIC2 sites, where studied, are in cardiovascular differentiation genes [PMID:29061339].

## Biology and disease

Hic1-null mice die perinatally with developmental defects - acrania, exencephaly and limb abnormalities - that overlap the structures affected in Miller-Dieker syndrome [PMID:10655551], consistent with HIC1 contributing to that contiguous gene deletion phenotype. Heterozygous Hic1 mice are viable but develop a sex-dependent spectrum of malignant tumors, with age-dependent hypermethylation and silencing of the remaining wild-type allele [PMID:12539045], which is a textbook demonstration of an epigenetically inactivated tumor suppressor. Mechanistically, HIC1 binds and represses the SIRT1 promoter; because SIRT1 deacetylates p53, loss of HIC1 raises SIRT1 and blunts p53-dependent responses to DNA damage, forming a regulatory circuit with p53 that also explains why HIC1 is p53-inducible [PMID:7585125,16269335]. HIC1 promoter hypermethylation is among the more common epigenetic lesions across human carcinomas, medulloblastoma and leukemia [PMID:23566242]. HIC2 has been shown to control isoform switching during cardiovascular maturation [PMID:29061339] and lies in the distal 22q11 region, but its human disease role is not established.

## Reading a hit

The honest summary is that a short TGCC-type match is close to worthless on its own. The informative element is longer, the database matrices capture only 7-11 bits of it, and the sequence is GC-rich and CpG-island-associated, so it overlaps the recognition space of SP1-SP4, the KLFs and other C2H2 GC-box factors. Two things make a HIC call more credible: multiple sites in the same promoter, which is what the BTB-dependent cooperativity requires, and a target gene or cell context in which HIC1 is expressed rather than methylated. Within the family, HIC1 and HIC2 are indistinguishable at 0.98 similarity, and the Vierstra archetypes are named AC0435:HIC and AC0477:HIC without a paralogue assignment, so a hit identifies the pair. On provenance, the better entries are in vitro: JASPAR MA0739.2 and MA0738.2 are HT-SELEX matrices [PMID:23332764] and the HOCOMOCO HIC1 model is grade A with PSM evidence [PMID:37971293]. Two weaker entries deserve flags - JASPAR MA0739.2 is derived from mouse Hic1 rather than the human protein, a cross-species transfer that is unproblematic here given how conserved the fingers are but should be recorded; and the HOCOMOCO HIC2 model carries ChIP-only evidence (code P, grade B) and matches the rest of the family poorly (0.75), so it is the entry most likely to reflect indirect binding.
families.caveats: The short TGCC(A/G) form quoted for this family is a fragment of a longer selected consensus, (C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC, rendered on the other strand; the database matrices hold only 7-11 bits, are GC-rich and CpG-island-associated, and therefore overlap SP/KLF and other GC-box motifs. Single matches are not interpretable: the BTB domain blocks binding to isolated sites and supports cooperative binding to clustered ones, so look for several sites in one promoter. HIC1 and HIC2 are indistinguishable (0.98 similarity) and the Vierstra archetypes do not assign a paralogue. Note JASPAR MA0739.2 is a mouse Hic1 matrix, and the HOCOMOCO HIC2 model is ChIP-only and a poor fit to the rest of the family.

timeline.finding: HIC-1 was identified at 17p13.3 through a site hypermethylated in tumor DNA, shown to be expressed in normal tissue, underexpressed and hypermethylated in tumor cells, and inducible by wild-type p53 - a tumor suppressor candidate defined epigenetically rather than by mutation.
timeline.methods: methylation-directed cloning, expression analysis, p53 induction and colony suppression assays
timeline.open: What sequence the zinc fingers recognize and which genes they control.

timeline.finding: Hic1-null mice were shown to die perinatally with acrania, exencephaly, cleft palate and limb defects that match structures affected in Miller-Dieker syndrome, supporting a contribution of HIC1 loss to that 17p13.3 deletion phenotype.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, developmental phenotyping

timeline.finding: Mice heterozygous for Hic1 developed a sex-dependent spectrum of spontaneous tumors in which the remaining wild-type allele was densely methylated rather than mutated, making HIC1 a worked example of a tumor suppressor inactivated by methylation in both alleles' turn.
timeline.methods: heterozygous mouse cohorts, tumor histology, promoter methylation analysis

timeline.finding: Site selection with recombinant HIC1 gave the optimal sequence (C/G)NG(C/G)GGGCA(C/A)CC with a GGCA core read by fingers 3 and 4, and showed that the BTB domain blocks binding to a single site while supporting cooperative binding to concatemerized sites - so the functional unit is a cluster, not one match.
timeline.methods: selection and amplification of binding sites, EMSA with single and multimerized probes, chromatin immunoprecipitation, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether endogenous target promoters carry the multiple sites the full-length protein needs.

timeline.finding: SIRT1 was identified as a direct HIC1 target: HIC1 and SIRT1 form a repression complex on the SIRT1 promoter, and loss of HIC1 raises SIRT1, which deacetylates p53 and blunts DNA-damage responses, closing a circuit with the p53 that induces HIC1.
timeline.methods: chromatin immunoprecipitation, promoter reporters, apoptosis assays in HIC1-deficient cells

timeline.finding: HIC1 was shown to antagonize Wnt signaling without binding target promoters, by associating with TCF-4 and recruiting it and beta-catenin into HIC1 nuclear bodies - a mechanism that detaches part of this factor's output from its motif.
timeline.methods: co-immunoprecipitation, imaging of nuclear bodies, TCF reporter assays

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX measured both paralogues directly and returned short ATGCC-type models of 8 to 11 bits, much shorter than the 12-base consensus from site selection; these compact models are what the collections now carry, and the discrepancy with the longer in vitro consensus was never resolved.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX across human transcription factors
timeline.open: Whether the short model is the real preference or an artifact of using isolated DNA-binding domains that bypass BTB-dependent cooperativity.

timeline.finding: Hic2 was given its own phenotype - control of haemoglobin and sarcomeric isoform switching during cardiovascular maturation in mouse embryos - showing that the two paralogues, which are indistinguishable by motif, are not interchangeable in vivo.
timeline.methods: mouse mutants, expression profiling of embryonic heart and blood

open: The length of this family's site is unsettled: site selection with the full-length protein returned a 12-base GC-rich consensus, while HT-SELEX returned 6 to 8 informative bases, and no experiment has tested whether the difference comes from using isolated zinc-finger domains, which bypass the BTB-dependent cooperativity, or from the longer consensus overstating flanking preference.

Whether functional HIC1 elements must occur in clusters in the genome is unknown: cooperativity across concatemerized sites was demonstrated in vitro, but no genome-wide occupancy study has reported how many sites a bound promoter typically carries.

How much of HIC1's effect on Wnt targets requires DNA binding is unresolved, because the factor both represses promoters directly and sequesters TCF-4 and beta-catenin into nuclear bodies, and the two routes have not been separated with a binding-deficient allele.

HIC1 and HIC2 are indistinguishable by motif yet have different mutant phenotypes, and it is not established whether that reflects expression domains, different partners, or a sequence preference too subtle for the current models, the more so since the only HIC2 model with in vivo evidence is ChIP-only and fits the family poorly.

families.name: IKZF (Ikaros)
families.def: GGGAA core Ikaros sites. IKZF1-5.
families.short: The Ikaros family (IKZF1 Ikaros, IKZF2 Helios, IKZF3 Aiolos, IKZF4 Eos, IKZF5 Pegasus) are lymphoid zinc-finger proteins with an N-terminal C2H2 array that binds DNA and a C-terminal pair of fingers that mediates homo- and heterodimerization. They recognize a GGGAA core, present in lymphocyte-specific regulatory elements and also in pericentromeric satellite repeats, to which Ikaros localizes by direct DNA binding. IKZF1 is required for the development of all lymphoid lineages, is deleted in BCR-ABL1 and Ph-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia where it predicts poor outcome, and, with IKZF3, is the protein whose thalidomide-analog-induced degradation explains how lenalidomide works in myeloma. The GGGAA core is shared with ETS and NF-kB sites, which makes these motifs hard to trust.
families.long:
## The factors

Five human Ikaros-family proteins are encoded by IKZF1 to IKZF5: Ikaros, Helios, Aiolos, Eos and
Pegasus. Each has an N-terminal array of C2H2 zinc fingers that binds DNA and a separate C-terminal
pair of fingers that is not used for DNA contact but mediates homodimerization and heterodimerization
among family members [PMID:7969165]. Alternative splicing of IKZF1 produces isoforms (Ik-1 through Ik-5 in the
original description) carrying different combinations of the N-terminal fingers; these differ in
sequence specificity and affinity, with the full-length forms binding the whole set of recognition
sequences found in lymphocyte-specific regulatory elements and the short forms binding only a subset [PMID:7969165].
The short forms are also poorly nuclear and are weak activators, which is the basis of their
dominant-negative behavior [PMID:7969165,7585946].

Expression is lymphoid and largely restricted: IKZF1 and IKZF3 across B and T lineages, IKZF2 in
regulatory T cells and some other compartments, IKZF4 in regulatory T cells, IKZF5 more broadly.
Only IKZF1, IKZF2 and IKZF3 have motif models in the databases behind this family. The proteins work
in complexes rather than alone, associating with NuRD (Mi-2/CHD4) and with histone deacetylases, and
they localize to pericentromeric heterochromatin [PMID:10970879,29278858].

## The motif

The agreed core is GGGAA, written TTCCC on the other strand [PMID:7969165]. Extended forms appear in the databases
as TGGGAATAC and similar; the representative archetype for this family has that consensus. None of
these carries much information beyond the five-base core, and that is the central problem for this
family, because GGGAA is not distinctive. It is contained within the ETS core GGA(A/T) and within the
NF-kB half-site GGGRNNYYCC, so an Ikaros matrix, an ETS matrix and an NF-kB matrix can all score the
same DNA.

The collection makes this concrete. The JASPAR IKZF3 matrix has the consensus CAGGAAGTG, whose
nearest neighbors across all four databases are ETS models rather than Ikaros models; the JASPAR
IKZF2 matrix, AGGAAG, likewise resembles ETS more than it resembles the rest of its own family; and
two Vierstra archetypes in this family are explicitly named for mixed groups, IKZF with ZNF and IKZF
with NFKB. Family cohesion is correspondingly low. Ikaros also binds within centromeric DNA repeats,
and targeting to pericentromeric foci depends on the DNA-binding finger domain together with the
dimerization domain [PMID:10970879], so part of the genuine binding repertoire is repetitive sequence that motif
scanners will report en masse.

## Where it acts

Ikaros-family sites are found at promoters and enhancers of lymphoid genes, including the
immunoglobulin and T-cell-receptor loci, and co-occur with EBF1, PU.1/SPI1, RUNX1 and E2A at B- and
T-lineage regulatory elements [PMID:29278858,39017838]. Because PU.1 is itself an ETS factor that prefers a purine-rich GGAA
core, Ikaros and PU.1 sites are often indistinguishable in sequence at the same elements, and
composite occupancy is common. The other distinctive location is pericentromeric heterochromatin,
where Ikaros accumulates in foci; this was shown to require direct DNA binding rather than
recruitment through Mi-2 [PMID:10970879], and is consistent with Ikaros sites inside satellite repeats. Genome-wide,
a five-base core occurs on the order of a million times, so scanning alone cannot define an Ikaros
cistrome.

## Biology and disease

Ikzf1-null mice lack B cells and have profound defects across lymphoid lineages, establishing IKZF1
as required for the development of all lymphoid lineages [PMID:7923373]; mice expressing dominant-negative isoforms
develop T-cell leukemia [PMID:7585946]. In humans, focal deletions and point mutations of IKZF1 are a defining
feature of BCR-ABL1-positive B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and of Ph-like ALL [PMID:18408710], and IKZF1
deletion is associated with a substantially worse outcome [PMID:19129520], which is why it is now assayed in risk
stratification. Germline dominant-negative IKZF1 variants cause a combined T-, B- and myeloid-cell
immunodeficiency [PMID:29889099], and other IKZF1 variants cause common variable immunodeficiency [PMID:26981933].

The best-known pharmacology is degradation, not transcription. Thalidomide, lenalidomide and
pomalidomide act as molecular glues that recruit a zinc finger of IKZF1 and IKZF3 to cereblon, the
substrate receptor of the CRL4-CRBN ubiquitin ligase, causing their selective degradation; this
accounts for the activity of these drugs in multiple myeloma [PMID:24292625,24292623]. A systematic screen of the human C2H2
zinc-finger proteome identified eleven such degrons and predicted that more than 150 zinc fingers can
engage the drug-CRBN interface [PMID:30385546], which turned the Ikaros story into a general strategy for targeting
zinc-finger transcription factors.

## Reading a hit

Treat an Ikaros hit as a weak, ambiguous call. Three problems stack. First, the informative core is
five bases, so matches are everywhere. Second, that core is shared with ETS and NF-kB, and the
databases themselves are contaminated: at least one JASPAR Ikaros matrix in this family is closer to
ETS models than to Ikaros models, and two archetypes are named for IKZF together with ZNF or NFKB.
If you get an Ikaros hit at a lymphoid enhancer, PU.1 or another ETS factor is at least as likely to
be the direct binder. Third, no sequence argument distinguishes IKZF1 from IKZF2 or IKZF3, and IKZF4
and IKZF5 have no models here. Ikaros models are ChIP- and selection-derived in these collections
rather than backed by a structure of the protein on DNA, and Ikaros works in NuRD and HDAC complexes,
so indirect binding is a live possibility for any individual peak. A credible Ikaros call needs
lineage-appropriate expression, a peak from a well-controlled experiment, and ideally loss of the
peak on IKZF1 degradation rather than a motif match.
families.caveats: The informative core is only GGGAA, which is shared with ETS (GGAA) and NF-kB (GGGAA) sites, so an Ikaros match is rarely attributable to an Ikaros protein. The databases show the contamination directly: the JASPAR IKZF3 matrix here has ETS models as its nearest neighbors across all four sources, the IKZF2 matrix also resembles ETS more than its own family, and two Vierstra archetypes are named IKZF/ZNF and IKZF/NFKB. Family cohesion is low as a result. No model distinguishes IKZF1 from IKZF2 or IKZF3, and IKZF4 and IKZF5 have none. Ikaros additionally binds satellite repeats and acts within NuRD and HDAC complexes, so peaks need not reflect its own specificity.

timeline.finding: The Ikaros gene is shown to encode a set of alternatively spliced zinc-finger proteins whose N-terminal finger combinations differ in specificity and affinity, and Ikzf1-null mice are shown to lack all lymphoid lineages, so the family is defined simultaneously as a variable DNA-binding activity and as a requirement for lymphopoiesis.
timeline.methods: cDNA isolation and binding-site analysis of isoforms; germline gene targeting in mouse
timeline.open: The recognition sequence was a short purine-rich core whose specificity relative to other GGAA-binding factors was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Mice expressing a dominant-negative Ikaros isoform develop T-cell leukemia and lymphoma rapidly, linking loss of Ikaros DNA-binding function to malignancy rather than only to development.
timeline.methods: Targeted mouse mutant expressing a DNA-binding-deficient isoform

timeline.finding: Ikaros is shown to be targeted to pericentromeric heterochromatin by its own DNA-binding fingers together with the dimerization domain, not by recruitment through Mi-2, so part of its genuine binding repertoire is repeat DNA.
timeline.methods: Domain mutagenesis with imaging of pericentromeric localization, binding assays on satellite repeats
timeline.open: What fraction of genome-wide Ikaros signal comes from repeats rather than single-copy regulatory elements.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide copy-number analysis finds focal IKZF1 deletions, often removing the N-terminal fingers and leaving a dominant-negative product, in most BCR-ABL1-positive B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias.
timeline.methods: SNP-array copy-number profiling and sequencing of patient samples

timeline.finding: IKZF1 deletion is shown to mark a high-risk subgroup of B-ALL with substantially worse outcome, moving the gene into clinical risk stratification.
timeline.methods: Genomic profiling with outcome analysis in clinical trial cohorts

timeline.finding: Two groups show that lenalidomide works by making cereblon bind IKZF1 and IKZF3 and degrade them, which reinterprets a decades-old drug as a targeted removal of these factors rather than a transcriptional modulator.
timeline.methods: Quantitative proteomics, CRBN binding and ubiquitination assays, cell-based degradation

timeline.finding: Germline IKZF1 variants are shown to cause human immunodeficiency: haploinsufficiency presenting as common variable immunodeficiency with progressive B-cell loss, and, in a later series, dominant-negative variants causing combined T-, B- and myeloid-cell disease.
timeline.methods: Exome sequencing in patient cohorts with functional assays of variant proteins

timeline.finding: IKAROS is shown to assemble lineage-specific chromatin interactions over megabase distances in B-cell precursors, with contacts from IKAROS-bound enhancers crossing CTCF boundaries, which recasts the family as a genome-organizing activity rather than only a promoter and enhancer repressor.
timeline.methods: Loss- and gain-of-function with HiChIP and Hi-C, chromatin profiling
timeline.open: Whether these long-range interactions require the GGGAA core at the contacting elements or the dimerization and NuRD interfaces alone.

open: Whether the matrices labeled IKZF in these databases measure Ikaros specificity at all is unsettled: the JASPAR IKZF3 and IKZF2 models score closer to ETS matrices than to other Ikaros models, and PU.1 and other ETS factors occupy the same lymphoid elements, so co-occupancy and indirect binding cannot be excluded for any of them.

No structure of an Ikaros-family protein on DNA has been reported, so which fingers read the GGGAA core, and why the splice isoforms differ in specificity, remain inferred from binding assays rather than observed.

How much of Ikaros occupancy in vivo is at satellite and other repeat DNA rather than at single-copy regulatory elements has never been quantified, although pericentromeric targeting is known to require its own DNA-binding domain.

Whether the long-range chromatin interactions attributed to IKAROS depend on sequence-specific binding at the contacting elements, or on its dimerization and NuRD interfaces, is open, and this determines whether a motif hit is informative about genome organization at all.

families.name: BCL11A / BCL11B
families.def: TGACCA-containing sites. BCL11A, BCL11B.
families.short: BCL11A and BCL11B (originally CTIP1 and CTIP2) are paralogous C2H2 zinc-finger repressors with six fingers, of which a C-terminal cluster binds DNA while the N-terminal region recruits NuRD. They are best known not as motif proteins but as switches: BCL11A silences the fetal gamma-globin genes and is the target of approved gene-editing therapies for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia, while BCL11B enforces T-lineage commitment, so that its loss converts T cells into natural-killer-like cells. Reported DNA preferences conflict. In vitro selection on BCL11A gave a GC-box-like GGCCGG core, whereas the site it occupies at the gamma-globin promoter is written TGACCA. The family's matrices are heterogeneous and several look like other factors' motifs.
families.long:
## The factors

BCL11A and BCL11B were isolated as COUP-TF-interacting proteins 1 and 2 (CTIP1 and CTIP2) [PMID:10744719] and are
also known as EVI9 (BCL11A) and RIT1 (Bcl11b in mouse). Both are large C2H2 zinc-finger proteins with
six fingers: an N-terminal region that includes the COUP-TF interaction domains and a short
NuRD-interacting motif, and a C-terminal cluster of fingers that carries the DNA-binding activity.
Neither is a simple monomeric binder. BCL11A forms a tetramer through a single zinc finger (ZnF0),
and tetramer formation is required both for steady-state protein accumulation and for gamma-globin
repression, because an engineered monomer fails to engage its corepressor complex [PMID:39607926]. BCL11A's original
in vitro selection likewise recovered binding by an oligomeric complex rather than a monomer [PMID:12196208].

Expression is tissue-restricted and largely complementary. BCL11A is expressed in B cells, adult
erythroid cells and brain; BCL11B is T-cell-specific among hematopoietic cells and is also expressed
in skin, tooth and central nervous system [PMID:10744719]. Both repress transcription, and the repression seen in
reporter assays was not reversed by the class I/II HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A [PMID:12196208].

## The motif

The literature gives two answers and they do not agree. A selection procedure for high-affinity
CTIP1 (BCL11A) sites recovered the core GGCCGG, described at the time as closely related to the
canonical GC box [PMID:12196208]. Separately, the functionally best-characterized BCL11A element is in the HBG1 and
HBG2 (gamma-globin) promoters about 115 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site, where
BCL11A binds directly and where naturally occurring hereditary-persistence-of-fetal-hemoglobin point
mutations disrupt binding and raise gamma-globin expression [PMID:29610478]; the JASPAR matrix built from that class
of data has the consensus CTGACCA. The family data consensus here, TGACC, follows the second form,
and we give TGACCA as the headline consensus because it is the site with direct functional
validation. But the GGCCGG form is not an error: two of the eight matrices assigned to this family
(a CIS-BP BCL11B model with consensus TCCGGCC and a Vierstra archetype with THCGGCC) are
GGCCGG-related, and they are the ones that agree with the in vitro selection.

Cohesion in this family is the lowest in the zinc-finger set at 0.50, and the individual matrices are
worth listing because they illustrate what goes wrong. Besides the TGACC and GGCCGG groups, a CIS-BP
BCL11A model and a Vierstra archetype share the consensus TTTCACTTCCTC, and the archetype is named
BCL11A/IRF, reflecting the IRF/ISRE-like TTTC core. One Vierstra BCL11B archetype has a long,
high-information consensus (GTGAACGCNDNHGCTACAC) with no close neighbor anywhere in the four
databases. And the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix has the consensus AAACCACAA, whose reverse complement,
TTGTGGTTT, contains the RUNX core TGTGGT; its nearest neighbors across all four databases are RUNX
models rather than BCL11 models, and it is flagged in these data as belonging with RUNX. Since RUNX1
and RUNX3 are dominant occupants of T-cell regulatory elements, where BCL11B ChIP is performed, the
simplest reading is indirect binding or co-occupancy at RUNX sites rather than a genuine BCL11B
specificity; we are not aware of literature that settles this either way.

## Where it acts

BCL11A acts through a small number of intensively studied elements rather than a diffuse cistrome:
sites in the beta-globin cluster, its own erythroid-specific +58 intronic enhancer (whose common
variants set fetal-hemoglobin level) [PMID:24115442], and B-lymphoid and neural regulatory regions. BCL11B occupies
T-lineage enhancers and promoters, frequently alongside RUNX, TCF7, GATA3 and ETS factors. Both
proteins sit in NuRD-containing complexes, so much of their genomic footprint is complex-driven.

## Biology and disease

BCL11A is the developmental-stage-specific repressor of fetal hemoglobin: it is expressed in adult
but not fetal erythroid cells, knockdown reactivates HbF, and it occupies discrete sites in the
beta-globin cluster [PMID:19056937]. Because its erythroid enhancer is dispensable outside erythroid cells,
disrupting that enhancer raises HbF without compromising B-cell development [PMID:24115442], which is the basis of
the CRISPR-Cas9 therapy now approved for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent
beta-thalassemia [PMID:33283989]. Heterozygous BCL11A microdeletions and variants (2p15-p16.1) cause an
intellectual-disability and autism-spectrum phenotype (Dias-Logan syndrome) with persistent fetal
hemoglobin but otherwise near-normal blood counts [PMID:25938782].

BCL11B is the T-lineage commitment factor. It is first expressed immediately before commitment,
suppresses natural-killer-cell and progenitor programs [PMID:20595614], and is required for alpha-beta T-cell
differentiation and survival [PMID:12717433]; deleting it converts T cells at all developmental stages into
natural-killer-like cells that retain cytotoxic activity [PMID:20538915]. In disease, BCL11B is targeted by
enhancer-hijacking translocations in T-cell and T/myeloid acute leukemias [PMID:34103329], and germline heterozygous
variants cause immune dysregulation with severe atopic disease [PMID:34887873].

## Reading a hit

Do not trust a BCL11 motif hit. The family has no single validated consensus: the in vitro selection
and the functionally validated gamma-globin element point at different sequences, and both are short
(five to seven informative bases). Several matrices in the family are almost certainly other factors'
motifs recovered from ChIP data, most clearly the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix that scores as a RUNX site.
Nothing distinguishes BCL11A from BCL11B in sequence. And because BCL11A works as a tetramer bound to
a corepressor complex and BCL11B works within NuRD, occupancy in vivo depends on partners as much as
on sequence, so peaks are a poor guide to intrinsic specificity and motif hits are a poor guide to
peaks. Practical advice: for BCL11A, work from the known validated elements (the gamma-globin -115
region and the +58 enhancer) rather than from a genome-wide scan; for BCL11B, check whether your hit
is better explained as a RUNX site before attributing it here.
families.caveats: Trust this family least. There is no agreed consensus: in vitro selection on BCL11A gave a GC-box-like GGCCGG core, while the functionally validated site at the gamma-globin promoter is written TGACCA, and both appear among the family's matrices. Cohesion is 0.50. At least three matrices look like other factors: two Vierstra/CIS-BP models with an IRF-like TTTCACTTCC consensus (one archetype is named BCL11A/IRF), and the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix whose AAACCACAA consensus is the RUNX core and whose nearest neighbors in all four databases are RUNX models, most plausibly indirect binding at RUNX sites in T cells. BCL11A and BCL11B are not separable by sequence, and both act within corepressor complexes.

timeline.finding: CTIP1 and CTIP2, later renamed BCL11A and BCL11B, are isolated as COUP-TF-interacting zinc-finger proteins expressed in brain and the immune system and shown to repress transcription.
timeline.methods: Yeast two-hybrid and biochemical interaction screening, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether they bound DNA themselves or acted only as COUP-TF cofactors.

timeline.finding: In vitro selection gives CTIP1/BCL11A a high-affinity core of GGCCGG, closely related to the GC box, recovered by an oligomeric rather than monomeric complex, and shows repression independent of COUP-TF and insensitive to trichostatin A.
timeline.methods: SELEX-type binding-site selection, EMSA, reporter assays with HDAC inhibition
timeline.open: The selected GC-box-like site was never matched to a validated genomic element.

timeline.finding: Bcl11b is shown to be required for alpha-beta T-cell differentiation and survival in mouse, giving the paralogue a defined developmental role.
timeline.methods: Conditional and germline mouse knockouts with immunophenotyping

timeline.finding: BCL11A is identified as the developmental-stage-specific repressor of fetal hemoglobin: it is present in adult but not fetal erythroid cells, its knockdown reactivates gamma-globin, and it occupies discrete sites in the beta-globin cluster.
timeline.methods: GWAS follow-up, expression analysis, knockdown in primary erythroid cells, ChIP
timeline.open: Which sequence BCL11A reads at those sites was not resolved; the occupied regions did not match the GGCCGG selection.

timeline.finding: Two studies show Bcl11b is the T-lineage commitment factor: it is required at the commitment checkpoint, and deleting it at any stage converts T cells into natural-killer-like cells.
timeline.methods: Stage-specific conditional deletion in mouse, transcriptional profiling, functional assays

timeline.finding: An erythroid-specific enhancer in BCL11A intron 2, containing the common variants that set fetal-hemoglobin level, is identified and shown to be dispensable outside erythroid cells, which converts a transcription factor that cannot be drugged into a cell-type-specific target.
timeline.methods: Fine-mapping of GWAS variants, enhancer dissection with reporter and genome editing

timeline.finding: Hereditary-persistence-of-fetal-hemoglobin point mutations at the gamma-globin promoter are shown to act by disrupting direct BCL11A binding, giving the family its one element where a specific sequence, a bound factor and a human phenotype all line up; the matrix from this class of data reads CTGACCA, not the GGCCGG of the in vitro selection.
timeline.methods: Genome editing of promoter variants in erythroid cells, binding assays
timeline.open: Why the functionally validated site and the selected site are unrelated sequences is unexplained.

timeline.finding: BCL11A is shown to work as a tetramer assembled through a single zinc finger, with tetramerization required for protein accumulation and for gamma-globin silencing, so the unit that engages DNA and the corepressor complex is not a monomer and intrinsic specificity cannot be read off a monomer-based matrix.
timeline.methods: Structural and biochemical analysis of the oligomerization domain, engineered monomer in erythroid cells

open: The family has two incompatible consensus sequences and no accepted reconciliation: in vitro selection on BCL11A gives a GC-box-like GGCCGG core, while the functionally validated gamma-globin element and the matrices derived from that class of data give TGACCA.

Whether the JASPAR Bcl11B matrix reflects any BCL11B specificity is unresolved: its reverse complement contains the RUNX core TGTGGT and its nearest neighbors in all four databases are RUNX models, which is consistent with indirect binding at RUNX-occupied T-cell elements, but no published experiment settles it.

How a tetrameric BCL11A engages DNA is unknown, including whether the four subunits contact several copies of a short core or whether only one subunit binds sequence specifically, which determines whether any single-site matrix can describe this family.
Whether BCL11A and BCL11B differ in intrinsic specificity at all has not been tested; they are pooled here because their matrices are not separable, yet their biological targets barely overlap.

families.name: ZNF460 / ZNF317-like
families.def: Long composite KZFP motifs characterised by ChIP-exo; covers ZNF460 and the closely related ZNF317.
families.short: ZNF460 and ZNF317 are poorly characterized human C2H2 zinc-finger proteins grouped here because their database motifs cluster together, not because a published experiment showed they read the same sequence. The family is the least coherent in this part of the atlas: its eight matrices split into two unrelated groups, one a long AGTCTGCTGT-type word from ZNF317 in vitro data and the other a GC-rich GCCTCAGCCTCCC-type word from ZNF460 that closely resembles Alu consensus sequence. No single consensus is given here because the data do not support one. Almost everything known about either protein comes from high-throughput surveys of zinc-finger binding specificity rather than from focused study.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF460 and ZNF317 are human C2H2 zinc-finger proteins with tandem finger arrays. Neither has been the subject of a dedicated structural or biochemical study, and the literature on them is thin enough that this entry is mostly a description of data quality rather than of biology. They are grouped as one family because their motifs are nearest neighbours across the four databases, not because anyone has demonstrated shared specificity; the pairing should be read as a statement about matrix similarity. Both fall within the broad class of zinc-finger proteins surveyed in genome-wide characterizations of human KRAB and non-KRAB zinc fingers, where hundreds of members were assayed at once by ChIP-exo and related methods [PMID:28273063,37730438]. They are broadly but not highly expressed. There is no reported dimerization, no described cofactor, and no knockout phenotype in a mammalian model for either gene.

## The motif

This family has the lowest cohesion in the batch (0.49 on the atlas's internal scale), and the reason is visible in the matrices. They fall into two groups that have nothing in common. The first is long and AT/AC-mixed: the CIS-BP ZNF317 matrix reads GAGAAGTCAGCTGTCADTCTTAT, the Vierstra archetype AC0085 reads AGTCTGCTGT, one ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO ZNF317 matrix reads GAHTGACAGCTGACTTCTCA, and JASPAR MA1593.2 reduces this to ACAGCAGA. The second group is GC-rich: JASPAR MA1596.1 for ZNF460 reads GCCTCAGCCTCCCGAG, the CIS-BP ZNF460 matrix reads CGCCGCCTCCCC, and the low-grade HOCOMOCO ZNF460 matrix reads GGGGGGCG. The GCCTCAGCCTCCC word is worth naming for what it is: that sequence is a near-exact match to a well-known segment of the Alu consensus, so a matrix built on it will report Alu copies rather than a specific protein-DNA preference. The second ChIP-derived ZNF317 matrix (ATGGAAGCCAGAAGACAATGGAA) has no close neighbour anywhere in the collection. For this reason no `consensus` field is given for this family: quoting either group as the consensus would misrepresent the data, and averaging them would be meaningless.

## Where it acts

There is little to say that rests on evidence. If the GC-rich ZNF460 matrices are reporting Alu sequence, then matches will be distributed like Alus: hundreds of thousands of copies, concentrated in gene-rich, GC-rich regions and in introns, and heavily represented near promoters simply because Alus are. The AGTCTGCTGT-type ZNF317 word is longer and less repeat-like, and would be expected to occur at more modest frequency, but no published mapping study describes where ZNF317 actually binds in a genome or which genes it regulates. Neither protein has a named composite element or an established partner. Surveys of human zinc-finger proteins provide the only genome-scale occupancy context, and they treat these two as members of a large set rather than as individually characterized factors.

## Biology and disease

Direct functional work is limited to recent cancer and vascular papers, all of which study the protein rather than the motif. ZNF460 has been reported to inhibit HMGCL and activate PI3K signalling in colon cancer [PMID:41969486], to act downstream of KMT2D in a COL9A1-dependent extracellular-matrix stiffening mechanism that maintains a colorectal cancer stem-cell pool [PMID:40591048], and to promote GSDME-driven pyroptosis through transcriptional activation of PKM2 in aortic dissection [PMID:41923736]. These studies identify target genes but do not establish a binding consensus, so they cannot be used to validate the matrices above. ZNF317 has no comparable literature. Neither gene is a recognized Mendelian disease gene or a recurrent cancer driver, and neither appears among the primate-specific KRAB zinc fingers whose control of endogenous retroviruses has been worked out in detail. Where the literature is this thin, the right summary is that these are annotated but essentially uncharacterized factors.

## Reading a hit

Be cautious to the point of scepticism. First, decide which of the two motif groups your hit belongs to, because they are not the same element and the family label hides that. If the match is to the GC-rich GCCTCAGCCTCCC-type word, check whether it falls in an Alu; if it does, the hit is almost certainly reporting the repeat and not ZNF460 occupancy. If the match is to the longer AGTCTGCTGT-type word, you have a more specific sequence but almost no functional literature to interpret it against. Second, look at the evidence codes. The ZNF460 HOCOMOCO matrix is grade C with in vitro (S) evidence only and is a low-information G-run; the ZNF317 HOCOMOCO matrices are ChIP-only (P, grade B) and disagree with each other. Third, do not report a hit as identifying ZNF460 versus ZNF317: the grouping itself is data-driven, and nothing in the literature says these two proteins share a site. A match in this family is best treated as a flag to inspect the underlying sequence manually rather than as an assignment to a factor.
families.caveats: Treat this family as unreliable. Its matrices split into two unrelated groups, a long AGTCTGCTGT-type ZNF317 word and a GC-rich ZNF460 word whose sequence (GCCTCAGCCTCCC) closely matches Alu consensus, so matches to the latter most likely report a repeat rather than protein occupancy. Internal cohesion is 0.49, the lowest in this batch, and the two ChIP-derived ZNF317 matrices disagree with each other; the ZNF460 HOCOMOCO matrix is grade C with low information content. The pairing of ZNF460 with ZNF317 is a clustering result, not a published finding of shared specificity. No consensus is quoted because the data do not support one, and there is no focused literature on either protein's DNA binding.

timeline.finding: A genome-wide survey of human KRAB zinc-finger protein binding by ChIP-exo in HEK293T cells includes ZNF317; JASPAR's ZNF317 matrix (MA1593) is derived from that ChIP data.
timeline.methods: ChIP-exo of tagged KZFPs, de novo motif discovery
timeline.open: No in vitro selection confirmed the ChIP-derived ZNF317 word, and ZNF460 had no comparable characterization.

timeline.finding: In colorectal cancer, KMT2D-mediated H3K4me1 at a COL9A1 enhancer is reported to recruit ZNF460 to activate COL9A1, supporting cancer stem-cell self-renewal.
timeline.methods: Knockdown, ChIP, mouse tumor models
timeline.open: No ZNF460 binding motif was defined at the enhancer.

timeline.finding: ZNF460 is reported to bind the PKM2 promoter and activate it, driving GSDME-dependent pyroptosis in aortic dissection; the binding sites were predicted with JASPAR and checked by luciferase reporter and ChIP assays.
timeline.methods: JASPAR site prediction, luciferase reporter, ChIP, knockdown in mouse models
timeline.open: The prediction relied on a ZNF460 matrix whose core resembles Alu sequence.

timeline.finding: ZNF460 is reported to repress HMGCL and raise PI3K phosphorylation in colon cancer cells, and its high expression associates with poor prognosis.
timeline.methods: Cell proliferation assays, western blot, TCGA and single-cell analyses

open: Whether ZNF460 has a sequence preference of its own is unknown: its JASPAR and CIS-BP matrices are GC-rich words that match Alu sequence, and its only in vitro-supported HOCOMOCO matrix is a grade-C G-run, so none of the three is an established ZNF460 site.

Whether ZNF317's two ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices describe one site or two is unresolved: one matches the AGTCTGCTGT-type word shared with CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetype, while the other (ATGGAAGCCAGAAGACAATGGAA) resembles nothing else in the collection.

The recent ZNF460 target-gene studies do not show sequence-specific binding: the PKM2 study predicted its sites from JASPAR, which for ZNF460 means an Alu-like matrix, and the COL9A1 and HMGCL studies define no site, so whether ZNF460 reaches these genes through a motif of its own is open.

families.name: HINFP (MIZF)
families.def: Histone H4 promoter site GTCCGCGGTA. HINFP.
families.short: HINFP, also called HiNF-P and originally cloned as MIZF, is a seven-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that reads a short CGGAC core, usually written CGGACGTT. Its best-characterized job is at the replication-dependent histone H4 genes, where it binds a conserved cell-cycle element in the proximal promoter and, using the cyclin E/CDK2 substrate NPAT/p220 as coactivator, switches on H4 transcription at the G1-to-S transition. It is the endpoint of a linear pathway from growth-factor-induced cyclin E/CDK2 activity to histone synthesis. The same protein was independently identified as a partner of the methyl-CpG-binding protein MBD2 and acts as a repressor in that context, so the motif can mean activation or repression depending on the promoter.
families.long:
## The factors

HINFP is a single gene with no paralogue sharing its specificity. The protein has seven C2H2 zinc fingers; deletion analysis showed that five of the seven are required for DNA binding [PMID:14752047], so the array is used as one continuous reading head rather than as separable modules. It was discovered twice. As MIZF it was pulled out as a binding partner of MBD2, a methyl-CpG-binding protein, and characterized as a sequence-specific repressor that recruits MBD2-associated silencing activity [PMID:11553631,14752047]. As HiNF-P it was purified as the factor required for E2F-independent activation of the replication-dependent histone H4 multigene family [PMID:14585971]. The activating function depends on a coactivator rather than on a dimerization partner: HINFP binds NPAT/p220, a substrate of cyclin E/CDK2, and NPAT phosphorylation at the G1 restriction point converts the bound HINFP into an activator [PMID:14585971,19590016]. HINFP is broadly expressed and conserved; the Drosophila homolog exists and is functional [PMID:34620709].

## The motif

The site is short. Cyclic amplification and selection of targets gave the consensus CGGACGTT, with a conserved CGGAC core that is the invariant part [PMID:14752047]; the trailing GTT positions are preferred but not essential. Written on the other strand this is AACGTCCG, which is the orientation most database matrices use, and the family's dataConsensus GCGGACG is simply the core with an extra 5' guanine. Only about six to eight positions carry information, and the core sits within a CpG dinucleotide context, which matters because methylation of that CpG is relevant to the MBD2 connection. One feature of the data is worth flagging: the strongest archetype in this family, the Vierstra AC0649 matrix, reads GCGGACGTTCAACGTCCGC, which is two CGGAC cores in inverted orientation separated by five base pairs. Whether that reflects a genuine preference for a palindromic arrangement or simply the frequent occurrence of paired sites in the sequences used to build the archetype is not settled in the literature; treat the single core as the unit and the palindrome as a common arrangement. HINFP has no close paralogue, so there is no within-family ambiguity, but the CGGAC core is short enough to be a substring of longer GC-rich motifs from other families.

## Where it acts

HINFP sites are proximal promoter elements. The canonical location is Site II of the human histone H4 genes, a conserved element a short distance upstream of the start site that is present across the replication-dependent H4 multigene family; chromatin immunoprecipitation and genomic footprinting confirmed occupancy in vivo [PMID:14585971]. In the nucleus this activity is spatially concentrated: the H4 gene clusters assemble into histone locus bodies, subnuclear structures where HINFP, NPAT and the histone genes co-localize during S phase [PMID:37094694,37017672]. Beyond histone genes, database searches identified the CGGACGTT word in many human promoters, and HINFP was shown to bind and repress the RB1 promoter through it [PMID:14752047]. The motif is common enough that most genomic matches are not functional elements, and published HINFP ChIP-derived matrices in HOCOMOCO differ noticeably from the in vitro word, which is a sign that some of those peak sets contain indirect or low-specificity binding.

## Biology and disease

The HINFP-NPAT axis is the link between the cyclin E/CDK2 restriction point and the burst of histone gene transcription that packages newly replicated DNA. Reducing HINFP slows entry into S phase [PMID:14585971]; in mouse, Hinfp is required for early embryonic cell cycles [PMID:19590016], maternal Hinfp protein sustains pre-implantation development [PMID:27609454], and the histone H4 deficiency caused by Hinfp loss is made worse by removing p53, indicating that cells sense the shortfall as a checkpoint problem [PMID:26030398]. In Drosophila, loss of Hinfp derepresses most transposable elements and causes DNA damage in somatic tissues; the key mediator is Histone1, the linker histone, whose expression collapses without Hinfp, so higher-order chromatin assembly fails [PMID:34620709]. The same work found that Hinfp loss enhances Ras-driven tissue growth and ageing phenotypes [PMID:34620709]. On the repression side, MIZF/HINFP-mediated silencing of RB1 was described during myogenic differentiation [PMID:15541338]. There is no established Mendelian HINFP disease, and cancer associations are indirect, mostly through the histone gene/cell-cycle axis.

## Reading a hit

A match to CGGACGTT is only moderate evidence. Ask first whether the hit is in a proximal promoter, and second whether it is at a replication-dependent histone gene, where the prior probability of function is far higher than anywhere else. Isolated CGGAC cores in enhancers or gene bodies are usually chance matches. Because the protein has no paralogue, a real site means HINFP, but the converse trap is that the core is a substring of longer GC-rich words, so check whether a better-scoring motif from another family covers the same position. Direction of effect cannot be read from the sequence: the same element activates histone H4 genes with NPAT and represses RB1 with MBD2. The in vitro-supported HOCOMOCO matrix is the safer choice; the ChIP-derived ones in this family are internally inconsistent.
families.caveats: The core is short, so chance matches are frequent and a hit outside a proximal promoter usually means little. The strongest prior is a replication-dependent histone H4 promoter. HINFP has no paralogue, so a genuine site implicates one protein, but the CGGAC core sits inside many longer GC-rich motifs and can be claimed by other families. Evidence quality within the family is uneven: the in vitro matrix and the SELEX-derived consensus agree, while two ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices give noticeably different words, one of them with low information content, which suggests indirect or poorly resolved binding in those peak sets. Finally, the motif does not predict direction, since HINFP both activates and represses.

open: Whether HINFP prefers paired, inverted CGGAC cores is unresolved: the Vierstra AC0649 archetype is a palindrome of two cores separated by five base pairs, whereas target-site selection defined a single CGGACGTT site and the cited biochemistry tested only the single site.

How one protein activates histone H4 genes with NPAT and represses RB1 through MBD2 using the same core is unexplained; the activating role rests on histone-gene genetics and the repressive role on reporter and overexpression assays.

Whether histone H4 is HINFP's critical target in all animals is open: mouse work centres on H4 expression, while in Drosophila the decisive target for transposon repression is the linker histone gene Histone1, and Histone4 expression does not rescue.

Why the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO HINFP matrices diverge from the in vitro word (one reads CGGACCBRGGTGAGGACAG) is unexplained; they may record indirect or low-specificity binding rather than a second HINFP site.

families.name: GCM (glial cells missing)
families.def: GCM box ATGCGGGT. GCM1, GCM2.
families.short: GCM1 and GCM2 (glial cells missing 1 and 2) are the only human members of a small metazoan family that binds DNA through the GCM domain, a conserved 150-residue region with a fold unlike any other transcription factor class: two subdomains held together by structural zinc ions, reading the major groove with a five-stranded beta-sheet rather than an alpha-helix. They recognize an 8-bp GCM box, AT(G/A)CGGGT, as monomers, with no half-sites or spacing rules. Despite the name, the mammalian proteins are not gliogenic: GCM1 is required for placental labyrinth branching and trophoblast fusion, and GCM2 for parathyroid gland development, where loss-of-function and activating mutations cause hypoparathyroidism and hyperparathyroidism respectively.
families.long:
## The factors

GCM (glial cells missing) proteins are a small metazoan family with two human members, GCM1 (also GCMa) and GCM2 (GCMb); *Drosophila* has *gcm* and *gcm2*. They share a highly conserved 150-residue N-terminal region, the GCM domain, which carries all of the sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and sits next to a bipartite nuclear localization signal; the transactivation function maps to the divergent C-terminal half [PMID:9114061,12682016]. There is no dimerization module — the GCM domain binds its site as a monomer — and no relationship to any other DNA-binding class [PMID:12682016]. Expression is narrow. GCM1 is expressed in placental trophoblast, with lower levels in kidney and thymus; GCM2 is expressed in the developing parathyroid and, at lower levels, in a few brain regions [PMID:10888880,10910362,15353544]. Despite the name, the mammalian proteins have no established role in gliogenesis: the glia-versus-neuron switch is the *Drosophila* function, and it was the fly gene that gave the family its name [PMID:15353544]. With only two paralogues and highly restricted expression, GCM is one of the most self-contained families in this atlas.

## The motif

The GCM box is an 8-mer, AT(G/A)CGGGT, determined by binding-site selection for *Drosophila* GCM and reproduced for both mammalian proteins [PMID:8962155,9114061,15353544]. The models here agree closely: JASPAR, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetypes all give ATGCGGGT, and family cohesion is 0.92. Note that two of the HOCOMOCO entries (GCM1.H14CORE.0.S.B, GCM2.H14CORE.0.SM.B) report the consensus as ACCCGCAT, which is the reverse complement of the same element — an orientation convention, not a different specificity. One short CIS-BP profile (M02020_2.00, TGCGGG) is simply a trimmed version of the same core.

The structural story is what makes this family unusual. The crystal structure of the murine GCMa GCM domain bound to its octameric site, at 2.85 A, revealed a fold with no precedent: two subdomains tethered together by one of two structural zinc ions, and a five-stranded beta-sheet that protrudes into the major groove perpendicular to the DNA axis [PMID:12682016]. Almost every well-known DNA-binding class reads the major groove with an alpha-helix; GCM does it with a beta-sheet, and the zinc ions are structural rather than part of a classical zinc finger. That is why the recognized sequence looks like nothing else: the GC-rich CGGGT half is read by beta-strand side chains in a geometry not available to helical readers [PMID:12682016]. Because the element is a single 8-mer with high information content and no half-site structure, there are no spacing rules to worry about and no composite arrangements to score. GCM1 and GCM2 are not distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

GCM boxes act in promoters and proximal enhancers of a small number of tissue-restricted genes. The best-documented GCM1 targets are the syncytin-1 (*ERVWE1*) promoter in human trophoblast, and *Itga4*, *Rb1* and syncytin A in mouse placenta [PMID:12397062,18167345]; GCM1 activity is regulated by cAMP/PKA signaling in trophoblast [PMID:16166624]. GCM2 acts in parathyroid precursor cells [PMID:10910362]. Because both factors are so restricted, the great majority of sequence matches genome-wide are unoccupied in any given cell type. An exact 8-mer of this composition is expected tens of thousands of times in the human genome, and GC-rich promoter sequence produces additional weak partial matches, so the motif is informative only when paired with the right cell type. The GCM box is not part of any named composite element.

## Biology and disease

In *Drosophila*, *gcm* is a binary switch: cells that express it become glia, cells that do not become neurons [PMID:7553844,7553843]. The mammalian phenotypes are entirely different. *Gcm1*-null mouse embryos fail to initiate chorioallantoic branching morphogenesis and die from a defective placental labyrinth [PMID:10888880]; the fusion of trophoblast into syncytium depends on GCM1-driven syncytin expression [PMID:10888880,12397062]. *Gcm2*-null mice have no parathyroid glands yet are viable with normal serum parathyroid hormone, which was first attributed to the thymus [PMID:10910362]; later lineage and thymectomy work showed that the thymus is not an auxiliary source of serum PTH, and that thymic PTH comes mainly from small misplaced parathyroid clusters [PMID:21203493]. In humans, loss-of-function *GCM2* mutations, including substitutions that disrupt DNA binding by the GCM domain, cause autosomal recessive familial isolated hypoparathyroidism [PMID:15863676], while activating *GCM2* variants cause familial isolated hyperparathyroidism [PMID:27745835] — a clean case of a transcription factor with disease alleles in both directions.

## Reading a hit

A GCM box match is one of the more trustworthy family-level calls in this atlas. The fold is unique, the element is an 8-mer with high information content, and no other human family in this collection reads it: across the eight member motifs, similarity to the nearest non-GCM motif (0.67-0.80) sits well below within-family similarity. The evidence is also good — the HOCOMOCO entries rest on in vitro selection (codes `S` and `SM`), not on ChIP alone, so the claim "these proteins bind this sequence" is directly supported rather than inferred from co-occupancy.

What the match does not license is a call on which paralogue, or on occupancy. GCM1 and GCM2 are indistinguishable by motif; the discriminator is tissue, and outside trophoblast and parathyroid neither is expressed at a level that would make a site functional. Watch for two practical traps: databases report this motif in both orientations (ATGCGGGT and ACCCGCAT), so a scan that only checks one strand will miss half the sites; and permissive thresholds on GC-rich promoter sequence will produce partial matches to the CGGGT half that have little to do with GCM.
families.caveats: The GCM box is a high-information 8-mer read by a structurally unique domain, so family-level assignment is reliable — nothing else in this atlas reads ATGCGGGT, and the HOCOMOCO models rest on in vitro selection rather than ChIP alone. GCM1 and GCM2 cannot be told apart from sequence; use tissue instead, since GCM1 is essentially trophoblast-restricted and GCM2 parathyroid-restricted, so most matches are unoccupied in most cell types. Two mechanical points: the element is reported in both orientations across databases (ATGCGGGT and its reverse complement ACCCGCAT), and permissive scoring on GC-rich promoter sequence yields partial matches to the CGGGT half that are not GCM sites.

open: Whether GCM proteins use paired sites is unresolved: the structure and biochemistry show a monomer on one 8-mer, but the Vierstra archetype AC0550 is a 14-bp palindrome of two inverted GCM boxes (TGCGGGTACCCGCA), and it is not known whether this reflects cooperative binding without a dimerization module or only the avidity of two monomers in selection assays.

Whether the low-level expression of mammalian GCM genes in brain has any function is open: the Drosophila glial switch has no established mammalian counterpart, and the knockout phenotypes characterized so far are confined to placenta and parathyroid.

families.name: PLAG / PLAGL
families.def: GRGGC(N6-8)GGG bipartite sites. PLAG1, PLAGL1/ZAC1, PLAGL2.
families.short: The PLAG proteins - PLAG1, PLAGL1 (also called ZAC1 or LOT1) and PLAGL2 - are C2H2 zinc-finger factors with seven fingers that read a bipartite G-rich site: a GRGGC core and a GGG cluster separated by roughly six to eight base pairs. Finger 3 contacts the G-cluster and fingers 6 and 7 contact the core, so the two halves are read by different parts of one protein. PLAG1 is the classic translocation target in salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma, where promoter swapping with CTNNB1 or LIFR switches it on; PLAGL2 is also transforming, while PLAGL1/ZAC1 is an imprinted, maternally silenced growth suppressor whose loss of imprinting causes transient neonatal diabetes. All three activate IGF2.
families.long:
## The factors

Three human genes make up this family. PLAG1 (8q12) was identified as the gene activated by promoter
swapping in pleomorphic adenomas of the salivary gland carrying t(3;8)(p21;q12), which fuses the CTNNB1
promoter to the PLAG1 coding region [PMID:9020842]; a second recurrent translocation, t(5;8)(p13;q12), puts PLAG1 under
the LIFR promoter. PLAGL1 (6q24), independently named ZAC1 for zinc finger with apoptosis and cell-cycle
arrest [PMID:9184226] and LOT1 for lost on transformation, and PLAGL2 (20q11) complete the set. All three carry seven
Cys2-His2 zinc fingers in a conserved N-terminal DNA-binding domain plus a C-terminal
serine/threonine/proline-rich transactivation domain, and all bind DNA as monomers. The DNA-binding
domains are highly similar in sequence [PMID:11888928], which is the central problem for interpreting a hit. PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 are broadly expressed in embryonic tissues and largely silenced after birth; PLAGL1 is expressed
from the paternal allele only [PMID:10655556], in pituitary, brain, pancreatic islets and many embryonic tissues.
PLAG1 activity is further tuned by SUMOylation of its transactivation domain.

## The motif

The literature consensus is bipartite: a GRGGC core and a G-cluster. The binding-site selection that
defined it placed seven random nucleotides between the core and a G-cluster written RGGK [PMID:10646861]; the
same group's later target-gene screen quoted it as GRGGC(N)6-8GGG, allowing six to eight [PMID:14712223]. How far
the spacer can vary has not been measured directly, but to the extent it does, the element is better described
as two half-sites than as a fixed-width matrix. Mutational and
binding work assigned the two halves to different fingers: finger 3 engages the G-cluster, fingers 6 and
7 engage the GRGGC core, so a single molecule bridges the gap [PMID:10646861].

The data in this atlas are consistent with that but compress it. The JASPAR PLAG1 model
(GGGGCCCAAGGGGG, 14 bp) and the equivalent CIS-BP and Vierstra models (CCCCCTTGGGCCCC) [PMID:25215497,32728250] span the whole
bipartite element with the short end of the spacer; the PLAGL2 and PLAGL models collapse to an 8-bp
GGGCCCCC, effectively just the G-rich halves. The atlas medoid, GGGCCCCC, is therefore shorter than the
literature consensus rather than in conflict with it: fixed-width position weight matrices cannot
represent a variable spacer, so the databases store the tightest-spaced version. Expect real sites to be
longer and more variably spaced than any of these matrices.

The three paralogues are not equivalent in vitro. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 bind the same bipartite site and both
transform NIH3T3 cells, whereas PLAGL1/ZAC1 binds a distinguishable, more homogeneously G-rich sequence
and arrests rather than promotes growth [PMID:11888928,9184226]. The CIS-BP PLAGL1 model here is a 4-bp CCCC inferred from mouse
Plagl1 at 88% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497], so it carries almost no information and should not be used
for scanning.

## Where it acts

PLAG-family sites are G-rich and land preferentially in GC-rich, CpG-island promoters. The best-validated
target is IGF2: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 both bind the IGF2 P3 promoter region and up-regulate it, and IGF2
induction accompanies PLAG1- and PLAGL2-driven transformation [PMID:10646861,11888928]. PLAGL1/ZAC1 sits at the top of an
imprinted gene network that includes IGF2, H19, CDKN1C, DLK1 and MEST, and coordinates their expression
during embryonic growth [PMID:17084362]. Because the sites are G-rich, they overlap the binding preferences of KLF/SP
factors, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and other GC-box readers, and PLAG matches are common in the CpG-island
promoters of housekeeping genes where none of these factors is necessarily the functional occupant.

## Biology and disease

PLAG1 is the defining oncogene of salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma [PMID:9020842] and also of lipoblastoma, where
the HAS2 or COL1A2 promoter is fused to the entire PLAG1 coding sequence, again a promoter swap rather than
a chimeric protein [PMID:10987300]. PLAGL2 is amplified and overexpressed in glioma and colorectal cancer and
promotes proliferation partly through WNT-dependent [PMID:20478531] and partly through IGF2/ASCL2-dependent routes [PMID:37310750].
PLAGL1/ZAC1 has the opposite behaviour: it induces apoptosis and G1 arrest [PMID:9184226], is imprinted with maternal
silencing [PMID:10655556], and relaxation of that imprint at the 6q24 HYMAI/PLAGL1 locus causes transient neonatal
diabetes mellitus [PMID:10655556,11448939]. Zac1-null mice are growth-restricted [PMID:17084362], consistent with a network role in embryonic
growth. Outside disease, a regulatory variant at the bovine PLAG1-CHCHD7 interval is one of the largest
single-locus effects on stature and carcass weight in cattle [PMID:22607022,29215042], a reminder that PLAG1 dosage controls
growth in normal physiology.

## Reading a hit

A PLAG match is a G-rich, GC-box-like element, so the honest conclusion from sequence alone is "a G-rich
promoter element," not "a PLAG site." KLF, SP, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and ZNF263 all compete for the same
matches, and G-rich matrices produce many chance hits in CpG islands. Within the family, PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 cannot be told apart by sequence; PLAGL1 is somewhat distinguishable in vitro, but the PLAGL1
matrices available here are too short (4-8 bp) to exploit that. Because the true element is bipartite,
with a spacer of about seven bases that later work quotes as six to eight, a fixed-width matrix will miss differently spaced real sites and may score
contiguous G-runs that are not functional sites. Check for the two halves explicitly if the call
matters. Expression is the strongest discriminator: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so in adult
tissue a PLAG match is more likely to be a generic GC-box unless a fusion or amplification is known.
families.caveats: The real element is bipartite, a GRGGC core and a G-cluster seven bases apart in the original selection and quoted as six to eight in later work, and a fixed-width matrix represents only one spacing, so the matrices here are truncated or tightest-spaced versions that will both miss differently spaced sites and over-call plain G-runs. Matches overlap KLF/SP, EGR, MAZ and other GC-box factors, and G-rich models hit CpG-island promoters frequently by chance. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 share a specificity and cannot be separated by sequence; PLAGL1/ZAC1 differs in vitro, but its models here (CCCC, TGGGGCCA) are too short to use, and the CIS-BP PLAGL1 entry is inferred from mouse at 88% DBD identity. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so adult-tissue matches deserve extra scepticism.

timeline.finding: PLAG1 is identified as the 8q12 gene activated in pleomorphic adenomas with t(3;8)(p21;q12), where promoter swapping with CTNNB1 drives expression of an intact PLAG1 coding sequence.

timeline.open: PLAG1 was a predicted zinc-finger protein with no known DNA-binding specificity.

timeline.finding: Zac1 (PLAGL1) is cloned as a zinc-finger protein that induces apoptosis and G1 arrest and suppresses tumor formation, the opposite of PLAG1's oncogenic behavior.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; proliferation, apoptosis and nude-mouse tumorigenicity assays

timeline.finding: The PLAG1 site is defined as a bipartite element, a GRGGC core and a G-cluster separated by seven random nucleotides, contacted by fingers 6-7 and finger 3 respectively; IGF2 promoter 3 is a bound and activated target.

timeline.open: Whether PLAGL1 and PLAGL2 read the same element was untested.
