timeline.methods: Restriction landmark genome scanning; allele-specific RT-PCR; methylation analysis; reporter assays

timeline.finding: Despite highly homologous DNA-binding domains, the three PLAG proteins split in DNA binding: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 both need the GRGGC core and the G-cluster, with finger 3 reading the cluster, whereas PLAGL1 recognizes only an extended core; PLAG1 and PLAGL2 transform NIH3T3 cells and induce IGF2, in contrast to growth-suppressive PLAGL1.
timeline.methods: Transformation and nude-mouse assays; DNA-binding assays; expression analysis
timeline.open: Which residues give PLAGL1 its different preference was not identified.

timeline.finding: Zac1 knockout causes intrauterine growth restriction, and Zac1 is placed in a network of co-regulated imprinted growth genes, directly regulating Igf2/H19 through a shared enhancer.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice; microarray meta-analysis; binding and expression assays

timeline.finding: PLAGL2 is identified as an oncogene targeted by amplification or gain in malignant glioma, where it suppresses neural stem cell differentiation partly by modulating Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
timeline.methods: Integrated copy-number and expression genomics; neural stem cell differentiation assays; transcriptome analysis

timeline.finding: In colorectal cancer, PLAGL2 drives transformation with only modest effects on canonical Wnt signaling, acting instead through direct targets IGF2 and ASCL2, which revises the Wnt-centered model for this tissue.
timeline.methods: Gain- and loss-of-function in CRC lines and intestinal cells; reporter assays; rescue with ASCL2
timeline.open: Whether the glioma and colorectal mechanisms differ by tissue or reflect a disagreement is unresolved.

open: The spacer is stated inconsistently: the original PLAG1 selection placed seven random nucleotides between the GRGGC core and the G-cluster, while the consensus usually quoted allows six to eight, and no genome-wide measurement has established how much spacer variation PLAG1 tolerates in vivo.

How PLAGL1 acquires a DNA preference different from PLAG1 and PLAGL2, despite a highly homologous DNA-binding domain, has not been explained structurally, and the PLAGL1 matrices in these databases (CCCC and TGGGGCCA) are too short to show the difference.

Whether PLAGL2's oncogenic activity runs through WNT signaling is disputed: in glioma and neural stem cells it was attributed in part to Wnt/beta-catenin modulation, whereas in colorectal cancer its effect on canonical WNT signaling was minimal and IGF2 and ASCL2 carried the effect.

families.name: OSR1 / OSR2
families.def: Odd-skipped related zinc fingers; GC-rich sites. OSR1, OSR2.
families.short: OSR1 and OSR2 (odd-skipped related 1 and 2) are the two vertebrate members of the Odd family of C2H2 zinc-finger proteins, homologs of Drosophila odd-skipped. OSR1 carries three tandem C2H2 fingers and OSR2 five, and both bind the 8-mer GCTACTGT, established by in vitro selection. Despite the C2H2 class label, this motif is not GC-rich — the central TACTG carries most of the information. Both proteins are mesenchymal and developmentally restricted: OSR1 is required for the metanephric mesenchyme and hence for kidney formation, OSR2 for palatal shelf growth, and loss of either causes a distinct mouse malformation. A knock-in experiment showed that Osr1 can replace Osr2 in palate and skull development, so their different phenotypes are attributed to where they are expressed rather than what they bind.
families.long:
## The factors

OSR1 and OSR2 (odd-skipped related 1 and 2) are the two vertebrate members of the Odd family of C2H2 zinc-finger proteins, named for *Drosophila* odd-skipped (*odd*), which together with *sob* and *bowl* forms a related fly group [PMID:8878683]. The two human proteins are small and consist of little besides their finger array: OSR1 has three tandem C2H2 fingers (residues 175-253), while OSR2 has five (172-306), the fifth degenerate [PMID:19389375]. That difference matters for the motif, since more fingers means more base pairs contacted. OSR2 additionally exists as two alternatively spliced isoforms, with three or five fingers [PMID:19389375]. Both act mainly as repressors in reporter assays and both are mesenchymal: OSR1 in intermediate mesoderm, the metanephric mesenchyme that gives rise to the kidney, and in cardiac and lateral plate mesenchyme [PMID:16223478,16790474]; OSR2 in palatal mesenchyme and tooth germ [PMID:15175245,19251632]. Neither is broadly expressed in adult tissues, and neither has a large paralogue set — with two genes, this is a two-member family in the strictest sense. A knock-in experiment in mice replaced the Osr2 coding region with Osr1 cDNA: it completely rescued the cleft palate and cranial skeletal defects of Osr2-null mice, though not eyelid closure, which also failed with an Osr2 cDNA knock-in and tracked altered expression of the knock-in allele. The authors concluded that the distinct phenotypes come from divergent cis-regulatory sequences rather than from different biochemistry; the study did not test the reverse swap, Osr2 in the Osr1 locus [PMID:19389375].

## The motif

The consensus supported by the data is GCTACTGT, an 8-mer derived from in vitro selection (HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX) [PMID:28473536]. Six of the eight models here — from JASPAR, CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and the Vierstra archetypes — give GCTACTG or GCTACTGT, and family cohesion is 0.92, so this is a well-agreed motif.

It is worth stating plainly that this contradicts a common shorthand. C2H2 zinc-finger factors are often assumed to read GC-rich sequence, and this family is sometimes described that way, but GCTACTGT is not GC-rich; the central TACTG is the most distinctive part, and the informative positions span a mixed-composition 7-8-mer. Anyone scanning with a GC-rich expectation will look in the wrong places.

Two orientation and length details follow from the structure. The JASPAR OSR2 profile MA1646.2 has a consensus of CAGAAGC, which is the reverse complement of GCTTCTG — the same core with one substitution, reported on the opposite strand; databases are not consistent about strand here. And the longest model in the family, the HOCOMOCO OSR2 methyl-HT-SELEX matrix (tGCTACTGaagtaGC, 15 bp, 18.2 bits), reads as an inverted repeat: GCTACTG at the 5' end and, on the other strand at the 3' end, GCTACTT. That arrangement is consistent with OSR2's larger finger array or with two-site occupancy, but no structure of either protein on DNA has been reported, so which fingers make which contacts is not established. OSR1 and OSR2 are not distinguishable from sequence.

## Where it acts

Because both factors are mesenchymal and developmentally restricted, the sites that matter are developmental enhancers in mesenchyme rather than housekeeping promoters, and the motif is not CpG-island associated. No named composite element exists for this family, and no well-characterized partner motif has been established — a genuine gap rather than an omission. An exact 8-mer of this composition is expected on the order of tens of thousands of times in the human genome, which puts OSR matches firmly in the "too common to mean anything alone" category.

## Biology and disease

The mouse phenotypes are clean and non-overlapping. *Osr1*-null embryos fail to form the metanephric mesenchyme and have no kidney, along with heart and urogenital defects [PMID:16223478,16790474]; conditional and lineage work has since shown that Osr1-expressing mesenchymal cells also initiate lymph node formation [PMID:37160119]. *Osr2*-null mice have cleft palate, caused by reduced proliferation and disturbed patterning of the palatal shelf mesenchyme [PMID:15175245], and Osr2 also functions in tooth germ development [PMID:19251632]. Human Mendelian disease links are weaker than the mouse data would suggest; the clearest reported human connection is regulatory rather than coding, with enhancer variation at *OSR2* associated with susceptibility to mandibular incisor agenesis [PMID:42470271].

## Reading a hit

A GCTACTGT match identifies the family, not the member. The mouse knock-in result makes this more than a technical caveat: Osr1 can stand in for Osr2 in palate and skull development [PMID:19389375], so there is no reason to expect sequence to separate them, and any call between OSR1 and OSR2 has to come from expression data.

Three practical points. First, check strand — at least one database profile in this family is reported as the reverse complement (CAGAAGC), so a single-strand scan will miss half the matches. Second, weigh the evidence: the strongest models here are in vitro (HOCOMOCO codes `SM` for OSR1 and `PSM` for OSR2, the latter grade A), so the claim that these proteins bind this sequence is well supported and not a ChIP-only inference; the weakest, OSR2.H14CORE.1.M.C, is grade C and much longer, and the extra flanking positions in it should not be treated as a requirement. Third, the motif is short and common, so a hit is only informative in a mesenchymal context where one of the two genes is actually expressed. Outside kidney, palate, tooth and related mesenchyme, a match is very unlikely to be occupied.
families.caveats: The motif itself is well agreed (cohesion 0.92, six of eight models giving GCTACTG/GCTACTGT, with in vitro HOCOMOCO evidence at codes SM and PSM), so family assignment is sound. What it cannot do is name the protein: OSR1 and OSR2 read the same site, and a mouse knock-in showed that Osr1 can replace Osr2 in palate and skull development, so only expression data can separate them. The 8-mer is common enough to occur tens of thousands of times by chance, and both genes are restricted to developing mesenchyme, so matches outside kidney, palate, tooth or related mesenchyme are unlikely to be occupied. Check strand: one JASPAR profile reports the reverse complement (CAGAAGC). Do not expect a GC-rich site here.

open: Whether OSR2 reads the same core in cells as in vitro is unresolved: every in vitro model gives GCTACTG(T), and the HOCOMOCO model that combines ChIP-seq with SELEX gives GCTACCG, but the JASPAR OSR2 profile, built from ChIP-seq alone, gives CAGAAGC, the reverse complement of GCTTCTG, with a T where the in vitro site has an A.

Which zinc fingers contact the site, and whether the five-finger OSR2 isoform reads a longer site than the three-finger proteins, is unknown: no OSR-DNA structure has been reported, and the longest model (the 15-bp HOCOMOCO OSR2 methyl-HT-SELEX matrix, grade C) could reflect either an extended footprint or two-site occupancy.

families.name: RNA-binding proteins with inferred DNA motifs
families.def: Factors whose motif comes from an RNA-binding assay or from inference, so the DNA motif should be read with caution: CPEB1, LIN28B and MBNL2. MBNL1 has no matrix in these databases.
aka: RNA-binding proteins with inferred DNA motifs
RBP motifs in a DNA motif database
families.short: This is not a motif family. It is a warning label. The factors here have motifs that came out of RNA-binding proteins run through DNA assays, or out of inference, so the matrices filed under their names should be read with real caution. Three proteins are present - CPEB1, LIN28B and MBNL2, plus a generic MBNL archetype - across eight models, at cohesion 0.50. All three are bona fide RNA-binding proteins with well-mapped RNA elements, and for CPEB1 the DNA matrix is simply that RNA element with T written for U: its models read TTTTAT and AATAAAA, the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element and its own reverse complement. Scanning genomic DNA against these is usually a mistake. Read the RNA literature instead, and look up the RNA motif.
families.long:
## The factors

Three proteins, eight models. MBNL1 is named in the definition but has no model here, and the "and similar" resolves to nothing further: the bucket is smaller than its label implies.

CPEB1 was identified as the specificity factor for cytoplasmic polyadenylation during Xenopus oocyte maturation [PMID:7954828]. It binds the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element, UUUUAU, in mRNA 3' untranslated regions using two RRMs and a ZZ zinc-binding domain that close on it in a fly-trap arrangement [PMID:24990967], and it lengthens poly(A) tails to control translation [PMID:7954828]. MBNL2 is a muscleblind-like protein with tandem CCCH zinc fingers that read YGCY motifs - GC steps embedded in pyrimidines - in single-stranded pre-mRNA to control alternative splicing [PMID:20071745]. LIN28B carries a cold-shock domain and a pair of CCHC zinc knuckles; the knuckles read a GGAG element in the preE loop of pre-let-7, the cold-shock domain contributes little sequence specificity, and the protein blocks let-7 maturation [PMID:22078496]. Its documented nuclear activity is indirect: in neuroblastoma it occupies active promoters through protein-protein interaction with the zinc finger ZNF143 [PMID:32601179].

## The motif

There is no consensus. The reported aATAAAA is only the medoid, CIS-BP M03581.

CPEB1 contributes three models: HOCOMOCO CPEB1.H14CORE.0.S.B reads TTTTAT (9.9 bits) and CPEB1.H14CORE.1.S.B reads TTTTATttTtTTt (15.1 bits), both from HT-SELEX alone at grade B [PMID:37971293], and CIS-BP M03581 reads AATAAAA (10.8 bits). TTTTAT is the CPE with T for U. ATAAAA is the exact reverse complement of TTTTAT, which is why those models agree at 0.94 - and it is also the whole problem in miniature. An RNA element is strand-specific; a DNA scan is not. Scan for the CPEB1 matrix and half your hits are reverse-complement copies that correspond to no RNA element at all.

MBNL contributes three: CIS-BP M04659 (MBNL2) cGCtTcGCtT at 8.8 bits, HOCOMOCO MBNL2.H14CORE.0.B.B cGCTT at 8.3 bits from a protein-binding microarray alone at grade B, and the Vierstra archetype AC0360:MBNL:CCCH_ZF, tGCtTcGCtT. Those contain CGCT, a YGCY motif. A microarray presents double-stranded DNA, so a real duplex preference was measured - for a protein whose physiological target is single-stranded.

LIN28B contributes two, CIS-BP M04663 and the Vierstra archetype AC0341:LIN28B:CSD, both reading CGCGATAtaaCaGCG at 16.6 and 15.9 bits. These are the most information-rich models here and the only ones with no match in any other family. Neither LIN28B's RNA specificity nor its documented nuclear mechanism predicts a 15-bp CG-flanked matrix [PMID:22078496,32601179], so do not read 16.6 bits of information as 16.6 bits of biological confidence.

There are four routes by which an RNA-binding protein acquires a DNA motif. First, direct DNA assay of a protein admitted to a transcription-factor census [PMID:29425488] on the strength of a nucleic-acid-binding domain: HT-SELEX for CPEB1, a microarray for MBNL2. Second, inference by domain similarity, which propagates a measured matrix to relatives and across species [PMID:31133749]. Third, indirect ChIP, where a protein tethered to chromatin by a partner yields the partner's motif [PMID:32601179]. Fourth, archetype clustering, which merges similar matrices under a joint label [PMID:32728250].

## Where it acts

On RNA, in every case: CPEB1 at cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements in mRNA 3' untranslated regions, MBNL2 at YGCY in introns and around regulated exons, LIN28B on pre-let-7 and target mRNAs [PMID:24990967,20071745,22078496]. No validated genomic DNA element exists for any of the three. The arithmetic is decisive: TTTTAT and its reverse complement are expected roughly four million times in 3.1 Gb at human base composition, and GCTT about twenty million times. No threshold localises anything. Restricting a scan to transcribed sequence does not help: a DNA-space match is blind to which strand is transcribed, to whether the position survives splicing, and to whether it lies in the 3' untranslated region where CPEB1 works.

## Biology and disease

The disease biology here is RNA biology. In myotonic dystrophy type 1, a CTG expansion produces CUG-repeat transcripts that recruit and sequester muscleblind proteins, and the resulting loss of MBNL activity misregulates splicing [PMID:10970838,20071745]; that is a disease of an RNA element, which no DNA scan for an MBNL matrix would find. CPEB1 governs translational activation in oocyte maturation and local translation at synapses [PMID:7954828,24990967]. LIN28B is an oncofetal factor overexpressed in neuroblastoma, where it potentiates MYCN-driven tumour formation partly by repressing let-7 and partly at promoters through ZNF143 [PMID:32601179].

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit here as a red flag, not a result. Name the matrix, state which assay produced it - S is HT-SELEX and B is a protein-binding microarray in the HOCOMOCO model name - then ask which question you were answering. If you want to know whether the protein binds your sequence as RNA, take the RNA motif from an RNA motif compendium; large collections of RNA-binding specificities exist, and a CPEB1 or MBNL model from one is the right tool [PMID:23846655]. If you want to know what bound your genomic site, discard these matrices and look at the next best hit.

Do not over-correct. Proteins that genuinely bind both exist, and the founding example is in this atlas: TFIIIA/GTF3A binds the internal control region of the 5S rRNA gene as duplex DNA and also binds the 5S RNA transcript, a dual specificity described in 1980 [PMID:7001457]; reviews of dual DNA- and RNA-binding proteins document many more [PMID:12364590,25269475]. An RNA-binding label is not automatically disqualifying. The test is whether a duplex-DNA measurement exists for your protein, whether the candidate site sits where that protein is known to act, and whether the genomic context makes sense at all. For the three proteins here, at least one of those answers is no.
families.caveats: Not a family, and not really a set of DNA motifs. Three RNA-binding proteins are represented by eight models at cohesion 0.50: CPEB1 from HT-SELEX alone, MBNL2 from a protein-binding microarray alone, both at HOCOMOCO grade B, and LIN28B from CIS-BP plus its Vierstra archetype. Two of the CPEB1 models are the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element UUUUAU written as TTTTAT and its own reverse complement, which is the difficulty in miniature: RNA elements are strand-specific and DNA scanning is not. MBNL1, named in the definition, has no model here. Do not build a consensus, do not scan genomic DNA against these matrices, and if you need a CPEB1 or MBNL specificity take it from an RNA motif resource.

timeline.finding: The transcription factor that binds a control region inside the Xenopus 5S RNA gene is the same abundant oocyte protein that is stored in complex with 5S RNA, and 5S RNA inhibits 5S gene transcription by binding it. One protein can read a specific DNA element and a specific RNA.
timeline.methods: In vitro transcription in oocyte nuclear extracts, binding and competition assays
timeline.open: The structural basis of the dual specificity was unknown.

timeline.finding: CPEB is enriched by RNA affinity chromatography on the U-rich cytoplasmic polyadenylation element, cloned, and shown by immunodepletion and add-back to be required for cytoplasmic polyadenylation in Xenopus egg extracts. Its specificity is defined on RNA, through two RNA recognition motifs.
timeline.methods: RNA affinity chromatography, cDNA cloning, immunodepletion and add-back
timeline.open: How the RNA recognition motifs select the CPE was not known.

timeline.finding: A systematic in vitro survey reports RNA motifs for RNA-binding proteins from 205 genes in 24 eukaryotes, finds them deeply conserved and inferable from RNA-binding-domain sequence, and shows they agree with in vivo RNA-binding data. RNA-binding proteins gain a motif resource of their own, separate from the DNA collections.
timeline.methods: RNAcompete in vitro binding to designed RNA pools, comparison with in vivo RNA-binding data

timeline.finding: Solution structures of the tandem RRMs of CPEB1 and CPEB4, free and RNA-bound, show an unusual free-state arrangement that closes on the U-rich element on binding, a fly-trap mechanism behind sequence-specific RNA recognition.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, functional assays
timeline.open: The structures explain RNA recognition; they do not address why selection on DNA recovers the same sequence.

timeline.finding: The human transcription factor census classes CPEB1, LIN28B and MBNL2 as transcription factors on the strength of high-throughput in vitro DNA motifs. It notes that the CPEB1 HT-SELEX motif could be an artefact of single-stranded DNA binding by a well-characterized RNA-binding protein, and that MBNL2 has HT-SELEX motifs although the family largely binds RNA. MBNL1 is excluded as an ssDNA/RNA-binding protein.
timeline.methods: Expert curation of candidate transcription factors
timeline.open: The single-stranded-DNA explanation was raised, not tested.

timeline.finding: Archetype clustering, introduced with the reference footprint atlas, groups matrices from several collections under the names of the factor groups they contain. The archetypes used here include AC0341:LIN28B:CSD and AC0360:MBNL:CCCH_ZF, filed alongside the DNA-binding families.
timeline.methods: Motif clustering; DNase I footprinting in 243 cell and tissue types
timeline.open: An archetype name records which matrices clustered, not whether the protein binds DNA in cells.

timeline.finding: In neuroblastoma cells LIN28B occupies active gene promoters through protein-protein interaction with the sequence-specific zinc finger ZNF143, and a LIN28B mutant that cannot block let-7 processing still potentiates MYCN-driven tumours. This is a documented route by which an RNA-binding protein appears in ChIP-seq at sites set by a partner's motif.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, co-immunoprecipitation, in vivo tumour models

timeline.finding: The HOCOMOCO collection, rebuilt in 2024 and since extended to v14, carries two CPEB1 models from HT-SELEX alone and an MBNL2 model from a protein-binding microarray alone, all at grade B: none of the RNA-binding-protein models here has support from a second assay type.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX and protein-binding-microarray motif discovery, expert curation, benchmarking

open: Whether the CPEB1 HT-SELEX models record duplex-DNA binding or the selection of single strands is unresolved. The human transcription factor census raised the single-stranded-DNA explanation and found no published evidence that CPEB1 binds DNA, while the TTTTAT models match the RNA element the protein is known to read.

The LIN28B matrix is not explained by anything known about the protein. CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetype give a 15-bp CG-flanked CGCGATAtaaCaGCG at about 16 bits, whereas Lin28 structures describe recognition of let-7 precursor loops by two separate domains, and the protein's documented promoter occupancy in neuroblastoma is indirect, through ZNF143.

Whether MBNL2's measured duplex-DNA preference means anything in cells is open. Protein-binding-microarray and HT-SELEX data recover a GCTT-containing preference on double-stranded DNA that is consistent with the protein's YGCY RNA specificity, but the work cited here establishes no cellular DNA-binding function for any muscleblind protein.

families.name: TAL1 / LYL1 (hematopoietic)
families.def: E-box CAGCTG/CAGGTG within composite GATA-E-box elements. TAL1, TAL2, LYL1.
families.short: TAL1 (SCL), LYL1 and TAL2 are haematopoietic and endothelial class II basic helix-loop-helix proteins with no intrinsic DNA-binding activity: they bind only as heterodimers with the class I E-proteins E12/E47, TCF4 or TCF12. In blood cells the functional unit is larger still — a pentameric complex in which LMO2 bridges the TAL1-E47 dimer to GATA1 or GATA2 with LDB1 — and it reads a composite element made of an E-box followed about nine base pairs later by a GATA site. TAL1 is required for all primitive haematopoiesis and is the most frequently activated oncogene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The family is the atlas's clearest example of a motif that is really a composite, and partly a partner's.
families.long:
## The factors

TAL1 (also called SCL), LYL1 and TAL2 are class II bHLH proteins of the blood and endothelial lineages. TAL1 is the founding member, identified through the chromosomal rearrangements that activate it in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. None of them binds DNA on its own: binding-site selection showed that TAL1 polypeptides have no intrinsic DNA-binding activity, presumably because they cannot homodimerise, and acquire it only on heterodimerising with a class A (class I) partner — E12, E47, TCF4/E2-2 or TCF12/HEB [PMID:8289805]. In blood cells TAL1 rarely acts as a bare heterodimer either. It sits in a pentameric complex in which the LIM-only protein LMO2 bridges the TAL1-E47 dimer to GATA1 (or GATA2), with LDB1/NLI completing the assembly [PMID:9214632]; a crystal structure of LMO2 bound to the SCL:E47 bHLH heterodimer shows how the bridge is made [PMID:23831025]. Expression: TAL1 in haematopoietic stem cells, erythroid, megakaryocytic and mast lineages and in endothelium; LYL1 in stem, endothelial and myeloid cells; TAL2 is narrowly expressed and poorly characterised. Because all three depend on the same E-proteins and the same partners, there is no expectation that they differ in sequence preference.

## The motif

The TAL1 heterodimer's selected consensus is AACAGATGGT, which decomposes into a half-site read by the class A partner (AACAG) and one read by TAL1 (ATGGT) [PMID:8289805]. In erythroid cells, an unbiased search of TAL1 ChIP-seq peaks gave CAGNTG as the preferred E-box [PMID:20566737], which is why the atlas consensus is written that way; the representative model here is the Vierstra archetype `AC0077:LYL/OLIG:bHLH` with consensus AACAGCTG.

The functional site in blood is not the E-box alone. The LMO2/LDB1 complex binds a bipartite element: an E-box, canonically CAGGTG, followed roughly nine base pairs downstream by a GATA site (WGATAA) [PMID:9214632]. This composite E-box-GATA element is the signature of TAL1 activity at erythroid and megakaryocytic enhancers, and it is the reason this family is a textbook case of an indirect or composite motif. The highest-information TAL1 model in HOCOMOCO, `TAL1.H14CORE.0.P.B`, reads TGGNNNNNVCAGATAAG — the 3' end of an E-box, a short spacer, and then AGATAAG, which is the GATA motif. The atlas flags this model as matching the GATA family, and it is right to: viewed as a position weight matrix, most of the information in that "TAL1 motif" is GATA information. A second flagged model, JASPAR TAL1::TCF3 MA0091.2 (ACCATCTGTT), matches the MYOD family instead. So of seven motifs assigned here, the two best known are each closer to another family than to their own label.

There is a further structural limitation: every HOCOMOCO model in this family carries the evidence letter `P` (ChIP-seq) with grade B or C. There is no HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX model for TAL1 or LYL1 in the collection at all. Cohesion is 0.75 over just seven motifs, the smallest and weakest of the tissue-specific bHLH families here.

## Where it acts

TAL1 occupies thousands of sites in erythroid and megakaryocytic cells, concentrated at lineage-specific enhancers of red-cell and platelet genes rather than at CpG-island promoters. About four fifths of erythroid targets require TAL1's own DNA-binding activity; the remaining fifth, enriched among the highest-affinity peaks, are occupied by a DNA-binding-deficient TAL1, which is direct evidence that some "TAL1 sites" are recruitment sites, not recognition sites [PMID:20566737]. Target sets are lineage-specific: TAL1 occupies largely different regions in erythroid and megakaryocytic cells [PMID:21179004]. Co-occurring motifs are GATA (GATA1 in erythroid cells, GATA2 in progenitors), KLF1, NFE2, RUNX1 and FLI1; simultaneous mapping of GATA1/GATA2, RUNX1, FLI1 and SCL in megakaryocytes showed heavy combinatorial overlap [PMID:21571218]. In T-ALL, TAL1 forms a core regulatory circuit with GATA3, RUNX1 and MYB at large enhancer clusters [PMID:22897851].

## Biology and disease

*Tal1*/*Scl*-null mouse embryos make no blood: yolk-sac haematopoiesis is absent and the embryos die at mid-gestation, the cleanest demonstration that this factor sits at the top of the haematopoietic hierarchy [PMID:7624372,7830794]. In humans, TAL1 is the most commonly activated oncogene in T-ALL, through t(1;14)(p32;q11), through the *SIL-TAL1* interstitial deletion, and through small somatic insertions in a non-coding region upstream of *TAL1* that create a MYB binding site and nucleate a new super-enhancer [PMID:25394790]. LYL1 is activated by t(7;19) in T-ALL. The TAL1-driven circuit in T-ALL is a candidate therapeutic target because it depends on the large enhancer clusters it creates.

## Reading a hit

Little in this family licenses a factor-level conclusion. CAGNTG or AACAGATGGT is an ordinary E-box and matches E-proteins, MYOD-family and NEUROD-family models; the archetype covering LYL1 is named LYL/OLIG because the two could not be separated. If you want evidence of TAL1 complex activity, look for the composite architecture — an E-box and a WGATAA about nine bases apart — and not for the E-box alone. Conversely, if a GATA-like motif is the top hit in a TAL1 ChIP experiment, that is the expected result for the composite element and is not evidence that TAL1 binds GATA sites directly; the same logic applies in reverse to GATA1 experiments recovering E-boxes. Because this family has no in vitro model, "TAL1 binds this sequence" rests on the older biochemistry rather than on the database entries, and the database entries should be read as occupancy models for a multiprotein complex.
families.caveats: Read this family's database entries as occupancy models for a complex, not as recognition sequences. Every HOCOMOCO model here is ChIP-only (evidence letter P, grade B or C); there is no HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX model for TAL1 or LYL1. The highest-information TAL1 model is essentially the GATA motif with an E-box fragment upstream, which is the composite E-box-GATA element rather than a TAL1 recognition site, and a second widely used model (JASPAR TAL1::TCF3) matches the MYOD family. The bare E-box CAGNTG carries almost no discriminating information. TAL1, TAL2 and LYL1 are not separable from sequence; the archetype covering LYL1 also covers OLIG.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection shows TAL1 has no intrinsic DNA-binding activity and cannot homodimerise, but as a heterodimer with E12, E47, E2-2 or HEB it selects AACAGATGGT, an asymmetric E-box in which each partner reads its own half-site.
timeline.methods: in vitro binding-site selection with recombinant proteins
timeline.open: Whether the selected site is the one used in blood cells was untested.

timeline.finding: Two groups show that Tal1/Scl-null mouse embryos make no blood at all, with yolk-sac haematopoiesis absent and death at mid-gestation.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting

timeline.finding: The functional element in erythroid cells is redefined as a composite: LMO2 bridges a TAL1-E47 dimer to GATA1 with LDB1/NLI, and the assembled pentamer binds an E-box (CAGGTG) followed about nine base pairs downstream by a GATA site, so the free E-box is not the unit of recognition.
timeline.methods: co-immunoprecipitation and gel-shift assays on a bipartite element
timeline.open: How strict the nine-base spacing is, and whether the same architecture operates outside erythroid cells.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide mapping in primary erythroid cells gives CAGNTG as the TAL1-preferred E-box, and shows that while most targets need TAL1's own DNA-binding activity, about one fifth — concentrated among the highest-affinity peaks — still recruit a DNA-binding-deficient TAL1.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq plus rescue with a DNA-binding mutant
timeline.open: Which partner tethers TAL1 at the binding-independent sites was not resolved.

timeline.finding: TAL1 is shown to occupy largely different regions in erythroid and megakaryocytic cells, and simultaneous mapping of GATA1/GATA2, RUNX1, FLI1 and SCL in megakaryocytes shows heavy combinatorial overlap, so the target set is set by partners and lineage rather than by the E-box.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in two haematopoietic lineages

timeline.finding: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia TAL1 is found at the centre of a self-reinforcing core regulatory circuit with GATA3, RUNX1 and MYB at large enhancer clusters.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and knockdown in T-ALL lines

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of (SCL:E47)bHLH:LMO2:LDB1 on DNA shows that LMO2 strengthens the SCL-E47 heterodimer but rotates E47 in a way that weakens its own contact with DNA, shifting DNA binding onto other complex members — a structural basis for TAL1 acting without reading DNA itself.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography with biochemistry
timeline.open: How far this explains the binding-independent occupancy seen genome-wide.

timeline.finding: Small somatic insertions in a precise noncoding site upstream of TAL1 are shown to create a MYB binding motif that nucleates a new super-enhancer and recruits the RUNX1-GATA3-TAL1 complex, activating the oncogene by motif creation rather than by translocation.
timeline.methods: targeted sequencing of noncoding regions, ChIP and editing in T-ALL lines

open: Whether the matrices stored for this family describe TAL1 recognition or complex occupancy is unresolved: every HOCOMOCO model is ChIP-only, no HT-SELEX or methyl-SELEX model exists for TAL1 or LYL1, and the one published selection consensus (AACAGATGGT) does not match the ChIP-derived CAGNTG well.

The split between direct and tethered binding is unsettled: about one fifth of erythroid TAL1 targets, concentrated among the strongest peaks, remain occupied by a DNA-binding-deficient protein, and a crystal structure shows LMO2 weakening the heterodimer's own DNA contact, but which partner holds TAL1 at those sites genome-wide has not been established.

It is unclear whether the composite E-box-GATA element requires the roughly nine-base spacing reported for the erythroid pentamer or merely prefers it, and no spacing-aware matrix for the composite element exists in these databases, so scans must look for the two parts separately.

Whether TAL1, TAL2 and LYL1 differ in sequence preference at all has never been tested side by side in vitro; the Vierstra archetype covering LYL1 is named LYL/OLIG because footprint-derived motifs for the two groups could not be separated.

families.name: BHLHE40 / BHLHE41 (DEC1/2)
families.def: Class B E-box CACGTG repressors of the circadian and hypoxia programs.
families.short: BHLHE40 and BHLHE41 - also known as DEC1/STRA13/SHARP-2 and DEC2/SHARP-1 - are bHLH repressors without a leucine zipper that bind the class-B E-box CACGTG and shut down transcription, both by competing for E-boxes with activating dimers such as CLOCK-BMAL1 and by recruiting histone deacetylases without contacting DNA. Their own promoters carry hypoxia response elements, so they couple HIF signalling to the E-box landscape. A BHLHE41 missense change causes familial natural short sleep in humans and mice, BHLHE40 is required for pathogenic T cell cytokine output, and the two together control alveolar macrophage identity. Because they read the same site as circadian activators, the sequence alone cannot tell you whether an E-box is being activated or repressed.
families.long:
## The factors

BHLHE40 and BHLHE41 are two closely related basic helix-loop-helix repressors that have accumulated an unusual number of names: BHLHE40 is also DEC1, STRA13, SHARP-2 and BHLHB2; BHLHE41 is also DEC2, SHARP-1 and BHLHB3. Unlike MYC, MAX, USF and the MiT/TFE proteins, they are plain bHLH proteins with no leucine zipper; they homodimerize, heterodimerize with each other, and contain a C-terminal repression region rather than an activation domain. They were found independently several times - as a retinoic-acid-inducible gene that blocked mesodermal and promoted neuronal differentiation of P19 cells, as neuronal-activity-coupled enhancer-of-split- and hairy-related proteins, and as clock components [PMID:9284045,9532582,12397359] - which is why the nomenclature is so tangled. Both are broadly expressed and strongly inducible: their promoters contain functional hypoxia response elements and are direct HIF targets [PMID:12354771], and they also respond to serum, TGF-beta and retinoic acid. That makes them stimulus-driven repressors superimposed on a constitutive E-box landscape. They repress by two mechanisms: competing for E-boxes with activating bHLH dimers, and binding proteins - notably BMAL1 and histone deacetylases - without necessarily contacting DNA [PMID:12397359,12657651]. The atlas assigns 7 motifs here (2 JASPAR, 3 HOCOMOCO, 2 CIS-BP) over both symbols, cohesion 0.93, with BHLHE40 (MA0464.3) as the representative.

## The motif

The site is the class-B E-box CACGTG [PMID:12297495,12657651], the same 6-bp palindrome read by MYC-MAX, USF and MiT/TFE, with each CAC half-site contacted by the conserved histidine, glutamate and arginine of one basic region. In vitro, BHLHE40 homodimers bind best when the core is preceded by a T and/or followed by an A [PMID:12297495], and the models for both paralogues mostly show the same T/A flanks. The BHLHE41 models carry the longer extended palindrome GTCACGTGAC or GTCACGTGC - the USF and CLEAR-box form - and the JASPAR and CIS-BP BHLHE40 models read tCACGTGa and CACGTGa. The one G-flanked model is the A-grade HOCOMOCO BHLHE40 model, GCACGTG, which prefers G over T before the core but keeps a weaker A after it, so it is still compatible with the in vitro preference. The BHLHE40 models are shorter and carry less flanking information than the BHLHE41 ones, and the similarity scores show BHLHE41 models matching other families' motifs about as well as they match BHLHE40's. One HOCOMOCO BHLHE40 model is not a single site at all but a tandem pair, CACGTGnnnvgCACGTGa: two E-boxes separated by five base pairs. Clock-gene promoters do carry tandem E-boxes, but there the spacing that supports rhythmic transcription is six or seven base pairs, and a five-base spacer nearly abolished oscillation of a Per2 reporter [PMID:18177499], so the model should not be read as the circadian element. The Vierstra footprint archetype covering these motifs is labelled AC0066:USF/BHLHE:bHLH, an explicit statement that USF and BHLHE40/41 motifs did not separate in footprint data [PMID:32728250].

## Where it acts

These factors act at promoter-proximal E-boxes in accessible chromatin, in three recurring contexts: circadian genes, where they sit on the same E-boxes used by CLOCK-BMAL1 in PER and DBP promoters [PMID:12397359]; hypoxia-responsive genes, where they are both HIF targets and themselves repressors, giving a feed-forward loop [PMID:12354771,18345027]; and immune and metabolic loci, where BHLHE40 in particular is induced by activation signals [PMID:11668339]. Because a substantial part of their repression is protein-mediated, a fraction of their ChIP signal can be expected at sites they do not contact directly. Their binding does not mark a cell type: both are widely expressed, and what changes is induction level and the time of day.

## Biology and disease

DEC1 and DEC2 were shown to repress CLOCK-BMAL1-driven transactivation of the mPer1 promoter [PMID:12397359] and to shift the behavioural clock, placing them in the negative limb of the mammalian oscillator alongside the cryptochromes. The clearest human genetic result is a BHLHE41 missense change (reported as P385R, and numbered P384R in the same group's later work) segregating with the familial natural short sleep trait; the same substitution shortens sleep in transgenic mice [PMID:19679812,29531056]. Immunologically, Bhlhe40-deficient mice show defective T cell activation and develop autoimmune disease [PMID:11668339], and Bhlhe40 is required for the cytokine output that makes T cells pathogenic in autoimmune neuroinflammation [PMID:24699451]. Both paralogues together control alveolar macrophage self-renewal and identity [PMID:31414712]. They have also been linked to hypoxic repression of specific targets, including the mismatch-repair gene MLH1 [PMID:18345027] and SREBP-1c, and to tumour behaviour, though the direction varies by tissue.

## Reading a hit

A CACGTG hit does not distinguish BHLHE40 or BHLHE41 from MYC-MAX, USF, MITF/TFE3/TFEB, SREBP, HIF-ARNT or CLOCK-BMAL1. In the circadian case this ambiguity is biologically real rather than a technical limitation: the same E-box is an activating element when CLOCK-BMAL1 occupies it and a repressing one when DEC1/DEC2 do [PMID:12397359], so the sequence alone cannot even tell you the sign of the effect. BHLHE40 and BHLHE41 are not distinguishable from one another by sequence; models for both favor the same T/A flanks, and the differences in model length are not a reliable discriminator. Because both repress partly through protein interaction, a ChIP peak without a motif is an expected outcome here, not necessarily an artifact - and conversely, a motif match is not evidence that repression at that site is DNA-binding-dependent.
families.caveats: A CACGTG match cannot separate BHLHE40/41 from MYC-MAX, USF, MITF/TFE, SREBP, HIF-ARNT or CLOCK-BMAL1, and the Vierstra archetype carrying these motifs is explicitly labelled USF/BHLHE because the two did not separate in footprint data. The two paralogues are not distinguishable from each other: models for both favor a T before and an A after the core, and only one HOCOMOCO BHLHE40 model prefers a G before it. Since both repress partly by protein-protein interaction with BMAL1 and HDACs, motif-free ChIP peaks are expected, and a motif match does not establish that repression at that site requires DNA binding.

open: How much DEC repression requires DNA binding is not known: DEC1 and DEC2 repress CLOCK-BMAL1 both by competing for E-boxes and by binding BMAL1, and DEC2 also acts on MyoD, E-proteins and SP1 without DNA contact, but the relative contributions at endogenous targets are not established.

Whether the tandem HOCOMOCO BHLHE40 model (CACGTGnnnvgCACGTGa, HT-SELEX only, grade C) reflects cooperative binding to paired E-boxes in cells has not been established; its five-base spacing differs from the six or seven bases of the tandem E-box element of clock genes, so circadian promoters do not by themselves support it.

families.name: BCL6 / BCL6B
families.def: STAT-like TTCCTAGAA bound by the BTB-ZF repressors BCL6, BCL6B.
families.short: BCL6 and its paralogue BCL6B (BAZF) are BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressors that bind a nine-base site, TTCCTAGAA, which is a TTCNNNGAA element of the same class that STAT dimers use. That overlap is not incidental: BCL6 represses interleukin-4-induced, STAT6-dependent genes by occupying sites that STAT6 would otherwise use, so the same sequence can be an activating STAT element or a repressed BCL6 element depending on which protein is present. BCL6 is required for germinal center formation and for follicular helper T cells, and its deregulation by chromosomal translocation or promoter mutation occurs in a large fraction of diffuse large B-cell lymphomas. A hit to this motif is ambiguous between BCL6, BCL6B and the STAT family.
families.long:
## The factors

Two paralogues: BCL6 (also LAZ3, ZBTB27) and BCL6B (BAZF, ZBTB28). Both have the standard BTB-ZF architecture - an N-terminal BTB/POZ domain, a central region with PEST and RD2 repression motifs, and six C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers [PMID:8692924]. The BTB domain obligately homodimerizes, and the dimer creates a lateral groove at the interface into which the SMRT and NCOR corepressors dock through a short peptide; the crystal structure of that complex explained how one BTB dimer recruits corepressor and provided the target site for the small-molecule BCL6 inhibitors and degraders developed since [PMID:14690607]. Repression is therefore corepressor-dependent and also involves BCOR and HDAC recruitment. BCL6 is expressed at high levels in germinal center B cells and in follicular helper T cells, at lower levels in macrophages and other tissues [PMID:9171827,19628815]; BCL6B is expressed in endothelium, some T-cell subsets and neural tissue and is much less studied. The two proteins bind DNA as dimers, and the six fingers give a footprint consistent with a nine- to twelve-base site.

## The motif

The site is written in the literature as TTCCTAGAA, sometimes generalized to TTCCT(A/C)GAA [PMID:7945383,11374866]. Parsed as TTC-CTA-GAA it is a TTCNNNGAA element - structurally the same family of sites that STAT dimers occupy as gamma-interferon activated sequences (GAS elements) [PMID:9110977,11374866]. All the matrices here are consistent with that once strand is taken into account: the HOCOMOCO grade-A BCL6 model reads GCTTTCGAGGAAT and JASPAR MA0463.3 reads GCTTTCGAGGAA, whose reverse complements are TTCCTCGAAAGC, while the BCL6B HT-SELEX models read TGCTTTCTAGGAATTCA, reverse-complementing to TTCCTAGAAAGCA [PMID:23332764]. So BCL6 models favor TTCCTCGAA and BCL6B models TTCCTAGAA; both fit TTCCTNGAA, and the difference at that one central position is the only sequence feature that even hints at a paralogue distinction. It is not enough to act on: the BCL6 and BCL6B models are 0.91-0.97 similar, and the Vierstra archetype for the family is named AC0665:BCL/BCL6B, an explicit statement that the two were not separable. Information content is high for a C2H2 family - the BCL6B matrices reach nearly 30 bits because they include long flanks - but much of that comes from the flanking bases selected in vitro rather than from the core, and long high-information matrices of this kind tend to overfit. One entry in the family contradicts the rest outright: CIS-BP M00227, labelled BCL6, reads TAATTAA and its nearest cross-database neighbors are PRD-like homeodomain motifs. It does not belong with the other BCL6 models.

## Where it acts

BCL6 binds promoters and enhancers of genes that must be held off during the germinal center reaction: DNA damage response and checkpoint genes (TP53, CDKN1A, ATR), differentiation genes (PRDM1), and cytokine and chemokine genes [PMID:21900183,22894929]. In T cells it represses the Th1, Th2 and Th17 programs while promoting the follicular helper program [PMID:19628815]. Because the site is a GAS-type element, BCL6 sites overlap physically with STAT sites at shared loci - the germline immunoglobulin epsilon (Iepsilon) promoter is the worked example, where BCL6 occupancy blocks STAT6-driven transcription and IgE class switching [PMID:10490661]. TTCCTNGAA is AT-rich, CpG-free and about nine informative bases, so chance occurrences are frequent; occupancy is set by BCL6 abundance, which is itself tightly controlled by phosphorylation-triggered degradation and by MYC-driven transcription in the germinal center.

## Biology and disease

Bcl6-null mice form no germinal centers, cannot mount high-affinity antibody responses, and develop a lethal inflammatory syndrome with eosinophilia and Th2-skewed cytokine production [PMID:9110977,9171827] - a phenotype that connects directly to the STAT6 antagonism. Bcl6 is also required for follicular helper T cell development, and enforced Bcl6 expression drives T cells into that program [PMID:19628815]. In human disease, BCL6 is the most frequently translocated locus in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: chromosomal rearrangements juxtapose heterologous promoters to the BCL6 coding sequence and prevent its normal downregulation [PMID:8235596], and point mutations in the BCL6 promoter region have the same effect. BCL6 is also deregulated in follicular lymphoma and in some T-cell lymphomas. The BTB lateral groove has been exploited pharmacologically, with peptide and small-molecule inhibitors and BTB-directed degraders in development [PMID:14690607]. BCL6B has no comparable disease association and is best described as an understudied paralogue.

## Reading a hit

The central caution is the STAT overlap. A TTCNNNGAA match is compatible with BCL6, with BCL6B, and with STAT1, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A/B and (with the N4 spacing) STAT6; the sequence does not distinguish a repressed BCL6 site from an activated STAT site, and at some loci the same element is both at different times. If your interest is signaling, do not read a BCL6 motif hit as evidence against STAT involvement, or vice versa - the correct inference is that the locus is contested. Within the family, BCL6 and BCL6B are not separable; the slight preference of BCL6 models for a central C and BCL6B models for a central A is within the noise of a single position. Evidence quality is otherwise good: HOCOMOCO BCL6 and BCL6B core models are grade A with PSM evidence, and JASPAR MA0463.3 and MA0731.1 are HT-SELEX, so direct binding is well supported [PMID:23332764,28473536]. Two practical exclusions: discard CIS-BP M00227 (TAATTAA), which is a homeodomain-like site mislabelled as BCL6, and be wary of scoring with the full 17-position BCL6B matrix, whose extreme information content comes largely from in vitro-selected flanks that are unlikely to be conserved in real promoters. Cell context is the strongest supporting evidence: a germinal center B cell or follicular helper T cell makes a BCL6 call reasonable.
families.caveats: The site is a TTCNNNGAA GAS element, so a match is ambiguous between BCL6, BCL6B and the STAT family; BCL6 is documented to repress STAT6-dependent genes by competing for overlapping sites, so a hit indicates a contested element rather than a settled assignment. BCL6 and BCL6B motifs are 0.91-0.97 similar and the Vierstra archetype merges them by name. The nine-base core is AT-rich and CpG-free and occurs often by chance. Two specific data problems: CIS-BP M00227 labelled BCL6 is a homeodomain-like TAATTAA site that does not belong in this family, and the 17-position BCL6B HT-SELEX matrix draws much of its information from selected flanks.

timeline.finding: BCL-6 was cloned from the chromosome 3q27 translocations of diffuse large-cell lymphoma and found truncated in its 5' noncoding region in a third of cases, identifying a zinc-finger gene whose expression is deregulated in that disease.
timeline.methods: positional cloning of translocation breakpoints, Southern blotting of tumor panels
timeline.open: Whether the protein binds DNA and what it does transcriptionally.

timeline.finding: A recombinant BCL6 zinc-finger fusion selected the 14-base site (T/A)NCTTTCNAGG(A/G)AT, and full-length BCL6 was then shown to repress from that site through an autonomous N-terminal repression region including the POZ domain - defining both the word and the activity.
timeline.methods: random-oligonucleotide selection, EMSA, DNase I footprinting, transfection reporters
timeline.open: Which genes carry the site in vivo.

timeline.finding: Two BCL6 knockout lines showed loss of germinal centers with a lethal Th2-skewed inflammatory disease, and the recognition site was noted to resemble STAT binding sequences, with BCL6 able to repress interleukin-4-induced transcription from a STAT6 site - the first statement that this motif is contested between a repressor and a signaling activator.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, immunophenotyping, reporter assays on STAT sites

timeline.finding: BCL6 was shown to bind several STAT6 elements with different affinities and to repress interleukin-4-induced germline epsilon transcription; BCL6-null mice switched to IgE more readily, and the defect disappeared in BCL6-STAT6 double knockouts, making the competition genetically explicit.
timeline.methods: EMSA on STAT6 elements, class-switch assays, double-knockout mice

timeline.finding: The consensus for the paralogue BAZF/BCL6B was determined as ATTCCTAGAAAG, essentially the BCL6 site, and both proteins were shown to bind natural STAT6 elements weakly, with a single C-to-T substitution in the interleukin-4 STAT6 site strongly increasing binding - locating the discrimination between a GAS element and a BCL6 site at one or two bases.
timeline.methods: binding-site selection, EMSA with natural and mutated STAT6 probes

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the BCL6 BTB homodimer bound to a SMRT peptide showed that two corepressor fragments dock symmetrically into a lateral groove formed at the dimer interface, explaining how dimerization and repression are coupled and giving a druggable surface.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography at 2.2 A with biochemical and cellular validation

timeline.finding: Bcl6 was shown to be required for follicular helper T cell development and sufficient to drive that program while suppressing other helper lineages, extending the factor's role from the B-cell germinal center to its T-cell partner and in a DNA-binding-dependent manner.
timeline.methods: conditional and retroviral expression in mouse T cells, immunization experiments

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX re-measured both paralogues in vitro and returned the same TTCCTNGAA core with long flanks, which is what the current JASPAR and HOCOMOCO models encode; the in vitro data confirm direct binding but do not separate BCL6 from BCL6B.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX across human transcription factors

open: Whether BCL6 and the STAT factors actually compete for the same genomic elements, or occupy adjoining but distinguishable subsets, is unsettled: biochemistry shows that one or two bases shift the preference between a GAS element and a BCL6 site, but no genome-wide study has classified occupied TTCNNNGAA elements by which protein binds them in which state.

The only hint of a sequence difference between the paralogues is a central C in BCL6 models against a central A in BCL6B models, and it is unknown whether this is a real preference or a sampling difference between the experiments behind the two matrices.
BCL6B has no disease association and little functional literature, so whether it is a redundant copy of BCL6 in endothelium and T-cell subsets or has its own target set has not been tested.

The CIS-BP entry M00227 labelled BCL6 reads TAATTAA and clusters with PRD-like homeodomain motifs, and nothing explains whether this is a mislabelled model or a record of some indirect association; no BCL6 literature reports binding to an AT-rich homeodomain-type site.

families.name: DACH / SKI-family corepressors
families.def: DACH1/DACH2 (DD1 winged-helix, binds forkhead-like sites and competes with FOXM1) and the SKI/SnoN/SKOR corepressors (SKI, SKIL, SKOR1, SKOR2), whose DNA contact comes from a SAND-like motif in the Ski homology domain. Their ChIP motifs often resemble those of the homeodomain partners they are recruited by.
families.short: These are transcriptional corepressors, not classical sequence-specific activators. DACH1 and DACH2 are the vertebrate Dachshund proteins, and SKI, SKIL/SnoN, SKOR1 and SKOR2 are the Ski family; all share a Dachshund homology domain with a winged-helix fold related to forkhead. They work mostly by being recruited: DACH proteins into SIX/EYA complexes and onto forkhead sites where they compete with FOXM1, the Ski proteins onto SMAD complexes to shut down TGF-beta signalling, and SKOR1/SKOR2 onto homeodomain factors such as LBX1. The motifs in this family therefore look borrowed. The best-supported models, TTAATTAC for SKOR1 and SKOR2, are indistinguishable from homeodomain dimer sites, which is what you would expect from proteins that arrive at DNA on someone else's back.
families.long:
## The factors

Two lineages sit in this family because they share one domain. DACH1 and DACH2 are the vertebrate
homologues of *Drosophila* dachshund, a retinal determination gene. Their conserved N-terminal region, the
Dachshund homology domain or DD1, was solved crystallographically and turned out to adopt a winged-helix
fold of the kind used by forkhead proteins, with a surface consistent with DNA binding [PMID:12057194]; a second conserved
region, DD2, mediates protein-protein interaction. The Ski family, SKI, SKIL (SnoN), SKOR1 and SKOR2,
carries a homologous Dachshund homology domain; the crystal structure of the human SKI domain confirmed the
same fold and identified a SAND-like element within it as the likely DNA-contacting surface [PMID:15130471]. None of these
proteins has a homeodomain, a zinc finger or a leucine zipper. All of them function primarily as
corepressors that recruit histone deacetylase and N-CoR complexes to sites chosen by a partner: DACH
proteins into SIX-EYA complexes on SIX target promoters, SKI and SnoN onto SMAD2/3 and SMAD4 complexes at
TGF-beta response elements, and SKOR1 and SKOR2, originally named Corl1 and Corl2, onto the homeodomain
protein LBX1 and related factors in developing neurons [PMID:12215533,10485843,15528197].

## The motif

There is no single well-founded consensus, and the two lineages point in different directions. For the DACH
proteins, the functional claim from cell biology is that DACH1 binds forkhead-type sequences and thereby
competes with FOXM1 for its targets [PMID:20351289]; the winged-helix fold of DD1 makes that structurally plausible. The
database models for DACH1 and DACH2, however, are HT-SELEX motifs reading CAATCGTCATAATT and TGACGATTG,
which are not forkhead sites, are the weakest-matching members of this family internally, and should be
treated as provisional [PMID:23332764]. For SKOR1 and SKOR2 the models are much stronger and mutually consistent: in vitro
selection and methyl-selection give TTAATTAC and CTTTAATTAA, around 15 to 16 bits, reproduced in CIS-BP as
TTAATTACAGNT [PMID:23332764,28473536]. Read as a homeodomain site, TTAATTAC is a TAAT/ATTA arrangement of exactly the type that
LHX, ALX and ARX homeodomains bind as cooperative dimers, and that is what the data show: the
nearest neighbours of these models outside the family are LHX, ALX and ARX homeodomain motifs, at
similarities of 0.88 to 0.93. Whether the Ski/Dachshund winged helix genuinely prefers this sequence, or
whether the selection experiments captured the preference of an associated homeodomain partner, is not
settled. The family consensus offered here, TTAATTAC, is therefore the observed motif, not a validated
statement about which protein reads it.

## Where it acts

DACH1 occupies promoters and enhancers in complexes with SIX1 and EYA proteins, where the three together
convert a SIX-bound site from repressed to activated via CREB-binding protein [PMID:12215533], and at forkhead sites where
DACH1 opposes FOXM1-driven proliferative programs. SKI and SnoN are found wherever SMAD complexes are, so
their apparent binding footprint is the SMAD-binding element landscape of TGF-beta and BMP signalling [PMID:10485843].
SKOR1 and SKOR2 are restricted to specific neuronal lineages: SKOR1 in dorsal horn interneurons with LBX1 [PMID:15528197],
SKOR2 in cerebellar Purkinje cell precursors, where it is a selective marker and drives early
differentiation [PMID:18522874,24491816]. The practical consequence is that these factors' genome-wide occupancy tracks the
expression and occupancy of their partners, so composite elements in the useful sense are the partner's
elements: a SIX site, a SMAD-binding element, or an LBX1-type homeodomain site.

## Biology and disease

DACH1 restrains proliferation: it inhibits cyclin D1 and breast tumour growth [PMID:16980615], binds SMAD4 to attenuate
TGF-beta signalling [PMID:14525983], and attenuates forkhead signalling [PMID:20351289]. It is downregulated in several carcinomas, and
transcriptome-wide association work identified DACH1 as a kidney disease risk gene contributing to fibrosis,
making it a candidate target in chronic kidney disease [PMID:33998598]. DACH1 and DACH2 act redundantly in Mullerian duct
development. SKI and SnoN are proto-oncoproteins by virtue of repressing TGF-beta growth inhibition [PMID:10485843], and
SKI mutations cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome [PMID:23023332]. SKOR2/Corl2 is required for early Purkinje cell
differentiation [PMID:24491816]. The SKOR1 locus, formerly LBXCOR1, was one of the three regions identified in the first
genome-wide association study of restless legs syndrome, alongside MEIS1 and BTBD9 [PMID:17637780].

## Reading a hit

Be sceptical in a specific way. A TTAATTAC hit is a good homeodomain dimer site and a poor SKOR
identification: if you scan with the SKOR1 or SKOR2 model you will recover LHX, ALX and ARX sites, and in
this family's own data those motifs are the nearest neighbours. Conversely, if a ChIP experiment on any of
these proteins yields a homeodomain or SMAD or forkhead motif, the most likely explanation is indirect
binding through the partner that recruited them, which is the mechanism these proteins are known for. The
DACH1 and DACH2 models are the weakest members of the family internally and do not match the forkhead-like
specificity that the functional literature describes, so a DACH1 motif hit should not be used as evidence
of DACH1 occupancy. In practice, use expression of the partner, not the motif, to decide whether a DACH or
Ski family protein is plausibly at a locus.
families.caveats: This family's motifs probably belong to other proteins. DACH and Ski family members have no homeodomain, no zinc finger and no leucine zipper; they are corepressors recruited by SIX/EYA, SMAD or homeodomain partners, and their conserved Dachshund homology domain has only a plausible, not a demonstrated, sequence preference. The strongest models here, SKOR1 and SKOR2 reading TTAATTAC, sit among LHX, ALX and ARX homeodomain motifs at 0.88 to 0.93 similarity, which is the expected signature of partner carry-over. The DACH1 and DACH2 models do not match the forkhead-like specificity the functional literature reports and are the weakest members internally. Do not call occupancy for these factors from a motif hit alone.

timeline.finding: SKI is shown to bind Smad2, Smad3 and Smad4 and to repress TGF-beta target genes from the Smad complex, establishing that a protein with no classical DNA-binding domain reaches TGF-beta response elements by riding on a partner.
timeline.methods: coimmunoprecipitation, reporter assays and mutational analysis in mammalian cells
timeline.open: Left open whether SKI contributes any sequence preference of its own at those elements.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the Dachshund homology domain of DACH shows a winged-helix fold of the type used by forkhead proteins, with a surface compatible with DNA binding, which is the structural basis for every later claim that these corepressors can contact DNA directly.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of the isolated domain
timeline.open: No DNA was present in the structure and no bound sequence was identified.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the Dachshund homology domain of human SKI confirms the same winged-helix fold in the Ski lineage and identifies a SAND-like element as the probable DNA-contacting surface, unifying the two lineages on structure rather than on sequence preference.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of the isolated domain
timeline.open: Again without DNA, so the predicted contacts remained untested.

timeline.finding: Corl1, later named SKOR1, is identified as a neuronal lineage-specific corepressor that binds the homeodomain protein Lbx1, which gives a concrete mechanism by which a Ski-family protein can be delivered to homeodomain sites.
timeline.methods: yeast two-hybrid, interaction mapping and expression analysis in mouse neural tube

timeline.finding: DACH1 is shown to attenuate forkhead signaling and to compete with FOXM1 at forkhead target genes, the main functional evidence that the DACH winged helix engages forkhead-type sequences.
timeline.methods: reporter assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation and expression analysis in cancer cell lines
timeline.open: Occupancy at forkhead sites could also reflect displacement of FOXM1 through protein contact rather than direct DNA binding by DACH1.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX on recombinant proteins produces the first measured models for this family and contradicts the functional picture: the DACH1 and DACH2 models are not forkhead-like, while SKOR models select a TTAATTAC arrangement that is a classic homeodomain dimer site.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Selection on a recombinant protein cannot exclude that a copurified or added homeodomain partner shaped the result.

timeline.finding: Methylation-sensitive HT-SELEX reproduces the SKOR1 and SKOR2 preference for TTAATTAA-type sites, making the homeodomain-like SKOR motif the best-supported model in the family while leaving its attribution unresolved.
timeline.methods: methyl-HT-SELEX

timeline.finding: A transcriptome-wide association study in human kidney identifies DACH1 as a risk gene for chronic kidney disease whose reduced expression contributes to fibrosis, giving the DACH lineage a human genetic phenotype outside cancer.
timeline.methods: transcriptome-wide association analysis with mouse and cell validation

open: It is unknown whether the Dachshund homology domain binds DNA directly in cells: both crystal structures show folds compatible with DNA binding, but neither contains DNA, and no protein-DNA complex or validated site has been reported for any member.

Whether TTAATTAC is the SKOR proteins' own preference or the preference of an associated homeodomain is unsettled: the site is a canonical LHX, ALX and ARX dimer element and the nearest neighbours of the SKOR models across all four databases are those homeodomain motifs, but no experiment has separated the two possibilities.

The functional literature and the database models disagree for DACH1: cell biology reports competition with FOXM1 at forkhead sites, while in vitro selection gives sequences that are not forkhead-like, and no study has tested the selected sequences for DACH1 occupancy or activity.

Whether SKOR1 is the gene through which the restless legs syndrome association acts is not established: the associated variants are non-coding, and the locus was named for SKOR1 by proximity rather than by a demonstrated effect on the protein.

families.name: TFAP4 (AP-4)
families.def: Palindromic E-box CAGCTG. TFAP4.
families.short: TFAP4 (AP-4) is a single-gene bHLH-LZ family with no close paralogue. Unusually for the class, a second zipper-like dimerization motif restricts it to homodimers, so it does not form the combinatorial heterodimers that dominate the rest of the bHLH class. It binds the palindromic class-A E-box CAGCTG, usually written extended as AACAGCTGAT. TFAP4 is a direct MYC target and represses the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A (p21), placing it in a MYC-driven cell-cycle circuit whose direction is context-dependent - growth-promoting in several carcinomas, tumour-suppressive in B lymphocytes. Because CAGCTG is shared with the E-proteins and with most tissue-restricted bHLH factors, a match is weak evidence for AP-4 specifically.
families.long:
## The factors

TFAP4 (AP-4) is a single-gene family: there is one human TFAP4 protein and no close paralogue, which makes it one of the few bHLH families where the usual paralogue problem does not apply. It is a basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper protein, but with an unusual architecture. Beyond the bHLH and the adjacent leucine zipper, AP-4 carries a second, more distal zipper-like dimerization motif; biochemical dissection showed that these multiple dimerization surfaces restrict it to homodimers and prevent it from partnering the other bHLH-ZIP proteins [PMID:2123466]. Functionally that puts AP-4 in the opposite position from the E-proteins: it does not form the combinatorial heterodimers that dominate the rest of the bHLH class, so its DNA-binding activity depends on its own expression level rather than on the availability of a partner. AP-4 was discovered as an enhancer-binding factor that cooperates with AP-1 to activate SV40 late transcription in vitro [PMID:2833704], and it is expressed broadly but at levels that follow proliferative signals, because TFAP4 is a direct MYC target gene [PMID:18818310]. The atlas assigns 6 motifs here (4 JASPAR, 1 HOCOMOCO, 1 CIS-BP), all labelled TFAP4, with cohesion of only 0.77 - the lowest in this batch - for reasons explained below.

## The motif

The AP-4 site is the palindromic class-A E-box CAGCTG, six base pairs, read as two CAG half-sites by the basic region of each monomer in the homodimer [PMID:2123466]. In the general bHLH scheme, CACGTG is the class-B E-box read by the MYC/MAX/USF/MITF group and CAGCTG (and CACCTG) is the class-A E-box read by the E-proteins and by tissue-restricted bHLH factors [PMID:10611221]; AP-4 is a class-A binder that happens to be a bHLH-ZIP. In the databases the motif is usually written extended, AaCAGCTGaT or CAGCTGtT, adding a weak preference for A/T immediately outside the core; that extra information is small and comes mainly from local DNA shape rather than from direct base contacts [PMID:23562153]. The low cohesion score has two concrete causes. First, two of the six models are not CAGCTG at all but CATATG-type CANNTG variants (aaCAtaTGtt in JASPAR MA1570.1, AhCATATG in CIS-BP), so the family contains two different E-box classes. Second, two of the models are JASPAR heterodimer profiles in which the TFAP4 half-site is fused to an ETS half-site - ACCGGAAACAGCTG with FLI1, cCGGAAGCAGsTG with ETV1 - which are composite models of a TFAP4-ETS pair rather than definitions of the AP-4 site itself. Across all four databases, the nearest neighbours of the TFAP4 models are usually motifs labelled with some other factor: label agreement is only 0.1-0.2. That is not an error in the databases; it is a statement that CAGCTG is not an AP-4-specific sequence.

## Where it acts

CAGCTG is a 6-bp palindrome and therefore expected several hundred thousand times in the human genome, and unlike CACGTG it contains no CpG and so is not depleted. AP-4 occupancy is concentrated at promoters of cell-cycle and proliferation genes, overlapping heavily with MYC-responsive promoters, which is unsurprising given that TFAP4 is MYC-induced. It can act as an activator or a repressor at the same class of site; at CDKN1A it is a repressor [PMID:18818310]. The JASPAR composite models suggest AP-4 half-sites adjacent to ETS half-sites as one recurring arrangement, and the founding observation was cooperation with AP-1 at the SV40 late enhancer, so AP-4 sites are best interpreted as part of composite promoter modules rather than as stand-alone elements.

## Biology and disease

AP-4 sits in a MYC-driven cell-cycle circuit. TFAP4 is induced directly by MYC and represses the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A (p21), so MYC can suppress p21 indirectly through AP-4 [PMID:18818310]; AP-4 is required for mitogen- and MYC-induced cell-cycle progression [PMID:25261373], and it attenuates DREAM-complex-mediated repression downstream of p53 [PMID:36831504]. The relationship is not uniformly oncogenic: in B lymphocytes, MYC was found to suppress tumorigenesis through TFAP4-dependent restriction of stemness, so the direction of the effect is context-dependent [PMID:34283887]. There is no well-established Mendelian disease attributed to TFAP4 in the sources reviewed here.

## Reading a hit

A CAGCTG match is close to uninformative about AP-4 on its own. The same core is the preferred site of TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, of MYOD and the myogenic bHLHs, of ASCL and NEUROD proteins, of TWIST/HAND, and of many other class-A binders, and it is common enough to occur by chance roughly every few kilobases. Nothing in the flanking preference reliably separates AP-4 from those. Use a CAGCTG hit as "class-A E-box", then argue from expression, from ChIP data and from promoter context. Do not treat the two JASPAR TFAP4::ETS models as TFAP4 motifs; they are composite dimer models. Do not treat the CATATG models as the canonical AP-4 site either.
families.caveats: CAGCTG is the generic class-A E-box: TCF3/TCF4/TCF12, MYOD, ASCL, NEUROD, TWIST and many others read it, and nothing in the flanking preference separates AP-4 from them. The site contains no CpG, so it is not depleted and occurs by chance every few kilobases. Family cohesion is only 0.77 because two of the six models are CATATG-type variants rather than CAGCTG, and two are JASPAR heterodimer profiles in which a TFAP4 half-site is fused to an ETS half-site; those composite models should not be used as AP-4 site definitions. Label agreement for these models is 0.1-0.2, meaning their nearest neighbours across databases usually carry a different factor name.
