timeline.finding: The dioxin-responsive element of the CYP1A1 enhancer was narrowed to the core 5'-TA/TGCGTG-3', with flanking bases required for full enhancer activity, giving the family its first sequence definition.
timeline.methods: Enhancer deletion and point mutagenesis with protein-DNA binding assays
timeline.open: Which subunit of the receptor complex read which half of the element.

timeline.finding: Binding-site selection with AHR, ARNT and SIM resolved the half-sites: ARNT supplies the 3' GTG in every complex while AHR prefers a 5' T(C/T)GC, so the XRE and the hypoxia response element differ mainly at the base immediately 5' of CGTG.
timeline.methods: In vitro binding-site selection (SELEX) with recombinant proteins

timeline.finding: Mice lacking Ahr were shown to be resistant to TCDD and to develop reduced liver size, hepatic fibrosis and immune defects, establishing that dioxin toxicity is mediated by the receptor rather than by nonspecific chemical injury.
timeline.methods: Mouse germline knockout with toxicological challenge

timeline.finding: AHRR was identified as an AHR-induced repressor that competes with AHR for ARNT and for the same response element, making the family a negative-feedback circuit and leaving the two proteins with one indistinguishable motif.
timeline.methods: Cloning, reporter assays, expression analysis

timeline.finding: Genome-wide ChIP-seq in TCDD-treated cells found 2,594 AHR-bound, 1,352 ARNT-bound and 882 co-bound regions, of which only about 60% contained a core GCGTG, and recovered a symmetrical GTGCGTG variant de novo; peaks were densest within 1 kb of transcription start sites but extended up to 100 kb away.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq with de novo motif discovery
timeline.open: Whether the core-free co-bound regions reflect tethering or unrecognized variant elements.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the AHR-ARNT heterodimer on a DRE showed ARNT curling around AHR in an intertwined asymmetric architecture and identified the contacts that discriminate the DRE from the hypoxia response element, placing specificity in local base contacts plus the dimerization interfaces.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Cryo-EM of the agonist-bound cytosolic Hsp90-XAP2-AHR complex resolved how the unliganded receptor is held before nuclear translocation, completing the path from ligand binding to DNA occupancy.
timeline.methods: Cryo-electron microscopy

timeline.finding: Systematic binding measurements across bHLH-PAS proteins reported 12-15 bp footprints in which flanking-base preferences, not the shared core, separate family members, revising the view that a 6-7 bp XRE core captures the specificity of this complex.
timeline.methods: High-throughput in vitro binding across family members
timeline.open: Whether the flanking information is recoverable from the ChIP-derived models that make up this family.

open: Whether the symmetrical GTGCGTG element recovered de novo from AHR ChIP-seq is a genuine second binding mode or a composite of overlapping canonical sites has not been settled, and no in vitro measurement for AHR discriminates between the two.

About 40% of AHR/ARNT co-bound regions contain no core element, and it remains open whether these reflect tethering of the receptor through other factors, degenerate sites below the scoring threshold, or a distinct low-affinity mode.

Whether AHR and AHRR can be distinguished at the level of DNA at all is unresolved: the two existing models are ChIP-derived and near-identical, and there is no in vitro specificity measurement for AHRR to compare against.

It is unclear whether the single base 5' of CGTG plus weak flanking preferences is sufficient in practice to separate an XRE from a hypoxia response element in genomic sequence, since the in vitro work says the discriminating information lies in the flanks while every collected model here encodes little beyond the core.

families.name: TBP / TATA
families.def: TATA box TATAWAWR. TBP, TAF1.
families.short: The TATA box is the oldest known eukaryotic core promoter element and the binding site of TBP, the TATA-box-binding protein. TBP is a saddle-shaped, internally pseudo-symmetric protein that straddles about eight base pairs of AT-rich DNA, reads them entirely from the minor groove, kinks the duplex at both ends and bends it by roughly 80 degrees. It works within TFIID for RNA polymerase II and within SL1 and TFIIIB for polymerases I and III, so a single protein serves all three. Because minor-groove contacts barely distinguish A:T from T:A, the element carries little information: the canonical TATAWAWR is present in only a small minority of human promoters, most of which are instead GC-rich and TATA-less. A TATA match on its own is therefore very weak evidence of anything.
families.long:
## The factors

TBP is a single small protein, about 180 residues in its conserved core, encoded by one gene. Its
fold is a pseudo-symmetric saddle: two structurally similar halves, each contributing a curved
beta sheet that forms the concave underside, with helices on the convex top surface where general
factors and activators dock [PMID:8413605,8413604]. TBP does not act alone. For RNA polymerase II it is the anchoring
subunit of TFIID, a roughly one-megadalton complex of thirteen or more TAF subunits [PMID:27007846]; for
polymerase I it sits in SL1 and for polymerase III in TFIIIB. Two paralogues exist, TBPL1
(TRF2/TLF) and TBPL2 (TRF3), which have the TBP fold but altered DNA-contacting surfaces and do
not bind TATA boxes; neither has a motif in the databases used here. TAF1, the largest TFIID
subunit, is included in this key because its motif models are attributed to a promoter-binding
component of the same machinery, but TAF1 is not a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein in the
way TBP is: its promoter contacts involve the initiator and downstream regions [PMID:27007846], and it carries
histone-acetyltransferase and bromodomain activities.

## The motif

The literature consensus is the eight-base TATAWAWR, most often realized as TATAAAAG or TATATAAG,
positioned roughly 25-30 bp upstream of the transcription start site in a focused promoter [PMID:17123746,28808065]. The
co-crystal structures of plant (Arabidopsis) and yeast TBP on TATA DNA showed why the information content is
low: TBP makes no major-groove base contacts at all [PMID:8413605,8413604,7634103]. It binds the minor groove, where an A:T and a
T:A base pair present nearly the same pattern of hydrogen-bond acceptors, and inserts pairs of
phenylalanine side chains between the first two and last two base pairs, kinking the helix at both
ends and bending the whole element by about 80 degrees while partially unwinding it [PMID:7634103,10617571]. What TBP
really reads is a short run of deformable, narrow-minor-groove AT-rich DNA, and later work showed
that a wide range of AT-rich variants are bound with comparable affinity [PMID:10617571]. The consequence for
motif models is direct: every matrix in this family is a low-information AT-rich model. The
representative here, the Vierstra archetype AC0057, is TATAAAAG; JASPAR MA0108.3 is TATAAAA;
HOCOMOCO's TBP model is CTATAAAAGG [PMID:37971293]. There is no half-site structure and no spacing rule, and
because TBP is a monomer on a pseudo-symmetric site, orientation is only weakly determined by
sequence, which is one reason TATA-box orientation prediction is unreliable. Family cohesion here
is only 0.64, and two of the five motifs are flagged as belonging elsewhere, discussed below.

## Where it acts

TATA boxes belong to focused, or sharp-initiation, promoters: a single dominant start site,
AT-rich surroundings, no CpG island [PMID:16645617]. These are a minority of mammalian promoters. A genome-scale
analysis found that about 76% of human core promoters have no TATA-like element, are GC-rich and
are enriched for SP1 sites; about 24% have something TATA-like, but only about 10% of those match
the canonical TATAWAWR, which puts canonical TATA boxes at a few percent of human genes [PMID:17123746]. Broad,
dispersed-initiation promoters in CpG islands dominate the mammalian genome, and these use the
initiator, downstream elements and TFIID-DNA contacts rather than a TATA box [PMID:16645617,28808065]. Functionally the
split is informative: TATA-less promoters skew toward housekeeping genes, while TATA-containing
promoters are enriched for highly regulated, stimulus-responsive and tissue-specific genes,
including many that are strongly induced by stress or hormones [PMID:17123746]. The cryo-EM structure of
promoter-bound human TFIID shows TBP on the TATA region while TAF subunits contact the
initiator and downstream promoter, so the TATA box is one anchor point in an extended,
multi-contact interaction rather than the sole determinant of where transcription starts [PMID:27007846].

## Biology and disease

TBP is essential in every organism tested; there is no viable null. Its N-terminal region in
humans contains a polyglutamine tract, and expansion of that tract to roughly 43 repeats or more
causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 17, a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder,
placing TBP among the polyglutamine diseases [PMID:11448935]. Mutations in individual TAFs cause developmental
syndromes and intellectual disability, and TAF1 variants are associated with X-linked
neurodevelopmental disease. TATA-box variants in individual promoters cause disease in their own
right, the classic cases being promoter mutations that reduce beta-globin expression in
beta-thalassemia and the TATA-box polymorphism in the UGT1A1 promoter that contributes to
Gilbert syndrome.

## Reading a hit

Treat a TATA match as almost no evidence. TATAWAWR is an eight-base AT-rich pattern with two
degenerate positions, expected by chance roughly once every few kilobases on either strand, which
is hundreds of thousands of matches in a human genome, the overwhelming majority of them nowhere
near a promoter. A match is only interesting if it sits 25-30 bp upstream of an annotated or
measured start site in a promoter that otherwise looks focused and AT-rich. It also says nothing
about TBP itself, since TBP is present at essentially all active promoters, including TATA-less
ones, where it is positioned by TFIID rather than by sequence. This family is also a good place to
see what happens when a ChIP-derived matrix is assigned to the wrong protein. The HOCOMOCO model
TAF1.H14CORE.0.P.B is AAGATGGCGGC, which is the YY1 motif, not a TBP-like or TAF1-specific
sequence; YY1 sites are common at focused promoters, so a TAF1 ChIP experiment recovers them [PMID:22955990,29224777].
Likewise the CIS-BP TBP entry M08231_2.00 is TATTTGCATA, whose core ATTTGCAT is the POU octamer
read in reverse. Neither model should be used as a TATA box.
families.caveats: The TATA box is the least informative element in common use: eight AT-rich bases read entirely from the minor groove, where A:T and T:A are nearly interchangeable, so the matrix cannot be much better than the physics allows. Expect hundreds of thousands of chance matches per genome and only a few percent of human promoters to carry a real one. A match means nothing without position 25-30 bp upstream of a start site. Two of the five motifs under this key are not TATA boxes: the HOCOMOCO ChIP-derived TAF1 matrix is the YY1 motif, and the CIS-BP TBP entry M08231_2.00 is the POU octamer. Family cohesion is correspondingly low at 0.64.

timeline.finding: A single T-to-G point mutation in the TATAAAA ('Goldberg-Hogness') box of the conalbumin promoter drastically reduces specific transcription in vitro, establishing the TATA box as a functional promoter element.
timeline.methods: Site-directed mutagenesis, in vitro transcription
timeline.open: The protein that recognizes the element was unknown.

timeline.finding: Co-crystal structures of plant and yeast TBP on TATA DNA show a saddle-shaped protein binding a widened, underwound minor groove, with phenylalanines kinking the DNA at both ends and no major-groove base contacts.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How TBP accommodates the variety of natural TATA sequences.

timeline.finding: Structure of the TFIIB-TBP-TATA ternary complex: TFIIB recognizes the preformed TBP-DNA complex and its N-terminal domain forms the downstream face, where it could fix the start site.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Whether TBP itself chooses an orientation on a nearly symmetric site.

timeline.finding: Structures of TBP on ten natural TATA variants show the same DNA deformation in every case; A-to-T and T-to-A transversions leave the minor-groove face unchanged, explaining why many AT-rich sequences are bound.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Genome-wide CAGE mapping of mouse and human start sites splits promoters into a sharp, conserved, TATA-enriched class and a broad, CpG-rich class.
timeline.methods: CAGE tag sequencing

timeline.finding: A genome-scale analysis estimates that about 76% of human core promoters lack any TATA-like element and that only about 10% of the TATA-like ones match the canonical TATAWAWR, overturning the textbook picture of the TATA box as a general core-promoter element.
timeline.methods: Computational promoter analysis

timeline.finding: Cryo-EM of human TFIID bound to promoter DNA shows every core promoter element contacted by TFIID subunits, with TAF1 and TAF2 holding the downstream promoter and TFIIA bridging TBP-TATA to lobe B.
timeline.methods: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy
timeline.open: How TBP is placed at the majority of promoters that lack a TATA box.

open: How much orientation is intrinsic to TBP is unsettled: the TFIIB-TBP-TATA structure fixes the complex's polarity, but TBP alone reads a nearly symmetric minor-groove surface, and the share of orientation set by TBP, by TFIIB and by flanking sequence has not been agreed.

How TBP is positioned at TATA-less promoters, which are most human promoters, is unresolved: TFIID contacts initiator and downstream elements, but whether TBP still engages a degenerate AT-rich sequence near -30 or is placed purely by TAF contacts is not settled.

Two of the five matrices under this key are other factors' motifs, YY1 for the ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO TAF1 model and the POU octamer for CIS-BP M08231_2.00; whether these record indirect binding at promoters or misattribution in the source data is not stated by the databases.

families.name: WT1
families.def: EGR-like GC-rich site with distinct KTS-isoform preference. WT1.
families.short: WT1 is the Wilms tumor suppressor, a four-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger protein whose last three fingers are closely related to those of EGR1 and which binds essentially the same GC-rich site. In vitro selection also found a slightly different high-affinity site, GCGTGGGAGT, called the WTE. Alternative splicing inserts three amino acids (lysine-threonine-serine) between fingers three and four, and the +KTS form binds DNA poorly and localizes to splicing-factor compartments, so WT1 is a DNA-binding protein only in part. Expression is restricted to developing kidney and gonad, podocytes, mesothelium and epicardium. The WT1 matrices in motif databases are ChIP-derived and G-rich rather than EGR-like, which matters when reading a hit.
families.long:
## The factors

WT1 was isolated as a zinc-finger gene at the Wilms tumor locus on human chromosome 11p13, spanning about 50 kb (Call et al. 1990) [PMID:2154335]. The protein has four Cys2-His2 fingers; fingers 2-4 align with the three fingers of EGR1, and finger 1 adds further contacts [PMID:17716689]. Two alternative splice events generate four main isoforms: insertion or omission of exon 5 (17 amino acids) in the N-terminal region, and insertion or omission of the tripeptide lysine-threonine-serine (KTS) between fingers 3 and 4. The KTS insertion is the consequential one. The -KTS protein localizes to nuclear compartments occupied by transcription factors, while the +KTS protein concentrates in splicing-factor domains (Larsson et al. 1995) [PMID:7736591], WT1, unlike EGR1, also binds RNA through the same zinc fingers (Caricasole et al. 1996) [PMID:8755514], in a region that overlaps the DNA-binding surface (Bardeesy and Pelletier 1998) [PMID:9512553]. Which isoform does so is unsettled: RNA selection found +KTS isoforms unable to bind the selected ligands [PMID:9512553], while an NMR study found -KTS and +KTS binding a stem-loop RNA with similar affinity, the KTS insertion instead abolishing high-affinity DNA binding [PMID:32955251]. So one gene produces a DNA-binding transcriptional regulator and an RNA-binding protein from the same finger array, and the ratio between them is under splice control. WT1 expression is restricted: nephron progenitors and podocytes in kidney, Sertoli and granulosa cells in gonad, mesothelium, epicardium and spleen, with additional roles in heart and nervous system (Hastie 2017) [PMID:28811308]. WT1 has no close paralogue; its nearest relatives by DNA-binding domain are the EGR proteins.

## The motif

WT1 binds the EGR-1 consensus, which was how its sequence specificity was first demonstrated: a bacterially expressed WT1 finger region bound the EGR-1 site (Rauscher et al. 1990) [PMID:2244209]. A whole-genome PCR selection later identified a distinct preferred 10-mer, GCGTGGGAGT, termed the WTE, which is similar to but not the same as the EGR-1 consensus GCG(G/T)GGGCG (Nakagama et al. 1995) [PMID:7862142]. The difference is the penultimate triplet: GGGAGT in the WTE against GGGCG in the EGR site. The four-finger domain has been solved on DNA by X-ray crystallography and NMR on both 14-bp and 17-bp duplexes, which resolved the position of finger 1 (Stoll et al. 2007) [PMID:17716689]. Here the atlas data and the literature agree only in part. Both HOCOMOCO models (WT1.H14CORE.0.P.B, GGGGGAGGA; WT1.H14CORE.1.P.B, GCGGGGGAGG) and the JASPAR profile (MA1627.2, CCTCCCCCAC, which is GTGGGGGAGG on the other strand) are G-rich runs without the EGR signature CACGC, whose nearest neighbors outside the family are EGR, SP/KLF, ZNF281 and ZBTB17 models [PMID:37971293]. The longer model is not a bare G-run: GCGGGGGAGG matches the biochemically defined WTE, GCGTGGGAGT, at 8 of 10 positions, including the adenine at position 8 that contributes most to WTE affinity, and differs only at position 4 and at the 3' thymine [PMID:7862142]. Family cohesion is nonetheless low, 0.57. The remaining two matrices carry no usable signal: the Vierstra archetype AC0095:WT/FOXC is an AT-rich model (ATATATT) whose nearest neighbors are K50-class homeodomain motifs, and the CIS-BP entry M00243_2.00 has 0.1 bits of information. In the other direction, a HOCOMOCO matrix labelled ZBTB17/MIZ1 (ZBT17.H14CORE.0.P.B, GTGGGGGAGGGG) has its nearest neighbor across all four databases in this family - a sign of how much these ChIP-derived models share with the general G-rich promoter element.

## Where it acts

WT1 sites sit in GC- and GA-rich promoter-proximal sequence, and the genes WT1 controls are concentrated in the programs it is expressed in: nephron and podocyte differentiation, gonadal development, epicardial and mesothelial identity (Hastie 2017) [PMID:28811308]. Because WT1 and EGR1 recognize overlapping sequences, they compete at shared sites [PMID:7862142], and which one occupies a site is determined by which protein is present - EGR1 only transiently after stimulation, WT1 only in the restricted lineages that express it. The G-rich matrices in the databases, by contrast, point at CpG-island promoters generally, where MAZ-, ZNF281- and SP-family sites are also abundant.

## Biology and disease

Wt1-null mice fail at an early step of kidney development, with defective ureteric bud outgrowth and no metanephros, together with gonadal and mesothelial defects (Kreidberg et al. 1993) [PMID:8395349]. In humans, germline WT1 mutations cause two distinct syndromes that map onto the protein's two functions. Denys-Drash syndrome arises from germline missense mutations concentrated in the zinc fingers and combines urogenital malformation, nephropathy and Wilms tumor (Pelletier et al. 1991) [PMID:1655284]. Frasier syndrome arises from donor splice-site mutations in intron 9 that specifically abolish the +KTS isoform, producing gonadal dysgenesis and progressive glomerulopathy without the same Wilms tumor risk (Barbaux et al. 1997) [PMID:9398852] - direct evidence that the KTS isoform ratio, not just total WT1, matters in vivo. Somatic WT1 mutations occur in a minority of Wilms tumors, and WT1 is also reported to be highly expressed in acute leukemias [PMID:28811308].

## Reading a hit

Be careful here, because the label and the matrix disagree. The structurally and biochemically characterized WT1 site is EGR-like (the EGR-1 consensus, or the WTE), but every informative WT1 matrix in these databases is a ChIP-derived G-rich model at grade B [PMID:37971293]. A hit to one of those models tells you the sequence belongs to the GGGAGGG family of G-rich promoter elements - shared with MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281, ZNF148, VEZF1 and at least one ZBTB17 matrix - and does not on its own establish that WT1 binds there, though the longer HOCOMOCO model is 8 of 10 matched to the WTE. Conversely, a strong hit to an EGR matrix is also a candidate WT1 site, and one Vierstra archetype is labelled AC0519:EGR/WT precisely because the two could not be separated. Ignore the two uninformative entries: AC0095:WT/FOXC is an AT-rich homeodomain-like model, and M00243_2.00 carries essentially no information. Two further constraints are biological rather than sequence-based. WT1 is expressed in few cell types, so in most samples there is no WT1 available to bind. And even in those cell types, roughly half the WT1 protein may be the +KTS isoform, which binds DNA poorly because the three-residue insertion sits between fingers 3 and 4 [PMID:32955251].
families.caveats: The WT1 label and the WT1 matrices point in different directions. Biochemistry and structure say WT1 binds an EGR-like GC-rich site (the EGR-1 consensus, or the WTE GCGTGGGAGT); all informative database matrices here are ChIP-derived, grade B, and G-rich (GGGGGAGGA), sitting among the SP/KLF, ZNF281 and EGR models, although the longer one (GCGGGGGAGG) does match the WTE at 8 of 10 positions. Family cohesion is only 0.57, one matrix has 0.1 bits, and one Vierstra archetype labelled WT is an AT-rich homeodomain model. A hit therefore identifies a G-rich promoter element and does not establish WT1 occupancy. Also check that WT1 is expressed at all, and remember that the +KTS isoform binds DNA poorly.

timeline.finding: WT1 is cloned at the 11p13 Wilms tumor locus as a four-zinc-finger gene, and site selection with its finger region recovers sequences similar to the EGR-1 consensus; a finger mutation from a Wilms tumor patient abolishes binding.
timeline.methods: Positional cloning; selection from degenerate oligonucleotides, gel shift
timeline.open: Whether WT1 prefers a site of its own, distinct from EGR1's, was not known.

timeline.finding: Germline point mutations in the zinc fingers of one WT1 copy, nine of ten in finger 3, are found in Denys-Drash syndrome and directly affect DNA recognition, tying the DNA-binding domain to urogenital development.
timeline.methods: Mutation screening of coding exons in patients

timeline.finding: Wt1-null mouse embryos fail to form kidneys and gonads: the metanephric blastema undergoes apoptosis and the ureteric bud does not grow out, with additional mesothelial, heart and lung defects.
timeline.methods: Gene targeting in mice

timeline.finding: Whole-genome PCR selection identifies the WTE, GCGTGGGAGT, which WT1 binds with 20- to 30-fold higher affinity than the EGR-1 site; the A at position 8 and the 3' T contribute most, fingers 2-4 are required for recognition, and finger 1 raises affinity about tenfold.
timeline.methods: Whole-genome PCR selection, affinity measurements, site and finger mutagenesis
timeline.open: Whether native WT1 targets in kidney use WTE-type sites rather than EGR-type sites was not established.

timeline.finding: The KTS splice choice decides whether WT1 sits mainly with splicing factors or in transcription-factor domains, and WT1, unlike EGR1, binds specific Igf-2 RNA sequences through its fingers (1996), proposing a post-transcriptional role. RNA selection in 1998, however, found that the +KTS isoforms could not bind the selected RNAs.
timeline.methods: Immunolocalization, immunoprecipitation; RNA binding assays; in vitro RNA selection with isoform comparison
timeline.open: Which isoform carries the RNA-binding function was left contested.

timeline.finding: Frasier syndrome is caused by donor splice-site mutations in intron 9 that are predicted to remove the +KTS isoform, giving gonadal dysgenesis and progressive glomerulopathy without Wilms tumor: direct evidence that the KTS isoform ratio matters in vivo.
timeline.methods: Mutation analysis in patients

timeline.finding: X-ray and NMR structures of the four-finger domain on 14- and 17-bp DNA show fingers 2-4 deep in the major groove making base-specific contacts, while finger 1 follows the groove in a non-canonical orientation without base contacts, anchoring WT1 and raising affinity but adding little specificity.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy

timeline.finding: The ChIP-derived WT1 models in HOCOMOCO v14 are G-rich (GCGGGGGAGG, GGGGGAGGA) and lack the EGR signature CACGC, sitting among the SP/KLF, ZNF281 and EGR models; the longer one still matches the biochemically defined WTE at 8 of 10 positions, so the models depart from the EGR-1 site without being unrelated to the selected WT1 site.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq-derived motif models, cross-database clustering
timeline.open: Whether these models reflect direct WT1 binding or co-occupancy of G-rich promoters is untested.

open: Whether the ChIP-derived WT1 matrices are indirect or a genuine WT1 preference is unresolved: they cluster with the MAZ and ZNF281 G-rich motifs, yet the more informative one, GCGGGGGAGG, matches the biochemically defined WTE (GCGTGGGAGT) at 8 of 10 positions, including the A at position 8 that contributes most to WTE affinity.

Which WT1 isoform binds RNA is contested: the +KTS form co-localizes with splicing factors and has been described as the RNA-binding isoform, but in vitro RNA selection found that +KTS isoforms could not bind the selected RNAs while the -KTS isoforms could, and a later NMR study found the two isoforms binding a stem-loop RNA with similar affinity.

Whether WT1 acts as an oncogene or a tumor suppressor in leukemia is unsettled: it is highly expressed in many acute leukemias, while the somatic WT1 mutations found in acute myeloid leukemia are mostly frameshifts expected to inactivate the protein.

families.name: ZEB
families.def: E-box-like CACCTG bound by ZEB1/ZEB2 zinc fingers.
families.short: ZEB1 and ZEB2 are large C2H2 zinc-finger repressors that bind the E-box-like sequence CACCTG, written CAGGTG when read on the other strand. Each protein carries two widely separated zinc-finger clusters, either of which can engage a site, so one molecule can hold two boxes at once. ZEB proteins contain no basic helix-loop-helix domain, yet they compete for the same CAGGTG boxes that bHLH activators use, so an E-box hit does not imply a bHLH factor. Both paralogues repress epithelial genes, E-cadherin (CDH1) above all, and are central to epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss-of-function mutations cause posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (ZEB1) and Mowat-Wilson syndrome (ZEB2), and high ZEB1 marks poorly differentiated carcinomas.
families.long:
## The factors

Humans have two paralogues: ZEB1 (also TCF8, deltaEF1, AREB6, ZFHX1A) and ZEB2 (SIP1, ZFHX1B, SMADIP1), each roughly 1,100-1,200 residues. Their architecture is atypical. Instead of one contiguous finger array, each protein carries two widely separated C2H2 clusters - three to four fingers near the N terminus and three near the C terminus - flanking a central region that includes a degenerate homeodomain which does not itself bind DNA. Remacle and colleagues showed that each cluster binds a target site on its own, so a single molecule works with two hands and can occupy two sites simultaneously [PMID:10487759]. ZEB proteins do not dimerize through a leucine zipper or a helix-loop-helix; repression is delivered by recruited partners, chiefly CtBP through a central interaction domain, plus NuRD and HDAC complexes. ZEB2 was independently isolated as a SMAD-interacting protein in a yeast two-hybrid screen [PMID:10400677], and both paralogues couple TGF-beta signaling to transcription. ZEB1 is expressed in mesenchymal tissue, T cells and corneal endothelium; ZEB2 in neural crest derivatives, the central nervous system and blood. Both are induced during epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and are restrained post-transcriptionally by the miR-200 microRNA family [PMID:18483486].

## The motif

The literature writes the site CACCTG, or equivalently CAGGTG on the opposite strand: a 6 bp member of the CANNTG E-box class, sometimes called the E2-box or Z-box [PMID:8065305,9544704]. Essentially all the information sits in those six positions. Each three-finger cluster reads about one base triplet per finger from the major groove, which accounts for a footprint of roughly 6 bp and for the absence of strong flanking preference [PMID:9544704]. The family data matches this: the CIS-BP and JASPAR models are rendered CACCTG and CTCACCTG while the HOCOMOCO models read CAGGTG and CAGGTGAG, which is the same motif on the other strand (the reverse complement of CAGGTGAG is CTCACCTG). This is a strand convention, not a disagreement. Information content is low, 10-12 bits, and the ZEB1 and ZEB2 models are effectively interchangeable, with cross-database similarities of 0.94-0.99, so sequence alone cannot tell the two paralogues apart. Because each protein has two independent hands, tandem CACCT(G) boxes bind more strongly than a single box [PMID:10487759], and validated targets such as CDH1 carry two or more [PMID:11430829]; no fixed spacing is required.

## Where it acts

ZEB sites occur in proximal promoters of epithelial structural genes - the E-pal element of CDH1 is the textbook case [PMID:11430829] - and in large numbers of distal enhancers in mesenchymal and carcinoma cells. CACCTG contains no CpG, so it is not depleted by genome-wide CpG loss: a strict 6 bp match occurs roughly once every 2 kb counting both strands, on the order of a million times in the human genome. Occupancy is therefore set by chromatin state and competition, not by site availability. ZEB1 ChIP-seq peaks overlap extensively with SNAI1/SNAI2 peaks and with bHLH factor peaks, because all of them use the same box. Functional partners include SMAD2/SMAD3 (especially for ZEB2), CtBP, NuRD and, in some settings, YAP; the best-characterized regulatory circuit is the mutual repression between ZEB1 and the miR-200 family [PMID:18483486].

## Biology and disease

ZEB1 and ZEB2 repress epithelial genes including CDH1, EPCAM, CRB3 and LGL2 [PMID:11430829,17486063], and are required for EMT in gastrulation, neural crest migration and organ fibrosis. Mouse deltaEF1 (Zeb1) mutants show skeletal defects and impaired thymocyte development [PMID:9126927]. Zeb1 also couples EMT to cellular senescence through the CDKN2A locus, so loss of Zeb1 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts triggers premature senescence [PMID:18192284]. In humans, heterozygous ZEB1 mutations cause posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy type 3, with ectopic COL4A3 expression in corneal endothelium [PMID:16252232], while truncating mutations and deletions of ZEB2 cause Mowat-Wilson syndrome (intellectual disability, microcephaly, Hirschsprung disease and a distinctive face) [PMID:11279515]. In carcinomas, ZEB1 expression tracks with loss of apicobasal polarity and dedifferentiation [PMID:17486063]. One honest qualification: ZEB-driven EMT is firmly established in culture and in development, but in human tumors the transition is usually partial, and how much full EMT contributes to metastasis is still argued; current consensus statements describe a spectrum of hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal states rather than a binary switch [PMID:27368099].

## Reading a hit

A CACCTG/CAGGTG match is among the least specific hits a scan can return. Plausible binders include the bHLH E-proteins TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, MYOD and MYF, TWIST and HAND, NEUROD and ATOH, MAX and USF, and the C2H2 repressors SNAI1-3, SCRT1/2 and ZBTB18. An E-box hit therefore does not imply a bHLH factor. Nothing in the 6 bp core distinguishes ZEB from these alternatives; only context does. Two boxes within a short window, in a mesenchymal or TGF-beta-stimulated cell type, and near an epithelial gene, is a reasonable circumstantial case for ZEB. A single isolated box is not. Note also the evidence types: the HOCOMOCO ZEB1 and ZEB2 models are ChIP-seq-derived (evidence code P, grade B) [PMID:37971293] and the JASPAR ZEB1 matrix MA0103.4 is ChIP-seq-derived [PMID:37962376], so they report where ZEB was found, not necessarily what ZEB binds directly; the CIS-BP entries for both genes are direct rather than inferred. Low label agreement in the family data (0.2-0.4) means the nearest neighbours of these matrices across databases are often non-ZEB E-box models, which is expected rather than a sign of error.
families.caveats: Trust the family, not the member, and not even the family without context. The 6 bp CACCTG core is shared with bHLH activators, SNAIL/SCRATCH, INSM and ZBTB18, so a hit licenses "E-box" and nothing more; ZEB1 and ZEB2 motifs are indistinguishable from each other at 0.94-0.99 similarity. The site is common enough to occur roughly a million times by chance in the genome, so single matches carry almost no evidence. HOCOMOCO ZEB1/ZEB2 and JASPAR MA0103.4 are ChIP-derived and can reflect indirect or co-binding. Paired boxes, an epithelial target gene and a mesenchymal or TGF-beta context are what make a ZEB call defensible.

timeline.finding: Random-oligonucleotide selection with deltaEF1 (ZEB1) returned CACCT, and deltaEF1 was shown to compete with the bHLH activator E47 at the E2 box CACCTG and to block MyoD-driven myogenesis - the first evidence that a zinc-finger protein reads an E-box.
timeline.methods: site selection, EMSA, reporter and myogenic conversion assays
timeline.open: Whether repression worked only by occluding the box or also through an intrinsic repression domain.

timeline.finding: Deletion analysis separated two repression mechanisms - binding-site competition, which needs both finger clusters, and active repression through the N-terminal NR domain - and deltaEF1 mutant mice showed that the factor is required in vivo, with a 100-fold reduction in thymocyte number.
timeline.methods: domain deletion, reporter assays, mouse gene targeting
timeline.open: How a protein with two separated finger clusters engages DNA.

timeline.finding: Each zinc-finger cluster was shown to bind a CACCT site independently, and the highest-affinity natural sites are bipartite, one CACCT plus one CACCTG with variable spacing and orientation; a single molecule binds with two hands.
timeline.methods: EMSA with isolated clusters, promoter mapping, transgenic Xenopus reporters
timeline.open: Whether bipartite sites are the rule at endogenous targets genome-wide.

timeline.finding: ZEB2/SIP1 was shown to repress E-cadherin through both E2 boxes of the CDH1 promoter and to induce invasion, and SIP1 mutations were found to cause Hirschsprung disease with intellectual disability, linking the motif to an epithelial program and to human disease.
timeline.methods: promoter mutagenesis, conditional expression in MDCK cells, patient sequencing

timeline.finding: Heterozygous truncating mutations in TCF8/ZEB1 were shown to cause posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy, with ectopic COL4A3 expression in corneal endothelium, providing a human loss-of-function phenotype for ZEB1 itself.
timeline.methods: linkage and mutation screening, immunohistochemistry

timeline.finding: ZEB1 was shown to repress the miR-200 family, which in turn targets ZEB1, defining a double-negative feedback loop; in parallel, Zeb1 mutant mouse fibroblasts were found to senesce prematurely through p15INK4b and p21 rather than through the Ink4a pathway.
timeline.methods: chromatin immunoprecipitation, reporter assays, mouse genetics

timeline.finding: Reviews and subsequent consensus guidelines reframed EMT as a set of partial, reversible states rather than a binary switch, which revised how a ZEB-driven program in a tumor should be described and cautioned against inferring full EMT from marker or motif evidence.
timeline.methods: review and consensus statement
timeline.open: How much, if any, complete EMT occurs in human carcinomas and whether it is needed for metastasis.

open: It is unresolved how often ZEB proteins actually use both finger clusters in the genome: the highest-affinity in vitro sites are bipartite CACCT plus CACCTG elements with variable spacing, but every database matrix for ZEB1 and ZEB2 models a single 6 bp box, and no survey has reported what fraction of occupied sites carries two boxes.

Whether ZEB1 and ZEB2 differ at all in sequence preference is unknown rather than settled: their models are 0.94-0.99 similar, so paralogue-specific target sets reported in different tissues may reflect expression and cofactors rather than DNA recognition, and no assay has yet separated the two possibilities.

The contribution of ZEB-driven EMT to human metastasis remains disputed, with cell-culture and developmental work supporting a full transition and consensus statements on human tumors favoring partial, hybrid states that are hard to distinguish from other sources of mesenchymal gene expression.

What decides whether a given CAGGTG box is occupied by a ZEB protein or by a bHLH factor is not established; competition for the same core was demonstrated biochemically in the 1990s, but whether in vivo selectivity comes from flanking sequence, chromatin state or relative protein abundance has not been resolved.

families.name: ZNF384 / ZNF362
families.def: AT-rich TAAAAA-type site at extracellular-matrix gene promoters, shared by the near-identical paralogues ZNF384 and ZNF362.
families.short: ZNF384 and its near-identical paralogue ZNF362 are C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind homopolymeric runs of A on one strand and T on the other. They are unusual among zinc fingers in reading the minor groove of an A-tract rather than the major groove of a mixed sequence, and only three of their fingers contact DNA. ZNF384 was cloned twice, as CIZ, a partner of the adaptor p130Cas that activates matrix metalloproteinase genes, and as Nmp4, a nuclear matrix factor at the type I collagen alpha-1 promoter. In human leukaemia ZNF384 is a recurrent fusion partner: rearrangements joining its C-terminal region to EP300, TCF3, TAF15 and others define a subtype of B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF384 and ZNF362 are paralogues whose zinc-finger arrays are close enough that no assay distinguishes their sequence preferences; the family therefore has two members and one motif. Splice variants of ZNF384 contain between five and eight C2H2 fingers, together with an SH3-binding region overlapping a putative AT-hook and a polyglutamine-alanine repeat [PMID:11867614]. Mapping the DNA-binding function showed that only fingers 2, 3 and 6 are needed for association with the A-tract element [PMID:11867614], so most of the array does something other than read bases. ZNF384 was described independently as CIZ, a protein that binds the focal-adhesion adaptor p130Cas and activates matrix metalloproteinase promoters [PMID:10669742], and as Nmp4, one of a set of nuclear matrix proteins occupying the rat COL1A1 promoter [PMID:10972987]. The N-terminus carries a strong activation domain that is masked in the full-length protein and becomes productive once the fingers engage DNA, and the polyglutamine-alanine repeat then contributes to activation, suggesting an allosteric switch triggered by binding [PMID:11867614]. Both proteins are broadly expressed.

## The motif

This is the atlas entry whose consensus is least word-like. The element is a homopolymeric (dA:dT) tract: eight or more consecutive adenines on one strand, equivalently eight or more thymines on the other. The literature usually writes it as poly(dA:dT) rather than as an IUPAC string, and the AT-rich promoter sites in COL1A1 and the MMP genes are described as TAAAAA-type runs [PMID:10669742,11112339]. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are, as far as is known, the only C2H2 zinc-finger proteins that bind within the minor groove of such a tract [PMID:11867614], which is why only three fingers are involved: there are no distinguishing major-groove bases to read. All five matrices in this family are A- or T-runs of seven to twelve positions, differing mainly in run length and in whether they specify a flanking base; the HOCOMOCO ZNF362 matrix adds a 3' C and the ZNF384 matrix a 3' GT. Information content is therefore low in the usual sense while being high in a positional sense, because the requirement is a structural one: an uninterrupted, narrow-minor-groove A-tract. ZNF384 and ZNF362 cannot be distinguished from sequence at all.

## Where it acts

Occurrences are promoter-proximal in the characterized cases, notably the COL1A1 and MMP promoters in osteoblasts, and genome-wide mapping of Nmp4 in bone cells recovered a large target set biased toward extracellular-matrix and secretory-pathway genes [PMID:26244796,37147466]. A-tracts are, however, everywhere: they are among the most abundant simple sequence features in mammalian genomes, occur heavily in intergenic and intronic DNA, and are also intrinsically nucleosome-disfavouring, which means they influence chromatin accessibility independently of any protein binding them. That double life is the central interpretive problem for this family. There is no named composite element with a partner factor, and the reported cofactor interactions are protein-protein rather than DNA-adjacent: p130Cas for CIZ, and the nuclear matrix for Nmp4.

## Biology and disease

Nmp4/ZNF384 is best understood in bone as a brake. Nmp4-null mice respond more strongly than wild type to anabolic parathyroid hormone therapy, gaining more trabecular bone [PMID:19189321], and their osteoblasts show enhanced secretory capacity [PMID:37147466]; the factor has accordingly been described as closing the PTH anabolic window [PMID:19766748]. Nmp4 loss also alters innate immune responses to influenza A [PMID:32152414] and modifies serum-induced arthritis [PMID:37147466], so the effects are not skeletal alone. The prominent human disease link is oncogenic and structural rather than transcriptional-regulatory in the ordinary sense: ZNF384 is a recurrent fusion partner in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, with EP300, TCF3, TAF15, CREBBP and other 5' partners fused to a nearly complete ZNF384 coding region [PMID:27634205,34529760]. These ZNF384-rearranged leukaemias form a distinct transcriptional subtype with a characteristic immunophenotype [PMID:27634205], they include mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia cases, and additional classes of ZNF384 aberration have since been described [PMID:34529760]. Because the fusion retains the zinc-finger array, the chimeric protein is thought to redirect a strong heterologous activation domain to ZNF384's A-tract sites.

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit here as a statement about DNA structure first and about protein occupancy second. Eight-base A-tracts occur many hundreds of thousands of times in the human genome, so a match on its own is close to uninformative; conversely, a long A-tract found in an accessibility or ChIP dataset may reflect nucleosome depletion or an alignment artefact rather than ZNF384 binding. The family also overlaps other AT-rich motif families, and any tool that scans for homopolymer runs will find these sites regardless of which factor is labelled. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are indistinguishable, so a hit identifies the pair. HOCOMOCO's evidence codes for this family include in vitro data (S and M), so direct binding to A-tracts is real; what is not licensed by a hit is the conclusion that a particular tract is a regulated element.
families.caveats: This is a structural motif, not a word, and its abundance makes single hits nearly uninformative: eight-base A-tracts appear hundreds of thousands of times genome-wide. A-tracts are also intrinsically nucleosome-disfavouring, so their enrichment in open chromatin and in ChIP peak sets can arise without any ZNF384 binding, and an A-tract hit in an accessibility dataset should not be read as occupancy. ZNF384 and ZNF362 are indistinguishable from sequence, and the motif overlaps other AT-rich families. In vitro evidence supports direct minor-groove binding, so the protein-motif link itself is sound; only the interpretation of individual genomic matches is weak. Context, notably promoter position and extracellular-matrix or secretory target genes, does most of the work.

timeline.finding: CIZ is cloned as a ligand of the p130Cas SH3 domain; target-site selection gives the DNA-binding consensus (G/C)AAAAA(A), which occurs in matrix metalloproteinase promoters, and CIZ binds the MMP-1 promoter and raises MMP-1 and MMP-3 transcription.
timeline.methods: Far-Western screening, cyclic amplification and selection of targets (CASTing), reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether the protein bound the short consensus or a longer A-tract, and how, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: The nuclear matrix proteins NP/Nmp4, which bind the rat COL1A1 promoter in osteoblast-like cells, are reported to include isoforms identical to CIZ; CIZ overexpression raises type I collagen mRNA through a consensus site in the collagen promoter.
timeline.methods: Nuclear matrix fractionation, imaging, overexpression and reporter assays

timeline.finding: Nmp4 binds within the minor groove of homopolymeric (dA:dT) DNA, the first C2H2 proteins known to do so; fingers 2, 3 and 6 mediate binding, and a strong N-terminal activation domain that is masked in the full-length protein becomes active once the protein is bound to the A-tract.
timeline.methods: DNA-binding assays with deletion mutants, GAL4 fusion transactivation assays
timeline.open: No structure was determined, so how C2H2 fingers engage a minor groove remained unknown.

timeline.finding: Nmp4-null mice gain more femoral trabecular bone than wild type under anabolic PTH treatment, establishing Nmp4 as an attenuator of the PTH bone-building response.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, densitometry and micro-CT

timeline.finding: Nmp4 ChIP-seq in preosteoblasts, embryonic stem cells and blood cell lines gives a genome-wide target set; ovariectomized Nmp4-null mice keep the improved PTH response, with more osteoprogenitors.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, gene ontology analysis, ovariectomy model, micro-CT
timeline.open: ChIP alone could not separate direct A-tract binding from occupancy at accessible, nucleosome-depleted tracts.

timeline.finding: ZNF384 fusions, with TCF3, EP300 and other 5' partners, are found in 4.1% of 291 childhood B-cell precursor ALL cases; the fusion-positive leukemias share weak CD10 and aberrant CD13/CD33 expression and a distinct expression signature.
timeline.methods: Whole-transcriptome sequencing, RT-PCR, immunophenotyping

timeline.finding: Leukemias with the ZNF384-fusion expression signature but no canonical fusion are found to carry a new class of aberration in the last exon of ZNF384 that disrupts the C-terminal portion of the protein, showing that these 'ZNF384r-like' cases are the same genetic subtype.
timeline.methods: Targeted reanalysis of sequencing data in three patients
timeline.open: How a C-terminal disruption phenocopies fusions that keep the entire ZNF384 coding sequence was not explained.

open: How a C2H2 array recognizes an A-tract is unknown: biochemistry places binding in the minor groove through fingers 2, 3 and 6, but there is no structure, so whether ZNF384 reads bases or the narrow minor-groove shape of an uninterrupted tract is unresolved.

Whether ZNF384 is mainly an activator or a repressor is unsettled: A-tract binding unmasks activation of the COL1A1 promoter in reporter assays and CIZ overexpression raises MMP and collagen expression, whereas knockout mice behave as if Nmp4 represses osteoblast and PTH-responsive genes.

Why canonical fusions, which retain the complete ZNF384 coding sequence, and last-exon aberrations that disrupt its C-terminus produce the same leukemia expression signature is unexplained, as is whether either depends on A-tract binding.

families.name: ZNF768
families.def: MYC-box-like TGGCAGCAGC repeat. ZNF768.
families.short: ZNF768 is a C2H2 zinc-finger protein whose binding site sits in the core region of mammalian-wide interspersed repeats (MIRs), an old family of SINE retrotransposons. The site is bipartite: GCTGTGTG and CCTCTCTG separated by about twenty unconstrained bases, so the two halves are usually reported separately and most motif databases hold only one of them. ZNF768 binding is concentrated in euchromatin and at promoters of expressed genes, and its own N-terminus contains a heptad repeat array structurally reminiscent of the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, which is where the frequent comparison to MYC-box-like repeats comes from. The literature is recent and small: two primary characterizations plus mouse work linking it to RAS-induced senescence and p53.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF768 is a single human gene with no paralogue that shares its specificity, and the entire family here consists of its own matrices. The protein has a C-terminal C2H2 zinc-finger array and, unusually, an N-terminal region built from a heptad repeat array that is structurally related to the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II [PMID:30476274]. That array evolved in placental mammals, is absent in marsupials and monotremes, and varies in length between species, which raises the possibility that it performs CTD-like scaffolding functions in gene regulation [PMID:30476274]. The resemblance of these repeats to MYC homology boxes is the origin of the "MYC-box-like" description attached to this family in some annotations; the description refers to the protein's repeats rather than to a MYC-type DNA element, and no E-box-like binding has been reported. ZNF768 is broadly expressed, is a phosphoprotein, and is destabilized when RAS signalling is activated [PMID:34404770].

## The motif

The characterized site is bipartite. Affinity purification and genome-wide mapping identified specific binding to GCTGTGTG followed, about twenty base pairs later, by CCTCTCTG, with the intervening sequence unconstrained [PMID:30476274]. This spacing is the reason the four databases disagree so visibly. The two ChIP-derived HOCOMOCO matrices, 23 and 21 base pairs long, are adjacent windows on the same long site and even share their overlapping flank: one contains CTCAGAGAGG (the reverse complement of CCTCTCTGAG) and the other ends in CACACAGC (the reverse complement of GCTGTGTG). The CIS-BP matrix and the Vierstra archetype both read CTTAACCTCTCTGAG, essentially the CCTCTCTG half with its native MIR flank, and JASPAR MA1731.2 reduces it to the eight-base CCTCTCTG core. No matrix in any of the four databases spans the whole bipartite element, because standard motif discovery does not model a twenty-base gap. The family consensus quoted here therefore writes the gap explicitly; the dataConsensus CTTAACCTCTCTGAG is the 3' half only. Because the site is embedded in a repeat family, the "flanks" that motif discovery recovers are MIR consensus sequence rather than base contacts, and should not be read as specificity determinants.

## Where it acts

ZNF768 occupancy tracks MIRs, and MIRs are old enough to be widely fixed and heavily fragmented, with hundreds of thousands of copies in the human genome. Binding is preferentially associated with euchromatin and with promoter regions of genes that are actively expressed, and in the two cell lines examined (the B-cell line Raji and the osteosarcoma line U2OS) it marked genes expressed in a cell-type-specific manner [PMID:30476274]. Mass spectrometry of ZNF768 complexes recovered the Elongator components ELP1, ELP2 and ELP3 along with other nuclear factors, pointing to a role at expressed genes rather than in silencing [PMID:30476274]. MIR-derived sequences are independently known to act as enhancers and to be rewired during changes in pluripotency [PMID:40296153], so the sequence class is regulatorily active with or without ZNF768. There is no named composite element pairing ZNF768 with another factor.

## Biology and disease

The functional literature is small and recent, and it is worth saying plainly that the connection between the DNA motif and the phenotypes below has not been closed. ZNF768 protein is destabilized when oncogenic RAS is activated, and its levels fall in replicative, stress-induced and oncogene-induced senescence [PMID:34404770]. Depleting ZNF768 impairs proliferation and induces senescence, altering expression of cell-cycle effectors and established p53 targets; overexpressing it helps cells bypass RAS-induced senescence, and it interacts with p53 and suppresses p53 phosphorylation and activity [PMID:34404770]. ZNF768 is amplified or overexpressed in a range of tumours [PMID:34404770]. Mouse work supports this axis from both directions: ZNF768 loss amplifies p53 action and reduces lung tumorigenesis [PMID:40133474], and a Cre-inducible ZNF768 overexpression model has been generated [PMID:40473701]. None of these studies identifies the MIR-embedded motif as the mediator, so the relationship between the binding site and the senescence phenotype is currently an open question rather than an established mechanism. There is no human Mendelian disease linked to ZNF768.

## Reading a hit

Expect a hit here to be a hit on a MIR. Because the recognized sequence lies in a repeat core, a match tells you first that you are in a MIR element and only second that ZNF768 might bind, and the two statements are not interchangeable: the great majority of MIR copies are not occupied. Only one half of the bipartite site is modelled by most matrices, and CCTCTCTG on its own is an eight-base CT-rich word that overlaps other CT-rich families, so a single-half match in non-repeat sequence is weak. Check whether the two halves occur with the expected spacing. All the direct evidence in this family is ChIP-derived (HOCOMOCO evidence code P for both matrices), with no HT-SELEX support, so direct binding by the purified protein is not independently confirmed here. Repeat-derived motifs are also a known source of artefacts in occupancy data, including spurious apparent binding at repetitive and organellar sequences [PMID:40163815], so verify mappability before interpreting a hit.
families.caveats: Two structural problems. The site is bipartite with an unconstrained twenty-base gap, and no database matrix models it, so every available matrix covers one half; scores are not comparable and half-site matches are weak. And the site lives inside MIR SINEs, which means a match mainly reports the presence of a MIR, not occupancy: MIR copies number in the hundreds of thousands and only a small subset is bound. Evidence in this family is ChIP-only (HOCOMOCO codes P, grade B), with no in vitro confirmation of direct binding to the motif, and the recovered flanks are MIR consensus sequence rather than demonstrated base contacts. The senescence and p53 biology is not yet tied to the motif.

timeline.finding: ZNF768 is found to bind a bipartite motif, GCTGTGTG(N20)CCTCTCTG, in the core of MIR retroelements, preferentially in euchromatin and at promoters of expressed, cell-type-specific genes; it associates with the Elongator subunits ELP1-3, and its N-terminus carries a placental-mammal-specific heptad repeat array related to the RNA polymerase II CTD.
timeline.methods: Affinity purification, ChIP-seq, motif analysis, mass spectrometry of ZNF768 complexes, comparative sequence analysis
timeline.open: How the finger array spans a 20-base-pair unconstrained gap, and why ZNF768 binds some MIR copies and not others, were not addressed.

timeline.finding: ZNF768 is identified as a phosphoprotein destabilized by oncogenic RAS; its depletion induces senescence through cell-cycle and p53 target genes, its overexpression helps bypass RAS-induced senescence, it binds p53 and represses p53 phosphorylation and activity, and it is often amplified or overexpressed in tumors.
timeline.methods: Knockdown and overexpression in cultured cells, co-immunoprecipitation, cancer genomics, immunohistochemistry
timeline.open: The senescence phenotype was not linked to binding at the MIR motif.

timeline.finding: A reanalysis of 6,153 ENCODE ChIP experiments lists ZNF768 among 12 C2H2 zinc-finger proteins with some evidence of occupancy over the mitochondrial genome, and notes that such chrM signal is not always reproducible between antibodies or protocols.
timeline.methods: Reanalysis of ENCODE ChIP-seq with deep-learning occupancy models

timeline.finding: Znf768-null mice are viable with an early growth defect; their fibroblasts show higher p53, premature senescence and genotoxic sensitivity, and deletion of ZNF768 suppresses KRAS G12D-driven lung tumors.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice, mouse embryonic fibroblasts, KRAS G12D lung cancer model

timeline.finding: Whole-body ZNF768 overexpression in mice gives no apparent phenotype and does not promote chemically induced fibrosarcoma or KRAS G12D-driven lung adenocarcinoma, so raising ZNF768 levels is not sufficient to drive tumors.
timeline.methods: Cre-inducible Rosa26 transgenic mice, tumor models

open: Whether ZNF768's binding at MIR elements mediates its effects on proliferation and senescence is not established: the motif and the RAS-p53 phenotypes come from separate studies, and the phenotypes have not been attributed to occupancy at MIR sites.

Whether ZNF768 drives tumors or only supports them is unsettled: it is often amplified or overexpressed in tumors and its deletion reduces KRAS-driven lung tumorigenesis in mice, yet whole-body overexpression did not promote fibrosarcoma or KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma.

How one protein reads two eight-base half-sites separated by an unconstrained 20-base-pair gap is unknown in the absence of a structure or in vitro selection data, and no database matrix models the whole element, so whether either half alone is sufficient for binding is open.

families.name: MTF1
families.def: Metal response element TGCRCNC. MTF1.
families.short: MTF1 (MTF-1) is a six-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds the metal response element, a short TGCRCNC core first defined as the 12-base-pair repeat that makes metallothionein promoters metal-inducible. MTF1 is constitutively present but only becomes an activator when free zinc rises, so the same site is quiet in resting cells and strongly occupied after exposure to zinc, cadmium, copper or other heavy metals, and under oxidative and hypoxic stress. Metallothionein promoters carry several MREs in tandem, and that clustering, rather than any single site, is what produces a large induction. Mouse Mtf1 knockout is embryonic-lethal with liver degeneration. Because the core is only seven informative bases, isolated genomic matches are common and mostly meaningless.
families.long:
## The factors

MTF1 is a single gene with no paralogue that shares its specificity; the human protein was cloned in 1994 after the mouse factor was identified biochemically as the zinc-responsive activity binding the metallothionein-I enhancer [PMID:3208749,8467794,8065932]. Its DNA-binding region is a tandem array of six C2H2 zinc fingers [PMID:8467794], and the fingers differ from each other in how tightly they hold zinc. That heterogeneity is the basis of metal sensing: at low free zinc some fingers are unloaded and the array binds DNA poorly, while rising zinc fills them and licenses binding [PMID:8026472]. Three separate transactivation domains (acidic, proline-rich and serine/threonine-rich) lie C-terminal to the fingers [PMID:7610056], and nuclear import, phosphorylation and interaction with coactivators add further layers of regulation; the Hippo kinases LATS1 and LATS2 phosphorylate MTF1 and dampen the heavy-metal response [PMID:35027733]. Homologues exist from Drosophila to mammals and the protein is broadly expressed, with the highest activity in liver.

## The motif

The metal response element was defined genetically before any protein was known: a 12-base-pair motif repeated several times in metallothionein promoters was shown to be sufficient to make a heterologous gene metal-inducible [PMID:6095286], and fine mapping narrowed the essential part to a core now written TGCRCNC (reverse complement GNGYGCA) [PMID:2725504]. Only about seven positions carry real information, and the strongest of these are the invariant TGC and the following purine. The in vitro matrices in this family extend the core with flanking preferences: the HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX word is GCCGTGTGCAAAA (reverse complement TTTTGCACACGGC), which is the TGCACAC core with a 5' GCC and a 3' A-tract, and JASPAR MA0863.1 is the same element written on the other strand. The family consensus quoted here is the literature core, TGCRCNC, because that is what functional work defines; the longer database words reflect flanking base preferences measured in vitro and should not be treated as required. Individual MREs vary considerably and have been grouped into subtypes with different affinities. There are no half-sites and no dimerization: MTF1 binds as a monomer to a single core, and the potency of a promoter comes from having several cores in a row.

## Where it acts

MREs sit in proximal promoters, typically within a few hundred base pairs of the start site, and the classic arrangement is a tandem cluster: the mouse and human metallothionein promoters carry five or more [PMID:6095286,8467794]. Beyond metallothioneins, target-gene searches identified zinc transporters (including SLC30A1/ZnT1), selenoprotein and glutathione-pathway genes, and stress-response genes, so the element marks a metal-and-oxidative-stress promoter module rather than a tissue-specific enhancer [PMID:11266553]. Occupancy is inducible, which sets this motif apart from most in the atlas: in unstressed cells many strong MREs are unoccupied, and the same promoter can go from no signal to heavy signal within an hour of zinc or cadmium exposure. MTF1 also handles the opposite extreme, activating a different gene set under copper starvation [PMID:15833915], so the direction of the response depends on context. No named composite element pairs MTF1 with another factor, but MREs frequently sit next to antioxidant response elements and major late transcription factor sites in the same promoters.

## Biology and disease

Cells lacking MTF1 lose both basal and metal-induced metallothionein expression and become hypersensitive to cadmium [PMID:8026472,9582278]. Mouse Mtf1 knockout dies around embryonic day 14 with liver degeneration [PMID:9582278]; Drosophila MTF-1 null flies are viable in normal conditions but cannot survive heavy-metal load or copper starvation [PMID:12505988,15833915], which frames the factor as a homeostatic buffer rather than a developmental regulator. In humans the interest is largely toxicological and oncological, though the evidence is from cell and animal models rather than from patients: cadmium induces MTF1 in prostate epithelial cells, and silencing it blocks the spheroid formation and xenograft growth of cadmium-transformed cells [PMID:40520016]; MTF1-driven metallothionein induction raises the cisplatin IC50 of cancer lines several-fold, and re-expressing MT1A or MT2A partly restores resistance to MTF1-null cells [PMID:39920630]; and a genome-wide screen in mouse embryonic stem cells recovered Mtf1 as a suppressor of mutant huntingtin toxicity, with forced expression reducing aggregates and motor defects in R6/2 mice [PMID:37407555]. There is no classical Mendelian MTF1 disease.

## Reading a hit

TGCRCNC is short. A genome of three billion base pairs contains millions of matches, the great majority of which are never bound, so a single MRE match in a promoter is weak evidence on its own. Two things strengthen it: a tandem cluster of two or more cores within about 100 base pairs, and a promoter whose expression is metal-, zinc- or cadmium-responsive. Conversely, absence of MTF1 signal in a resting-cell ChIP dataset says nothing, because occupancy requires induction. Paralogue ambiguity is not an issue here, since no other human factor is known to read this word, but the short core does overlap by chance with parts of longer GC-rich motifs, so check whether a hit is better explained by a neighbouring family. The in vitro (S/M) evidence behind the HOCOMOCO and CIS-BP matrices supports direct binding, so this is one motif where the label is well grounded.
families.caveats: The protein-to-motif link is solid: MREs were defined functionally, MTF1 was purified on them, and the database matrices rest on in vitro selection rather than ChIP alone. The weakness is length. With roughly seven informative positions, matches occur by chance throughout the genome and most are not bound, so a lone MRE is not evidence of regulation. Require a tandem cluster, or a demonstrated metal response, before calling a site functional. Occupancy is also conditional: MTF1 only binds when free zinc is elevated, so both positive and negative ChIP results depend entirely on the metal status of the cells assayed. The longer in vitro consensus adds flanking preferences that functional MREs frequently violate.

timeline.finding: Deletion and linker-scanning mutants of the mouse metallothionein-I promoter, assayed by microinjection into mouse eggs, pin metal regulation to a 12-base-pair sequence repeated several times in the promoter; one copy placed in a thymidine kinase promoter confers limited metal regulation and two copies confer as much as the whole MT-I promoter.
timeline.methods: Promoter mutagenesis, oligonucleotide insertion, microinjection into mouse eggs
timeline.open: No protein binding the element had been identified.

timeline.finding: A zinc-inducible binding activity, named MTF-1, is detected on the mouse MREd element, and the zinc-dependent formation of the complex in vitro tracks zinc-inducible transcription in cells; Sp1 binds the same element with a similar but non-identical interference pattern.
timeline.methods: Band-shift assays, methylation interference, transient transfection
timeline.open: It was unclear whether MTF-1 or Sp1 carried the metal response, and MTF-1 had not been cloned.

timeline.finding: Point mutagenesis of MREd separates the two: the conserved core TGCPuCXC is critical for metal induction while substitutions in the flanks, including the putative Sp1 site, barely matter, and two copies act cooperatively.
timeline.methods: Point mutagenesis with reporter assays in transient transfection

timeline.finding: Mouse MTF-1 is cloned: a 72.5-kDa protein with six zinc fingers and separate acidic and proline-rich activation domains, whose DNA complex increases in zinc-treated cells and whose ectopic expression activates MRE-driven reporters; the human gene follows in 1994, and mapping of the activation domains in 1995 shows they work constitutively, so metal responsiveness is conferred by the zinc-finger region together with the acidic and proline-rich region in the intact protein.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, band-shift assays, reporter assays, GAL4 domain-swap analysis

timeline.finding: Disruption of both Mtf1 alleles in mouse embryonic stem cells silences metallothionein I and II and abolishes activation of metal-responsive promoters by zinc, cadmium, copper, nickel and lead, establishing MTF-1 as required for basal as well as induced expression and as a zinc sensor.
timeline.methods: Homologous recombination in embryonic stem cells, expression and reporter analysis

timeline.finding: Mtf1-null mouse embryos die around day 14 with impaired hepatocyte development and liver decay, and their fibroblasts are hypersensitive to cadmium and hydrogen peroxide; a later target-gene search finds few robust additional targets and shows that some apparent ones reflect the dying liver rather than direct regulation.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockout, histology, cytotoxicity assays, microarray and promoter-reporter screening
timeline.open: Which targets besides the metallothioneins explain the lethal phenotype remained unsettled.

timeline.finding: Drosophila MTF-1 knockouts are viable but sensitive to copper, cadmium and zinc, and unexpectedly also to copper depletion; in 2005 this is explained when MTF-1 is shown to activate the copper importer Ctr1B through the same MRE motifs under copper starvation, so one factor and one element serve both detoxification and acquisition.
timeline.methods: Targeted gene disruption in Drosophila, metal challenge, promoter analysis and reporter assays
timeline.open: How the same element directs opposite responses to copper load and copper starvation was not resolved.

timeline.finding: The Hippo pathway kinases LATS1 and LATS2 phosphorylate and inhibit MTF1 independently of YAP and TAZ; heavy-metal exposure inhibits LATS, with zinc binding LATS directly, adding a signaling layer to metal sensing.
timeline.methods: Kinase assays, mass spectrometry, cell-based metal toxicity assays

open: What MTF1 regulates besides the metallothioneins is still unsettled: the knockout dies of liver degeneration while metallothionein-null mice are viable, yet a systematic target search recovered only a few candidates and showed that some differential expression reflected the dying liver rather than direct regulation.

How one element produces opposite responses is unexplained: MREs of the same type drive metallothionein induction under copper load and Ctr1B induction under copper starvation, so what distinguishes the two promoter contexts is unknown.

The relationship between the literature core TGCRCNC and the longer in vitro word is unresolved: HT-SELEX and methyl-SELEX matrices add a 5' GCC and a 3' A-tract to the core, and whether those flanks matter at functional MREs has not been tested.

How zinc occupancy of the six fingers is converted into DNA binding is not settled at the structural level, since the fingers differ in zinc affinity but no structure of the array on an MRE across a range of zinc concentrations has been reported.

families.name: ZFP57 / imprinting
families.def: Methylated TGCCGC hexamer at imprinting control regions. ZFP57, ZNF445.
families.short: ZFP57 is a KRAB zinc-finger protein that reads a six-base sequence, TGCCGC, but only when the CpG inside it is methylated. That combination of a short site and a methylation requirement lets it mark the methylated parental allele at imprinting control regions, the germline-methylated switches that restrict about two dozen loci to expression from one parent's chromosome. ZFP57 binds together with the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1 and DNA methyltransferases, shielding those regions from the wave of demethylation that follows fertilization. The larger zinc finger ZNF445 reads the same element and covers most of the same regions, which is why loss of ZFP57 alone produces imprinting defects with incomplete penetrance. In humans, recessive ZFP57 mutations cause transient neonatal diabetes with hypomethylation at multiple imprinted loci.
families.long:
## The factors

ZFP57 (6p22.1, formerly C6orf40) is a KRAB zinc-finger protein with a short tandem array of C2H2 fingers, of which only the first two are needed for sequence recognition. Like other KZFPs it carries an N-terminal KRAB domain that binds the corepressor TRIM28/KAP1 [PMID:28273063], and in mouse embryonic stem cells ZFP57 and KAP1 occupy imprinting control regions (ICRs) together with DNA methyltransferases and the hemimethylated-DNA-binding protein NP95/UHRF1 (Quenneville et al. 2011) [PMID:22055183]. ZFP57 is a maternal-zygotic effect gene: protein and transcript are supplied by the oocyte and the gene is also expressed in the embryo (Li et al. 2008) [PMID:18854139]. ZNF445 (3p21.31, also catalogued as ZKSCAN15/ZSCAN47) is a much larger zinc finger that binds the same regions, can be traced back to the origins of imprinting, and is expressed earlier in the embryo than ZNF/ZFP57 (Takahashi et al. 2019) [PMID:30602440]. This entry holds five matrices for the two proteins; a sixth label, the Vierstra archetype AC0364, is annotated only as "ZFP".

## The motif

The literature consensus is the hexamer TGCCGC carrying a methylated CpG [PMID:22055183]. A 1.0 Angstrom crystal structure of the two relevant Zfp57 fingers on fully methylated DNA shows finger 1 contacting the 5' half (TGC) and finger 2 the 3' half (CGC). The two 5-methylcytosines are read asymmetrically: one packs against Arg178, which simultaneously contacts the neighbouring 3' guanine in a 5mC-Arg-G arrangement, while the other is read through a layer of ordered water. Affinity falls for unmodified DNA and for the oxidation products of 5mC, and two point mutations found in patients abolish binding (Liu et al. 2012) [PMID:23059534]. The atlas matrices agree with this. JASPAR MA1583.2 is TGCCGCA; HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetype all give GCGGCA, which is the reverse complement of TGCCGC, so the apparent disagreement with the literature consensus is only a choice of strand [PMID:37962376,37971293]. Family cohesion is 0.76, the highest value among the zinc-finger entries in this group and the level expected of a genuinely single motif. One member does not fit: the CIS-BP model for ZNF445 (M07674) is a 29 bp, 31-bit matrix unrelated to the hexamer, and nothing else in the atlas resembles it.

## Where it acts

ICRs, also called germline differentially methylated regions, number on the order of 20 to 25 in human and mouse and include the regions controlling SNRPN, KCNQ1OT1, H19/IGF2, GNAS and PLAGL1. ZFP57 and KAP1 bind only the H3K9me3-bearing, DNA-methylated allele, so occupancy is monoallelic by construction (Quenneville et al. 2011) [PMID:22055183]. Binding is not confined to ICRs: several tens of additional methylated loci carry the hexamer and lose methylation when ZFP57 is deleted in ES cells [PMID:22055183], and allele-specific ZFP57 binding also occurs at non-imprinted monoallelically expressed regions (Strogantsev et al. 2015) [PMID:26025256]. Real ICRs usually contain a cluster of hexamers rather than one copy, and clustering discriminates far better than any single match.

## Biology and disease

Mice lacking only zygotic Zfp57 show partial neonatal lethality; removing maternal and zygotic function together is close to fully embryonic lethal, and maternal methylation imprints fail to be established at the Snrpn region (Li et al. 2008) [PMID:18854139]. In humans, recessive ZFP57 mutations cause transient neonatal diabetes mellitus with mosaic hypomethylation at multiple imprinted loci, the first heritable multi-locus imprinting disorder compatible with life (Mackay et al. 2008) [PMID:18622393], with long-term clinical follow-up reported later (Boonen et al. 2013) [PMID:23150280]. Penetrance is incomplete, which is what motivated the search that found ZNF445: in mice Zfp445 and Zfp57 together maintain all but one ICR, and in humans ZNF445 is intolerant of loss-of-function variation, suggesting it carries more of the load than ZFP57 (Takahashi et al. 2019) [PMID:30602440].

## Reading a hit

A six-base site occurs by chance roughly once every few kilobases per strand, so an isolated TGCCGC match licenses no conclusion. Three things make a hit interesting: the CpG is methylated in your sample, several copies cluster within a few hundred bases, and the interval overlaps an annotated germline DMR. Position-weight-matrix scanning cannot see methylation, so a scan returns candidate sites only. ZFP57 and ZNF445 cannot be separated from sequence. Neither can every GCGGC-containing zinc-finger motif: the HOCOMOCO model for ZNF729, a KRAB zinc finger with no known imprinting role, is TGCGGCAG, and its nearest neighbour anywhere in the atlas is the ZFP57 matrix. The HOCOMOCO ZFP57 model itself is ChIP-derived (evidence code P, grade B), so confidence that this protein binds this sequence rests on the structure and biochemistry in the primary papers rather than on the motif model.
families.caveats: A TGCCGC match is a candidate, not a site. The hexamer is short enough to appear roughly a million times in the genome, and the property that makes it functional, CpG methylation, is invisible to motif scanning. Treat a hit as meaningful only with methylation data, clustered copies, or germline-DMR annotation. The motif does not distinguish ZFP57 from ZNF445, and short GCGGC-containing motifs of unrelated KRAB zinc fingers such as ZNF729 score almost as well. The ZFP57 models in HOCOMOCO and the Vierstra set are ChIP-derived or unnamed; the in vitro and structural support comes from the primary literature, not from these matrices.
