timeline.finding: Knocking out Zfp57 in mouse showed it is a maternal-zygotic effect gene required to maintain both maternal and paternal methylation imprints: zygotic loss gives partial neonatal lethality, loss of both maternal and zygotic function is highly penetrant embryonic lethality, and maternal imprints at Snrpn fail to be established.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, methylation analysis of imprinted loci
timeline.open: What DNA sequence ZFP57 recognized, and whether it bound imprinting control regions directly, were unknown.

timeline.finding: Mutations in ZFP57 were found in seven pedigrees with transient neonatal diabetes and mosaic hypomethylation at several imprinted loci, the first heritable multi-locus imprinting disorder compatible with life.
timeline.methods: human genetics, methylation profiling of imprinted loci
timeline.open: The incomplete and mosaic pattern of hypomethylation had no mechanistic explanation.

timeline.finding: ZFP57 and KAP1 were shown to bind the H3K9me3-bearing, DNA-methylated allele of imprinting control regions in embryonic stem cells, and the recognized element was identified as the methylated hexanucleotide TGCCGC, present in all imprinting control regions and in several tens of other methylated loci.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and ChIP-chip in mouse ES cells, deletion of Zfp57, Kap1 and DNMTs, motif discovery
timeline.open: How a zinc finger could require methylation of its own recognition site was not explained structurally.

timeline.finding: A 1.0 Angstrom crystal structure of the two relevant Zfp57 fingers on fully methylated DNA showed the hexamer read across two fingers with the two 5-methylcytosines contacted asymmetrically, one through a 5mC-Arg-G interaction with Arg178 and the other through ordered water, with reduced affinity for unmodified DNA and for 5mC oxidation products.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays on modified DNA

timeline.finding: Allele-resolved mapping in hybrid ES cells assigned allele specificity to about two-thirds of ZFP57 sites and showed that parental-origin-specific, methylation-dependent binding occurs only at germline differentially methylated regions, while other sites are biallelic or vary with genetic background, including endogenous retrovirus targets and a newly imprinted gene, Fkbp6.
timeline.methods: allele-specific ChIP-seq in C57BL/6J x Cast/EiJ hybrid ES cells

timeline.finding: ZNF445 was shown to bind imprinting control regions in mouse and human and to act with ZFP57 in maintaining all but one mouse ICR; because ZNF445 is expressed earlier and is intolerant of loss-of-function variation in humans, the ZFP57-centered account of imprint maintenance was revised toward a two-factor model in which ZNF445 may carry more of the human load.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, mouse knockouts, human population constraint data
timeline.open: No human with biallelic ZNF445 loss has been described, so its clinical importance is inferred rather than observed.

open: The division of labour between ZFP57 and ZNF445 in humans is unsettled: mouse genetics assigns imprint maintenance to the two factors jointly, while human expression timing and constraint data suggest ZNF445 carries more of it, and no patient with biallelic ZNF445 loss has been reported to test this.
Why ZFP57 loss produces mosaic, incompletely penetrant hypomethylation that varies between loci and between patients has no mechanistic explanation.

The CIS-BP model for ZNF445 is a 29 bp matrix unrelated to the methylated hexamer, which contradicts the literature claim that ZNF445 reads the same element as ZFP57; neither the matrix nor a hexamer-based ZNF445 model has been checked against in vitro binding data.

Whether ZFP57 binding outside germline differentially methylated regions, at biallelic endogenous retrovirus copies and at background-dependent monoallelic sites, has any regulatory consequence is untested.

families.name: Telobox (TERF1/TERF2/ZBTB48)
families.def: Telomeric TTAGGG repeat binders. TERF1, TERF2, ZBTB48/TZAP.
families.short: The telobox factors TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2) bind the vertebrate telomeric repeat TTAGGG through a single Myb-type helix-turn-helix domain that is, structurally, a homeodomain-like fold. Both work as preformed homodimers, and the dimer reads two YTAGGGTTR half-sites whose spacing and orientation are almost unconstrained, so the footprint on a tandem repeat array is flexible rather than fixed. ZBTB48 (TZAP) is a zinc-finger protein that binds the same telomeric and subtelomeric variant repeats and triggers telomere trimming. Because the motif is the telomeric repeat itself, a match in the genome is almost always either a true telomere, a subtelomeric region, or an interstitial telomeric sequence - not a conventional regulatory element.
families.long:
## The factors

Human telomeres end in several kilobases of tandem TTAGGG repeats, bound by the six-protein shelterin
complex. Two shelterin subunits supply the double-stranded DNA contact: TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2) [PMID:7502076,9326950].
Each has an N-terminal domain (acidic in TRF1, basic in TRF2), a central TRFH homodimerization domain, and
a C-terminal Myb/SANT-type helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain [PMID:7502076,9326950]. The Myb domain here is a single repeat, not
the three-repeat array of c-MYB, and crystal and NMR structures show that it adopts a homeodomain-like
fold, the same solution the budding-yeast telomere protein Rap1 uses [PMID:9739097,15608617]. Both proteins bind DNA as preformed
homodimers in which the two DNA-binding domains are independent structural units on a flexible tether [PMID:15608617,10523316]. The
family name comes from the telobox, a Myb-related telomeric DNA-binding motif recognized as a conserved
module across yeast, plants and humans [PMID:8614633].

ZBTB48, also called TZAP or HKR3, is grouped here because it binds the same sequence, but it is a
different protein class: a BTB/POZ zinc-finger factor, not a telobox protein. It binds telomeric and
subtelomeric variant repeats directly [PMID:28500257], competes with TRF1 and TRF2 for long telomeres [PMID:28082411], and also acts as a
conventional transcriptional activator at a small set of promoters [PMID:28500257]. TRF1 and TRF2 are broadly expressed [PMID:9326950]
and essential; ZBTB48 is a more transient telomere visitor.

## The motif

The literature consensus is the telomeric repeat itself, TTAGGG, and in practice the unit the protein
reads is the 7-9 bp half-site YTAGGGTTR [PMID:10523316]. High-resolution crystal structures of the TRF1 and TRF2
DNA-binding domains on telomeric DNA show that both recognize the same TAGGGTT site, that two of the three
G-C base pairs characteristic of the repeat are read specifically, and that an unusually large number of
ordered water molecules mediate the protein-DNA interface [PMID:15608617]. SELEX with dimeric TRF1 defined the site as
bipartite: two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with essentially no constraint on distance or relative orientation,
simultaneously contacted by one dimer, with the intervening DNA looped out [PMID:10523316]. A tandem repeat array
therefore does not have one canonical binding register.

The matrices in this atlas all describe fragments of this repeat in one orientation or the other: AGGGTT
(HOCOMOCO TERF1), AACCCTA (CIS-BP TERF2), TCCCTAA and GGTCCCTDA (ZBTB48/TZAP), GGTCCCT (a Vierstra ZBTB
archetype). These are the same repeat unit read on opposite strands and phased differently, which is why
the atlas medoid, TCCCTAA, looks unlike TTAGGG at first glance - it is CCCTAA, the reverse complement,
shifted by one. Family cohesion is about 0.81, and the residual spread is phase and strand, not genuine
specificity differences. None of these short matrices captures the dimeric bipartite logic, so a scan
reports individual half-sites rather than functional dimer footprints. The members are not distinguishable
from sequence: TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same repeat.

## Where it acts

Almost everywhere this motif occurs it is a telomeric repeat. ChIP-seq for TRF1 and TRF2 recovers
telomeres, subtelomeric regions, and a defined subset of interstitial telomeric sequences (ITSs) -
internal blocks of degenerate TTAGGG repeats scattered through the genome, many of them near or within
gene introns - plus some centromeric and pericentromeric satellite DNA [PMID:21423270]. ITSs are themselves unstable and
are recombination-prone. ZBTB48 additionally binds subtelomeric variant repeats [PMID:28500257]. So the honest description
of the genomic distribution is: chromosome ends, subtelomeres, ITSs and satellite arrays, with only a
small number of genuine promoter sites, such as the ZBTB48 target MTFP1 [PMID:28500257]. This motif is not a promoter
element in the ordinary sense, and CpG-island promoter enrichment is not expected.

## Biology and disease

TRF1 is a negative regulator of telomere length: overexpression shortens telomeres progressively and a
dominant-negative form lengthens them, in telomerase-positive cells [PMID:9034193]. TRF2 protects chromosome ends from
being processed as double-strand breaks; its inhibition causes end-to-end chromosome fusions [PMID:9476899] and triggers
an ATM-dependent damage response, and TRF2 is implicated in the t-loop structure at telomeres, although
the crystal structures show no DNA distortion that would explain that activity [PMID:15608617]. ZBTB48/TZAP binds
preferentially to long telomeres, where shelterin density is low, and initiates telomere trimming - rapid
deletion of telomeric repeats - which sets an upper limit on telomere length [PMID:28082411]; it is also a negative
regulator of telomere length in cancer cells regardless of their telomere-maintenance mechanism [PMID:28500257]. Telomere
dysfunction through these routes connects to senescence, genome instability in cancer, and the
telomere-biology disorders, and TRF1 and TRF2 are reviewed as shelterin components in that context.

## Reading a hit

The practical rule for this family is different from every other family in the atlas: a match is a
telomeric repeat, so ask where it is before asking who bound it. If the hit is at a chromosome end or in a
subtelomere, it is telomeric. If it is internal, the most likely explanation is an interstitial telomeric
sequence or a satellite array, and a TTAGGG-rich internal block will score highly whether or not any
protein binds it. Only after excluding those should a hit be read as a regulatory element. The members
cannot be separated by sequence - TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read TTAGGG - and the short matrices available
represent single half-sites rather than the flexible bipartite site a TRF dimer actually occupies, so
scores will not track dimer affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 at 92%
DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on the human protein, the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is
ChIP-only (grade B), and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for the broad ZBTB group rather than for
ZBTB48 specifically.
families.caveats: This motif is the telomeric repeat, so most matches are telomeric, subtelomeric, interstitial telomeric sequence or satellite DNA rather than regulatory elements - check location before interpreting. TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same TTAGGG repeat and cannot be separated by sequence. The available matrices (6-9 bp fragments in both orientations; the medoid TCCCTAA is the reverse complement, phase shifted) capture single half-sites, whereas TRF dimers bind two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with almost no spacing or orientation constraint, so scores do not track real affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 (92% DBD identity), the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is ChIP-only at grade B, and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for ZBTB generally.

timeline.finding: A nuclear activity, TRF, is found in human, mouse and monkey cells that binds duplex TTAGGG repeat arrays but not closely related repeats such as TTGGGG or TTAGGC.
timeline.methods: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays with nuclear extracts
timeline.open: The protein behind the activity was unidentified.

timeline.finding: TRF (later TRF1) is cloned as a telomeric protein with one Myb-type DNA-binding repeat that colocalizes with telomeric DNA in interphase and at metaphase chromosome ends.
timeline.methods: Protein purification and cDNA cloning; immunofluorescence

timeline.finding: The telobox is defined as a Myb-related telomeric DNA-binding motif shared by yeast Tbf1, several plant proteins and human TRF and a second human protein.
timeline.methods: Deletion mapping; sequence comparison; DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: TRF2 is cloned as a distant TRF1 homologue with a very similar Myb-related domain that also binds duplex TTAGGG; the two proteins exist predominantly as separate homodimers.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; in vitro binding; dimerization assays; metaphase localization
timeline.open: Why two proteins read one repeat, and whether they discriminate between sites, was unknown.

timeline.finding: SELEX with dimeric TRF1 reveals a bipartite site of two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with no constraint on spacing or orientation, contacted simultaneously by one dimer with the intervening DNA looped out.
timeline.methods: SELEX; binding affinities; DNase I footprinting; electron microscopy

timeline.finding: Crystal structures of the TRF1 and TRF2 DNA-binding domains on telomeric DNA show both recognize the same TAGGGTT site through homeodomain-like folds, reading two of the three G-C pairs, with many water-mediated contacts.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography (2.0 and 1.8 angstrom)
timeline.open: No DNA distortion was seen that would explain TRF2's proposed role in t-loop formation.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide ChIP-seq maps TRF1 and TRF2 beyond telomeres to a subset of interstitial telomeric sequences and to centromeric and pericentromeric satellites, often near genes or in introns.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq
timeline.open: Whether these extratelomeric sites have regulatory function was not tested.

timeline.finding: Two groups characterize ZBTB48 (TZAP) as a C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds telomeric and subtelomeric variant repeats directly, prefers long telomeres with low shelterin, triggers telomere trimming, and also activates a small set of genes including MTFP1.
timeline.methods: Telomere-binding protein screens; ChIP-seq; RNA-seq; telomere-length assays

open: How TRF2 promotes t-loop formation is unexplained: TRF2 is implicated in t-loops, but its DNA-binding domain does not distort the duplex in crystal structures, so the activity must come from other parts of the protein or complex.

Whether TRF1 and TRF2 binding at interstitial telomeric sequences and satellites has a regulatory role is unsettled: ChIP-seq places them at a subset of such sites, often near genes or within introns, and a role in long-range chromosome organization and gene regulation has been proposed but not demonstrated.

families.name: SRF
families.def: CArG box CCW6GG. SRF.
families.short: The CArG box is the site of a single protein, serum response factor, which binds as a homodimer through a MADS box - the same fold MEF2 uses, reading a different sequence. The element is CC(A/T)6GG: a ten-base near-palindrome in which the outer CC and GG carry the specificity and the six central A/T positions are effectively free, giving a well-defined but degenerate site. SRF is expressed almost everywhere and is constitutively bound to many of its sites; what changes with signalling is not occupancy but which coactivator family it recruits - the ETS-domain TCF proteins downstream of MAP kinase, or the actin-regulated MRTF proteins downstream of Rho. Both bind the same CArG box, so the motif does not tell you which programme is running.
families.long:
## The factors

SRF is one protein, encoded by one gene, and this family has one member. Its DNA-binding and dimerisation function sits in a MADS box of about 57 residues with two extensions: an N-terminal one that MEF2 lacks, and a C-terminal B-box that docks one class of cofactor [PMID:3203386,7744019]. The crystal structure of the SRF core on a serum response element showed that the dimer binds an alpha-helix into the widened major groove of each half-site and that the recognised feature is as much DNA shape as base identity - the intrinsic and induced bend of the CArG box is what SRF reads [PMID:7637780]. SRF is broadly and constitutively expressed, and its activity is set by cofactors rather than by its own abundance or nuclear entry. Two families compete for it. The ternary complex factors ELK1, ELK4 (SAP-1) and ELK3 dock on the B-box through a short peptide and simultaneously contact an adjacent ETS site with their own ETS domain; they are activated by ERK and p38 phosphorylation, and the ternary-complex structure showed that the B-box contact dominates their recruitment [PMID:11406578]. The myocardin-related transcription factors MRTFA (MKL1/MAL), MRTFB and MYOCD instead bind the MADS domain itself [PMID:15014501], and MRTFA and MRTFB are sequestered by monomeric actin until Rho-driven actin polymerisation releases them [PMID:12732141].

## The motif

The CArG box is CC(A/T)6GG, ten bases, a near-palindrome [PMID:1748287]. Nearly all of the information is in the outer CCW and WGG; the six central positions are constrained only to be A or T, which is why the element is often described as heavily degenerate - one genome-wide survey characterised it as a 1,216-fold degenerate cis element once CArG-like variants are included [PMID:16365378]. Contacts from the MADS helix reach the guanines of the GG step and the adjacent bases, and basic residues clamp the phosphate backbone across the bend [PMID:7637780]. Literature and data agree here: the four models (JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP and one Vierstra archetype) converge on CCATATATGG, with family cohesion 0.93, the highest in this batch. The useful contrast is with MEF2, the other vertebrate MADS family: both read a ten-base A/T-cored near-palindrome, but SRF requires CC and GG at the ends where MEF2 requires CTA and TAG. That difference is small in edit distance but large in practice; a few in vitro MEF2 models in these collections drift into CArG-like CCAAATATGG, so the database boundary is less clean than the protein boundary. One further practical point: the cofactor switch does not change the motif. A TCF-driven serum response element, such as the c-fos SRE, is a CArG box plus a nearby ETS site [PMID:3524858,11406578]; an MRTF-driven CArG box, such as those in cytoskeletal genes, is frequently a CArG box with no ETS site at all. The presence or absence of the flanking ETS site, not the CArG itself, is what distinguishes the two.

## Where it acts

CArG boxes are predominantly proximal promoter elements, usually within a few hundred base pairs of the transcription start site, which sets SRF apart from the enhancer-biased MEF2. They are not CpG-island features. A comparative-genomics screen of conserved CArG elements near human and mouse orthologous transcription start sites recovered more than 100 candidate targets and validated 60 of 89 tested; 26 of those encode cytoskeletal, contractile or adhesion proteins [PMID:16365378]. The characteristic composite is the serum response element itself - CArG plus an ETS site - at immediate-early genes including FOS and EGR1 [PMID:3524858]. In smooth muscle, CArG and CArG-like elements cluster in the promoters of ACTA2, MYH11, TAGLN and CNN1 [PMID:15014501].

## Biology and disease

SRF sits at the junction of growth-factor signalling and the actin cytoskeleton. Deleting Srf in the mouse blocks mesoderm formation and is lethal in early gastrulation [PMID:9799237]; conditional deletion in the developing heart produces myocardial defects and embryonic lethality [PMID:15169892]. In fibroblasts, the immediate transcriptional response to serum is dominated by Rho-actin signalling to the MRTF coactivators rather than by the TCF arm, and conversely the TCF arm handles much of the ERK-driven immediate-early response [PMID:24732378]. The target set explains the phenotypes: smooth muscle contractile genes, cytoskeletal and focal-adhesion genes, and the immediate-early genes. SRF has been implicated in cardiac hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy, in vascular smooth-muscle phenotypic switching in atherosclerosis, and, through MRTFA, in tumour-cell migration and mechanotransduction. Sun and colleagues described SRF as an ancient regulator of the actin cytoskeleton [PMID:16365378].

## Reading a hit

A CArG hit is more interpretable than most, for three reasons: there is only one protein in the family, so there is no paralogue problem; the site is ten bases with four well-constrained positions; and SRF is expressed nearly everywhere, so a match is not disqualified by cell type. The limits are the degeneracy and the position bias. CCW6GG still occurs often by chance, and the A/T core means AT-rich regions produce false positives, so a match carries much more weight in a proximal promoter than in random intergenic DNA. Note one artefact of how this atlas is built: because SRF is a single-member family, every SRF model's nearest neighbours in motif space are mostly outside the family - label agreement is 0.3 for all four - and those neighbours are MEF2 and other MADS motifs. That is a property of a singleton family, not a sign the labels are wrong. Finally, the hit says nothing about which cofactor arm is active: for that, look for an ETS site within roughly 20 bp (TCF-type), or its absence at a cytoskeletal gene (MRTF-type).
families.caveats: Unusually for this atlas, there is no paralogue problem: SRF is the only member, so a CArG hit names the protein. The real limits are degeneracy and position. CC(A/T)6GG constrains only four bases, so chance matches are frequent and AT-rich sequence inflates them; weight a hit far more heavily in a proximal promoter, where real CArG boxes concentrate, than in intergenic DNA. A hit also says nothing about which coactivator arm is active, since TCF and MRTF use the same element - look for an adjacent ETS site to distinguish them. The low label-agreement values on all four SRF models reflect the family being a singleton surrounded by MEF2 and other MADS motifs, not mislabelling.

timeline.finding: A protein-binding site in the c-fos promoter, the serum response element, is identified as the sequence that mediates the gene's transcriptional response to serum factors.
timeline.methods: Gel-shift assays, binding competition and methylation interference; promoter reconstitution in transfected cells
timeline.open: The protein that bound the element had not been isolated.

timeline.finding: cDNA clones encoding SRF, a ubiquitous nuclear protein that binds the c-fos serum response element, are isolated; SRF binds DNA as a dimer, and its DNA-binding and dimerisation domain is homologous to two yeast regulators - the founding observation of the MADS box.
timeline.methods: Protein purification and cDNA cloning; DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: Comparison with three SRF-related proteins (later MEF2) fixes the SRF site as CC(A/T)6GG against their CTA(A/T)4TAG, with the difference in specificity mapping to the basic N-terminal part of the MADS domain; the two groups do not heterodimerise.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; DNA-binding assays with recombinant proteins

timeline.finding: The structure of the SRF core on a serum response element shows DNA binding, dimerisation and accessory-factor docking integrated in one compact MADS-box unit, and that the intrinsic and induced conformation of the DNA is the principal feature recognised.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: The SAP-1-SRF-DNA ternary-complex structure shows the ternary complex factor's B-box peptide docking on the SRF MADS domain while its ETS domain binds the adjacent ETS site, with the B-box contact dominating the interaction.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Actin dynamics control SRF activity through the coactivator MAL (MRTFA): monomeric actin holds MAL in the cytoplasm until Rho-driven polymerisation releases it, defining a second, TCF-independent route to CArG activation.
timeline.methods: Cell biology: reporter assays, localisation and actin perturbation
timeline.open: How much of SRF's target set each cofactor arm controls.

timeline.finding: Of 960 serum-responsive SRF target genes in fibroblasts, most are controlled by MRTFs rather than TCFs, and much SRF binding is itself serum-inducible because MRTF-SRF complexes are needed to displace nucleosomes - overturning the expectation, drawn from c-fos, that the TCF arm dominates the immediate response to serum.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq of SRF, MRTF and TCF; transcriptomics with pathway-specific perturbations

open: How many CArG-like sites are functional is unsettled: the 1,216-fold degeneracy counts the 64 perfect CC(A/T)6GG sequences plus every single-mismatch variant, and while some single-mismatch elements are validated SRF targets, the high-information motif models score most of them poorly.

Whether a CArG box's cofactor arm can be predicted from sequence is unresolved: an adjacent ETS site permits TCF recruitment, but genome-wide data show that most serum-responsive CArGs are MRTF-controlled and that SRF binding itself can depend on MRTF-driven nucleosome displacement, so the decision rule involves chromatin as well as the flanking ETS site.

families.name: CSL / RBPJ
families.def: GTGGGAA. RBPJ (SUH), plus NOTCH-dependent dimer sites.
families.short: CSL is the DNA-binding transcription factor at the end of the Notch pathway, named for its three orthologues: CBF1/RBPJ in mammals, Suppressor of Hairless in Drosophila and LAG-1 in C. elegans. Humans have one broadly expressed gene, RBPJ, plus the pancreas-restricted paralogue RBPJL. RBPJ binds the seven-base element GTGGGAA, often written on the other strand as TTCCCAC, and does so whether or not Notch is active: without a Notch intracellular domain it recruits corepressors, and with one it assembles an activating ternary complex with Mastermind-like coactivators. Some Notch targets carry two sites in a head-to-head pair with fixed spacing, an SPS, which allows two Notch complexes to dimerize. Notch signaling through RBPJ controls lateral inhibition, T-cell specification and vascular development, and is constitutively activated in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
families.long:
## The factors

There is essentially one CSL protein per genome. In humans the gene is RBPJ (older names RBP-J,
RBPSUH, CBF1); the paralogue RBPJL (RBPSUHL) is restricted to pancreatic acinar cells, where it
replaces RBPJ in the PTF1 complex. RBPJ is expressed in nearly every tissue. It is not a
Notch-specific protein in the sense of being present only when Notch is: RBPJ is constitutive,
and Notch activation changes what RBPJ does rather than whether it exists. The DNA-binding
module has three parts: an N-terminal domain with a Rel-homology-like fold, a beta-trefoil
domain (BTD) and a C-terminal domain [PMID:15297877]. The crystal structure of CSL on DNA showed that the
Rel-like domain and the BTD grip the site from opposite faces, with the BTD doing double duty as
the docking site for the RAM peptide of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD) [PMID:15297877,16530045]. On Notch
activation, NICD binds RBPJ and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1-3) to form the
ternary complex [PMID:16530045]; in the absence of NICD, RBPJ binds corepressors such as SPEN/SHARP and
associated histone deacetylases and demethylases. So the same protein on the same sequence can
repress or activate [PMID:15975935].

## The motif

The literature consensus is GTGGGAA, usually written with a 5' pyrimidine as YGTGGGAA, and its
reverse-strand form is TTCCCAC [PMID:8152928]. Only about six or seven positions carry information, and the
models in these databases are short accordingly: the representative motif here is TTCCCA, which
is simply the reverse complement of TGGGAA with the 5' GT trimmed off, and JASPAR's RBPJ matrix
(TGGGAA) is the same element on the forward strand. The GGG at the center is the least tolerant
part of the site. Only one symbol, RBPJ, appears across all four databases, so there is no
paralogue problem inside the family, and the four models agree closely (cohesion 0.93). The
difficulty is external. TGGGAA and its complement TTCCCA sit inside the purine-rich sequence
space used by ETS cores (GGAA), NFAT (GGAAA) and the half-sites of NF-kB and STAT models, and
the label-agreement statistics for all four RBPJ motifs are low (0.3) precisely because their
nearest neighbours across the four databases frequently belong to those families. A separate
feature is site architecture rather than sequence: some Notch-responsive promoters carry two
CSL sites in head-to-head orientation with a spacer of roughly 15-17 bp, the Su(H)-paired site
or SPS, first described in the Drosophila Enhancer of split complex [PMID:7590239]. The spacing and orientation
matter because they allow the ankyrin repeat domains of two Notch molecules to contact each
other across the DNA, which sharpens the response [PMID:17284587,16365048]. No PWM captures an SPS; you have to look for
two matches at the right distance and orientation.

## Where it acts

RBPJ sites are found in both promoters and enhancers, and the best-studied targets are the HES
and HEY families (HES1, HES5, HEY1, HEY2), DTX1, NRARP, and, in lymphoid cells, PTCRA, IL2RA and
MYC. Genome-wide, RBPJ and Notch1 occupy thousands of sites, and occupancy is dynamic: in
Drosophila, Su(H) binding at target enhancers is transient and only partly overlaps its
Notch-independent binding [PMID:17545467], and in mammalian cells RBPJ occupancy at many sites increases on
Notch activation rather than being fixed [PMID:23651858]. Conversely, a subset of sites is occupied by CSL
without Notch and functions in default repression, keeping targets off in cells that have not
received a signal [PMID:15975935,23651858]. RBPJ co-occurs with lineage factors that determine which of its sites are
used: TCF/LEF and GATA3 in T cells, ETS and RUNX factors at lymphoid enhancers [PMID:21737748], and PTF1A
through RBPJL in pancreas.

## Biology and disease

Rbpj-null mouse embryos die around embryonic day 10 with defects in somitogenesis and
vasculature, phenocopying loss of Notch1 more closely than any single ligand mutant. Through
Notch, RBPJ drives lateral inhibition in neurogenesis, T-cell versus B-cell specification,
arterial-venous specification and intestinal secretory-versus-absorptive choice [PMID:27507209]. Activating
NOTCH1 mutations that stabilize NICD are the commonest genetic lesion in T-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia, and the resulting Notch1/RBPJ complexes bind a largely conserved set of
enhancers in human and mouse leukemia cells [PMID:21737748]. Notch loss of function causes disease as well:
NOTCH3 in CADASIL, JAG1 and NOTCH2 in Alagille syndrome, and inactivating NOTCH1 mutations in
squamous carcinomas, where the pathway is tumor-suppressive. RBPJ itself is mutated in Adams-Oliver
syndrome.

## Reading a hit

The important caution is interpretive, not statistical: a match to the RBPJ motif, and even
measured RBPJ occupancy, does not mean Notch signaling is active at that site. RBPJ binds
constitutively and represses in the unsignaled state, so the sequence marks a potential Notch
response element, not a signaled one. To claim active signaling you need evidence for NICD or
MAML at the site, or a change in output on gamma-secretase inhibition. The site is also short:
six or seven informative bases occur often by chance, and the purine-rich core is easily
confused with ETS, NFAT or NF-kB half-sites, which is what the low label-agreement scores in
these data reflect. Two matches in head-to-head orientation about 15-17 bp apart are much
stronger evidence than one [PMID:17284587].
families.caveats: One factor, RBPJ, so a hit does not have a paralogue problem inside the family; the risk is outside it. The informative core is only six or seven bases and overlaps ETS, NFAT and NF-kB purine-rich half-sites, which is why all four RBPJ models here score low label agreement against the other databases. The HOCOMOCO model (SUH.H14CORE.0.P.B) is ChIP-derived, so it reports where RBPJ was found, not what RBPJ binds in isolation. Most importantly, RBPJ occupies sites constitutively and represses without Notch, so neither a sequence match nor a ChIP peak licenses the conclusion that Notch signaling is active.

timeline.open: What the protein did at its sites, and its link to Notch, were not addressed.

timeline.finding: Su(H) directly activates Enhancer of split complex genes in response to Notch through multiple binding sites in their proximal upstream regions, making the site a Notch response element.
timeline.methods: Drosophila reporter transgenes, binding-site mutagenesis, genetics

timeline.finding: Crystal structure of CSL on DNA: Rel-like N- and C-terminal domains with an inserted beta-trefoil domain; the N-terminal domain and the beta-trefoil domain contact the DNA, and a hydrophobic pocket on the beta-trefoil domain is proposed as the Notch docking site.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: How Notch binding converts a DNA-bound repressor into an activator.

timeline.finding: Su(H) represses Notch targets by default, through the same binding sites it uses for activation, in cells that receive no Notch signal; Hairless, Groucho and CtBP confer the repressive activity.
timeline.methods: Drosophila cis-regulatory analysis, reporter mutagenesis

timeline.finding: Structure of the CSL-NotchIC-Mastermind ternary complex on DNA: the RAM domain binds the beta-trefoil domain, the C-terminal domain unexpectedly organizes the interface with the ankyrin repeats and Mastermind, and CSL changes conformation on complex formation.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Head-to-head paired CSL sites in HES/E(spl)-type promoters require cooperative dimerization of two Notch transcription complexes to activate transcription.
timeline.methods: Structure-guided mutagenesis, reporter assays
timeline.open: How many Notch targets genome-wide depend on paired rather than single sites.

timeline.finding: Su(H) occupancy at E(spl) target genes rises transiently after Notch activation, contradicting the prevailing model of CSL statically bound to its enhancers.
timeline.methods: ChIP at 11 target loci before and after Notch activation

timeline.finding: The first RBPJ ChIP-seq in mammalian cells shows binding that rises with Notch activation at essentially all NICD-co-occupied sites, plus a separate class of sites bound statically regardless of Notch status. This revised the static-occupancy model in mammals as well.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq for RBPJ, NICD, p300 and histone marks under active and inhibited Notch

open: How much of RBPJ's genomic occupancy is Notch-independent is unsettled: the default-repression model has RBPJ sitting on its sites and exchanging corepressors for NICD, whereas ChIP in Drosophila and in mouse myogenic cells finds binding at Notch-responsive sites rising on signaling, with static binding confined to a separate set of sites.

What fraction of Notch targets depend on paired sites is unclear: cooperative dimerization on head-to-head SPS elements is required at HES-type promoters, yet most RBPJ sites are single, and the Notch paralogues differ in how well they use paired versus single sites.

How RBPJ shares sites with ZNF143 is unresolved: in T-ALL cells many RBPJ sites lie inside ZNF143 motifs and the two proteins bind such DNA mutually exclusively in vitro, which suggests exchange in cells, but the exchange was inferred rather than observed.

families.name: PROX1 (Prospero)
families.def: Prospero-domain homeodomain-like factor PROX1.
families.short: PROX1 is the human counterpart of Drosophila Prospero, and it binds DNA with a module unlike any other homeodomain: a highly divergent homeodomain fused to a conserved Prospero domain, the two folding into one structural unit called the homeo-prospero domain. That unit reads a non-canonical site, TAAGACG, rather than the TAAT core used by ordinary homeodomains, and the Prospero domain both aligns the protein on DNA and masks a nuclear export signal, coupling DNA binding to where the protein sits in the cell. PROX1 is essential for lymphatic endothelium, lens fibre elongation, liver and pancreas development and dentate gyrus identity, and it also works without its own site by tethering to nuclear receptors. A single human gene, so no paralogue ambiguity.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has effectively one member in human, PROX1, a 737-residue protein; PROX2 is a shorter relative
with much less supporting data. PROX1 was cloned as the vertebrate homologue of *Drosophila* Prospero, a
pan-neural factor required for proper differentiation of neuronal lineages [PMID:7908825,9380747]. The DNA-binding module sits at
the C terminus and is unusual enough that standard domain annotation does not register a homeobox in PROX1
at all. It consists of a highly divergent putative homeodomain immediately followed by a conserved
Prospero domain, and the crystal structures showed that these two regions are not separable: they fold as a
single structural unit, the homeo-prospero domain [PMID:12429095]. The homeodomain region retains a three-helix fold
similar to a canonical homeodomain, the Prospero domain is a four-helix bundle, and the recognition helix
bridges the two [PMID:12429095,15837198]. PROX1 binds as a monomer through this unit; it has no zinc fingers, leucine zipper or
other dimerisation module. Both the fly and human proteins also act on other transcription factors: 
Prospero modulates the DNA-binding properties of conventional homeodomain proteins such as Deformed [PMID:9380747], and
PROX1 modulates nuclear receptors, in both cases through the same conserved C-terminal region that binds
DNA but through activities that are formally independent of it [PMID:9380747].

## The motif

The functionally validated Prospero target sequence is TAAGACG, which is not a homeodomain site: there is
no TAAT core, and the bases contacted are read by residues that do not correspond to the canonical
homeodomain specificity positions [PMID:9380747,15837198]. The co-crystal structure of the homeo-prospero domain with DNA showed
Lys1290, Asn1294 and Asp1297, invariant across the family, making the specific contacts, and it reconciled
two different sequences that had previously been proposed as Prospero targets, the TAAGACG element and a
looser SELEX-derived pyrimidine-rich consensus [PMID:15837198]. The Prospero domain does not itself contact many bases; its
job is to align the protein correctly on the site. In vitro selection on human PROX1 extends the site to an
eleven-position model, AAGACGCCTTA, whose reverse complement reads TAAGGCGTCTT [PMID:23332764]; the TAAGACG core of the
literature consensus is contained in it, and the extra positions are a weakly specified 3' half that makes
the whole thing look like a loose near-palindrome of two AAG-type half sites. All four database models in
the family agree on this shape, with a cohesion of 0.89, and the only weak entry is a shortened HOCOMOCO
model reduced to CGTCTT [PMID:37962376]. Because there is one gene, there is no paralogue problem: the motif and the
protein correspond one to one.

## Where it acts

PROX1 acts at promoters and enhancers of lineage genes in the tissues where it is expressed: lymphatic
endothelium, lens, liver, pancreas, heart, lymphocytes and dentate gyrus granule cells. A large part of its
genomic footprint, though, is not explained by its own site. PROX1 functions as a corepressor and
coregulator of nuclear receptors, including liver receptor homologue-1, the oestrogen-related receptor
ERRalpha with its coactivator PGC-1alpha, and the retinoic-acid-related orphan receptors; in these
complexes it is recruited to the receptor's own response element [PMID:20194433]. So PROX1 ChIP peaks are expected to be
enriched for nuclear receptor half sites as well as for TAAGACG, and in bioenergetic gene programs the
nuclear receptor element may be the only motif present. There is no widely used name for a PROX1 composite
element.

## Biology and disease

Prox1-null mouse embryos fail to form a lymphatic vasculature: lymphatic endothelial cells do not bud from
the embryonic veins, which established PROX1 as the switch for lymphatic endothelial identity [PMID:10499794]. Forced PROX1
expression in blood vascular endothelial cells reprogrammes them toward a lymphatic phenotype, and this
remains one of the cleaner examples of single-factor endothelial fate conversion [PMID:12198161]. Prox1 loss also blocks
lens fibre elongation, causing a cataract-like phenotype [PMID:10080188], and blocks hepatocyte migration during liver
development [PMID:10888866]. In the brain, Prox1 postmitotically specifies dentate gyrus granule cell identity in
preference to CA3 pyramidal identity [PMID:22791897]. Through ERRalpha/PGC-1alpha, PROX1 restrains mitochondrial and
bioenergetic gene expression [PMID:20194433]. In cancer the direction of effect is context-dependent and contested; in
intestinal tumorigenesis a PROX1-positive tumour stem or progenitor population has been described that
contributes to tumour growth [PMID:39841093], while other settings report tumour-suppressive behaviour.

## Reading a hit

A good TAAGACG or AAGACGCCTTA match is unusually informative for a homeodomain-class family, because the
site shares nothing with the TAAT core that hundreds of other homeodomain factors use, and because there is
only one human protein that reads it. Two limits. The site is short and only moderately constrained, so
chance occurrence is not negligible in a large search space, and matches should be weighted by whether
PROX1 is expressed in the tissue at all; it is off in most adult somatic cell types. More importantly, the
converse inference fails: a PROX1 ChIP peak with no TAAGACG is not evidence against PROX1 involvement,
because much of what PROX1 does genomically is tethered to nuclear receptors. The available models rest on
in vitro selection, which supports the statement that PROX1 binds this sequence, and the crystal structure
supports it independently; that is a stronger evidence base than most families in this atlas.
families.caveats: One gene, one motif, so no paralogue ambiguity, and the site is structurally validated by a co-crystal of the homeo-prospero domain with DNA. The limits are elsewhere. TAAGACG is only seven constrained positions, so chance matches are common in large searches and should be filtered by whether PROX1 is expressed. The database models come from in vitro selection, which is good evidence for sequence but not for occupancy. And a large fraction of PROX1 genomic action is indirect: it is recruited as a coregulator by nuclear receptors including LRH-1, ERRalpha and RORs, so PROX1 ChIP peaks are expected to carry nuclear receptor elements rather than, or in addition to, this motif.

timeline.finding: Prox1 is cloned as the likely mouse homologue of Drosophila prospero and found to be expressed in young neurons, developing lens, pancreas, liver and heart, matching the fly expression pattern.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning and in situ expression analysis in mouse embryos
timeline.open: Nothing was known about what sequence the protein binds, or whether it binds DNA directly at all.

timeline.finding: Prospero is shown to be a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein with preferences unlike those of canonical homeodomains, and to separately modulate the DNA binding of homeodomain partners such as Deformed, with both activities mapping to the conserved C-terminal region but operating independently.
timeline.methods: in vitro DNA binding, enhancer assays and deletion mapping in Drosophila
timeline.open: Two different target sequences were in circulation, a defined element and a looser selection-derived consensus, and they had not been reconciled.

timeline.finding: Prox1-null mouse embryos arrest lymphatic endothelial budding from the embryonic veins while blood vessel development proceeds normally, and separately fail lens fibre elongation, giving the vertebrate protein two sharply defined requirements.
timeline.methods: targeted mouse knockouts with histology and marker analysis

timeline.finding: The structure of the DNA-binding region shows that the divergent homeodomain and the adjacent Prospero domain form a single structural unit, the homeo-prospero domain, and that the Prospero domain both contributes to DNA binding and masks a nuclear export signal inside the homeodomain region.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of the unliganded domain
timeline.open: The apo structure could not say which bases the unit reads.

timeline.finding: The co-crystal with DNA shows the invariant residues Lys1290, Asn1294 and Asp1297 contacting a non-canonical site, with the Prospero domain aligning the protein rather than reading many bases, and reconciles the two sequences previously proposed as Prospero targets; it also indicates that exposure of the nuclear export signal is not directly coupled to DNA binding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography of the protein-DNA complex

timeline.finding: PROX1 is shown to act as a negative modulator of ERRalpha and its coactivator PGC-1alpha at bioenergetic genes, establishing that a large part of its genomic action is tethered to nuclear receptors rather than driven by its own site.
timeline.methods: coimmunoprecipitation, reporter assays and genome-wide location analysis in liver cells
timeline.open: How much of PROX1 occupancy overall is tethered rather than direct was not quantified.

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX on recombinant human PROX1 extends the site to an eleven-position model, AAGACGCCTTA, which contains the TAAGACG core of the literature consensus plus a weakly specified second half, and this model underlies the JASPAR, CIS-BP and archetype entries for the family.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: In vitro selection says what the protein can bind, not which of those sites it occupies in a cell.

timeline.finding: Lineage tracing in intestinal adenomas identifies PROX1-positive cells as slow-cycling tumor stem or progenitor cells that self-renew, supply multiple tumor lineages and survive irradiation through enhanced DNA damage repair, sharpening but not settling the contested role of PROX1 in cancer.
timeline.methods: mouse lineage tracing with patient-derived organoids and xenografts
timeline.open: Other tumor settings report PROX1 as growth-suppressive, and the determinants of the direction of effect are unknown.

open: No PROX1 motif derived from occupancy exists: all four database models come from in vitro selection, so whether TAAGACG-type sites are the ones PROX1 actually binds genome-wide, and in which tissues, has not been shown by ChIP.

The proportion of PROX1 genomic action that is tethered to nuclear receptors rather than driven by its own site is unknown, which matters because the two modes predict different motif content under a peak and cannot be told apart from a motif hit.

Whether PROX2 reads the same sequence is untested: it is annotated as a Prospero-domain relative but has no measured binding model, so motif hits in this family are implicitly attributed to PROX1 alone.

The direction of PROX1 effect in cancer is contested: lineage tracing in intestinal tumors describes a self-renewing, radioresistant PROX1-positive stem or progenitor population, while other tumor types report loss of PROX1 as the oncogenic event.

families.name: Other HMG-box
families.def: HMG-box factors outside SOX and TCF/LEF: HMG20A/20B, BBX, HMGB-like archetypes.
families.short: This entry holds the HMG-box factors that are neither SOX nor TCF/LEF: HMG20A (iBRAF), HMG20B (BRAF35) and BBX (bobby sox homolog). They share only the fold. HMG20A and HMG20B are paralogous subunits of chromatin complexes - HMG20B of the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC complex that keeps neuronal genes off in non-neuronal cells, HMG20A of KMT2A/MLL complexes that turn them on - so their genomic distribution is largely set by whichever partner recruits the complex. BBX is a poorly characterized protein that groups phylogenetically with CIC rather than with SOX. The three measured motifs are unrelated to each other and to the SOX core, and this is the least coherent family in the HMG class; a hit here should be treated as a lead, not an identification.
families.long:
## The factors

Three proteins are collected here, and what they have in common is a single HMG box, not a site.
HMG20B, originally named BRAF35 (BRCA2-associated factor 35), is a core subunit of the BHC
complex that pairs LSD1 (KDM1A) and CoREST with histone deacetylases and represses neuronal
genes in non-neuronal cells [PMID:12032298]. HMG20A, its paralogue, was named iBRAF for inhibitor of BRAF35: it
opposes that complex and instead recruits KMT2A/MLL to drive neuronal gene expression [PMID:16227968], and it is
also found in a KMT2A-associated PHF5A-PHF14-HMG20A-RAI1 subcomplex [PMID:37709746]. HMG20B has a separate
mitotic function that depends on its interaction with the BRC repeats of BRCA2 [PMID:21399666]. Both are broadly
expressed. BBX is a larger, much less studied protein, broadly expressed with enrichment in the
central nervous system, which phylogenetic analysis places with CIC (capicua) in an HMG-box
subfamily distinct from both SOX and TCF/LEF [PMID:25079045]. The important structural point is that most HMG
boxes are architectural rather than sequence-reading domains: the HMGB1/HMGB2 type binds and
bends DNA with little sequence preference, and only a minority of the superfamily - SOX,
TCF/LEF, CIC and a few others - has demonstrable sequence specificity [PMID:7774012]. Nothing published
establishes that HMG20A or HMG20B selects a specific sequence in cells.

## The motif

There is no single consensus for this family, which is why none is given. The four models here
disagree with each other; cohesion is 0.45, the lowest of the HMG-class families. BBX gives the
most informative model, and it is the family medoid: CIS-BP reports TGAACRVCGTTCA (15.1 bits), the human HT-SELEX matrix of Yin et al. 2017,
and the Vierstra archetype AC0363 reports TGAACRNYGTTCA (15.8 bits) [PMID:25215497,28473536,32728250]. These are the same 13-base element - an inverted repeat, since TGAAC and GTTCA are reverse complements, with three variable bases between them - but not two measurements of it: Vierstra archetypes are clusters of models compiled from existing collections [PMID:32728250], so AC0363 most likely re-renders the same in vitro data. The half-site resembles the TGAAT half of the dimeric,
palindromic sites that appear in SOX models (Vierstra TGAATGTGCAGTCA, HOCOMOCO SOX1
TGAATANCATTCAT), differing at one position, which is consistent with BBX reading DNA in the same
general way as other sequence-specific HMG boxes. HMG20A's single HOCOMOCO model,
HM20A.H14CORE.0.SB.A, reads TCCCTAGGC (11.5 bits); its fourth field carries S, so it rests on
HT-SELEX rather than on ChIP, and it is graded A. CCTAGG is itself palindromic but bears no
relation to the SOX or TCF/LEF core. The HMG20B model, CIS-BP M02487_2.00, is ATTATAT (10.5
bits) and is inferred from the mouse protein at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497]; a short AT-rich
string of this kind is what a non-sequence-specific HMG box tends to produce in a selection
experiment, and it should not be read as a recognition sequence.

## Where it acts

For HMG20A and HMG20B the practical answer is: wherever the complex goes. LSD1-CoREST-HDAC is
recruited to neuronal gene promoters largely by REST binding its own RE1/NRSE element [PMID:12032298], and KMT2A
complexes are recruited by their own targeting subunits; HMG20A and HMG20B come along as
subunits. Locations reported for them therefore track partner occupancy - neuronal gene
promoters, pancreatic islet regulatory regions where HMG20A is required for beta cell
maturation [PMID:29449530], adipocyte loci where HMG20A acts through MEF2C [PMID:36142473], and KMT2A targets in pancreatic
cancer stem cells [PMID:37709746]. BBX has been mapped less. Its 13-base palindrome is specific by the standards
of this atlas: with two degenerate inner positions, TGAACRVCGTTCA is expected only a few hundred
times in a 3.1 Gb genome, against tens of thousands for the nine-base HMG20A model and millions
for a bare six-base HMG core.

## Biology and disease

HMG20B is required for repression of the neuronal program in non-neuronal cells and for
completion of mitosis [PMID:12032298,21399666], and its splicing has been implicated in breast cancer [PMID:39731153]; the HMG20A locus
is a genome-wide-association signal for type 2 diabetes, and HMG20A is needed for functional
maturity of pancreatic beta cells [PMID:29449530], restrains adipogenesis through MEF2C [PMID:36142473], and supports the stem-
cell state in pancreatic cancer. The HMG20A/HMG20B antagonism is a clean example of two
paralogues with the same DNA-binding domain having opposite effects by virtue of the complexes
they join. BBX has been linked to phosphate homeostasis through regulation of FGF23 in bone [PMID:39482539], and
is maternally expressed and CNS-enriched in zebrafish and mouse [PMID:25079045]. None of the three has an
established monogenic human disease.

## Reading a hit

Treat this family as a fold, not a motif: the models do not resemble one another and the family
cohesion is 0.45. The BBX palindrome is worth taking seriously as a sequence - it is long enough to be rare - but its presence in two databases is not independent confirmation, and the label rests on in vitro selection with no structural or functional follow-up, so "BBX site" is provisional, and because
the half-sites resemble those of dimeric SOX sites you should exclude SOX before settling on
BBX. An HMG20A match does not license the conclusion that HMG20A occupies the site: the HT-SELEX
evidence supports "this protein can bind this sequence", while in cells HMG20A is a passenger in
LSD1-CoREST and KMT2A complexes whose distribution is set by REST and other partners, so check
for an RE1/NRSE element nearby. The HMG20B model is mouse-inferred and low in information; do
not use it to call sites. More generally, a weak AT-rich match labelled with an HMG-box protein
is more likely to reflect a shape preference than a recognition sequence.
families.caveats: Low confidence throughout. This is a fold-defined group with no shared consensus and the lowest cohesion in the HMG class (0.45) across only four models. The BBX 13-base palindrome appears in two databases that most likely share one in vitro source, so they do not confirm each other; it is rare enough to be useful, but rests on in vitro selection alone and its half-sites overlap those of dimeric SOX sites. The HMG20A motif has HT-SELEX support, yet HMG20A acts as a subunit of LSD1-CoREST and KMT2A complexes, so genomic locations attributed to it may belong to REST or another recruiting factor. The HMG20B model is inferred from mouse at 94% DNA-binding-domain identity and is an uninformative AT-rich string.

timeline.finding: BRAF35 (HMG20B) is purified as a subunit of the BHC complex, which joins LSD1 and CoREST to histone deacetylases and is recruited by REST to the RE1/NRSE element of neuronal genes; a point mutation in the BRAF35 HMG domain blocks REST-mediated repression.
timeline.methods: Complex purification and mass spectrometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation, reporter assays
timeline.open: The HMG domain mattered for repression, but no sequence preference was defined for BRAF35 itself.

timeline.finding: HMG20A, named iBRAF, is shown to antagonize BRAF35: it accumulates at neuronal gene promoters during differentiation, recruits the methyltransferase MLL and raises H3K4 trimethylation, activating the genes BRAF35 helps repress.
timeline.methods: Chromatin immunoprecipitation, knockdown and overexpression in P19 cells

timeline.finding: HMG20B acquires a function unrelated to transcription: it binds the BRC5 repeat of BRCA2, and its depletion blocks completion of cell division.
timeline.methods: RNA interference, in vitro binding, peptide competition

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX of human BBX gives a 13-base palindrome, TGAACGCCGTTCA, the only informative model in this group; the CIS-BP BBX model (TGAACRVCGTTCA) is the same matrix. A 2014 phylogenetic analysis had already placed BBX with CIC in an HMG-box subfamily separate from SOX and TCF/LEF.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX (as compiled in JASPAR and CIS-BP); earlier phylogenetics and expression analysis
timeline.open: No structure, no genomic occupancy data and no functional test of the proposed BBX site.

timeline.finding: HMG20A is linked to beta cell biology: it is expressed in human and mouse islets, reduced in islets from type 2 diabetic donors, needed for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, and the diabetes-associated rs7119 variant lowers its expression in a reporter assay.
timeline.methods: Expression profiling, knockdown in islets and cell lines, chromatin immunoprecipitation, reporter assays

timeline.finding: Clustering human motif collections into archetypes keeps the BBX palindrome as its own archetype, AC0363, rather than folding it into the SOX or TCF/LEF clusters, which is the strongest evidence that it is a distinct element.
timeline.methods: Genomic footprinting and motif clustering
timeline.open: Archetypes are clustered from the same motif collections, so this is not an independent measurement of the BBX site.

timeline.finding: HMG20A is found in a PHF5A-PHF14-HMG20A-RAI1 subcomplex that binds the histone methyltransferase KMT2A in pancreatic cancer stem cells, reinforcing the picture of HMG20A as a complex subunit rather than a site-selecting factor.
timeline.methods: Proteomics, chromatin profiling, inhibitor and xenograft experiments

timeline.finding: The first mammalian loss-of-function phenotype for BBX: Bbx-null and osteocyte-specific Bbx-deleted mice have raised serum FGF23, low serum phosphate and reduced bone mass, and BBX suppresses vitamin D-induced Fgf23 promoter activity.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockouts, serum chemistry, promoter and interaction assays
timeline.open: Whether BBX acts at the Fgf23 promoter through its own palindromic site or through its interaction with the vitamin D receptor was not resolved.

open: Whether HMG20A and HMG20B select DNA sequences in cells at all is unresolved: HT-SELEX gives HMG20A a grade-A model for TCCCTAGGC, yet both proteins are documented as subunits of LSD1-CoREST and KMT2A complexes whose placement is set by REST and other targeting factors, and no ChIP-derived motif exists for either.

How BBX represses FGF23 is open: the mouse work shows both a vitamin D receptor interaction with ubiquitin-dependent BBX degradation and an effect on Fgf23 promoter activity, without establishing whether a BBX site in that promoter is occupied.

families.name: REST (NRSF)
families.def: 21-bp RE1/NRSE TTCAGCACCACGGACAGCGCC. REST.
families.short: REST, also called NRSF, is a single zinc-finger protein that recognizes RE1 (the neuron- restrictive silencer element), a 21-base-pair site that is one of the longest and most information- rich transcription-factor motifs in the human genome. Eight of its nine zinc fingers read two half-sites separated by a two-base spacer, which is why the element is long and unusually specific. REST recruits SIN3-HDAC and CoREST-LSD1 complexes to silence neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells, and is removed or degraded as neurons differentiate. Human and mouse genomes contain roughly one to two thousand canonical RE1s, many spread by transposable elements, plus a larger set of weaker non-canonical variants. Unusually for a PWM, a strong RE1 match is good evidence of real REST binding.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has one member. REST (RE1-silencing transcription factor) was identified twice in 1995:
as NRSF, a coordinate repressor of multiple neuron-specific genes [PMID:7871435], and as REST, a silencer protein
that restricts type II sodium channel expression to neurons [PMID:7697725]. It contains nine C2H2 zinc fingers,
eight of which form the DNA-binding array, plus a separate C-terminal finger [PMID:25092546]. REST is not itself a
catalytic repressor; it carries two repression domains that dock different corepressor machinery, an
N-terminal region that binds SIN3A with HDAC1 and HDAC2, and a C-terminal region that binds
CoREST/RCOR1, which in turn brings the demethylase LSD1/KDM1A and associated activities such as
G9a, CTDSP1 and MeCP2 [PMID:25092546]. REST is expressed broadly in non-neuronal tissue and in neural stem cells,
and its protein level falls sharply at neuronal differentiation [PMID:25092546]. A truncated splice variant, REST4,
lacks most of the finger array. There is no paralogue in these databases, so the family and the
protein coincide.

## The motif

The canonical RE1/NRSE is written TTCAGCACCACGGACAGCGCC, 21 base pairs [PMID:7871435,7697725]. It is best read as two
half-sites, a left half around TTCAGCACC and a right half around GGACAGCGCC, separated by a
two-nucleotide spacer that carries almost no information. Separate groups of zinc fingers engage the
two halves, which is the structural reason a single monomer can specify 19 informative positions [PMID:33849071];
by contrast most vertebrate factors specify six to ten. The spacer explains a discrepancy readers
will notice: the canonical string has AC at those two positions, while the JASPAR and HOCOMOCO
matrices show a weak preference for at, and the data consensus for this family is
TCAGCACCatGGACAGCgcC. These are the same element, differing only where the model is uninformative.
Non-canonical RE1s are common and functionally important. They include half-site RE1s, in which only
the left or right half is present; compound elements with expanded spacers; and single-substitution
variants throughout [PMID:17581960]. Binding-affinity work shows that canonical motifs give strong occupancy at
targets shared by all cell types, whereas atypical motifs give weak occupancy at cell- and
tissue-specific targets, and, unexpectedly, that the weak sites are the most evolutionarily
constrained [PMID:19401398].

## Where it acts

RE1 elements sit in promoters, first introns and distal regions of neuronal genes: ion channels,
synaptic vesicle proteins, neurotransmitter receptors, neuronal microRNAs and splicing factors.
Position-specific scoring searches of the human genome recover on the order of 1,300 canonical RE1s
(about 1,000 in mouse) [PMID:16899447], and a comparative-genomics model built from conserved occurrences produced
842 high-confidence human sites at 733 genes [PMID:16963704]; larger surveys that admit weaker matches reach a few
thousand [PMID:15240883,17581960]. The number is small for a vertebrate motif, which is the practical consequence of the
element's length. RE1s are present in all sequenced vertebrate genomes and absent from invertebrates
and protochordates, as is REST itself. A substantial fraction lie in repeats, and many RE1s fall
into closely related families associated with transposable elements, implying that transposon-
mediated duplication carried the element to new target genes during vertebrate evolution [PMID:16899447]. The REST
cistrome is not conserved in detail: it is substantially larger in human than in mouse embryonic
stem cells [PMID:25990720].

## Biology and disease

REST silences neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells and keeps them repressed in progenitors,
releasing them as neurons mature. Its regulation is therefore mostly post-transcriptional, through
splicing to REST4 and through ubiquitin-dependent degradation at differentiation. The first
mammalian ChIP-sequencing experiment was performed on NRSF [PMID:17540862], and the resulting maps established the
tight coupling between the motif and occupancy that makes this factor unusual.

Several diseases turn on REST dosage. Wild-type huntingtin sequesters REST in the cytoplasm; mutant
huntingtin fails to, so REST enters the nucleus, occupies RE1s and represses target genes including
BDNF, contributing to Huntington disease pathology [PMID:12881722]. In the ageing human cortex, nuclear REST rises
and is required for stress resistance, and is lost in Alzheimer disease [PMID:24670762]. Germline truncating REST
mutations predispose to Wilms tumor [PMID:26551668], and REST loss or degradation has been reported in epithelial
tumors, so it behaves as a tumor suppressor in some contexts while its gain of function drives
pathology in others.

## Reading a hit

This is the family where a PWM hit means the most. With about 19 informative positions, a full-length
canonical RE1 match essentially does not occur by chance in a three-gigabase genome, and the great
majority of strong matches are occupied wherever REST is expressed. There is no paralogue problem:
the motif belongs to one protein. Two caveats remain. First, half-site and other non-canonical RE1s
score poorly and will be missed by a threshold tuned to the canonical element [PMID:36777181,17581960], yet they carry the
cell-type-specific part of the regulon, so a negative result at a neuronal gene is weak evidence.
Second, occupancy is not the same as repression: REST is bound at many sites in cells where the
target is expressed anyway, and the functional output depends on which corepressor complex is
recruited and on REST protein level, which falls in neurons. Because the element is long and
distinctive, ChIP-derived REST models are relatively clean, and an RE1-like motif appearing in
another factor's ChIP data usually means that factor is part of a REST corepressor complex.
families.caveats: This is the best case for trusting a PWM hit: a full canonical 21-bp RE1 has roughly 19 informative positions, has no paralogue competing for the label, and is rare enough that chance matches are negligible. The failure mode is the opposite of usual: thresholds set for the canonical element miss half-site and other non-canonical RE1s, which are numerous, weakly bound and carry the tissue-specific part of the regulon. A hit also does not imply repression, since REST occupies sites in cells where the target is expressed and its protein level and corepressor choice determine the output. Conversely, an RE1-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data usually means that factor sits in a REST corepressor complex.

timeline.finding: The same protein is reported twice in one year, as NRSF, a repressor acting on a shared element in many neuron-specific genes, and as REST, which restricts type II sodium channel expression to neurons; both define the 21-base RE1/NRSE.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning, DNA-binding and reporter assays
timeline.open: How many RE1s exist in the genome, and whether the element was always this long, were unknown.

timeline.finding: A combined computational and biochemical survey catalogs 1,892 human and 1,894 mouse RE1s and shows an in vivo hierarchy: some sites are occupied at endogenous REST levels and others only when REST is raised.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide PSSM search in human, mouse and Fugu with biochemical validation
timeline.open: Which of the predicted sites are occupied in any given cell type.

timeline.finding: Two independent catalogs converge on roughly 1,000-1,300 canonical RE1s per mammalian genome, far fewer than for a typical vertebrate motif, and show that many RE1s belong to sequence families carried by transposable elements.
timeline.methods: PSSM genome search plus BLAST clustering; comparative-genomics model trained on conserved sites
timeline.open: Whether transposon-borne RE1s are functional silencers or passengers.

timeline.finding: Serial analysis of chromatin occupancy in a kidney cell line recovers far more REST-occupied sites than the canonical catalogs, and defines non-canonical motifs: half-site RE1s and versions with expanded spacers.
timeline.methods: Serial analysis of chromatin occupancy (ChIP with tag sequencing)
timeline.open: Whether non-canonical sites are bound with enough affinity to repress, or are low-occupancy background.

timeline.finding: NRSF is the subject of the first mammalian ChIP-sequencing experiment, producing genome-scale occupancy maps whose peaks align tightly with RE1 matches, which is why this motif became the standard demonstration that sequence can predict binding.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Measured in vivo binding affinities split the regulon: canonical RE1s are strongly occupied at targets shared across cell types, while atypical low-affinity sites give cell-type-restricted occupancy, and those weak sites are the most evolutionarily constrained.
timeline.methods: Quantitative ChIP across cell types with affinity ranking, comparative sequence analysis
timeline.open: Why selection would preserve weak sites more strongly than strong ones.

timeline.finding: The REST cistrome in human embryonic stem cells is substantially larger than in mouse, so the regulon defined by occupancy is not conserved in detail even where the motif is.
timeline.methods: Comparative ChIP-seq analysis in human and mouse ESCs

timeline.finding: A massively parallel reporter assay tests RE1s directly for silencing and finds a minimum REST binding strength below which cofactors do not assemble, and that non-canonical motifs silence only when their half sites are aligned at particular spacings, qualifying the view that any half-site RE1 is a functional element.
timeline.methods: Modified massively parallel reporter assay (MPRAduo) across RE1s and 1,500 variants
timeline.open: The assay measures episomal silencing, so which of these elements silence in their native chromatin is still untested.

open: How much of the non-canonical RE1 repertoire is functional is contested: affinity-based work argues that weak, atypical sites carry the cell-type-specific part of the regulon and are the most conserved, whereas reporter-based testing finds that non-canonical motifs silence only when their half sites sit at particular spacings.

Why the weakest RE1s are the most evolutionarily constrained has no accepted explanation; one possibility is that weak occupancy is itself the regulated quantity, another that these sites are constrained for reasons unrelated to REST.

Whether the much larger human than mouse REST cistrome reflects ongoing transposon-mediated expansion of the RE1 repertoire, or differences in cell state and assay sensitivity between the compared datasets, is unresolved.

What determines whether an occupied RE1 is actually repressed is unsettled, since REST is bound at many sites in cells where the target gene is expressed, and the corepressor complex recruited is not predictable from the site.

families.name: ZBTB33 (Kaiso)
families.def: KBS TCCTGCNA and methyl-CpG CGCG sites. ZBTB33.
families.short: ZBTB33, better known as Kaiso, is a BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressor with only three C2H2 fingers and two distinct ways of reading DNA. It binds the non-methylated consensus TCCTGCNA - the Kaiso binding site, or KBS, whose minimal core is CTGCNA - and, separately, methylated CpG dinucleotides, with higher affinity for the KBS of the two. Crystal structures show both modes use the same first two fingers, with methylcytosine read through CH-to-O hydrogen bonds. Kaiso was found as a partner of p120-catenin, which blocks its DNA binding, and it links adhesion to transcription. Note that all four database matrices for ZBTB33 describe a CGCG-containing palindrome, TCTCGCGAGA, not the KBS.
families.long:
## The factors

Kaiso is a single-gene family. ZBTB33 encodes a roughly 670-residue protein with an N-terminal BTB/POZ dimerization and repression domain and, unusually for a BTB-ZF factor, only three C2H2 zinc fingers at the C terminus plus a short C-terminal extension. It was isolated in a yeast two-hybrid screen for partners of the Armadillo-family adhesion protein p120-catenin [PMID:10207085], and was later identified as the DNA-binding component of a mammalian methyl-CpG-binding activity that acts as a methylation-dependent repressor [PMID:11445535]; it recruits the N-CoR corepressor complex [PMID:14527417], and its Xenopus orthologue is required to keep genes silent before the mid-blastula transition [PMID:15548582]. p120-catenin binding inhibits Kaiso's DNA binding in both of its modes [PMID:12087177], which is the mechanistic basis for the claim that Kaiso couples cadherin-based adhesion to transcriptional output: when p120 is released from junctions it can sequester Kaiso off DNA. Repression is delivered through recruited corepressors including N-CoR and the MTG16/CBFA2T3 corepressor [PMID:11445535,23251453]; Kaiso is also regulated by phosphorylation, with modification at Thr606 driving cytoplasmic accumulation and reduced repression of CDH1 [PMID:35851744]. Kaiso is broadly expressed and is not restricted to a lineage.

## The motif

This is the family where the phrase "dual specificity" is literal, and where the databases and the literature describe different things. Site-selection experiments defined a sequence-specific consensus, TCCTGCNA, with a minimal sufficient core of CTGCNA; two copies occur in the human and mouse matrilysin (MMP7) promoters [PMID:12087177]. The same work showed that Kaiso separately possesses a methyl-CpG-dependent binding activity, requiring consecutive methylated CpGs and biochemically distinct from KBS binding, and that affinity for the KBS is the higher of the two [PMID:11445535,12087177]. Only zinc fingers 2 and 3 are needed for sequence-specific binding [PMID:12087177]. Crystal structures of the Kaiso zinc-finger domain bound to the KBS and to a symmetrically methylated sequence from the E-cadherin promoter explain how one small domain does both jobs: bases are read in the major groove by residues in the first two fingers, using classical hydrogen bonds for the KBS and methyl CH-to-O hydrogen bonds for methylcytosine, while the C-terminal extension past finger 3 binds the opposing minor groove and is required for high affinity [PMID:22949637]. That extension is disordered in the free protein and folds on binding. Now the discrepancy: all four matrices in this family - the JASPAR ENCODE-derived MA0527.2 [PMID:23693142], both HOCOMOCO KAISO models (evidence P, grade B), and CIS-BP M08094 - read TCTCGCGAGA or a close variant. That palindrome is the CGCG element found at TATA-less, CpG-island-associated bidirectional promoters [PMID:30332484]. It is CpG-containing, so it is compatible with the methyl-CpG mode, but it is not the KBS, and it is not what site selection returned. In other words, the collections capture one Kaiso mode and miss the other entirely. Genome-wide work with Kaiso-knockout cells as a control reports both: CGCG and CTGCNAT are the two principal enriched motifs, with about 60 percent of sites containing both [PMID:39702290].

## Where it acts

Kaiso sites are overwhelmingly promoter-proximal and CpG-island-associated. ChIP in Kaiso-knockout-controlled experiments places Kaiso at CpG islands with a preference for methylated ones and for islands with partial methylation at their 5' or 3' boundaries, including a class showing wave-like methylation [PMID:39702290]. Canonical KBS-containing targets include MMP7 (matrilysin) and Wnt-pathway genes [PMID:12087177,23251453]; the methylation-dependent mode has been studied at the CDH1 promoter. Because the CGCG element is a general bidirectional-promoter feature, Kaiso motif hits cluster where CpG-island promoters cluster rather than at tissue-specific enhancers. Named partners are p120-catenin (negative), N-CoR, MTG16, and, at Wnt targets, the TCF/LEF-beta-catenin machinery.

## Biology and disease

Kaiso-deficient mice are viable and fertile, and on an Apc(Min) background they show reduced intestinal tumor burden and longer survival [PMID:16354691], which put Kaiso forward as a tumor-promoting repressor rather than a suppressor. Much of the disease literature concerns Kaiso's subcellular distribution in carcinoma: nuclear versus cytoplasmic Kaiso correlates with p120-catenin status and with prognosis in several tumor types [PMID:30419310], and Thr606 phosphorylation shifts the balance toward the cytoplasm, releasing CDH1 [PMID:35851744]. Kaiso has also been linked to clonal hematopoiesis and myelodysplastic phenotypes [PMID:39702290], and to DNA-damage responses in breast cancer cells. The tumor-biology claims are more contested than the biochemistry: reported effects of Kaiso depletion vary between cell systems and between the two binding modes, and the field has not settled how much of Kaiso's function depends on methyl-CpG reading versus KBS binding.

## Reading a hit

First decide which motif you matched. A hit to a database ZBTB33 matrix is a hit to the TCTCGCGAGA CGCG element, which is a common CpG-island promoter feature also matched by other GC- and CpG-reading factors; on its own it is closer to evidence of "this is a CpG-island bidirectional promoter" than of Kaiso occupancy. A hit to TCCTGCNA is the literature KBS, but it is short, degenerate at one position, and therefore frequent by chance. Second, note that every matrix here is ChIP-derived: JASPAR MA0527.2 is ENCODE ChIP-seq and both HOCOMOCO models carry evidence code P at grade B, with no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model in this family's data [PMID:28473536,37971293]. That is exactly the situation in which indirect binding cannot be excluded, and published Kaiso ChIP-seq datasets have been noted to conflict with the in vitro binding data [PMID:23693142,39702290]. Third, methylation state is part of the specificity, and no PWM encodes it: a CpG-containing match that is unmethylated in your cell type may not be a Kaiso site at all, and vice versa. The practical recommendation is to pair a motif hit with methylation data and, where possible, with a knockout-controlled occupancy dataset.
families.caveats: Kaiso has two binding modes and the databases represent only one. All four ZBTB33 matrices here read the CGCG palindrome TCTCGCGAGA - a generic CpG-island bidirectional-promoter element - rather than the site-selection consensus TCCTGCNA, so the same gene symbol can mean two different motifs depending on the source. Every matrix in this family is ChIP-derived (ENCODE JASPAR; HOCOMOCO evidence P, grade B), with no in vitro model, and published Kaiso ChIP datasets are known to conflict with in vitro data, so indirect binding is a live possibility. Methylation state is part of the specificity and no position weight matrix captures it; interpret hits alongside methylation data.
