timeline.finding: Kaiso was cloned in a two-hybrid screen for p120-catenin partners as a BTB/POZ protein with only three C2H2 fingers, placing an adhesion cofactor in contact with a transcriptional repressor.
timeline.methods: yeast two-hybrid, co-immunoprecipitation, immunolocalization
timeline.open: What sequence, if any, Kaiso recognizes.

timeline.finding: Kaiso was identified as a methylation-dependent repressor that requires at least two symmetrically methylated CpGs, preferentially in the sequence CGCG, and as a component of the MeCP1 methyl-CpG binding activity.
timeline.methods: methyl-DNA affinity purification, mass spectrometry, transfection reporters
timeline.open: Whether Kaiso also reads unmethylated sequence specifically.

timeline.finding: Site selection defined the unmethylated Kaiso binding site TCCTGCNA with the minimal core CTGCNA, showed that fingers 2 and 3 suffice for it, established that the KBS is bound with higher affinity than methyl-CpG sites, and showed that p120-catenin blocks both modes.
timeline.methods: random-oligonucleotide site selection, EMSA with finger deletions, competition assays
timeline.open: How one three-finger domain can read two unrelated kinds of site.

timeline.finding: Kaiso-null mice were found to be viable and fertile with no overt developmental or expression phenotype, but crossing them to Apc(Min) mice delayed intestinal tumorigenesis, which framed Kaiso as tumor-promoting rather than as an essential repressor.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, tumor-susceptibility crosses, expression analysis

timeline.finding: Crystal structures of the Kaiso zinc-finger domain on the KBS and on a symmetrically methylated E-cadherin sequence showed that the same first two fingers read both, using classical hydrogen bonds for the KBS and methyl CH-to-O bonds for methylcytosine, with a C-terminal extension that is disordered until it folds into the opposing minor groove.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays

timeline.finding: Analysis of ENCODE Kaiso ChIP-seq together with methylation maps reported that Kaiso occupies unmethylated, highly active promoters in vivo rather than methylated DNA, contradicting the model built from the in vitro methyl-binding work and leaving the two literatures in open conflict.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and DNA methylation data integration
timeline.open: Whether the discrepancy reflects antibody quality, chromatin accessibility or a genuinely different in vivo mode.

timeline.finding: The TCTCGCGAGA palindrome that all the ZBTB33 matrices describe was characterized in its own right as a conserved, methylation-sensitive element that drives bidirectional transcription at TATA-less CpG-island promoters, showing that the catalogued Kaiso motif is also a general core-promoter feature.
timeline.methods: motif analysis of CpG-island promoters, nascent-transcript mapping, reporter assays

timeline.finding: Kaiso ChIP in Caki-1 cells with a Kaiso-knockout line as the negative control recovered both motifs - CGCG and CTGCNAT, with about 60 percent of sites carrying both - and placed Kaiso at CpG islands with a preference for methylated and partially methylated ones, partially reconciling the in vitro and in vivo pictures.
timeline.methods: knockout-controlled ChIP-seq, methylation profiling, binding-deficient mutant comparison

open: Whether Kaiso prefers methylated or unmethylated DNA in cells is still contested: an ENCODE-based analysis concluded that it occupies unmethylated, actively transcribed promoters, while knockout-controlled ChIP in kidney carcinoma cells reports enrichment at methylated and partially methylated CpG islands, and the crystal structures show that the protein is capable of both.

Which of the two binding modes carries Kaiso's biological function is unresolved, since no study has separated KBS-dependent from methyl-CpG-dependent target genes in the same cells with separation-of-function mutants beyond the single E535A allele.

It is unclear how much of a match to the catalogued TCTCGCGAGA matrix says anything about Kaiso at all, because the same element independently drives bidirectional transcription at TATA-less CpG-island promoters and would be recovered in any ChIP experiment centered on such promoters.

Whether Kaiso promotes or restrains tumor growth in humans is unsettled: loss delays intestinal tumorigenesis in Apc(Min) mice, whereas the correlative human data depend on whether the protein is nuclear or cytoplasmic and point in both directions across tumor types.

families.name: MECOM / EVI1
families.def: Two-finger-cluster GATA-like and GACAAGATA sites. MECOM, PRDM16-EVI1 module.
families.short: MECOM, better known as EVI1, is a 145-kDa C2H2 zinc-finger protein with two separate finger clusters that bind two different sequences. The N-terminal cluster of seven fingers reads a 15-bp GATA-like site, GA(C/T)AAGA(T/C)AAGATAA, whose core is GACAAGATA; the C-terminal cluster of three fingers reads the unrelated GAAGATGAG. EVI1 is normally expressed in hematopoietic stem cells, kidney and lung, and is silenced in most differentiated blood cells. It is one of the strongest adverse prognostic markers in acute myeloid leukemia, where 3q26 rearrangements such as inv(3)(q21q26) do not create a fusion protein but move a GATA2 enhancer next to MECOM, switching the gene on. Germline MECOM mutations cause radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.
families.long:
## The factors

MECOM (MDS1 and EVI1 complex locus, 3q26.2) encodes EVI1, first found as the site of retroviral
integration in murine myeloid leukemia cell lines [PMID:2842066]. The protein carries two physically separate arrays of
Cys2-His2 zinc fingers, seven at the N terminus and three near the C terminus [PMID:2842066,2017172], plus a CtBP-interaction
motif and an acidic domain; it can act as a repressor or an activator depending on partners. A longer
read-through transcript, MDS1-EVI1, adds a PR/SET domain and is the reason EVI1 was once numbered
PRDM3. Unlike the PRDM family proper, the two finger clusters of EVI1 are used as independent
DNA-binding modules, which is why this atlas treats MECOM separately. EVI1 binds as a monomer, not an
obligate dimer, and one protein can engage both site types. Expression is restricted: hematopoietic stem
and progenitor cells, kidney, lung and developing heart and limb, with silencing on myeloid and
lymphoid differentiation. There is only one human gene, so there is no paralogue ambiguity within the
family, but there is considerable ambiguity with GATA factors.

## The motif

The proximal (N-terminal, fingers 1-7) cluster recognizes a 15-nucleotide consensus,
GA(C/T)AAGA(T/C)AAGATAA, which contains a tandem pair of GATA-like half-sites [PMID:8321231]. Fingers 4-7 make the
sequence-specific contacts; fingers 1-3 do not detectably bind DNA on their own but bias the first
position toward GACAA over GATAA and are needed for optimal occupancy of the full 15-mer [PMID:8321231]. The functional
minimal core is GACAAGATA [PMID:8557637], and a single amino-acid change (R205N) abolishes high-affinity binding to it [PMID:16006653].
Because GATAA is embedded in the site, EVI1 and GATA factors have overlapping but not identical
preferences: EVI1 binds erythroid GATA-1 target sites only weakly, while GATA-1 can bind and activate
through a GACAAGATAA element [PMID:8557637]. The distal (C-terminal, three-finger) cluster binds a completely different
and shorter consensus, GAAGATGAG [PMID:8183551].

The database consensus in this atlas, TTATCTTATCT (and the 14-bp TATCTTATCWTATC archetype), is the
reverse complement of the proximal site written as tandem AGATAAGATAA half-sites; JASPAR renders the
same thing as AGATAAGATAA. So the literature consensus and the data agree once strand and finger cluster
are accounted for, and the longer Vierstra archetype simply captures more half-site repeats. No
widely used matrix in these databases represents the distal GAAGATGAG site, which is worth remembering:
scanning with a MECOM matrix tests only one of EVI1's two specificities.

## Where it acts

EVI1 occupancy in fibroblasts and myeloid cells maps to conserved GACAAGATA-like motifs within about
10 kb of transcription start sites of a defined target set, including GATA2, ZFPM2/FOG2, GADD45G, SKIL,
KLF5, DCN and MAP3K14 [PMID:16006653]. Sites are found in both promoters and distal elements. Because the proximal site
is a doubled GATA half-site, EVI1 peaks overlap GATA1/GATA2 peaks in hematopoietic cells, and in
erythroid or megakaryocytic chromatin a WGATAA-rich region is ambiguous between the two families. EVI1
also functions through protein interactions with a large partner network, including CtBP and
polycomb-associated proteins, so a fraction of its ChIP signal is likely tethered rather than
sequence-driven.

## Biology and disease

Conditional deletion of Evi1 in mice depletes hematopoietic stem cells and impairs repopulation, and
also blocks transformation by leukemic fusion oncogenes, making EVI1 required for both normal and
malignant stem-cell self-renewal [PMID:18682242]. High EVI1 expression marks roughly 6-11% of adult acute myeloid
leukemia and is associated with poor outcome [PMID:26729571]. The clearest mechanism is enhancer hijacking: in
inv(3)(q21q26) and t(3;3)(q21;q26), the breakpoint does not create a fusion protein but relocates a
distal GATA2 hematopoietic enhancer to the MECOM locus, driving EVI1 expression while leaving the
other GATA2 allele haploinsufficient [PMID:24703711]. Two independent studies established this, one by mapping the
rearranged enhancer in patient genomes [PMID:24703711] and one by deleting the orthologous mouse enhancer [PMID:24703906]. Germline missense mutations in MECOM, one of them de novo and all three clustered in the eighth zinc finger of the C-terminal domain, cause radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia [PMID:26581901],
a bone-marrow-failure syndrome with a skeletal phenotype, confirming a developmental role beyond blood.

## Reading a hit

A MECOM match is a doubled GATA-like element, so the first alternative hypothesis is a GATA factor, not
EVI1 - especially in erythroid, megakaryocytic or endothelial cells where GATA1/GATA2 are abundant and
EVI1 is usually off. The 15-bp full site is long enough to be reasonably specific, but the shorter
matrices in these databases (10-11 bp, essentially two WGATAA half-sites) will match tandem GATA sites
indiscriminately. A hit on the distal GAAGATGAG specificity will not be found at all with the available
matrices. There is only one human MECOM gene, so a true EVI1 hit has no paralogue problem, but the
CIS-BP model is inferred from mouse Evi1 at 98% DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on the
human protein [PMID:25215497], and the Vierstra archetypes are named for MECOM without claiming separability from GATA.
Treat a hit as evidence for a GATA-type element and use expression data to decide whether EVI1 is a
plausible occupant.
families.caveats: The proximal EVI1 site is a tandem GATA-like element, so matches are shared with GATA1-GATA6 and TRPS1; in blood and endothelium a GATA factor is usually the more likely occupant, since EVI1 is off in most differentiated cells. The shorter matrices here are effectively two WGATAA half-sites and match tandem GATA sites indiscriminately. EVI1's second specificity, GAAGATGAG, is not represented by any matrix in these databases, so a MECOM scan tests only one of two binding modes. The CIS-BP model is inferred from mouse Evi1 (98% DBD identity), not measured on human EVI1. Part of EVI1's ChIP signal is likely tethered through its large protein-interaction network rather than direct.

timeline.finding: Evi-1 is identified as a common retroviral integration site activated in IL-3-dependent mouse myeloid leukemia lines, encoding a protein with two zinc-finger domains of seven and three fingers.
timeline.methods: Provirus integration mapping; cDNA and genomic cloning
timeline.open: Whether the protein bound DNA, and what sequence, was unknown.

timeline.finding: Purified Evi-1 is shown to be a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein with a high-affinity site, TGACAAGATAA, protected in DNase I footprints.
timeline.methods: Random-oligonucleotide selection by gel shift-PCR; DNase I footprinting
timeline.open: Which of the ten fingers made the contacts was not resolved.

timeline.finding: The N-terminal seven-finger domain recognizes a 15-nucleotide consensus, GA(C/T)AAGA(T/C)AAGATAA; four of the seven fingers are required, and fingers 1-3 bias the first position toward GACAA.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection and amplification; finger deletion mutants

timeline.finding: The C-terminal three-finger domain is shown to bind a different consensus, GAAGATGAG, which, unlike the N-terminal site, follows the standard C2H2 recognition rules.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection; finger-swap and point mutagenesis; reporter assays
timeline.open: The site did not support reporter activation, leaving its function in cells unclear.

timeline.finding: Fingers 1-7 require the GACAAGATA core and bind erythroid GATA-1 target sites only weakly, arguing against simple occupation of GATA sites by EVI1.
timeline.methods: Methylation interference; quantitative gel shift; genomic fragment selection; cotransfection

timeline.finding: A single-residue mutant (R205N) abolishes high-affinity binding, and native EVI1 occupies GACAAGATA-like motifs near target genes including Gata2, Zfpm2 and Gadd45g in myeloid cells.
timeline.methods: DNA-binding mutants; EVI1-VP16 target screen; ChIP

timeline.finding: Two groups independently show that inv(3)/t(3;3) leukemias activate EVI1 by repositioning a distal GATA2 hematopoietic enhancer to the MECOM locus rather than by creating a fusion protein.
timeline.methods: Functional genomics and enhancer excision in AML cells; BAC transgenic mice with and without the enhancer

timeline.finding: A de novo MECOM missense mutation and two further missense mutations, all clustered in the eighth zinc finger (C-terminal domain), are found in radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.
timeline.methods: Exome sequencing; ChIP-qPCR; reporter assays
timeline.open: The mutants were tested at an ETS-like EVI1 site rather than at GAAGATGAG, so which C-terminal specificity matters in vivo was left open.

open: What the C-terminal finger cluster reads in cells is unsettled: in vitro selection gave GAAGATGAG, whereas the disease-causing mutations in finger 8 were assayed at an ETS-like EVI1 site, and no matrix in these databases represents either specificity.

Whether EVI1 antagonizes GATA factors by competing for shared sites is unresolved: GATA-1 can bind and activate through the GACAAGATAA element, but EVI1 binds erythroid GATA-1 sites only weakly, so direct site competition and indirect interference remain alternative models.

families.name: ZFX / ZFY
families.def: CpG-island GGCCT core at promoters. ZFX, ZFY.
families.short: ZFX and its Y-linked paralogue ZFY are thirteen-finger C2H2 zinc-finger activators that bind a short GC-rich site containing a GGCCT core. Their placement is the interesting part: they bind inside CpG-island promoters a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of the transcription start site, between the open region at the TSS and the first downstream nucleosome, and they activate the promoters they occupy. Together with the related ZNF711, they occupy the majority of active CpG-island promoters in a cell. ZFX loss slows proliferation, which is why the gene recurs in growth-based CRISPR screens, and ZFX supports embryonic and hematopoietic stem-cell self-renewal. Germline ZFX variants cause an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder.
families.long:
## The factors

ZFY was cloned in 1987 from the sex-determining region of the human Y chromosome and proposed as the
testis-determining factor [PMID:3690661], a role later taken by SRY [PMID:1695712]. Its X-linked paralogue ZFX has a similar gene
structure, escapes X inactivation [PMID:2500252], and was recognized early as a probable transcriptional activator
with alternative isoforms [PMID:2512506]. The third member, ZNF711, is also X-linked and has an overlapping binding
pattern [PMID:32406922]. All three are ubiquitously expressed, which is unusual among C2H2 factors and consistent
with a housekeeping role at promoters.

The proteins have an acidic N-terminal region and thirteen C2H2 zinc fingers. Mutational dissection
shows that fingers 11 to 13 are necessary and sufficient for DNA binding, and that these fingers
together with the N-terminal region constitute a functional transactivator [PMID:32406922]; the remaining ten fingers
are not required for site recognition. In the databases behind this family, only ZFX has matrices,
and the four of them agree closely (cohesion 0.91), so this is one of the more internally consistent
zinc-finger families despite the short motif.

## The motif

The consensus is GC-rich and short. The core that all models share is GGCCT, and the fuller form used
by JASPAR and CIS-BP is GCCBMGGCCT, which is also the data consensus for this family; the HOCOMOCO
ChIP-derived version, CCAGGCCBCG, is the same core with different flanks. There is no crystal or NMR
structure of the ZFX fingers on DNA, so which bases the three DNA-binding fingers contact is inferred
from the standard C2H2 recognition rules rather than observed. With roughly five to eight informative
positions, the motif is one of the least specific in routine use, and it is intrinsically GC-rich, so
matches are dense wherever GC content is high. Reported analyses note that the GGCCT motif occurs
throughout the genome but at higher density inside CpG islands, which is where occupancy is found [PMID:29429977].

ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 are not separable by sequence in practice, and their genomic binding patterns at
CpG-island promoters are essentially the same. ZNF711 also has its own reported motif, and where the
two are distinguished, ZFX appears to be the dominant of the pair, with ZNF711 playing a subordinate
role at shared promoters [PMID:32406922].

## Where it acts

This family is a promoter family, and the position of binding is its defining feature. ChIP in four
cancer cell lines recovered roughly 9,000 ZFX sites, most of them in CpG-island promoters, and genes
with ZFX-bound promoters were expressed at higher levels than unbound ones [PMID:29429977]; knocking ZFX down
down-regulated many of them, so ZFX is an activator. The binding position is about 240 base pairs
downstream of the transcription start site of responsive promoters, and nucleosome-occupancy and
methylome sequencing places it between the nucleosome-free region at the TSS and the first downstream
nucleosome [PMID:29429977]. Taking ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 together, the union of their bound promoters covers on the
order of 10,000 CpG-island promoters, a large majority of the active CpG-island promoters in a cell [PMID:32406922].
Mechanistically, reducing ZFX lowers histone H4 acetylation and increases RNA polymerase II pausing
at target promoters [PMID:38726870], which is consistent with a role in promoter architecture and early elongation
rather than in enhancer-driven, cell-type-specific regulation.

## Biology and disease

Zfx-null mice are viable but smaller, with reduced self-renewal of embryonic and hematopoietic stem
cells [PMID:17448993], so the gene supports proliferative capacity rather than specifying a lineage. That fits the
cancer literature, in which ZFX expression correlates with proliferation and outcome across several
tumor types, and in which Zfx facilitates tumorigenesis driven by Hedgehog-pathway activation [PMID:25164012].
Because ZFX contributes to growth in many cell types, bi-allelic ZFX knockouts reduce cell growth and
combined ZFX/ZNF711 knockouts cause major proliferation defects [PMID:32406922], which is why ZFX turns up repeatedly
as a hit in growth-based genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens; readers should be aware that a ZFX hit
in such a screen usually reflects this general proliferative requirement rather than a
pathway-specific dependency. In human genetics, germline ZFX variants cause an X-linked
neurodevelopmental disorder with a recurrent facial gestalt [PMID:38325380]. ZFY, on the Y chromosome, has a distinct
role in male germ-cell development [PMID:37354519].

## Reading a hit

A GGCCT-containing match is weak evidence by itself: the motif is short, GC-rich, and denser in CpG
islands, so hits accumulate in exactly the sequence people usually submit. Position is the most useful
filter. A match a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of a CpG-island TSS is a plausible ZFX site;
the same match in an intergenic or AT-poor enhancer is probably not. The hit identifies the family
rather than the protein: ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 bind the same sequence, and which one matters depends on
the sex and expression of the cells. Note also that the CIS-BP human ZFX motif in this collection is
transferred from mouse Zfx rather than measured on the human protein, though at 99% DNA-binding-domain
identity that transfer is harmless. Finally, because ZFX sits at a large fraction of all active
promoters, a ZFX-like motif recovered from another factor's ChIP data is more likely to reflect
promoter co-occupancy than that factor's own specificity.
families.caveats: The motif is short (roughly five to eight informative positions) and GC-rich, so hits are dense in CpG islands and GC-rich sequence generally, and a match alone means very little. Position carries more information than score: credible sites lie a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of a CpG-island transcription start site. ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 read the same sequence and cannot be separated, and only ZFX has matrices here; the CIS-BP entry is transferred from mouse Zfx, benign at 99% DNA-binding-domain identity. No structure of these fingers on DNA exists, so the base contacts are inferred. Because ZFX occupies most active CpG-island promoters, a ZFX-like motif in another factor's ChIP data usually means co-occupancy.

timeline.finding: A zinc-finger gene, ZFY, is cloned from the sex-determining region of the human Y chromosome and proposed as the testis-determining factor.
timeline.methods: Deletion mapping of the Y chromosome in sex-reversed individuals, cDNA cloning
timeline.open: No DNA-binding site was known, and the assignment rested on map position.

timeline.finding: The X-linked paralogue ZFX is shown to have the same gene structure, to escape X inactivation, and to encode alternative isoforms with the features of a transcriptional activator, making the pair a dosage-related gene family rather than a male-specific switch.
timeline.methods: Genomic and cDNA comparison, X-inactivation escape assays, domain analysis

timeline.finding: SRY is identified as the testis-determining factor, removing the role that had motivated interest in ZFY and leaving the family without an assigned function for a decade.
timeline.methods: Positional cloning in sex-reversed individuals, sequence analysis

timeline.finding: Zfx-null mice are viable but small, with reduced self-renewal of embryonic and hematopoietic stem cells, giving the family a proliferative rather than a lineage-specifying role.
timeline.methods: Conditional mouse knockout with stem-cell transplantation and self-renewal assays

timeline.finding: ChIP in human tumor cell lines places roughly 9,000 ZFX sites overwhelmingly in CpG-island promoters, about 240 base pairs downstream of the start site, between the nucleosome-free region and the first downstream nucleosome, and knockdown lowers expression of bound genes, so ZFX is an activator positioned by promoter architecture rather than by enhancer context.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in four cell lines, knockdown with RNA-seq, nucleosome-occupancy and methylome sequencing
timeline.open: Whether ZFY and ZNF711 occupy the same promoters was untested.

timeline.finding: Treating ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 as one family shows their bound promoters cover on the order of 10,000 CpG islands, that zinc fingers 11-13 are necessary and sufficient for DNA binding, and that losing ZFX and ZNF711 together causes major proliferation defects.
timeline.methods: CRISPR bi-allelic knockouts in HEK293T, RNA-seq, structure-function analysis of ZFX mutants

timeline.finding: Reducing ZFX lowers histone H4 acetylation and increases RNA polymerase II pausing at target promoters, which recasts the family as acting on promoter chromatin and early elongation rather than on recruitment of the polymerase.
timeline.methods: Degron and knockdown of ZFX with chromatin profiling and nascent transcription assays

timeline.finding: Germline ZFX variants are shown to cause an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder with a recurrent facial gestalt, establishing that a factor sitting at most active CpG-island promoters is dosage-sensitive in human development.
timeline.methods: Clinical exome and genome sequencing in a patient cohort with functional assays

open: How ZFX is positioned a couple of hundred base pairs downstream of the start site is unexplained: the GGCCT core is short and common in CpG islands, so either an unidentified feature of promoter architecture selects the bound copy, or the position reflects nucleosome placement rather than sequence.

Whether ZFX, ZFY and ZNF711 differ at all in intrinsic specificity is untested; their measured motifs are the same and their promoter occupancy overlaps, so the apparent dominance of ZFX over ZNF711 at shared promoters has no sequence explanation.

No structure of the ZFX fingers on DNA has been determined, so which bases fingers 11-13 contact is inferred from the standard C2H2 recognition rules rather than observed, and the GCCBMGGCCT and CCAGGCCBCG forms in the databases have not been reconciled structurally.
Whether the transcriptional effects of ZFX loss are direct or follow from a general proliferation defect is hard to separate, which is also why ZFX recurs as a hit in growth-based CRISPR screens.

families.name: ZNF410
families.def: Long GC-rich site clustered at the CHD4 promoter. ZNF410.
families.short: ZNF410 is a five-finger C2H2 zinc-finger protein that recognizes a long, information-rich element, and it is the clearest known case of a mammalian transcription factor with essentially one target gene. Two conserved clusters near CHD4, which encodes the ATPase of the NuRD chromatin remodeling complex, together carry 27 copies of the motif; comparable clusters occur nowhere else in the genome. Removing ZNF410 lowers CHD4 protein by about 60 percent, which is enough to de-repress the fetal haemoglobin genes without obvious toxicity, and the factor was found in CRISPR screens for fetal haemoglobin silencers. Matches to the motif are therefore biologically meaningful mainly when they fall in those clusters, and isolated hits elsewhere rarely correspond to occupied, functional sites.
families.long:
## The factors

ZNF410 is a single, conserved protein with no close paralogue in the human genome: a tandem array of five C2H2 zinc fingers flanked by N- and C-terminal regions that are not themselves DNA-binding domains [PMID:36660822]. It is broadly expressed. The pentadactyl array is the whole of the sequence-reading apparatus, and crystallographic and solution work shows it binds DNA as a monomer with 1:1 stoichiometry [PMID:33301730,36660822]. An unusual regulatory feature sits outside the fingers: AlphaFold modeling combined with small-angle X-ray scattering indicates that an acidic, serine/threonine-rich hairpin loop in the N-terminal region folds back onto the DNA-binding face of the finger array, mimicking the charge and shape of DNA [PMID:36660822]. Full-length ZNF410 binds DNA less tightly than the isolated finger array, both in vitro and in cells, consistent with the loop having to be displaced before binding [PMID:36660822]. This is an autoinhibitory mechanism layered on top of ordinary sequence specificity.

## The motif

The element is long for a five-finger protein: a 15-base-pair site, usually written from the CHD4 clusters as CATCCCATAATA with two or three further specified positions at the 5' end (reverse complement TATTATGGGATG) [PMID:23332764,33301730]. All four databases in this family agree closely on it, and the family is among the most cohesive in the atlas. Five fingers contacting fifteen base pairs is the canonical three-base-pairs-per-finger arrangement [PMID:38754172], and the element contains no internal repeat or half-site: it is read in one pass, with no spacing rule and no dimerization. Information content is high and spread across the whole word, with the central CCCAT and the 3' AATA both contributing; the AT-rich 3' end is what distinguishes this motif from the many GC-rich promoter motifs it would otherwise resemble. Because ZNF410 has no paralogue, there is no paralogue ambiguity within the family: a strong match means ZNF410 or nothing.

## Where it acts

In erythroid cells, ZNF410 chromatin occupancy is concentrated almost entirely at CHD4 [PMID:33859416]. Two regulatory elements, one upstream of the promoter and one intronic, carry 27 ZNF410 motifs between them [PMID:33859416]; no other locus in the human or mouse genome has a comparable cluster, and the two clusters are conserved across mammals [PMID:33301730]. Deleting them reproduces the effect of deleting ZNF410 itself, so essentially all of the factor's relevant output runs through this one gene [PMID:33859416]. Occurrences of the isolated motif do exist elsewhere in the genome, and weak ZNF410 signal has been reported at some of them, but they do not measurably affect transcription [PMID:33301730]. Mechanistically this is thought to be a matter of local concentration: a tight array of sites builds enough occupancy to activate, while single sites do not. The clusters sit in an open, CpG-island-adjacent promoter context rather than in tissue-specific enhancers.

## Biology and disease

ZNF410 came out of CRISPR screens of transcription factors for regulators of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) [PMID:33301730,33859416]. It is not a direct repressor of HBG1/HBG2; it activates CHD4, and CHD4/NuRD in turn silences the gamma-globin genes [PMID:33301730]. Knocking out ZNF410, or its mouse homolog Zfp410, drops CHD4 protein by roughly 60 percent and raises HbF substantially in adult-type erythroid cultures and in xenotransplantation, without the cellular or organismal toxicity seen when CHD4 itself is removed [PMID:33859416]. That partial, buffered effect is why ZNF410 attracted interest as a therapeutic target for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia, alongside BCL11A and the HBG promoter BCL11A site [PMID:38728575,37924864]. Outside erythropoiesis the phenotype is mild, consistent with a factor whose only strong target is a chromatin-remodeler subunit. There is no established human disease caused by ZNF410 mutation, and no recurrent cancer association.

## Reading a hit

A strong match to this 15-base-pair word is good evidence for ZNF410 specifically, because the protein has no paralogue and the motif is long. What a hit does not license is the inference that the site is used. The lesson of this family is that a single occurrence of even a high-information motif is usually not a functional element; what mattered at CHD4 was 27 of them in two clusters. If your hit is a lone site, treat it as a sequence match rather than a regulatory element unless you have occupancy or perturbation data. Conversely, if you find a dense cluster of ZNF410 motifs at a locus, that is worth following up, and genome-wide scans for such clusters have been used to argue that CHD4 really is unique [PMID:33301730,33859416]. The database matrices here are a mixture of in vitro (HT-SELEX/methyl-SELEX) and derived archetypes and agree well, so matrix choice matters little.
families.caveats: Trust a hit for the protein but not for function. ZNF410 has no close paralogue, the motif is 15 base pairs long, and the in vitro and ChIP matrices agree, so a strong match is genuinely ZNF410's word rather than a shared GC-rich site. The problem is the opposite of the usual one: isolated matches occur throughout the genome and are largely inert, because ZNF410 needs the dense clusters found only at CHD4 to produce an effect. Do not read a single hit as a regulatory element, and be wary of published ZNF410 peak lists that include weak non-CHD4 sites. Full-length ZNF410 also binds more weakly than its isolated finger array, so in vitro affinities overstate cellular occupancy.

timeline.finding: High-throughput SELEX of human transcription factors yields a ZNF410 motif, the in vitro basis of the JASPAR matrix for this family, years before any target gene of the protein was known.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX
timeline.open: Where ZNF410 bound in cells, and what it regulated, was unknown.

timeline.finding: A CRISPR screen for fetal hemoglobin regulators identifies ZNF410 as a factor that in erythroid cells directly activates a single gene, the NuRD subunit CHD4, through two conserved clusters of its binding sites with no counterpart elsewhere in the genome; crystallography defines how the five fingers read the 15-base-pair site.
timeline.methods: CRISPR-Cas9 screen, ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, xenotransplantation, in vitro binding assays, X-ray crystallography
timeline.open: Why isolated copies of the same motif elsewhere in the genome have no effect was not explained.

timeline.finding: An independent screen reaches the same conclusion and quantifies it: the two CHD4 regulatory elements carry 27 ZNF410 motifs between them and account for the whole effect of ZNF410 on fetal globin, and knockout of ZNF410 or mouse Zfp410 lowers CHD4 by about 60%, enough to derepress fetal hemoglobin while avoiding the toxicity of removing CHD4 itself.
timeline.methods: CRISPR screen, ChIP-seq, enhancer deletion, mouse knockout, erythroid differentiation assays

timeline.finding: Full-length ZNF410 binds DNA less tightly than its isolated finger array; small-angle X-ray scattering with AlphaFold modeling indicates an acidic, serine/threonine-rich hairpin loop in the N-terminal region lies on the DNA-binding face of the fingers, mimicking DNA and acting as an autoinhibitory switch that must be displaced.
timeline.methods: Small-angle X-ray scattering, AlphaFold modeling, binding assays in vitro and in cells
timeline.open: What displaces the hairpin loop in cells, and whether it is regulated, is unknown.

timeline.finding: A distal CHD4 enhancer transcribed as an enhancer RNA is reported to differ between beta-thalassemia patients with high and low fetal hemoglobin, with a candidate variant at a predicted ZNF410 site, placing the ZNF410-CHD4 axis among the modifiers of fetal hemoglobin now under review as therapeutic targets.
timeline.methods: Patient transcriptome sequencing, eQTL and binding-site prediction, inhibition experiments in HUDEP-2 cells
timeline.open: The ZNF410 site involvement was predicted rather than demonstrated by binding or editing.

open: Why a dense cluster of sites activates CHD4 while isolated copies of the same 15-base-pair motif elsewhere in the genome do not measurably affect transcription is unexplained; local concentration is the proposed reason but the threshold has not been measured.

What relieves the autoinhibition is unknown: the N-terminal hairpin loop occupies the DNA-binding surface and lowers the affinity of the full-length protein, but no signal, modification or partner that displaces it has been identified.

Whether ZNF410 does anything outside erythroid cells is unresolved: it is broadly expressed and highly conserved, yet its occupancy in the cells examined is concentrated at CHD4 and no phenotype outside erythropoiesis has been described.

Whether partial loss of CHD4 is a safe way to raise fetal hemoglobin in patients is unsettled: the roughly 60% reduction caused by ZNF410 loss avoids toxicity in cultured cells, xenografts and mice, but no clinical data test this therapeutic window.

families.name: VEZF1
families.def: CT/GC-rich sites in vascular promoters. VEZF1.
families.short: VEZF1, originally cloned twice as DB1 and as Vezf1, is a broadly expressed six-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger protein first defined on CT/GC-rich promoter elements and on the chicken beta-globin HS4 insulator, where its sites protect against DNA methylation. It has no established consensus sequence: the matrices in motif databases reduce either to a plain poly-C/poly-G run (JASPAR MA1578.2 is six positions long) or to GGGGGAGGGGG, which is the MAZ motif. That is the central problem with this family - the data cannot separate it from MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281 or ZNF148. Its documented functions are in vascular development, in maintaining DNA methylation levels through Dnmt3b, and in slowing elongating RNA polymerase II.
families.long:
## The factors

VEZF1 is one protein, cloned independently twice. It was first isolated as DB1, one of three Cys2/His2 zinc-finger cDNAs recovered by screening with the CT/GC-rich region (positions -76 to -47) of the human interleukin-3 promoter; the other two clones were EGR1 and EGR2. DB1 encoded a novel 516-residue protein with six zinc fingers, expressed ubiquitously across human tissues, and it bound the IL-3 element constitutively while EGR1 bound only after T-cell activation (Koyano-Nakagawa et al. 1994) [PMID:8035792]. Independently, a retroviral entrapment screen in mouse identified Vezf1 (vascular endothelial zinc finger 1) as a gene whose expression is restricted to vascular endothelial cells and their precursors in the yolk sac blood islands (Xiong et al. 1999) [PMID:9986727]. The two literatures have not fully merged: one describes a ubiquitous factor, the other an endothelial one, and current work generally treats VEZF1 as broadly expressed with a particular requirement in endothelium. The chicken homolog is BGP1, which has binding sites in the beta-globin locus including the upstream HS4 insulator (Gowher et al. 2008) [PMID:18676812]. There are no paralogues; the gene is also catalogued as ZNF161.

## The motif

This family has no consensus sequence that the literature agrees on. The IL-3 element VEZF1 was cloned on was described only as a CT/GC-rich region [PMID:8035792]. The one short site mapped since is the 6-bp ACCCCC in the endothelin-1 promoter, which recombinant VEZF1 binds and whose 2-bp mutation abolishes the response [PMID:11504723], and the HS4 insulator elements it was purified on are G-rich [PMID:20062523]. These point to C/G runs without defining a consensus, and the matrices assembled here do not converge. The medoid (CIS-BP M01172_2.00) is CCCCCCAC and the JASPAR profile (MA1578.2) is CCCCCC - six positions, a poly-C run, which will match an enormous number of genomic positions and carries almost no discriminating information. The two HOCOMOCO models are longer but point somewhere else: VEZF1.H14CORE.0.P.C is GGGGGAGGGGG and VEZF1.H14CORE.1.P.B is a 23-position G-run, GGGGGGGGGGAGGGGGAGGGGGG [PMID:37971293]. The first of those has its single best-matching matrix, across all four databases, inside the MAZ family rather than in its own - so as a matter of data, VEZF1's motif is MAZ's motif. The family flags it as a suspect assignment for exactly that reason. Cohesion across the four matrices is 0.69, and label agreement for each of them is 0 to 0.1, meaning that for every one of them the nearest neighbors are mostly labelled with some other factor. Two things follow. First, there is no sequence feature that identifies a VEZF1 site as opposed to a MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281 or ZNF148 site; the single-base discriminator that separates the GGGAGGG group from the SP1 GC-box (an A where the GC-box has a C, Song et al. 2001) [PMID:11395515] is the only sequence-level distinction available anywhere in this neighborhood, and it does not help here. Second, a poly-C or poly-G match should be treated as a statement about base composition, not about a transcription factor.

## Where it acts

VEZF1 sites were characterized at promoters (IL-3, endothelin-1) and at an insulator [PMID:8035792,11504723,20062523]. In the chicken beta-globin HS4 element, the G-rich sub-elements bound by VEZF1 are the part that confers protection from DNA methylation: they can defend a transgene from encroaching methylation independently of the enhancer-blocking activity of the same insulator (Dickson et al. 2010) [PMID:20062523]. Genome-wide in HeLa S3 cells, VEZF1 binding correlates strongly with peaks of Ser2-phosphorylated elongating RNA polymerase II, reflecting a VEZF1-dependent slowing of elongation (Gowher et al. 2012) [PMID:22308494]. That is an unusual place for a zinc-finger factor to act and is one of the few properties that distinguishes VEZF1 functionally from its motif neighbors, though it is a property of the protein, not something readable from a match.

## Biology and disease

Vezf1 is required for vascular development in a dose-dependent manner: targeted inactivation in mice causes vascular defects and embryonic lethality with localized hemorrhage, and heterozygotes are affected (Kuhnert et al. 2005) [PMID:15882861]. Vezf1-null embryonic stem cells fail to form normal vascular structures on differentiation (Zou et al. 2010) [PMID:20431070]. In endothelial cells VEZF1 acts pro-angiogenically, in part by repressing the anti-angiogenic factor Cited2 (AlAbdi et al. 2018) [PMID:29794136], and it activates the endothelin-1 promoter (Aitsebaomo et al. 2001) [PMID:11504723]. Its most striking phenotype is epigenetic: deleting both copies of Vezf1 in mouse embryonic stem cells reduces expression of the full-length active isoform of the Dnmt3b methyltransferase and causes widespread loss of DNA methylation genome-wide (Gowher et al. 2008) [PMID:18676812]. So VEZF1 influences methylation both indirectly, through Dnmt3b levels, and locally, through methylation-protecting elements. No human Mendelian disease has been established for VEZF1.

## Reading a hit

Treat a VEZF1 match with more suspicion than almost any other entry in this atlas. All four matrices are derived from binding data in cells (ChIP-seq for both HOCOMOCO models, at grades B and C) [PMID:37971293] and none is an in vitro model, so none of them is evidence that VEZF1 itself prefers that sequence. Two of them are so short or so uniform - CCCCCC, and a 23-base G-run - that they function as composition filters. The most informative model has its best match inside the MAZ family. In practice, then: a VEZF1 hit means "G-rich or C-rich promoter sequence", and the candidate binders include MAZ, PATZ1, ZNF281, ZNF148, the ChIP-derived WT1 models and, one base away, the SP1/KLF GC-box. If you specifically need VEZF1, the useful evidence is not the motif but the context in which VEZF1 has documented function: methylation-protected insulator sub-elements, and regions where elongating Pol II accumulates. Confirm with VEZF1 ChIP or knockdown rather than with a score.
families.caveats: This is the least trustworthy family in the batch. VEZF1 has no agreed literature consensus: the one short site mapped in a promoter is ACCCCC in endothelin-1, and its insulator elements are G-rich. Of the four matrices, JASPAR's is six positions of poly-C, one HOCOMOCO model is a 23-base G-run, and the most informative model has its single best match across all four databases inside the MAZ family - the data cannot tell VEZF1 from MAZ, and flags the assignment as suspect. All models are ChIP-derived; none is in vitro. Read a hit as a statement about G/C-rich composition, not about VEZF1, and confirm by ChIP or knockdown.

timeline.finding: DB1 is cloned as one of three zinc-finger cDNAs binding the CT/GC-rich element of the IL-3 promoter, alongside EGR1 and EGR2: a six-finger protein whose mRNA is present in all human tissues tested and which binds the element constitutively, while EGR1 binds only after T-cell activation.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning with a promoter element, gel shift with specific antibodies, transfection
timeline.open: The bound sequence was defined only as a 30-bp CT/GC-rich region.

timeline.finding: A retroviral entrapment screen identifies mouse Vezf1, homologous to DB1, with expression restricted to vascular endothelial cells and their yolk-sac precursors, the opposite of the ubiquitous pattern reported for human DB1.
timeline.methods: Gene-trap screen, in situ hybridization
timeline.open: The two expression reports were not reconciled.

timeline.finding: VEZF1/DB1 activates the endothelin-1 promoter through a 6-bp element, ACCCCC; recombinant protein binds it and a 2-bp mutation abolishes the response, the one short site mapped for VEZF1 in a promoter.
timeline.methods: Deletion mutagenesis, gel shift with recombinant protein and endothelial nuclear extracts, transfection

timeline.finding: Vezf1-null mouse embryos show vascular remodeling defects, loss of vascular integrity and localized hemorrhage, and heterozygotes show lymphatic hypervascularization, establishing a dose-dependent vascular requirement.
timeline.methods: Gene targeting in mice, ultrastructural analysis

timeline.finding: Deleting both Vezf1 copies in mouse ES cells causes loss of DNA methylation at LINE-1 elements, minor satellites, some imprinted genes and several CpG islands, attributed to a large drop in Dnmt3b.
timeline.methods: Knockout ES cells, methylation and expression analysis
timeline.open: How a zinc-finger factor controls Dnmt3b levels was unknown.

timeline.finding: VEZF1 is purified as the factor that binds the methylation-protection sub-elements of the chicken HS4 insulator, which are separable from the CTCF-dependent enhancer-blocking part; G-rich VEZF1 elements alone protect the APRT CpG-island promoter from methylation.
timeline.methods: Stable reporter assays, protein purification on DNA elements, methylation analysis
timeline.open: Whether VEZF1 protects CpG islands genome-wide was proposed but not tested.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide, VEZF1 binding coincides with peaks of Ser2-phosphorylated elongating Pol II reflecting VEZF1-dependent slowing of elongation, including near VEZF1 sites in the dnmt3b gene, with effects on alternative splicing.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in HeLa S3, Pol II ChIP in knockout ES cells, splicing analysis

timeline.finding: The HOCOMOCO v14 VEZF1 models are ChIP-only G-runs (grades B and C), and the more confident has its best match in the MAZ family, so the database models cannot separate VEZF1 from other G-rich binders.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq-derived motif models, cross-database comparison

open: Whether VEZF1 is a broadly expressed factor or an endothelial one is unresolved: the human DB1 cloning found its mRNA in all tissues tested, whereas the mouse studies describe expression largely restricted to endothelium and its precursors, with additional mesodermal and neuronal sites.

What VEZF1 itself recognizes is not pinned down: the one element mapped in a promoter is the 6-bp ACCCCC in endothelin-1, the insulator elements it was purified on are G-rich, and the database matrices are poly-C or poly-G runs whose best matches lie in the MAZ family; whether these reflect one preference for C/G strings is unknown.

Whether VEZF1 affects genome-wide methylation mainly through Dnmt3b, by slowing Pol II and shaping splicing within the dnmt3b gene, or also by directly protecting CpG islands, as its insulator sub-elements do in reporter assays, has not been separated experimentally.

families.name: NRF1
families.def: Palindromic GCGCATGCGC at nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene promoters. NRF1.
families.short: NRF1 (nuclear respiratory factor 1, also alpha-PAL) is a single-gene family whose DNA-binding domain belongs to no common fold class, its closest relatives being sea urchin P3A2 and Drosophila Erect wing. It binds as a homodimer to a palindrome, GCGCATGCGC, with each subunit contacting one GCGC half; motif models extend this to TGCGCATGCGC. The site contains two CpG dinucleotides in its most informative positions, so it is strongly associated with CpG-island promoters and is blocked by cytosine methylation. NRF1 sites sit in promoters of nuclear genes for mitochondrial proteins, including cytochrome c, cytochrome c oxidase subunits and TFAM, making NRF1 the main nuclear coordinator of mitochondrial biogenesis. It should not be confused with NFE2L1, also abbreviated Nrf1.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has exactly one human member: NRF1, nuclear respiratory factor 1, also called alpha-PAL for "alpha palindromic-binding protein". It was defined functionally, by mutational and binding analysis of the somatic cytochrome *c* promoter, before it was cloned [PMID:2166701]. Its DNA-binding domain lies in the N-terminal half of the protein and belongs to no previously described class; the closest relatives are the sea urchin developmental regulator P3A2 and the *Drosophila* protein Erect wing (EWG), and the three define a small, conserved family unrelated to zinc fingers, helix-turn-helix, bZIP or any other common fold [PMID:8253388]. The C-terminal half, which carries the activation function, is divergent between the three [PMID:8253388]. NRF1 binds as a homodimer [PMID:38055835] and is broadly expressed; it is a housekeeping factor rather than a tissue-specific one, and its activity is modulated by phosphorylation of an N-terminal serine cluster and by coactivation from the PGC-1 family [PMID:18391175]. Because there is one gene, the usual paralogue problem does not arise — but a nomenclature problem does, described under **Reading a hit**.

## The motif

NRF1 recognizes a palindrome, GCGCATGCGC, and the palindromic character is the defining feature: each subunit of the homodimer contacts one GCGC half, and the guanine contacts on the two strands mirror each other [PMID:2166701,38055835]. The motif models in this collection extend it slightly, to an 11- or 12-mer — the HOCOMOCO and Vierstra consensus is TGCGCATGCGC — so the element is equally well described as a tandem pair of TGCGC half-sites separated by a single base [PMID:38055835]. The palindrome is the older rendering; the extended repeat is what the matrices encode. Some models (JASPAR MA0506.3, CIS-BP M08177_2.00) place a C rather than an A/T at the central position, giving TGCGCCTGCGC, which reflects tolerance at the one position that is not part of either half-site [PMID:38055835].

Two features follow directly from the composition and matter in practice. First, the site contains two CpG dinucleotides, and both fall in the positions that carry the most information. Second, it is therefore methylation-sensitive: cytosine methylation within the site blocks NRF1 binding, and in cells lacking DNA methyltransferases NRF1 gains occupancy at sites it cannot bind in wild-type cells. NRF1 was the factor used to demonstrate this competition genome-wide [PMID:26675734], and it also scores as methylation-avoiding in systematic methyl-SELEX surveys [PMID:28473536]. Family cohesion is 0.94, the highest tier in this atlas: all four models are effectively the same matrix.

## Where it acts

NRF1 sites are promoter elements, not distal enhancers, and they are strongly associated with CpG islands — which follows from the motif itself, since an unmethylated CpG-rich 10-mer is exactly what a CpG island is made of. The original targets were nuclear genes for mitochondrial proteins: somatic cytochrome *c*, cytochrome *c* oxidase subunits, a ubiquinone-binding subunit of the reductase complex, and the RNA component of RNase MRP, which functions in mitochondrial DNA replication [PMID:2166701]. NRF1 also activates the promoter of *TFAM*, the mitochondrial transcription factor A gene, which is the direct mechanistic link between a nuclear promoter element and mitochondrial genome expression [PMID:8108407]. Beyond respiratory genes, NRF1 sites occur in many broadly expressed promoters, frequently alongside GABP (historically NRF-2), SP1 and YY1 sites [PMID:8383622,18391175]. An exact 10-mer of this composition is expected only a few thousand times in 3 Gb of uniform sequence, and because CpGs are depleted outside CpG islands, genuine matches concentrate in island promoters rather than being spread across the genome.

## Biology and disease

NRF1 is the central nuclear factor coordinating expression of the respiratory apparatus with the mitochondrial genome. Mouse *Nrf1* knockouts die at peri-implantation stages with depleted and unstable mitochondrial DNA [PMID:11134350], a phenotype consistent with loss of *Tfam* and related targets rather than with a single metabolic defect. Through *TFAM*, *TFB1M/TFB2M* and the mitochondrial ribosome and import machinery, NRF1 sets the capacity of oxidative phosphorylation, and its activity is the point at which PGC-1-family coactivators act during mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle and brown fat [PMID:18391175]. The methylation dependence also gives NRF1 a role as a readout of the epigenome: in promoters that become hypermethylated, NRF1 occupancy is lost even though the sequence is intact [PMID:26675734], so changes in NRF1 target expression can reflect methylation change rather than any change in the factor.

## Reading a hit

The most common error with this family is not motif-related at all, it is naming. "NRF1" in this atlas means nuclear respiratory factor 1 and nothing else. It is not NFE2L1, which is also routinely abbreviated Nrf1 and belongs to the CNC-bZIP antioxidant-response family; it is not NFE2L2/NRF2; and it is not NRF-2, which turned out to be GABP, an ETS-domain factor [PMID:8383622]. A hit on GCGCATGCGC says nothing about antioxidant response elements or the KEAP1-NRF2 pathway.

With one gene in the family, a match is unusually close to a protein-level call, and the evidence supports direct binding: HOCOMOCO's NRF1.H14CORE.0.PS.A combines ChIP-seq with HT-SELEX at grade A, so this is not a ChIP-only inference. The 10-11-mer is long and information-rich enough that a strong match in a CpG-island promoter is genuinely suggestive. What a match does not tell you is occupancy, and here the gap is specific and checkable: because the site carries two CpGs and NRF1 will not bind a methylated site, a perfect match inside a methylated region is probably unbound, so check methylation state [PMID:26675734]. Finally, the Vierstra archetype here is AC0555:NRF:Unknown: the class is recorded as unknown, and the label names clustered factor annotations, not a validated protein.
families.caveats: Two cautions dominate. First, nomenclature: this family is nuclear respiratory factor 1, not NFE2L1 (also abbreviated Nrf1), not NFE2L2/NRF2, and not NRF-2, which is GABP; a hit here has nothing to do with antioxidant response elements. Second, methylation: the palindrome carries two CpGs in its most informative positions and methylation blocks binding, so an intact match inside a methylated region is likely unoccupied — check methylation state, not just sequence. Otherwise this is a strong family. One gene, cohesion 0.94, all four models essentially identical, and HOCOMOCO grade A evidence combining ChIP-seq with HT-SELEX, so the motif is not a ChIP-only inference.

timeline.finding: NRF-1 is defined as an activator binding the somatic cytochrome c promoter, and functional sites with the same guanine contacts are found in genes for cytochrome oxidase subunit VIc, the ubiquinone-binding protein of the reductase complex and the RNA of RNase MRP.
timeline.methods: Promoter mutagenesis, EMSA, methylation interference, competition binding
timeline.open: The protein had not been cloned, so its DNA-binding domain was unknown.

timeline.finding: The second nuclear respiratory factor, NRF-2, is purified and identified as GABP, a multisubunit ETS-domain activator, so NRF-1 and NRF-2 are unrelated proteins with unrelated sites.
timeline.methods: Protein purification, peptide sequencing, DNA binding

timeline.finding: NRF-1 is cloned; its N-terminal DNA-binding domain is shared with sea urchin P3A2 and Drosophila EWG and is unrelated to known DNA-binding motifs, founding a new class.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, deletion mapping, recombinant DNA binding, reporter assays
timeline.open: The structure of the new DNA-binding domain remained unknown until 2024.

timeline.finding: The TFAM (mtTFA) promoter is shown to depend mainly on an NRF-1 site, linking a nuclear promoter element directly to mitochondrial transcription.
timeline.methods: Promoter mutagenesis, in vitro transcription with recombinant protein

timeline.finding: Nrf1-null mouse embryos die between E3.5 and E6.5, and null blastocysts have markedly reduced mitochondrial DNA.
timeline.methods: Gene knockout, blastocyst culture, mtDNA quantification

timeline.finding: In mouse ES cells lacking DNA methylation, NRF1 occupies several thousand additional sites; restoring de novo methyltransferase activity remethylates them and evicts NRF1, showing genome-wide that methylation, not sequence, restricts its binding.
timeline.methods: DNase-seq, ChIP-seq, DNMT knockout and rescue, motif deletion

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of an NRF1 homodimer on ATGCGCATGCGCAT shows a dimerization domain with an SRF MADS-like dimer interface linked flexibly to a helical DNA-binding domain; one monomer makes a U-turn so that the two DBDs read the two TGCGC half-sites from opposite sides of the DNA.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, ITC, mutagenesis, reporter assays
timeline.open: The isolated DBD binds a single TGCGC half-site in vitro; whether that happens in cells was not tested.

open: Whether the central base pair of the site is constrained is not settled: JASPAR MA0506.3 and CIS-BP M08177_2.00 place a C there (TGCGCCTGCGC), whereas the HOCOMOCO model and the 2024 crystal structure use the A/T form, and binding measurements show only about a three-fold preference for a central AT over CG.

Whether NRF1 binds isolated TGCGC half-sites in vivo is unknown: its DNA-binding domain alone binds a half-site in vitro, but the full-length protein needs cooperation between the dimerization and DNA-binding domains to bind the intact palindrome and to activate transcription.

Which factors keep NRF1 sites unmethylated is only partly understood: NRF1 cannot bind methylated sites and depends on neighboring motifs or other factors to keep its sites hypomethylated, and whether NRF1 itself helps maintain that state once bound has not been established.

families.name: NPAS3 / NPAS4 / other PAS
families.def: Neuronal PAS-domain bHLH factors binding E-box variants.
families.short: NPAS3 and NPAS4 are neuronal bHLH-PAS transcription factors, relatives of CLOCK, HIF and AHR that heterodimerize with the same shared beta subunits ARNT and ARNT2 and read E-box-like sites built around a CGTG core. NPAS4 is an immediate-early gene induced by neuronal activity rather than by growth factors, and it controls the number of inhibitory synapses formed on excitatory neurons. NPAS3 is a broader brain factor whose disruption segregates with schizophrenia in one family. This is the thinnest family in the group: only three motif models exist, all derived from chromatin immunoprecipitation, and the NPAS4 and NPAS3 models do not actually resemble each other. A match here is best treated as a generic E-box variant unless neuronal, activity-dependent evidence supports more.
families.long:
## The factors

NPAS1 (MOP5) and NPAS3 (MOP6) were cloned together as bHLH-PAS proteins with expression largely restricted to the central nervous system (Zhou et al. 1997) [PMID:9012850]. NPAS4, also called NXF, was identified separately as a neuron-specific bHLH-PAS factor that competes with SIM2 at the drebrin promoter (Ooe et al. 2004) [PMID:14701734]. All share the class domain layout, a basic helix-loop-helix domain followed by PAS-A and PAS-B, and none binds DNA usefully alone. Co-immunoprecipitation from mouse brain recovers ARNT2 as the major NPAS4 partner with ARNT1 as a minor band; both heterodimers are active in reporter assays, and ARNT1 mRNA is found in some NPAS4-expressing regions lacking ARNT2 (Ooe et al. 2009) [PMID:19284974]. ARNT is therefore the shared beta subunit here exactly as it is for HIF and AHR. NPAS4 is an immediate-early gene, unusual in being induced by calcium influx and neuronal activity rather than by growth factors, and its expression is confined to neurons. NPAS3 is more broadly distributed in brain. NPAS1 has no motif model in JASPAR, HOCOMOCO, CIS-BP or the Vierstra archetypes, so it does not appear in this family's data even though it belongs to the group by domain. The family holds only three motifs, one from JASPAR and two from HOCOMOCO.

## The motif

There is no single well-established consensus, and the two members do not share one, so this entry gives no family consensus string. For NPAS4 both available models center on a short CGTG core with a 5' T and a 3' A: HOCOMOCO NPAS4.H14CORE.0.P.B is TCGTGa and JASPAR Npas4 (MA1995.2) is TCGTGAC. That is an E-box-like half-site pair but not a canonical E-box: the position carrying C in CACGTG, or T in the HRE TACGTG, is absent from the core. Read through the pairing rules established for this class, in which the ARNT-type subunit contributes the 3' GTG half-site and the partner supplies the 5' half (Swanson et al. 1995) [PMID:7592839], the NPAS4 model is best understood as ARNT's GTG plus a non-canonical NPAS4 half-site. NPAS3 is different. Its single model, NPAS3.H14CORE.0.P.C, is gkACGTGc, an ordinary ACGTG site, and its nearest neighbor across all four databases lies outside this family: similarity 0.97 to a motif in another family versus 0.81 to the other NPAS models. The pooled consensus for the family, TCGTGa, is essentially the NPAS4 model alone. Recent systematic profiling of prototypical bHLH-PAS proteins including NPAS4 reports footprints of 12-15 bp in which preferences for bases flanking the core, together with DNA shape, carry the discriminating information rather than the core itself (Bersten et al. 2026) [PMID:41495897]. The practical consequence is that a 6-7 bp core model for these factors cannot be specific.

## Where it acts

NPAS4 works at activity-regulated promoters and enhancers in neurons, where its induction follows depolarization within minutes and its targets include genes that set the number and distribution of inhibitory synapses on excitatory cells (Lin et al. 2008) [PMID:18815592]. In hippocampal CA3 it drives a transcriptional program required for contextual memory formation (Ramamoorthi et al. 2011) [PMID:22194569]. Two features limit where these sites matter: expression is restricted to neurons and occupancy requires activity, so in resting neurons and all non-neural tissue nearly all matches are unoccupied. The genome-wide picture is less settled than for the other bHLH-PAS families, and a prominent genome-wide study of NPAS4 heterodimers was retracted in 2024 (Cell 2024) [PMID:38870944], so published site counts and partner-specific cistromes for this family should be treated as provisional. Both HOCOMOCO models here derive from ChIP-seq rather than from in vitro selection.

## Biology and disease

Loss of Npas4 in mice reduces the number of inhibitory synapses formed on excitatory neurons and removes an activity-dependent brake on excitation (Lin et al. 2008) [PMID:18815592]; conditional deletion in CA3 impairs contextual fear memory (Ramamoorthi et al. 2011) [PMID:22194569]. The factor has since been linked to seizure susceptibility, social behavior and cognitive flexibility (Sun and Lin 2016) [PMID:26987258]. For NPAS3, a balanced translocation that disrupts the gene segregates with schizophrenia in an affected family (Kamnasaran et al. 2003) [PMID:12746393], and Npas3-null mice show abnormal neurodevelopment, altered neurotrophin and reelin signaling, and behavioral abnormalities (Brunskill et al. 2005) [PMID:16190882]. Neither gene is an established cancer driver.

## Reading a hit

This family has the weakest evidence base of the bHLH-PAS groups in the atlas. All three models are ChIP-derived (HOCOMOCO evidence letter P, grades B and C) [PMID:37971293], so they support "this region was occupied in cells" rather than "this protein binds this sequence"; there is no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model for either factor. Because the NPAS4 and NPAS3 models do not resemble each other, a hit should be reported against the specific model, not the family: a match to the NPAS3 model is in practice a match to a generic ACGTG E-box and is closer to the HIF/ARNT class than to NPAS4. The NPAS4 core is five informative base pairs and occurs by chance very often. Cell type and stimulus are more informative than the score: a site is only plausible in neurons and after activity. A hit cannot separate NPAS4 from NPAS3, nor either from HIF, AHR, SIM or ARNT homodimer complexes reading overlapping cores, and it says nothing about which beta subunit, ARNT1 or ARNT2, was present.
families.caveats: Trust this family less than the other bHLH-PAS groups. Only three models exist, all from ChIP-seq at grade B or C, so none is in vitro evidence of direct binding, and indirect or tethered binding cannot be excluded. The two members do not share a motif: the NPAS3 model is a generic ACGTG E-box whose nearest neighbors sit in another family, while the NPAS4 model is a short TCGTG core. Report the model, not the family. NPAS1 has no model at all. A prominent genome-wide study of NPAS4 heterodimers was retracted in 2024, so cistrome-level claims for NPAS4 are provisional. Neuronal identity and recent activity are stronger evidence than any match score.

timeline.finding: NPAS1 (MOP5) and NPAS3 (MOP6) were cloned as bHLH-PAS proteins whose expression is largely restricted to the central nervous system, extending the ARNT-partner class beyond the circadian and hypoxia branches.
timeline.methods: Molecular cloning, expression analysis in mouse tissue
timeline.open: No DNA-binding specificity was determined for either protein.

timeline.finding: A balanced translocation disrupting NPAS3 was found to segregate with schizophrenia in one affected family, the first disease link for the group.
timeline.methods: Cytogenetics and breakpoint mapping in a single pedigree
timeline.open: A single pedigree cannot establish that loss of NPAS3 is sufficient to cause the phenotype.

timeline.finding: NPAS4, then called NXF, was identified as a neuron-specific bHLH-PAS factor that competes with SIM2 at the drebrin promoter, placing a second neuronal member in the class.
timeline.methods: Cloning, reporter assays, promoter binding

timeline.finding: Npas4 was shown to be an immediate-early gene induced by calcium influx and neuronal activity rather than by growth factors, and to control the number of inhibitory synapses formed on excitatory neurons, giving the family a defined cellular function.
timeline.methods: Mouse knockout and knockdown, electrophysiology, imaging

timeline.finding: Co-immunoprecipitation from mouse brain recovered ARNT2 as the major NPAS4 partner with ARNT1 as a minor band, both active in reporter assays, confirming that these factors use the same shared beta subunits as HIF and AHR.
timeline.methods: Co-immunoprecipitation from brain, reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether ARNT1- and ARNT2-containing heterodimers occupy different sites.

timeline.finding: Conditional deletion of Npas4 in hippocampal CA3 was shown to impair contextual fear memory, tying the activity-dependent program to a specific behavior.
timeline.methods: Conditional mouse knockout, behavioral testing, expression profiling

timeline.finding: Retraction: Cell withdrew 'Genomic decoding of neuronal depolarization by stimulus-specific NPAS4 heterodimers'. The retraction notice is recorded here because the withdrawn paper is the most-cited genome-wide source for this family; its site counts and partner-specific cistromes should not be used.
timeline.methods: Journal retraction notice
timeline.open: No replacement genome-wide dataset for NPAS4 heterodimers has taken its place.

timeline.finding: Systematic in vitro profiling of prototypical bHLH-PAS proteins including NPAS4 reported 12-15 bp footprints in which flanking-base preferences and DNA shape, not the short core, carry the discriminating information, implying that the 5-7 bp ChIP-derived models in this family cannot be specific.
timeline.methods: High-throughput in vitro binding across family members

open: Whether NPAS3 and NPAS4 share a motif at all is unresolved: they are grouped by domain, but the NPAS3 model is an ordinary ACGTG E-box whose nearest neighbor across the four databases lies in another family (0.97) rather than with NPAS4 (0.81).

The true extent of the NPAS4 site is disputed: the available ChIP-derived models give a 5-7 bp TCGTG core, while in vitro profiling of the class reports 12-15 bp footprints whose specificity rests on flanking bases and shape.

Which beta subunit operates where is unsettled; co-immunoprecipitation from brain recovers ARNT2 as the dominant NPAS4 partner, yet ARNT1 transcripts are present in NPAS4-expressing regions that lack ARNT2, and no sequence feature separates the two heterodimers.

There is currently no reliable genome-wide map of NPAS4 occupancy: the most prominent such study was retracted in 2024 and has not been replaced, so the number and location of genuine NPAS4 sites are unknown.

families.name: Other bHLH
families.def: bHLH factors and archetypes not covered above, incl. MYRF-like and unclassified E-box archetypes.
families.short: A residual bucket rather than a real family: it holds bHLH motifs that could not be placed in any of the defined bHLH families. In the current release that is three models, all labelled SOHLH2, a germ-cell-restricted bHLH protein that heterodimerizes with SOHLH1 and controls spermatogonial differentiation and early folliculogenesis in mice. All three read an ordinary class-B E-box with a G/C flank (CACGTGC), and the data flags each one as resembling MYC/MAX or BHLHE40/41 motifs instead. The family definition also reserves space for MYRF-like factors and unclassified E-box archetypes, though none are assigned here. A hit means "canonical E-box", not SOHLH2.
families.long:
## The factors

This is a residual bucket, not a protein family. The atlas groups bHLH motifs that could not be placed in one of the defined bHLH families - MYC/MAX, USF, MITF/TFE, SREBP, TFAP4, BHLHE40/41, the E-proteins, HES/HEY, MYOD, NEUROD/ATOH, HAND/TWIST, TAL/LYL, CLOCK/BMAL, HIF/ARNT and the others - and in the current release that leaves exactly one gene with motifs: SOHLH2. SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 (spermatogenesis- and oogenesis-specific basic helix-loop-helix 1 and 2) are germ-cell-restricted bHLH proteins. They are expressed in spermatogonia and in oocytes rather than in somatic tissue [PMID:16564520,16765102], they heterodimerize with each other and each can also homodimerize [PMID:22056784]. Whether they also pair with E-proteins, the usual partners of tissue-specific bHLH proteins in the class I/class II scheme [PMID:10611221], was not tested in that work. The family definition also reserves this bucket for MYRF-like factors and for unclassified E-box archetypes. MYRF is worth a word because its inclusion in a bHLH-adjacent bucket is a naming accident rather than a structural claim: myelin gene regulatory factor is a membrane-bound, self-cleaving transcription factor whose DNA-binding domain is an Ndt80/PhoG-like beta-sandwich that trimerizes, with no helix-loop-helix at all [PMID:28623291]. No MYRF motif is assigned here in the current data. The atlas assigns 3 motifs to this family: one JASPAR, one HOCOMOCO and one CIS-BP model, all labelled SOHLH2, with SOLH2.H14CORE.0.S.C as the representative.

## The motif

All three models read a class-B E-box with G/C flanks: CACGTGC in HOCOMOCO (HT-SELEX evidence, quality grade C), GCACGTGC in JASPAR (MA1560.2) [PMID:37971293,37962376], and a low-information gCACGtG in CIS-BP carrying only 8.1 bits of total information. The data consensus for the family is therefore CACGTGC, which is simply the canonical palindrome CACGTG with one extra flanking base. There is no family-specific motif here, and the family data says so explicitly: each of the three models is flagged as resembling a different family. The HOCOMOCO model's nearest neighbours across all four databases are BHLHE40/41 motifs; the JASPAR and CIS-BP models' nearest neighbours are MYC/MAX motifs. Label agreement - the fraction of a motif's nearest neighbours that carry the same factor label - is 0 to 0.2 for all three. The cohesion figure of 0.92 describes only how similar the three SOHLH2 models are to each other, which is not informative when all three come from the same gene. In short, a SOHLH2 model is a CACGTG E-box that happens to be labelled SOHLH2, and nothing in its information content separates it from the canonical MYC or BHLHE40 site.

## Where it acts

Because the site is an ordinary CACGTG E-box, matches occur throughout the genome: a 6-bp palindrome is expected several hundred thousand times in 3 Gb, reduced somewhat by CpG depletion but still far beyond the number of sites any factor occupies. Nothing is known here about promoter versus enhancer preference or chromatin context, because none of the three models is ChIP-derived - the HOCOMOCO model carries only in vitro (HT-SELEX) evidence, and there is no Vierstra footprint archetype in this family [PMID:32728250]. SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 expression is confined to germ cells, so whatever occupancy exists is restricted to spermatogonia and oocytes and has not been mapped genome-wide at the scale available for the common factors. Reported targets sit in the spermatogonial differentiation program, which the two proteins control jointly [PMID:22056784].

## Biology and disease

The phenotypes come from mouse genetics. Sohlh1-null mice fail spermatogonial differentiation [PMID:16564520]. Sohlh2-null males are sterile because differentiating type A spermatogonia degenerate [PMID:18339773], and Sohlh2 is separately required in females for early folliculogenesis and for oocyte-specific gene expression [PMID:18753606]. The two genes act together rather than redundantly: the double mutant phenocopies the single mutants, and SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 coordinate the spermatogonial differentiation step [PMID:22056784]. That is consistent with an essential role for the SOHLH1-SOHLH2 heterodimer, but heterodimerization is not obligate: each protein can also homodimerize [PMID:22056784]. Human evidence is thin by comparison and consists largely of individual case reports in infertility cohorts, so the human disease picture should be treated as provisional. There is no cancer or developmental syndrome robustly attributed to either gene.

## Reading a hit

Treat a hit against anything in this bucket as a hit against a generic CACGTG E-box and nothing more. This family exists so that motifs which do not belong to a defined bHLH family are not silently forced into MYC/MAX or BHLHE40/41; it is a holding pen, and membership is expected to change between releases as the assignments are revised. Concretely: do not report a "SOHLH2 site" on the basis of a sequence match. If a BHLH_OTHER model is your top hit, rescore the same sequence against MYC_MAX, USF, MITF_TFE, BHLHE40_41, CLOCK_BMAL and HIF_ARNT and expect comparable scores, then argue from expression - SOHLH2 is only a plausible candidate in germ-cell material. None of these three models has ChIP support, so they say nothing about in vivo occupancy either way.
families.caveats: This bucket has no motif of its own. All three assigned models are CACGTG E-boxes whose nearest neighbours across the four databases belong to other families - BHLHE40/41 for the HOCOMOCO model, MYC/MAX for the JASPAR and CIS-BP models - with label agreement between 0 and 0.2. None is ChIP-derived, and the CIS-BP model carries only 8.1 bits of information. A match therefore licenses no factor assignment at all; report it as a canonical E-box. Membership in a residual bucket is provisional by construction and should be expected to change as the family assignments are revised, so do not build a pipeline that depends on this key's contents.
