timeline.finding: A phylogenetic classification of 242 bHLH proteins groups them into lineages and five higher groups by E-box binding, motif features and presence of a leucine zipper, and finds that zipper-containing bHLH proteins are not a monophyletic group.
timeline.methods: Phylogenetic analysis of bHLH sequences

timeline.finding: Comparative genomics of fly, nematode and vertebrate bHLH genes defines 44 orthologous families, the framework into which unplaced bHLH proteins are later sorted.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide sequence searches, phylogenetic analysis

timeline.finding: SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 are identified as germ-cell-specific bHLH factors expressed in spermatogonia and oocytes, and Sohlh1-null males fail spermatogonial differentiation.
timeline.methods: Gene discovery, expression analysis, mouse gene targeting

timeline.finding: Sohlh2 knockout males are sterile because differentiating type A spermatogonia degenerate, and knockout females lose oocytes and misexpress oocyte-specific genes.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting (independent male and female studies), histology, expression analysis

timeline.finding: SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 heterodimerize in testis and each can also homodimerize, the double mutant phenocopies the single mutants, and the proteins directly regulate Gfra1, Sox3 and Kit.
timeline.methods: Protein interaction assays, double-knockout mice, expression profiling, promoter binding assays

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the MYRF DNA-binding domain shows an Ndt80-like beta-sandwich that trimerizes, confirming that MYRF has no bHLH despite its place in this bucket.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, mutagenesis

timeline.finding: Current JASPAR and HOCOMOCO releases carry SOHLH2 models that read a plain G/C-flanked CACGTG, supported only by in vitro data and indistinguishable from MYC/MAX and BHLHE40/41 motifs.
timeline.methods: Database curation of in vitro-derived motifs
timeline.open: No in vivo binding data exist for SOHLH2 in these collections.

open: Which dimer reads DNA in germ cells is unresolved: SOHLH1 and SOHLH2 heterodimerize in testis and each can also homodimerize, but the only motifs available are for SOHLH2 alone, and no SOHLH1 model exists to show whether the heterodimer reads the same site.

Whether SOHLH2 has any specificity beyond the canonical E-box is unknown: its three models are in vitro-only, their nearest neighbours are BHLHE40/41 and MYC/MAX motifs, and label agreement is 0 to 0.2.

families.name: Ndt80/PhoG-like (C11orf9/MYRF)
families.def: Ndt80-like DNA-binding domain archetypes, incl. MYRF.
families.short: This family is named after the budding yeast meiotic activator Ndt80, whose DNA-binding domain defines an immunoglobulin-like fold shared by the human proteins MYRF and MYRFL. MYRF, myelin regulatory factor, is the only well-characterized vertebrate member. It is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that trimerizes and cleaves itself using a domain related to bacteriophage tailspike proteins; the released N-terminal fragment enters the nucleus and binds DNA. The measured site is the palindromic eight-base TGGTACCA, consistent with binding by a symmetric oligomer. MYRF is required for oligodendrocyte differentiation and for making and maintaining central nervous system myelin, and human MYRF variants cause a cardiac-urogenital syndrome and disorders of sex development.
families.long:
## The factors

The family is defined by a DNA-binding fold, not by a lineage of related regulators. It takes its
name from Ndt80, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae transcription factor that is activated at pachytene
and turns on roughly 150 middle sporulation genes, including the B-type cyclins, once meiotic
recombination is complete [PMID:9660952,12411490]. The crystal structure of the Ndt80 DNA-binding domain showed an
immunoglobulin-like fold, with functional similarities that suggested an evolutionary link to the
p53 family [PMID:12411490]. Human proteins carrying the same Ndt80/PhoG-like domain are MYRF (myelin regulatory
factor, formerly C11orf9 or MRF) [PMID:19596243] and its paralogue MYRFL, which is poorly characterized. MYRF is
unusual for a transcription factor: it is synthesized as a type-2 transmembrane protein in the
endoplasmic reticulum, assembles into a homotrimer, and then cleaves itself through an
autoproteolytic intramolecular chaperone domain that is related to the corresponding domain of
bacteriophage tailspike proteins, the first time that domain was found in a eukaryotic protein [PMID:23966832,23966833].
Cleavage separates the transmembrane C-terminal region from an N-terminal fragment that carries
the DNA-binding domain and a nuclear localization signal [PMID:23966833]. MYRF expression is essentially
restricted to oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system [PMID:19596243], with some expression in Schwann
cells and other tissues [PMID:29446546]; it is not a broadly expressed factor.

## The motif

All three models in these databases converge on TGGTACCA, an eight-base perfect palindrome, which
is what a symmetric trimeric or dimeric binder would be expected to select: the half-site is TGGT,
read on both strands. The CIS-BP MYRF model and the Vierstra archetype AC0396 are identical to
each other [PMID:25215497,32728250]. Chromatin immunoprecipitation of the cleaved N-terminal fragment showed it binding
oligodendrocyte and myelin gene enhancers through a defined consensus [PMID:23966833], which is consistent with
this palindrome. Information is concentrated in the TGGT/ACCA core; there are no established
spacing rules, and because the site is symmetric, orientation cannot be called from sequence. The
family is not fully coherent here (cohesion 0.73, three motifs). The one discordant model is
HOCOMOCO's MYRFL entry, a long grade-A model with ChIP-seq, HT-SELEX and GHT-SELEX support (GTGCCAGGCNGTGACATCCC) whose best similarity to
any other member of the family is only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL should not be assumed to share a
site on the current evidence. The yeast middle sporulation element that Ndt80 reads is a different
sequence again, with a GC-rich 5' half whose pyrimidine-guanine steps are recognized by arginine
side chains through a combination of hydrogen bonding and stacking, and an AT-rich 3' half read
through the minor groove [PMID:12411490,16531239]; it is useful as structural background but not as a human motif.

## Where it acts

MYRF sites are found at promoters and, more characteristically, at oligodendrocyte-specific distal
enhancers of myelin genes, including MBP, PLP1, MAG and CNP [PMID:23966833]. Enhancer mapping at the Plp1 locus
identified two oligodendrocyte-specific enhancers, both acted on by MYRF, whose contacts with the
gene are among the strongest in that cell type [PMID:34230963]. MYRF works with SOX10 at many of these elements,
so a MYRF match near a SOX10 dimer site in oligodendrocyte-accessible chromatin is a much stronger
signal than the match alone. As an eight-base fixed palindrome, TGGTACCA is expected by chance on
the order of tens of thousands of times in a human genome, most of them in closed chromatin and in
cell types where MYRF is absent.

## Biology and disease

Mice lacking Myrf in the oligodendrocyte lineage fail to myelinate the central nervous system [PMID:19596243], and
inducible deletion in adults causes loss of myelin and of mature oligodendrocyte identity [PMID:22956843], so MYRF
is required for maintenance as well as for differentiation. In humans, de novo MYRF variants cause
a syndrome of congenital cardiac and urogenital anomalies, often with congenital diaphragmatic
hernia [PMID:29446546], and MYRF haploinsufficiency has been reported in both 46,XY and 46,XX disorders of sex
development [PMID:30985895]. The link between a myelin regulator and cardiac and gonadal development is not
explained by the oligodendrocyte role, and likely reflects earlier developmental expression.

## Reading a hit

The palindrome is short and fully specified, so chance matches are common and the sequence alone
carries no cell-type information. A MYRF match matters only in a cell that expresses MYRF, which
in practice means the oligodendrocyte lineage; elsewhere the same eight bases are inert. Do not
assume that a match to the MYRFL model is equivalent to a MYRF site: that model is discordant with
the MYRF palindrome in these data. Because MYRF requires autoproteolytic release to reach the
nucleus, the presence of MYRF protein in a tissue does not establish that its DNA-binding fragment
is present, which is an unusual extra step between motif and function. Treat the yeast Ndt80 MSE
as a separate element that shares only the fold.
families.caveats: Only three motifs and two proteins sit under this key, and one of them disagrees with the other two: the HOCOMOCO MYRFL model matches the MYRF palindrome at only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL cannot be assumed interchangeable. TGGTACCA is eight fixed bases and a perfect palindrome, so chance matches number in the tens of thousands per genome and orientation is undefined. The site is only interpretable in cells expressing MYRF, essentially the oligodendrocyte lineage. MYRF also needs autoproteolytic cleavage before its DNA-binding fragment reaches the nucleus, so protein presence does not imply DNA binding. The yeast Ndt80 MSE shares the fold but not the sequence.

timeline.finding: Ndt80 acts at pachytene of yeast meiosis to activate middle sporulation genes, including the B-type cyclins, and recombinant Ndt80 binds a conserved sequence upstream of them, the middle sporulation element (MSE).
timeline.methods: Yeast genetics, ectopic expression, DNA binding with recombinant protein
timeline.open: The structural basis of MSE recognition, and whether the fold had relatives outside fungi.

timeline.finding: Crystal structure of the Ndt80 DNA-binding domain, free and on an MSE: an immunoglobulin-like fold whose arginines read 5'-pyrimidine-guanine steps by hydrogen bonding to the guanine and stacking on the pyrimidine; functional parallels suggest a link to the p53 family.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays with MSE mutants

timeline.finding: Structures of Ndt80 on ten MSE variants explain its specificity: YpG steps in the GC-rich 5' end read by arginines, and an AT-rich 3' end read through the minor groove with a preference for poly(A)-poly(T) tracts.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: Myelin gene regulatory factor (MRF, now MYRF), a protein with a DNA-binding domain homologous to a yeast transcription factor, is expressed by postmitotic oligodendrocytes and required for CNS myelin gene expression and myelination.
timeline.methods: RNA interference, overexpression, conditional knockout mice
timeline.open: Whether MYRF binds DNA directly; reports of a transmembrane domain and lack of nuclear localization argued against it.

timeline.finding: Deleting MYRF from mature oligodendrocytes in the adult causes delayed but severe demyelination and loss of mature oligodendrocyte identity, so MYRF is needed to maintain myelin, not only to make it.
timeline.methods: Inducible conditional knockout

timeline.finding: Two independent groups show MYRF is a membrane-bound precursor that trimerizes and cleaves itself through a domain related to bacteriophage tailspike chaperones; the released N-terminal fragment enters the nucleus and, by ChIP-seq, binds oligodendrocyte and myelin gene enhancers through a defined consensus. This settled the earlier doubt about whether MYRF is a transcription factor at all.
timeline.methods: Biochemistry, reconstitution in E. coli and yeast, ChIP-seq

timeline.finding: Exome studies tie de novo MYRF variants to a syndrome of cardiac and urogenital anomalies and to 46,XY and 46,XX disorders of sex development, implicating MYRF well outside the CNS.
timeline.methods: Exome sequencing, case-control burden analysis
timeline.open: Which MYRF targets act in the affected non-neural tissues.

open: Whether MYRF and MYRFL share a binding site is unresolved: the MYRF models converge on the palindrome TGGTACCA, whereas the only MYRFL model, a grade-A HOCOMOCO model supported by ChIP-seq, HT-SELEX and GHT-SELEX, is a long unrelated sequence (GTGCCAGGCNGTGACATCCC).

How a trimerizing protein reads a two-fold palindrome is not explained: MYRF trimerizes through its chaperone domain before cleavage, but TGGTACCA has the symmetry expected of a dimeric binder, and the references here do not establish the stoichiometry of the released DNA-binding fragment on DNA.

Whether MYRF uses the same sites and targets outside the CNS is open: de novo variants cause cardiac, urogenital and gonadal anomalies, but target predictions for those tissues rest on reanalysed ChIP-seq from other cells rather than binding data from the affected tissues.

families.name: HMGA (AT-hook)
families.def: AT-rich minor-groove binding. HMGA1, HMGA2.
families.short: HMGA1 and HMGA2 have no sequence specificity worth scanning for. They bind the minor groove of AT-rich DNA through short basic peptides called AT-hooks, which were described from the outset as recognizing DNA structure rather than base sequence, and they will bind essentially any run of A and T. The family holds three motifs, and the data show what that means: the HMGA1 models are ATTTTTA in JASPAR and TAaAATAtAtA in HOCOMOCO, the HMGA2 model is four bases at 2.2 bits, and not one of the three has another model in this family as its nearest neighbour. All three resemble models in other families more than they resemble each other. Do not treat a match here as a binding site.
families.long:
## The factors

HMGA1 and HMGA2 are small, extremely basic, intrinsically disordered nuclear proteins of about 100 residues. They are architectural chromatin factors, among the most abundant non-histone proteins in embryonic and transformed cells, and they work by bending, straightening and unwinding DNA and by making the surrounding chromatin more permissive [PMID:11602345]. HMGA1 exists as two main splice variants, historically called HMG-I and HMG-Y, which differ by an eleven-residue internal segment; HMGA2 was originally called HMGI-C. Both carry three AT-hooks in the N-terminal two-thirds and an acidic C-terminal tail.

The AT-hook itself was defined in 1990 from the mammalian HMG-I proteins as a novel peptide motif for recognizing DNA structure, built around a short palindromic core of the form Arg-Gly-Arg-Pro flanked by lysines and arginines [PMID:1692833]. It was subsequently found in a wide variety of otherwise unrelated DNA-binding proteins - chromatin remodellers, transcription factors and others - where it typically serves as an auxiliary anchor rather than as the specificity-determining module [PMID:9742243]. That is the key point for this page: the AT-hook is an affinity device, not a recognition device.

## The motif

A crystal structure of an HMGA AT-hook bound to AT-rich DNA shows the peptide lying in the narrow minor groove, making van der Waals and water-mediated contacts with the floor of the groove, and the same site can be occupied competitively by small-molecule minor-groove binders [PMID:39478017,1692833]. Minor-groove width and narrowness are what the hook reads; the identity of the individual A and T bases is largely irrelevant, and a run of A:T base pairs in almost any arrangement will do. There is no discriminating base pair in the sense that a zinc-finger or homeodomain motif has one.

The three atlas models reflect this exactly. JASPAR MA2124.1 for HMGA1 gives ATTTTTA at 11.9 bits. HOCOMOCO HMGA1.H14CORE.0.P.B gives TAaAATAtAtA at 12.4 bits, but its evidence code is P - ChIP-only - and its grade is B, so there is no in vitro support for it in the atlas. The CIS-BP model M00751 for HMGA2 is the four-base Aata at 2.2 bits, transferred from mouse at 100 percent domain identity, and carries no usable information.

The diagnostic statistic is the nearest-neighbour analysis. For all three models the within-family nearest neighbour is undefined - no model in this family is another's closest match - while the best out-of-family similarity is 0.72 for the HOCOMOCO model, 0.81 for the JASPAR model and 0.80 for the CIS-BP model. Every model here looks more like something in another family than like its own family-mates. Reported cohesion of 0.54 flatters the situation. An ATTTTTA-style heptamer is not distinguishable from a homeodomain TAAT site, an ARID AT core, a FOX forkhead flank, or unremarkable AT-rich intergenic sequence; at human base composition a given AT-only heptamer is expected several hundred thousand times in the genome.

## Where it acts

Because binding is structural, HMGA proteins are found across AT-rich DNA, in nuclear scaffold and matrix-attachment regions, in nucleosome-poor and linker DNA, and at the AT-rich flanks of enhancers. Where they matter functionally, it is through cooperation. The textbook case is the interferon-beta enhancer, where HMG I(Y) is required for NF-kB-dependent virus induction [PMID:1330326] and then for assembly of the complete enhanceosome together with ATF-2/c-Jun and IRF proteins [PMID:8548797]: HMGA bends the DNA into the geometry the other factors need, and its own contribution to sequence recognition is nil. The generalisation is that an HMGA site is defined by its partners, not by its sequence, which is why HMGA occupancy maps are broad and shallow rather than peaked.

## Biology and disease

HMGA2 is the mouse pygmy gene: the pygmy phenotype was mapped to disruption of Hmgi-c, giving small, lean mice and establishing HMGA2 as a growth regulator [PMID:7651535]. In humans, HMGA2 variants and microdeletions cause Silver-Russell syndrome and related growth-restriction phenotypes [PMID:38516887], and common variants at the locus are associated with adult height. HMGA2 is also one of the most recurrent fusion partners in benign mesenchymal tumours: translocations at 12q14-15 in lipoma, uterine leiomyoma and related lesions repeatedly truncate HMGA2 after its AT-hooks, generating fusions such as HMGA2-SETBP1 that remove the acidic tail while retaining DNA binding [PMID:7606786,26202160]. HMGA1 is re-expressed in most aggressive carcinomas, is a driver in breast cancer [PMID:11602345,29518471], and is also involved in insulin receptor regulation and metabolic disease.

## Reading a hit

Effectively, do not read it. If you scan with these models, expect several hundred thousand matches, no ability to separate HMGA1 from HMGA2, and no ability to separate either from any other AT-preferring factor or from bulk AT-rich sequence. HMGA occupancy cannot be predicted from sequence at the resolution a motif scan implies, and a strong score here carries no information about function. If an AT-rich region genuinely matters in your data, the useful questions are whether it is a matrix-attachment or nucleosome-depleted region and which sequence-specific factors bind alongside - HMGA is the geometry, not the address.
families.caveats: HMGA proteins are not sequence-specific: the AT-hook reads minor-groove structure, and any run of A and T will bind. Say it plainly - a match here is not a binding site. All three models are mutually dissimilar enough that none is another's nearest neighbour, while each has an out-of-family match at 0.72 to 0.81, so the family does not cohere. The HOCOMOCO HMGA1 model is ChIP-only (grade B) with no in vitro support in the atlas; the CIS-BP HMGA2 model is four bases at 2.2 bits and unusable. Expect hundreds of thousands of genome-wide matches, indistinguishable from homeodomain, ARID and forkhead AT preferences or from bulk AT-rich sequence.

timeline.finding: The DNA-binding unit of the HMG-I proteins was mapped to three conserved repeats of the consensus T-P-K-R-P-R-G-R-P-K-K; a synthetic peptide bound the narrow minor groove of A/T stretches like the intact protein and was competed by netropsin, distamycin and Hoechst 33258, and the motif was named the AT-hook, a module for recognizing DNA structure.
timeline.methods: Peptide binding assays, drug competition, molecular modelling
timeline.open: Whether the hook reads base sequence or groove geometry.

timeline.finding: HMG I(Y) was shown to be required for NF-kB-dependent virus induction of the interferon-beta gene, binding the center of the PRDII element in the minor groove while NF-kB contacts the major groove, and stimulating NF-kB binding.
timeline.methods: DNA-binding assays, promoter mutagenesis, antisense inhibition

timeline.finding: Rearrangements at 12q14-15 in lipomas were found to disrupt HMGI-C (HMGA2), producing chimeric transcripts that fuse its AT-hooks to a LIM or acidic transactivation domain.
timeline.methods: Positional cloning at a tumor breakpoint, chimeric transcript isolation

timeline.finding: The mouse pygmy dwarfism mutant was traced to inactivation of Hmgi-c, establishing HMGA2 as a growth regulator acting outside the growth hormone-IGF endocrine pathway.
timeline.methods: Mouse genetics and gene mapping

timeline.finding: Virus induction of interferon-beta was shown to require assembly of an enhanceosome in which HMG I(Y) binds three sites in the enhancer, promotes cooperative binding of the other factors in vitro and is required for their transcriptional synergy in vivo.
timeline.methods: In vitro complex assembly, helical-phasing mutants, transfection assays
timeline.open: How HMGA is placed at enhancers that lack a partner-defined geometry.

timeline.finding: The NMR structure of the second and third HMG-I(Y) AT-hooks on a PRDII-containing dodecamer revealed an architectural minor-groove motif built on a central Arg-Gly-Arg that stabilizes B-DNA for factors binding the opposite major groove; the third hook lacks one contacting module and binds about 100-fold more weakly.
timeline.methods: Multidimensional NMR spectroscopy

timeline.finding: Database searches found AT-hooks in a wide variety of eukaryotic nuclear proteins, usually alongside other DNA-binding or chromatin domains, and characterized the motif as an auxiliary minor-groove tether rather than a primary recognition domain.
timeline.methods: Sequence pattern searches and classification

timeline.finding: A 1.40 A crystal structure of HMGA AT-hook 1 in the minor groove of AT-rich DNA showed moderate groove widening and binding to neighbouring DNA molecules, unlike AT-hook 3, which bends DNA; antikinetoplastid minor-groove drugs competed with the hook for binding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, SPR, isothermal titration calorimetry
timeline.open: Whether the three hooks of one HMGA molecule act on DNA in the same way in chromatin.

open: Whether HMGA binding has any sequence preference beyond A/T content is unresolved: structures show the hooks reading minor-groove width, yet individual hooks differ about 100-fold in affinity and in whether they bend or only widen DNA, so it is not known whether particular AT arrangements are favoured in cells.

It is not settled whether the hooks prefer homopolymeric A-tracts or alternating A/T sequence: the JASPAR HMGA1 model is A-tract-like (ATTTTTA) while the ChIP-only HOCOMOCO model is alternating (TAaAATAtAtA), and the atlas data cannot separate a genuine preference from chromatin context.

How HMGA occupancy is targeted in cells is open: the interferon-beta enhanceosome shows partner-dependent placement, but whether genome-wide occupancy follows partner factors, nucleosome-depleted AT-rich DNA or the protein's modification state has not been resolved.

families.name: Cold-shock domain (YBX)
families.def: Y-box CTGATTGGC. YBX1 and CSD archetypes.
families.short: A one-protein family. YBX1 (YB-1) carries a cold-shock domain, the eukaryotic descendant of the bacterial CspA nucleic-acid-binding fold, and it is at least as much an RNA-binding protein as a transcription factor: it packages messenger RNA, unwinds RNA secondary structure and prefers single-stranded nucleic acid over duplex DNA. Three motifs agree closely with one another - cohesion is 0.95, the highest in this part of the atlas - and all read the same eight base pairs, GATGGTAC, or its reverse complement GTACCATC. Note that this in vitro site is not the classical Y box, CTGATTGGC, with which YB-1 is historically identified; the two should not be conflated.
families.long:
## The factors

The cold-shock domain is one of the oldest nucleic-acid-binding folds, a five-stranded beta-barrel of the OB-fold class, conserved from the bacterial cold-shock proteins such as CspA into eukaryotes [PMID:11851341,32087051]. Human cold-shock-domain proteins include the Y-box family YBX1, YBX2 and YBX3, the unrelated CSDE1/UNR and the LIN28 proteins, but only YBX1 contributes motifs to this atlas, so the family is effectively a single-protein entry.

YBX1 was cloned in 1988 as the complementary DNA encoding a protein that binds the Y box of the major histocompatibility complex class II promoter - hence the name Y-box binding protein 1 [PMID:3174636]. The Y box itself is an inverted CCAAT element [PMID:3174636], and Y-box sequences were subsequently shown to be required for basal expression of other promoters, notably the human multidrug resistance gene MDR1 [PMID:8095499]. Domain architecture is an alanine/proline N-terminal region, the single cold-shock domain, and a long charged C-terminal region with alternating basic and acidic clusters that does most of the RNA binding and mediates mRNP packaging [PMID:11222770,32087051].

Functionally YBX1 is dual. It acts as a transcription factor at some promoters, but the bulk of the cellular protein is cytoplasmic and bound to messenger RNA, where it packages transcripts, unwinds secondary structure and thereby restrains stress granule assembly [PMID:34469566]. In vitro, YB-1 binds single-stranded nucleic acids in preference to duplex DNA and even displays a 3' to 5' exonuclease activity [PMID:11222770]. Any interpretation of a YBX1 motif has to be made against that background.

## The motif

The three models are essentially the same site read on the two strands. HOCOMOCO YBOX1.H14CORE.0.SM.B gives GTACCATC at 13.0 bits with evidence code SM - HT-SELEX plus methyl-HT-SELEX, so genuine in vitro support - though graded B. The CIS-BP model M04661 and the Vierstra archetype AC0342 both give GATGGtAC, the reverse complement, at 9.9 and 8.8 bits. Pairwise similarity within the family reaches 0.98, and out-of-family similarity stays at 0.63 to 0.65 - the widest margin between within-family and out-of-family matches anywhere in this group of entries. On the internal statistics, this is a clean, well-behaved eight-base-pair motif.

The complication is historical rather than statistical. The site these models describe is built around a CCAT/ATGG core; the classical Y box that gave YBX1 its name is built around CCAAT, one base longer [PMID:3174636]. The atlas ontology labels this family with the Y box CTGATTGGC, and that string does not match the models the family actually contains. Both observations can be true - YB-1 was purified on a Y-box probe, and in vitro selection recovered a CCAT-centred site - but they are not interchangeable, and a scan using these models is not a scan for Y boxes. If your interest is in Y-box or CCAAT-element regulation, the NFY family is the appropriate place to look.

Structural work explains why the duplex-DNA numbers are modest. The solution structure of the YB-1 cold-shock domain identified the canonical aromatic surface that binds nucleic acid [PMID:11851341], and a later structure of the domain on DNA showed that binding is regulated by phosphorylation, with the phosphorylated protein altering its engagement of single-stranded DNA [PMID:32710623]. Comparative work shows the domain discriminates RNA from DNA largely through non-bonded interactions rather than hydrogen-bond readout [PMID:26147853], which is another way of saying that base identity is not read as strictly as in a classical DNA-binding domain.

## Where it acts

Reported YBX1 promoter targets cluster in proliferation and stress-response genes and in drug-resistance genes such as MDR1, and the protein is recruited to MHC class II and other CCAAT-containing promoters. But most YBX1 in a cell is on messenger RNA, not chromatin, and the genomic occupancy that has been mapped is correspondingly broad. In practice a YBX1 site is defined by the promoter it sits in and the partners present rather than by the eight base pairs alone.

## Biology and disease

YBX1 is essential in mouse: knockout embryos fail in early development with defective neural tube formation and reduced proliferation [PMID:17082189]. In human cancer YBX1 is one of the most consistently overexpressed nucleic-acid-binding proteins, associated with proliferation, drug resistance, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and poor prognosis across many tumour types, and it has been pursued as a therapeutic target [PMID:38255791]. Much of that activity is post-transcriptional - mRNA stabilisation and translational control, including roles in m6A-dependent regulation - rather than transcriptional, which is a further reason not to read YBX1 biology off a DNA motif scan.

## Reading a hit

The motif is technically sound and the family is internally consistent, so a strong GATGGTAC match is a defensible YBX1 candidate site - but only a candidate. Three cautions apply. First, eight base pairs with 10 to 13 bits will still match tens of thousands of times genome-wide, so require promoter context and YBX1 expression. Second, do not treat the hit as a Y box or a CCAAT element; it is neither, and NFY is the family that reads CCAAT. Third, remember what YBX1 mostly does: it binds single-stranded nucleic acid and RNA in preference to duplex DNA [PMID:11222770,11851341], so a sequence match is weak evidence of chromatin occupancy and no evidence at all of transcriptional function. Corroborate with ChIP or footprint data before assigning a regulatory role.
families.caveats: This family is one protein, YBX1, and its three models are the same eight base pairs on opposite strands, so the high cohesion of 0.95 reflects redundancy rather than breadth of support. The models describe a CCAT-centred site, not the CCAAT-based classical Y box CTGATTGGC that the family is named for, and they should not be used to find Y-box or CCAAT elements - that is NFY's motif. The HOCOMOCO model has genuine HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX support but is graded B. Most importantly, YB-1 prefers single-stranded nucleic acids and RNA over duplex DNA and is largely a cytoplasmic mRNA-packaging protein, so a DNA motif match is weak evidence of occupancy and none of function.

timeline.finding: YB-1 was cloned by probing an expression library with Y-box oligonucleotides from an HLA class II promoter; its binding had an absolute requirement for the inverted CCAAT box and relative specificity for the Y box, and its levels correlated inversely with HLA-DR beta mRNA.
timeline.methods: Expression-library screening with double-stranded DNA probes, binding assays
timeline.open: Whether YB-1 recognizes CCAAT sequence directly in cells.

timeline.finding: An inverted-CCAAT Y-box consensus between -82 and -73 of the human mdr1 promoter was shown to be required for basal expression and for nucleoprotein binding in nuclear extracts.
timeline.methods: Promoter deletion and mutation, reporter assays, DNase I footprinting, EMSA
timeline.open: Which protein acts at the mdr1 Y box, since both YB-1 and CCAAT-binding factors were candidates.

timeline.finding: YB-1 was found to bind single-stranded nucleic acids preferentially; its cold-shock domain was necessary but not sufficient for double-stranded DNA binding, its C-terminal tail bound single-stranded DNA and RNA independently and mediated homodimerization, and the protein had intrinsic 3' to 5' exonuclease activity.
timeline.methods: Domain deletion binding assays, in vitro translation, co-immunoprecipitation, nuclease assays

timeline.finding: The first structure of a eukaryotic cold-shock domain, from YB-1, showed a closed five-stranded beta-barrel of the OB-fold type with a positively charged aromatic surface; the isolated domain preferred single-stranded pyrimidine-rich sequence and bound DNA weakly and hardly specifically, so other domains must contribute to YB-1 DNA binding.
timeline.methods: NMR spectroscopy, DNA-binding measurements
timeline.open: What, if anything, gives full-length YB-1 sequence specificity on duplex DNA.

timeline.finding: YB-1 knockout mice were embryonic lethal with exencephaly, abnormal neuroepithelial proliferation and reduced actin assembly, and knockout fibroblasts grew poorly and resisted transformation.
timeline.methods: Mouse gene targeting, embryo and fibroblast analysis

timeline.finding: Molecular dynamics validated by binding assays indicated that the YB-1 cold-shock domain binds nucleic acids in a sequence-dependent way with higher affinity for RNA than DNA, discriminating the two through non-bonded interactions.
timeline.methods: Molecular dynamics simulation with experimental validation

timeline.finding: The structure of the YB-1 cold-shock domain with its C-terminal extension, alone and bound to a single-stranded DNA heptamer, showed all seven nucleotides contacting the protein and the extension forming an additional binding site; S102 phosphorylation destabilized the domain and sharply reduced single-stranded DNA binding.
timeline.methods: Protein structure determination, DNA-binding assays
timeline.open: Whether phosphorylation switches YB-1 between transcriptional and translational roles in cells.

timeline.finding: YB-1 was shown to unwind mRNA secondary structure without ATP, using the cold-shock domain to destabilize stem-loops and the disordered C-terminal domain to secure unwinding, and to facilitate stress granule disassembly in HeLa cells.
timeline.methods: In vitro unwinding assays, structural modelling, cell-based stress granule assays

open: Whether YB-1 recognizes double-stranded DNA sequence-specifically at all is disputed: the database models give a clean eight-base CCAT-centred site with HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX support, while structural and biochemical work finds that the isolated cold-shock domain binds duplex DNA weakly and hardly specifically, prefers single-stranded pyrimidine-rich sequence and binds RNA with higher affinity.

How the CCAT-centred in vitro site relates to the Y box is unresolved: the original cloning showed an absolute requirement for the CCAAT box, which the selected site lacks, and it is not known whether YB-1 at Y-box promoters reads sequence directly, binds locally single-stranded DNA, or depends on the CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y.

Whether S102 phosphorylation, which destabilizes the cold-shock domain and sharply reduces single-stranded DNA binding, switches YB-1 between transcriptional and translational roles has been proposed from structural work but not established in cells.

families.name: Other / unclassified
families.def: Motifs whose factor has no assigned structural family here: LCOR and LCORL (psq-type HTH) and LRRFIP1. Cofactors without a DBD are in CHROMATIN; unnamed archetypes are in ZNF_UNNAMED.
families.short: This is not a motif family. It is the residual category for motifs whose factor has no assigned structural family in this ontology, and in the current data it holds three matrices for three proteins. Two are the paralogous corepressors LCOR and LCORL, which carry a psq-type helix-turn-helix rather than a homeodomain and whose models are 4-5 bit A-rich strings that carry almost no information. The third is LRRFIP1, cloned as GC-binding factor 2, whose only model is a GC-rich matrix derived from ChIP-seq alone and resembles neither of the others. Internal cohesion is 0.60 and no member has a same-family neighbour that it matches. Read a hit here as unassigned rather than as shared biology, and re-report it to whichever named family the sequence actually matches.
families.long:
## The factors

Three motifs, three proteins. The definition is broader than the contents: it also covers chromatin regulators without a classical DNA-binding domain and unlabelled archetypes, but both of those have entries of their own, so what lands here is proteins believed to bind DNA whose domain has no family of its own.

Two of the three are paralogues. LCOR, ligand-dependent corepressor, is recruited to agonist-bound nuclear receptors through a single LXXLL motif and represses both by binding histone deacetylases directly and by recruiting CtBP corepressors through two consensus motifs; it attenuates receptor signalling rather than activating a programme of its own [PMID:12535528]. LCORL is its larger relative. Both carry a psq-type helix-turn-helix - the pipsqueak fold, a member of the homeodomain-like superfamily - which is a real DNA-binding domain [PMID:29425488], but this atlas has no pipsqueak family and the fold is not a homeodomain, so neither protein has anywhere else to go.

The third, LRRFIP1, entered the literature as GCF2, found by cross-hybridisation with the cDNA of the GC-rich repressor GCF and shown to bind and repress epidermal growth factor receptor promoter fragments through a major site at nucleotides -249 to -233 [PMID:2556218,9705290]. It has no recognised DNA-binding domain [PMID:29425488]; the part of it that has been solved is a dimeric coiled coil, and its best-documented activity is cytosolic, as a nucleic-acid-binding protein that drives interferon-beta production through beta-catenin [PMID:20453844].

## The motif

There is no consensus for this bucket and none should be quoted. The CnAAa string the pipeline reports is only the medoid of three unrelated matrices, and the medoid is the weakest of the three.

The three entries: CIS-BP M02433, labelled LCOR, reads CnAAa and carries 4.1 bits; its provenance record marks it as taken from a Meleagris gallopavo - wild turkey - protein whose DNA-binding domain is 100 percent identical to the human one [PMID:25215497]. CIS-BP M01304, labelled LCORL, reads cchAAa and carries 4.9 bits. The two match each other at 0.97, but each also matches a motif in another family at 0.83-0.84: at five bits an A-rich matrix is not distinguishable from anything else A-rich. LCORL turns up again in the forkhead entry as part of the Vierstra archetype AC0014:FOXR/LCORL, a 3.4-bit AAa matrix pooled with genuine forkhead models [PMID:32728250]. The third entry, HOCOMOCO LRRF1.H14CORE.0.P.B for LRRFIP1, reads aaGCTCGC with 9.6 bits. Its evidence code is P alone - ChIP-seq, with no in vitro assay - and grade B means two experiments of that one type [PMID:37971293]. It has no same-family neighbour anywhere in its top thirty; its best match outside the bucket is only 0.66. Family cohesion is 0.60.

The pipeline treats residual buckets as places where membership says nothing about what a matrix should look like, so it suppresses the suspect flag and reports a resemblance instead; the reported zero suspect motifs is a property of that rule, not a sign that these three belong together.

## Where it acts

Not established as a cis-element for any of the three. LCOR and LCORL act as corepressors recruited by nuclear receptors, so their functional footprint on the genome is at oestrogen, glucocorticoid and related receptor sites [PMID:12535528], and finding CNAAA under a peak tells you nothing about which receptor brought the corepressor there. The one mapped element for LRRFIP1 is the GC-rich region of the EGFR promoter around -240 [PMID:9705290]; its ChIP-derived matrix will pick out promoter-proximal GC-rich sequence, as most ChIP-only GC-rich models do whatever protein they are labelled with. A five- or six-base A-rich matrix of the kind LCOR and LCORL contribute matches several million times in 3.1 Gb on either strand, so a scan against them returns noise at any threshold that returns anything.

## Biology and disease

None of the three has a Mendelian disease attributed to it, but the biology is real. LCOR primes interferon responses in mammary epithelium; miR-199a represses it to protect normal and cancerous mammary stem cells from interferon-induced differentiation and senescence, and that axis is active in poorly differentiated ER-negative breast tumours and associated with poor outcome [PMID:28530657]. LCORL sits in the NCAPG-LCORL interval, one of the most reproducible loci for body size and stature in human and livestock association studies; knockout mice are born small, stay lean, eat less, have reduced circulating IGF-1 and show improved glucose tolerance [PMID:39467326]. LRRFIP1 represses the EGFR and RhoA promoters as GCF2 [PMID:9705290,30709060], regulates Wnt/beta-catenin signalling through a specific spliced isoform [PMID:28322931], and acts in innate immunity as a cytosolic sensor of double-stranded RNA and DNA [PMID:20453844].

## Reading a hit

Do not report a match here as a match to a family motif. Report the matrix instead, then ask what it is. If the hit is M02433 or M01304, the honest reading is that a four- to five-bit A-rich matrix matched, which is no evidence, and the LCOR matrix is in any case a cross-species transfer from a bird. If it is LRRF1.H14CORE.0.P.B, read it as a GC-rich model built from ChIP-seq alone and compare the sequence against the GC-box families - KLF/SP, MAZ, EGR, NRF1 - before crediting LRRFIP1 with the site. More generally, a residual category exists so that well-supported families are not diluted by unresolved single cases, and a hit in it should be read as unassigned. For LCOR and LCORL the informative question is not what they bind but which nuclear receptor recruited them; for LRRFIP1 it is which GC-box family the sequence belongs to, and whether the protein was in the nucleus at all.
families.caveats: Treat this as an administrative category, not a biological one. It holds three matrices for three proteins whose medoid similarity is 0.60, and the group has no shared consensus: two are 4-5 bit A-rich matrices for the corepressors LCOR and LCORL, one of them transferred from a wild turkey protein, and the third is a 9.6-bit GC-rich model for LRRFIP1 supported by ChIP-seq alone at grade B. No member has a same-family neighbour it actually matches. The reported zero suspect motifs reflects a pipeline rule that suppresses the flag inside residual buckets, not internal agreement. Do not build a consensus, a logo or a representative matrix for this group, and re-report any hit to the named family the sequence matches.

timeline.finding: GCF2, the protein now called LRRFIP1, is cloned by differential hybridization with the cDNA of the GC-binding repressor GCF; it binds epidermal growth factor receptor promoter fragments at a major site between -249 and -233 and represses the promoter only when that site is intact.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, promoter-fragment binding assays, reporter cotransfection with site mutation
timeline.open: Whether the protein occupies that site, or any GC-rich site, in cells was not tested.

timeline.finding: LCoR is defined as a ligand-dependent corepressor: it is recruited to agonist-bound nuclear receptors through a single LXXLL motif and represses by binding HDACs directly and by recruiting CtBP corepressors, so its genomic placement is set by the receptor.
timeline.methods: Protein interaction assays in vitro and in cells, reporter assays, HDAC inhibitor treatment
timeline.open: Whether LCoR makes any sequence-specific DNA contact of its own, rather than riding on the receptor, was not addressed.

timeline.finding: LRRFIP1 is recast as a cytosolic nucleic-acid sensor that binds exogenous double-stranded RNA and DNA and drives interferon-beta production through beta-catenin and IRF3, moving its best-supported activity out of the nucleus.
timeline.methods: Knockdown and overexpression in macrophages, viral and bacterial infection, protein interaction assays
timeline.open: How this activity relates to the GC-rich promoter binding reported for GCF2 was not addressed.

timeline.finding: The CIS-BP survey measures DNA preferences for more than 1,000 transcription factors from 131 eukaryotes and finds that closely related DNA-binding domains almost always share them. That rule is what lets CIS-BP file a matrix measured on a wild turkey protein, with a DNA-binding domain 100% identical to the human one, under human LCOR.
timeline.methods: Protein-binding microarrays, motif inference by DNA-binding-domain identity

timeline.finding: The human transcription factor census keeps LCOR and LCORL as likely sequence-specific factors with a pipsqueak DNA-binding domain and high-throughput in vitro motifs, LCOR's taken from an ortholog at 100% identity. It judges LRRFIP1 unlikely to be a sequence-specific factor and records nothing that would indicate DNA binding.
timeline.methods: Expert curation of candidate transcription factors
timeline.open: The census note on LRRFIP1 does not engage with the 1998 report of EGFR-promoter binding by GCF2, so the disagreement was recorded rather than resolved.

timeline.finding: The reference footprint atlas clusters matrices from several collections into archetypes named after their members. LCORL's low-information A-rich matrix is pooled with forkhead models in AC0014:FOXR/LCORL.
timeline.methods: Motif clustering; DNase I footprinting in 243 cell and tissue types
timeline.open: An archetype name records which matrices clustered, not which protein binds.

timeline.finding: HOCOMOCO is rebuilt from motif discovery in more than 14,000 ChIP-seq peak sets plus HT-SELEX data. In the current release LRRFIP1's only matrix is a GC-rich ChIP-seq-only model, LRRF1.H14CORE.0.P.B (grade B), even though the census had found no evidence that the protein binds DNA.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq motif discovery, expert curation, benchmarking
timeline.open: Whether aaGCTCGC is LRRFIP1's own preference or that of a co-bound GC-box factor has not been tested in vitro.

open: Whether LRRFIP1 binds DNA sequence-specifically at all is unresolved. The 1998 GCF2 study reported repression through a mapped site in the EGFR promoter; the human transcription factor census found nothing indicating DNA binding; and the only matrix for the protein is ChIP-derived, with no in vitro assay behind it.

Whether the pipsqueak-type helix-turn-helix of LCOR and LCORL has a sequence preference worth modelling is not settled. The in vitro assays recorded for both yield only 4-5-bit A-rich matrices, while the biochemistry of LCOR describes recruitment by agonist-bound nuclear receptors rather than direct recognition of a DNA sequence.

families.name: CTCFL (BORIS)
families.def: CTCF-like core bound by the testis paralogue CTCFL.
aka: Brother of the Regulator of Imprinted Sites
families.short: CTCFL, usually called BORIS, is the single paralogue of CTCF. The two proteins share an almost identical eleven-zinc-finger array and therefore the same DNA sequence preference, so the CTCFL matrices in motif databases are simply shorter, noisier versions of the CTCF core. What differs is the protein outside the fingers and, above all, where and when it is made: CTCFL is normally confined to a narrow window of male germ-cell development, and is re-expressed in many tumors, where it is used as a cancer-testis antigen. A CTCFL motif match is a CTCF-family match; deciding which of the two proteins is bound requires expression data or an antibody, not sequence.
families.long:
## The factors

CTCFL (also BORIS, for Brother of the Regulator of Imprinted Sites) was identified as a paralogue of CTCF whose exons encode the same eleven-zinc-finger domain, and therefore the same DNA-binding potential, attached to entirely different amino- and carboxy-terminal regions (Loukinov et al. 2002) [PMID:12011441]. It is the only CTCF paralogue in mammals. Expression is the main distinction. CTCFL is normally restricted to the testis, appearing transiently in male germ cells before the onset of meiosis, at a stage that coincides with erasure of methylation marks; immunohistochemistry on testis sections places it alongside Stra8-positive cells and shows that it overlaps in time with ubiquitously expressed CTCF rather than strictly replacing it (Sleutels et al. 2012) [PMID:22709888]. Outside the germ line, CTCFL is silent in normal somatic tissue but is aberrantly activated in a wide range of tumors [PMID:24657531,32334335], which is why it is catalogued as a cancer-testis antigen. Neither protein needs to dimerize to bind DNA. The N and C termini of CTCFL differ from those of CTCF; the CTCF N terminus carries the cohesin interaction needed for loop formation, and in chimera-complementation experiments the N terminus, C terminus and zinc-finger region each contributed to targeting the two paralogues to distinct sites (Nishana et al. 2020) [PMID:32393311].

## The motif

Because the zinc-finger arrays are effectively the same, so is the sequence preference: CTCFL binds the CTCF core. The three CTCFL matrices in this atlas make the point. HOCOMOCO's CTCFL.H14CORE.0.P.B (CCRCCAGGGGGCGC) and CIS-BP's M07930_2.00 (GCGCCCCCTGGCGG, the reverse-complement orientation of the same sequence) both reproduce the CCASYAGRKGGC core that CTCF reads through zinc fingers 3-7 [PMID:28529057], and JASPAR's CTCFL profile (MA1102.3) is only 8 positions long (CAGGGGGC) - a fragment of that core, not a distinct motif [PMID:37962376,37971293]. What is *not* captured by any of these matrices is the upstream module that CTCF's fingers 9-11 read, so the CTCFL models are on average shorter and carry less information than the CTCF ones (11.7-15.7 bits here versus up to 22.5 bits for CTCF). That is a property of the models, not evidence of a different specificity. The practical statement is blunt: no position-weight matrix separates CTCFL from CTCF, and none should be expected to. What can be distinguished is site *architecture* rather than site sequence. Comparing CTCF and BORIS occupancy genome-wide, Pugacheva et al. (2015) found that BORIS is largely confined to a subset of regulatory elements containing clustered CTCF motifs, which they called 2xCTS elements, whereas single-motif sites (1xCTS) are bound by CTCF alone; 2xCTS elements are preferentially active promoters and enhancers in both germ cells and BORIS-positive cancer cells [PMID:26268681]. So the discriminating feature is the presence of two adjacent core motifs, not the sequence of either one.

## Where it acts

In germ cells and in BORIS-expressing cancer lines, CTCFL occupies a minority of the CTCF site repertoire, concentrated at the clustered 2xCTS class at active promoters and enhancers, and enriched in regions that escape the histone-to-protamine transition (Pugacheva et al. 2015) [PMID:26268681]. Its binding in germ cells is accompanied by testis-specific transcriptional regulators that selectively occupy the BORIS-bound subset (Rivero-Hinojosa et al. 2017) [PMID:28145452]. Nucleosome context also differs: in mouse ES cells, induced CTCFL bound promoters with loosely assembled nucleosomes and colocalized with the histone variant H3.3, whereas CTCF favored sites flanked by phased nucleosomes, and the authors proposed that nucleosome composition specifies where each protein binds (Sleutels et al. 2012) [PMID:22709888]. In cancer, BORIS binding has been mapped to the promoters of cancer-testis antigen genes MAGEA2, MAGEA3 and MAGEA4, where it accompanies their transcriptional activation in lung cancer (Bhan et al. 2011) [PMID:21558405].

## Biology and disease

The germ-line role is the well-supported one: transient CTCFL expression during pre-meiotic male germ-cell development, coincident with epigenetic reprogramming, and regulation of testis-specific genes. Its disease relevance is as an ectopically activated gene. Conditional expression of BORIS in normal cells is sufficient to demethylate and derepress MAGE-A1 and to reactivate other cancer-testis genes (Vatolin et al. 2005) [PMID:16140943], and BORIS occupancy at MAGEA promoters tracks their activation in tumors (Bhan et al. 2011) [PMID:21558405]. CTCF and CTCFL are both altered in cancer, but in opposite directions - CTCF behaves as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor while CTCFL is typically gained or de-repressed (Marshall et al. 2014; Debaugny and Skok 2020) [PMID:24657531,32334335]. Claims that BORIS acts as a simple antagonist of CTCF have not held up cleanly, since the two are co-expressed in germ cells and co-occupy 2xCTS sites [PMID:22709888,26268681].

## Reading a hit

Treat a CTCFL match as a CTCF-family match. The sequence cannot tell you which paralogue is bound, and in almost every human tissue the answer is CTCF, because CTCFL is not expressed: check CTCFL mRNA in your cell type before entertaining it at all. All three database CTCFL matrices derive from chromatin immunoprecipitation in cells where CTCF is also present, so they inherit CTCF's specificity by construction; the HOCOMOCO model carries ChIP-only evidence at grade B [PMID:37971293]. If you have a reason to care about CTCFL specifically, the informative feature is not the motif but whether the region contains two closely spaced core motifs, since the clustered configuration is what BORIS occupancy tracks. And because JASPAR's CTCFL profile is only 8 bp, it will match far more often than a full CTCF core model - do not read those extra hits as CTCFL-specific sites.
families.caveats: CTCFL and CTCF share an almost identical zinc-finger array, so no matrix can separate them and a CTCFL hit is really a CTCF-core hit. In normal somatic tissue CTCFL is not expressed, so the biologically relevant binder is CTCF unless you have expression evidence otherwise. All three database CTCFL models are derived from ChIP in CTCF-containing cells, and JASPAR's is only 8 bp long, which makes it match promiscuously. If CTCFL is genuinely the question, look for two clustered core motifs rather than for a CTCFL-specific sequence, and confirm with an antibody or CTCFL expression data.

timeline.finding: BORIS is discovered as a testis-specific CTCF paralogue with the same 11-zinc-finger exons and therefore the same DNA-binding potential, but different N and C termini; it was reported to be expressed mutually exclusively with CTCF and up-regulated as methylation marks are erased in male germ cells.
timeline.methods: Gene cloning, expression analysis in testis
timeline.open: Its genomic binding sites, and whether it ever meets CTCF in the same nucleus, were unknown.

timeline.finding: Conditional expression of BORIS in normal fibroblasts demethylates and de-represses the cancer-testis gene MAGE-A1 and reactivates other cancer-testis genes, linking ectopic BORIS to the cancer-testis antigen program.
timeline.methods: Conditional expression in normal cells, promoter methylation and expression assays
timeline.open: Whether BORIS acts directly at these promoters in tumors was not shown.

timeline.finding: BORIS occupancy at the MAGEA2, MAGEA3 and MAGEA4 promoters accompanies their transcriptional activation in lung cancer.
timeline.methods: ChIP and expression analysis in lung cancer cells and tissue

timeline.finding: Imaging of testis shows CTCFL is present only transiently before meiosis and co-localizes with CTCF in the same nuclei, overturning the earlier mutual-exclusion model; Ctcfl-deficient mice are sub-fertile, and genome-wide CTCFL binds a CTCF-like consensus at about 5,700 sites, only about 3,700 of which overlap CTCF's.
timeline.methods: Immunohistochemistry, live imaging of seminiferous tubules, knockout mice, ChIP-seq
timeline.open: Why only a subset of CTCF-like sites recruits CTCFL could not be explained by the core motif.

timeline.finding: Comparative CTCF and BORIS ChIP-seq defines two classes of CTCF sites: clustered double motifs (2xCTS), co-occupied by BORIS and enriched at active promoters and enhancers, and single motifs (1xCTS) bound by CTCF alone. Site architecture, not motif sequence, predicts BORIS binding.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in BORIS-positive cancer lines and germ cells, knockdown and ectopic expression
timeline.open: How the two proteins are arranged on a 2xCTS element was not resolved by occupancy data.

timeline.finding: Testis-specific transcriptional regulators, including TAF7L, which interacts physically with BORIS, co-occupy subsets of BORIS-bound regions in mouse male germ cells.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq overlap in germ cells, co-immunoprecipitation

timeline.finding: Inducible complementation with CTCF, CTCFL and chimeric proteins shows that the CTCF N terminus carries the cohesin interaction needed for convergent-site loops, and that the N terminus, C terminus and zinc-finger region each help target the two paralogues to distinct sites.
timeline.methods: Inducible complementation with chimeric proteins, ChIP-seq, Hi-C, RNA-seq
timeline.open: Which zinc-finger differences produce distinct targeting, and at which positions of the site, was not mapped.

timeline.finding: In JASPAR 2024 and HOCOMOCO v14, all CTCFL matrices are ChIP-derived and reproduce the CTCF core; the JASPAR profile is an 8-bp fragment (CAGGGGGC) and none captures the upstream module.
timeline.methods: Database curation of ChIP-seq-derived models

open: Whether CTCFL's zinc fingers carry any sequence preference of their own is disputed: the original description emphasized a DNA-binding domain shared with CTCF, while chimera complementation found that the zinc-finger region helps direct each paralogue to distinct sites, and every CTCFL matrix in these databases is ChIP-derived, so no in vitro model exists to settle it.

How CTCF and CTCFL are arranged on the clustered 2xCTS elements they co-occupy is not established: occupancy data show both proteins at the same regions but cannot say whether each takes one motif or whether they bind together.

Whether ectopic CTCFL contributes to transformation or marks a demethylated, germline-like state in tumors is unsettled: its expression is sufficient to demethylate and de-repress cancer-testis genes in normal cells, but a requirement for it in tumor growth has not been established across cancer types.

families.name: INSM1 / INSM2
families.def: INSM1 and INSM2. The matrices here are GC-rich (TGTCAGGGGGCG) rather than E-box-like, and all three trace back to one compiled model, so the apparent agreement between databases is one matrix repeated.
families.short: INSM1 (originally IA-1, cloned from a human insulinoma) and its paralogue INSM2 are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger repressors of neuroendocrine and neuronal differentiation. Despite the family's historical placement alongside the Snail-type repressors, every matrix in this family is a GC-rich, GGGG-containing element - TGTCAGGGGGCG, or GCCCCCTGACA read on the other strand - not a CANNTG E-box. Structural work shows INSM1's fingers bind DNA with little intrinsic specificity for that element and that INSM1 reaches GGGG-containing loci largely by riding with CTCF, and TEAD1 sites through a direct TEAD1 contact. INSM1 is required for pancreatic beta cell and intestinal endocrine development and is now a standard immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine tumors.
families.long:
## The factors

INSM1 was isolated as IA-1 from a human insulinoma cDNA library and encodes a roughly 510-residue protein with five C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers and a proline-rich N terminus [PMID:1634555]. INSM2 is its single paralogue, considerably less studied and without a motif of its own in any of the four databases surveyed here. Recent structural work resolves the whole five-finger module and shows it is unusually flexible: finger 1 adopts a non-canonical CCHC fold and does not contact DNA at all, instead binding the TEAD domain of TEAD1 through hydrophobic contacts, while fingers 2 and 3 bind DNA but, because the interdomain linker is long and flexible, without specificity for the GGGG-containing element that the factor is classically associated with [PMID:40038295]. The functional consequence, as reported in that work, is that INSM1 is recruited to genomic targets substantially through partner proteins - CTCF at GGGG-element loci, TEAD1 at TEAD-target promoters - rather than through autonomous high-affinity recognition [PMID:40038295]. Repression at the insulin promoter involves recruitment of cyclin D1 and HDAC3 [PMID:18417529]. INSM1 expression is tightly restricted: transient in neural and endocrine progenitors during development, essentially absent from adult differentiated tissue, and re-expressed in neuroendocrine neoplasia [PMID:1634555,31113827].

## The motif

All three matrices in this family describe the same GC-rich element. JASPAR MA0155.1 renders it TGTCAGGGGGCG, CIS-BP M08445 renders it CGCCCCCTGACA, and the Vierstra archetype AC0533:INSM reads TGCCCCCTGACA; the first is simply the reverse complement of the other two. The informative block is the CCCCC/GGGGG run plus the adjacent TGAC, roughly 15 bits over 11-12 positions [PMID:11842116]. There is no CANNTG E-box anywhere in it. This matters because the family is conventionally described, including in this atlas's own family definition, as carrying "SNAI-like E-box repressor sites": that statement reflects protein-level kinship with the Snail-type C2H2 repressors and the shared habit of repressing differentiation programs, not the matrices, which are unambiguously not E-boxes. Readers looking for an INSM1 E-box will not find one in these data. Two further points constrain how much the consensus is worth. The JASPAR entry is typed COMPILED and traces to literature annotation rather than to a high-throughput binding experiment [PMID:11842116,37962376], and the CIS-BP and Vierstra entries match it at 0.99-1.00 - so the family's apparent perfect internal cohesion is not three independent confirmations but one consensus propagated through three collections. And the structural data argue that fingers 2-3 have limited intrinsic preference for this element, so the matrix is better read as a description of where INSM1 is found than of what it binds tightly in isolation [PMID:28160313,40038295].

## Where it acts

Mapped INSM1 sites are promoter-proximal. The best-characterized single example is the proximal rat insulin I/II promoter, where a GG-to-AT substitution in the INSM1 core site raises promoter activity three- to twenty-fold and abolishes INSM1-dependent repression, and where INSM1 occupancy has been confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation in beta cell lines, fetal mouse pancreas and human islets [PMID:18417529]. Genome-wide, INSM1 co-localizes with CTCF at GGGG-element loci and with TEAD1 at TEAD targets [PMID:40038295], so a large fraction of INSM1 occupancy is expected to be at sites that are primarily another factor's. Because the element is GC- and CpG-rich, it is concentrated in CpG-island promoters, where it competes for space with the many other GC-box-reading C2H2 families.

## Biology and disease

Insm1-null mice fail to make pancreatic beta cells and intestinal endocrine cells in normal numbers, with endocrine progenitors arrested before terminal differentiation [PMID:16951258]. In the developing neocortex Insm1 acts across neurogenic lineages, promoting the generation and expansion of basal progenitors [PMID:18940587], and in the zebrafish retina insm1a is required for photoreceptor differentiation [PMID:23747542]; in the inner ear Insm1 promotes proliferation of delaminated otic progenitors [PMID:26545349]. The clinical relevance is mostly diagnostic and oncologic. INSM1 protein is now widely used as an immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine differentiation across small cell lung carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors and related neoplasms, generally with better specificity than chromogranin or synaptophysin [PMID:31113827]. In neuroblastoma, INSM1 stabilizes N-MYC protein in a positive-feedback circuit [PMID:26456864], and INSM1 has been proposed as a therapeutic target and as a promoter for tumor-selective gene delivery [PMID:31113827].

## Reading a hit

Treat a match here as weak evidence. First, the consensus is GC-rich and CpG-island-like, which means it overlaps the recognition space of SP/KLF, ZBTB7, MAZ, PATZ1 and many other C2H2 GC-box readers; a CCCCC run with a flanking TGAC is not a specific INSM1 signature. Second, the sequence model rests on a single compiled matrix reproduced in three collections, not on independent in vitro determinations: there is no HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX model for INSM1 or INSM2 in HOCOMOCO in these data, so the "this protein binds this sequence" test is not met by the usual standard. Third, the structural evidence indicates that INSM1's fingers lack strong specificity for this element and that genomic recruitment leans on CTCF and TEAD1 [PMID:40038295], which means an INSM1 ChIP peak carrying the motif may well be a CTCF site. Fourth, INSM2 has no motif at all, so nothing here can be attributed to it. If you have an INSM1 hit, the strongest supporting evidence is cell type: transient neural or endocrine progenitors, or a neuroendocrine tumor.
families.caveats: This family's consensus is not an E-box, despite the "SNAI-like" label, which refers to protein kinship rather than to the matrices. The apparent perfect cohesion across JASPAR, CIS-BP and Vierstra reflects one compiled matrix propagated into three collections, not three independent measurements; there is no HOCOMOCO in vitro model here. Structural work indicates INSM1's DNA-binding fingers have little intrinsic specificity for the GGGG element and that occupancy depends heavily on CTCF and TEAD1, so a motif-positive INSM1 peak may belong to a partner. The element is GC-rich and overlaps many other C2H2 GC-box motifs. INSM2 has no motif; do not read a hit as evidence about it.

timeline.finding: IA-1 was cloned by subtraction from a human insulinoma library as a 510-residue protein with five C2H2 fingers, expressed in neuroendocrine tumor lines and undetectable in normal adult tissue.
timeline.methods: subtractive cDNA cloning, Northern blotting
timeline.open: Whether the protein bound DNA, and at what sequence.

timeline.finding: A selected and amplified random-oligonucleotide assay with the bacterially expressed IA-1 DNA-binding domain gave the GC-rich consensus TG/TC/TC/TT/AGGGGG/TCG/A, showed that fingers 2 and 3 suffice for activity through that site, and mapped the repression function to residues 168-263; this single determination is the origin of the matrix later carried by JASPAR, CIS-BP and the Vierstra archetypes.
timeline.methods: random-oligonucleotide selection with a GST-DBD fusion, reporter assays, promoter database search
timeline.open: Whether the full-length protein binds this element with high affinity in cells.

timeline.finding: Insm1-null mice were shown to form pancreatic and intestinal endocrine precursors that arrest before terminal differentiation, with loss of hormone and secretory-machinery gene expression, giving the factor a developmental requirement independent of any motif evidence.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, expression profiling, histology

timeline.finding: A functional INSM1 site was mapped in the proximal rat insulin I/II promoter, where a two-base substitution raised promoter activity several-fold and abolished repression and where occupancy was confirmed in beta cell lines, fetal pancreas and human islets; in the same period Insm1 was shown to have a pan-neurogenic role in generating basal progenitors in the neocortex.
timeline.methods: promoter mutagenesis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, mouse and in utero electroporation experiments

timeline.finding: A solution NMR structure of INSM1 zinc fingers 4 and 5 showed a conventional head-to-tail arrangement but only weak binding to the published consensus, the first direct signal that the five-finger module may not read this element tightly.
timeline.methods: solution NMR, NMR titration, isothermal titration calorimetry
timeline.open: Whether the fingers that were not resolved, 1 to 3, supply the missing affinity.

timeline.finding: INSM1 was established in diagnostic practice as an immunohistochemical marker of neuroendocrine differentiation with better specificity than chromogranin or synaptophysin, which made the protein widely assayed even though its binding specificity remained based on one 2002 experiment.
timeline.methods: review of immunohistochemical series and functional studies

timeline.finding: Structural and biochemical analysis of the whole five-finger module reversed the standard reading of this family's motif: finger 1 adopts a CCHC fold and binds the TEAD domain of TEAD1 rather than DNA, fingers 2 and 3 bind DNA without specificity for the GGGG element, and INSM1 reaches its genomic targets with CTCF and TEAD1, so the catalogued matrix describes where INSM1 is found rather than what it binds.
timeline.methods: NMR and crystallographic analysis of the zinc-finger module, binding assays, ternary complex reconstitution, genomic co-localization

open: Whether INSM1 has any intrinsic preference for the GC-rich element attributed to it is now in dispute: selection with the isolated DNA-binding domain returned the TGAC-plus-GGGGG consensus that all three databases carry, while structural work on the intact five-finger module reports that fingers 2 and 3 bind DNA without specificity for it and that occupancy depends on CTCF and TEAD1.

It is unresolved what fraction of motif-containing INSM1 ChIP peaks are bound directly, since the same GGGG element is a CTCF-associated feature and no knockout-controlled occupancy study with a DNA-binding-deficient INSM1 mutant has been reported.
INSM2 has no motif in any of the four collections and essentially no binding literature, so whether it reads the same element as INSM1, a different one, or binds DNA at all is unknown.

families.name: ZBTB18 (RP58)
families.def: ZBTB18 (RP58): a C2H2 repressor reading the E-box-like site MACATCTGKM, core CATCTG/CAGATG - an E-box read by zinc fingers rather than by a bHLH.
families.short: ZBTB18, first described as RP58, is a BTB/POZ zinc-finger repressor that binds an E-box-like site, (A/C)ACATCTG(G/T)(A/C), whose CATCTG core reads CAGATG on the opposite strand. It is a C2H2 protein, not a bHLH one, so the E-box it occupies is a site that basic helix-loop-helix activators can also use - which makes competition, not just repression, part of how it works. RP58 concentrates in condensed chromatin and represses target promoters through its POZ domain. In the brain it controls the multipolar-to-bipolar transition of newborn cortical neurons and is required for cerebellar growth; human ZBTB18 mutations cause autosomal dominant intellectual disability and figure in 1q43-q44 deletion syndrome with corpus callosum malformation.
families.long:
## The factors

ZBTB18 is a one-member family in this atlas. The gene, also known as RP58 and ZNF238, encodes a 522-residue protein with an N-terminal POZ/BTB domain - the feature that first placed it alongside BCL6 - and four C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers [PMID:9756912]. The POZ domain mediates homodimerization and autonomous repression; it does not contact DNA. An early and still striking observation is that almost all RP58 protein localizes to condensed chromatin regions by immunogold electron microscopy [PMID:9756912], which was the basis for proposing that this factor links sequence-specific repression to chromosome organization. ZBTB18 is expressed most prominently in the developing and adult central nervous system, in cortical and cerebellar neurons, and also in skeletal muscle and other tissues [PMID:32959890]; it is not a lineage-restricted factor in the way GFI1 or ThPOK are. In neurons it behaves as a differentiation-promoting repressor: it shuts down programs belonging to other cell identities rather than activating neuronal genes directly.

## The motif

The binding site was determined by cyclic amplification and selection of targets with recombinant protein, giving the high-affinity consensus (A/C)ACATCTG(G/T)(A/C) [PMID:9756912]. The internal CATCTG is a CANNTG E-box variant, and read on the opposite strand the same site presents CAGATG as its core. This is worth stating carefully because the two renderings look like different motifs: the JASPAR HT-SELEX matrix MA0698.2 reads TCCAGATGTT and the HOCOMOCO grade-A model reads CCAGATGTG, both of which are the reverse complement of the selected consensus, not a disagreement with it [PMID:23332764,37971293]. Note also that the family definition used in this atlas describes the site as "E-box-like CACATG"; the experimentally selected core is CATCTG (equivalently CAGATG), with an A at the position where CACATG has a C, so the shorter label is slightly off and should not be used for scanning. Information content is 11-15 bits over nine or ten positions - better than a bare 6 bp E-box but still modest. Four adjacent fingers could cover more sequence than the consensus specifies, and the flanking A/C and G/T degeneracies suggest that only two or three fingers contribute strong base contacts. The family data flags one entry as inconsistent: the CIS-BP model M08257 for ZBTB18 reads CGCAGCTGCG, a canonical CAGCTG bHLH E-box whose nearest neighbors across databases fall in the NEUROD/ATOH family rather than with ZBTB18, and which matches no other ZBTB18 model. With only three matrices in the family, that single outlier drags the measured cohesion down to 0.79.

## Where it acts

ZBTB18 acts mainly at promoters of genes belonging to alternative differentiation programs. In developing neurons it represses transcriptional programs linked to non-neuronal cell identity, including programs that correspond to glioblastoma subtypes [PMID:33903225], and the sites it uses are promoter-proximal E-boxes rather than distal enhancer clusters. Because the core is a CANNTG box with no CpG, matches are not concentrated in CpG islands and occur throughout the genome; a nine-position match with two degenerate positions still arises tens of thousands of times by chance in 3 Gb. The important co-occurrence to keep in mind is with bHLH factors: NEUROG2, NEUROD and ASCL1 bind overlapping CANNTG boxes in the same neuronal promoters, and the sequence alone cannot say which occupied a site.

## Biology and disease

Mouse Rp58 mutants show defective cortical development: newborn neurons fail to complete the multipolar-to-bipolar transition needed for radial migration [PMID:23395638], and cerebellar growth and patterning are disrupted, with abnormal development of both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons [PMID:22513377]. In humans, heterozygous ZBTB18 loss-of-function and missense variants cause autosomal dominant non-syndromic intellectual disability 22 (MRD22), with developmental delay, seizures and frequent corpus callosum abnormalities [PMID:38215144]; ZBTB18 lies in the critical region of 1q43-q44 deletion syndrome, and its loss is a principal candidate for the corpus callosum and microcephaly phenotypes in that contiguous gene syndrome [PMID:36192753]. Missense variants have been shown to differ in how much they impair DNA binding versus repression, so the allelic series is informative rather than uniform [PMID:35083747]. In glioblastoma, ZBTB18 behaves as a tumor suppressor that is silenced epigenetically, and restoring it represses mesenchymal and lipid-metabolic programs [PMID:28512252].

## Reading a hit

The CATCTG/CAGATG core makes this an E-box family, with all the attendant ambiguity. Candidates for any CANNTG match include the bHLH factors of the NEUROD/ATOH, ASCL, NEUROG, TCF3/4/12, MYOD and TWIST groups, and among C2H2 proteins the SNAIL, ZEB and INSM-related repressors. An E-box hit is not evidence of a bHLH factor, and equally it is not evidence of ZBTB18. What tilts the balance toward ZBTB18 is the specific internal composition: CATCTG rather than CACCTG, CAGCTG or CACGTG, with the flanking A and G/T. The best-supported matrix here is JASPAR MA0698.2, which is HT-SELEX-derived and thus direct in vitro evidence [PMID:23332764], and the HOCOMOCO model is grade A with PSM evidence, so "ZBTB18 binds this sequence" is well established [PMID:37971293]. Do not use the CIS-BP entry M08257 (CGCAGCTGCG): it looks like a NEUROD/ATOH-class site, and scanning with it will return bHLH sites labelled as ZBTB18. Finally, since ZBTB18 is one gene, there is no paralogue problem inside the family - but the outside-the-family problem is severe, and a hit should be reported as "E-box consistent with ZBTB18" rather than as a ZBTB18 site.
families.caveats: The site is an E-box variant, so the crowd of bHLH factors plus SNAIL, ZEB and INSM-related C2H2 repressors all compete for interpretation of a match; report an E-box, then argue for ZBTB18 from the internal CATCTG composition and the cell type. The commonly quoted "CACATG" shorthand for this family is not the selected consensus and should not be scanned. Trust JASPAR MA0698.2 (HT-SELEX) and the HOCOMOCO grade-A model, which are reverse-complement renderings of the same site; discard the CIS-BP entry CGCAGCTGCG, which the cross-database analysis places with NEUROD/ATOH and which accounts for this family's low internal cohesion. Single gene, so no paralogue ambiguity within the family.
