timeline.finding: RP58 was cloned as a POZ-domain zinc-finger protein, its high-affinity site was selected as (A/C)ACATCTG(G/T)(A/C) - an E-box core read by zinc fingers - and the protein was shown to repress from that site and to sit almost entirely in condensed chromatin.
timeline.methods: binding-site selection (CAST), reporter assays, immunogold electron microscopy
timeline.open: Whether the protein competes with bHLH activators for the same boxes in cells.

timeline.finding: Neural deletion of Rp58 in mice caused severe cerebellar hypoplasia with failure of Purkinje neuron, Bergmann glia and granule neuron development, showing that the factor is required for both glutamatergic and GABAergic lineages rather than for one neuronal class.
timeline.methods: conditional mouse knockouts, lineage-specific deletion, histology

timeline.finding: RP58 was shown to be required cell-autonomously for the multipolar-to-bipolar transition of newborn cortical neurons, acting by repressing Ngn2 and the Ngn2-Rnd2 pathway, which put a proneural bHLH gene directly downstream of this repressor.
timeline.methods: conditional deletion with in utero electroporation, rescue by Ngn2 knockdown

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX returned the same site from the other strand, TCCAGATGTT, independently confirming the 1998 selection and giving the collections an in vitro model for ZBTB18.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX across human transcription factors

timeline.finding: ZBTB18 was found to be silenced by promoter hypermethylation specifically in the mesenchymal subtype of glioblastoma, and re-expression suppressed the aggressive phenotype, framing it as an epigenetically inactivated tumor suppressor.
timeline.methods: methylation and expression profiling of tumors, re-expression and xenograft assays

timeline.finding: Transcriptome analysis of Rp58 mutant cortical neurons showed that the repressed program consists largely of genes belonging to other cell identities, including mesodermal, pluripotency and glioma signatures, so the factor maintains neuronal identity by exclusion rather than by activating neuronal genes.
timeline.methods: mouse conditional knockouts with RNA sequencing and gene set enrichment, glioma stem cell experiments

timeline.finding: Functional dissection of patient missense alleles showed that they differ in whether they impair DNA binding or repression, and reviews of 1q43q44 deletions placed ZBTB18 as the principal candidate for the corpus callosum and microcephaly components of that contiguous gene syndrome.
timeline.methods: variant functional assays in neural cells, array CGH and clinical correlation
timeline.open: Whether any single gene in the 1q43q44 interval accounts for the callosal phenotype on its own.

open: The CIS-BP entry M08257 reads CGCAGCTGCG and its cross-database neighbors are NEUROD/ATOH motifs, and it is unresolved whether ZBTB18 has a genuine secondary preference for a CAGCTG box or the model simply carries the wrong label; nothing in the literature reports CAGCTG binding by this protein.

Whether ZBTB18 and proneural bHLH factors contest the same boxes in neurons is not established: ZBTB18 represses the Ngn2 gene, which is a regulatory relationship rather than site-level competition, and no experiment has shown the two protein classes exchanging at individual CANNTG sites.

Which fingers of the four carry the specificity is unknown, since there is no structure of the ZBTB18 zinc-finger array on DNA and the degeneracy at the flanking positions of the selected consensus only suggests that two or three fingers make strong base contacts.

It remains unsettled how patient missense alleles cause disease, because the tested variants fall on a spectrum between loss of DNA binding and loss of repression, and whether some act as dominant negatives through the dimerizing POZ domain has not been determined.

families.name: SALL
families.def: AT-rich double zinc-finger sites. SALL1-4.
families.short: SALL1 to SALL4 are the human Spalt-like proteins: large C2H2 zinc-finger factors built from several clusters of paired fingers, with a short N-terminal motif that recruits the NuRD corepressor complex. Their DNA binding is unusual in being defined by base composition rather than by a sequence. A single C-terminal pair of fingers in SALL4 reads AT-rich DNA, and a crystal structure shows why it is promiscuous: the contacts use small side chains in the major groove, so many different AT-rich combinations are accepted. There is consequently no reliable consensus string for this family. SALL1 mutations cause Townes-Brocks syndrome and SALL4 mutations Okihiro syndrome; SALL4 is also the cereblon substrate whose degradation explains thalidomide limb teratogenicity.
families.long:
## The factors

The four human SALL genes, SALL1 to SALL4, are homologues of Drosophila spalt. Each protein is large
and built from several clusters of C2H2 zinc fingers, usually a set of paired fingers (three or four
double-finger clusters) plus one unpaired finger, separated by long low-complexity linkers. A short
motif at the extreme N terminus recruits the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex,
and NuRD recruitment accounts for much of the repressive activity attributed to these proteins; the
same interaction is required for SALL4's contribution to reprogramming [PMID:37208322]. SALL4 is highly expressed in
embryonic stem cells and in germ-cell and hepatocellular tumors but silenced in most adult tissues,
which is why it is used as an immunohistochemical marker. SALL1 is prominent in kidney and limb,
SALL3 in the nervous system. Mouse work shows Sall1, Sall2 and Sall4 are each required for neural
tube closure [PMID:18818376].

## The motif

Only one of the SALL clusters binds DNA in SALL4: a pair of fingers near the C terminus (ZFC4).
Inactivating that one cluster drastically reduces SALL4's genome occupancy and reproduces the
phenotype of a complete Sall4 knockout, including precocious differentiation of embryonic stem cells
and embryonic lethality, whereas deleting two of the other clusters is phenotypically neutral [PMID:33406384]. What
that cluster reads is AT-richness rather than a defined word: SALL4 was recovered in a screen for
proteins that bind AT-rich motifs, and genes are de-repressed on SALL4 loss in proportion to their AT
content [PMID:33406384]. Protein-binding-microarray and CUT&RUN experiments define an AT-rich consensus [PMID:33406418], and the
crystal structure of the C-terminal fingers on AT-rich DNA explains the flexibility: recognition uses
small hydrophobic and polar side chains in the major groove, so many different combinations of A and
T are accepted [PMID:36635047]. We therefore give no consensus string for this family; any single IUPAC word
overstates what the protein specifies.

The database situation reflects this awkwardly. Of the three matrices assigned here, only the SALL3
model (consensus TTATGAATTATGATAT, HOCOMOCO grade A with HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and ChIP-seq support) is
the AT-rich motif the literature describes, and it has no close neighbor among the other family
members. The SALL1 and SALL4 models are ChIP-only (grades C and B) and are GC-rich, with the
consensus GGGTGGGG, which is also the family's data consensus and its medoid. GGGTGGGG is a GC-box-
and KLF/SP-like sequence, and the most economical explanation is that these ChIP-derived models
capture a co-occupancy or promoter signal rather than SALL binding preference. Cohesion in this
family is 0.51, essentially because the literature motif and the database medoid disagree.

## Where it acts

SALL4 occupancy is broad and follows base composition: it accumulates over long AT-rich domains and
at AT-rich genes, a distribution unlike the punctate enhancer occupancy of most transcription
factors, and it acts largely to hold such genes down [PMID:33406384]. That makes the relevant genomic feature a
region rather than a site. Reported partners include NuRD and, in pluripotent cells, the core
pluripotency factors [PMID:37208322]. SALL1 in kidney and limb, and SALL4 in limb and heart development, act at
developmental enhancers, but no well-validated composite element carrying a named SALL site is
established in the way that exists for, say, GATA or ETS composites.

## Biology and disease

Heterozygous truncating SALL1 mutations cause Townes-Brocks syndrome (imperforate anus, thumb
malformations, dysplastic ears and hearing loss, with variable renal and cardiac involvement) [PMID:9425907,20301618].
Heterozygous SALL4 mutations cause Okihiro (Duane-radial ray) syndrome [PMID:12393809], which overlaps the
radial-ray phenotype of Holt-Oram syndrome and includes Duane anomaly. The SALL4 phenotype is
mechanistically informative in two directions. First, the Okihiro missense mutations that fall inside
the C-terminal fingers reduce overall DNA binding without abolishing the AT preference and shift the
protein's association with AT-rich genomic sites, which supports their pathogenicity [PMID:36635047]. Second, SALL4
is a thalidomide-dependent cereblon neosubstrate: thalidomide and its analogs recruit SALL4 to
cereblon for degradation, and this provides a molecular explanation for thalidomide limb
teratogenicity, since chemical SALL4 loss phenocopies genetic SALL4 loss [PMID:30190590,30067223]. A crystal structure of the
SALL4-pomalidomide-cereblon-DDB1 complex shows how the degron is presented [PMID:32251415].

## Reading a hit

There is little to read. This family specifies base composition rather than a word, so a PWM hit is
close to meaningless on its own: an AT-rich match is expected anywhere in AT-rich DNA, and the same
matrices score homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A sequence. The four paralogues are not separable, and
in these databases only SALL1, SALL3 and SALL4 have models at all. The specific trap is the opposite
of the usual one: if your hit came from the GC-rich GGGTGGGG matrices labelled SALL1 or SALL4, you
have almost certainly matched a GC-box-like sequence, and a KLF, SP or other GC-box factor is the
more likely direct binder; those two models are ChIP-only and disagree with every in vitro
measurement of SALL4 specificity. A credible SALL4 claim rests on AT-rich domain-level enrichment,
on the effect of degrading or mutating the ZFC4 cluster, or on the clinical genetics, not on a motif
match.
families.caveats: SALL proteins read base composition, not a word: a C-terminal finger pair in SALL4 binds AT-rich DNA promiscuously, and the crystal structure shows the contacts accept many A/T combinations. We give no consensus for that reason, and an AT-rich hit is expected throughout AT-rich DNA and overlaps homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A signals. The paralogues are indistinguishable, and SALL2 has no model here. Worse, the family's medoid and data consensus come from ChIP-only SALL1 and SALL4 matrices that are GC-rich (GGGTGGGG, a GC-box/KLF-like sequence) and contradict every in vitro measurement; cohesion is 0.51. Matches to those two models are most likely GC-box factors, not SALL.

timeline.methods: Positional cloning and mutation screening in families

timeline.finding: SALL4 mutations are shown to cause Okihiro (Duane-radial ray) syndrome, whose radial-ray limb phenotype overlaps that of thalidomide embryopathy.
timeline.methods: Linkage analysis and mutation screening in families
timeline.open: The resemblance to thalidomide embryopathy had no mechanistic explanation.

timeline.finding: Mouse mutants show Sall1, Sall2 and Sall4 are each required for neural tube closure, establishing partially overlapping developmental requirements across the family.
timeline.methods: Single and compound mouse mutants with embryo phenotyping

timeline.finding: Two groups identify SALL4 as a thalidomide-dependent cereblon neosubstrate, so the drug degrades the protein whose mutation causes the overlapping limb syndrome; chemical loss phenocopies genetic loss.
timeline.methods: Quantitative proteomics of drug-treated cells, CRBN binding and ubiquitination assays, zebrafish and chicken limb models

timeline.finding: A crystal structure of the SALL4-pomalidomide-cereblon-DDB1 complex shows how a SALL4 zinc finger is presented as a drug-induced degron, explaining the species and analog specificity of the effect.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography

timeline.finding: SALL4 is recovered in a screen for proteins that read AT-rich motifs: a single C-terminal pair of zinc fingers accounts for genome occupancy, inactivating it reproduces the null phenotype, and genes are de-repressed in proportion to their AT content, so the protein reads base composition rather than a word; a parallel study defines an AT-rich consensus by protein-binding microarray and CUT&RUN.
timeline.methods: Proteomic screen with AT-rich baits, mutant mouse and ESC genetics, genome-wide occupancy; protein-binding microarray and CUT&RUN
timeline.open: Whether the AT-rich consensus derived in vitro adds anything beyond composition was not resolved.

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the SALL4 C-terminal zinc fingers on AT-rich DNA shows recognition through small hydrophobic and polar side chains in the major groove, which explains why many A/T combinations are accepted, and Okihiro missense mutations in these fingers reduce binding without changing the AT preference.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography with binding assays and genomic occupancy of mutants

timeline.finding: The N-terminal NuRD-interacting motif is shown to be required for SALL4's contribution to reprogramming, tying the family's repressive output to a recruited complex rather than to its own binding site.
timeline.methods: Reprogramming assays with interaction-deficient mutants, complex purification

open: Whether SALL4 recognizes anything more specific than base composition is unsettled: protein-binding microarray and CUT&RUN data are reported as an AT-rich consensus, while the structural and genomic work describes flexible recognition of many A/T combinations over long domains, and the two readings differ on whether a position weight matrix is meaningful here at all.

The GC-rich GGGTGGGG models labeled SALL1 and SALL4 in HOCOMOCO contradict every in vitro measurement of SALL4 specificity; whether they capture an unrecognized GC-box-like binding mode or simply promoter co-occupancy in ChIP has not been tested directly.
Whether SALL1, SALL2 and SALL3 share SALL4's AT preference is unknown: only SALL3 has an in vitro-supported model in these databases, and it is not close to any other family member's motif.

Whether degradation of SALL4 alone accounts for thalidomide limb teratogenicity remains open, since other cereblon neosubstrates have been proposed to contribute and the drug degrades many zinc-finger proteins.

families.name: RREB1
families.def: RAS-responsive element, GC-rich. RREB1.
families.short: RREB1 is a large C2H2 zinc-finger protein, originally identified as the factor binding the RAS-responsive element of the human calcitonin promoter in medullary thyroid carcinoma cells. It has around fifteen fingers and prefers a long C-rich word, CCCCAAACCACCCC, reported when the protein was cloned and reproduced by the database matrices. It is a downstream effector of RAS and TGF-beta signalling: in the TGF-beta pathway RREB1 partners with SMAD complexes to direct fibrogenic and developmental epithelial-mesenchymal transitions, and it has been implicated in metastatic enhancer priming. The motif's length is its main virtue and its main problem, since much of it is a C-run that overlaps several other GC-rich promoter families, and a fragment of the protein has been reported to bind an unrelated sequence instead.
families.long:
## The factors

RREB1 is a single gene, with no paralogue in the human genome that shares its specificity, and this family therefore has one member and three closely agreeing matrices. The protein is large and carries a long array of C2H2 zinc fingers, on the order of fifteen, which is consistent with the long element the databases recover; as with other very large finger arrays, it is unlikely that all fingers contact DNA in a single binding event. It has appeared under several names: RREB-1, from the RAS-responsive element of the calcitonin promoter [PMID:8816445]; Finb, from work on a Raf-responsive zinc-finger protein that binds divergent sequences [PMID:10390538]; and zinc finger protein 368. Multiple splice variants exist and have been catalogued in urologic cancers [PMID:21703425]. RREB1 is broadly expressed and is not a dedicated tissue-restricted factor.

## The motif

The consensus CCCCAAACCACCCC was reported in the paper that cloned RREB-1 as the protein binding the distal RAS-responsive element of the human calcitonin promoter [PMID:8816445], and the database matrices reproduce it. They are not independent of that report: JASPAR lists its RREB1 matrix, MA0073.2, as SELEX data from the same paper, the CIS-BP M02665 matrix is effectively identical to it (pairwise similarity 0.998 in this collection), and the Vierstra archetype AC0602 is a slightly shortened version. The full 19-base form CCCCAAACCACCCCCCCCC is C-rich throughout with a short internal A-tract, and the information is carried mainly by the CCCCAAACCA portion; the 3' C-run is low in information and will match almost any C-rich stretch. There is no half-site, no spacing rule and no dimerization requirement described. The one conflicting result came from a four-finger RREB1 fragment (LZ321), which bound a GGTCCT-containing tramtrack site and the calcitonin element with similar affinity but did not bind a consensus RREB1 site [PMID:10390538]; the secretin promoter study described potentiation of BETA2/NeuroD rather than a new consensus [PMID:12482979]. The literature and data consensuses therefore agree; what is unsettled is whether the protein, through other parts of its long finger array, also reads unrelated sequences.

Several families in this atlas read C-rich promoter words, and they are easy to confuse. ZNF281/ZNF148 (ZBP-89) read CCCCACCCC; ZBTB7A/B/C read GACCCCCCCC; SP/KLF-type GC boxes are GGGGCGGGGC, that is G-rich on the same strand where RREB1 is C-rich plus CpG-containing; ZBTB17/MIZ1 reads core-promoter GC-rich sites. The RREB1 word's distinguishing feature is the internal AAA: CCCCAAACCACCCC has a purine interruption in the middle of the C-run that GC boxes and ZBTB7 sites lack, and it contains no CpG dinucleotide, which sets it apart from the CpG-island-associated GC-rich families. A hit with no internal A-tract is more likely one of the neighbouring families.

## Where it acts

There is less genomic mapping for RREB1 than for most families of comparable size, and no ChIP-derived matrix appears in HOCOMOCO for it at all, which is itself informative. The characterized sites are promoter-proximal: the calcitonin promoter RAS-responsive element, the secretin promoter, and the SLC39A1/hZIP1 zinc-transporter promoter, where RREB1 overexpression down-regulates the gene in prostate cancer [PMID:19802870,21360563]. In the TGF-beta pathway the interesting occupancy is enhancer-associated and combinatorial: RREB1 and SMAD complexes act together at enhancers controlling SNAI1 and other EMT effectors [PMID:31915377], and RREB1 has been placed in the mechanism by which TGF-beta and RAS jointly unmask primed enhancers to drive metastasis [PMID:39243762]. So the motif can be expected both at C-rich proximal promoters and at signal-dependent enhancers, and in the latter case the relevant unit is a composite RREB1-SMAD arrangement rather than an isolated RREB1 site.

## Biology and disease

RREB1 was found through a differentiation response to RAS in human medullary thyroid carcinoma [PMID:8816445]. Its best-supported function now is as a RAS effector within TGF-beta signalling: it directs the choice between fibrogenic and developmental EMT programs [PMID:31915377], and in mouse models contributes to enhancer priming for metastasis [PMID:39243762]. Independent lines of work report RREB1 repressing the zinc transporter hZIP1 in prostate cancer, altering p16 expression and proliferation in gastric cancer [PMID:34666611], and being subject to splice-variant changes in urologic tumours. The RREB1 locus is also recurrently altered in melanoma, and copy-number gain at RREB1 is used diagnostically in melanocytic-lesion FISH panels [PMID:36325821], which is one of the more concrete clinical connections. Common variants in and near RREB1 appear in genome-wide association studies of type 2 diabetes and birth weight [PMID:32210733]. No Mendelian RREB1 disorder is established.

## Reading a hit

Treat the long C-rich word as a family-level signal at best. The 5' CCCCAAACCA segment carries the discriminating information; the 3' C-run does not, so check that your match covers the informative half rather than sliding along a homopolymeric C stretch. A hit without the internal A-tract is probably a GC box or a ZNF281/ZBTB7-type site. There is no paralogue problem, but there is a provenance problem: the JASPAR and CIS-BP matrices are near-duplicates and JASPAR attributes its matrix to the 1996 cloning paper's SELEX data, so agreement between them is not independent confirmation, and there is no ChIP-derived matrix to check against. For signalling questions, look for a nearby SMAD-binding element, because the functionally demonstrated RREB1 activity in TGF-beta responses is composite. A single promoter-proximal hit does not license the conclusion that a gene is RAS- or TGF-beta-responsive.
families.caveats: The consensus is the one reported when RREB-1 was cloned, and the matrices reproduce it, but the support is narrower than three matrices suggest: JASPAR attributes its matrix to that paper's SELEX data and the CIS-BP matrix is a near-duplicate, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and no ChIP-derived matrix is available to cross-check. A later study of a four-finger fragment found binding to an unrelated GGTCCT site and none to the consensus. The word is long but much of its length is a low-information C-run that will match many GC-rich promoters, overlapping the ZNF281, ZBTB7, ZBTB17 and SP/KLF families; only the CCCCAAACCA portion discriminates. Functionally demonstrated activity in TGF-beta signalling is composite with SMAD, not standalone.

timeline.finding: RREB-1 is cloned by affinity screening as the protein binding the distal RAS-responsive element of the human calcitonin promoter in medullary thyroid carcinoma cells; its reported consensus is CCCCAAACCACCCC, and overexpression increases RAS- and RAF-induced transactivation of the calcitonin promoter.
timeline.methods: Affinity screening of an expression library, binding-site analysis, reporter assays
timeline.open: How a single factor with a long finger array selects sites genome-wide was untested.

timeline.finding: A liver cDNA isolated on a Drosophila tramtrack site, GGTCCT, turns out to encode RREB1; the protein binds that site and the calcitonin RRE with similar affinity (Kd 50-60 nM) yet does not bind a consensus RREB1 site, and only the two C-terminal fingers of the fragment are needed, so RREB1 is reported to read divergent sequences.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning, gel-shift binding with multiple ligands, finger deletion, enhancer reporter assays
timeline.open: The relationship between the published consensus and the divergent sites was left unexplained.

timeline.finding: On the secretin promoter, Finb/RREB-1 has no intrinsic activation domain and does not activate alone; it requires both DNA binding and physical interaction with BETA2/NeuroD to potentiate transcription, which places it between classical activators and coactivators.
timeline.methods: Promoter mutagenesis, expression cloning, protein interaction and reporter assays

timeline.finding: RREB-1 is shown to bind a site in the hZIP1 (SLC39A1) promoter region and to repress the zinc transporter in prostate cancer cells, with follow-up work linking its overexpression to the loss of zinc accumulation in prostate tumors.
timeline.methods: Luciferase reporters, site-directed mutagenesis, gel shift, ChIP

timeline.finding: RREB1 is identified as the RAS effector that partners TGF-beta-activated SMAD factors in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition: MAPK-activated RREB1 recruits SMADs to SNAI1, and chromatin accessibility then decides whether the resulting program is fibrogenic or developmental.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide binding and expression analysis, proteomics, carcinoma cells and mouse epiblast progenitors
timeline.open: What marks the enhancers that RREB1 can use was not yet defined.

timeline.finding: The chromatin basis is worked out: RREB1 localizes to H4K16ac/K20ac-marked, H2A.Z-loaded nucleosomes at enhancers of IL11, PDGFB, HAS2 and SNAI1, priming them for activation by a SMAD4-INO80 remodeling complex on TGF-beta input, which assembles a metastasis program in lung adenocarcinoma.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, histone mark and nucleosome profiling, mouse metastasis models

open: Whether RREB1 has one binding specificity is unsettled: the 1996 cloning paper reported the consensus CCCCAAACCACCCC that the in vitro matrices now reproduce, while a 1999 study found that a four-finger fragment of the protein bound a dissimilar GGTCCT-containing site and the calcitonin element with comparable affinity but did not bind a consensus RREB1 site at all.

Which of the roughly fifteen fingers contact DNA is unknown: a fragment containing four fingers bound two unrelated ligands through its two C-terminal fingers, so the long array may provide alternative reading heads rather than one continuous interface, which would explain the reported sequence promiscuity.

Where RREB1 binds genome-wide is poorly documented for a factor of this prominence: no ChIP-derived matrix exists in HOCOMOCO, and the three available matrices are near-duplicate in vitro products, so it is not known how much endogenous occupancy falls on the C-rich word versus on composite RREB1-SMAD enhancers.

Whether RREB1 acts as an activator, a repressor or a potentiator is context-dependent in a way that is not understood: it potentiates BETA2/NeuroD without an intrinsic activation domain, represses hZIP1, and with SMAD4 activates EMT and fibrogenic genes.

families.name: MYT1 / ST18 (CCHC zinc finger)
families.def: AAAGTTT core neural repressor sites. MYT1, MYT1L, ST18.
families.short: MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 are the three human members of the MYT/NZF family, which uses an unusual non-classical zinc finger (described as C2HC or CCHHC, not the C2H2 fold of most zinc-finger transcription factors) arranged in two widely separated clusters of fingers. Each cluster binds DNA independently and recognizes the same short AT-rich element, reported as AAAGTTT, and affinity rises sharply when two copies are present, so the functional element is effectively bipartite. The family matters most in neurons: MYT1L is one of the three factors that convert fibroblasts to induced neurons, where it works by repressing non-neuronal programs. MYT1L haploinsufficiency causes a human neurodevelopmental syndrome with obesity. The available motif models for this family are weak.
families.long:
## The factors

MYT1 was cloned in 1992 by its binding to cis-regulatory elements of the myelin proteolipid protein
gene and named myelin transcription factor I [PMID:1280325]. Its zinc fingers do not belong to the classical C2H2
class: the original description assigned them a Cys-X5-Cys-X12-His-X4-Cys arrangement (C2HC) [PMID:1280325], while
later structural work on the same domain in this family describes it as a non-classical CCHHC-type
finger [PMID:24820620], and both names appear in the literature. MYT1 has six such fingers arranged in two widely
separated clusters. Critically, each cluster binds DNA independently and recognizes the same
sequence, which led to the proposal that one protein can bridge a proximal and a distal site in the
same promoter [PMID:1280325].

Humans have three members: MYT1 (also MyT1, NZF-2, PLPB1), MYT1L (MYT2) and ST18 (MYT3). ST18 was
cloned as the third member of the neural zinc finger factor family, NZF-3; unlike MyT1 and NZF-1,
which activate transcription in reporter assays, NZF-3 represses [PMID:9478997]. Expression across mouse nervous
system development is broadly overlapping but not identical among the three [PMID:24214099]. MYT1 and MYT1L are the
neural members in practice [PMID:8530187,24214099]; MYT1 and ST18 are additionally expressed in pancreatic islet beta cells [PMID:32359405].
Only MYT1 and MYT1L have motif models in the databases behind this family; ST18 is assigned here on
domain grounds.

## The motif

The consensus reported for these proteins is AAAGTTT, and the key measurement is that a single copy
binds, but a bipartite element containing two copies of the consensus is bound with markedly higher
relative affinity [PMID:9478997]. That is the expected behavior for a protein with two independent finger clusters
of identical specificity, and it means the real recognition unit is a pair of short AT-rich cores
rather than one longer site. Recognition chemistry has been examined for the NZF-1 finger domain,
where hydrogen bonding contributes to base discrimination [PMID:24820620].

The motifs actually available are thin. HOCOMOCO's MYT1 model, the only one in this family with an A
grade, has the consensus AAACTTTTBNAAA and rests on two in vitro assays, HT-SELEX and GHT-SELEX; its MYT1L
model is ChIP-only at grade C with the consensus AAAGTT; and the CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is not
measured on a human protein at all but inherited from a Caenorhabditis elegans relative at 79%
DNA-binding-domain identity. The data consensus for the family, AAAGTT, therefore reflects six
weakly informative positions, one of them from a nematode. A six- or seven-base AT-rich core carries
roughly the same information as a TATA box, which sets a hard ceiling on what any MYT PWM can
resolve.

## Where it acts

MYT1L occupancy, mapped during fibroblast-to-neuron reprogramming, is unusual in two ways: the
binding sites are largely the same in neurons and in fibroblasts, and they are preferentially in
already-open chromatin [PMID:28379941]. In other words this factor is not selecting sites by cell-type-specific
accessibility; its targets are distributed across the somatic lineage programs it represses. Sites
are found at promoters and in accessible regulatory regions of genes belonging to non-neuronal
lineages, including several components of Notch signaling such as Hes1 [PMID:28379941]. Because the core is short and
AT-rich, matches are dense in AT-rich intergenic and intronic DNA and overlap in scoring space with
other AT-preferring models, including homeodomain and forkhead sites and poly-A tracts.

## Biology and disease

MYT1L is one of the three transcription factors, with ASCL1 and POU3F2/BRN2, that convert mouse
fibroblasts into functional induced neurons [PMID:20107439], and it is dispensable for the initial steps but
important for the quality and stability of the resulting neurons [PMID:24243019]. Its mechanism is repressive: MYT1L
directly represses many different somatic lineage programs while sparing the neuronal program, and it
does so by recruiting a SIN3B-containing complex through an N-terminal domain [PMID:28379941]. That makes it a
counterexample to the assumption that developmental repressors are lineage-specific.

In humans, heterozygous MYT1L deletions and truncating variants (2p25.3) cause MYT1L syndrome:
intellectual disability, autistic features and obesity [PMID:25232846,32065501]. Mouse models reproduce the behavioral and
metabolic phenotype, including obesity [PMID:35538503,34614421], and human neuron models show maturation defects, some of
which have been reversed pharmacologically in these systems [PMID:36782060]. On the metabolic side, the Myt factors
act together in beta cells, where their combined loss allows over-activation of stress-response genes
and impairs postnatal beta-cell proliferation and function [PMID:32359405]. ST18 has been studied mainly outside the
nervous system, as a candidate tumor suppressor and in beta-cell function [PMID:15489893].

## Reading a hit

Be conservative. The motif is a short AT-rich core, so matches are common by chance and cannot be
distinguished from other AT-preferring factors on sequence alone; a single AAAGTTT is weak evidence
even in an otherwise plausible context. A tandem pair of cores in one element is a better signal,
because affinity for the bipartite arrangement is substantially higher. A hit does not identify the
paralogue: MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 share one specificity and the databases cannot separate them, and
ST18 has no measured human matrix here at all. Two provenance problems are worth stating plainly:
the CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is a cross-species transfer from a C. elegans protein, and the HOCOMOCO
MYT1L model is ChIP-only at the lowest quality grade. Given that MYT1L's binding sites are mostly in
pre-existing open chromatin and that its repressive function works through a recruited SIN3B complex,
a MYT1L ChIP peak without a motif is a normal observation rather than an anomaly, and a motif hit
without accessibility is not worth much.
families.caveats: The evidence base is weak for a whole family. The recognition unit is a six- to seven-base AT-rich core, which occurs constantly by chance and overlaps homeodomain, forkhead and poly-A signals; only a tandem pair of cores is a meaningfully specific element. MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 cannot be separated by sequence, and ST18 has no human matrix here. The CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is transferred from a Caenorhabditis elegans protein at 79% DNA-binding-domain identity, and the HOCOMOCO MYT1L model is ChIP-only at grade C; only the MYT1 model has in vitro support. Since MYT1L binds mostly in already-open chromatin and represses via a recruited SIN3B complex, peaks without motifs are expected.

timeline.finding: MyTI is cloned by binding to the myelin proteolipid protein gene; its six fingers use a Cys-X5-Cys-X12-His-X4-Cys arrangement unlike C2H2 or C2C2 fingers, and the two separated finger clusters bind DNA independently and read the same sequence.
timeline.methods: Expression screening with DNA probes, EMSA with zinc chelation, sequence and secondary-structure analysis
timeline.open: The recognized sequence was defined only within the PLP regulatory elements, and no structure of the finger existed.

timeline.finding: The third family member, NZF-3/ST18, is cloned and shown to bind a single AAAGTTT copy but with markedly higher relative affinity to a bipartite element with two copies, and to repress rather than activate reporters, so the family contains both signs of output on one consensus.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, EMSA on single and bipartite elements, cotransfection reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether the bipartite preference reflects one protein using both clusters or two proteins binding adjacent sites.

timeline.finding: MYT1L is identified as one of three factors (with ASCL1 and POU3F2/BRN2) that convert mouse fibroblasts directly into functional neurons, which moved the family from myelin-gene regulation to cell-fate control.
timeline.methods: Combinatorial factor screening with electrophysiology on induced neurons
timeline.open: What MYT1L contributes mechanistically to reprogramming was not known.

timeline.finding: In the reprogramming hierarchy ASCL1 acts first as the on-target pioneer factor, with MYT1L dispensable for initiating conversion but required for the quality and maturation of the induced neurons.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq of reprogramming factors, chromatin accessibility, staged reprogramming experiments

timeline.finding: Biophysical analysis of the NZF-1 finger domain characterizes the non-classical CCHHC finger and the hydrogen bonds that contribute to base discrimination, giving the family's recognition chemistry its first direct treatment.
timeline.methods: Peptide binding studies with mutational and spectroscopic analysis
timeline.open: No structure of a MYT finger cluster bound to DNA has been reported.

timeline.finding: Mapping of 2p25.3 deletions in patients narrows the critical interval to MYT1L and links haploinsufficiency to intellectual disability with obesity, establishing the human phenotype.
timeline.methods: Array-based deletion mapping and clinical phenotyping of a patient series

timeline.finding: MYT1L is shown to work as a repressor of many different non-neuronal lineage programs at once, acting through a recruited SIN3B complex, and to bind largely the same, already-accessible sites in fibroblasts and neurons, which overturns the expectation that a cell-fate factor selects cell-type-specific sites.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq in fibroblasts and neurons, transcriptomics, domain mapping and complex purification
timeline.open: Why occupancy is so similar between cell types while the transcriptional effect is not.

timeline.finding: Mouse Myt1l haploinsufficiency reproduces the human phenotype, including obesity and behavioral alterations, and human neuron models show maturation defects that can be reversed genetically and pharmacologically in those systems.
timeline.methods: Mouse behavioral and metabolic phenotyping, human iPSC-derived neuron models with drug treatment

open: Whether the functional unit is one AAAGTTT core or a pair is unresolved: the bipartite element is bound with much higher affinity in vitro, but no genome-wide analysis has shown that occupied regions carry two correctly spaced cores.
No structure of a MYT finger cluster on DNA exists, so which bases the CCHHC fingers contact, and why the preference is this short and AT-rich, are inferred rather than observed.

Whether MYT1, MYT1L and ST18 differ at all in sequence preference is untested; ST18 has no measured human matrix in these databases, and the only CIS-BP human MYT1L motif is transferred from a Caenorhabditis elegans protein.

How MYT1L represses only non-neuronal programs while occupying nearly the same sites in fibroblasts and neurons is unexplained, and it is not known whether the selectivity comes from partner availability, from the SIN3B complex, or from the chromatin state of the target genes.

families.name: Other bZIP
families.def: bZIP factors not covered above, e.g. CREBZF, CREBL2, and unclassified bZIP archetypes.
families.short: This is not a family. It is the residual bucket in which bZIP motifs land when they do not belong to any of the defined bZIP families, and in the current data it holds exactly two entries, both from CIS-BP: a cyclic-AMP-response-element-like matrix labelled CREBL2 that was inherited from a Drosophila protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity, and a short, low-information ACGT-core matrix labelled CREBZF (Zhangfei/SMILE) taken from the mouse ortholog. The two do not resemble each other, and each is closer to a member of another family than to its bucket-mate. Read a hit here as unassigned rather than as a shared motif, and read the underlying proteins as bZIPs that act largely by partnering with, and destabilizing, other bZIPs rather than through a well-mapped element of their own.
families.long:
## The factors

Only two proteins have a motif model in this bucket. CREBZF, also called Zhangfei or SMILE, is a bZIP whose documented mode of action is not sequence-specific activation but interference with other bZIPs. It suppresses CREB3 (Luman) and CREB3L3 (CREBH), both ER-stress transducers in the ATF6/CREB3 family, and it binds XBP1s through its leucine zipper and triggers its proteasomal degradation, reducing induction of unfolded-protein-response genes [PMID:24155933]. Depleting CREBZF has the opposite effect, raising UPR transcript and protein levels [PMID:24155933]. CREBL2 was cloned as a transcript from the chromosome 12p13 interval between ETV6 and CDKN1B, a region recurrently deleted in leukemia [PMID:9693048], and has since been reported to interact with CREB1 and to promote adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells [PMID:21728997], and to influence metabolism in muscle and liver [PMID:31882710]. Neither protein has an established DNA-binding specificity determined on the human protein. For scale: the human bZIP class has on the order of fifty to sixty members [PMID:12192032,29425488], and the named families in this atlas account for nearly all of the ones with motif models. Several human bZIPs have no model at all in JASPAR 2024, HOCOMOCO v14, CIS-BP or the Vierstra archetypes - ATF5 and NFE2L3 (NRF3) among them - and so appear in no family, including this one.

## The motif

There is no consensus for this bucket and none should be quoted. The two entries are as follows. CIS-BP M03649, labelled CREBL2, reads GTGACGTCAT - a cyclic-AMP response element. Its provenance record marks it as inferred from a Drosophila melanogaster protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497], and the family data notes that it resembles the CREB/ATF family. CIS-BP M01813, labelled CREBZF, reads AAACGTAK, a short motif carrying 10.8 bits in total, determined on the mouse ortholog, whose DNA-binding domain is 100 percent identical to the human one. The internal cohesion of the pair is 0.60, the lowest of the eight bZIP groups in this atlas, and for each entry the nearest neighbour across all four source databases lies in a different family. In other words the bucket fails the definition of a family used here - a set of motifs it is reasonable to believe are the same motif - and it fails it by design. Averaging these two matrices, or scanning with a single representative for the group, would mix a CRE with an unrelated short ACGT core.

## Where it acts

Not established, for either protein, in the sense that matters for a motif atlas: there is no published genome-wide occupancy map tied to a validated element for CREBZF or CREBL2 in human cells. Scanning with the CREBL2 matrix will return the same promoter-proximal, CpG-island-associated sites that a CREB1 or ATF7 matrix returns, because it is a CRE; that reflects the borrowed Drosophila specificity rather than measured CREBL2 occupancy. The CREBZF matrix is short and will match very frequently, and its hits should not be treated as CREBZF binding sites. Where CREBZF does act functionally is at unfolded-protein-response genes, but as a partner and destabilizer of XBP1s and of CREB3-family activators [PMID:24155933], so its effect appears at their elements rather than at one of its own.

## Biology and disease

CREBZF behaves as a brake on the unfolded protein response. It reduces induction of UPR genes after thapsigargin treatment, an effect that depends on its leucine zipper and on degradation of XBP1s, and knocking it down in primary sensory neurons increases UPR gene expression [PMID:24155933]. Mouse and cell work has since linked CREBZF to hepatic lipogenesis and steatosis in diet-induced insulin resistance, where it represses Insig-2a in association with ATF4 [PMID:29637572], to adipose-tissue macrophage inflammation that promotes insulin resistance [PMID:38286660], and to repression of adipose browning, with glucose stabilizing the protein through reversible acetylation [PMID:38588421]. CREBL2 has no disease attributed to the gene itself; the 12p13 region in which it sits is deleted in leukemia, but the deletions are not mapped to CREBL2, and the functional literature is small: CREBL2 promotes adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells [PMID:21728997], restrains glycolysis and triglyceride synthesis in muscle and liver cells [PMID:31882710], and mediates the effect of miR-195-5p on Schwann cell proliferation and migration after nerve injury [PMID:37469605]. Neither protein has a knockout phenotype that is routinely cited as defining a cis-element.

## Reading a hit

Do not report a match here as a match to a motif. If a scan returns M03649 (CREBL2), read it as a cyclic-AMP response element and report it to the CREB/ATF family, with the caveat that the matrix is a cross-species transfer from an insect protein at 64 percent domain identity and is not evidence about human CREBL2. If it returns M01813 (CREBZF), the match carries little information and no established in vivo target; it does not license the conclusion that CREBZF binds that sequence in human cells. More generally, a residual bucket exists in a motif ontology so that the well-supported families are not diluted by unresolved single cases, and its contents should be read as unassigned rather than as shared biology. If the question is which bZIP is bound at your site, the informative version of that question is which of the named families - AP-1, CREB/ATF, ATF6/CREB3, C/EBP, MAF, NFE2/BACH or PAR bZIP - the sequence best matches, and whether the flanks let you tell them apart at all.
families.caveats: Treat this as an administrative category, not a biological one. It holds two CIS-BP matrices whose internal similarity is the lowest of any bZIP group here (cohesion 0.60), and both are cross-species transfers: the CREBL2 model comes from a Drosophila protein at 64 percent DNA-binding-domain identity and is simply a CRE, and the CREBZF model comes from mouse and carries little information. Neither protein has a validated human element. A hit in this bucket should be re-reported to whichever named family the sequence actually matches, or left unassigned. Do not build a consensus, a logo or a representative matrix for the group, and do not infer that CREBZF and CREBL2 share a site.

timeline.finding: CREBL2 is cloned as a transcript from the chromosome 12p13 interval between ETV6 and CDKN1B, a region deleted in leukemia.
timeline.methods: Positional cloning, transcript mapping
timeline.open: No DNA-binding specificity or function was determined.

timeline.finding: CREBL2 interacts and co-localizes with CREB and promotes adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells in a CREB-dependent way, pointing to action through a partner rather than a site of its own.
timeline.methods: Overexpression and knockdown, protein interaction and co-localization, CREB activity assays
timeline.open: Whether CREBL2 binds DNA directly, alone or with CREB, was not tested.

timeline.finding: CREBZF (Zhangfei) suppresses induction of most unfolded-protein-response genes by binding XBP1s through its leucine zipper and causing its proteasomal degradation; knockdown in sensory neurons raises UPR gene expression.
timeline.methods: Overexpression and siRNA knockdown, protein interaction, reporter assays
timeline.open: No CREBZF-specific DNA element was identified.

timeline.finding: Large-scale specificity mapping shows that closely related DNA-binding domains almost always share sequence preferences, the basis on which CIS-BP infers motifs, including the CREBL2 matrix transferred from a Drosophila protein at 64% domain identity.
timeline.methods: Protein-binding microarrays across eukaryotes, DBD-identity inference
timeline.open: Whether the inference holds for CREBL2 specifically was not tested.

timeline.finding: Crebl2, the mammalian ortholog of Drosophila REPTOR-BP, mediates part of the transcriptional response to mTORC1 inhibition and restrains glycolysis and triglyceride synthesis in muscle and liver cells.
timeline.methods: Knockdown in C2C12 and Hepa1-6 cells, metabolic assays

timeline.finding: Glucose stabilizes CREBZF through CBP/p300-mediated Lys208 acetylation, reversed by HDAC3, and adipose-specific loss of CREBZF enhances browning and thermogenesis, with CREBZF repressing thermogenic genes together with PGC-1alpha.
timeline.methods: Adipose-specific knockout mice, acetylation mapping, human adipose expression

open: Whether CREBZF binds DNA in a sequence-specific way at all is unresolved: its documented actions are through heterodimerization with and destabilization of other bZIPs, and its only motif model, CIS-BP M01813 from the mouse protein, is a short, low-information ACGT-core matrix with no validated in vivo site.

Whether the CRE-like CREBL2 matrix describes human CREBL2 is untested: it is inferred from a Drosophila protein at 64% domain identity, no in vitro or ChIP-derived model exists for the human protein, and the functional work places CREBL2 as a partner of CREB rather than as an independent DNA-binding factor.

families.name: ZBTB17 (MIZ1)
families.def: Core-promoter GC-rich MIZ1 sites; MYC partner. ZBTB17.
families.short: ZBTB17, universally called MIZ1, is a BTB/POZ protein with an unusually long array of C2H2 zinc fingers that binds core-promoter regions around transcription start sites. On its own it activates genes including the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors CDKN2B (p15INK4b) and CDKN1A (p21); when MYC binds its C-terminal helix, the same sites are converted into repressed ones, which is the main route by which MYC turns genes off. MIZ1 is therefore best understood as a promoter-anchored platform rather than as a classical enhancer-binding factor. There is no reliable in vitro sequence model for MIZ1: the two available matrices are both ChIP-derived and mutually inconsistent, one resembling a WT1-type GC/GA-rich site and the other a homeodomain ATCGAT site.
families.long:
## The factors

ZBTB17/MIZ1 is a single-gene family. It encodes a roughly 800-residue protein with an N-terminal POZ/BTB domain and a long C-terminal array of a dozen or more C2H2 zinc fingers, plus a short amphipathic helix near the C terminus. It was isolated in a two-hybrid screen for MYC-interacting proteins and named Myc-interacting zinc finger protein 1 [PMID:9312026]. The MYC interaction is the defining feature: it requires the helix-loop-helix region of MYC and the C-terminal helix of MIZ1, and it converts MIZ1 from an activator into a component of a repressive complex [PMID:9312026], in part by recruiting DNA methyltransferases and other corepressors and in part through the POZ domain, whose integrity is required for MYC to override MIZ1 [PMID:9312026]. MIZ1 binds DNA as a POZ-mediated oligomer and is broadly expressed. Beyond MYC it partners with the related MYCN and with TGF-beta-driven SMAD complexes; MIZ1 without MYC has a growth-arrest function [PMID:9312026,11283613].

## The motif

This entry has to be honest about a gap. The original characterization localized MIZ1 binding to the initiator regions of the adenovirus major late promoter and the cyclin D1 promoter [PMID:9312026] - that is, to sequence at and immediately around the transcription start site - and subsequent genome-wide work has consistently placed MIZ1 at core promoters. Core promoters are defined more by composition and position than by a compact recognizable word, and no position weight matrix in the surveyed collections has been derived from an in vitro binding experiment with MIZ1. The family contains exactly two matrices and they do not agree; measured cohesion is 0.11, the lowest value in this part of the atlas, and both entries are flagged as inconsistent with their label. The HOCOMOCO model ZBT17.H14CORE.0.P.B reads GTGGGGGAGGGG. It carries evidence code P (ChIP-seq only) at grade B, and its nearest cross-database neighbors sit in the WT1 family [PMID:37971293], which is to say it looks like a generic G-rich/GA-rich promoter element rather than something specific. The JASPAR model MA2102.1 reads AATCGATT. It is ChIP-seq-derived from the GTRD collection [PMID:37962376], and its nearest neighbors are paired-class homeodomain motifs - ATCGAT is a recognizable CUX/homeodomain-type word. It does have one counterpart in the MIZ1 literature: an in vitro Bind-n-Seq experiment reported ATCGAT as the site bound by the MIZ1 zinc-finger domain and ATCGGTAATC as the site bound by the full-length protein, with a matching long motif recovered from MIZ1 ChIP-seq peaks that lie away from core promoters - a result that has not been reproduced elsewhere and that sits awkwardly with the core-promoter occupancy reported by everyone else [PMID:24983942]. Of the two, the G-rich HOCOMOCO model is the less implausible, because G-rich runs are common at the CpG-island core promoters where MIZ1 is found; but "less implausible" is not the same as validated, and a reader should not treat either matrix as MIZ1's intrinsic specificity. If you need to find candidate MIZ1 sites, the more defensible predictor is position - within a few dozen base pairs of an annotated start site in a CpG-island promoter - rather than either matrix.

## Where it acts

MIZ1 is a core-promoter factor. Its occupancy is concentrated in a narrow window around transcription start sites of CpG-island promoters, and the functional consequence of MIZ1 binding at a promoter depends on whether MYC is present at the same site. Documented MIZ1-bound promoters include CDKN2B (p15INK4b), CDKN1A (p21), CDKN2A, and, in the Schwann cell system, the H3K36me2 demethylase gene Kdm8 [PMID:11283613,29217679]. Genome-wide, MYC-dependent repression at high MYC levels maps preferentially to MIZ1-bound promoters, and the resulting repressed set is what distinguishes tumor-specific MYC expression profiles from the shared activated set [PMID:25043018]. MIZ1-dependent repression also couples the circadian clock to the cell cycle, with MYC/MIZ1 repressing clock genes [PMID:27339797].

## Biology and disease

Miz1-null mouse embryos die during gastrulation, so the gene is required early [PMID:14560010]. Conditional deletions give tissue-specific phenotypes, including a Schwann cell proliferation defect that leads to peripheral nerve demyelination [PMID:29217679]. The main biomedical interest is as the partner through which MYC represses transcription. MIZ1-mediated repression of CDKN2B is the mechanism by which MYC blocks the TGF-beta-induced cell-cycle arrest program [PMID:11283613], and TGF-beta signaling itself adjusts the balance between MYC, MIZ1 and SMAD proteins at that promoter [PMID:11283614]. Because MIZ1 is required for MYC-driven repression but not for MYC-driven activation, MIZ1 has been used experimentally to separate the two arms of MYC function in tumors, and MYC mutants unable to bind MIZ1 are impaired in transformation in several models [PMID:25043018,32071436]. MIZ1 is not itself a recurrently mutated cancer gene at appreciable frequency.

## Reading a hit

Treat any ZBTB17 motif hit as unreliable evidence about MIZ1. Both matrices are ChIP-derived with no in vitro backing, so they report where the factor was found under one set of conditions, not what it binds [PMID:37962376,37971293]; and the two disagree with each other so completely that at most one of them can be describing MIZ1. If you matched MA2102.1 (AATCGATT), the more likely explanation is that you found a CUX- or paired-homeodomain-type site, either co-bound in the original ChIP or captured as a passenger motif in the peak set. If you matched the HOCOMOCO G-rich model, you have found a G-rich promoter element that many C2H2 factors - WT1, SP/KLF, MAZ, ZBTB7 - could also read [PMID:32728250]. In neither case does the hit license the conclusion that MIZ1 binds there. The productive question for MIZ1 is positional and contextual: is the site a CpG-island core promoter, is the gene a cell-cycle inhibitor or clock gene, and is MYC bound at the same promoter? MIZ1 ChIP-seq with a validated antibody, or the pattern of MYC-dependent repression, is far more informative than sequence. Since ZBTB17 is a single gene, there is no paralogue problem here - the problem is that the motif itself is not established.
families.caveats: Do not trust either matrix. ZBTB17 has only two entries in the surveyed collections, both ChIP-derived with no in vitro support, and they are mutually incompatible: the HOCOMOCO model (evidence P, grade B) reads a G-rich GTGGGGGAGGGG that the cross-database analysis places with WT1, and JASPAR MA2102.1 reads AATCGATT, a homeodomain/CUX-type word with no basis in the MIZ1 literature. Family cohesion is 0.11. The literature instead describes MIZ1 as binding core-promoter and initiator regions, which no compact PWM captures well. Predict candidate MIZ1 sites from position in a CpG-island core promoter and from MYC co-occupancy, not from motif score.

timeline.finding: Miz-1 was cloned in a two-hybrid screen for MYC partners, shown to bind the initiator regions of the adenovirus major late and cyclin D1 promoters and to activate from them, and shown to be converted into a repressive complex when MYC binds it through its C-terminal helix.
timeline.methods: yeast two-hybrid, EMSA on promoter fragments, reporter assays, growth arrest assays
timeline.open: No compact consensus - binding was described by position at the start site rather than by a word.

timeline.finding: Two papers established the physiological consequence: MYC represses the CDK inhibitor p15INK4b by joining MIZ1 at the promoter initiator, and TGF-beta signaling relieves that repression while a SMAD complex contacts MIZ1 to activate the same promoter.
timeline.methods: chromatin immunoprecipitation, promoter reporters, MYC alleles defective in MIZ1 binding

timeline.finding: Miz1-null mouse embryos were shown to arrest before gastrulation and to die around embryonic day 7.5 with widespread ectodermal apoptosis, while p21 expression was unchanged and p57 was lost, showing the factor is essential and that its target set in vivo is narrower than reporter assays suggested.
timeline.methods: mouse gene targeting, embryo expression analysis

timeline.finding: An in vitro Bind-n-Seq experiment reported compact MIZ1 motifs for the first time - ATCGAT for the zinc-finger domain and ATCGGTAATC for the full-length protein - and recovered a matching motif in MIZ1 ChIP-seq peaks, which were mostly distal rather than promoter-proximal; this is the only sequence determination behind the JASPAR matrix and it has not been reproduced.
timeline.methods: Bind-n-Seq, competition EMSA with mutant probes, MEME-ChIP on two ChIP-seq datasets
timeline.open: Whether these motifs are MIZ1 sites or sequences shared with homeodomain proteins present in the same peak sets.

timeline.finding: Profiling of MYC gain and loss showed that the ratio of MYC to MIZ1 at a promoter predicts whether the gene is activated or repressed, and that the MIZ1-dependent repressed set is what makes tumor MYC profiles differ from the general amplification seen in normal cells.
timeline.methods: inducible MYC systems, ChIP-seq and expression profiling, mouse tumor models

timeline.finding: MYC/MIZ1 complexes were shown to repress the core clock genes BMAL1, CLOCK and NPAS2, so that high MYC dampens the circadian clock while promoting proliferation, with the inverse MYC-BMAL1 relationship confirmed across 102 human lymphomas.
timeline.methods: inducible expression in cell lines, ChIP, clock reporter assays, tumor cohort analysis

timeline.finding: Deletion of the Miz1 POZ domain in mouse Schwann cells was shown to derepress the H3K36me2 demethylase gene Kdm8, keeping cells in the cycle and causing a peripheral neuropathy - a direct target and a tissue phenotype for MIZ1 independent of MYC levels.
timeline.methods: conditional mouse alleles, RNA sequencing, chromatin and histone methylation analysis

timeline.finding: A review of MYC interactomes argued that much of MYC's activity is exerted on the transcription machinery rather than through specific target genes, which weakens the older picture of MIZ1-bound promoters as a discrete, sequence-defined repressed gene set.
timeline.methods: review of interactome, genomic and biochemical studies

open: Whether MIZ1 has a compact binding word at all is unresolved: the founding work and most occupancy studies describe binding by position at core-promoter initiators, while the single in vitro determination reports ATCGAT-type motifs enriched at distal rather than promoter-proximal peaks, and the two catalogued matrices agree with neither each other nor the literature, with family cohesion of 0.11.

It is unknown whether the G-rich HOCOMOCO model represents MIZ1 at all: G-rich runs are generic at CpG-island core promoters, the model's nearest cross-database neighbors are WT1 motifs, and no experiment has tested whether MIZ1 binds such a run in vitro.

How a protein with a dozen fingers that binds as a POZ-mediated oligomer engages DNA is unresolved, and this may be why no position weight matrix fits: there is no structure of the MIZ1 finger array on DNA, and nothing establishes how many fingers contact bases or whether several subunits bind adjacent sequence.

families.name: GTF3A (TFIIIA)
families.def: 5S rRNA internal control region. GTF3A.
families.short: GTF3A encodes TFIIIA, the transcription factor in which the C2H2 zinc finger was first recognized, and the protein that made the zinc finger a general concept. It is an RNA polymerase III factor with nine fingers that binds the internal control region of 5S ribosomal RNA genes, a roughly 50-base-pair sequence inside the transcribed region rather than upstream of it, and nucleates assembly of TFIIIC and TFIIIB. TFIIIA also binds 5S rRNA itself, storing it in the 7S ribonucleoprotein particle of amphibian oocytes. Because the functional element is a long internal sequence rather than a short word, the short motifs held in databases for this factor are abstractions and should be treated with caution.
families.long:
## The factors

TFIIIA, the product of the human GTF3A gene, is a single protein with no paralogue. Its DNA-binding region is a tandem array of nine C2H2 zinc fingers; the repeating zinc-binding unit was identified in this protein in the mid-1980s and gave the fold its name [PMID:4040853], so every other family in this atlas classed as C2H2 zinc finger traces its nomenclature here. The human gene was cloned in 1995 on the basis of homology to the long-studied Xenopus laevis protein [PMID:7789179]. TFIIIA is not a conventional gene-specific activator: it is a basal factor for one class of RNA polymerase III promoter, and its role is to bind DNA and then recruit TFIIIC, which in turn positions TFIIIB and polymerase III [PMID:41783558]. It works as a monomer, with no dimerization and no partner requirement at the DNA-binding step. It is broadly expressed, as 5S rRNA is needed by every cell. TFIIIA is also an RNA-binding protein: in Xenopus oocytes it sequesters 5S rRNA in the 7S particle, and its nuclear import depends on that dual capacity [PMID:3456603,15146977].

## The motif

The functional element is the internal control region (ICR) of the 5S rRNA gene, which lies inside the transcribed sequence rather than upstream of it, in the middle third of the roughly 120-base-pair Xenopus gene. Mutational analysis of the 5S promoter defined several separable blocks within it [PMID:2992947,3004969], and the crystal structure of the six N-terminal fingers bound to 31 base pairs of the gene explained why the element is so long [PMID:9501194]: the fingers are not wound continuously in the major groove. Some sit in the major groove, one crosses the minor groove, and the array spans the whole duplex, so six fingers cover a stretch that continuous major-groove binding would need far more fingers to reach [PMID:9501194]. The consequence for motif analysis is that TFIIIA does not have a conventional short consensus. The nine-base word CTCCCATCC held by CIS-BP and by the Vierstra archetype for this family is a database abstraction extracted from high-throughput data, not the element defined by 40 years of functional work, and the two databases agree with each other only because one is derived from the other. There is no half-site, no spacing rule, and no paralogue to confuse: this family has just two matrices and a single member.

## Where it acts

In the human genome the genuine targets are the 5S rRNA gene arrays, a tandem cluster on chromosome 1 plus dispersed 5S-derived pseudogenes, and the element sits within the gene body rather than in a promoter. Some tRNA-like and SINE-derived sequences contain ICR-like stretches, and RNA5SP141, a 5S pseudogene, is a functionally important TFIIIA product because its transcript is a RIG-I ligand [PMID:36399538]. This is not a motif that marks enhancers, CpG islands or cell-type-specific regulatory regions, and it has no known composite elements with other transcription factors; its partners are the polymerase III machinery, TFIIIC and TFIIIB. TFIIIA binding also has a chromatin consequence beyond transcription: bound TFIIIA blocks nucleotide excision repair within the 5S gene, so the footprint is a locally repair-refractory region [PMID:10064604].

## Biology and disease

The Xenopus 5S system was for decades the main model for developmental gene switching and for storage of a ribosomal RNA in a protein particle, and much of the classical literature is amphibian. Human genetics has caught up recently. Biallelic GTF3A mutations predispose to herpes simplex encephalitis by disrupting biogenesis of RNA5SP141, the host-derived RIG-I ligand needed for the innate antiviral response [PMID:36399538], which is a striking example of a basal polymerase III factor producing a narrow immunological phenotype. In zebrafish, the somatic paralogue gtf3aa is required for somatic 5S rRNA transcription and affects embryonic organ development [PMID:41783558]. There is no established cancer driver role. 5S rRNA supply itself feeds into the ribosomal-protein/p53 surveillance pathway [PMID:21957041], so severe loss of TFIIIA function is expected to be poorly tolerated.

## Reading a hit

Be sceptical. A match to CTCCCATCC is not useful evidence for TFIIIA occupancy, because the real element is a long internal control region and the short word is a low-information abstraction; the same nine bases occur in many GC/CT-rich promoters that belong to other families. The practical test is positional: TFIIIA acts inside 5S rRNA genes and 5S-derived sequences, so if the hit is not in one of those, it almost certainly does not mean TFIIIA. If you actually want to find 5S genes, sequence homology to the 5S rRNA gene is the right tool, not motif scanning. Neither of the two matrices in this family is backed by a published in vitro binding experiment for the human protein, and there is no ChIP-seq-derived matrix here at all, so the evidence base for the motif as a scanning model is thin and we say so rather than dressing it up.
families.caveats: This family should be read as a weak entry. Both matrices are short, low-information and mutually derived, and neither corresponds to the element that functional work defines, namely the roughly 50-base-pair internal control region inside the 5S rRNA gene. A CTCCCATCC match therefore carries almost no specific information about TFIIIA, and will often be better explained by one of the many CT/GC-rich promoter families. Positional context does almost all the work: TFIIIA binds within 5S rRNA genes and 5S-derived pseudogenes, so a hit elsewhere should not be attributed to it. There is no ChIP evidence in this family and no paralogue problem, only a mismatch between the biological element and the motif format.

timeline.finding: Sequence and metal analysis of Xenopus TFIIIA reveals nine repeated zinc-binding units of the Cys2-His2 type, defining the zinc finger and the fold that names the largest family of eukaryotic DNA-binding proteins. In the same year, point mutations and transversions across the 5S gene split its internal control region into a box A element, two spacers and a 3' block that carries the main TFIIIA binding domain, and show that the spacing between the blocks must be preserved.
timeline.methods: Protein sequence and metal analysis, oligonucleotide mutagenesis with in vitro transcription and complex formation assays
timeline.open: How nine fingers were arranged on a 50-base-pair internal element was unknown.

timeline.finding: Nuclease protection in the 7S particle maps the TFIIIA footprint on 5S rRNA to nucleotides 64-116 and notes two CCUGG helices also present in the binding site on the gene, suggesting the protein recognizes a shared structural feature in the gene and its product.
timeline.methods: Ribonuclease protection of the 7S ribonucleoprotein

timeline.finding: The human TFIIIA gene GTF3A is cloned by homology to the Xenopus protein: 423 amino acids with nine C2H2 fingers, 58% amino acid identity to the Xenopus factor, broadly expressed, mapped to 13q12.3-q13.1.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, northern analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the six N-terminal fingers on 31 base pairs of the 5S gene promoter shows the fingers placed differently along the duplex, some in the major groove and one crossing the minor groove, so TFIIIA reads several separated sequence blocks with fewer fingers than continuous major-groove winding would require; this is why the element has no short consensus.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography at 3.1 A

timeline.finding: Bound TFIIIA suppresses nucleotide excision repair of UV photoproducts across the internal control region in vitro, while repair proceeds normally just outside the footprint, showing that the binding site is a locally repair-refractory stretch.
timeline.methods: In vitro repair assays with Xenopus oocyte nuclear extracts on the TFIIIA-5S rDNA complex

timeline.finding: Compound heterozygous loss-of-function GTF3A mutations are found in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency and herpes simplex encephalitis; ChIP-seq identifies the 5S pseudogene RNA5SP141 as a TFIIIA target, and mutant cells fail to make this RIG-I ligand and to mount antiviral responses, giving a basal polymerase III factor a narrow immunological phenotype.
timeline.methods: Patient genetics, patient fibroblasts and gene-edited cells, ChIP-seq, infection assays

timeline.finding: Knockout of the zebrafish somatic paralogue gtf3aa suppresses somatic 5S rRNA transcription, reduces mature mono- and polyribosomes, and causes slow growth with impaired eye, heart, liver, swim bladder and intestinal development; the mutants die by seven days post-fertilization.
timeline.methods: Zebrafish knockout, expression profiling, ribosome profiling of larvae

open: What the two database matrices for this family represent is unclear: CTCCCATCC is a nine-base abstraction from high-throughput data with no published in vitro binding experiment for the human protein behind it, while the functionally defined element is a roughly 50-base-pair internal control region read by fingers spaced along both grooves.

Whether TFIIIA recognizes a shared structural feature in the 5S gene and the 5S rRNA, as the matching CCUGG helices in the two footprints suggested, or uses separable surfaces for DNA and RNA has not been settled structurally, since the crystal structure covers only six fingers on DNA.

How many TFIIIA targets exist beyond the 5S genes is open: ChIP-seq identified the pseudogene RNA5SP141 as a functionally important target, and whether other 5S-derived or SINE-derived loci are genuinely transcribed through TFIIIA is not established.

Why loss of a factor needed for all 5S rRNA synthesis produces a narrow phenotype in humans, susceptibility to herpes simplex encephalitis, while zebrafish gtf3aa mutants die as larvae with broad organ defects, is unexplained; the human mutations are hypomorphic, but how much 5S output is required has not been measured.

families.name: CAMTA
families.def: CGCG box bound by the calmodulin-binding CG-1 domain. CMTA1/CAMTA1, CAMTA2.
families.short: CAMTA1 and CAMTA2 (calmodulin-binding transcription activators) are the two human members of a family defined by the CG-1 domain, an N-terminal DNA-binding module unrelated to any other class, followed by a TIG domain, ankyrin repeats and calmodulin-binding IQ motifs. The IQ motifs make the family a direct link from calcium signaling to a DNA-binding domain. The element established for CG-1 is the plant CGCG box, (A/C/G)CGCG(G/T/C); site selection with mammalian CAMTA2 gave a related but distinct consensus, (T/C)GCANTGCG, which the human CAMTA2 motif model matches exactly, while the CAMTA1 model is short and low in information. CAMTA2 also acts as a coactivator recruited by NKX2-5. Loss of CAMTA1 causes ataxia in mice and congenital ataxia in humans, and a WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion drives epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
families.long:
## The factors

CAMTA stands for calmodulin-binding transcription activator. Humans have two genes, *CAMTA1* and *CAMTA2*, and they are listed in HOCOMOCO under the older symbols CMTA1 and CMTA2 — worth knowing when searching, because the two spellings are not interchangeable in database queries. The domain layout is the same in plants and animals: an N-terminal CG-1 domain, which carries the DNA-binding activity, followed by a TIG (transcription factor immunoglobulin) domain, two ankyrin repeats that mediate protein-protein interaction, and a C-terminal set of IQ motifs that bind calmodulin [PMID:11925432,17689537]. The name comes from that last feature: calcium-loaded calmodulin binding to the IQ region is the regulatory input, which makes CAMTAs one of the few direct links from calcium signaling to a sequence-specific DNA-binding domain [PMID:11925432]. The CG-1 domain has no similarity to any other DNA-binding class and was first characterized in plants, where the family is larger — Arabidopsis has six members (AtSR1-6) induced by cold, salt, UV-B, wounding and hormone signals [PMID:8075408,12218065]. In humans both genes are expressed most strongly in heart and brain [PMID:16678093,17689537]. Notably, CAMTA2 was characterized biochemically not as a direct DNA-binding activator but as a coactivator recruited by the homeodomain factor NKX2-5, so part of the family's activity at chromatin is tethered rather than motif-driven [PMID:16678093].

## The motif

The element established for this domain family is the CGCG box, a 6-bp site written (A/C/G)CGCG(G/T/C), defined for the Arabidopsis CG-1 protein AtSR1 by direct binding-site analysis [PMID:12218065]. This is the consensus given above. A mammalian consensus was established separately: four rounds of gel-shift selection from random oligonucleotides with a recombinant mouse CAMTA2 fragment gave (T/C)GCANTGCG, a palindrome around one variable central base, bound by a CAMTA dimer and dependent on an adjacent A/T-rich stretch; mutating the core abolished both binding and reporter activation [PMID:25049392]. The HOCOMOCO CAMTA2 matrix, CGCAATGCG — a GC-rich flank on either side of a central AT, architecturally a short inverted repeat rather than a tandem CGCG — is an exact instance of that consensus, while the CAMTA1 matrix is shorter and weaker, CGCAtt, with only 9.4 bits of information. The two agree with each other only moderately (family cohesion 0.79), and for the CAMTA1 model the most similar motif anywhere across the four databases lies outside this family rather than inside it.

The honest reading is that the plant and mammalian sites are related but distinct, as the mammalian work itself concluded [PMID:25049392]: both are short CG-rich elements read by the same conserved domain, but the mammalian consensus carries a central A/T and GCG arms where the plant box is a tandem CGCG. Both human models carry HOCOMOCO evidence code `PSGI` at grade A, meaning they combine ChIP-seq with three in vitro assays: HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq; the in vitro component is what keeps them credible, but the CAMTA1 motif remains low in information content, and there is no published vertebrate CG-1-DNA structure to explain which base contacts matter.

## Where it acts

With only two models, and both of low information content, there is little reliable information about genomic distribution for the human factors. What is documented is functional context rather than motif context: CAMTA2 acts at cardiac gene promoters through NKX2-5, in opposition to class II histone deacetylases (notably HDAC5), and its nuclear activity is regulated by HDAC5 export [PMID:16678093]. In plants, CGCG boxes are found in promoters of ethylene-signaling, abscisic-acid-signaling and light-perception genes, often in multiple copies [PMID:12218065] — the multiplicity is part of how a weak site becomes functional. A 6-mer consensus like VCGCGB will match hundreds of thousands of positions in a 3-Gb genome, so occurrence carries essentially no information on its own; matches are concentrated in CG-rich promoter sequence for compositional reasons rather than biological ones.

## Biology and disease

The mouse phenotypes are neurological and cardiac. *Camta1*-null mice develop ataxia with Purkinje cell degeneration [PMID:25049392], and CAMTA2 overexpression drives cardiac hypertrophy while its loss blunts the hypertrophic response [PMID:16678093]. In humans, intragenic *CAMTA1* rearrangements cause non-progressive congenital ataxia, with or without intellectual disability [PMID:22693284], and a described *CAMTA1* mutation produces a characterized neuropsychological and neuroimaging phenotype [PMID:24145135]. *CAMTA1* lies within the commonly deleted 1p36 region in neuroblastoma and behaves as a tumor suppressor candidate there, with reduced expression associated with worse outcome [PMID:21385898]. The most striking cancer connection is a fusion: *WWTR1* (TAZ)-*CAMTA1* is the defining driver rearrangement in epithelioid hemangioendothelioma [PMID:21885404], where the CAMTA1 portion supplies constitutive nuclear localization and transcriptional output to the TAZ coactivator [PMID:35740643].

## Reading a hit

Treat a CAMTA match as weak evidence. The two available models are short and low in information, they agree with each other only moderately, and for CAMTA1 the nearest neighbour across the databases is outside the family — so a hit may equally reflect a different CG-rich motif. CAMTA1 and CAMTA2 cannot be distinguished from one another. The consensus quoted at the top of this entry is the plant CGCG box; the mammalian site defined by selection is (T/C)GCANTGCG [PMID:25049392], so scanning human sequence with the plant box is an assumption rather than a result.

Two structural cautions about the evidence. First, CAMTA2's best-documented mode of action in mammals is as an NKX2-5 coactivator [PMID:16678093], so ChIP-derived signal for CAMTA2 may reflect a homeodomain site rather than a CG-1 site — the classic indirect-binding case, where the tagged protein "has" the motif of whatever recruits it. Second, both matrices are partly ChIP-derived (`PSGI`), and even at grade A that mixture cannot separate direct from tethered binding. Use a CAMTA hit to raise a hypothesis in a calcium-responsive, heart- or brain-expressed promoter, and verify with a direct binding assay before relying on it.
families.caveats: This is one of the weakest families in the atlas for sequence-based calling. Only two motifs exist, both HOCOMOCO, both low in information content (9.4 and 16.5 bits), cohesion is 0.79, and for the CAMTA1 model the most similar motif across all four databases lies outside the family. The consensus given here, the CGCG box, comes from plant work on the same conserved domain; the mammalian site defined by selection with CAMTA2 is (T/C)GCANTGCG, which the CAMTA2 model matches and the plant box does not. CAMTA1 and CAMTA2 are indistinguishable. Because CAMTA2 is documented to act as an NKX2-5 coactivator, ChIP-derived signal may report a homeodomain site rather than a CG-1 site. Confirm with a direct binding assay.
