timeline.finding: A partial cDNA for CG-1, a light-induced parsley protein, is isolated by DNA-ligand screening; CGCG is required in its binding site, the first observation for what became the CG-1 domain.
timeline.methods: Expression-library DNA-ligand screen, DNA binding
timeline.open: Only a partial clone; no target gene and no relation to calmodulin was known.

timeline.finding: Calmodulin-probe screening defines the CAMTA family across multicellular organisms, including human, Drosophila and C. elegans, with a shared CG-1, TIG, ankyrin and IQ layout; human CAMTA1 and CAMTA2 activate transcription in yeast and a 25-residue region binds calmodulin with nanomolar affinity in the presence of calcium.
timeline.methods: Calmodulin-binding library screen, sequence comparison, yeast reporter assays, binding assays

timeline.finding: Arabidopsis AtSR1 is shown to bind a 6-bp CGCG box, (A/C/G)CGCG(G/T/C), through an N-terminal domain conserved among AtSR1-6; multiple CGCG boxes occur in ethylene, abscisic-acid and light-signaling promoters.
timeline.methods: DNA binding assays, promoter survey
timeline.open: Defined for a plant protein; vertebrate CAMTA specificity was not measured.

timeline.finding: An expression screen for activators of the cardiac ANF gene identifies CAMTAs as coactivators that work at least partly through the homeodomain factor NKX2-5 and are opposed by class II HDACs; CAMTA2-mutant mice show a blunted hypertrophic response.
timeline.methods: Expression screen, co-immunoprecipitation, reporter assays, mutant mice
timeline.open: Whether CAMTA2 also binds CG-1 sites in cardiac chromatin was not resolved.

timeline.finding: A WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion, joining the N-terminus of TAZ to the C-terminal part of CAMTA1 under the WWTR1 promoter, is found in virtually all epithelioid hemangioendotheliomas and in no other vascular tumor tested.
timeline.methods: Transcriptome sequencing, cytogenetics, FISH

timeline.finding: Intragenic CAMTA1 copy-number changes, all within the CG-1 domain, segregate with non-progressive congenital cerebellar ataxia with or without intellectual disability.
timeline.methods: Array CGH, family segregation, sequencing

timeline.finding: Global or neural deletion of Camta1 in mice causes ataxia with Purkinje cell degeneration; the same study derives the mammalian CAMTA consensus, (T/C)GCANTGCG with an adjacent A/T-rich stretch bound by a CAMTA dimer, and finds such sites upstream of many of the dysregulated neuronal genes.
timeline.methods: Conditional knockout mice, expression profiling, gel-shift site selection, reporter assays
timeline.open: Only a CAMTA2 fragment was stable enough to use, so whether CAMTA1 binds the same site was not tested.

open: Whether CAMTA1 reads the same site as CAMTA2 is untested: the mammalian consensus (T/C)GCANTGCG was derived with a CAMTA2 fragment, because no stable CAMTA1 protein could be purified, and the CAMTA1 motif model (CGCAtt, 9.4 bits) is too short to show a second half-site.

How much CAMTA activity requires its own DNA binding is unclear: CAMTA2 was identified as a coactivator recruited by NKX2-5, whereas the CAMTA1 rearrangements that cause congenital ataxia fall in the CG-1 DNA-binding domain, so direct and tethered binding may carry different weight in the two paralogues.

families.name: LIN54 / DREAM (CHR)
families.def: Cell-cycle genes homology region TTYGAA. LIN54 in the DREAM/LIN complex.
families.short: LIN54 is the DNA-binding subunit of the MuvB core, the module shared by the repressive DREAM complex and the activating MMB (B-MYB-MuvB) and FOXM1-MuvB complexes. It reads a very short promoter element called the CHR, the cell cycle genes homology region, whose consensus is TTYGAA (most often TTTGAA or TTCGAA). Recognition is unusual: two tandem cysteine-rich CXC (tesmin/CRC) domains grip the duplex and two tyrosine side chains insert into the minor groove, with no zinc finger or helix-turn-helix involved. The CHR is the reason so many G2/M promoters - CCNB1, CCNB2, CDK1, CDC25C, PLK1, AURKA, UBE2C - share the same short TTYGAA, switching from repressed in G0/G1 to activated in G2/M.
families.long:
## The factors

LIN54 (also called MIP120, and CXCD1) is one of five subunits of the MuvB core, together with LIN9,
LIN37, LIN52 and RBBP4 [PMID:17531812,22391450]. MuvB is the shared module of three complexes that act sequentially through the
cell cycle. In quiescence and early G1 it assembles with E2F4, DP1 and the RB-family pocket protein p130
(RBL2) to form DREAM, which represses [PMID:17531812]. On entry into S phase p130 and E2F4 leave and B-MYB (MYBL2) binds,
giving MMB; later FOXM1 is recruited, giving FOXM1-MuvB, which activates the same promoters in G2 and M [PMID:22391450].
LIN54 is the only subunit with sequence-specific DNA-binding activity, so it supplies the address for all
three complexes [PMID:19725879,27465258]. There is a single human LIN54 gene, so there is no paralogue ambiguity, and the protein
is broadly expressed in proliferating and quiescent cells alike. Its DNA-binding module is not a zinc
finger: it consists of two tandem cysteine-rich CXC domains, related to the tesmin/CRC domain family, and
both are required for high-affinity binding [PMID:27465258]. The Drosophila orthologue Mip120 is part of the dREAM/MMB
complex with the same architecture [PMID:28522430].

## The motif

The CHR was defined genetically in 1995 as a short element in the CCNA2, CDC25C and CDK1 promoters, sitting
just downstream of a second element, the CDE, in a CDE-CHR tandem [PMID:7556094]. The literature consensus is TTYGAA -
in practice TTTGAA or TTCGAA - and the atlas data agree: the JASPAR LIN54 model is TTTGAAT and the CIS-BP
model is ATTCAAA, which is the same element on the reverse strand [PMID:25215497]. Family cohesion is 0.99, essentially
one motif in two orientations.

One genuine disagreement is worth flagging. The genome-wide survey by Engeland's group defined the
functional spectrum around TTYGAA [PMID:25106871], while the crystallographic study of LIN54 bound to DNA reported the
biochemically selected consensus as TTYRAA, which admits TTTAAA and TTCAAA as well [PMID:27465258]. Both statements are
in the literature; the practical difference is whether a central G is required. The structure explains why
the information content is so low: specificity comes from two tyrosine residues inserting into the minor
groove rather than from major-groove base readout, a mode that reads a short AT-rich stretch with modest
discrimination [PMID:27465258]. That tyrosine-mediated contact is required for MuvB recruitment to target promoters in
cells [PMID:27465258].

The element is 6 bp of low-complexity sequence. That is the single most important fact for reading a hit:
TTTGAA occurs roughly every few kilobases in random sequence.

## Where it acts

CHR elements are promoter elements, not enhancer elements, and they sit close to the transcription start
site [PMID:19725879,27465258], typically within about 20-100 bp downstream of it. They occur in most late (G2/M) cell-cycle genes
that bind DREAM, MMB or FOXM1-MuvB: CCNB1, CCNB2, CDK1, CDC25C, PLK1, AURKA, AURKB, BUB1, CENPF and UBE2C
among many others [PMID:25106871]. Inverse-orientation CHRs are functional [PMID:22064854]. Some promoters use a CDE-CHR tandem in which
an E2F4-contacted CDE enhances DREAM binding, and some use a CHR alone; the CHR, not the CDE, is the
element that is strictly required [PMID:22064854]. By contrast, canonical MYB-binding and forkhead-binding sites are
under-represented in these promoters, even though B-MYB and FOXM1 act there - they arrive by protein
interaction with MuvB rather than by binding their own sites [PMID:25106871,22391450]. The structural work also suggests MuvB
binding near the start site helps position downstream nucleosomes [PMID:27465258]. The p53-p21-DREAM axis routes p53
signalling to these same CHR promoters, so CHR-containing G2/M genes are among the most reliably
p53-repressed genes in the genome [PMID:20015071].

## Biology and disease

The CHR is the mechanistic answer to a common observation: that G2/M genes behave as a tightly coordinated
module with almost identical expression timing. They share one element and one binding protein. Loss of
LIN54 or other MuvB subunits impairs mitotic gene expression and cell-cycle progression [PMID:19725879,22391450], and a LIN54
mutant in the CXC region mislocalizes to the cytoplasm and blocks the cycle [PMID:22895175]. DREAM disruption
de-represses G2/M genes in quiescence [PMID:17531812,28799433], which is one route by which RB-pathway and p53-pathway lesions in
cancer produce the proliferation signature seen in tumour expression profiles. The CHR is therefore less
a disease gene than the promoter grammar through which two of the most commonly disrupted tumour
suppressor pathways act.

## Reading a hit

A CHR match tells you a G2/M cell-cycle promoter is plausible; it does not tell you that LIN54 is bound.
Six low-complexity bases match far too often for a single hit to be evidence. What raises confidence is
context, not score: the match should be in a promoter, within roughly 100 bp of the transcription start
site, in a gene whose expression peaks in G2/M, and ideally accompanied by a CDE a few bases away. Outside
that context, treat TTTGAA as background. There is no paralogue problem, because LIN54 is the only protein
known to read this element, but there is an interpretation problem in the other direction: because MuvB
carries B-MYB, FOXM1, E2F4 and p130 to the DNA, ChIP-seq for any of those factors will return CHR
elements without those factors binding DNA themselves, and a CHR hit under a FOXM1 or MYBL2 peak is
usually indirect. The CIS-BP LIN54 model is inferred from chicken LIN54 at 99% DNA-binding-domain
identity [PMID:25215497] rather than measured on the human protein, and note the TTYGAA-versus-TTYRAA disagreement when
choosing how strict to be about the central base.
families.caveats: The CHR is 6 bp of low-complexity sequence (TTYGAA; TTTGAA and TTCGAA), so it matches frequently by chance and a single hit carries almost no information. Confidence comes from context: promoter location within roughly 100 bp of the transcription start site, a gene with G2/M-peaking expression, and often an adjacent CDE. Two consensus definitions coexist - TTYGAA from genome-wide promoter analysis and TTYRAA from in vitro selection with the LIN54 CXC domains - so whether a central G is required is unsettled. LIN54 is the only known reader, so there is no paralogue problem, but B-MYB, FOXM1, E2F4 and p130 all reach CHRs through MuvB, so their ChIP peaks contain CHRs indirectly. The CIS-BP model is inferred from chicken LIN54 (99% DBD identity).

What confines MuvB to a few hundred promoters when TTYGAA occurs every few kilobases is not fully explained: proximity to the start site, an adjacent E2F4-bound CDE and NF-Y-bound CCAAT boxes are all implicated, but their separate contributions have not been resolved.
Whether MuvB bound near the start site positions downstream nucleosomes is a model suggested by the structural study, not an established mechanism.

families.name: CDC5L
families.def: Myb-like repeat factor with a spliceosomal role; MBS-like site. CDC5L.
families.short: CDC5L is the human orthologue of fission yeast Cdc5, a protein with two N-terminal Myb/SANT-like repeats whose main established job is not transcription at all: it is an essential component of the spliceosomal Prp19/CDC5L complex required for the second catalytic step of pre-mRNA splicing, and it is visible in cryo-EM structures of the human spliceosome. A site-specific DNA-binding activity was reported for the N-terminal region, and CDC5L also promotes G2/M progression and participates in the ATR-dependent S-phase checkpoint. Its motif evidence is weak: the two models in these databases disagree completely with each other, and one is inherited from an Arabidopsis protein rather than measured on human CDC5L. Treat any hit with caution.
families.long:
## The factors

CDC5L (also CDC5, CEF1) was named for Schizosaccharomyces pombe cdc5+, cloned in 1994 as an essential gene
whose product has homology to c-MYB [PMID:8313892]. The protein carries two Myb/SANT-like repeats near the N terminus -
fewer than the three repeats of c-MYB itself - followed by a long low-complexity C-terminal region with a
latent transcriptional activation domain [PMID:11082045]. A mammalian homologue was shown to regulate G2 progression and
mitotic entry [PMID:9468527]. There is a single human gene and no close paralogue, so within this family there is no
member ambiguity; the ambiguity is about whether the protein functions as a DNA-binding transcription
factor at all.

The best-established function is in splicing. CDC5L is the scaffold of a multiprotein complex in nuclear
extract - the CDC5L/Prp19 complex, containing PRPF19, PLRG1, BCAS2, CTNNBL1, HSPA8 and others - that joins
the spliceosome in an ATP-dependent step and is required for the second catalytic step of pre-mRNA
splicing [PMID:11101529]. Immunodepleting it blocks splicing product formation without preventing spliceosome assembly [PMID:11101529].
The complex is resolved in cryo-EM structures of the human catalytic spliceosome [PMID:29301961]. CDC5L also interacts
with ATR and is required for the S-phase cell-cycle checkpoint [PMID:19633697]. Orthologues behave similarly: Arabidopsis
CDC5 (AtCDC5) is part of the MOS4-associated complex (MAC) with MOS4 and PRL1, which is required for plant
innate immunity and for splicing and microRNA biogenesis [PMID:17575050,28947490]; AtCDC5 was shown to have DNA-binding activity [PMID:8917598,17575050],
which is where the plant-derived motif in these databases comes from [PMID:25215497]. CDC5L is broadly and constitutively
expressed, as befits a core splicing factor.

## The motif

There is no reliable consensus for human CDC5L, and this entry does not assert one. A 12-bp sequence bound
specifically and with high affinity by the N-terminal region of human Cdc5 was identified in 2000, together
with human genomic fragments containing similar sequences that bound with comparable specificity, and the
interaction could activate transcription in a reporter [PMID:11082045]. That paper explicitly noted that previous attempts
by others had failed to find a preferential binding site for Cdc5-family proteins [PMID:11082045], which sets the
expectation for how well-determined this specificity is.

The two models in this atlas disagree with one another, and the disagreement is the single most important
fact about this family. The CIS-BP model, M02698, has consensus GCGCTGAGC - and it is not measured on the
human protein: it is transferred from Arabidopsis thaliana CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497]. The
Vierstra archetype AC0311:CDC5L:Myb/SANT has consensus GATTTAACATA [PMID:32728250], an AT-rich sequence with no resemblance
to the CIS-BP model. Family cohesion is 0.21, essentially no agreement, and neither model's best match in
any other family exceeds about 0.72. There are no JASPAR or HOCOMOCO models. So the honest description is
that this family contains two mutually inconsistent models, one of which is a cross-species inference and
the other of which is a footprint-derived archetype named for a factor whose footprints may reflect
something else entirely.

## Where it acts

There is no well-mapped genomic distribution for human CDC5L binding sites. The 2000 study recovered human
genomic fragments containing sequences related to its 12-bp site and suggested these are specific,
low-abundance sequences rather than a common promoter element [PMID:11082045], but genome-wide occupancy data for CDC5L as
a DNA-binding factor are essentially absent. Because CDC5L is abundant, nuclear and associated with
co-transcriptional splicing machinery, it is highly likely to crosslink to actively transcribed gene
bodies and promoters in ChIP experiments without binding DNA sequence-specifically. That is precisely the
situation in which a footprint- or ChIP-derived "CDC5L motif" is likely to be the motif of whatever else
occupies those regions. In Arabidopsis, AtCDC5 acts through the MAC complex on defence gene expression and
on splicing [PMID:17575050,28947490], again a mixture of direct and indirect routes.

## Biology and disease

Loss of Cdc5 function is lethal in fission yeast [PMID:8313892]. In mammalian cells, overexpressing CDC5L shortened G2,
and a dominant-negative mutant lacking the C-terminal activation domain slowed G2 progression and delayed
entry into mitosis [PMID:9468527]. The S-phase checkpoint function requires the CDC5L-ATR
interaction [PMID:19633697], linking it to the DNA damage response. In the Arabidopsis system, MAC components including
AtCDC5 are required for SNC1-mediated innate immunity [PMID:17575050] and for correct splicing under stress [PMID:28947490]. In human
disease, CDC5L is reported as overexpressed in several cancers, but the mechanistic accounts are
inconsistent and mostly correlative, and it is not established whether any such effect runs through DNA
binding rather than through splicing. There is no monogenic human disease attributed to CDC5L. The
literature is thin on the transcription-factor side and rich on the splicing side, and motif databases
reflect the former more confidently than the evidence supports.

## Reading a hit

Do not read a CDC5L hit as evidence that CDC5L binds your sequence. The two available models are mutually
contradictory (cohesion 0.21), which alone should prevent a specific call. The CIS-BP model is inherited
from Arabidopsis CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity, so it reports a plant protein's preference, and
a GCGCTGAGC match in human sequence is at least as likely to be a coincidence or another Myb/SANT-type or
CRE-adjacent element. The Vierstra archetype is a footprint cluster labelled CDC5L; footprint archetypes
are named after the factor group that dominated a cluster, not after a demonstrated binder, and CDC5L's
abundance at transcribed regions makes an indirect explanation plausible. There is no paralogue problem,
but there is a class problem: CDC5L's demonstrated essential activity is in splicing, and a DNA match
gives you no purchase on that. If a CDC5L hit matters to your analysis, verify it directly rather than
relying on the database label.
families.caveats: The two models in this family contradict each other: CIS-BP gives GCGCTGAGC and the Vierstra archetype gives GATTTAACATA, with cohesion of only 0.21 and no JASPAR or HOCOMOCO model to arbitrate. The CIS-BP entry is not measured on human CDC5L at all - it is transferred from Arabidopsis thaliana CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity - and the Vierstra entry is a footprint cluster named for CDC5L rather than a demonstrated binding preference. A 12-bp human Cdc5 site was reported once, but earlier attempts to find any preferential site for Cdc5-family proteins failed. CDC5L's established essential role is in pre-mRNA splicing, and as an abundant nuclear protein at transcribed regions it is a good candidate for indirect crosslinking. Treat any hit as unverified.

open: Whether human CDC5L acts as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor in cells is unresolved: a 12-bp high-affinity site and reporter activation were reported in 2000 after earlier failures to find any preferred site, while its established essential role is as a core spliceosome component.

Which, if either, database model describes human CDC5L is unknown: the CIS-BP GCGCTGAGC model is transferred from Arabidopsis CDC5, whose reported site CTCAGCG it contains on the opposite strand, the Vierstra GATTTAACATA archetype is an unrelated footprint cluster, and the relation of either to the 12-bp site reported for the human protein has not been established.

families.name: SPZ1
families.def: Testis-specific bHLH-Zip factor. SPZ1.
families.short: SPZ1 is a single-gene family: one bHLH-Zip protein, with a basic helix-loop-helix domain followed by a leucine zipper, the same architecture as MYC, USF and the SREBPs. It was isolated from mouse testis, where expression is confined to testis and epididymis and is reduced by testosterone and retinoic acid. Unlike its palindrome-reading relatives, the one experimentally derived matrix is asymmetric, AGGGTAACAGC, from a small mouse SELEX experiment; the only other entry in the databases is a footprint archetype with a completely different, G-rich consensus. There is no ChIP-seq or in vitro human model. Overexpression studies link SPZ1 to MAPK-driven proliferation and transformation and to TWIST-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition in liver cancer.
families.long:
## The factors

SPZ1 (spermatogenic Zip 1) is a single gene with no human paralogues, and this family therefore has exactly one member. It was isolated from a mouse testis cDNA library and described as a bHLH-Zip protein: a basic helix-loop-helix domain followed by a leucine zipper, the same domain architecture as MYC, MAX, USF1/2, TFE3 and the SREBPs [PMID:11165476,10611221]. In mouse, expression is restricted to testis and epididymis, with protein detected in the nuclei of Leydig cells, and transcript levels are reduced by testosterone and by retinoic acid [PMID:11165476]. Nothing comparable to the structural, genetic and genomic literature that exists for the other bHLH families exists for SPZ1; there is no crystal structure, no knockout phenotype in the published record retrieved here, and no genome-wide binding map. The functional work that does exist is about overexpression: Spz1 driven downstream of mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling promotes proliferation, transformation of cultured cells and tumour formation in mice [PMID:15899793], and SPZ1 has since been reported to promote TWIST-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition in liver cancer [PMID:28368406], chemoresistance in breast cancer lines [PMID:30076850], and interleukin-6 induction in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells [PMID:39440046]. Whether endogenous human SPZ1 does any of this outside the testis is not established.

## The motif

The family contains two entries, and they do not agree with each other.

The primary one is JASPAR MA0111.1, a SELEX-derived matrix for the *mouse* protein (UniProt Q99MY0), traceable to the original 2001 report, which described a nine-base asymmetric target site selected by random selection and PCR [PMID:37962376,11165476]. The retrieved matrix is 11 columns wide and its column sums are 12, meaning it was built from about a dozen selected sequences — an extremely small sample by modern standards. Its consensus reads AGGGTAACAGC, with position 7 weakly A or T. Two things are worth noting about that string. It is asymmetric, unlike the palindromic CACGTG-type E-boxes that the other bHLH-Zip proteins read, and its 3' end, AACAGC, is the 5' half of a class A E-box with an A/T flank (AACAGCTG) but is not followed by a complete second half-site. Whether the selected element is a bona fide degenerate E-box variant or something else is not resolvable from one small SELEX experiment.

The second entry is the Vierstra archetype `AC0575:SPZ:Unknown`. Its consensus is GGRGGGT, a G-rich sequence with no resemblance to the SELEX model, and its structural class is recorded as unknown. Archetypes are named after whichever factor group dominated a cluster of footprint-derived motifs, so this is a claim about clustering, not about SPZ1 recognition [PMID:32728250]. The two entries match each other poorly and match nothing else in the collection: the best similarity of either to any motif outside the family is 0.62 and 0.69 respectively, and family cohesion is 0.33, the lowest value in this part of the atlas. There is no HOCOMOCO model for SPZ1 at all — no ChIP-seq, no HT-SELEX, no methyl-SELEX — and no CIS-BP entry [PMID:25215497].

## Where it acts

Unknown. With no ChIP-seq or footprint-verified model, there is no evidence in the collection about promoter versus enhancer preference, chromatin context, CpG association, typical occupancy count or co-occurring partners. The expectation for a bHLH-Zip protein would be dimerisation through the zipper and binding as a dimer, but SPZ1's dimerisation partner, if it has one, has not been identified in the material retrieved here.

## Biology and disease

Restricted testis and epididymis expression in mouse, Leydig cell nuclear localisation, and downregulation by testosterone and retinoic acid are the only well-supported endogenous observations [PMID:11165476]. A role in spermatogenesis was proposed on that basis but has not been demonstrated genetically in the literature retrieved. The cancer literature is overexpression-based: SPZ1 downstream of MAPK signalling drives proliferation, transformation and tumorigenesis in mouse models [PMID:15899793]; SPZ1 promotes TWIST-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition and oncogenesis in human liver cancer [PMID:28368406]; and reports link it to chemoresistance in drug-resistant breast cancer cells and to Wnt5a/interleukin-6 signalling in nasopharyngeal carcinoma [PMID:30076850,39440046]. These are consistent in direction but come from a small literature centred on a few groups.

## Reading a hit

Treat an SPZ1 match with real skepticism. The only sequence model with any experimental basis is a mouse SELEX matrix built from roughly twelve sequences, so its position weights are not well estimated, and using it on human sequence is a cross-species application even though the human and mouse proteins are orthologous. The only other entry, the SPZ archetype, is a different sequence entirely and is labelled with an unknown structural class, so the two cannot be reconciled. There is no in vitro human model and no ChIP evidence of any kind. In practice a hit to this family should be read as "the sequence resembles a poorly characterised mouse SELEX consensus", not as "SPZ1 binds here", and it should not be used to support a mechanistic claim without direct experimental follow-up. If SPZ1 came up as a top hit in a scan of human regulatory regions, the prior that the result is meaningful is low, and the prior that a better-supported factor explains the same sequence is high.
families.caveats: This is the weakest family in the batch and should be read as provisional. Its two motifs do not agree with each other: the JASPAR SELEX matrix (mouse, roughly twelve selected sequences) reads AGGGTAACAGC, while the Vierstra archetype AC0575:SPZ:Unknown reads a G-rich GGRGGGT and carries an unknown structural class. Cohesion is 0.33, and neither entry resembles anything else in the collection. There is no HOCOMOCO model at all for SPZ1 — no ChIP-seq, no HT-SELEX, no methyl-SELEX — and no CIS-BP entry, so nothing here establishes a human binding preference. A hit means the sequence resembles a small mouse SELEX consensus, nothing more.

timeline.finding: The helix-loop-helix classes are set out in the form the atlas still uses, with the bHLH-Zip group (MYC, MAX, USF, TFE3, SREBP) defined by a leucine zipper appended to the bHLH and by dimeric binding to palindromic E-boxes — the class SPZ1 was later assigned to.
timeline.methods: review of structural and biochemical literature

timeline.finding: Spz1 is isolated from a mouse testis cDNA library as a bHLH-Zip protein expressed in testis and epididymis, with protein in Leydig cell nuclei and transcript reduced by testosterone and retinoic acid; random selection and PCR give a nine-base asymmetric target site, the matrix later deposited as JASPAR MA0111.1.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, Northern blot, immunohistochemistry, in vitro site selection
timeline.open: The selected site rests on about a dozen sequences and was never confirmed by an independent assay, and no dimerization partner was identified.

timeline.finding: Spz1 is placed downstream of mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling: overexpression promotes proliferation, transforms cultured cells and produces tumours in mice.
timeline.methods: overexpression in cell lines and transgenic mice
timeline.open: Whether endogenous Spz1, whose expression is testis-restricted, does any of this was not addressed.

timeline.finding: Successive genome-scale compilations leave SPZ1 essentially unmodelled: CIS-BP (2014) carries no SPZ1 motif, the human footprint archetypes (2020) place a G-rich cluster AC0575:SPZ:Unknown with unknown structural class, and JASPAR 2024 still offers only the 2001 mouse SELEX matrix.
timeline.methods: database compilation; genomic footprint clustering
timeline.open: The archetype and the SELEX matrix are different sequences and no experiment reconciles them.

timeline.finding: SPZ1 is reported to promote TWIST-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition and oncogenesis in human liver cancer, the first proposed mechanism for the human protein.
timeline.methods: knockdown and overexpression in liver cancer cells and xenografts
timeline.open: Whether SPZ1 acts here through its own DNA binding or through protein-protein interaction with TWIST.

timeline.finding: SPZ1 is linked to chemoresistance and aggressiveness in drug-resistant breast cancer cell lines.
timeline.methods: cell-line knockdown and overexpression

timeline.finding: SPZ1-mediated Wnt5a signalling is reported to induce interleukin-6 and promote progression in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells, extending a small overexpression-based literature.
timeline.methods: cell-line manipulation and expression assays
timeline.open: No genome-wide binding map or knockout phenotype has yet been reported for SPZ1 in any system.

open: The family's two entries describe different sequences and cannot both be SPZ1's site: the mouse SELEX matrix reads AGGGTAACAGC while the footprint archetype AC0575:SPZ:Unknown reads a G-rich GGRGGGT, and no independent experiment exists to decide between them.

Whether SPZ1 binds DNA as a homodimer, as a heterodimer with another bHLH-Zip protein, or chiefly through protein partners is unknown, since no dimerization partner has been identified and the selected site is asymmetric rather than palindromic like the sites read by other bHLH-Zip proteins.

It is unresolved whether the selected element is a degenerate E-box variant at all: its 3' end, AACAGC, is the 5' half of a class A E-box with an A/T flank, but no complete second half-site follows, and one small selection experiment cannot settle the question.

Whether endogenous human SPZ1 has any function outside the testis is unestablished: the proliferation, EMT, chemoresistance and interleukin-6 reports all rest on overexpression or knockdown in cell lines, and no knockout phenotype or genome-wide binding map has been published.

families.name: CASZ1 (castor)
families.def: Castor-type multi-zinc-finger factor; AT-rich composite site. CASZ1.
families.short: CASZ1 is the single human orthologue of Drosophila castor, a large multi-zinc-finger transcription factor that in flies specifies a late temporal window of neuroblast identity. The human gene sits at 1p36.22 and produces two main isoforms with different numbers of C2H2 zinc fingers. Its binding preference is poorly characterized: the only motif in these databases is a long, AT-rich composite model from in vitro selection, and no consensus has been established by focused biochemistry. CASZ1 is required for cardiac and vascular morphogenesis in Xenopus and mouse, its expression is low in high-risk neuroblastoma where 1p36 is frequently deleted, and common variants at the CASZ1 locus are among the earliest replicated blood-pressure associations.
families.long:
## The factors

CASZ1 (castor zinc finger 1, CST, ZNF693) is the vertebrate orthologue of Drosophila castor, which was
cloned in 1992 as a novel zinc-finger protein required for the development of a subset of CNS neurons [PMID:1418995] and
is best known as one of the temporal identity factors that mark a late window in neuroblast lineages. The
human gene is at 1p36.22. It encodes a large protein with multiple C2H2 zinc fingers arranged in an
unusual pattern, and two principal isoforms are described, commonly referred to by their finger counts
(an eleven-finger and a five-finger form), which differ at the C terminus. CASZ1 binds DNA as a monomer
as far as is known; no obligate dimerization partner has been reported, though it binds
congenital heart disease protein 5 (CHD5, also called tryptophan-rich basic protein or WRB, a chromosome 21 gene unrelated to the chromodomain helicase CHD5) [PMID:24993940], and in retinal progenitors it associates with the NuRD nucleosome-remodelling complex [PMID:33594190]. There is one human gene, so there is no paralogue problem within the family, but there is also
very little comparative information to lean on. Expression is highest in heart, vasculature and
neural-crest-derived sympathetic tissue, with additional expression in kidney and lung.

## The motif

This family has no established consensus, and this entry does not invent one. The only model in these
databases is a single HOCOMOCO matrix, CASZ1.H14CORE.0.SGI.A, with the data consensus
TTTTGGGGNAAAATNNGNNDTTT - a 23-position, mostly AT-rich composite with two loosely specified blocks
separated by a degenerate middle. Its evidence code (S, G, I) is three in vitro assays, HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq, and it carries a grade-A quality flag [PMID:41203846], so the measurement is credible as a measurement; what is
missing is independent confirmation and any focused structural or mutational work assigning positions to
particular fingers. There is no JASPAR, CIS-BP or Vierstra model for CASZ1 in this atlas, so cohesion is
undefined (recorded as zero because there is nothing to compare against), and the motif's nearest
neighbour in any other family reaches only about 0.64 similarity - it does not clearly resemble any other
known element.

A long AT-rich model with a degenerate middle behaves in a scan much like a low-complexity filter. The
information is spread thinly over many positions, poly-T and poly-A tracts will score, and the effective
specificity is much lower than the length of the model suggests. Nothing is known about half-sites,
spacing rules or which of the many CASZ1 zinc fingers contact DNA. Whether the two isoforms have different
specificities has not been tested.

## Where it acts

Direct, validated CASZ1 target genes are few. The best-characterized is EGFL7, which CASZ1 binds and
activates in endothelial cells; CASZ1 depletion phenocopies EGFL7 loss in vascular sprouting, and
restoring Egfl7 rescues the defect, acting through RhoA and focal-adhesion localization [PMID:23639441]. In neuroblastoma
cells, restoring CASZ1 changes the expression of a broad set of growth- and differentiation-related genes,
but these were identified by expression profiling rather than by direct occupancy, so most are downstream
rather than bound [PMID:21252912]. Genome-wide occupancy maps for CASZ1 in human cells are sparse. The practical
consequence is that there is no established picture of whether CASZ1 works from promoters or enhancers,
what chromatin context its sites occupy, or which factors it co-occurs with. The literature here is thin
and should be described as thin.

## Biology and disease

CASZ1 is required for heart and blood-vessel development. In Xenopus, loss of CASZ1 blocks differentiation
of cardiac precursor cells at the ventral midline [PMID:18410736], and CASZ1-depleted embryos fail to form a branched,
lumenized vascular network; human endothelial cells depleted of CASZ1 show altered adhesion, morphology
and sprouting [PMID:23639441]. CASZ1 associates with CHD5 to maintain myocardial tissue integrity [PMID:24993940]. In humans, a
heterozygous CASZ1 missense variant (p.L38P) segregating with ventricular septal defect in one family was
reported with reduced transactivation in reporter assays, the first link between CASZ1 and congenital
heart disease [PMID:27693370]; this rests on a single pedigree and should be treated as suggestive. In neuroblastoma, low
CASZ1 expression correlates with older age at diagnosis, high-risk classification, 1p loss of
heterozygosity and MYCN amplification, and with worse survival; restoring CASZ1 in neuroblastoma lines
induces differentiation and suppresses tumorigenicity, making it a candidate for the 1p36 tumour
suppressor [PMID:21252912]. Separately, common variants at the CASZ1 locus were among the loci identified in early
genome-wide association studies of blood pressure and hypertension [PMID:19430479], though the causal gene and mechanism
at that locus have not been settled.

## Reading a hit

Treat a CASZ1 match as weak. The model is a single long AT-rich composite from one database; there is no
replication across databases, no structure, and no defined core, so a match does not license the
conclusion that CASZ1 bound the sequence. AT-rich models of this shape also overlap the preferences of
homeodomain, forkhead, HMG and other minor-groove AT readers, and they score poly-A/poly-T tracts, so
sequence composition alone can produce hits. There is no paralogue ambiguity within the family, because
there is only one gene, but that is not reassurance - it just means the usual family-versus-member caveat
is replaced by a cruder one: the motif itself is not well enough established to support a specific call.
Use a CASZ1 hit as a hypothesis to test with expression and occupancy data in a tissue where CASZ1 is
actually expressed (heart, endothelium, sympathetic neuroblast lineage), and do not build an argument on
the match alone.
families.caveats: The whole family rests on one HOCOMOCO matrix, a 23-position AT-rich composite with a degenerate middle. Its evidence includes in vitro selection at grade A, so the measurement is credible, but there is no independent model in JASPAR, CIS-BP or Vierstra to corroborate it, cohesion is undefined, and no structural or mutational work assigns positions to specific zinc fingers. Long AT-rich models function partly as low-complexity filters: poly-A and poly-T tracts score, and the preferences overlap homeodomain, forkhead and HMG factors. Whether the two CASZ1 isoforms differ in specificity is untested. There is only one human gene, so no paralogue problem - but a match should be treated as a hypothesis, not an identification.

timeline.finding: Drosophila castor is cloned in an enhancer-detection screen as a zinc-finger protein expressed in a subset of CNS neuroblasts and required for their development.
timeline.methods: Enhancer-detection screen; mutant analysis
timeline.open: No DNA-binding specificity was determined.

timeline.finding: Vertebrate CASTOR (CASZ1) is shown to be required in Xenopus for differentiation of cardiac precursors at the ventral midline.
timeline.methods: Morpholino depletion; fate mapping in Xenopus

timeline.finding: A CASZ1 variant (rs880315, P = 2.1 x 10^-7) is reported among the systolic blood pressure association signals of the CHARGE genome-wide association study.
timeline.methods: Genome-wide association meta-analysis
timeline.open: The signal fell short of conventional genome-wide significance (5 x 10^-8) in that study, and no causal gene was assigned.

timeline.finding: Low CASZ1 expression in neuroblastoma correlates with high-risk features and poor survival, and restoring CASZ1 induces differentiation and suppresses tumorigenicity, nominating it as a 1p36 tumour suppressor.
timeline.methods: Quantitative RT-PCR in tumors; restoration in cell lines; expression profiling
timeline.open: Responsive genes were found by expression profiling, not occupancy, so direct targets remained unknown.

timeline.finding: CASZ1 is shown to directly regulate EGFL7 to promote vascular assembly; Egfl7 restores the defects of CASZ1-depleted endothelial cells.
timeline.methods: Xenopus depletion; human endothelial cell knockdown; direct-target analysis; rescue

timeline.finding: CASZ1 is found to interact directly with congenital heart disease protein 5 (CHD5/WRB), and the interaction is needed for cardiac morphogenesis in Xenopus.
timeline.methods: Protein interaction assays; Xenopus loss of function

timeline.finding: A heterozygous CASZ1 missense variant (p.L38P) co-segregating with ventricular septal defect in one family reduces transcriptional activity in reporter assays.
timeline.methods: Candidate-gene sequencing in 172 patients; pedigree segregation; luciferase assays
timeline.open: A single pedigree; no replication.

timeline.finding: Cross-platform data on poorly studied human transcription factors (HT-SELEX, genomic HT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq) underlie the first CASZ1 motif, the grade-A HOCOMOCO v14 model that is the only CASZ1 model in this atlas.
timeline.methods: HT-SELEX; GHT-SELEX; SMiLE-seq; cross-platform motif benchmarking
timeline.open: No independent laboratory, mutational or structural work has yet tested the model or assigned it to particular fingers.

open: Whether the single CASZ1 model describes a defined recognition site or a broad AT-rich preference is unresolved: it is reproducible across three in vitro platforms, but no independent study, mutational analysis or structure has identified a core or tied positions to particular zinc fingers.

Whether CASZ1 itself is the causal gene behind the blood-pressure association at its locus is unsettled: the association comes from genome-wide association data, and the cited work does not connect it to a CASZ1-dependent mechanism.

Whether CASZ1 variants cause human congenital heart disease is unresolved: the p.L38P variant co-segregates with ventricular septal defect in one pedigree and reduces reporter activity, but no independent family has been reported in the cited work.

families.name: CIC (capicua)
families.def: HMG-box repressor binding TGAATGAA octamer. CIC.
families.short: CIC (capicua) is a single HMG-box repressor and the transcriptional sensor of ERK/MAPK signaling. It binds an eight-base octamer, TGAATGAA or TCAATGAA, and recruits Groucho/TLE and SIN3-histone deacetylase complexes to switch target genes off; MAPK activity removes CIC from those sites and lets them fire. Unusually for an HMG-box protein, the HMG box alone cannot bind DNA - a distant C-terminal motif called C1 is required with it, and the two together form a bipartite recognition surface. CIC is inactivated in most IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, with mutations clustering in the C1 domain, and the CIC-DUX4 fusion defines a subset of undifferentiated round cell sarcoma. Its main direct targets are the PEA3/ETS genes ETV1, ETV4 and ETV5.
families.long:
## The factors

This family has one member. CIC is the human ortholog of Drosophila capicua, a large protein
(roughly 2,500 residues in the long isoform) containing a single HMG box near its N-terminus
and, far away at the C-terminus, a short conserved motif called C1. CIC is a repressor: it
recruits Groucho/TLE in flies and interacts with the SIN3 complex in human cells, repressing
through histone deacetylation [PMID:10652276,25569482,29844126]. It is broadly expressed, and its defining regulatory feature is
that it is the downstream sensor of receptor tyrosine kinase signaling - high ERK/MAPK activity
both downregulates CIC protein and abolishes its binding to target genes, which is how the
pathway activates them [PMID:10652276,29844126]. Phylogenetically CIC does not sit with SOX or TCF/LEF but forms a
distinct HMG-box subfamily together with BBX [PMID:25079045]. The mechanistic surprise is that the CIC HMG box
does not bind DNA on its own [PMID:28278156]. The HMG box and the C1 domain are both necessary for binding
octameric sites, they do not act by dimerizing, and they require no cofactor, so they appear to
form a single bipartite DNA-binding surface - a third solution, alongside the SOX and TCF/LEF
ones, to the problem that a lone HMG box binds DNA too weakly [PMID:28278156,40967212].

## The motif

The literature consensus is the octamer TGAATGAA, with TCAATGAA and related variants also
functional, generally written T(G/C)AATG(A/G)A; on the opposite strand it reads TTCATTCA. These
"capicua octamers" were identified as general response elements for RTK signaling in Drosophila [PMID:21270056]
and the same binding mechanism operates in human cells [PMID:28278156]. The element bears no resemblance to the
SOX core AACAAT or to the TCF/LEF element CTTTGWW. Allowing the two degenerate positions,
TGAATGAA-like octamers are expected a few hundred thousand times in a 3.1 Gb double-stranded
genome. The databases, however, do not carry this motif. The only CIC model in JASPAR, HOCOMOCO,
CIS-BP or the Vierstra archetypes is CIS-BP M00195_2.00, derived from mouse Cic at full DNA-
binding-domain identity, with consensus TGCTGAC at 12.7 bits [PMID:25215497]. TGCTGAC is exactly the left half
of the MAF recognition element, whose palindromic forms are TGCTGACTCAGCA and TGCTGACGTCAGCA [PMID:8264639],
and the model's nearest neighbor across all four databases is a MAF-family motif at 0.966
similarity, with no neighbor inside its own family. Two things make that entry implausible as a
capicua site: the sequence is a MARE half-site and nothing like TGAATGAA, and a measurement made
on an isolated CIC DNA-binding domain would not be expected to recover the real site, because
the HMG box needs the distant C1 domain to bind at all [PMID:28278156]. We therefore do not recommend using this
model to call CIC sites; scan the published octamer instead.

## Where it acts

CIC octamers sit in enhancers and promoters of MAPK effector genes involved in cell-cycle
control and proliferation, most prominently the PEA3 subfamily of ETS factors, ETV1, ETV4 and
ETV5. In Drosophila the octamers in the huckebein enhancer recruit Groucho, the same elements
mediate both Torso and EGFR responses in the embryo and a further EGFR response in the wing, and
a simple combination of activator sites plus capicua octamers is enough to generate complex
expression patterns [PMID:21270056]. Occupancy is conditional rather than constitutive: CIC binding is lost
where MAPK activity is high, so a genuine site can be unoccupied in the cell you are studying [PMID:29844126].

## Biology and disease

CIC is mutated in most IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas [PMID:21817013], and single amino acid
substitutions found in those tumors prevent CIC from binding its targets [PMID:29844126]; the C1 domain is a
mutation hotspot, which the bipartite binding mechanism explains [PMID:28278156]. Loss of CIC raises histone
acetylation and transcription at MAPK target genes and supports mitogen-independent growth [PMID:29844126], so
CIC behaves as a tumor suppressor whose inactivation phenocopies EGFR/RAS/MAPK activation. The
reciprocal case is the CIC-DUX4 fusion produced by t(4;19) or t(10;19), which defines a subset
of undifferentiated round cell sarcoma resembling Ewing sarcoma and upregulates PEA3 family
genes [PMID:16717057]; the C1 domain is preserved in the fusion protein.

## Reading a hit

With one member there is no paralogue problem inside the family, but three other cautions apply.
First, the octamer is short: a few hundred thousand matches are expected by chance, so a hit is
a candidate, not a site. Second, if your match came from the CIS-BP CIC model, treat it as a
MAF-family half-MARE rather than a capicua site, and rescan using TGAATGAA/TCAATGAA. Third, the
reverse complement of the octamer, TTCATTCA, is the unit of the highest-affinity HBP1 binding
site TTCATTCATTCA [PMID:10562551], so TGAATGAA-type matches are ambiguous between CIC and HBP1, both HMG-box
repressors. No ChIP-derived CIC motif exists in these collections, so nothing here is
contaminated by indirect binding - but equally, nothing here has been validated against CIC ChIP
data.
families.caveats: The published CIC site and the only database model for CIC disagree completely. The literature octamer is TGAATGAA; the single CIS-BP entry reads TGCTGAC, which is the MAF recognition element half-site, and its nearest neighbors across all four databases are MAF motifs. Since the CIC HMG box cannot bind DNA without the distant C1 domain, a domain-only assay would not be expected to recover the true site, so we treat that model as unusable for calling CIC sites and recommend scanning the octamer directly. Even then the octamer is only eight bases and occurs a few hundred thousand times by chance, its reverse complement is the HBP1 site unit, and CIC occupancy is abolished by high MAPK activity.

timeline.finding: capicua is identified in Drosophila as an HMG-box repressor of terminal and dorsoventral genes that interacts with the Groucho corepressor and is inactivated at the embryonic poles by Torso RTK signaling.
timeline.methods: Drosophila genetics, in vitro interaction assays
timeline.open: The DNA sequence Cic recognizes was not identified.

timeline.finding: A recurrent t(4;19) translocation fuses human CIC to DUX4 in Ewing-like sarcoma; the fusion protein binds the ERM/ETV5 promoter and raises PEA3-family gene expression, the first direct link between CIC and human tumors.
timeline.methods: Translocation cloning, expression profiling, promoter binding and transformation assays

timeline.finding: Two results arrive together: octameric Capicua sites are shown to be general RTK response elements in Drosophila, mediating Torso, embryonic EGFR and wing EGFR responses and recruiting Groucho at the huckebein enhancer; and exome sequencing finds CIC somatically mutated in most 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas.
timeline.methods: Drosophila enhancer dissection and chromatin immunoprecipitation; exome sequencing of tumors
timeline.open: Why mutations clustered in the C-terminal C1 region, far from the HMG box, was unexplained.

timeline.finding: The CIC HMG box is shown not to bind DNA on its own: the HMG box and the distant C1 domain are both required for binding TGAATGAA-like octamers, without dimerization or cofactors, and this explains why C1 is a mutation hotspot in oligodendroglioma while being retained in CIC-DUX4.
timeline.methods: Domain deletion and binding assays in Drosophila and human cells
timeline.open: How two distant domains cooperate on one octamer was a model without a structure.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide mapping shows human CIC bound at MAPK effector genes controlling the cell cycle and proliferation, with binding abolished where MAPK activity is high; CIC interacts with the SIN3 complex, and oligodendroglioma point mutations abolish target binding.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq in several cell types, proteomics, mutant rescue

timeline.finding: The crystal structure of the human CIC HMG-box-C1 module on an ETV5 promoter octamer confirms the bipartite mechanism: the HMG box reads the minor groove and bends the DNA by about 66 degrees, while C1 folds into a helix-turn-helix that inserts into the narrowed major groove on the opposite face, adding affinity but making no base-specific contacts.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics, binding assays on cancer variants
timeline.open: With no base-specific C1 contacts observed, how the C1 domain sharpens sequence selectivity rather than only raising affinity is still inferred rather than shown.

open: The only database model for CIC contradicts the published site: CIS-BP gives TGCTGAC, a MAF half-site whose nearest neighbors are MAF motifs, while the literature octamer is TGAATGAA, and since the CIC HMG box cannot bind without the distant C1 domain, a domain-only measurement is not expected to recover the real element; the entry in CIS-BP has not been retracted or re-measured.

How the C1 domain contributes sequence selectivity is unresolved: deletion experiments show it is required for specific octamer binding, but the crystal structure finds it making no base-specific contacts, and the proposal that it selects indirectly by destabilizing unfavorable DNA conformations has not been tested.

Which corepressor human CIC uses is unsettled: Drosophila Cic represses through Groucho via a motif that appears to be a dipteran innovation, whereas human CIC has been shown to act through the SIN3 histone deacetylase complex, and whether TLE proteins contribute in human cells remains open.

Whether genuine CIC octamers can be distinguished from HBP1 sites by sequence is unknown: TGAATGAA read on the other strand is the repeated unit of the HBP1 element, no ChIP-derived motif for either protein exists in these collections, and no study has compared their genomic occupancy.

families.name: HBP1
families.def: HMG-box factor binding an AT-rich site at cell-cycle promoters. HBP1.
families.short: HBP1 is a single HMG-box transcriptional repressor and cell-cycle inhibitor, identified as a target of the retinoblastoma protein family. Its highest-affinity site, found in the human CD2 locus control region, is the twelve-base element TTCATTCATTCA, which is explicitly not the canonical HMG-box consensus used by SOX and TCF/LEF proteins; read on the other strand it is three tandem copies of TGAATGAA, the octamer that CIC recognizes. HBP1 represses the N-MYC and cyclin D1 promoters, opposes E2F at N-MYC, activates p16 and p21, and arrests the cell cycle even under strong growth signals. It is suppressed by AKT signaling and by several microRNAs, and behaves as a tumor suppressor without being a commonly mutated cancer gene.
families.long:
## The factors

One protein. HBP1 (HMG-box transcription factor 1) is a roughly 514-residue nuclear protein with
a single HMG box. It was cloned twice independently: first by expression cloning in a potassium
transport-defective yeast screen [PMID:7937077], and then as a repressor that binds the retinoblastoma family [PMID:9030690].
It carries two RB-interaction motifs, LXCXE and IXCXE, and interacts selectively with RB and
p130 but not p107; HBP1, RB and p130 all rise during differentiation while p107 falls [PMID:9030690]. HBP1 is
broadly expressed. Functionally it is a repressor and a brake on proliferation: it represses the
N-MYC promoter and acts there as the opposite signal to E2F-1 [PMID:9030690], represses CCND1 [PMID:11500377], activates CDKN2A
(p16) and CDKN1A (p21) [PMID:23249948], and its expression arrests the cell cycle even in the presence of
optimal proliferation signals [PMID:9030690]. Much of its effect is exerted through proteins rather than DNA -
it neutralizes LEF1, TCF4 and MYC in the WNT/beta-catenin pathway [PMID:11500377,30683982]. It sits downstream of growth
factor signaling in two ways: AKT phosphorylates HBP1 and inhibits its transcriptional activity [PMID:30683982],
and the PI3K/PKB/FOXO pathway controls HBP1 transcription by regulating FOXO binding to the HBP1
promoter [PMID:24762137].

## The motif

The consensus given here, TTCATTCATTCA, is the highest-affinity HBP1 binding sequence described.
It was found in HSS3 of the human CD2 locus control region and binds more tightly than the HBP1
sites reported earlier in cell-cycle promoters [PMID:10562551]. The authors noted explicitly that it differs
from the canonical (T/A)(T/A)CAA(A/T)G consensus of other HMG-box proteins [PMID:10562551,8190643], so HBP1 should not
be scanned with a SOX or TCF/LEF model. The element is a tandem trimer: read on the opposite
strand it is TGAATGAATGAA, three copies of the octamer TGAATGAA that CIC binds, and both
proteins are HMG-box repressors, which makes sequence-only discrimination between them
impossible at the level of a single octamer. Length matters a great deal here. An exact twelve-
base match is expected only a few hundred times in a 3.1 Gb double-stranded genome, which makes
a full match informative; a single TTCATTCA octamer is expected of order a hundred thousand
times and is not. The motif model carried in these databases is of no use for scanning: the sole
entry, CIS-BP M00194_2.00, derived from mouse Hbp1 at full DNA-binding-domain identity, contains
1.1 bits of information in total [PMID:25215497], and its consensus string collapses to a single degenerate
base. Species is not the problem - the DNA-binding domains are identical - the problem is that
the model records almost no preference. Its best similarity to any motif outside the family is
0.797, and being a one-member family it has no within-family comparison.

## Where it acts

The place HBP1 binding was best characterized is unusual. HSS3 of the hCD2 locus control region
has no enhancer activity of its own but is required to prevent position-effect variegation:
transgenes carrying an HSS3 deletion of the HBP1 sites variegate when they integrate into
centromeric or telomeric heterochromatin [PMID:10562551]. The interpretation offered was architectural - HBP1
binds and bends the DNA, making protein-DNA and protein-protein contacts more likely and raising
the probability that an active locus is established [PMID:10562551]. Elsewhere HBP1 is documented at cell-cycle
gene promoters, including N-MYC, CCND1, CDKN2A, CDKN1A and DNMT1 [PMID:9030690,11500377,23249948]. There is no genome-scale map
of HBP1 occupancy in these collections, and no HBP1 model from ChIP-seq in any of the four
databases.

## Biology and disease

HBP1 behaves as a cell-cycle inhibitor and candidate tumor suppressor. It contributes to
oncogene-induced senescence downstream of RAS and to terminal differentiation, and its
repression of DNMT1 links it to the senescence program [PMID:23249948]. It is not among the frequently mutated
cancer driver genes, but its expression is lower in several tumor types than in matched normal
tissue, and alterations of HBP1 have been reported in invasive breast cancer [PMID:17616670]. Loss of HBP1
expression is more often post-transcriptional or signaling-driven than mutational: miR-155,
miR-17-92 and miR-29a each reduce HBP1 levels in different tumor contexts [PMID:30683982], and growth factor
signaling through PI3K/PKB/FOXO downregulates HBP1 transcription while AKT inactivates the
protein directly [PMID:24762137,30683982].

## Reading a hit

Do not use the database model for this family; at 1.1 bits it will match essentially anywhere.
If you want HBP1 candidate sites, scan the published element TTCATTCATTCA, and treat a full
twelve-base match as meaningful and a single octamer as not. The main interpretive hazard is
CIC: the octamer unit is identical, so a TTCATTCA or TGAATGAA hit is compatible with either
protein, and expression data or the presence of a tandem trimer versus a lone octamer is what
separates them. Do not read a SOX- or TCF/LEF-type WWCAAWG match as an HBP1 site; HBP1 was
explicitly shown not to use that consensus [PMID:10562551]. Because there is no ChIP-derived HBP1 model here,
nothing in this entry is contaminated by indirect binding - but equally, nothing has been tested
genome-wide. Finally, remember that a large part of HBP1's activity is protein-protein: absence
of a site near a gene HBP1 regulates does not mean HBP1 is not involved.
families.caveats: Low confidence in any motif-based call. The single database model for HBP1 carries 1.1 bits and is unusable for scanning; the entry here gives the published high-affinity site instead, which rests mainly on one study of the human CD2 locus control region. The octamer unit of that site is identical to the CIC recognition octamer read on the other strand, so single-octamer matches cannot be assigned to HBP1 rather than CIC. A full twelve-base match is rare enough to be informative; a partial one is not. HBP1 also works substantially through protein-protein antagonism of LEF1, TCF4 and MYC, so its regulatory targets need not contain an HBP1 site at all.

timeline.finding: HBP1 is cloned from rat by its ability to suppress a potassium transport defect in yeast, turns out to encode a 513-residue HMG-box protein unrelated to any transporter, and is found to rise with differentiation in adipocyte and myogenic cell lines.
timeline.methods: Expression cloning in yeast, Northern blots
timeline.open: Neither a DNA-binding site nor a transcriptional function had been demonstrated.

timeline.finding: HBP1 is isolated as a target of the retinoblastoma family: it carries LXCXE and IXCXE motifs, binds RB and p130 but not p107, represses the N-MYC promoter in opposition to E2F-1, and its expression arrests the cell cycle despite optimal growth signals.
timeline.methods: Interaction cloning, co-immunoprecipitation, reporter assays, cell-cycle analysis

timeline.finding: HBP1 is shown to separate cell-cycle exit from differentiation: in C2C12 myoblasts it blocks MyoD-family-driven muscle differentiation while leaving cell-cycle exit intact, with the outcome set by the RB/HBP1 ratio.
timeline.methods: Ectopic expression in muscle cells, reporter assays

timeline.finding: The highest-affinity HBP1 site is identified as TTCATTCATTCA in HSS3 of the human CD2 locus control region, explicitly different from the canonical HMG-box consensus; deleting it makes transgenes variegate when they land in heterochromatin.
timeline.methods: Site selection and binding assays, transgenic mice
timeline.open: Whether this element is used at HBP1's cell-cycle target promoters, or anywhere else in the genome, was not tested.

timeline.finding: HBP1 is shown to inhibit Wnt signaling by binding TCF/LEF proteins and blocking their DNA binding, and to repress cyclin D1: a large part of its activity does not require an HBP1 site at all.
timeline.methods: Co-immunoprecipitation, EMSA, reporter and growth assays

timeline.finding: During senescence HBP1 represses DNMT1 through a site at -115 to -134 of its promoter while activating p16, and the two opposite activities are shown to proceed through different DNA sequences and different protein acetylation states.
timeline.methods: Promoter mapping, chromatin immunoprecipitation, senescence assays
timeline.open: Leaves unclear what single sequence, if any, defines an HBP1 site.

timeline.finding: HBP1 is placed downstream of growth factor signaling as a FOXO target: FOXO binds a conserved site in the HBP1 promoter, PDGF and FGF lower HBP1 mRNA through PI3K and PKB, and HBP1 knockdown increases fibroblast proliferation.
timeline.methods: Microarray meta-analysis, reporter assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation, knockdown

timeline.finding: A synthesis of the field argues that HBP1 behaves as a tumor suppressor without being a recurrently mutated driver, lost instead through microRNAs such as miR-155, miR-17-92 and miR-29a and through direct AKT phosphorylation.
timeline.methods: Review of published genetic, expression and signaling data

open: Whether TTCATTCATTCA is the sequence HBP1 uses generally is unresolved: it was defined at one locus, the cell-cycle promoters HBP1 regulates were mapped to different and shorter sequences, and the repression and activation functions were shown to work through different DNA sequences, so no single element has been validated across targets.

Whether HBP1 has any strong intrinsic sequence preference is unclear: the published CD2 element is a high-affinity site, yet the only in vitro model in these databases carries 1.1 bits, and no modern high-throughput measurement of HBP1 specificity has been published to settle whether the weak model reflects the protein or a failed assay.

Nothing distinguishes an HBP1 site from a CIC site by sequence: the HBP1 element read on the other strand is three copies of the CIC octamer TGAATGAA, no genome-wide occupancy map exists for either protein in these collections, and whether the two repressors compete at shared sequences has not been examined.

How much of HBP1's regulatory output requires DNA binding is open: it represses cyclin D1 and Wnt targets by sequestering LEF1, TCF4 and MYC, so the relative contributions of site occupancy and protein-protein antagonism at any given target gene are unmeasured.

families.name: PURA / PURB
families.def: PUR-repeat GGN-rich single-strand-capable binders. PURA, PURB.
families.short: PURA and PURB (Pur-alpha and Pur-beta) are PUR-repeat proteins that bind purine-rich DNA and RNA, with a strong preference for single strands rather than duplex. The PUR element was defined as a repeated purine-rich sequence upstream of the human c-MYC P1 promoter, at a site of DNA bending inside a replication initiation zone, and was given the consensus GGNNGAGGGAGARRRR. The PUR repeats fold into a Whirly-like domain, and Pur-alpha can unwind double-stranded DNA rather than simply read it. These proteins act mostly as repressors, best characterized on the smooth muscle alpha-actin promoter, where they bind the GGN-repeat strand of core enhancer elements. De novo PURA variants cause PURA syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder with neonatal hypotonia, seizures and severe developmental delay.
families.long:
## The factors

Three PUR-repeat genes exist in humans: PURA (Pur-alpha), PURB (Pur-beta) and the less studied
PURG. PURA and PURB are broadly expressed, with PURA especially abundant in brain. The proteins are
built from tandem PUR repeats; crystallography of Pur-alpha showed that two repeats pack together
into a single Whirly-like domain, a fold otherwise associated with plant single-stranded
nucleic-acid-binding proteins, presenting an unusual continuous binding surface rather than the
discrete base-reading elements of a zinc finger or helix-turn-helix [PMID:19846792]. A third repeat mediates
dimerization between molecules [PMID:19846792]. This architecture explains the central functional fact about the
family: PUR proteins are not conventional double-stranded sequence-specific transcription factors.
They bind purine-rich single-stranded DNA and RNA with high affinity, and Pur-alpha can actively
unwind duplex DNA rather than reading it intact [PMID:26744780,23018800]. Pur-alpha also binds RNA, including
trinucleotide-repeat transcripts [PMID:26744780], and localizes to stress granules, so its functions extend beyond
transcription into RNA handling and, in the original work, into DNA replication [PMID:1545807].

## The motif

The literature element comes from mapping a site of DNA bending 1.6 kb upstream of the human c-MYC
P1 start site, near the center of a reported replication initiation zone. Methylation interference
mapped specific guanosine contacts in a 24-mer, and the derived consensus was GGNNGAGGGAGARRRR, a
sixteen-base purine-rich element found at replication origins and in gene flanking regions from
yeast to human [PMID:1545807]. In practice the element is usually described more loosely as a GGN repeat, and
binding is strand-selective: the purine-rich strand is bound, the complementary
pyrimidine-rich strand is not [PMID:1545807,16436378]. There is no half-site grammar, no spacing rule, and no palindrome.
The data here disagree with this, and the disagreement is worth stating plainly. This family
contains exactly one motif, the HOCOMOCO model PURB.H14CORE.0.B.B, whose consensus is ACCCAC, six
bases and only 7.6 bits of information. Its reverse complement, GTGGGT, is GT-rich rather than
purine-rich in the GGN sense, it is far shorter than the published PUR element, its evidence code B marks it as a protein-binding-microarray (PBM) measurement rather than derived from HOCOMOCO's own ChIP-seq or
SELEX data, and its nearest neighbours across all four databases lie outside this family (best
cross-family similarity 0.73, label agreement 0). There is no PURA motif in these databases at all,
and with a single member the family has no internal cohesion to measure. The honest position is
that the published PUR element is a single-strand, purine-rich sequence that a position-weight
matrix over double-stranded DNA is the wrong tool for, and that the one matrix available under this
key should not be treated as a validated model of PUR binding.

## Where it acts

Documented PUR-protein sites are promoter-proximal and, in the original work, at replication
origins. The best-characterized regulatory target is the mouse and human smooth muscle alpha-actin
promoter, where Pur-alpha and Pur-beta bind the GGN-repeat-containing strands of several cis
elements within a core enhancer and repress transcription [PMID:16436378]. Knockdown showed Pur-beta to be the
dominant repressor in fibroblasts, with the combined action of both proteins needed for full
repression, and the two proteins had indistinguishable binding affinity and specificity in vitro
but distinct protein-interaction profiles, which is how cell-type-specific behavior arises from a
shared site [PMID:16436378]. PUR proteins also occur at the c-MYC upstream region where the element was found, and
Pur-alpha associates with RNA and with cytoplasmic granules in neurons [PMID:19846792,23018800], so not all of its binding
is chromatin-associated.

## Biology and disease

Pura-null mice are viable at birth but develop severe neurological abnormalities with arrested
postnatal brain development and impaired proliferation of neuronal and hematopoietic precursors [PMID:19846792,23018800].
In humans, de novo PURA variants and 5q31.3 microdeletions that remove PURA cause PURA syndrome:
profound neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulty, seizures or seizure-like movements, and severe
developmental delay with little or no speech [PMID:25342064,25439098,29097605]. An early series proposed that disruption of PUR repeat III gives a more severe phenotype [PMID:25342064], and the Pur-alpha-DNA structure shows how some missense changes would impair nucleic-acid binding [PMID:26744780], but a study of 32 individuals found no significant correlation between mutation class and severity [PMID:29097605]. PURB has no established monogenic disease association.

## Reading a hit

Do not read a hit under this key as evidence of PUR binding. The only matrix available is a
six-base, 7.6-bit model that does not resemble the published purine-rich PUR element and whose
closest relatives in the motif databases belong to other families. More fundamentally, PUR proteins
prefer single-stranded purine-rich DNA and can unwind duplex [PMID:26744780], so scanning double-stranded genomic
sequence with a PWM is not a test of PUR binding even in principle. If you care about PUR proteins
at a locus, the useful evidence is a long GGN-rich or polypurine tract on one strand, ideally at a
site with known single-strand character, plus direct biochemical or crosslinking data. Treat any
automated PURB annotation in a scan result as a placeholder.
families.caveats: This is the weakest family in the atlas. It contains one motif, a six-base 7.6-bit HOCOMOCO model for PURB from a protein-binding microarray, with no PURA motif and no internal cohesion. That model (ACCCAC) does not match the published purine-rich PUR element, GGNNGAGGGAGARRRR, and its nearest neighbours in all four databases lie in other families. PUR proteins bind single-stranded purine-rich DNA and RNA and can unwind duplex DNA, so a double-stranded PWM scan is not a valid test of their binding. A hit here should be treated as an annotation placeholder, not as evidence that PURA or PURB binds the sequence.

timeline.finding: A HeLa protein of about 28 kDa binds the purine-rich strand of a repeated element (PUR) at a DNA bend 1.6 kb upstream of c-MYC, near a replication initiation zone; methylation interference maps guanosine contacts and gives the consensus GGNNGAGGGAGARRRR, also found at other origins and gene flanks from yeast to human.
timeline.methods: Gel shift, methylation interference, UV cross-linking
timeline.open: The identity of the protein and whether single-strand binding operates on chromosomal DNA.

timeline.finding: At the smooth muscle alpha-actin promoter, purified Pur-alpha and Pur-beta bind GGN-repeat strands of several enhancer elements with essentially identical affinity and specificity, and repress transcription; cell-type differences come from their distinct protein partners, with Pur-beta the dominant repressor in fibroblasts.
timeline.methods: RNA interference, binding assays with purified proteins, reporter assays

timeline.finding: Crystal structure of the Pur-alpha core: two PUR repeats pack into a Whirly-like PUR domain that binds nucleic acid through concave beta-sheet surfaces, and a third repeat mediates dimerization.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, SAXS, mutational binding studies

timeline.finding: De novo PURA mutations are found in children with severe neurodevelopmental delay, hypotonia and seizures, and PURA is identified as the gene behind the neurological core of 5q31.3 microdeletion syndrome.
timeline.methods: Trio exome sequencing in two independent cohorts
timeline.open: Whether mutation position predicts severity; repeat III disruption was proposed to be worse.

timeline.finding: Crystal structure of the Pur-alpha DNA/RNA-binding domain on single-stranded DNA shows base-specific recognition, DNA and RNA bound the same way, and the mechanism of duplex unwinding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, NMR, in vitro unwinding assays, Drosophila genetics

timeline.finding: Across 32 new and 22 published individuals with PURA syndrome, no significant correlation is found between mutation class and severity, against the earlier suggestion that repeat III disruption is more severe.
timeline.methods: Clinical delineation, structure-based classification of mutations

open: How much sequence PUR proteins actually read is unsettled: the original mapping gave a sixteen-base consensus (GGNNGAGGGAGARRRR), later functional work describes the sites only as GGN repeats, and the Pur-alpha-ssDNA structure shows base-specific contacts without by itself defining a consensus.

The only matrix under this key, the HOCOMOCO PURB model ACCCAC (GTGGGT on the other strand), does not resemble the published purine-rich element, and whether PURB has a genuine double-stranded preference that this model captures, or the model reflects weak signal, is untested.

Whether PURA mutation type predicts severity is disputed: an early series proposed that disruption of PUR repeat III is more severe, whereas a study of 32 individuals found no significant correlation between mutation class and severity.
